***Die-hard fans of the Stronghold series, please read this review before making your purchase.  You won't regret it.***
As a long time fan of the Stronghold series, this game was such a let down.  Yes, it is *technically* a Stronghold game, and it technically is the sequel to Crusader, but overall it is not even close to being on par with the rest of the series.
--First, the Good--
At its core, the concept of Stronghold is still the same here.  You'll start off building a settlement, gathering resources via a supply chain, ultimately crafting weapons to arm a force of soldiers.
There are familiar units: Archers, Macemen, Crossbowmen (Crusader).  Horse Archers, Slaves, Assassins(Arabic)..as well as some new ones, including the Healer and many other Arabic mercenaries not previously seen. You can build walls, towers, siege weapons and all sorts of defense mechanisms for keeping the black knight at bay.On top of that, many familiar faces return, such as The Rat, Richard the Lionheart and more.
The game is, of course, a 3d Model game, bringing the Crusader series at least one generation ahead.
And...that's about it.  Honestly.  If you were a fan of the original series, it may warm your heart to actually have some new Stronghold content to play with, but there really isn't anything new and exciting here.
--Now, the Bad...where do I begin?--
First of all, the game is somewhat broken.  There are plenty of times where characters models won't animate, and it's not uncommon for characters to simply float across the map in the standard model "christ pose" without any animation.  Even the oxen who carry the stone in the game would freeze when moving on an angle.  Stone walls are another mess.  Too often, staircases would end up with a wall piece right in the middle of them, creating a strange unrealistic graphical error.  These are only some of the visual phenomenen that occur while playing.
That brings me to another issue...wall building.  Not only do walls cost way too much in this game, but there is pretty much no room for creativity when building your castle.  In the original/Crusader 1, you had so much control over every little aspect of your wall design.  You could build walls of all different heights, staircase pieces, granulated walls all down to the very last square.  This gave us castle builders so much of a blank canvas that virtually anything was possible if we knew how to use those pieces the right way.
In Crusader 2, 90% of the wall building is done for you when clicking.  A wall piece is pre-built for you to include parapits on one side, a wall space, and parapits on the opposite side.  You can no longer just build a simple piece of stone wall, the basic building block (almost literally) of the original series' castle building element.  Sure, you can add towers and all kinds of siege weaponry, but the fun and joy of really creative a keep down to the last detail is completely lost here.
The cost of walls adds to another huge gripe with this game...balance.  It's my understanding that a patch has re-balanced some of the economy issues, but the game is still WAY too unbalanced when trying to get your city up and running.  Too often I find myself running out of resources right at the beginning of a match, even when set to give myself a huge advantage over my AI counterparts.  For example, a windmill in this game costs 200 wood.  In the original? 20.  So it costs literally 10 times as much here.  That would be fine, except woodcutters don't harvest 10 times as much wood here.  They harvest roughly the same amount as before.
This leads to a TON of waiting around to gather resources right from the git-go of any match.  Sure, there was always that element in the original (as with any RTS), but there is a considerable difference here.  I feel like I'm not getting anywhere, even though I have what would otherwise be the basics of a civilization in place.
Ah, civilization...a thriving, breathing melting pot of people going about their daily lives, each contributing to their society in their own way, all while maintaining their own unique personality...yeah, Stronghold Crusader 1 was a fantastic game.  Say goodbye to that here.
I mean, sure...you get to see the workers doing what they do in 3D, but it's not the same.  Peasants say NOTHING when you click on them.  No Monty Python-esque man impersonating a woman "morning your lordship!" or "no taxes is good taxes, that's my motto!", just silence.  No adding flowers, maypoles, dancing bears, gauntlets, guillotines, stretching
popularity control is just gone.
Speaking of voices (ha), this might be one of the most dissapointing aspects of Crusader 2, and I honestly didn't see it coming.
The voice acting in this game is TERRIBLE.  I mean that in every sense of the word.  I have friends who can do cooky voices that would have been better candidates.
A great example is the men-at-arms.  Remember the way they sounded in Stronghold 2?  They were dopey lummixes, and rightfully so given their rank.  Or how about their original counterpart, the spearmen?  They were rough, working class fighters ready to stick a spear in whatever you tell them to.
Here's what I want you to do:  We're gonna do a test.  I want you to read the next sentence I say in quotes out loud.  Don't use any exciting voice, or cooky impersonation, or anything.  Use your normal speaking voice.  Ready?  Okay, say this out loud:
"Man at arms, ready.  Close ranks."
Congratulations!  You've just landed a gig providing voice over work for a video game!
The level of enthusiasm in these vocal takes can only be described as the bare minimum.  Without trying to be funny, I've found myself honestly wondering if they simply had one of the programmers provide voices.  As annoying as he was, we all have to admit that at least The Rat had a memorable personality.  His voice has now been replaced with some Joe Everyguy off the street.  You'll forget him as soon as you end the game.
To be fair, I need to point something else out, though, about the voice over work, and that's that there are a lot of recycled vocal takes from previous games.  Archers still sound like archers, crossbowmen like crossbowmen, etc.  However, it's about 50/50 as far as which characters use the classic voices, and which use Joe Everyguy.
It might sound petty to be so bitter about this, but as (I'm assuming, since you've read this far) you are a die-hard Stronghold fan, then you KNOW how important the voices are to this series.  They are the character, the personality and the life of the game!  They're what make you feel like you are controlling living, breathing people of all different sorts, whose lives hang at your fingertips!
The original games did all of that in spades, and they weren't even 3D rendered!
--The Bottom Line--
I haven't played much of this game, but I'm fairly confident that won't change.  I could go on forever about the other issues that are impossible to ignore (such as the buildings and terrain feeling like they're from two different games), but I feel I've beaten my own horse to death here.
From what I gather, a team of less than 10 people programmed this game.  I don't mean this review as offense to them specifically.  They created a game, like they said they would.  They accomplished something that I, of course, haven't...but it's almost like giving credit to Nickelback.  I may hate their music, but at the end of the day they're creating albums and I'm sitting behind my keyboard judging people.
That being said, it doesn't mean that I have to LIKE Nickelback.
That was a bad way to end this review. Sorry to take a punch at an easy target.
Judge me all you want for that, just please don't buy this game.  It's something you can't take back.

So far, so good for a reboot of Train Simulator. The last game was looking pretty long in the tooth, and TSW brings a much needed refresh.
I play these games mostly to have a large model railroad, so the looks are as important as the realism to me. Every year that beecame more and more of a sticking point with TS, as the engine aged and aged - all while still being something of a system hog.
The bad news first - TSW is still a system hog. My best guess is that the physics are CPU dependent. I'm running a GTX 1080 and a 4.00 GHZ processor and even so, this thing chugs (ha, train puns!) at 1440 on virtually any settings. Frame rate is overall very low (20 fps in switching yards and city areas) and averages about 30-35 for me. I don't need blazing fast 60 fps, but it really detracts from what is overall a fantastic upgrade to TS.
The good news is that this is TS, but...well...more. Virtually every single thing I could think of on an engine is there and working - from in-cabin fans to fuse boxes to engine primers. Manual refuelling is here, and so is walking around. The walking around is cool for admiring a train, but it doesn't do much for me.
Lighting and reflections are great - take a moonlit spin in a train and watch the moon reflect on the engine and tracks, or sit in the cab and watch how the gauges are realistically lit from behind. If you can take the framerate hit, the foliage is finally up to par, for the most part. It's not the Witcher, but TS had some seriously sparse plant life, and TSW does not - it looks great and fills out the levels in a way that just wasn't possible before.
For a $40 starting price, a lot of people will be put off. TS has been on a bunch of insane sales over the years and $40 for three engines and one line will feel sparse. I don't mind, though - supporting the next generation of Doevetail's simulator is a winning proposition for me. If you have a relatively strong rig and you're looking for the next gen of train simulation, then this is a great start.
One last silly  note, though - the Doppler effect on sound is hilarious. I assume they'll patch it out, but you'll experience it even when you are just moving the exterior camera, making it nearly possible to do a record-scratch effect with the horn.

To fix the graphic issues and low FPS everyone is complaining about:
I set my resolution to the highest in game (my native is 1920x1080). In game its 3840x2160.
I set the view resolution (I think that's what its called. Its on the same menu as the game resolution option) to 100%, which is default.
And I set the Anti-Aliasing to TAA.
Everything else is set to max. I get an average of 60 FPS and everything is smooth and perfect.
Final Thoughts:
Because I understand early release games can have bugs and I am cool with that. I give TSW a thumbs up for the graphics (once you fix the resolution) and for the love of trains!

Right now I cannot recommend Train Sim World: CSX Heavy Haul.  Let me explain..
Right now, as of March 23, 2017, the game contains 9 tutorials.  Well, rather 6 tutorials and 3 train overviews that cover the 3 in-game locomotives.  On top of that, there are 8 "scenarios", all of which occur along the same line of track, which is approximately 50 miles in length, give or take a few miles.  Some of the scenarios are currently impossible to finish due to bugs, which I'm told are being worked on.
The next major issue with the game is that it's basically a slideshow.  I run an extremely high-end PC.  An i7 5960X with 16GB of DDR4 memory, a 1TB SSD drive, and an overclocked GTX 1080 graphics card.  I can run GTA5 in Ultra and get an average of between 100 and 110fps (and yes, my monitor can display every frame I throw at it).  I can run games like The Hunter: "Call of the Wild", Ghost Recon: Wildlands, Mafia 3, and many other high end games that have much better graphics than Train Sim World: CSX Heavy Haul and I still get 100+ FPS in most of them.  Oh, and that's while running my graphics at 1440p too.  On Train Sim World: CSX Heavy Haul, I'm lucky to get 40FPS.  The game averages between about 18 and 22 frames per second, and there are occasional pauses to load in new scenery along the line of about a half second.
I think of people attempting to play Train Sim World: CSX Heavy Haul on a lesser PC than mine, and experiecing even worse performance.  Egads!!  That must be awful!
It's sad too, because the graphics are the best I've seen to date for a "train game".  But this isn't a game really.  It's more of a "lite" simulation that you've have completed in a day or three, if you can stomach the persistently terrible framerates.  I'll call it a "Demo" of what could be in the future, but it is NOT in ANY way worth $39.99 as it is.  9 tutorials and 8 bad scenarios is an embarassment, and for $40 bucks is a slap in the face to the gamers that dish out their money for something that should keep their attention for at least a few hundred hours.  As it stands, Train Sim World: CSX Heavy Haul, definitely won't.
It's a waste of money for what is essentially a demo product.  Thumbs down for now.
Disclaimer, I DID receive a copy of 'Train Sim World: CSX Heavy Haul' for free from Dovetail for evaluation and review.  That has in no way affected my thoughts on the game or this review.  I will update this review if there are major changes to the game.

This is a decent game, but don't expect it to come near any of the main series.
The focus here is mainly on the gameplay and it is the strongest point of the whole package, alongside the soundtrack. There are 14 different characters that you can play as right from the start, allowing you to experiment and find the right combination that will compliment your playing style. The combat is solid for the most part, though towards the end it becomes more of a "who can one-shot the other faster" game.
Regarding the whole "HD" thing, well.. it's lackluster. The models of the main characters look amazing, almost on the level of FFXV, while the NPCs, enemies (excluding the Behemoth for some reason) and backdrops are straight from the PSP era and clash horribly, no matter how many effects, light options and blur you add.
If you're interested in achievements, the set that TYPE-0 provides is okay and fairly easy. You can get almost all of them in one playthrough.
To sum up: the story is trash, the HD conversion is half-baked and definitely needed more work, the music is beautiful, the gameplay is tight, the port is... slightly better than the other ones by Square-Enix, offering more graphical settings than usual but still miles away from the likes of MGSV. Get it on sale if you want.

Do you enjoy a great challenge? A phenomenal story with equally impressive gameplay? Do you wish to kill a ton o' bugs? Even if you said no to any of those questions, this game is definitely worth your precious time and money, although you must be patient with it at times and take your failures in stride.
Additionally, if you like Dark Souls and are looking for something new, Hollow Knight - or "Bug Souls," as I like to call it - is one of the BEST games I have ever played, and I don't say that lightly. Everything, from it's very rich and atmospheric environments, to the classic 2D sidescroller gameplay, to the variety of lovable characters will have you coming back for more and more.
When you die (oh, you'll DIE), picking up right where you left off is easy and quick. The platforming and combat go hand-in-hand, making tasks like epic boss fights and rescuing little grubs both challenging and easy. Speaking of epic boss fights, be prepared! There are quite a few of these in Hollow Knight. Most, if not all, of them are some of the most challenging and engaging battles I've waged in a long time.
Hollow Knight will have you hooked the moment you set foot in Dirtmouth. When it comes to the unique "Metroidvania" subgenre of platformers, Hollow Knight stands tall and proud.

Highly recommended!

Original Review: I honestly want to get into this game. As a kid both my brother and I put 1000 plus hours into SC1 easily so you could say we are big fans. The whole game just feels clunky and the entire possibility of running your own castle and making it a happy or horrid place to live in is totally gone. The game shifted towards more rts style and the graphics were better off as sprites in the old games. Sadly I wont be able to get any nostalgia  (or my money's worth) out of this unpolished, glitchy, foul turd. The only reason I bought it was to support FireFly Studios with the hopes that eventually they go back to the old style or ammend this F***ery by pumping out a SC1 expantion pack to take me back to chewing through a whole quench gum tin in a single game against 7 Wolfs.
Update: Two years out now there really hasnt been much that has changed other than some DLC added in you can buy and the game finally made the 5 dollar bin. For 5 bucks to help firefly work on the next game, I say go for it. Does it change this game? No. The glitchy aspects are not as bad and the game is just okay but now playable. If you loved Crusader you will feel familiar but it's not quite the same. Its like dating a super hot girl and then going for her average at best cousin two years later. Its a little wierd and dissapointing in certain aspects but still the same family so you know how things work. The game is not that good but there are some nuances about the game that I do like and I will list them so you can decide for yourself to support Firefly or not..
+Tiling system: I like how you clearly see your building space and limits, this is neccessary for 3d
+Unit  Types: The added variety adds a lot of cool things I wish were in the first Crusader but its nice to play with new troops
+Seige equipment:No more micromanaging engineers but then again you can pick them off stopping the build of a catapult either now
+Stock pile: only need one
+Armory: you only need one to house all your weapons now
+Market: auto buy and selling cuts micromanagement a lot
+Building and troop limits: It sucked at first but keeps the AI from mass hording you while they auto spawn from Dante's Inferno..
+AI comments: Some of the things the AI say are stupid but can be funny
+Firefly is still trying and in business to make another Stronghold game

Ok first things first: Buy it! ... just do it.
If you are still not sure... well I can go into detail, but just because it is you.
Story: You are comming to a town as a small soldier or so, in your believ, in his search for adventure.
Quickly you find the entrance to the biggest tunnel network that you can imagine and OLA let's do this.
But what is that, you find more and more about the history of this god forsaken place, meet funny and interesting characters along the way and you find more out about yourself.
Quickly you are in a rollercoaster which takes you for a ride and boy oh boy what a ride it is.
Like Dark Souls you can either rush through everything without learning much (even if that is still more than Dark Souls)
or you can look around and find more and more out. Trust me it is worth it.
Gameplay: It is an 2D-Jump'n Slash game. Like Dark Souls were Death can wait around every corner. You have a meele weapon and get spell-like abilities or real spells along your journey which opens paths and areas in visited places. Boss fights are ... well some are easy, some are normal and than there are the MOT... sorry. Uhm... really hard ones. A feeling of accomplishment is sure to rise.
Grafiks: It is a nice looking 2D Jump'n Slash game. With nice detailed design and "lively" background. It is nothing compared to a game like ori, but it is still beautiful and easy on the eyes. The effects are well balanced and you don't feel overwhelmed at all.
Verdict: It is a cheap beautiful and addicting game, which captivates you with it's vastly different ares and music. Some of the NPCs are lovely and you care about them, even if you don't meet them for an hour or so of gaming.
I played through most of the Game and looked mostly every corner and got 26 hours. (1 hour for the last boss... screw him but I feel amazing right now, for beating him). So all in all a really easy decision to buy it.

Very mixed feelings about this one.
First impressions of this game are amazing. The art style and music are fantastic. I instantly fell in love with the character design, the world's lore, how each section felt like it had a history to it. The controls are also tight, movement feels good, and combat isn't too bad.
Then the cracks start to show.
After the first few hours, difficulty levels really spike. As everyone else has mentioned there is also a Dark Souls like mechanic of going to retrieve your currency after you die. In addition to that, the map increases in size much faster than fast travel points become available. This amounts to a LOT of backtracking and it becomes an exercise in misery after a while, especially when you die a mile from your last rest spot. It also makes learning punishing areas harder because it takes so much longer to get back to the area.
What's there that is good is fantastic though, and I find it hard to fault the game for a lot of things I mentioned because I feel it's that way by design, not by oversight. This is how the game was intended to be. Some people like this hard, more punishing style of game. Personally, I'm not a huge fan.
I'm going to recommend it for the reasons it's good, just know what you're buying.

TL:DR version: The effects are nice but the camera/aiming/controls are a hassle!
I may end up liking the game more, but my immediate reaction is that while I enjoy what the game offers, I could see many people being turned off by its simplistic approach and somewhat clunky aiming mechanics. I was bummed to realize this plays more like an on-rails shooter/shmup (you choose when to move forward and have 180 degree aiming or at everything in "front" of you as you move forward, but if you want to aim "behind" you or look around far to your left or right, your view is restricted.) The player can slowly "back up" to explore previous areas, but this kills a lot of the rhythm of the game. Let's say you have just barely walked past/ ahead of an enemy on the game, if you are one step ahead of where they are, they can still hit you but there is nothing for the player to do aside from holding down or back to take slow steps backward until the only-facing forward 180 degrees POV allows you to then aim to your left or right (now that you can see the enemy ahead of you again) to take the enemy out -if you choose to- but most often you may be better off just running ahead and skipping the encounter altogether to avoid being hit.
The game's aiming seems to have really wonky anchor points at times for both the player character and the reticle, on both Xbox One controller and Mouse and Keyboard. The player's area of interaction seems to jump from zone to zone quite a bit.  Let's say you are trying to aim to your immediate bottom-left to strafe into and "keep an eye" on zones as you enter them, which may sometimes be very narrow corridors to shoot enemies and avoid being hit, the game's aiming will "bounce" your aim to face where it has deemed is looking ahead in certain areas, despite the enemies being able to already shoot at you from your far periphery, the player is at a disadvantage due to the shoddy camera movement and strange insistence on aiming ahead of you.
I had been expecting more of a platformer shooter with "fully 3D" (360 degree) aiming, not confined to the previously-mentioned rails feeling. You also have no jump button (unless it is possibly a pickup of some kind?) or roll to dodge enemy fire, which adds both more restriction to the overall player movement as well, but also adds to the 'elegance' needed to narrowly dodge enemy fire as found in other SHMUP/rail style shooter games (I could see this becoming immersive later in the game, with more enemy types and larger swarms of enemies...)
The effects of the game and gameplay beyond the POV restriction are still cool and fit the early 3D PS1 esque designs well, with the sound design being well done and the sound effects and soundtrack being appropriately chunky, the enemies exploding as their point total is shown and a heavy bass sound effect hitting is nice and gets you into building a large score. The soundtrack and game have a sort of surf rock / laid back presentation that fits it well, which I imagine changes up as the game progresses. The game includes powerup pickups and health dropped from enemies to give some variety.
The game fits its niche market well, and begins to embody a frantic Space Invaders / Panzer Dragoon aiming feel as you strafe and take out waves of enemies, but the way the game moves from zone to zone, with its restriction of the aiming only being available within your front vision (or less on some more clunky camera sections..i.e. navigating a narrow cityscape / balcony area) to be disorienting and annoying when trying to dodge enemy bullets and also line up shots of my own.
I will probably end up enjoying the game and may end up recommending it, and this shouldn't be thought of as a be-all end-all Non-Recommendation as I do think the game is entertaining, especially to those seeking a retro 3D game that can wrangle its somewhat crappy camera and enjoy it despite some lame deaths due to strange aiming mechanics.
At the somewhat "high" price of 14.99 for what is present, I think the game's sales and reception would improve if it the game were to move to a lower initial barrier of entry cost-wise (for example, I paid 8.00ish during a sale..) and it definitely needs to resolve or smooth some of the camera issues ( I can understand if full 360 degree aiming isn't possible with what's already made of the game, but the "bouncing" effect as you strafe into or try to aim to your immediate right or left during crammed sections is obnoxious)

Assassin's Creed. Very... interesting series for me to talk out. They start releasing a game a year on main gen consoles and PC since 2009, hell, they released two back in 2014, Unity and Rogue, and I guess they do it this year again. Heck, they could be releasing even more a year. What I am saying, ladies and gentlemen, is that this game makes Call of Duty jealous from the ridiculous releases each year. So, to quell our possible uprisings, Ubisoft decided to say, "We are sorry to hear that you are unsatisfied. Would you like an awesome pirate adventure?" The unanimous answer to that was, "...well now we do!" Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, which is not the fourth game but I would go nuts for counting up what game it actually is probably, is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome without a doubt, and is probably the best of the franchise, though I've only played this game twice, half of 3 and part of 2. Not very much, yeah, but this game is awesome. Want to know why? Of course you do, or else you wouldn't be reading this. So let's get into it, shall we?
STORY: Your name is Edward Kenway. Actually, you're some guy who works at a video game development place that uses Desmond Miles's DNA to both make games and
, but most of you only give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the pirate, so I'll tell you about the pirate. You go to the Carribean to try and make money to support you and your wife back in England. After you kill an assassin, you decide to impersonate him and go to a meeting in Havana, where it turns out that the Templars plan to find a place called the Observatory. Edward, seeing a way to make money, decides to try to go after it. He is then imprisoned, but breaks free and takes a ship and a crew that are willing to go after the observatory with him as long as they get paid. You are thrown unwillingly between the duel for power between the Assassins and the Templars as well, which is interesting to see how this plays out. The story is interesting, I was engrossed enough, there were a couple neat twists throughout the whole story. The ending was sweet, I'm glad I made it to the end. Oh yeah, and that DNA playing thing was good I guess. Overall great.
GAMEPLAY: Same♥♥♥♥♥♥as the last couple♥♥♥♥♥Creed games. You run around, have a lot of gadgets, you can do parkour. Stealth gameplay is fine, but I feel like sometimes it is kind of unfair, though it might just be because I suck. Combat is great, feels fairly satisfying. The parkour stuff is fine. Ship combat is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing as well, I love fighting on ships. Just remember, play with a gamepad. Keyboard controls are kind of bad.
GRAPHICS AND PERFORMANCE: Game looks damn good. Water looks very nice, environments are nice, kind of the same jungle-y areas for the most part, but still nice. This game takes a lot for it to run, however, so you might want to hold off on this unless you have a PC that can handle it. My rig could barely run it even. But if you have a good PC, it won't matter.
CHARACTERS AND VOICE ACTING: Edward Kenway is a good character. It's kind of interesting seeing him evolve from a man who only does something for a paycheck to a loyal member of the Assassin's (spoiler? meh, probably not.) You come across some notable members of pirate history, including Blackbeard, Black Bart, and some more guys who I probably could recognize if I paid attention better in social studies the day we went over these names. If this was a review of AC3 I could tell you every single ♥♥♥♥ing name in that game, I bet. xD You don't really have any notable members of your crew with the exception of Adewale, a slave who helps you escape your prison and take over your ship and becomes your First Mate. He's awesome as well. Not really any bad voice acting I'd say, character design is decent, so I can't really complain.
SIDE ACTIVITIES: Land activities are simple. You can go on assassin missions where you have to take a guy out, you can help other Assassin's out in order to find keys to a safe, you can raid storehouses, you can use your eagle vision to find Mayan keystones, you can syncronize points to reveal bits of the map, or you can just go around and look for collectibles. Seawise you can attack and conquer forts, which reveal parts of the map, you can go harpooning sea animals for crafting purposes, you can go on naval contracts that are essentially assassin missions but on a boat, and you can, of course, attack and plunder ships like a true pirate. You can also go underwater with assistance of a diving bell and explore underwater wrecks. Decent amount of variety with these, I think I might miss one or two but you get the idea. Nice amount of stuff to do.
FINAL VERDICT: Nice place to start off in the♥♥♥♥♥Creed saga. Any game that doesn't have Desmond Miles in it only gets points to me. 9/10, definately worth picking up sometime soon.

After some time spent in the game I've came to the point that I think I can have a proper opinion of it. Black Flag is a very enjoyable game, the venture into pirating serves the franchise well and serves up on of the best Assasin's Creed games for a long time. The game is, however, flawed, not deeply, but enough to be a annoyance at times.
Pros
-The world is beautiful in both visuals and sounds.
-The freedom, though limited early on, is quite impressive.
-Sea battles are exciting and sailing itself can be quite enjoyable and even relaxing as your crew sing a sea shanty.
-Submersive as the sea, easy to clock hours into the game without realising it.
-Characters and story are interesting enough to hold your attention.
Cons
-Almost every aspect of the game is buggy in one way or another, this can range from silly and funny to infuriatingly annoying. A few I've run into are excutions not, err, executing properly, enemies spawning right next to you when trying to be stealthy and your character leaping to his death when trying to get him to simply drop down one ledge.
-Bogged down from time to time with the real life story. Character out of the memories is infuriatingly stupid. (Trust me, you'll understand when the game first drags you out of the pirating and into the office)
-Controls can be finicky or not too well explained at times.
Despite it's flaws, Black Flag still comes off as well made though missing that slight bit of polish that could have turned this into a truly great game.

is a gun-blazing action-arcade romp through  a deliberately polygonal, block-y and hazy look to it that makes it reminiscent of late 90's 3D action games for the N64, PSX, and Saturn. This retro-flavored and post-apocalyptic appearance in tandem with the forward moving, almost on-rails nature of the shooting bring me back to what I loved most of the era.
An Americana lovechild between
post-apocalyptic wasteland sensibilities and
gritty rail-gunning low-poly N64 age badassery, the intuitive weapon combining of the iconic
with the forward-pressing level progression of
all wrapped in a hilariously satirical romp rife with action and macho-fueled patriotism that only a post-2016 America could truly be deserving of.
is entertaining and funny as hell, it's a nostalgic blast to play, a trip to look at, and it takes it's influences from the best-of-the-best using a formula from the golden-age of games that has stood the test of time.
What I love about
is how well each setting is communicated through such a raw polygonal style, every level really feels like a retro-flavored adventure that only the raddest of 80's and 90's action movies could deliver. The streets are as cold and oppressive as anything else in post-2016 America, and you really feel like it's your sole duty to rid the country of the authoritarian goons of the Canadian Army who now threaten your country's freedom.
The variety of areas keeps you on your feet and kept me hooked into the game to see where I was headed next, greeted by even more outlandish locales than the last. From fighting scorpions in painted red deserts, to mind-controlled apes in wild and primal jungles, fighting from psychedelic log-rafts in a surreal color-gradient forest and even animatronic dinosaurs in an amusement park.
The music is very lo-fi but also with strangely captivating melodies, like so many of the sounds you'd hear from old Japanese arcade cabinets. The sound effects, also, have a memorable grittiness like something you'd hear from an old Genesis game. The Hollywood movie satire through the dialogue of our masculine protagonist is consistently hilarious and beautiful, with moments like Sgt. Jon Dagger declaring stoically that he's already in a committed relationship... with America. There's also even an achievement which I believe may be referencing
's "Jet Generation", which would explain the very punk rock and DIY nature of the game.
One thing I'd really like to see added to the already slick gameplay of
is some form of a dodge or dash mechanic. Sometimes charging through the alleyways of a dead America while grenades pour out of the windows of abandoned apartment complexes can get a little hectic, and Sgt. Dagger just isn't quite nimble enough for me to maneuver out of harms way.
This was a seriously unexpected gem for me, and I know it will be for like-minded retro enthusiasts too. It's a shame many will likely be turned away by the crude throwback style of the visuals but for those with their curiosity piqued by the appearance, absolutely take the plunge because it's a fun and chaotic trip with a lot of weird variety.

Before getting into this review, I would just like to point out that there is more to farming than pigs and bad banjo tunes.
Now that the disgruntled country kid inside me is satisfied, what exactly is Space Farmers? Essentially, it's a coop only puzzle (maybe?) game, designed to be played in short 5 level runs through self contained rooms that each focus on a particular theme or item. At times that's as easy as running from point A-B, other times you'll need to direct a robotic bull by using a rather distracting hat, or move pigs onto buttons to keep doors from closing.
I rather like the idea of semi random, varied objectives and play styles something along the lines of WarioWare, with a short playtime requirement and some goofy customization options, but Space Farmers just comes across as so incredibly lazy in its design. It's constantly punishing for the slightest mistakes, never explains anything about itself (instead asking you to navigate outside of the game to a webpage to read a how-to), and forces you to replay the same tired levels over and over again do to there being no way to select which you want to play or even simply limit them to ones you haven't already gone through. The presentation is unremarkable and unpolished, with an unhelpful UI, and mediocre controller support, not to mention a general instability that saw the game crashing numerous times in just the hour or so I spent playing.
It's a tediously dull game all around, in ways that seem like so easily avoidable and amendable, but despite its frequent content updates its issues are so ingrained at this point that I'm not sure they could be fixed in a simple patch, leaving me pessimistic it will ever turn into something worthwhile.

I was a bit uncertain of purchasing this game as it had no reviews, and a rather unique look. I can  happily say that  all of my apprehentions were blasted away after completing the first mission. This game is a cool, fun, and challenging throwback to the early N64/Ps1 era Arcade style games. At times it reminded me of both Starfox and Timecrisis blended with something far dirtier, nuclear and grindhouse-y. The Levels contain many hidden/alternate paths that increase replay potential, and will keep highscore junkies searching for the perfect/fastest route. Each level has you starting with your standard single shot blaster, but you have 2 upgradable equipment slots that offer a large range of customization options. For example you can fill one slot with the explosive shot and the other with multi shot, after upgrading a few times you will be slinging a huge cluster of exploding bolts with each pull of the trigger. More than any game in recent memory, Cold Vengeance had me thinking i was back playing an arcade classic, only with more toxic waste.

This is an excellent game for competitive players who want the arena experience of WoW without worrying about grinding for gear or levels, or MOBA players who don't care much for level differences and farming/item purchases. It's a 2v2 or 3v3 pure PVP arena where nearly every single ability, including healing, is a skill-shot (meaning you have to aim and land it, not just click a target). There aren't a large number of abilities per character, so it is less about having a large ability toolkit and more about knowing how to anticipate your opponent's moves and use the abilities you have at the right time. I would highly recommend this game for individuals who want quick access to intense PVP fights without any of the outside work involved (farming, itemization, leveling, grinding, etc. etc.). There is a pretty nice balance between melee, ranged and support character options, and the Devs seem actively interested in maintaining the game's balance and adding new features and characters.

The game caught a lot of negative attention with its port to steam. 30 fps?! Texture resolutions?! And just like that, negative/mixed reviews. Now, don't get me wrong. I'm a 60 fps ♥♥♥♥♥, myself, but I'm not naive enough to expect a PSP to PC port to blow me away with its performance and graphics.
Before I dive too far into the game review, I will say that the game's story is incomplete on its own. Squeenix saw it fit to make the complete story spread across two games and a novel. That being said, there are plot holes and it will require some external research to get the whole story. This in itself is aggrivating, and I wish I knew this before jumping in.
That being said, Final Fantasy Type-0 is an enjoyable experience that doesn't overstay its welcome. Character progression isn't complex. You level up, pick a few skills to build on, and go on your way. You can alter your magic spells by spending the souls that you harvest from your fallen enemies, changing cast time, mp cost, power, etc. The new game plus system is a nice touch, especially since it ties in with the story... sort of. The varied gameplay for the characters is a nice touch, since everyone has their own fighting style and feel. Unfortunately there is a massive void of characterization and development in the game. Is it due to the PSP nature of the game forcing them to hold out on cutscenes? I don't know. All that I know is that outside of Rem and Machina, there isn't much development, and even theirs is minimal. All of the characters feel like cardboard cut-outs that are based on the typical Japanese stereotypes, and while this is usually a serious negative...
This is a Final Fantasy game. Anyone experienced with the Final Fantasy series knows to not expect amazing character or story development. We've been fed silent characters that look for the crystals because "plot stuff," and we enjoyed it. Final Fantasy has never been about the incredible writing or amazing character dialogue. It's been about the grind, the summons/magic, the flashyness of the designs, and the girly-man villians. The story and characters are just a bonus.
The grind is there if you want it. It's not necessary, thanks to the difficulty system and the new game + system, but it's there if you want to over level. Leveling doesn't increase your stats by a whole lot, but damage/defense is highly based on level and equipment. There are stat boosting items that are farmable if you are looking to max your stats.
Magic is ridiculous in this game. Not only is it the hardest hitting form of damage that you can do, but you can make it aoe or have homing. From 5 seconds into the game all the way until you finish it, magic is useful (unless the enemies are immune, which is rare). And Ultima... dear god Ultima is great in this game. It breaks the damage cap if 9999, its radius is huge, and it is visually satisfying.
Summons are quite strong as well. I didn't use them much, since I didn't prep a reraise to rez my summoner, and I really didn't want yet another character to level. Storywise, Summoning is pretty incredible, and gives it a reason to be feared by both the summoning party and the recipients of the summon's aggression.
With all of that being said, I do need to address some of the negatives to this game. There are really only two that I will cover, but they need to be covered, none-the-less. The camera is awful. Locking on to a target moves the camera to be at ground level, making the game trigger claustrophobia even worse than it already did with its ridiculously narrow field of view (PSP constraint). Nothing could have been done with the port to PC with this, but it's still frustrating.
PC Port-wise, the keyboard and mouse controls. Jesus tap-dancing Christ. Whoever designed this part of the game needs to be fired. Twice. The absolute least that they could have done was add the keymapping to a .ini file, but no, that would be too hard, I suppose.
TLDR: If you're a Final Fantasy fan, get it and enjoy it. If you're an action RPG fan, buy it, but try to make up your mind within two hours of gameplay in case you want to cash in on that refund. Oh, and buy a controller, you'll need it.

Update:
I've seen a lot of reviews complaining about lack of content.

Starmade is a fine Early Access title.

Valhalla Hills is a city builder that is quite similar to early Settlers games. Unfortunately the whole game feels highly unpolished and it's looking very unlikely that any of the issues will ever be fixed.
The basic city building gameplay is decent but not great. The production chains are rather simple and the game is missing a number of core features and UI tools I'd expect in a good city builder. I strongly disliked the courier network system, too. Combat is also pretty terrible, but that's frankly normal for the genre.
The procedurally generated maps are rather repetitive and there's no proper campaign mode. In Classic mode you simply keep playing through new random maps slowly unlocking new buildings and stronger enemies. The game could have used much more variation with the maps and the objectives. There's also the Open game mode where everything is unlocked from the beginning, but you are still playing on the same repetitive random maps so this feels somewhat pointless.
Production values are not particularly good either. I wasn't a big fan of the highly generic art style which reminded me quite heavily of mobile games. Music is decent but way too repetitive and the sound effects are minimal at best.
Perhaps the biggest issue, however, is that the game is full of bugs. I ran across two critical bugs and lots of minor issues. On one map the final portal was unreachable, so the only option was to restart. On another map my military units got stuck on the scenery and the only way to fix this was to create a brand new military camp. These bugs are even more annoying as the save system in the game is extremely limited.
With more development time and extra content Valhalla Hills could have been a pretty solid city builder. Unfortunately, the game was released way too early and many of the bugs and problems were never fixed. As it is, you are much better off playing something like Settlers II 10th Anniversary Edition instead.
I played the classic mode long enough to unlock almost all the buildings but didn't ascend any of my vikings to Valhalla yet. The game just got too repetitive for me to continue.
The good:
- Core gameplay is decent enough, if not particularly deep
The bad:
- Extremely repetitive maps
- Poorly designed UI

Hollow Knight, a charming 2D action-platformer with delightful hand-drawn visuals, is a triumph in its genre.  Much like Terraria was a surprising and pleasing interpretation of what Minecraft's basic principles could be in the 2D space, Hollow Knight is, in many ways, what Dark Souls set out to do so well, but translated deftly into a 2D space with its own masterful spins and unique identity.  From rich and illusive lore that slowly reveals itself through the environment, interactions with NPCs, and player theory, to challenging and tightly-controlled combat and platforming, to the elation of discovery and surprise, Hollow Knight embodies and builds on what made Dark Souls so indescribable yet utterly compelling.
The world of Hollow Knight is a desolate one, though with hidden beauty and otherworldly majesty.  It takes place in the stunningly realized Hallownest, a world once home to a bustling insect population, now reduced to ruin and memory.  You play as an insect of tiny proportion wielding a Nail, a sword-like tool for keeping one safe in the depths of the forgotten kingdom.  Your goal is not apparent yet, but you plunge into the world below, fighting off deranged insects who were once citizens of this forsaken place and other such perils to uncover what happened to the once-proud kingdom.
Hallownest is completely hand-drawn, and has an emotive, undeniable charm in both scenery and populace.  The environment and characters of this world all show loving craftsmanship and subtly clue the player into the themes and state of the land.  Friendly NPCs offer pieces of story and items for sale, while they talk and grunt in their memorable and crazy made-up insect language.  Caves show their wear and age with beautiful attention to detail and lore, and open up into countless other ecosystems as you plot your way through the massive map.  Much of this world is accompanied by a stirring soundtrack as well, with haunting timbre and melodias piano pieces setting the tone for the mysterious and sad Hallownest.  Clear care was put into making each area feel unique not just visually, but musically as well, and you'll find yourself pausing the action to take in the sensory pleasures.
Discovery is one of the greatest joys in the game, and constantly delights the player with hidden passages, discoverable shortcuts, and a breadth of charms and skills to upgrade the player's combat and platforming abilities with.  You start off with your Nail and the simple ability to jump, but throughout the game, you'll learn magic derived from a Soul meter which fills as you attack enemies, allowing you to heal and use offensive magic, gain Charms which add special new traits to your character when equipped, and learn other abilities which aid in platforming, like a dash or wall-jump ability.  Much of the game world is ingeniously blocked off if you lack the proper platforming ability to navigate it as well, and makes the joy of discovering a new traversal skill feel like gaining a key to a new world.
Hollow Knight is a magical game; effortlessly engrossing and inspirational in its imagination.  It's easy to pick up and hard to put down, with a pluck of your heartstrings or tantalizing new joy to uncover with just a few more minutes of play time.  The care put into making this game is evident, and your time with it more than worthy.  Hollow Knight channels the greatness of 2D classics like Metroid and Castlevania, with their perfected controls and sense of progression, while blending the nebulous and primordial world-building and storytelling of Dark Souls.  It's a testament to the talented developers behind this game that Hollow Knight not only draws inspiration from such classics, but builds on them in meaningful and impactful ways; maybe even surpassing them.  Hollow Knight is a sight to behold, and in every sense of the word, a masterpiece.

For the record, before AC IV - BF I've only played AC II and AC III. Out of those 3 this is by far the best! It takes concepts from both those earlier games and expand upon them, the best example being the naval combat from AC III that is now put closer to its full potential.
Short technical overview:
I ran the game on a FX-6300 @ 4.1 GHz, 8GB RAM and a GTX 970. Phys-x turned off, because it affects all foliage in the game making it VERY demanding. Anti aliasing was also turned down pretty low. I had almost constant 60 fps in open areas and out on the seas. In cities 40-55 depending on foliage and population. In dense forest and vegetation it went to 40-45 with occasional drops to about 38.
With phys-x turned on I would get stuttering when vegetation textures was loaded. It could be my CPU but I don't know.
Game review:
The game is beautiful! The jungles, the swamps, the seas, the cities, they all look stunning and feel varied. They have done a good job adding a vertical feel to the world using a combination of trees, buildings and varied terrain. It's a huge step up from AC III.
There are several kinds of collectibles and side missions that I actually felt compelled to complete, but I was a bit saddened that I didn't get anything but an Uplay achievement for collecting all the animus fragments. Collecting the uncharted chests and fragments became a pain in the end as you have to constantly stop your ship, swim to an island and back to your ship. I suggest picking them up on the way early on when you are still so mesmerized about how pretty the game is that you don't mind the grind. Or forget them entirely. You might not be able to 100% the game anyway because of Uplay. See further down for explanation.
The naval combat gave a well needed change of setting to the usual running and provided a fun and rewarding way to earn money for upgrades. One flaw I found was that the best equipment was a bit too easy to get. Money is easy to get with a little bit of grinding on the seas and then the best set of swords and pistols are yours. I thought even better ones would be unlocked later on but no. I was fully equipped from the store very early in the game. You don't have to grind, but piracy is fun and will gain you money very quickly.
The crafting system is very much like the one in Farcry 3 where you need different animal skins and bones to make different objects. How does that make any sense? Why do I need BLACK jaguar skin? What's wrong with regular jaguar? Or even rabbit? I see what why they are doing this but I would really have liked to see a different kind of crafting system.
The free running then. So much fun and so annoying at the same time. We need one button for plain old running and one button for free running. I don't know how many times I've wanted to run through a doorway and have Kenway trying to climb the wall beside it. Even if it's impossible to climb it. One time I lost a tailing mission because Kenway insisted on climbing instead of running. He fell down, I tilted the analog stick to the left to make him run around the obstacle and watched as he climbed it again. And then a third time, making me lose my target.
So, on to one of the worst things of all. Uplay. It tries to connect to Uplay each time I start the game, but I get no indication as to whether it succeeds or not. But in game I've never been able to access the minigame "Kenways fleet" because the Ubisoft servers were unavailable. Meaning I can't get the last upgrade for my ship and I can't get all the chests. If I just missed out of some multiplayer I wouldn't care, but I can't get access to all single player content. What's up with that?!
In conclusion: AC IV is a great game. It's fun, immersive and beautiful. It's dragged down by Uplay and the sometimes annoying free run system. If you have enjoyed other AC games then this is definitely for you! If you like to try an AC game then this is a great starting point! If you want something graphically less demanding I would recommend AC II. As always with Ubisoft games do your research! They seem to all be buggy to some extent and there might be a problem you find game breaking. Some people claim they can't get the game to run at all due to Ubisoft servers being offline.
Edit:
I totally forgot about the part where you exit the animus and walk around at Abstergo. So here goes my opinion: It pretty much sucks.
I usually don't have a problem with FPS but these parts give me motion sickness. They are really slow an awkward and just rips you out of the otherwise so immersive game to force you through some incredibly forced story. I forgot about them in my review earlier because I always avoided exiting the animus for as long as i could. At least these parts are so infrequent and short that I could forget about them, that's says something.
Edit 2: Spelling and text cleanup
Edit 3: I have refreshed my memory on AC II and I take back the "Assassin's Creed refined part". There really is a ton of stuff to do in AC IV but it really does lack some of the sense of purpose that AC II had. Both the combat and the free climbing is also better featured in AC II than in AC IV. I'll try to stop editing this now...

EDIT: Its now been about three weeks since my initial review. In this time, I have done quite a bit of exploring of the route and its activities, tweaked my graphics settings, and joined in the beta testing of the updates. I think the first and most important point to note here is, since my review below, there have been 2 patches with a third in beta. These updates have brought with them noteable improvements in performance that has given me the opportunity to play at high settings and still maintain decent performance on my mid-range (i7-6700, GTX960m 4GB, 16GB RAM) laptop.
After spending more time with the route I have come to one conclusion. This is just another TS2017 route just built on new graphics and physics engines. While there are amazing improvements over the previous generations in areas like signal visibility, in-cab interactivity and features, and the ability to stop and walk around, there are still the same old DTG TrainSimulator complaints - No life in the towns, no defect detectors(even though the metal bungalo scenery is in place), among others. On the scenarios I have two major complaints. First, there is no Quick Drive. So no consist builder/editor, no ability to start a train from anywhere at any time. Second, nearly all the scenarios and services have you out on the main line except for one where you will fill coal hoppers and two in the yard. Of the two yard scenarios, the first one is simply showing off the features of the yard in the new platform (working the turntable, starting a cold engine, self-serve fueling a locomotive) disguised as a scenario to be moving and servicing incoming and outgoing power. The last scenario is basicly a free-for-all in the yard. I am disappointed that there is nothing involving switching cars, or utilizing the hump yard.
Overall, I changed my recommendation to "Yes" because DTG is working on the performance problems. Just understand that what you are getting is still the same old DTG TrainSimulator game just in a shiny new Unreal package.
-----------------------
ORIGINAL: Visually the game is beautiful and a drastic graphic improvment over previous generations of Train Simulator games. Unfortunatley, like many of the other reviews already state, there is a  problem with the optimization leading to in-game performance that ranges from unplayable to just good on the best of machines.
Features and gameplay have been vastly improved with the ability to leave the engineer's seat and to interact with some of the locomotive systems. This new feature while a great addition to the game can also be extremely frustrating as you often have a conductor in the cab with you during the scenarios but you are unable to task them with appropriate duties like changing switches or cutting off cars leading to a lot of on/off type activity between running the locomotive and walking.
Overall, I would recommend Run8 before TSW for the simulation experience. I think that TSW as it is now is a great starting platform that with work can be built into an unbeatable rail simulator. As it stands today, I can't in good consience recommend buying the game until the performance issues are corrected.

I decided to change my review of Raceroom.
After now playing most of the other games / sim AC ,RF2  & the older Simbin game's I have had time to see some major forwards step since Simbin changed to  Sector 3 racing .
Al this years updates have changed this game & set new levals across the board.
Better sounds , yes Better than what already the best sound engine out there .
The FFB is also 2nd to none even with older wheel like the G27 it shines .
The whole package as been improved , now including online that is still only alpha or early Beta that knocks most other racing game into touch.
Yes still the big moaning isssue for most is the odd why they sell DLC . but once you understand that buying two packs that contain lots of the same items track wise , is not doubling up on the payments , that in fact Sector 3 will credit you for doubled up content so there should me no risks of paying for the same tracks twice over.
The money you save can be then used to buy extra cars or packs should you choose to.
Yes there is quite a bit of lame content add's in the cut screens & loading screens for DLC.
That is bit off putting so is the fact that only fraction of their content is been sold via steam , so the content you buy via staem is only covered by your Steam account & not directly through Sector 3 . I have no idea what the on- going deal with  Sector § & Steam is but its is a little messy .
I like buying my items via the Steam Card service I find this a lot safer than having to have my credit card details stuck on a Steam server waiting the next big hacking accounts scandle.
So I hope Sector 3 decide to push more stuff onto steam as that is the only way I will be buying more content from them in the long term.
The overal cost could be high should you want every car & track , But most have a pick & mix approch & stick with their favorite cars .
You only need one car from ever race series along with the tracks & bingo you can race in any event held online.
If you are realy good & can race realy fast then you should try the challanges that offer a wide range of prizes both in game credits or even hardware.
So I see this now as better value than the year in year out serial fest of the likes of F1 games.
Or the over hyped & money making Project Cars the former out part of Simbin now SMS.
For the most part you can not fault the game engine ,
The sounds are the best
The cars drive & handle well.
AI has improve by a large margin form this time last year.
The menus could still do with some work.
FFB is some of the best out there with lot tweaking to be had in the setting screen.
Online is very advanced for what is still Alpha standards.
Every update this year as improved the game.
Its not perfect they still need to make batter sales platform, but you get a lot for what you pay for it & you only need to add the content you want to & you can still race online.

I'll start this review off by pointing out that i have played this game on and off for over a year now. This is one of those rare gems of a game that keeps you coming back for more forever as it is constantly improving through its passionate and dedicated dev team and community.
But more then that. This is a game that has a nearly infinite depth in its mechanics and advanced build modes, logic systems, weapons systems..etc..etc which leaves you with nearly limitless possibilites in which to build whatever ship, base, station you can imagine.
The mulyiplayer aspect is often quite engaging as well with its caring community, factions and moderators that always have interesting events planned and fun things to do, ranging from huge PvP tournements like Blood and Steel where you bring the deadliest machine you can build to wage war against other teams. Along with server bosses or christmas events..etc..etc
Or even something as simple as taking a noob out to fight the pirates for the first time to hear them get excited when they get there first kill in their newly built fighter ship. Or even having to save that same noob later because he jump driven his ship into a star because thay havent learned that they should chart there course a little more carfully when traversing the cosmos.
All of these things add up to a game that is absolutley satisfying , so long as you can muster the patience to overcome the admittedly steep learning curve required to understand the workings of this game competently.
I certainly recommend this game to all who love space, sci fi, sandbox and voxel building games. But must say that it isnt for the faint of heart or those without much patience. But is for those who want to build the baddest mutha of a ship this side of the galaxy has seen

The HD graphics are definitely noticable in the student's character models, but otherwise the graphics look rather mundane. Not terrible though. Keep in mind that you will spend most of your time interacting and controlling these main characters so most of what you see is very crisp and detailed character models.
The artwork in general fits the story setting very well and I find that the game itself most closely resembles FFVIII when compared to other FF games (ie: highschool age students thrust into a war due to their unique abilities).
I haven't beaten the game yet so I might write another review upon completion.
Cheers!

The levels are linear where you only have to follow a single path available. Huge amount of enemies will spawn when you reach a huge open area. This is also indicated by the background music.
The plot is alright but you will tend to get a little confuse at first because you cannot familiarize with the names and the story telling is vague in the beginning.
I highly recommend this game if you are a fan of clean, simple, classic first person shooter.

I really wanted to like this game, and unlike a lot of people who start their reviews like this and then give a game a negative review I am going to do the opposite and give it a positive review. Why? Becuase the spirit and intention of the game was really good and I feel that two little things really betrayed the game and had the developers gotten those two things right, the reviews would not be mixed but positive instead. But before I get to the bit where I talk about those two things I would like to explain what I did like about this game:
This game tried to encompass that good old citybuilder feel that was so popular about 10-15 years ago but is a lot less so today. I'm talking about games like “Settlers” where there is a nice mix between economic factors and a little bit of warrior management, but not too much. God knows there are already enough military games out there! So when I saw this game I honestly really wanted it to be like “Settlers” especially given that the people that made Settlers apparently don’t want to make that game anymore and it’s getting harder and harder to find a fun non-modern citybuilder (of course we have Tropico and Cities Skylines to scratch that itch). But I longed for one set in history hence I really wanted this to work. Now from an artistic perspective they actually get a lot right. I like the art style and interface a lot and the music is very fitting and adds to the ambience.
The first thing that really betrays this game is the camera. It is awful and is something the devs should have really prioritized. When you’re playing a citybuilder you want to seamlessly switch between an overview of your civilization and a screen that shows a smaller area where you want to do your work. It was such a little thing but I’m sure had they got that right this game would have another 5 points up on it’s score.
The second thing that really bothered me was the level system. Often they would have us build a whole town on a tiny island just to find out that the creeps at the end were quite easy and that we didn’t need to build quite so much. Then we have to start again in the next island. No, they should have just put various objectives on a single map. That would have been more fun.
Look it’s a good game and had potential to be up there but sadly those two things make the game a bit annoying to play. Perhaps I may give it more of an effort in the future but for now I will give it a positive review as I believe these devs are going the right direction.

The Bridge is a somewhat pretentious but great puzzle game about surreal perspectives and geometry. The difficulty rating will surely make it memorable for those who manage to somehow reach its end.
Many things have been said about the Bridge. About the innovation of using puzzles based on impossible geometry (like the Penrose triangle). About the creativity of the hand-drawn black and white visual style. About the eerie, surreal story.
All of it is true. And all of it is (geatly) exaggerated.
First and foremost: the Bridge is nothing more than a set of rotation puzzles with good friction and momentum physics. Some levels are good. Some require a lot of tiresome fidgeting around to find that roughly 0.01° window to pull off the solution.
Don’t get me wrong: the puzzle design is great. It is also a little sadistic, especially in the second half of the game. This makes you to stop and think about the core of the problem instead of sheer trial and error, so it achieves that many other puzzle games could not.
Next to the difficulty, the most memorable feature of the Bridge is the visual style, which reminds us to the black & white underground obscure graphic novels from the late seventies. Strange as it may sound, but this surreal imagery really fits a logic-based puzzle game.
This warped mindset carries itself through the story, or more precisely the very conscious choice of not having any form of story whatsoever. It is just a collection of surrealistic monologues that try to make the player think deeper things into the levels than what they really are: a set of good rotational puzzles with really high difficulty.

Generally: Very good climatic game. Rules are taken from its precursor, board game. Good turn-based strategy, which gives long play and a lot of fun. About 6-7 DLCs, but onyl 4 are with missions. Other are skins and additional team.
Team planning/arming: Generally, it's based on preset settings of squads. No possible to rearm or reconfigure teams. No editor for missions. This is minus of this game. There is no progress for characters also. It means, each mission you start with the same preset characters and weapons. There is DLC called "Wolves chapter" which gives other one team, more prepared for close combat. And it gives more fun of playing, even if you finish campaing. But still, no possible to adjust or rearm team.
Missions: Be prepared for more costs if you want to get more missions. Basic campaign got 12 missions. DLCs cost much, and gives you about 3-5 missions. To recompensate it I can tell than missions last long time, about hour sometines. And to finish it you have to play many times to find out good way how to make it.
Bugs: But this game is fixed often and refined to the top. A lot of bugs/issues which you will find in forum, was already fixed. I didn't experience any problems.
AI: There is only sometimes AI "hanging", by stopping units in some corner, piling up and waiting. But this is not often, and happens in some missions in some cases only. The game very depends on AI pressure. So if there are not units running on you or spawning on your path, game from hard tension massacre changes for a walk. So, in some missions you struggle for survive but in some you have a heavy armored terminators just walking from entry to exit through whole map, maybe killing something on pass, but then you even do not notice a threat.
Long play: Prepare youself for long and hard play. Even in normal level, it is hard to finish base campaing. It took for me about two weeks to make it. One missions can last from 20 minutes to more than 1 hour.
Rules/chances: This game is based on dice rolls. It means all the time you can calculate your probability of kill/miss. Even if it looks like "chess" play, due to fixed number of action points, it has got command points and some random behaviour of opponent. It gives you mission not exact the same all time. However, playing a mission is kind of following general stratecic plan which is based on calculations. So it's "chess" plus some luck.
Cheats: You don't need any cheats in the game. This game got already cheat inside. By making "undo" on you action you can repeat last dice roll. In example, you move and shoot. When you miss, you can "undo" and repeat it untill you will not get it success. Real good players do not make it. Me also. And it pist me off that this possibility is, because it's not quite fair and good. It induces you, so sometimes you will want to use it. It is up to you. Play normal and "fair", or repeat every move many times.
Graphics: It is not the main case for such kind of game. Some predefined scenes for action like shoot/kill/die are shown where character is doing something. More its like top view of map. It is nice that this top view is not exactly ortogonal, but king of twisted which gives more expression on it. You can't rorate it freely rather than that, you can turn by full 90 degrees.
Climate: It is dark and deep climatic game, where you can feel terror and panic struggle for survive. Some actions require to sacrifice someone on mission. But even then you can try to save the character in very drastic situation. So this is fun.

Wow, this game is just incredible. I wasn't aware at all of what I was getting myself into when I started playing this, but once the map opened up my God did it open up. This is a Metroidvania style game that takes a lot of mechanical inspiration from both the obvious Metroid and Castlevania tropes, but also from Dark Souls in many ways. In Dark Souls, there were bonfires, and in this game there are benches. Souls are now Geo. Bosses will wreck you.
And yet, this game does not feel derivative. It definitely has its own identity, mostly due to the fact that it's 2D, and can take advantage of that for platforming and more player mobility. As you progress through the game, you will gain more abilities and moves that will make you much more agile. The "Charm" system is this game's version of speccing a character, and allow you to equip different passive and active abilities and perks.
This game is in the truest sense "open world", in that there really isn't a set path for the player to take. Virtually half of the content in the game is optional, although most likely you will want to experience that content, and most of it becomes imperative if you want to get the "good" ending. An average vanilla run of the game can take you about 20 hours, although to get 100%, that could easily go on 40 or 50 hours.
My only real complaint is that while the controls are definitely tight, they can at times prove to be frustrating, or to not exactly work as you intended. Some sections requiring tight jumps with little room for error can be very annoying, and sometimes you can fall to your death because your character simply wouldn't latch onto a wall correctly for a wall jump. That and traversing the map can occasionally be a chore, but these are minor qualms with an otherwise fantastic game.
Now that I've completed this game and Ori and the Blind Forest, I'm definitely hankering for some more Metroidvania goodness. I have high hopes for the DLC coming out later this month.

TLDR: 10/10 Perfectly executed story and consistently fun gameplay.
I was worried at first when booting up the game, as I didn't have a controller that was compatible with Hollow Knight. My fears were swiftly quelled after two minutes of platforming and slashing at foes. Even with a keyboard, the game felt very fluid and I never felt that platforming problems were a result of controls. The simple gameplay works to never overwhelm the player. Even whenI had all the spells and upgrades, I still never felt like I was desperately juggling the buttons and stumbling through the expansive world of Hallownest.
The world is massive and meant to be explored and backtracked, just like any Metroidvania should be. The game also doesn't restrict creativity to earlier areas of the game. The entire world is oozing with the passion Team Cherry had for this game. Unlike other Indie games, I never saw a part where the developers got sloppy and less creative with their enemies, music, or environments. With places ranging from a mining peak filled with gorgeous pink crystals, to a dark spiders den that always leaves you guessing about what horrors may be around the corner, or wilds where ash is always raining down from above, Hallownest is always unique and exciting to explore.
The Story of Hollow Knight is executed perfectly. It doesn't begin with boring narration or an overwhelming backstory. The player knows very little and just knows to head right. The Lore unfolds itself as the player progresses and learns the story, but doesn't know where they learn it since they are having so much fun exploring. The ending doesn't rely on story elements that were never explained, but rather ties the story together in a brilliant fashion.

Everything is kept simple yet complex, and this simplicity is tackled in a fashion that keeps the game exciting, but never overwhelming.

The original Call of Duty.
Negatives:
It has a few negatives because this game was made back when the studio was still learning their craft.
-It’s the only game in the series with a health bar. This isn’t that bad, but on Veteran, there are no health packs, and the AI and situations can be unforgiving (to put it mildly).
-The graphics are not the best. Not that this is actually a bad thing, but the character models live in the uncanny valley, and are difficult to look at.
-Somewhat repetitive, but this can be overlooked because you’re actually playing though different parts of the second world war.
-The tag line was “no one fights alone”, but because the AI was still pretty weak, there are some missions in which you operate almost entirely alone (say 1 out of 3?).
-Some areas have respawning enemies, which can make advancement difficult.
-The saving system in this game makes it a little difficult to just pick up and play one or two missions.
Positives:
-You generally have more control over your character than later installments (Black Ops through Ghosts), and are not forced to watch as many cutscenes or set pieces (they do still exist though).
-It’s not trying to be dark, gritty, and mature. It’s just trying to be a fun game.
-You really do feel like you’re in the middle of pretty epic battles, when they happen.
-Harder difficulties are actually hard.
Bottom line: I had a lot of fun with the different weapons and scenarios, and can forgive its mistakes because it was the studio’s first project.

Dungeon Defenders is a quirky little game where, on top of being a tower defense, you also have to run around and shoot things. Ever played Sanctum 1 or 2? Then keep your money, bud, cause this is just a less fun version.
The basic premise is you four heroes in training must hold the line against invading waves of heroes while the real heroes are out gettin donuts or somethin. I didn't pay attention to that bit. So you build turrets and collect resources dropped from chests and enemies to build turrets or to upgrade your abilities and weapons. In the end we have an tower defense third person shooter with rpg elements. It's got a cute little cell shaded graphic style that I can't help but find appealing and honestly the actual mechanics of it all aren't half bad if you can excuse the fact that projectile attacks are virtually useless if not awkward as a 14 year old trying to talk about his sexual experiences in a positive light. Yeah I bet you got it good last night, Uncle Paul.
So why not reccomend it? BECAUSE IT'S BOOOOOOOOORING. Honestly, the game is so unbelievably slow paced. Everything is slow, the enemies are slow, the projectiles are slow, the turrets are slow, every attack is slow and boring and lame. I'd call it a childrens game, but Kameo: Elements of Power was a childrens game and on the hardest difficulty can at least keep you paying attention. You know what else is a childrens game? The Legend of Zelda. A game that isn't combat orriented still has far superior combat mechanics and faster paced gameplay then a game that boasts it.
On top of the slow game play, it's just plain awkward. Projectile attacks can hardly be called skill shots, since the move barely any faster than the enemies and you never run out of amunition. Only the mage and the knight are really worth anything because the knight can literally just stop an entire wave with two turrets and shell them with cannonballs that are basically 2 hit kills on large enemies. The monk supposedly has healing abilities but there's never any need because you have to actually try to die in this game.
Simply put, it's boring. It's cute, it's quirky, it's unique(kinda), but it's just too slow. It's upgrade system is just a massive min/maxfest and leaves so much to be desired.
