The Stronghold series has always been extremely difficult to summarise, but I guess the unfortunate word that I tend to use is "frustrating". It hasn't ever recaptured that momentum that Stronghold Crusader delivered back in 2002, producing games that didn't deliver for a variety of different reasons.
Unfortunately, I don't think newcomers to the game will enjoy the game as much as we do. It still has a lot of content missing, and areas such as the menu's and HUD are definitely missing a much-needed improvement. The graphics aren't as good as you'd expect, and the AI is broken at times. Troops refuse to obey your commands due to bugs, and so on. It certainly wasn't what I was expecting, thats for sure.
With this said, I do rate Stronghold Crusader 2, and I do enjoy playing it. It has been great for a player like myself who grew up playing the original. Just to have the feel of Stronghold again, to get a taste of what originally made it so successful. Character dialogue is witty, the gameplay is fast, and the numerous scenario's that you partake in provide excellent replayability. The tutorial and majority of skirmishes are brilliant, even for me a few of them I kinda thought "..how the hell am I supposed to do that?!" but you eventually get into the groove of how the game dynamics work. Its good to progressively see yourself get better & better, as you challenge yourself further by adding multiple AI and restricting yourself to using certain units/buildings. I haven't completed the campaign as of yet, but so far its been extremely good fun.
So for fans of previous Stronghold titles, I am sure you will learn to appreciate the game for the quality it has, though somewhat trapped inside a conglomerate of faults. For newcomers I am skeptical as to how much you'd enjoy it, as there are other titles in this genre that do much more then what Stronghold Crusader 2 provides. Still, SC2 provides some memorable moments and entertaining game scenario's, yet lacks the full package we truly want to see that follows in the originals footsteps.

Played this game at a games con a little while ago, and thoroughly enjoyed the alpha build I played on, so when I found it was on steam, now a few months on, I knew I had to get hold of it, as of now, I've played about an hour of the game through with a friend and we both enjoyed the way the game played.
Things I loved:
[Level Design]  The game instantly throws you in at the deep end, with a rather complex first level, which is quite hard to one shot, but instead teaches you to learn the levels features, so on and so forth.  The first level took us around 15 tries, but by the end we knew how the level worked and had no trouble getting through it.
[Turnips]  I adore this in-game currency, firstly because it is not gained through micro transactions, you have to work to get them. Secondly, the way you use it, picture the scene, you are low on health, and have just reached a tough part in the level where you KNOW you are going to get hit, ta-da!  There is a health-dispenser that costs 10 turnips per 10% of your health restored, genius.  And not only can it be used for this, but the game has a decent variety of customization for the user, after a run of the game, you can go back and edit your player, some items are already unlocked for you, but with turnips, you can unlock some lovely clothing and character player models.  My favourite custom item being the fez.
[Co-op]  This is the most co-op based co-op game on the market as of right now,  well, that and portal 2, but for now we'll focus on the game shall we?  There are genius puzzles of the game for players to bang their heads on the desk at, not because it isn't fun, because it's difficult to get used too. No 2 puzzles in the game are similar, each level introduces a new way of solving it, one of my favourites is the invisible path level. You literally have to direct your partner through what to them looks like nothing but air.
Ok, we've done good things, but there were a few bit's and pieces of the game I wasn't so sure about:
[Menu]  This game has some absolutely fantastic elements in it, and I love it to bits, BUT the menu, the thing you see when you load the game up, could look... better...  compared to the rest of the game, it kind of let it down.
[Choosing levels]  When we had finished the first 5 or so levels, the game took us to a little hall, with a funny looking band playing music, and I was dumb enough to tell my friend to step on the pressure plate nearest to the entrance.  It started the game again...  And also seemed to shuffle in levels we hadn't played yet, at this point we decided to stop playing for the day, very confused.
That's all I really have to say about this fantastic Indie game.  Thanks for adding some awesome new things, and apologies for not finding everything so up to scratch.

I am an 80ies kid by heart, and have lived through all the shows, movies, music vids and fashion statements from that time. Zup! 5 is a minimalistic puzzle with explosions. The idea is simple and the gameplay is just as simple. A great game for relaxation.

The negatives I talked about?
1. When you have to wait for achievement pop-ups to stop before you can solve a level, there are *WAY* too many achievements. Or bad level design.
2. The game takes about 30 minute to complete: way too little content!
3. The music seems to be really short and loops probably hundreds of times in the 30 minutes.
4. Most puzzles are ridiculously easy -- so easy in fact that you *cannot* offer any other solution than the correct one.
All in all, if you've played one Zup! you've seen it all. This installment is probably the weakest one, so I'd recommend you rather try 1 or Zero if you only want one. For those who find this kind of easy clicking addictive and relaxing, a must buy. The simple and clean look is still captivating.

I dont understand all the bad reviews. This is not a 4x. it is not CIV 17.5. It is not a milsim, its just a mellow relaxing little twist on settlers. Especially settlers 1 & 2. I'm pretty sure you will like this if you liked the early settlers. (in my opinion, settlers started going downhill after 4).
I was hesitating to buy this, as i really like the genre, but it had so many negative reviews. I watched i video by petard (who loved it) and i decided to get it.
PRO:
* the scenery is pretty and the models are cute
* you have a little more control over your troops than early settlers, but still not a lot. This is not a game for heavy military strategy. thats one of the mistakes that the settlers series ended up making
* the terrain varies from map to map providing diffferent challenges
* roads are way easier to manage than in settlers 1
* resource movement (which stumps a lot of people it seems) is important, it doesnt "just happen"  (see below)
CON:
* music is nice, but a few more tracks would be better
* you do tend to start most games placing the same buildings in the same order
RESOURCE MOVENT:
(I want to call this out seperately since this is a common complaint of even some positve reviewers. I think it is a PRO but could legitimatly be seen as a CON by some people.)
As your village gets more spread out, resources will not be distributed the way you want without doing extra work. Each building has a limited range of influence, if you have a remote fishing hut, the fish will not get transported to your central stockpile. your villagers will only make the trek out to the hut when the are starving.
Since the fisherman stops fishing when his hut is full (5 fish) this could mean that people may not have enough to eat. (hunger really slows your vikings down). There are a number of strategies to deal with this in the game. Additional stockpile workers, additional stockpiles and couriers a the three most obvious.
This makes VH a game where you really have to think about storage an transport. Which i like  - this makes it more than just a settlers clone
SUMMARY:
if you want a military strategy or a deep 4X, look somewhere else.  If you want a relaxing town builder with cute vikings with resource management and a little fighting then you should probably get this

Hollow Knigh is a beautiful 2D combat based metriodvaina and has quickly become one of my favorite games of all time because of the following reasons:
* Great soundtrack that adds ambience, so much so that it makes each part of the massive world feel unique, I loved returning to the main city becuase of the amazing piano piece.
* Amazing art style with fluid animation, poofts of dust leave the characters legs as they jump, double jumping leaves white glowing feathers, little touches make the game feel alive.
* Interesting characters that are much more than exposition dumps, all having unique character, the majority move around the game world and have interesting small stories that develop with the player. The writing is also great, most of the time I would speak to everyone just to see their take on the world.
* Great enemy variety, including varied bossess and a massive bestiary that gives incentive to hunt down enemies repetedly.
* Badge system allows for customizable character, great to experiment with nearly all badges having a genuine impact on gameplay.
* Massive world with many nooks and crannies, gives a genuine feel of exploration. The world also has great variety in color, theme and feel. There is everything from lush jungles, bee hives and undeground areas crawling with bugs.

* Great feeling of momentum, always pushing you forward with new abilites, interesting enemies and upgrades.
*Interesting story that is pieced together with bits of information from the bestiary, character chatter and world landmarks.
* Staggering amount of content for the price, first playthrough will take 25+ hours or more for completionists, with multiple endings, achivements for speedrunning and even a perma death mode, the value for money is undeniable.
The game is not without it's downsides though:
* The game is slow to start and players without a natural inclanation to explore migh be left bored and purposeless.
* The game has a nice diffiuclty curve but those who want a more casual experience will be crushed near the late game
where you really have to concentrate to tackle the harder challenges.
* The game world is enormous and I could imagine those without a strong sense of direction could easily get lost.

Space Hulk is incredibly disappointing. As a fan of turn-based strategy games and the Space Hulk: Death Angel card game, I anticipated this title with what I thought were reasonable expectations, though this game did not come close to meeting them.
The graphics and animation have no notable qualities. The game is ugly, sluggish and plays like an iPhone title. One can easily waste a turn making a misclick and watching their lumbering character turn to face the wall.
The gameplay is pitiful in comparison to any recent turn-based strategy game. There is nothing to a lot of the maps other than setting up an overwatch, waiting for the genestealers to come to you and getting the requisite kills to complete the mission. The map layouts are simple and linear and would have been much better with an element of randomization like the card game mentioned above. That feature would have also added some replay value to this, which currently has none. There is no sense of exploration or cautious advance that XCOM: Enemy Unknown provides and no sense of personality or team relationships that is featured in Fire Emblem Awakening. There is also no character progression system that allows you to customize or favor individual units such as those systems offered in XCOM, Fire Emblem or Battle for Wesnoth.
I would not recommend this game to anyone; all, including Space Hulk fans, would be much better served playing XCOM, Fire Emblem or Battle for Wesnoth and passing on this one.

In each level, you have to get to the exit door. You do this by walking, rotating gravity, avoiding evil balls, pick up keys, and control a bunch of other mechanics. Most levels are clever, but can be solved with some trial-and-error. Some require precise movement/timing/alignment of gravity. This can get very annoying, but at least you can rewind as much as you want. There is some Escher stuff going on in the level design; paths that cross themselves.
This game will not appeal to everybody: it is very frustrating at times, especially when you want to get one of the balls to move in a certain direction but rotating gravity makes the dude slide to his death. If you want a slow, hand-drawn physics puzzle game and don't easily get dizzy, I can recommend this game, but only just. Worth playing, but not worth €9,99.

You can already tell by reading the title Dungeon Defenders (DD) that this game is trying something very new and very different; and you would be right! DD is a tower defense game with RPG and loot hoarding (it's "hoarding" not "whoring"), and manages to get the thrill of all of the above.
The plot too tries something just a "little" different; just enough to spice things up. You play as the children of 4 legendary heros whom - many years ago - defeated an ancient evil known only as....the...*facepalm*...The Old Ones, and locked them away in.....Eternia Crystals (they won't be there for "eternity", will they...?) . Anyway, after their major victory, (for reasons uknown) they traveled to a "far off land" (the writer's way of saying "JUST GET RID OF THEM!") and have left you in charge of defending the crystals. However, in your rough housing, you shatter a small Eternia Crystal, which attracts millions of creatures hoping to destroy the others. Whoops! Time to defend some dungeons!
You choose one of 4 classes.
Apprentice (mage) has powerful offensive towers, but they die fast.
Squire (warrior) has short range towers that are expensive, but they hit hard and he himself is a strong    melee fighter.
Huntress (why not just hunter?) has expendable traps, but mostly thrives off of her ranged damage.
Monk melees and has auras that buff/debuff. He brings utility and is mostly a brawler. (many others have been added via DLC).
The sound effects bring the fantasy world to immersive life. Aside from just the sounds of fighting, the beasts sounds are also a joy to hear. They let out their weird shrieks and grumbles and groans as they march toward your crystal. It's so hard to describe sound in a text review :(. What makes the sound good here is the attention to detail. As a ballista missile is sent flying, you can clearly hear that it's made of wood. The sound of wood slipping past the lumber of the bow itself, followed by the faint ratatatat of the string is stunning detail, for example. The narrator gives the game it's essence. His performance is legendary. He's a fantastic story teller with a great voice, as well as the filter they added to him.
The music is beyond most of what I've heard in video games. I won't say much. Just listen to this.
Graphically the game is freakin' GORGEOUS. It has that Warcraftian thick, blocky look, lovely color palettes, butter-smooth animations on all characters, and runs over 60fps. I'd go so far as to say that visually, the game is a new standard for fantasy games.
Once, you place your towers (or not), the game isn't just tower defense. You can also wade into the thick of combat slashing away at the goofy baddies, giving the game a large amount of variation.
Your decision of your toon's progression is divided into those 2 parts: "hero spec" or "builder spec". The idea is to have 1 or maybe 2 builders and 2 (or 3) fighters. How many structures you can build is limited by Defense Units (DU).
There's even boss fights which you must defeat while still maintaining defenses for trash mobs. With 4 players and the higher difficulty modes, bosses get INTENSE!
It's all so good! What could possibly go wrong!? Enter the expansion packs (DLC/xpacks). At first, they introduced a new level cap, loot, and a new dificulty: Nightmare. It was awesome at first, but there was a major underlying problem.
You see, I was one of the best "builders" in the community at the time. Not that I had the best gear, but I had a deep understanding of how the towers worked and how to place them. It wasn't long before I was solo'ing the most difficult modes with no help from teammates, who would stand by commenting "wow ur a good builder. i love ur set up D:" but amongst all of this, the xpacks brought new loot. That new loot was roughly 10x better than my gear. That means, no matter how good I got at building, my skill didn't matter. All that mattered was if I had bought the xpacks and grind, grind, grinded for better gear.
I was willing to do this, then another problem reered: always-online DRM. It runs off of Trendynet which requires you to be connected to their service constantly. If your internet even hiccuped, THE WHOLE SERVER SHUTS DOWN. This means when you're forced to play survival mode up to wave 25+ to FINALLY get gear upgrades, there's so many enemies eating up the bandwidth that the server shuts down! Worse yet, it's not just Trendy's connection that must be maintained, but ALSO STEAM'S!
YOU HAVE TO KEEP 2 ALWAYS-ONLINE DRM SERVICES PERMANENTLY CONNECTED AT ALL TIMES OR YOUR GAME IS OVER.
The community is also terrible. Not the worst I've seen, but they might as well just be empty player slots. They don't do or say anything but screw up the game or "ninja loot" (steal it). Get into anything past level 60 and it's a bunch of elitists that think they're hot s*** because they're one of the few who got that far.
If it's not elitists, it's people that are getting ran-through by their level 90 buddies that are geared out, which ruins the experience for me. "MOAR LEWT GIME LEWT GET THA LEWT!" why not enjoy the process? Where's the challenge?
The game quality itself is a 10, but the issues brought about by double DRM and the xpacks that inflated the gear too much, along with the brainless community,  bring the game down. For the most part, it's unplayable. If you can manage to get some friends to play, don't even hesistate. If you're solo, get it at a discount, but don't expect the game to give any love to solo players.
For some reason, it's impossible for developers to recognize solo players exist and scale the game down to be solo'able. Reduce enemies? Reduce number of crystals to defend? Reduce Boss HP? Why are solo players always out-right ignored in games like this?

What you have visited will then ONLY be shown on the map when you rest at the next save point. It certainly encourages the exploration of each nook and cranny of this gigantic labyrinth, yet sometimes you may find yourself completely lost with no mean of finding your way back where you came from because you didn't or COULDN'T find the map merchant due to his questionnable placement in the area (
). If finding your way through a blank void in the map for a while doesn't scare you, this game won't give you as much trouble as it gave me.

I'm an avid Metroidvania fan, and I've pretty much played them all. Hollow Knight is a STELLAR game and honestly the best I've played in years. The atmosphere of this game is not to be understated. There are several NPCs to interact with (some of which just for lore) and the world tells a haunting story of a ruined civilization through scenery and a few trinkets of words alone. The music is excellent and further drives the atmosphere department home. It's a world to get lost in for sure.
That is not to say the gameplay isn't absolutely on point, because it is. The combat in this game is very simple but so polished and well done that you never feel cheated when you get hit. Attacking and dodging are skills you have to master and mastering them is a friggen joy. Contrary to what you may hear, I did not think this game was especially difficult. I thought the difficulty curve was perfect honestly. Like I said, the combat is pretty much entirely skill based so the difficulty of the game is largely up to how quickly you can adapt. The boss fights are enthralling as the dreaded consequences of dying keeps you focused and engaged in a way not many other games can.
Did I mention this game is PACKED with content? My first playthrough landed at 30 hours, which is pretty typical for most players and at least double the next longest metroidvania I've ever played. There is a lot of backtracking though, so just be aware if that annoys you. This game is my GOTY without a question, and for 15$ it's actually borderline stealing.

The whole game is so lazy, that it took me all my will to continue with more levels in the mirrored worlds. It's just wasting your time instead of letting you play. This is an excellent game for competitive players who want the arena experience of WoW without worrying about grinding for gear or levels, or MOBA players who don't care much for level differences and farming/item purchases. It's a 2v2 or 3v3 pure PVP arena where nearly every single ability, including healing, is a skill-shot (meaning you have to aim and land it, not just click a target). There aren't a large number of abilities per character, so it is less about having a large ability toolkit and more about knowing how to anticipate your opponent's moves and use the abilities you have at the right time. I would highly recommend this game for individuals who want quick access to intense PVP fights without any of the outside work involved (farming, itemization, leveling, grinding, etc. etc.). There is a pretty nice balance between melee, ranged and support character options, and the Devs seem actively interested in maintaining the game's balance and adding new features and characters.

The Russian campaign begins on a foggy and gray river. You sit hunched down among 20 other comrades in a small, beat-up wooden raft, your only protection from the rain a worn red tarp full of holes flapping in the wind above your head. Your superiors circle around your small pit with machine guns and shout with a megaphone about reclaiming the motherland. German fighter planes strafe the rafts and blow them apart one at a time, until only yours remains. Some of your friends attempt to dive into the water, and your superiors turn around and shoot them. Your boat just manages it to make it to the opposite dock, where wounded Russians are being treated in a makeshift hospital. You line up with the rest of the survivors and pass a checkpoint, where the man in front of you is given a gun, and you are given five bullets. You have no weapon. With that, you begin running forward and almost immediately get knocked down by a mortar shell, and with your head swimming and your ears ringing, you continue up a hill as if in slow motion, where a long row of German machine gun nests lie in wait. You watch flag carriers and unarmed soldiers get mowed down around you, and you know your only option is to continue your suicidal advance. It's a unique set piece that I have not experienced in any other WWII shooter.
The rest of the game bored me. It's an important piece of FPS history and is the origin of many systems and styles still in use today. Yet while it remains very playable and occasionally exciting, there's nothing here you haven't done better countless times since.

First, to get this out of the way, there is no actual farming in Space Farmers. There are pigs and cows lurking around, and farmer characters to select, but you will not be collecting the harvest. Put away your thoughts of hovering tractors flying through fields of off-color fruits and vegetables. Instead of the zero gravity crop simulator you might expect from Steam in 2014, Space Farmers is instead a co-op puzzle game put out by the BumpkinBrothers. It’s a game that’s full of clever hooks and the kind of great moments you can only get when playing with a friend, but it’s held back by a bizarre progression that forces you to solve the same puzzles over and over again. Starmade is a small game in a massive world. There is building and designing to be had, fighting (apparently) and lots of other stuff.
Unfortunately, the game as a whole seems hollow. The only aspect I can really see in it is large scale coop or PvP. If that's your thing, go ahead and don't let me stop you. But if you're looking for something interesting and easy to play in your spare time, find something else.
In a more detailed analysis.
When I said "small game in a massive world" I meant that like any procedurally generated game (see Terraria for an example of what I'm talking about here), there is a limited amount of things you can have generated in an infinite universe. The asteroids and planets are almost identical throughout the galaxy. This not only makes no sense but gets quite boring. There are only a few colors (atmosphere color and dirt color / flora) of planets; there is yellow (desert), purple, green (Earth-like), and white (ice). Each of these has about four or so generation algorithms. So the terrain is essentially four types on planets. There is floating weird stuff that looks like noodles, there's plateau, hills, and spires. That's about it for planets.
Then there's the asteroids, which are hardly worth talking about since they have the same shape. They too have different colors (and different types of materials to harvest). But that's it.
There are about 6 (?) types of pirate station in the game. I have never seen them do anything at all. Just sit there.
There are some abandoned derelict stations which are incredibly well designed, but since walking around in them is so damn slow, you probably won't bother to explore them.
The crafting and the building is always on a massive scale. You will find yourself eventually using about a thousand (at least) factory enhancers (meaning 1000x the speed to craft items) for basically everything.
You'll eventually text edit your config files so you can place 10000 blocks at a time instead of 100.
The combat and ships designed for combat are simplistic. In this game, the more functional blocks you put on your ship, the more invincible it is. If you have shields that recharge at 2k a second and the enemy can only deal 1.99k a second, you literally
.
In combat the enemy AI basically works off these principles only: Go towards enemy. In you don't have any weapons run away. Fire weapons at enemy, repeat.
In non-combat situations, the AI is just not even there. There are seemingly no random attacks, patrols, factions, retaliations, or anything. There's a bunch of static stuff that shoots at you when you get too close and calls for drones.
The complexity of the game wears off extremely quickly. Unless you jump head first into logic (and get drowned in it), you'll know everything about how the game works and how to do just about anything that is possible in ~60 hours. Then there is no longer complexity. You'll realise the only reason you created a working airlock is because it looks cool when it opens.
In my opinion, this is – what a surprise – another case of “wait for it to be released”. I have not had a single early access game turn out to be any good. I'm hoping this will be different, but if they're releasing updates just to change the tool models, I don't know how likely that will be.

I got it as part of a bundle some time ago and decided to give it a try. The launcher was not the best experience. When I finally got in-game, the tutorial was broken. As if this was not annoying enough, without a tutorial I was *completely* lost and had no idea what to do. Oh, and the sound was bugged. It took me quite a while to find how to fix it. Then the performance was horrible and again it took me a while to find how to fix it (increase allocated memory, get Java 64x). So I ditched Starmade and was glad I did.
By the way: The tutorial was quickly fixed, and a new launcher is underway. This sums up quite nicely one of the positives of this game: The devs. They're active, they're quick, they're good. But most of all, they are just part of the community. I started watching a few tutorial videos and whatnot on youtube and only after I had watched quite a few I realized at least two of the youtubers were actually devs. They're so helpful and chill it's unbelievable.
After watching online some of the stuff people were doing with the game and how so many love it I decided to give it another go -- now with the knowledge of where to find solutions to the problems I'd certainly encounter: Youtube, and to some extent the forums. Oh and I'm so glad I didn't give up.
Then onto something that might be a pro or a con, depending what you're looking for: This game is whatever you make of it. So if you're looking to hop into space and find everything done and ready... keep looking. Here you start with pretty much nothing, in the middle of the vast space and next to a shop. Go from there, good luck. It's up to you what you want to build or do. Where you want to go. With whom you want to ally and play. And so on.
The big pro is that the limit is just your creativity. The possibilities are vast. If you like being creative, inventive, ingenious, and if you like to build not only your own game but a whole universe (ok, a whole "stronghold" in universe) -- then this is for you.
The cons stay pretty much on the realm of the interface. The interface
be pretty powerful but many many aspects are really non-intuitive. Also the launcher is really barebones (thankfully a new one coming). The tutorial is also quite lackluster, so there's no other way: To learn tricks and all the power the interface has you have to dedicate some time to watch tutorials and whatnot. Thankfully there's plenty of good ones so no excuses there.
Bugs exist, as well as some balance issues and whatnot. But it's a game in alpha so they are quite ok. And I know nowadays it's a bit old to put a half-arsed game out there and call it alpha as an excuse to have produced a crap game. But this is not the case with these guys: They're hard at work, and updates and content are being churned out quickly. All that with lots of transparency and community input. Just a couple of days ago I was in a Q&A session with them (and I'm a nobody!) that lasted some 3 hours, in which the replied to a ton of questions and played/had fun with the community. Thumbs up!
Pros:
Cons (bit hard to think of that many but I'll try so don't blame me for being a bit unfair):
It's hard to give a note. On the one hand if you're expecting a somewhat "polished", "arrive-and-play" type of experience, you'll be greatly disappointed. On the other hand, if you're into being creative and being responsive for the creation of your own experience, then this can easily be an 8/10 -- with the potential to go at least up to a 9 once a few things like the sounds are sorted.
I highly recommend it, if it's the kind of experience you're looking for and you are prepared to what's involved in grabbing it yourself.
ps: And as time passes the game only gets better with frequent updates. The ideas the devs still have "in the oven" make me very excited for the future of this title.

1. It's completely free, not even an in game option to buy anything with real currency.
2. The controls are simple.
3. Graphics are clean and cute.
4. Low Requirements.
5. Combat is fair, nothing too ridiculously unfair/annoying.
Cons:
1. Buggy/Glitchy; you can roll through/out of walls and sometimes shots go through an enemy, like the exploding enemies and scarabs.
2. Upgrade system/Glyph system while nice, are very limited and few options.
3. Soul collection radius is low, even with the glyph that increases radius. (You basically have to walk over each tiny soul)
4. There's no saved progression... (Main reason I'm giving a negative review)
5. Gets repetitive as there's only one map you're ever on.
End Note:
I'm not sure why people complain so much about the controls... I got to wave 28 in about an hour and a half using keyboard/mouse. While it would be easier to aim with a joystick - strafe has a "lock on target" type of effect which means you don't really have to aim yourself. After I reached wave 28 I exited to try and re-open with a lower resolution, because there were a lot of monsters in the wave and I wanted to make sure it was as smooth as possible... when I got back on I was level 1 again. Maybe you're into restarting/starting over, however I enjoy progression and with 0 save option it really left a poor taste in my mouth. If you're looking to kill time once or twice this would be the game for you.
10/10 would be a terrible driver again.

Short review:
Base building game focused on space (fitting necessary buildings into limited space) and resource (how do i make enough food while still growing my town) management, with some minor combat. You beat one map and go to a new one without any particular story, and you have to start your town from scratch each time. Gets quite repetitive after you've unlocked all the buildings and figured out an optimal build pattern. Some minor AI issues are quite annoying. Recommended for fans of the genre who don't mind simpler game mechanics.
Long review:
The main challenges of gameplay:
1 - build up your town while maintaining food supply. You'll learn pretty fast what build pattern works best for food, and how to place your food buildings so that your town is well covered.
2 - deal with threats. You'll need an early military to wipe out fixed threats like wolves and bears so your town can expand. Mid game military is dedicated to wiping out dwarf colonies so they stop harassing your town. Usually that's enough for the end game - killing the portal guardians.
3 - fitting everything in. Wheat farms are super important and they need empty fertile space around them, I generally had to plan my entire town on how to fit them in.
The major negatives of the game:
- Every map you start from scratch. It's fun at first but by my 15th map or so I was pretty sick of building the same exact buildings in the same exact order. Starts to feel real grindy and repetitive.
- You can't micromanage anything. You build a woodcutter, and it would be nice if he cleared the trees from your town, but he just chooses at random from stuff in range. This renders storage buildings completely useless because you can't tell them what NOT to store - specifically food, because you need food locations spread out to cover all your other work buildings.
- Bad AI problems. You have a nicely stocked bakery or fishery but your worker will walk right past it to trek way out into the wilderness to some berry bush... right next to the wolves' den. Blergh. Or your hunter will get stuck in a loop "looking for a better weapon" when there's plenty of low-tier enemies to hunt. You don't need a bone spear go kill some rabbits and get me some meat and leather!
- Managing military is a pain. Military units suck down resources so you have to assemble an army and then disband it every time you're done dealing with a threat. You can't tell military where to go, you can only move the military camp building around the map, and your units will fight things nearby. You learn to be careful with that placement as well because the units will fight willy nilly and your healers won't focus the lowest guy, so you need to compensate with careful building placement.
- randomized maps are sometimes crap. I had one map where the exit portal was completely 100% unreachable. Or start areas will have no trees realistically in reach with enemies in the nearby woods, making fighting them off nigh impossible. Or the entire map will be peppered with mini-fjords, leaving no real open space to build an actual town. By the time I was done playing I was just resetting the map to get a decent start layout.
- the big hyped "get your units to valhalla" theme doesn't seem to actually do anything. They get a gold star or whatever but they weren't noticeably amazing. Kind of a letdown really.
All that being said, I played the game a ton, and I greatly enjoyed it up til the point where it started felling repetitive - which was about 30 hours. Not bad at all! Still it's not something I can unreservedly recommend to everyone. You have to be a fan of the base building genre (see: gnomoria, rimworld, planetbase, dwarf fortress), you have to be interested in the space and resource management elements, and you have to be cool with the game being pretty shallow mechanically. If all that sounds good to you, I say give the game a try.

You know, people always make out the Vikings and Norse mythology in general to be a complex web of intricately-woven tales of honor, bravery, and combat. I mean, with some badasses like Odin, Thor, and Loki included in the mythology, it's pretty difficult to
be interested in their crazy tales. But.....what about the mythological figures no one talks about? Like Leko, the supposed son of Odin and the god of building? Does that not ring a bell? Well, I don't blame you, I'm pretty sure he's fictional, and he's coincidentally also the protagonist of this game.
Valhalla Hills begins with a brief cutscene describing the story of the game. Leko, that guy I mentioned earlier, has been banished from Valhalla by his own father, Odin, because he wasn't into fighting people or something. Poor bloke! Anyway, he now sets off to regain his father's favor by being honorable through whatever means possible. And by that, I mean building stuff and fighting stuff using his little Viking
people.
See, Valhalla Hills is a randomly-generated strategy game primarily focused on building with a side emphasis on combat. It's up to you, Leko, to open and enter the portal on each map through whatever means you choose. This may mean fighting the portal guardians using your Vikings or offering them various resources. Personally, I primarily like to offer resources because fighting can be pretty challenging. Regardless, just managing a town itself can be quite the struggle. You start with only a few Vikings, but by building a complex web of inter-connected buildings the process of maintaining a bunch of happy and healthy Vikings can be quite the struggle.
This is mainly because of the nature of the game. Valhalla Hills is not a story-based or progression-based RTS like what  you may be used to. Instead, the only story is given in one short cutscene, and the rest of the game plays out in randomly-generated maps with an arcade sort of feel to them. Each map could take anywhere from 10 minutes to an hour to complete, as it just depends on if you want to rush to enter the portal or not. However, depending on how you complete this task can alter how you play. If you want to fight your way to the portal, that can prove to be quite the ordeal because you would need to first build tools, harvest resources, make homes, make even more buildings, find a way to feed all of your Vikings, and finally make some soldiers to fight the portal guardians.
However, this is one area where I feel like the game is a little weak. It can be very,
difficult to properly balance soldiers with food production. See, soldiers eat a bunch of food even while just sitting around, which is frustrating because it requires a constant and large supply of food to them. Yet, they can't leave their military camp for some reason, so they need to have food near them. Yet, since you can't order Vikings around or move the soldiers' camp, you need to either only use them defensively or build your town far out near the portal. I know this sounds odd, and to me it really is. It basically makes the option of fighting the portal guardians basically implausible because it'd take ages to be able to build a town large enough to both place soldiers in a path all the way to the portal (which is typically far away from your starting area) and simultaneously feed them all. Sure, after a while you can unlock couriers to transport food near soldiers, but it's still a hassle, and it's frustrating trying to do a military-based run, which takes some of the fun out of that aspect of the game.
However, despite that, attempting peaceful runs is still quite fun. It's both challenging and enjoyable to try and balance the needs of non-military Vikings while keeping them busy. When you get a successful, bustling town running finally, it's a joy to just sit and watch all your Vikings go about their daily schedules. In that sense, the game can be really rewarding. Yet, there's even more rewards given to successful playstyles in the form of unlockables. And wow, this game has a ton! Only after a few hours of playing, I've unlocked a bunch of hats, buildings, environment types, and even new enemies. It definitely helps increase the replayability of the game, which is important for arcade-style games like this that caters to people who don't want to play for hours upon hours (though that is certainly an option). Though, if you do decide to keep at it and play for a while, eventually some of your Vikings will reach Valhalla itself. This is because every Viking gains honor as you play, and when they reach 100,000 they'll ascend to Valhalla. I don't think it does much, but it's still a nice addition.
And y'know, there's a lot of little intricate details that the game includes that are quite nice just to have. Each building explains what it does and there's a mini-tutorial given at the start for most of them. In addition to that, the depth of the seemingly simple economy is quite impressive. What seems like a simple progression of getting resources --> feeding vikings --> fighting stuff/collecting portal offerings is much more complicated than that. For example, if you only have 1 fisherman but have 50 Vikings, they'll eventually go hungry, causing them to work less and less until they stop working entirely, at which point you may become doomed to failure. Or, if you chop down too many trees but don't have someone who plants new ones, you'll struggle to get more wood which can collapse a large part of the town's economy. Likewise, if you hunt too many animals and don't have an animal breeder to balance the food supply, your townsfolk may starve eventually. Sure, these are all small details, but they add up to make a fun, challenging, and engaging experience.
The game may be a little complicated gameplay-wise, but it certainly isn't graphically. Everything has a simple, cartoony look to it that I think actually works quite well. The Vikings look cute (and you can give them hats!), the environments look simple but lovely, and the animations and lighting all flow in a nice, cohesive manner. In fact, I think that's the key to this game's graphical beauty: everything just flows nicely. Unreal Engine 4's lighting capabilities probably helps with that too. Yet, despite the game's aesthetic beauty, it still runs quite nicely, at least from my experience. My computer is a little old, but the game still ran very smoothly with no issues whatsoever. Sound-wise, it's what you might expect: some nice, pleasant tunes and standard sound effects for stuff like building placement. Nothing really stood out to me there.
Valhalla Hills can be a highly challenging experience, especially for those who are interested in focusing on combat. Yet, it's still certainly very satisfying to play, from witnessing the gradual progression of a tiny settlement to a bustling, sprawling city of Vikings. If you're interested in arcade-style RTS gameplay that's both fun and rewarding with beautiful graphics as well, this game is definitely worth checking out.

For the roughly $20 I spent on this, I'd say it was a terrific game. I'm not 100% sure I'd pay $40 for it, but it was still a lot of fun to play.
The game feels like a throwback in some respects, where it's just you against the world. But the production values are better than your average budget title. Some may recall that the original game had some rather...unsavory aspects in terms of Asian culture and stereotypes. You get some of that with this game, but it's oddly more...affectionate? I guess that's the word. It knows it's being goofy, but it can also be grounded in ways, too.
The action is terrific. The firearms are all fairly interesting, and aren't exactly your standard fare. Plus there's a nice upgrade system for weapons, skills, and powers. Those powers include things like being able to regenerate health, fire off a shockwave that knocks down enemies, and use special devastating katana attacks.
Which brings me to my favorite part of the game: slicin' stuff up with a katana. It's just FUN. And the enemies are quite susceptible to being sliced to bloody gibs.
Anyway, for a non-AAA title, I highly recommend it, especially if you're looking for a not-too-long FPS to screw around with.

Hollow Knight showed up on my Discover Queue and was love at first sight, A 2D metroidvania with awesome art, melancholy feel and beautiful music? I had to play it!
And I did, and the love turned into obsession. I couldn't let go of the controller, and it wasn't a ride on the park, no, it doesn't grab you by the hand, but that is one of the perks that makes it so special, so... classic.
From someone who grew playing Super Metroid, SotN and Demon's Crest; games I cherish and are part of my personal top 10 and most important, are the foundation of was to be considered the Metroidvania genre, Hollow Knight came like a storm to fulfill a void long due in the genre.
Yes, there are great Metroidvanias out there, principally from Indie Devs, but none has made so deep mark as Hollow Knight did, and here's why.

Hollow Knight looks simple, but as soon you start playing and exploring you realize how much effort and love was put into it. The areas are stunning, each one with their own feel and mood (Deepnest will make you squirm!)
The backgrounds are full of details as well the foreground, and it doesn't look like copy and paste, it feels seamless and alive.
The sprites are well done and have fluid movement, from the minor creatures to the bosses, all in place, there isn't a single thing that looks that it doesn't belong.

There is plenty of NPCs you encounter in the game, some more developed with their own personal quests and some less developed but with a piece of lore to add. And is easy to relate with some of them when you cross paths and start unveiling their reasons for being in Hallownest.
Their personalities are unique and add a lot of depth to the world.
I won't dive too much into the story to avoid spoilers, but know this, it feels more real than you imagine. It isn't your happy knight savior type of tale. It's bleak, melancholic and is easy to feel the burden as you progress. And while there are NPCs that help you out, you'll still feel the solitude following, almost claustrophobic, in a good immersive way.
The lore developed for this game is outstanding, the "bug society" feels functional and tangible and makes you want to know more about it.
Hollow Knight, as a faithful metroidvania, starts right. You don't have much, only a nail attack, short, slow, weak. You can't spam it, there's timing, and this is something I took some time to understand but when I did I realized how polished and fit to the game the mechanics are.
There are upgrades; life, spells, nail upgrades and the charm system, which allow you to combine charms to fit your playstyle. But none of these are OP endgame, you still can't spam the nail or tank/slash everything you see in front of you. There's tactics, pattern recognition, trial and error, a lot of trial and error!
The most important point in HK regarding fights is the healing, there isn't something as potion, you fill your "tank' with souls by hitting enemies and uses the soul to recharge your life, but you can't just hit heal and keep pushing, you have to stop and focus in order to heal, and this plays a huge part in the strategy part of the game as you need to find the right opening on the enemies patterns to be able to heal safely.
As a metroidvania, HK has upgrades which allow you to visit some previous unreachable parts, there is a lot of backtracking and exploration involved, but what makes HK stand out is the possibility of progressing to said areas early in the game with a bit of skill.
I won't get deep into it, but I'll give a hint.
The boss fights are a treat for sore eyes, isn't difficult to see people getting frustrated on the forums over the second boss encounter, and not without reason, it will get you off guard. but it will get you prepared for what will come.
As stated, you can't go tanking, there are patterns and tactics and it fits perfectly with the game mechanics, you have to time your attacks and find the openings, and while this sounds like a slow burn, the fights are actually really fast paced and full of enjoyable tension.

There's something very important in the 3 games I listed before, and is the music, all of them had iconic music, the type that you would listen out of the game, the kind that give you the chills, and with HK isn't different, the soundtrack is a piece of art and it blends masterfully with the game.
False Knight is probably my favorite track, but all of them is rightfully good, from Hornet's fast paced theme to the Demon's Crest feel of Soul Sanctum and the tension of Mantis Lords, the music plays a huge deal on the whole package.
I could go on and talk about the amazing sound fx, the character designs, the map extension, secrets and all, but there's something quite important for this game, and it's the feel of discovery.
This game is a piece of art, and while I'm sad I haven't got notice of it sooner, I'm really happy it came to fruition and turned out to be, for me, game of the year.
Thank you Team Cherry!

Hollow Knight is a fantastic game, as it features superbly charming visuals, deeply alluring music/sound effects, and an extremely fluid and tight control scheme, from the combat, to the platforming, and everything in between.
As one could see from my playtime, I did not rush myself through this game. I took my time and enjoyed marveling at all of the finely crafted regions and art spread throughout the game's world. After a fair number of hours playing through Hollow Knight, I feel that it is a strong contender to compete against other critically acclaimed platformers such as Metroid and Ori and the Blind Forest.
The hand-drawn art that comprises all of the visuals in this game are beautiful, and the animation for the game is executed very well. Hollow Knight's soundtrack is phenomenal in every sense of the word. Every single area in the game features music that suits it exquisitely. The main town of the game, the spooky areas that are dark and ominous, the boss fights, and areas that consist of a calmer tone, all have music that complements the art, progression, movement, and even combat of the game. Additionally, the game's soundtrack amplifies and deeply immerses and engrosses the player into Hollow Knight's atmosphere. Personally, my favorite piece of the soundtrack is the song that plays while in the City of Tears.
Controlling the protagonist in this game is very fluid and satisfying, and I do not believe it could have been done any better. Jumping and dashing from platforms to walls etc., feels very natural, and there was not a single moment in the game in which I felt as if I did not have full control of every action performed.
The game's combat features a fairly simplistic but graceful design, as a single button is dedicated to the vast majority of the offensive actions possible in the game. One's finesse and skill can be utilized to expertly fight the enemies in this game; your success in Hollow Knight's combat and platforming is entirely dependent on your own abilities, which is how it should be, being that this is a skill-based game. One particular aspect that stands out to me is the aerial combat. I have never before played a game in which mid-air combat felt so controllable, adaptable, flexible, and satisfying; it is an incredibly wonderful feeling, and it must be experienced first-hand in order to truly appreciate it. Dare I say it, I believe this game dethrones Ori and the Blind Forest from being my favorite Metroidvania platformer.
Hollow Knight is nothing short of a masterpiece, not only in terms of a great video game, but also a visual as well as audible treasure to behold. This game is truly a testament to what video games should be like today, as it clearly demonstrates that the developers genuinely care about their game. For that reason, I thoroughly commend and applaud Team Cherry for delivering such an amazing experience.
TL;DR
- A phenomenal platforming game
- Gorgeous art and animations (They are hand-drawn!)
- A magnificently crafted soundtrack by Christopher Larkin, featuring lovely vocals from Amelia Jones
- I have never experienced tighter, more fluid, and satisfying controls in a platforming game (Even from Nintendo)
- This game is a steal at 15 USD
- I regret not buying this on day one of its release
- Very well done, Team Cherry

As someone who rather likes puzzles, I was surprised to find myself utterly bored by this game.  The mechanics revolve around rotating the world and manipulating gravity, and while you might think that would make for some interesting logic puzzles, it just ends up being incredibly sluggish and grey.  You play through four chapters of decent but unremarkable puzzles, then you go into a mirrored world of pretty much the same four chapters but with additional complications.  I stopped playing soon after getting into the mirrored world because the game just felt more like homework than entertainment.
If you're looking for a good puzzle game, this isn't it.  Try Portal, Limbo, Braid, Antichamber, or The Talos Principle.
Edit:
Alright, I went back and finished the game.  The puzzles get more interesting towards the end, but also more finicky.  Some require  you being very patient and precise as you carefully slide things around.  Some require you to lodge yourself against the edge of a button so you can slide other things around.  Some require you to to swing balls back and forth to try to get enough momentum.  Basically, you feel like you're fighting against the game mechanics instead of using them.  The experience is just not joyful the way better puzzle games are.

This game deserves a lot of praise. Not only are the individual elements excellent on their own(art, sound, stage design), but they mesh together seamlessly to create a memorable experience. It truly stands out in the sea of indie metriodvania games.
It takes a slower, more methodical approach to the genre, allowing you to soak in its dark and whimsical atmosphere while emphaszing clever exploration and gameplay over big hp or damage numbers. The stage design is just phenomenal and I'm constantly astounded at how well thought-out everything is. The variety of enemies is huge( over 100!!!) and there're numerous strange and wonderful NPCS who would either aid or hinder you on your quest. Customization wise, there are 'charms', the game's equivalent of accessories, which you can mix and match to suit your playstyle. Be it a formidable mage, an able explorer, quick swashbuckler, there's something in it for everyone.
I hate bugs. I hate getting lost. And I'm not particularly fond of platforming. Hollow Knight has all of that. And I like Hollow Knight.

Story/Premise.
You are Leko, son of Odin. You have been cast out of Valhalla because, unlike the other Vikings, you prefer building to pillaging. In order to make your way back to Valhalla, you need to regain your honour by leading a ragtag group of exiled heroes through a series of maps and portals until you've amassed enough honour to ascend to Valhalla.
The introductory cutscene is the only actual bit of story you'll get. From then on, you clear map after map in order to earn honour.
.Game play.
-Main Menu-
In the main menu, you can view your individual Viking's progress towards returning to Valhalla. Once they've earned enough honour and ascended, they can be called back down with increased combat prowess.
You can also start a new map, continue your game, and change the options (graphics, sound, the standard stuff). Additionally, you can view your progress towards unlocks here, which are presented in the form of in-game "achievements"--some of which are also Steam achievements.
Let's jump in with a new map.
-Resource management-
Welcome to the hills, God of Building! Here in this verdant collection of islands, you'll be building a settlement and fighting off enemies and wildlife. Your Viking brethren will literally fall from the sky and, once they've landed, they'll gather around your starting crystal and wait for you to build.
When you build wood cutters and quarries next to wood and rocks respectively, Vikings are automatically assigned to the task of harvesting. These materials are used to build other buildings.
Food is the most important of your resources to manage, however, because, without it, your Vikings won't work. That means no building, no hunting, no fishing, and no harvesting. Everything screeches to a halt and your Vikings can die from hunger, which means you'll likely have to restart the map. This can be done by simply clicking "restart" in the main menu.
At first, you'll rely on the berry bushes that grow in each level. They'll soon run out, however, so you'll need to assign hunters and fisherman. Those wild animals and fish can be exhausted as well, so don't rely on them too much! Build farms and bakers so that your Vikings can have a viable food source.
The other materials can be refined in order to build more complex structures. These can also be used to create tools, which make more complicated tasks such as farming and bread baking, possible.
Vikings can also be considered a resource. You can request Vikings by building homes for them, which increases the max amount you can have at once. Take care because there's a max number of Vikings you can request, shown in the top, left corner of the U.I. If you send a bunch of them to their deaths in battle and have hit your cap for requests, you won't have enough Warriors to clear the map unless you shut down production buildings and stretch your workforce thin.
-City building-
As you progress, you unlock more options for sustainability in the hills. You begin with the ability to hunt and fish, which can exhaust its supply and run out. Once you've stripped an area of You quickly unlock more reliable options like baking and farming, which are self-sustaining. These, however, require refined materials. You also unlock things like foresters, which can replace the trees your wood cutter cuts down.
It's important to plan where you're putting your buildings. The terrain, which is sometimes more uneven than others, will hinder your placement: when you go to place a building, you're presented with three colours: green, yellow, and orange. These affect the building cost.
*Green-- the regular cost to build.
*Yellow--slightly increased cost in order to build an additional platform to compensate for the terrain.
*Orange--Greatly increased cost in order to build an additional platform to compensate for the terrain.
In true city builder style, you have no control over your Viking brethren. You can suggest tasks by placing buildings, but it's up to their discretion--and range--as to whether or not they'll hop to work. Once placed, a building has an effective range, which can be increased by linking them with paths. If your buildings are not in range of each other--say, your mill, tool maker, and wheat farm in range with your bakery--then they won't function.
-Battle-
Warrior units differ from your regular Vikings. They can take a beating and they also won't lift a figure to build or harvest. They'll still take up your food, though, so it's a good idea to limit your number of warriors until you're ready to go on the offensive. They are key to clearing the map. After you complete a random task--i.e, build a certain building or collect x amount of resources--you're allowed to open the Portal and face the enemies that await you. You have to defeat these Portal Guardians in order to use the Portal and go to the next map.
Battle consists of watching your Viking Warriors clash with various enemies--from wolves to otherworldly spirits. You don't play any part in it, but you can cheer them on as both parties take turns whacking each other.
After you've defeated the Portal Guardians, you'll be rewarded with a mass of honour and transported to the victory screen. In the post-battle victory screen, you'll see all of the nifty things you've unlocked by completing various objectives such as clearing various size maps or killing a certain number of enemies. Unlocks include more buildings, which offer more survival and combat options, map types, and terrains. You can also see your progress towards other unlocks by clicking an arrow to the next screen.
.Soundtrack.
The music is soaring and peaceful--a lot of wind instruments. It's the same throughout your building and warrior-rallying, changing only to reflect when your followers get into fights.
*I found the fight music to be a little grating, especially when it shifted frequently between the two tracks every few seconds because my warriors tended to wander about and stumble into combat on larger maps.
.Graphics/ Art Style.
Valhalla Hills is lovely. Your Vikings are stubby, cartoonish little men and women babble gibberish. The landscape--whether bright green and rife with life or crystalline white and flush with snow--is vibrant. Snow falls, the wind blows through the trees, and the waves lick at the shore to create an immersive atmosphere.
.Longevity/Difficulty.
You can clear maps in a few minutes or in over an hour depending on size. You can easily rush the objective or just sit around and develop a lovely little settlement--it's up to you. No two maps are the same so there's plenty of replayability if you just want to do a quick run or if you want to go on an honour collecting spree. Some maps are a juggling act. You'll need to prioritize getting  steady source of food, but you'll also need to manage building resources so that you don't run out and get stuck without the ability to build anything.
There are two modes, Classic and Open Game. Classic scales in difficulty as you unlock achievements and ease your way in. Open Game allows you to dive right in with everything unlocked from the get-go and is significantly more difficult.
.Bottom Line.
Valhalla Hills is both fun and engaging. You can play for a few minutes, or for a few hours and no two maps are the same so you'll spend your time figuring out how best to position your buildings. With two game modes and a variety of map sizes, you'll surely get your money's worth of game time. For fans of the city-building and strategy/RTS genres, Valhalla Hills is a definite yes.

Get it if you get it at a ridiculous discount, you're willing to forgive a game anything as long as it's wh40k or if you really don't have anything or anyone else to play with than a simple AI. (if the latter, there's better games for that out there)

There are many block building games and clones, and from the screenshots and videos of Starmade you may feel that this is just another one. I caution you to not fall into this line of thinking and give Starmade a chance. As of this writing, the game is completely free to play and downloadable from the developers website during it's alpha period.
Is it Minecraft in space? No. It's a starship game with a block building motif.
Like many people cutting their teeth with block building games, I felt restricted. Even with mods and redstone advancement I felt my creations were static and dead. I felt any attempts to construct creations of grandeur were less not a matter of creativity but more overcoming the limitations that the game enforced. Resource management and collection was more of a hinderance than anything, and I spent more time micromanaging furnaces than playing the actual game.
With Starmade I felt free to explore and expand in any way I chose. Even in survival mode the pursuit of expansion seemed more rewarding and the progression of my ships was smooth. The game developers provided basic tools (admittedly with a bit of a learning curve) throughout to make sure that you are able to build and play the game fast. You spend less time flying around collecting materials as asteroids with resources are plentiful and respawn throughout the galaxies. Automation, factories, logic, and filtering sort your materials the way YOU choose. Building tools that mirror and place blocks in bulk, with in-game guides make it fast and easy to lay down your ship designs. Blueprints and shipyards make saving your designs and testing out new things a breeze.
Any aspect of the game of interest to you? Focus on it! You can go as big or small as you want. Build planet-sized mining rigs, or quick-rapid fire fighter craft... or make small stealth ships to just explore the universe. Best of all, the developers and community are in constant communications... sharing ideas and opinions, fixing bugs and adding enhancements to the game constantly. The list of upcoming features is fantastic and after watching it's development for years I have yet to see them cancel or reject a truly anticipated feature.
Starmade is one of the few games that I allowed myself to fall into because I felt there were no limits.
I played for three years, primarily before it was Greenlit. Starmade was the one game I could always come home to. It became my favorite game to play anytime I had free moment. Sadly, I am writing this review now only as I am parting ways with it.
Space, by it very nature, is empty. When you are lacking content you have to make your own fun, and it's hard playing multi-player games alone. It is true there are quite a few Starmade servers with players on 24/7, but the current state of the game does not encourage teaming up with those who may be untrustworthy. Factions are available though somewhat limited at the time of this writing, and there are no 'personal' access blocks. That being said, I can't get a single one of my gamer friends interested in playing Starmade.
I am not a game developer and will not attempt to act as if I know the solution, but when I demo Starmade to my friends from the ground up all they see is the void of space and not much else. In most survival games the start is a mad rush to get yourself equipped and protected as soon as possible. Your first dirt hut is an amazing achievement. In Starmade, you may as well never even leave the starting shop if you so choose. There is no call to action, no shove out the door, no impending doom, nothing making a new user wish to 'do' anything.
I believe in Schine (the developers of Starmade).  I have no doubt that with their efforts and the support of the existing fan base they will absolutely polish and shine Starmade into a diamond. I just don't know how long that it will take. With that in mind, it's time for me to dock my ship for now, shut down the reactors, mothball the factories, and close up shop.
Edit: Note - As of Jan 16th, 0.19549 personal blocks have been added. I will update my review further when I come back to the game.

I came into Type-0 HD very sceptical. It's not often you see a game make a platform jump as huge as from PSP to firstly current generation consoles and then PC. Reviews of the PS4 and XBO versions were mostly positive, but with some reservations about the control system and the level of motion blur - both things which had been addressed by the time the PC version came to release.
For what is essentially a lightly updated PSP game, Type-0 has moments where it looks just as good as, say, a modern indie game. The character models of Class Zero have recieved the most attention during the update, having been completely remade, and they really do look just as good as any of the character models from any other recent Final Fantasy games, such as the XIII series. Everyone else, and everything else for that matter, has recieved nothing more than light texture updates, and as such can look incredibly dated or out of place when next to one of the newer models.
The storytelling in this game could have been much better. The story itself is fine, suitably convoluted in keeping with the rest of the Fabula Nova Crystallis, however it feels as though 90% of it arrives in the last chapter of the game (of which there are 8). I think this could have been spread out a bit better, which would have made the middle chapters a bit more engaging.
Tetusya Nomura has done, as usual, a fantastic job with the design in Type-0. Each member of Class Zero is identifiably unique despite sharing the same basic uniform, and each has a different set of weapons ranging from anything from a flute or deck of cards (how you hurt people with these, I dont know) to a scythe. The world is dark and gritty, which perfectly matches the more serious nature of this game compared to others in the Final Fantasy series. To clarify that, Type-0 is the first Final Fantasy to feature gruesome, bloody deaths. It's just a shame the English voiceovers aren't as good as the visual design. They are terrible, probably among the worst I've heard. It's too bad, because the English dub is really the only major complaint I have with this game.
When it comes to the control system, everything is fine. It's not great, just... fine. The camera can go a bit crazy sometimes during combat due to the lock-on system, but other than that, the improvements implimented on the PC version have mostly resolved any issues brought up previously. One comment I would make about combat is that it could do with a better way of switching between targeted enemies, the current system just feels like pot luck. Considering the action-oriented combat system, the game dosn't suffer badly at all from being locked at 30FPS, despite what some vocal members of the community will say. This framerate lock is inherent of the game engine, so unfortunately a workaround for higher framerates is unlikely, if not impossible.
The music in Type-0 is one of it's best features. It has a great orchestral main theme which can get stuck in your head for hours, and most town/battle/dungeon pieces are similarly catchy and enjoyable. There were only one or two occaisions where I thought the music got a little bit dull and lifeless, where it could have been improved.
Overall, I would recommend Type-0 to any fan of the Final Fantasy series, as long as they are well aware before diving in that this is a PSP remake and should set their expectations as such. With that in mind, I'm sure they'll be as impressed as I have been and will agree that Square Enix have done an incredible job in branching a game in the Final Fantasy series in a different, and intriguing direction.

Let me start this off by saying I'm a huge fan of Final Fantasy games both old and new, and am always excited by where they take the series. That said, this game preserves a few of the worst aspects of the series and doesn't quite make up for it enough with what it tries to do.
First, it's very obvious that this was a PSP game. Low-resolution textures, stilted cutscenes where characters just stand and talk at each other, and a camera that swings wildly for no reason at all while locked onto enemies make the game a lot harder to digest than one might expect from a different, bigger-budget title. Some games find ways to shine through these issues, but unfortunately Type-0 is not one of them.
Managing fourteen different party members is tiresome, and most of them don't recieve any character development besides a one-dimensional attribute. While the ability to navigate towns and the overworld as any character is a welcome touch, the symptom of this is your character doesn't have any meaningful interactions with the world, and often interacting with other characters shows you a scene that your character isnt even in. If you are the type of person that likes to understand ambient dialogue, you're out of luck. The english dub is atrocious, clearly made by paying the lowest-budget actors possible to simply read their lines off of a page. They also like to pause in their sentences where the subtitles stop on the screen, even if it makes no sense in the sentence. I'm guessing this is a symptom of some sort of PSP audio buffering where they had to divide up the audio files, but I've never noticed it in other heavily voice-acted PSP games so maybe I'm just giving them too much credit.
The story isnt necessarily bad, the world is an interesting take on the Nova Crystalis universe, and the opening cutscene is incredible. However, after the game's opening, the story is mostly told through stilted dialogue sequences and war documentary-style voiceovers, with very little in the way of actual character or action. The soundtrack is forgettable and plays softly in the background of these sequences, never shaping the emotion of the scenes.
The gameplay loop seems fun at first glance, but quickly becomes tiresome. The actual draw of the game, the missions, happen somewhat rarely, and much of the sidequests consist of wandering the empty overworld hunting for specific random battles. To make matters worse, you can only hold one sidequest at a time, though quests to deliver monster drops thankfully let you farm those drops while completing other missions. Still, this system often results in you wasting time trekking all the way back to turn in quest just so you can accept another quest that you could have completed at the same time. There's no excuse for this system, especially since the game is further slowed down by random battles on the overworld rather than a more modern approach such as overworld monsters.
The one thing this game does absolutely right is its combat. The breaksight/killsight system, essentially giving you "moments of opportunity" before or after enemy attacks to do massive damage, interrupt, and/or kill them, makes combat feel exciting and not the "mash the attack button" that other action rpgs such as Crisis Core devolve into. Each of the fourteen characters has different combos and feels unique to play, requiring different timing to hit killsights and letting you navigate the battlefield uniquely. Unfortunately, even the combat is marred somewhat by the camera not behaving well while locked onto enemies in close quarters, and since there's no manual aim, ranged characters will have difficulty hitting certain moving targets since the lock-on doesn't lead them properly. Still, even with these issues, I'm confident in saying that combat is a blast, and plenty challenging.
All in all, I can't find myself able to recommend this game, except perhaps to a small audience that's looking for fun action-rpg combat and doesn't mind a lot of grinding and lackluster characters. To the rest of us, we can hold out hope for some of Square's newer games in the future.

Probably one of my best game purchases ever. I played it for several hundred hours before finally buying it, and still play it at least 10 hours a week, usually in one session.
The best thing I can say for the game is that I keep forgetting it's early access. It's an amazing game already, and so much is coming still. I think it will eventually fill the promises it made, as well as all the failed ones that most, if not all, space sci-fi games made.
Pros:
-Ships are super-fun to design and build, and ship building is quite in-depth.
-Multiplayer is unbelievably smooth, even with hundreds of ships, small or large, all fighting. That said, your client might need the settings turned down if the ships are big enough. Some people (myself inluded) build ships larger than planets.
-The universe feels alive. They've redone the map, and it is glorious. We have blackholes (wormholes) now too, and a wide variaty of stations, planets and astroids now.
-Despite the above, it manages to highlight how big and empty space really is, which is something i enjoy.
-Docking is quite impressive and flexible, allowing for really cool effects to ships (Such as moving parts).
-
-Beautiful Graphics (if you like cube games)
-So many awesome features, Im not going to even attempt to list them
-Excelent Configurability
-Good Community
-Good mod support (never tested this, but I've heard no complaints about it)
-Procedurally generated, and absolutly HUGE.
-Probably forgot lots
-Most importantly: The game is always improving, very quickly too. The devs push large quantities of bugfixes and updates every 2 weeks. It's similer to Space Engineers in that respect. Does not feel like an alpha game, really.
Cons:
-They're missing the inverse-corner shape D: I should get around to suggesting this. But I'm too busy playing the game.
-AI still needs work, though it's getting better
-Factions need work as well, though that's coming in a future update
-Very large systems cause non-negligable client lag (negligable server lag though) (I mean multi-thousand block doors, etc)
-Very large ships cause some lag (500x300x300 m3 + on my craptop, but easily 10 - 1000+ times that for good laptops. Virtually unlimited for a solid desktop.)
-Alpha game. Lots of balance changes, content changes, etc.
-Tutorial needs a lot of work - it's outdated. Again. Mostly because of the update frequency.
Very addictive game, good if you like designing spaceships, or space combat. The game also fully supports mining, trading, etc, however, I stick to ship building, because that's my favorite part. This means I can't speak for those systems, but I've heard they're good.
If you want a good example of the game currently, get the demo - it's the full game, and it will be, until the game leaves Alpha. If you want a good idea of where the game is headed, and how it's changed/is changing, check the website, and look at the "news" tab.
For some of the best reviews about why I (and many others) like the game, read the funny reviews tab.
Edit: Forgot to mention the learning curve. I joined back when the tutorial, buggy as it was, was plenty. At the moment, however, the game has become so complicated that I'd recommend starting in MP and asking a player to teach you, or watching a youtube video.
