Once upon a time...no, wait, never mind.  I'm still bulding the U.S.S Defiant.
is a block-buildy game
The best way to explain it to people is, to start by imagining MineCraft.  Now, take your awesome castle, and put thrusters and guns on it.  That's StarMade...only, it's not
as engaging, even about seven months after my original review.
Some changes have happened, including a price hike to $14.99.  Thus, I'm taking the extra hours I've played in the intervening months into account, and doing a re-review.  Has it improved?  Well...you will see.
First, the visuals have improved greatly from my prior review, and the game overall looks pretty nice.  You can build some neat ships and stations.  The Pentas/Tetras/Corners allow for somewhat blocky re-builds of your favorite Sci-Fi ships, or your own custom creations.  Some recent texture updates from the developers have made good ships look even better!
Performance is also improved to the point where the game is at least playable on medium-grade machines.  This was a critical problem for me in my previous review, but the developers deserve credit for working to make the game behave more efficiently.  Good job there!
The UI has improved a lot in seven months too.  There are some issues with resizing individual windows, but the game is easily understandable via the UI, and gives you most of the tools you need to build ships, which is the game's primary mechanic.  The secondary mechanic, shooting stuff with your ship, is also well-accounted for, with shield, structural HP, and armor HP being presented well.  There are some placeholders about, as this game is still in development, but progress is being made.  I'm sure seven months in the future, the UI will be a lot better than it already is, and I look forward to that.
Before I get to anything heavy, I have to talk about the crafting system.  The crafting system is OK in a survival setting, and some much-needed tuning has happened...but ultimately, to make a decent ship, you need
of blocks, because in this game, bigger ship = better.  There's additional problems with that that we will get to, but the crafting system as it stands actually hampers the process of doing the main thing that you should be doing in a game about building starships:
To solve this, the crafting UI and system needs a pretty massive interface revamp, and some thought should be taken to all the 'wasted' blocks about, things like plantlife that could be leveraged to make more interesting builds.  It's as if the developers started off by copying MineCraft, then at some point decided, "oh yeah, the point of this game is to make ships!"
Next, there's a problem with how the shipbuilding mechanics in this game are balanced, specifically:
ship you make is a fighter.  You don't need crews to tend to large ships.  You just need your ship to be bigger than an enemy's, because a bigger ship fits more systems in it, and systems are what cause you to win fights, eat asteroids or planets, or whatever.  The recent Cargo system that was released yesterday will help prevent planet-eating miners from being quite as big of a problem as they were prior to this (good luck fitting a planet in your cargo holds), but those of you wondering whether or not to buy into this game should know that, especially in multiplayer, the shipbuilding mechanic is unfairly weighted towards building big ships; smaller ships are thus forced out of niches that are realistic, such as bombers/interceptors.
As big of problems as those points are, there was one critical problem in my prior review, that
This one, big, critical, overarching problem persists to this day, and it makes the entire game, all the well-crafted bits,
There are some feeble attempts to remedy this - specifically a "race gate" minigame setup was added to the game in a more recent release.
The reason I say, "there is nothing to do in StarMade", is tied more specifically to two things.
In Single-Player, there's really nothing to explore.  StarMade randomly generates universes, but other than finding slightly different ores on planets, you may as well not bother.  There are randomly generated space stations too, but do they reward anything?  Not really, unless you salvage the station.  In StarMade, you'll soon discover one thing: due to how the Crafting system works (above),
, or your lovingly-crafted spaceship will cease to be, and you will have to grind out a new ship.
In Multi-Player, it gets worse.  The Faction system in StarMade is...well, a faction system.  Ideally, players pool their resources to create fleets, stations, and stuff, thus providing a natural objective for PvP.  Sounds great, right?  Unfortunately, due to not designing the Faction system to account for humanity's darker impulses, the only way to secure anything you own, is to create a one-man faction, and set a planet or space station as the home base...rendering the systems inoperable by non-guildmembers, and storage secure.  In this way, your stuff is safe from griefing, and as far as I can tell, it's the way the game is designed to be played.  That's well and good...
.
The way I suggest for the developers to fix StarMade's pointlessness is two-fold.
First, there needs to be a meaningful progression that doesn't come out of your workbenches.  You should have to explore, and give exploration some meaning besides "where are the ores?"  If you want to create a civilian ship, ask yourself: why create a civilian ship?  Trade, mining, and ferrying come to mind.  Those are some great candidates for randomized quests that can be rewarded with blocks, money, or useful ship blueprints.  For that matter -
Existing ships can serve a great purpose - teaching new players the nuances of StarMade's shipbuilding mechanics.  In this way, players build better, interesting ships, which forges a stronger community and makes PvP more reasonable as an implicit objective.
Next,
.  Single-player factions destroy the fun of multiplayer in this game.  My suggestion is for players to have 'personal home' blocks that can be used to secure a personal space on a station or planet against anyone who's not them; all chests/cargo areas in that are similarly preserved.  Similarly, creating a faction should require a party of at least two people.  The home-base constraint can still apply, and should.   The game needs better in-faction control to help Factions defend against spies and ne'erdowells.

Ugh, where to start...
Graphics.  The graphics would be top notch, had this been a PS2 game.  The videos are the worst.  For something toting to be 'HD', they definitely missed their mark.
Acting.  I've never played a voiced FF game where the VAs sounded so...robotic.  There's no REAL emotion in them, they just sound like they're reading from a script in as minimalist a way as they can just to get it done.
Cutscenes/conversations.  One word: Clunky.  A lot of the conversations look like visual novels in a way...the people stand and/or move in certain positions/ways, and it continues to loop until you move onto the next part.  As well, Someone will be talking to one person, then the very next chat box pops up, and that person has been replaced with another person in the exact same spot.  In general, the movements of people within cutscenes and conversations is just as robotic, if not more, than the voice acting.
Combat.  The combat is clunky as hell.  There is absolutely no fluidity to how anything functions in combat.  As well, several times I found myself stuck in a case where an enemy would knock me down, and before I could get back up, they would knock me down again.  This would continue until either the unit models got far enough apart, or someone else interrupted it.  Most of the abilites get you stuck in animation so that you can't cancel it to dodge an incoming attack - once you start the attack, you're basically screwed until the attack is finished.
The characters.  Good lord.  There are, what, 14 playable characters in this game?  WTF?  This isn't a Suikoden game.  They're all thrown at you right from the start.  It's not like a typical game where you are introduced to them one or two at a time until you have the full crew.  You just suddenly get 14 characters all at once to pick and choose between.
Immersion.  Now, I'm not usually one to complain about immersion breaking in a game, but this game is very visceral, very emotional, and while I definitely love that part of it...suddenly moogles.  Like, what the hell.  It'd be like putting Moogles in Mad Max.  It's extremely jarring.  Even the Chocobos have been worked in a way to really fit into the visceral feel of the game.  But not the moogles.
Overall, I just really feel like this was done by some basement-dwelling division of Squenix.  It has absolutely none of the polish and luster that usually comes with a Final Fantasy title.  The voice acting is thrid rate, camera angles are terrible, controls are clunky, graphics are bad.  I just really can't find anything good to say about this game.

The game starts with a wonderful little story about how Leko ends up banished from Valhalla as he displays signs of creativity and enjoys building and doesn't seem to care for the traditional fighting ways of the Vikings. Odin tells him to go to Earth and become the God of the Builders and not to return. Leko, however, decides he can win a place in Valhalla with his father if he can just regain enough honor.
Valhalla Hills is reminiscent of some of the old great city builder strategy games but with it's own nice little spin. Rather than having every building unlocked for you from the start, you have to unlock them over time by regaining honor which you do by completing missions or various objectives. You do have the option to play in 'Open Mode' which allows everything to be unlocked from the start but this is significantly harder and I would not recommend this for people just starting out. The classic mode has a nice difficulty curve and teaches you what you need to know as it goes on, explaining each building or new feature to you as you unlock it preventing you from missing out on what vital buildings do.
The gameplay is pretty easy to learn if you are familiar with these types of games. You are guided through the basics like how to build, building speed, managing resources and such and each time you unlock something new, build a building for the first time or there is a new event it is explained. There is also a nice colour grid to help with placement which speeds things up a lot. Despite saying this, if you are new to this genre you might struggle. Though there is a lot that is explained to you there is also a lot that is missed out. I've played this genre for a many years but ended up making two crucial errors early on which messed up two entire missions because something very simple wasn't explained. This can become a huge problem which I'll explain further in the cons.
Each mission starts you with a few Vikings, some resources to get you started and an end portal on your map and your goal is to reach and open the end portal either killing or appeasing the guardians on the way. Your Vikings can be assigned various roles but from there onwards they will handle their duties themselves with no extra input from you (most of the time). They have basic needs as well and will require things like food and sleep with some extra needs/perks like some booze for the soldiers to keep them happy and strong. Its your job to build these things to fulfil the needs of your mortals so you can conquer each map and bring yourself closer to going home.
There is a nice selection of buildings from what I've seen so far but I feel the shape and design of the map can limit how you place them. The maps start of fairly small meaning your first few 'villages' will look fairly similar because certain buildings have to be placed near others for them to work successfully.
Despite me enjoying myself a lot so far there are some cons I would like to mention because they are noticeable. The first is that the story starts very, very strong and I was excited to play through and see more about Leko's struggles but from what I've seen there is no more to the story. The missions themselves start with no further addition to the storyline and it seems that the opening cutscene is all there is to it. This is very disappointing because the start itself was very engaging. My second issue is the fact that if you build wrong, even one building, chances are it'll mess up your entire mission. Resources are very scarce and once you have used one up you are screwed. For example, the woodcutter has a certain range where he can fell trees and there are only a certain amount of trees dotted around the map, once he destroys those trees that building is useless and I'll have to build another using logs (which can only be made in a woodcutter). If I have no logs, like I did then I'll have to demolish a building to get some as it's the only way I found to get more. Except, I had other buildings I had placed to be built and you cannot control the build priority at all so they started building those using up all my logs again. In the end I had to restart because they had all started to starve because they couldn't build the bakery. This needs to be fixed.
This forces you to build some things in a very specific order. My last gripe I think is directly related to my previous one. You have to create each tool you need yourself rather than it being automatically created if you have the resources. This becomes a very boring thing to do over and over again but I do believe this is in place because of how limited your resources are and to stop you using up everything making tools when you need buildings first.

Valhalla Hills is a real time town management game in which you play as Leko, son of Odin, who instead of being a distinguished and devoted warrior as his ancestors, prefers to spend his time building houses. Because of this Odin banishes you to live among the mortals on Earth until you regain your honour.
The game offers you two different modes to play, Classic and Open. Open mode offers a more challenging experience in which you have every building unlocked. On the other hand, Classic mode gradually increases in difficulty and unlocks more things as you play, and it is thus recommended to new players.
On Classic mode, the story starts nice and interesting but it quickly falls short and lacks any depth by only having a nicely put introductory cutscene. I still haven’t beaten the game but, from what I’ve played, there is no connection between each mission in terms of story, which I find to be rather disapointing.
The game plays very simple, different colors when placing buildings, and other elements of the UI make the game somewhat intuitive and easy to understand how everything works out. Still, it has been a while since I’ve played one of these management games, and so, I must say that the tutorial and instructions that this game gives you do not really teach you some essential things, other than what some buildings do, and because of that it took me a while to learn how resource and tool distributing systems worked out.
At its core, it plays like most town management games out there, especially ones like the Settlers series. You start with a small number of vikings, which you have no direct control of,  and a handfull of resources and from there you need to figure out the best way to prosper and expand your little settlement. Usually this means building basic resources buildings such as woodcutters, toolmakers and hunters or fishermen right off the bat and, afterwards, making sure you have a steady supply of resources coming from these places in order to feed the needs of your settlers.
On each mission the objective is always the same, you have to open a portal to Valhalla. First, you need to get a unit close to the portal in order to activate it and, after that, you need to deal with the guardians that come out of these portals. This can be done in two ways, by simply killing them with your soldiers or by performing sacrifices.
Valhalla Hills is overall a very good and pleasing title, it looks, sounds and plays great but sometimes I just wish it had something more going for it. Some of its mechanics are not well explained on the tutorial sections but after thinking for a little bit, you should start to realize how certain systems work. Eventually, you might also come across certain situations in which your vikings are wandering randomly with no idea what to do or take some time to perform a certain task, this can get somewhat infuriating but the fact that you can speed up time helps a lot. And last but by no means least, I really wish each mission was more varied other than just a bigger island to fight for and expand through and that the story was told by little bits spread across each mission, or establishing a link between them.
If you’re a huge fan of the genre and you’re looking for another city management game with a wonderful and charming setting I’d say you check this one out. Despite its lack of story depth and somewhat repetitive levels, at its core Valhalla Hills stands strong on its own. Eitherways, I suggest waiting for a sale because I think that the current price is somewhat high for what it initially offers.

Great artstyle, sketchy puzzles.  I really dig the penciled, black and white art direction of The Bridge, but the puzzles will make you feel more frustrated than smart.  It takes some obvious cues from games like Braid and reminds me of Monument Valley, but the easy to understand, reasonable difficulty curve of those titles are lost on The Bridge.  You move your avatar around and tilt the game world left or right while collecting keys and avoiding falling off the map or getting hit by a death ball.  The simple concept should lend itself to clean, heady puzzles, but fails as much as it succeeds.  The line art ends up getting in the way: it can be near impossible to tell what plane your character is standing or will end up while moving.  Many of the puzzles are also physics based and it's quite easy to screw something up by (reasonably) not thinking you should be finagaling the touchy objects as much as you have to.  This leads to frustrating solutions you'll most likely solve by endless tinkering and guesswork rather than looking at a level and feeling smart by reasoning it out.

For the roughly $20 I spent on this, I'd say it was a terrific game. I'm not 100% sure I'd pay $40 for it, but it was still a lot of fun to play.
The game feels like a throwback in some respects, where it's just you against the world. But the production values are better than your average budget title. Some may recall that the original game had some rather...unsavory aspects in terms of Asian culture and stereotypes. You get some of that with this game, but it's oddly more...affectionate? I guess that's the word. It knows it's being goofy, but it can also be grounded in ways, too.
The action is terrific. The firearms are all fairly interesting, and aren't exactly your standard fare. Plus there's a nice upgrade system for weapons, skills, and powers. Those powers include things like being able to regenerate health, fire off a shockwave that knocks down enemies, and use special devastating katana attacks.
Which brings me to my favorite part of the game: slicin' stuff up with a katana. It's just FUN. And the enemies are quite susceptible to being sliced to bloody gibs.
Anyway, for a non-AAA title, I highly recommend it, especially if you're looking for a not-too-long FPS to screw around with.

Wow, this game is just incredible. I wasn't aware at all of what I was getting myself into when I started playing this, but once the map opened up my God did it open up. This is a Metroidvania style game that takes a lot of mechanical inspiration from both the obvious Metroid and Castlevania tropes, but also from Dark Souls in many ways. In Dark Souls, there were bonfires, and in this game there are benches. Souls are now Geo. Bosses will wreck you.
And yet, this game does not feel derivative. It definitely has its own identity, mostly due to the fact that it's 2D, and can take advantage of that for platforming and more player mobility. As you progress through the game, you will gain more abilities and moves that will make you much more agile. The "Charm" system is this game's version of speccing a character, and allow you to equip different passive and active abilities and perks.
This game is in the truest sense "open world", in that there really isn't a set path for the player to take. Virtually half of the content in the game is optional, although most likely you will want to experience that content, and most of it becomes imperative if you want to get the "good" ending. An average vanilla run of the game can take you about 20 hours, although to get 100%, that could easily go on 40 or 50 hours.
My only real complaint is that while the controls are definitely tight, they can at times prove to be frustrating, or to not exactly work as you intended. Some sections requiring tight jumps with little room for error can be very annoying, and sometimes you can fall to your death because your character simply wouldn't latch onto a wall correctly for a wall jump. That and traversing the map can occasionally be a chore, but these are minor qualms with an otherwise fantastic game.
Now that I've completed this game and Ori and the Blind Forest, I'm definitely hankering for some more Metroidvania goodness. I have high hopes for the DLC coming out later this month.

I'm a W40K fan, having four armies. Space Marines, Tau, two Imperial Guard factions (Armageddon Steel Legion and the Death Korps of Krieg) and even more of the faction books. When I go to play a strategy game, I expect a reasonable challenge in which I win through craft, out-thinking my opponent, and as one might expect, through strategy and skill. This game is too simple to the point that once you've got the basics you know what you should do for every scenario, and even when you do just that, there's a good chance you'll lose anyway just because the computer decided that you'll miss 8 shots in a row, and decided arbitrarily to throw 8 'nids at you en masse.
Now I'm not the end-all, beat-all game critic here, but I came into this game wanting to love it, and left sorely disappointed. This is a very sad day for the Imperium indeed.

TLDR: 10/10 Perfectly executed story and consistently fun gameplay.
I was worried at first when booting up the game, as I didn't have a controller that was compatible with Hollow Knight. My fears were swiftly quelled after two minutes of platforming and slashing at foes. Even with a keyboard, the game felt very fluid and I never felt that platforming problems were a result of controls. The simple gameplay works to never overwhelm the player. Even whenI had all the spells and upgrades, I still never felt like I was desperately juggling the buttons and stumbling through the expansive world of Hallownest.
The world is massive and meant to be explored and backtracked, just like any Metroidvania should be. The game also doesn't restrict creativity to earlier areas of the game. The entire world is oozing with the passion Team Cherry had for this game. Unlike other Indie games, I never saw a part where the developers got sloppy and less creative with their enemies, music, or environments. With places ranging from a mining peak filled with gorgeous pink crystals, to a dark spiders den that always leaves you guessing about what horrors may be around the corner, or wilds where ash is always raining down from above, Hallownest is always unique and exciting to explore.
The Story of Hollow Knight is executed perfectly. It doesn't begin with boring narration or an overwhelming backstory. The player knows very little and just knows to head right. The Lore unfolds itself as the player progresses and learns the story, but doesn't know where they learn it since they are having so much fun exploring. The ending doesn't rely on story elements that were never explained, but rather ties the story together in a brilliant fashion.

Everything is kept simple yet complex, and this simplicity is tackled in a fashion that keeps the game exciting, but never overwhelming.
10/10

In AA your marines persist between missions, increasing in rank and receiving awards. The 2D graphics are much more to the point and easier to interact with. The UI is vastly more intuitive and quicker to work with. It's just a better game even though it has the same mechanics. Space Hulk is not worth the full price (£19.99 at time of review). For the most part, balancing is good (Jade is the only overpowered champ I have truly seen). With the cartoon-ish graphics the game will age perfectly like Torchlight.
I get a WoW pvp vibe, with a mix of basic MOBA when I play this title. I have found myself unable to stop playing because even though the matches are short, I thrive to see what I can do in my next match to get better.
There are always a need for improvements. You have to change your battlerites to get that perfect build for a champion that is giving you trouble. Maybe you need more healing if you're squishy, maybe you need more offense if you're not having enough impact, etc. All the skills in the game feel like they are doing something, and every one of the champions are fun to play.
This game is not hard to learn by no means, but it is very difficult to master. I have learned a specific champ in my *8 hours of gameplay. I feel comfortable with that champion, but that does not mean that I do not play other champions. You'll always find yourself switching up to suit for your specific cravings or needs. That being said there are not very many champions, but there are enough to do us consumers for the amount of time.
In Battlerite, you will find yourself bored of the cosmetic skins, weapons, and mounts. Yes they are not all in your face flashy, but I'm sure in due time there will be better cosmetics to earn/buy.
On the end note. This game is very fun. I have not gotten bored (yet) of the gameplay with multiple maps and many new challenges to face. I see this game going very far during Early Access and beyond. I do not want to see another BLC mistake with this game.

Its a brand new game, and so bugs and other problems are to be expected. In the haters defense, I do have the same issue with low frame rates, and very occasional lag spikes. I'm running an ASUS ROG-20 CB with an intel I-7 core with NVidia Ge force graphics cards, and 16GB or RAM. So yes, even multi thousand dollar gaming pcs have low frame rates and lag spikes with this game. However, I'm sure they can iron these out with patches and I'm used to having to play games on cheap Wal-Mart laptops, so I guess this doesn't bother me as much as others. It still runs more than good enough for me to play and enjoy playing for hours on end. For someone that wants to be an engineer for real, I can really appreciate the new features, like being able to walk around and climb on the equipment. Not to mention being able to actually refuel locomotives, and start them up or shut them down by actually throwing the switches and buttons, and not by pressing the Z key like in the railworks series. I know it will just get better with time and I think while there are some issues, this game shows a lot of promise.

Admittedly I will be a bit biased in this response as I am helping in the development for this game. However I will give the most honest answer I can.
It's been far too long since I should have made this post. I have been playing StarMade consistently for over a year and discovered it far before that. (There is a good chance I have hundreds of hours but I don't use steam to launch the game so that is surely incorrect in my hours played) Since then it has undergone massive changes and very much so in a positive direction. Visually and gameplay wise it continues to become an amazing game. This review will be from the perspective of an experienced player around December 2015
Graphics: This isn't any Star citizen, nor is it Space Engineers (a game it is often compared to) when it comes to graphics. The universe is cubed. It follows the trend set fourth by Minecraft (despite being planned long before MC made it's debut). I must say however, I never had such faith in the graphics of a voxel game. Even with shaders installed and a great texture pack, Minecraft can hardly come close to the visuals of StarMade. This is due to the use of built in normal, emission and specular maps. Additionally it has some very decent shadows as well. Like much of the rest of the game, a lot of this is configurable.
Scale: The universe is massive. Often times I will hear new players remark on how large a ship is. To me the same ship may be small. The feeling of walking around a kilometer long spaceship is awesome and getting to that point in the game is worth the money alone. Space itself is split up neatly into grids, which allow this universe to exist at this scale. From sectors to systems to galaxies, you could spend your entire time flying and never see the same stars again. The only area where scale is lacking is planets. These objects often sit under a kilometer in radius. That said, I know it is intended to bump up the scale where possible. Despite pushing a java game beyond what is possible, we will eventually reach it's limit's. At least for now those limits have yet to be reached.
Setting: The game is purely science fiction based. You can if you want turn on options for a more realistic experience, however the idea is that creativity should flourish and it should be fun to play. The universe is a bit empty right now, however rest assured. I myself am personally working on various assets that will be in the game and additionally we will see mechanics introduced that turn this into a bustling dynamic universe. Aliens, flora, space derelicts, cosmic anomalies. All of this is planned. Some of it is already in the game!
Building: Building has never been simpler. All blocks and materials are 1 cubic meter. I think this is the advantage this game has over similar titles. There is no need to build a large chunky machine that serves a specific purpose. Or to place it in a way on your build so that it actually functions. You can have a ship that makes just about no sense, but it will still work. If you like it, why should the game punish you for that? Additionally there are crazy awesome build tools. Templates for shapes, copy/paste, undo/redo, and symmetry planes just to name a few. All of this easily accessible from your ship.
Crafting: Crafting is simple and complex at the same time. There are 24~ resources that produce just about every block in the game, most of which you will eventually find a place for on your ship. These resources are fed into factories and can be automated and made more efficient.
Combat/gameplay: There is a lot to learn here and it will likely be where a new player will get stuck. Combat can be exciting, however I expect balancing as well as new features to be added till release. There are multiple approaches though; shield tanking, armor tanking, dps based. You can use missiles, lasers, cannons, or turrets or combinations of all of this. You can install jump drives to escape, you can install jump inhibitors to prevent escape! No idea is too crazy for StarMade and a lot of science fiction based features have made their way into the game simply because they are awesome.
I imagine learning how to play the game will be the hardest part for any new players. Learning to play is worth it however. The game's demo is free but will not be updated beyond beta or public release. As the game approaches full release the price will increase so now is the time! Take the time to learn and see what is possible and you will be getting your money's worth!
TLDR; Easy building with great tools. Simply yet deep crafting system that makes sense. Massive universe and massive scale. Anything in the realm of science fiction is a reality and may become a part of the game as it develops!

Your goal is to help Eets (the little white bug looking creature) reach the end of the level, you want to collect the 3 food items also, as an extra challenge. As you collect the food and the cake at the end of the level you unlock items you can use in your own Steamworkshop puzzles.
The game itself felt like an app I would play on an apple computer inside the computer store. The buttons themselves actually look like ones used on Angry Birds, so I’m pretty sure that’s how you should be playing this game, but it worked flawlessly with my mouse.
It’s a point and click game, that about sums it up. Before you start the game you are given a select few items to set down, then you play and use those items to help Eets finish the level.
I had no trouble with the achievements, once I had finished the game as far as I could go (I only had to skip about 4 levels, and still had most of the secret levels left), the rest of the achievements you can look up helpful guides. Basically think of this game as a free “100%” for your steam profile. Pretty neat, I think. :D

Curse of Mermos is one of those games you pick up to experiment with for one session, then forget about it the following week. It's in no way memorable or fun, seeing as the game just recycles itself over and over until you want to do your head in with a rock. Thank god this game is free; this review would have been a lot angrier if it wasn't.
You will only see 7-8 different types of enemies throughout the whole 30 wave game. You've got generic spiders, generic skeletons, generic skeleton
, generic mummies, and generic healers; each with only one flimsy attack to defend themselves with. Every enemy gets used so many times that you really have to hope and pray for somthing original to pop up.
Another thing to question is the game's complete lack of substance. The entirety of it is rinse and repeat: finish a couple waves, retrieve a trinket. Upgrade some stuff, finish more waves, retrieve a trinket. This repeats
until you're left with nothing but filler waves to make the game seem longer. Every wave up to wave 20 is extremely easy; there's never any need to use melee whatsoever (even when the game tells you "You won't escape the tomb without using melee" in a tip). All you really need to upgrade is agility, health, and bow damage. After getting the fourth trinket, the waves are literally
. I quit the game at round 28 because I literally became sad every time a new wave was ready to be played. It's
repetitive and boring. The enviornment doesn't even change for christ's sake; you're stuck in the same cluster of confined spaces for an eternity.
Before I keep ranting on and on, let me just simplify all of this: Curse of Mesmos is beyond bland. Every enemy is recycled to oblivion, the story that the game tries to pull off is non-existant, some attacks never even need to be used at all (despite the game saying so), and if you don't have a controller, you're screwed. This game is not worth your time in the slightest.

This game is very clever, too clever...
It does have an amazing art style and some really unique puzzles to solve, but there's a significant reason I don't recommend it to people like myself.
The game's difficulty curve is too steep. Levels are usually very easy or very hard, with not much inbetween. Within a couple hours you'll probably find yourself stuck. Puzzle games like this are a matter of patience, and I don't want to spend an hour solving a single puzzle. I don't get enough satisfaction from such a play session to want to have many more like it.
I beat a bunch of the early levels really fast and then spent a lot of time on the later levels. A couple times I ended up using a walkthrough for help, but yeah, that didn't feel too good.
After completing all 24 of the game's original levels you get to play extra challenging versions of those levels. They get new twists so you have to solve them in completely different ways. I beat a couple of the edited-version levels and then decided I didn't want to play the game anymore.
If you want a unique puzzle game and you have a ton of time and patience, and you're willing to spend half an hour experimenting on a level and still have no clue how to beat it, then this game is for you!
In all seriousness, this really is a well-designed puzzle game. I kinda feel bad for not recommending it, but the game just isn't for me. There is a small audience that will love this game, but make sure you think about it hard before deciding whether or not to get it.

With a little more time and work, The Bridge would've become an extra special gameplay experience, but due to the design, most puzzles feel like you're fighting and messing around with momentum rather than searching for an ah-ha moment. Regardless of a few smaller issues, there are still a ton of memorable maps which pay optical and physical illusions enough respect, while balancing player fun enough to mix good parts from both and make The Bridge an artistic puzzle platformer well worth grabbing.
The best parts of The Bridge are exactly what you see on the store front, a beautiful and imaginative art style that's unique and different enough to set this apart from others. The Bridge doesn't overstay its welcome, and the pleasant U.I. and ambiance serve to keep it casual and relaxing.
* Each level feels new and is a pleasure to explore. The floating design on the distant background helps everything feel dreamlike
There are a few moments where you actively need to think about how to approach the landscape and physics represented in the level, and suddenly you'll realize how to approach it and solve the problem, but these moments are too few and on the whole you'll be wrestling with momentum or gravity to move your character to the correct position, which feels a little too cheap and shallow.
* A distinct lack of music or even distinct ambient sounds is a loss, and would've worked to greatly compliment the art style
* The collectibles add nothing to the game, and are frustrating to collect, but can safely be ignored
* There's a ridiculous spike in difficulty on levels 4-5 that's very jarring
The Bridge clocks in with around 4-5 hours gameplay and may feel just a touch too highly priced on Steam at £6.99/9.99€/$9.99 when compared to other entries in this genre which are available for cheaper. When viewed alone, it's still a very reasonable price, and if you're a puzzler veteran, you'll probably see this as above average value for money, especially considering it regularly goes on sale for -80% and -90%, leaving it at just $0.99
* Due to the Developers confessed inspiration from, and love of the Braid game, and given the title of the game, it's possible that there's a subtly hidden story or message contained throughout the game
* There's a great AMA/Q&A with the Developers
* There's a free Trial/Demo version of The Bridge

The Stanley Parable is not a game.
It is a question.
There are choices.
And you can choose which choice to take.
You have control over reality in The Stanley Parable but you never know what will happen when,
You can hurl yourself over the stairwell and destroy another man's life.
You can even delve into different universes that break quantum physics and allows for giant amounts of creativity.
You can be a follower or a rebel.
It's all up to you.
The Stanley Parable is a game about choices.
And what happens when you stay in a broom closet for too long.

Wow, this game is just incredible. I wasn't aware at all of what I was getting myself into when I started playing this, but once the map opened up my God did it open up. This is a Metroidvania style game that takes a lot of mechanical inspiration from both the obvious Metroid and Castlevania tropes, but also from Dark Souls in many ways. In Dark Souls, there were bonfires, and in this game there are benches. Souls are now Geo. Bosses will wreck you.
And yet, this game does not feel derivative. It definitely has its own identity, mostly due to the fact that it's 2D, and can take advantage of that for platforming and more player mobility. As you progress through the game, you will gain more abilities and moves that will make you much more agile. The "Charm" system is this game's version of speccing a character, and allow you to equip different passive and active abilities and perks.
This game is in the truest sense "open world", in that there really isn't a set path for the player to take. Virtually half of the content in the game is optional, although most likely you will want to experience that content, and most of it becomes imperative if you want to get the "good" ending. An average vanilla run of the game can take you about 20 hours, although to get 100%, that could easily go on 40 or 50 hours.
My only real complaint is that while the controls are definitely tight, they can at times prove to be frustrating, or to not exactly work as you intended. To start off, I am a fan of the series. I played 'Stronghold' and 'Stronghold: Crusader' (and a bit of Stronghold 2) quite a few years ago and have rediscovered them again on Steam recently. While the two classics have been made compatible with newer hardware and are still fun to play (and are a no brainer if you find them on sale), you cant help but think they could do with a complete remake. I think this is the closest we will get for now...
When I first saw this game, I practically ignored it. Having experienced 'Stronghold 2' and 'Stronghold Legends' in the past, I knew the series wasnt in the best place. I also read/watched reviews of 'Stronghold 3' when it came out and decided it wasnt worth getting. This game being in the Steam sale caught my interest, and I decided to research it a little. I then decided it looked alright and went ahead with the purchase. Having bought this and played several hours, I have already decided it was definatly worth it!
The gameplay, unlike the other sequels, resembles the original two games, in my opinion. Although it may be basic in some areas, it is still enjoyable and i find is well balanced between the economy and combat aspects (you need to work efficiently on both to win). The graphics, while not too impressive by todays standards, look nice, and again, resemble the original 'Crusader' in some ways. The sound effects and voice acting can get a bit repetitive and annoying, but im sure these can be turned down/off in the options.
Although the game comes with several Campaign trails, I only played a couple, and then went straight into custom games, so I can't comment on them. There are plenty of maps to choose from, depending on the amount of opponents. There also seem to be lots of community maps too (which is a strong point of the original 'Stronghold'). The AI can present a real challenge in certain games and situations, but also can be too easy at lower difficulties, but I guess you can tailor the game to how difficult you want it.
Overall, I am enjoying this game from my first few hours, and it has restored a bit of confidence in the series for me. Hopefully, the amount of community maps will continue to grow, and I will continue to enjoy the game. Its not 100% perfect, but if you are a fan of the original two games, I would say this is at least worth looking in to.

TLDR: 10/10 Perfectly executed story and consistently fun gameplay.
I was worried at first when booting up the game, as I didn't have a controller that was compatible with Hollow Knight. My fears were swiftly quelled after two minutes of platforming and slashing at foes. Even with a keyboard, the game felt very fluid and I never felt that platforming problems were a result of controls. The simple gameplay works to never overwhelm the player. Even whenI had all the spells and upgrades, I still never felt like I was desperately juggling the buttons and stumbling through the expansive world of Hallownest.
The world is massive and meant to be explored and backtracked, just like any Metroidvania should be. The game also doesn't restrict creativity to earlier areas of the game. The entire world is oozing with the passion Team Cherry had for this game. Unlike other Indie games, I never saw a part where the developers got sloppy and less creative with their enemies, music, or environments. With places ranging from a mining peak filled with gorgeous pink crystals, to a dark spiders den that always leaves you guessing about what horrors may be around the corner, or wilds where ash is always raining down from above, Hallownest is always unique and exciting to explore.
The Story of Hollow Knight is executed perfectly. It doesn't begin with boring narration or an overwhelming backstory. The player knows very little and just knows to head right. The Lore unfolds itself as the player progresses and learns the story, but doesn't know where they learn it since they are having so much fun exploring. The ending doesn't rely on story elements that were never explained, but rather ties the story together in a brilliant fashion.

Everything is kept simple yet complex, and this simplicity is tackled in a fashion that keeps the game exciting, but never overwhelming.
10/10

I have finally gotten my hands on a copy of this medieval RTS Simulation game after it being wishlisted since its initial pre-release announcement. The reviews have been a mixed bag of tricks from the start so I wanted to give Firefly Studios plenty of time to bang out any kinks in the ol' armor before launching my assault and possibly bludgeoning this game into fragmented code. After a lengthy (and sometimes exhausting) battle, the dust has settled and as my gaze reflects upon the still-burning fires, the blood-soaked desert sands, and the rubbled remains of what once was a towering and majestic castle, I muster up the strength to utter a few last words with my last breath fading away - "I strongly recommend this game..."
A couple of reasons. First, this is an expensive game even after being released for almost a year. Not uncommon for many AAA titles, but let's face it - this is Steam and the majority of Steam users are known for pinching pennies and expecting everything on the cheap. Not totally unreasonable and for those who pay the hefty full price for this game, I understand why there may be some mixed feelings about it. The game is good, has a lot to offer, and is entertaining. But at the same time, there are a few bugs and issues in it still and don't appear to be getting fixed any time soon. They aren't necessarily being ignored though and Firefly Studios is still actively working on the game and new content for it.  Keep in mind, Stronghold Crusader 2 is a AAA title and its normal for periodical updates to be released as major patches that address many things at once rather than a multitude of weekly updates that may address one specific element as seen with smaller indie-type games.
Many gamers who have played the original Stronghold Crusader  before grabbing this long awaited sequel have been openly critical because the graphics are only slightly improved after more than a decade. Stronghold Crusader is very similar to the original, in fact, almost identical at first glance. But there are some differences -  new units (and special abilities added to others), a modified economic system, a change in the housing dynamic, co-op mode for multiplayer games, an automated purchase/sell system added to the market, weather/natural disaster random events, some new AI characters (and more planned as future DLC), troop formations added and improved, and a few other changes  or removed content from the original (such as the removal of moats and feasts). However, for the most part, Stronghold Crusader 2 is identical to its predecessor at a much loftier price so it draws a lot of criticism for this.
I review games individually based on their own content and whether they offer up gaming enjoyment to its players. This game is a lot of fun and has plenty to offer. The graphics are 3-D, unlike the original Crusader game. They will not leave you with that "wow" feeling, but they are still solid and detailed for a real-time strategy sim. The soundtrack to this game is a harmonic masterpiece that injects the player with a true sense of the environment and time period. There are several different game modes and each of them offer a numerous amount of gameplay. Hundreds of hours can be spent playing without ever trying out each one. There are a multitude of buildings that can be built and a nice variety of units available. A map editor has been included for easily creating and sharing your own designs with the Steam Community. And don't forget the most popular feature - Castle Building. This is what really makes the crusader series so great. Its one of the best castle building systems in gaming and while slightly different from previous versions, it still performs smoothly and allows for simple and fun creativity to give your kingdom its own personal touch.
In Stronghold Crusader 2 players will need to gather resources for building structures, creating weapons to train armed units, and produce enough food to support the populus. Fortifying your base is an important aspect as well, so players will want to protect their kingdom with castle walls and defensive structures like towers and traps. Naturally, you will need an army to defend your kingdom and attack your opponents. Each troop type requires specific weapons or armor to be crafted first and also have a price in gold. Gold can be earned by collecting taxes or by selling excess goods on the market. Troops can also be purchased from a mercenary post with gold. Governing your kingdom is very basic. It is based on overall happiness and there are several ways players can influence this statistic positively or negatively. To claim victory you must simply defeat all of the opposing lords on the map.
Stronghold Crusader 2 is packed full of gameplay content offered in a variety of game modes to ensure countless hours of entertainment. They include single player, co-op and multiplayer options. There are a variety of customization settings available to adjust the level of difficulty a player wishes to encounter, configure for team play, and map selection (in some cases). Computer AI players can be substituted or added in place of additional human players and each AI character has its own habits, strengths, and weaknesses that also influence how challenging the game will be.
Tutorial campaigns that play out as a campaign while progressively teaching the game's         concepts.
A chain of skirmishes versus AI characters that increase in difficulty as you progress.
Up to 8 players and team play. Players can be human or AI. Custom settings including map selection.
Build your mighty kingdom in peace and without fear of being attacked from any opponents.
Players can either join a server from the list or host their own game and can be played individually or as teams. There is also a simple in-game text chat available by pressing "Enter."
Skirmish maps designed by the Steam Community.
Stronghold Crusader 2 is a very entertaining medieval RTS castle-building simulation that is packed with gameplay and will continue to get better with time as more content is added. However, it does come at a considerable price. I recommend this game to all RTS lovers, but if you're on a tight gaming budget then i would wishlist it and wait for a sale. In the meantime, you might also consider buying the original Stronghold Crusader game to get a taste of the crusader experience.

The question I set out to answer when I bought this was simple, Is the fond memories I have of playing it just nostalgia, or even today, does it still hold up as the genre-defining FPS game it was 11 years ago?
The answer to that question is simple, Its not just all Nostalgia.
If you've never played the original, I highly recommend getting it, its a great way of seeing just how far the series has come and see the birth of a lot of things we take for granted. AI-controlled squadmates? That was here baby. "Ramirez DO EVERYTHING?" This game pioneered that.
The hardest time I had with the game was the fact that there is no sprint key, So you feel like you are running a lot slower than other CoD games, Oh and theres no regenerating health, which means getting shot is punishing. And you will die. A lot. The enemies in this game can still be tough little buggers frequently. But thats also what makes the game rewarding.
Flaws? Oh the game has them, Some are simply due to the age of the game, such as enviornments feeling quite linear and the draw distance feeling very low, these are just due to technical limitations of the day. THe bigger flaws to me would be that sometimes inputs are very.. picky.. on when they want to do what you need, and sometimes you seem to get stuck on debris. Also some areas feel very "narrow" and you end up hitting a corner. Oh and the squad AI, as innovative as it was back then, is still pretty bloody bad, I've watched them grenade each other or me from time to time. But hey these dont detract from the immense fun and challenge this game provides. And to me the missions in this one ended up being the ones I remembered the most.
Get it, You wont regret it

This is an excellent game for competitive players who want the arena experience of WoW without worrying about grinding for gear or levels, or MOBA players who don't care much for level differences and farming/item purchases. It's a 2v2 or 3v3 pure PVP arena where nearly every single ability, including healing, is a skill-shot (meaning you have to aim and land it, not just click a target). There aren't a large number of abilities per character, so it is less about having a large ability toolkit and more about knowing how to anticipate your opponent's moves and use the abilities you have at the right time. I would highly recommend this game for individuals who want quick access to intense PVP fights without any of the outside work involved (farming, itemization, leveling, grinding, etc. etc.). There is a pretty nice balance between melee, ranged and support character options, and the Devs seem actively interested in maintaining the game's balance and adding new features and characters.

Using TSW on the following PC Specification:
i7 6700 @ 3.40GHz
16 GB DDR4 3000MHz RAM
Samsung 850 Evo SSD
Windows 10 Home 64-bit
GeForce GTX 760 4GB
First of all... this is a good start to what will be the start of a TSW journey with many addons to come.
The UI is clean and easy to understand. The addition of having first person perspective for this game is good and makes you feel like you are part of the railroad staff. Even with an added trainspotting mode!
UE4 has a good reputation for creating a good base for which games sit with the graphics fidelity on the high side. I was cautious with the graphics settings and knocked a couple of options down from the high preset.
Started of with the tutorials which are narrated and easy to follow. It takes you through the main features of the locos and the various operations you can perform on and off track. I found these clear and easy to understand what is going on.
I then played through a basic "quick drive" scenario with the abiity to choose the weather conditions and time you wish to drive in. Pick a train service and off you go. Driving the whole length of the route took around 2 hours with some AI added to make things seems alive. The FPS remained pretty stable with a couple of a little pauses here and there just before loading crowded areas. I don't have an exact number for what the FPS stayed at but it was comfortable.
There were a few graphical artifacts such as reflections and the LCD panels in the cab and on the fuel display being heavily antiliased and distorted. - Somewhat fixed since review
Then entered FREE mode where I was set into the yard where I could get into whichever train I wanted then attach/detach the many freight wagons spaced out around me. This was a good opportunity to try out things without following tutorial instruction. The Cumberland yard was huge and plenty of trains to play with.
To sum up:
A great start to TSW, it could do with some more optimisation (correcting gfx artifacts and light anomolies). I look forward to how in depth UK stock can get with the same graphical quality shown with the CSX Heavy Haul introduction. It will be interesting to see how much the DLC will be for rolling stock and routes. Also there has been mention of VR support, multiplayer and the content editor which I presume will all be updated free of charge like the previous game. I'm very impressed on this introduction (even if US stock is not my focus) and I am very interested to see how the additions of DLC and new features add to the overall game!
Take the negative reviews with a pinch of salt, many were too eager to bash this game because their PC couldn't handle it on ultra settings. Knocking a few options down to high instead gave me a perfectly playable game with the above PC specs.

This is the story of a man named Carbon,
Carbon worked in his own home as a Part-time YouTuber were he was Carbon Helium. Carbon's job was simple: He sat at his desk in his room, and recorded footage of him playing games. Order's came to him via the comments on his videos, telling him what to play, how long, and who with. This is what Carbon did every day, of every month, of every year, and although others might have considered it boring, Carbon relished every moment someone commented on his video, as though he had been made exactly for this job. And Carbon was happy.
And then one day, Carbon downloaded the Stanley Parable, played it for a while, and posted a video on it. Then something very peculiar happened. Something that would forever change Carbon; something he would never quite forget. He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he realized that not one single comment had been made on his new video. No one had shown up to give him hatred, constructive feedback, or even say 'hi.' Never in all his years at home had this happened, this complete isolation. Something was very clearly wrong.
Shocked, frozen solid, Carbon found himself unable to move for the longest time. But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his room.
All of his friends were gone, what could it mean? Carbon then realised he had been playing this game for way too long. That the year was now 2097, and everyone he knew was dead.
10/10, lost all my friends

I can not stress how much I love this game. It just ticks all the box's for me like coop, tower defence and rpg. What else could I ask for?. Before I properaly start this review I should mention that I played the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game on my xbox but only recentyl purchased it on steam so I dont have many hours on it. Anyway I guess I should begin with the gameplay. The basic idea for the game is that theres is a crystal(s) on each map which you must defend at all cost because if even 1 of them gets destroyed you lose. You can do this by placing various defenses (depending on your class) ranging from traps to cannons to minions and using your hero. You can even level up your hero and collect loot making this game an rpg. Along with these basic missions there are also challenge maps which can varify from switching roles with the enemy to protecting an ogre. With all these varietys I would definatly recomend playing with friends with different classes in order to get the right type of towers and fighters. The games art style is nothing really special but it gets the job done. It does look pretty though and while im not normaly that big of a fan of medieval fantasy this game doesnt try to hard to be based around it so that doesnt really bother me. Hollow Knight showed up on my Discover Queue and was love at first sight, A 2D metroidvania with awesome art, melancholy feel and beautiful music? I had to play it!
And I did, and the love turned into obsession. I couldn't let go of the controller, and it wasn't a ride on the park, no, it doesn't grab you by the hand, but that is one of the perks that makes it so special, so... classic.
From someone who grew playing Super Metroid, SotN and Demon's Crest; games I cherish and are part of my personal top 10 and most important, are the foundation of was to be considered the Metroidvania genre, Hollow Knight came like a storm to fulfill a void long due in the genre.
Yes, there are great Metroidvanias out there, principally from Indie Devs, but none has made so deep mark as Hollow Knight did, and here's why.

Hollow Knight looks simple, but as soon you start playing and exploring you realize how much effort and love was put into it. The areas are stunning, each one with their own feel and mood (Deepnest will make you squirm!)
The backgrounds are full of details as well the foreground, and it doesn't look like copy and paste, it feels seamless and alive.
The sprites are well done and have fluid movement, from the minor creatures to the bosses, all in place, there isn't a single thing that looks that it doesn't belong.

There is plenty of NPCs you encounter in the game, some more developed with their own personal quests and some less developed but with a piece of lore to add. And is easy to relate with some of them when you cross paths and start unveiling their reasons for being in Hallownest.
Their personalities are unique and add a lot of depth to the world.
I won't dive too much into the story to avoid spoilers, but know this, it feels more real than you imagine. It isn't your happy knight savior type of tale. It's bleak, melancholic and is easy to feel the burden as you progress. And while there are NPCs that help you out, you'll still feel the solitude following, almost claustrophobic, in a good immersive way.
The lore developed for this game is outstanding, the "bug society" feels functional and tangible and makes you want to know more about it.
Hollow Knight, as a faithful metroidvania, starts right. You don't have much, only a nail attack, short, slow, weak. You can't spam it, there's timing, and this is something I took some time to understand but when I did I realized how polished and fit to the game the mechanics are.
There are upgrades; life, spells, nail upgrades and the charm system, which allow you to combine charms to fit your playstyle. But none of these are OP endgame, you still can't spam the nail or tank/slash everything you see in front of you. There's tactics, pattern recognition, trial and error, a lot of trial and error!
The most important point in HK regarding fights is the healing, there isn't something as potion, you fill your "tank' with souls by hitting enemies and uses the soul to recharge your life, but you can't just hit heal and keep pushing, you have to stop and focus in order to heal, and this plays a huge part in the strategy part of the game as you need to find the right opening on the enemies patterns to be able to heal safely.
As a metroidvania, HK has upgrades which allow you to visit some previous unreachable parts, there is a lot of backtracking and exploration involved, but what makes HK stand out is the possibility of progressing to said areas early in the game with a bit of skill.
I won't get deep into it, but I'll give a hint.
The boss fights are a treat for sore eyes, isn't difficult to see people getting frustrated on the forums over the second boss encounter, and not without reason, it will get you off guard. but it will get you prepared for what will come.
As stated, you can't go tanking, there are patterns and tactics and it fits perfectly with the game mechanics, you have to time your attacks and find the openings, and while this sounds like a slow burn, the fights are actually really fast paced and full of enjoyable tension.

There's something very important in the 3 games I listed before, and is the music, all of them had iconic music, the type that you would listen out of the game, the kind that give you the chills, and with HK isn't different, the soundtrack is a piece of art and it blends masterfully with the game.
False Knight is probably my favorite track, but all of them is rightfully good, from Hornet's fast paced theme to the Demon's Crest feel of Soul Sanctum and the tension of Mantis Lords, the music plays a huge deal on the whole package.
I could go on and talk about the amazing sound fx, the character designs, the map extension, secrets and all, but there's something quite important for this game, and it's the feel of discovery.
This game is a piece of art, and while I'm sad I haven't got notice of it sooner, I'm really happy it came to fruition and turned out to be, for me, game of the year.
Thank you Team Cherry!

Hollow Knight is a fantastic game, as it features superbly charming visuals, deeply alluring music/sound effects, and an extremely fluid and tight control scheme, from the combat, to the platforming, and everything in between.
As one could see from my playtime, I did not rush myself through this game. I took my time and enjoyed marveling at all of the finely crafted regions and art spread throughout the game's world. After a fair number of hours playing through Hollow Knight, I feel that it is a strong contender to compete against other critically acclaimed platformers such as Metroid and Ori and the Blind Forest.
The hand-drawn art that comprises all of the visuals in this game are beautiful, and the animation for the game is executed very well. Hollow Knight's soundtrack is phenomenal in every sense of the word. Every single area in the game features music that suits it exquisitely. The main town of the game, the spooky areas that are dark and ominous, the boss fights, and areas that consist of a calmer tone, all have music that complements the art, progression, movement, and even combat of the game. Additionally, the game's soundtrack amplifies and deeply immerses and engrosses the player into Hollow Knight's atmosphere. Personally, my favorite piece of the soundtrack is the song that plays while in the City of Tears.
Controlling the protagonist in this game is very fluid and satisfying, and I do not believe it could have been done any better. Jumping and dashing from platforms to walls etc., feels very natural, and there was not a single moment in the game in which I felt as if I did not have full control of every action performed.
The game's combat features a fairly simplistic but graceful design, as a single button is dedicated to the vast majority of the offensive actions possible in the game. One's finesse and skill can be utilized to expertly fight the enemies in this game; your success in Hollow Knight's combat and platforming is entirely dependent on your own abilities, which is how it should be, being that this is a skill-based game. One particular aspect that stands out to me is the aerial combat. I have never before played a game in which mid-air combat felt so controllable, adaptable, flexible, and satisfying; it is an incredibly wonderful feeling, and it must be experienced first-hand in order to truly appreciate it. Dare I say it, I believe this game dethrones Ori and the Blind Forest from being my favorite Metroidvania platformer.
Hollow Knight is nothing short of a masterpiece, not only in terms of a great video game, but also a visual as well as audible treasure to behold. This game is truly a testament to what video games should be like today, as it clearly demonstrates that the developers genuinely care about their game. For that reason, I thoroughly commend and applaud Team Cherry for delivering such an amazing experience.
TL;DR
- A phenomenal platforming game
- Gorgeous art and animations (They are hand-drawn!)
- A magnificently crafted soundtrack by Christopher Larkin, featuring lovely vocals from Amelia Jones
- I have never experienced tighter, more fluid, and satisfying controls in a platforming game (Even from Nintendo)
- This game is a steal at 15 USD
- I regret not buying this on day one of its release
- Very well done, Team Cherry

I've made a full video review of Valhalla hills here -
For those of you that prefer a written review, here it goes:
Valhalla Hills is a game very similar to the Cultures franchise and early Settlers games. In fact Valhalla Hills has been developed by Funatics Software - the same company that made these games, so it's to be expected. They've taken a well-loved pair of franchises and changed things up a little, in parts for the better - in parts for worse.
Normally games of this genre involve building up an army and destroying the opposition, In Valhalla Hills there is no specific enemy you must defeat to win the level, there is however a wide variety of enemies that are standing in the way between your settlement and your objective. To win the level in Valhalla Hills you need to enter the portal that lies at the top of the mountain and it's usually guarded pretty heavily - there’s also the option to win economically with a sacrifice (basically a bribe to the guards).
The aim of the game is to get your Vikings enough honour to enter Valhalla, which in a way makes some aspects of the game feel like a grind. Once a level is complete it's on to the next level to grind more honour! But I’m getting ahead of myself, let’s examine some game mechanics.
Production chains are pretty good actually, I'm happy with them. For the production chain of generating resources for buildings, we start with the basics - logs and quarry stone. These are good starting point for building your settlement and will be sufficient for a while. As you progress you'll need to refine these materials with another set of buildings, turning logs into planks and quarry stone into stone bricks. This is as far as the construction materials production chain goes, every structure in the game can be built with either; logs, quarry stone, planks or stone bricks. Like i said I’m happy with that, it's one step beyond what Settlers 3&4 offer but not a rabbit hole of complexity like in Cultures - a nice healthy middle ground. However this is the simplest production chain there is, it just gets more complex after that... mostly in a good way. There's a few irregularities I’ve noticed in the current build (v1.02.01) such as the kitchen, which takes the separate food items your Vikings have produced and combines them into a single unit of food (bread and meat become sandwiches) - this makes life easier for your hungry Vikings, but the nutritional value of the sandwiches is less than the sum of its parts - its wastefulness is a bit irritating!
The games AI seems to be a bit silly sometimes, they will stray too far and get attacked, after a bit of fighting back and losing health, they run off, then it seems like the AI resets and they head back to their exact previous location! The cycle of fighting, running and returning usually continues until they die. This issue is exacerbated by the inability to directly control your Vikings, they're off on their own and can't be commanded, Perhaps this is a feature, forcing you to quickly produce some troops and clear the local area - it's an RTS after all.
Speaking of the inability to control your Vikings, I get the feeling that Valhalla Hills is trapped in an identity crisis between the highly personal attachment to the Vikings that Cultures offers and the sense of distance from your people that Settlers has, where people are pretty much numbers and nothing more. It's a strange aspect to the game - You can follow your Vikings and rename them, but you can't directly control them and for the most part you have little influence on their daily activities.
Finally, if we think back to fighting up to the portal and the other main objective of the game - grinding enough honour to be worthy of Valhalla. I get a sense of "what’s the point?" there's currently no campaigns (once again, reviewing build v1.02.01) and no multiplayer. The only justification you have for your actions is the 2 minute long intro animation that plays when you load the game. There's also a feeling of "Where’s the sense of accomplishment?" once you make it to the portal, A little bit of music plays and **VICTORY!** appears on the screen, accompanied below by a [Next level] button, then it’s on to the next level to do it all again. There's currently a real lack of a feeling of accomplishment, it would be nice to see a statistics page like Setters 3 and 4 have. Show me the number battles I’ve won, show me the number of buildings I’ve built, rain some Godly Nordic lightening fireworks from the sky, something - anything!
I'm really on the fence as to recommend this game or not, it's definitely got a lot of potential. A thumbs up as of right now? Perhaps not. Please bare in mind that I’m biased because I love this kind of game, I’m a big fan of Cultures and I've been playing Settlers 3/4 on a weekly basis on my YouTube channel for over a year now. If you love the RTS genre, or you're a big fan of the Cultures and Settlers franchises and you're looking for a modern revamp then YES, give this game a try, I think you'll really enjoy it. If you're unsure, or you’re new to these kinds of games, then NO - perhaps save your money and either wait for a sale or first try one of the other similar titles available, I'd recommend you take a look at Cultures 2, Settlers 2 (10th anniversary addition), Settlers 3 and Settlers 4.
Hope you found this review helpful! Cya all at Odin’s dinner table!

Only way to tweak your character is between the rounds, where you get to choose 1 of 3 "battlerites"(a passive, which usually adds an additional effect to one of your skills), but EVERYONE gets one, so snowballing is non-existant.

-Going to be free-to-play at full release.

Well... No. At this (as they say) early state of development there are many reasons to just say 'no' to this game. I played a whole lot of racing games and racing sims and still I'm not fully aware where to put it Raceroom Racing Experience in. Sometimes, driving in R3E feels reasonably realistic, sometimes it's ridicoulusly arcade-ish.
Let's have a list of good aspects of R3E; There is a great AI, which often fights and struggles the same way you do. I don't want to say that they're completely flawless, hell no, but compared to other racing games, the AI in R3E is damn good.
The tracks come in a very polished manner and for me it was a pleasure to see such detailed tracks, full of life. Codemasters still does a better job in this but well, you can't be good at everything, right?
Also the cars look nice - not great, but nice. It's pretty hard to say when it is "enough" regarding details, because theoretically it's never enough if you want to simulate things. But sure there are restrictions in terms of hardware resources. And it's 'free' to play, so they want to reach a big audience of course.
All along the words 'free to play' is the biggest flaw in here. When you first download the game, there are waiting 2 cars in your garage on 2 tracks, with 3 and 2 versions of it. Of the the tracks is a R3E Fantasy track, which - don't get me wrong - is damn good.
Sector 3 Entertainment offers a test-drive in every car you may want to drive, at least. But let's face it - if you want to have a full garage, you're about to pay at least 120€, which is too damn high, considering that the cars are not even realistically balanced or even physically correct - yes, they are nice, but nice doesn't want me to pay that much money.
I purchased the ADAC GT Masters 2014 Package, the Hillclimb Package, as well as the track Bathurst and the Ruf GTRS12 (basically a Porsche 997 GT3). Hell yeah it was worth it, I had some fun, especially on Bathurst, and with some of the GT Masters tracks and cars... But the game still feels incomplete, everywhere pops up a "BUY NOW", "BUY NOW", "ON SALE", "ON SALE", advertisement everywhere - incredibly annoying.
I don't think that they ever change this, so this alone is a reason to give it a 'no'... On top of that comes the questionable physics and behaviour of some cars and the lack of settings of track conditions.
Oh and it was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥to get my Force Feedback into a playable state, although it fully supports my Logitec Driving Force GT (I know, it's far away from being the best, thanks! :D ), which to me was a antipathic moment, also...
Go download the thing and try it yourself, but invest some hours before you buy something.

The original Eets was a game with a new concept that took the gameplay of Lemmings and narrowed it down to one character, allowing for a lot more room for puzzle solving.
Eets Munchies, on the other hand, has you paying $7 for an iPhone style (and quality) game.
The resolution is capped in a very weird form that just ensures it was clearly built for mobile (going in fullscreen leads to big black bars on either side), and the system of "different worlds, few levels, 3 stars" that can be seen in games like Angry Birds is here.
The presentation of Eets is wonderful (even with resolution restraints) but the execution is off. Puzzles are either ridiculously easy or incredibly hard due to countless errors in timing. Think of it like the puzzles in Portal 2 compared to Portal: you understand how to set up the puzzle and you should get it done properly, but if your timing is off than your work is for nothing.
Not to mention of course that the only changes since the "beta" version were 2 other worlds, one of them being the "mystery" world, which is chock-full of those timing oriented puzzles.
Too easy, too short, and too little. Maybe buy this on iOS when it's cheaper and they plan on updating with more levels.

A truly incredible metroidvania that perfectly captures what makes the greatest games of the genre so interesting, challenging, rewarding, and ultimately worthwhile to play. Bolstering an immense depth of varied locations, abilities, bosses, and secrets, not to mention fantastic level design, Hollow Knight's main goal is very apparent: To immerse the player in a world that rewards exploration to the fullest. This is something that every metroidvania strives for, yet so many miss the mark by either not incentivising the player to explore further due to a lack of meaningful content, or by bloating themselves with far too many unneccessary features and systems which serve only to muddy the experience. Hollow Knight has accomplished the difficult task of finding a perfect amount of everything a player could expect from a metroidvania, and has added its own unique hand-drawn charm to it. I'm struggling to find anything in this game that I could consider a con.
Pros:
- Immensely rewarding world to explore in any fashion you choose.
- Very chalenging by the late game, but not over-bearingly so.
- A staggering amount of content for the pricepoint (100% achievement completion has taken me just under 50 hours).
- Beautiful, hand-drawn artstyle with fluid animation.
- Great variety of environments, characters, and enemies.
- Very atmospheric soundtrack.
- Interesting (albeit sparse) writing.
Cons:
- It ends (although there will be more content patches soon!).
I really can't stress enough how amazing this game is. Absolutely 100% my game of the year, well worth full price.
