Eets is a game about a little white... whatchamacallit thingy named Eets who is very hungry, and changes his walking behaviour via emotions: Happy, he'll just plod along at a leasurely pace and jump over edges, scared, he'll slowly creep and back away when he comes to an edge, and angry, he'll stomp around at a fast pace and pounce over edges like he's trying to win an olympic event- and you have to use these emotions and a bunch of activatable tools to get Eets to his goal of a nice tasty cake on a rope.  While I was a fan of the original Eets Chowdown (in fact, one of the first DLC I ever got on the Xbox 360) I do admit it had some flaws, most glaring of which was the precision of the puzzles combined with how very easy and tempting it was to just go "Give me the solution", and cheat your way to victory. While Eets Munchies has the same "Give me the solution" option, I'll be honest- I don't feel as tempted to actually USE it: So far the precision of the items is not as pixel perfect as the original, and those times where you do put something in the wrong place don't feel as frustrating.
Another great improvement is the music. Sound effects are replaced with a bunch of notes reminesent of the old Warner Bro's Coyote and Roadrunner cartoons, where Eets foot steps are punctuated by music depending on his mood.  Given that Eets is now no longer 3D rendered, and is now 2D animation, this also makes it tons easier to tell what his mood IS exactly (a feature that previously had to be conveyed in a little close-up image of Eets- especially if Eets starts off the level in the air.)
Add to that a level editor, and I'd say Eets is now a much better game then it's first outing.

Of course I did not complete The Stanley Parable, after all the end is never the end is never the end... However I pretty much saw all of what can be seen, both by playing the game (90%) and watching some easter eggs and the art ending on Youtube (10%). I didn't give a meaningful score to The Stanley Parable, because The Stanley Parable isn't a game: it's an interactive statement regarding (mostly but not only) gaming narrative. It's basically a very well thought thesis, only it's not written in words, but with code; a thesis built around paradoxes and illogicalities, such as the clearly and purposedly paradoxical main ending, the one you reach following the narrator's instructions step by step, resulting in the only outcome permitting Stanley to obtain freedom. However there are also paradoxes created unwillingly by the developer: the Unachievable Achievement, something you literally can't achieve in game if not in a completely random way, with the developer changing the way the random process worked with each patch, ended up becoming the only real and practical achievement of the game when gamers collaborated in real life to find a way to activate it through cheating, something that ended up being very difficult in and on itself, as the developer had tried to block cheating in many ways.

I really want to love this game.
When it's doing what's promised, being a melancholy metroidvania with an interesting world to explore, with fantastic art and sound and fun, interesting boss encounters; the game is a joy.
Sadly, the entire experience is soured by two things.
1: The controls aren't quite perfect. They're close, but they're *just* off enough to be an issue, and in a game of this type that's a dealbreaker. Even with v-sync disabled, there's a tiny, but noticable input lag and sometimes jumps don't even go off at all. Also the hitboxes for platform edges seem ever so slightly wrong sometimes too, appearing a fraction larger than they actually are.
2: The incomprehensible decision to copy Dark Souls' mechanics almost exactly and shoehorn them into a game that benefits from them in no way whatsoever. I've nothing against Dark Souls. In fact, I love Dark Souls. But I didn't want to play Dark Souls when I bought this. I particularly didn't want to play Dark Souls made by people who have no understanding of WHY Dark Souls works (I could play Lords of the Fallen for that, hurhur).
In terms of difficuilty, it's probably just right. Not too hard and not too easy. The problem is, I never felt like I was in any danger of losing my stuff whenever I did a (sometimes idiotically long) "corpse run" back to a boss. There's no risk vs reward angle when the risk doesn't exist. It just becomes filler. A chore.
It's depressing when developers sabotage their own game in such a fashion, because even with the somewhat flaky controls, this would've been a good game if not for the tiresome, and by now exceedingly overdone, cloning of Dark Souls mechanics for no reason.
Seriously. Indie devs. Stop it. You're not Dark Souls. You don't need to be Dark Souls.

My recommendation is only Valid to fans of Warhammer 40k & Squad Tactical Turned based games.
First off I have to say that like many others I was hoping for a Warhammer 40k: Space Hulk done like the excellent Xcom reboot from 2012.  I had seen, but never played the original Space Hulk, and have never got into the table top original.
After seeing it initially I thought oh, if it is like Incubation then I will still love it. It still did not have the variation that Incubation gave but I played through a few hours before having a copy purchased for me.  As such I can honestly say I knew what I was getting.
The Good:  To the best of my understanding it is a reasonably faithful recreation of the table top version and has the feel of a Warhammer game initially.
The Bad:  It is a recreation of the table top game with tolerable graphics, bland sound, and no atmosphere in either.  the game play easily gets repetitive and most stages can be completed by holding corridors with ordinary bolter armed dreadnoughts on overwatch. It is the height of Rinse and Repeat.  You have no sense of involvement in the squads or their members, meaning i feel no personal loss when a team member goes down other than annoyance, The price is too high for the game and I feel it should have been in the $15 range.
The Personal:  Having had it purchased knowing the faults you may wonder why. Well.....
1.  Warhammer, duh!  A fan does it and just fills in the blanks in his mind.  I imagine the sounds that
are missing, I picture the graphics being better and my imagination puts me there.
2.  Squad Tactical Turn based game.  I love them and so will forgive some.
3.  Despite there being very little variation it still is interesting in the begining each each turn in
planning out deployments and deciding how to achieve the objective. after the first 5 minutes
though it is all auto pilot.
4.  I grew up playing games on an Atari 2600, then Nintendo Famicom, Sega 16bit, and early PC
games like Wolfenstein and Blake Stone.  Graphics and sound are not the only things that attract
me I want solid game play mechanics and while simplistic this game feels solid in that aspect to
me.
I give this a personal score of 6/10 and only because I am ignoring the (personally feel) high price.  If i had to calculate the pricing into my view of the score i would make it 4.5/10.

I know we've seen "Set up a town, go through a portal" before - but there were always challenges in they way of that. Here there seems to be no challenge, and it all just seems terribly...pointless.
I am wrestling with the decision of whether or not to refund this game, and I have NEVER refunded a game before, that is the measure of how disappointed I am.

I started with Stronghold 2 and have played every other game since. You may have seen a lot of negative reviews on Stronghold Crusader II, allow me to counter those reasons.
"It's completely different to the first one"
- It isn't 'completely different' at all
- It has NEW features and units, it would be different
- The whole point of a NEW game is that it isn't 'identical' to the previous, why would you buy a sequel that was exactly the same?
"It's poorly optimised"
- I can run this game in 1080p and keep a solid 60FPS in most cases with all my settings on medium. I have a 3.1GHz processor and a discrete GPU, come on
- They recently released a new patch with a huge bunch of optimisation tweaks
"I hate it, so will you"
- Possibly the most ignorant review ever
- If you like Stronghold 2 and you like Stronghold Crusader, you will most likely enjoy this too
The new features really appeal to me. Not just in-game but lobby personalisation. Allowing you to set certain tradable goods, peace time, teams etc. Sure these were available in Stronghold 3 but the options are far better now.
If you are a lover of the Stronghold franchise, then give this game a chance. It's well worth the money, I assure you :)

I bought Demolition Inc. on sale after seeing the trailer. It looked like a fun puzzle blow up so I gave it a shot.

To think I preordered this game for 50 bucks, and for some reason I thought it would turn out good.
I was wrong. I could use that 50 bucks back too. Heres why:
-FAR less units than the original
-Absolute nightmarish AI with infinite resources. Expect them to already have a castle and an army headed your way in 5-7 minutes.
-I got bored of the campaign. Rather quickly too.
-Laggy for some reason
-Watered down gameplay. Once upon a time, Stronghold was known for being a castle-sim RTS. And boy, were the older games SO MUCH FUN. Now? Its a watery, poor RTS. Really Firefly? What happened? All you had to do was make a sequel to the original crusader. Does anyone remember having cool things like executing criminals and inspiring fear to your own people? How about the old Honor system? Castle feasts to gain honor? ITS ALL GONE HERE. Its a bit VERY sad that the original Crusader had about 42.7 times more content. I think you were better off doing a 3D remake. Not this.
-Instead of fixing the game, Firefly makes some DLC's. I understand you are a small company, but you already milked those that bought this 50 bucks each. At this point, you don't NEED more money.
-I don't know if this still happens, but even with 3 other people in a multiplayer game, it will either crash or disconnect. Fun.
-It takes FOREVER to get resources. I do not recall it taking THIS long in Stronghold 2 + Stronghold Legends.
-Again, Firefly could've had something going on here. but I couldn't tell you what happened. But the game just feels empty and not really finished.
-Am I done yet? No.
-There were interesting choices, like using the Havok engine for destruction. It DOES feel good when you tear down an enemy wall or tower. BUT the wall or tower will just re-appear momentarily.
-Strategy? What? You think this was Strategy? I've played this game long enough to tell you that even if you DID get an army of units, you'll notice there is NO thinking involved when you attack. This is because there are 2 main types of units, and a few Special Mercenary units that attack in different ways. The Mercenaries were an interesting touch, to be honest, but if you see a large force of Arabian Knights heading your way, you'll notice your archers basically tickle them to death from a distance with arrows. Literally the only way to counter the tougher units like Knights is with Knights. The only thing to be concluded about strategy here is that Archers are used for taking out unarmored units and enemy peasants, and the tougher Melee units are only good for countering units of the same type. Fun. On top of that, the AI still has infinite resources and can spam such said Knights and such said Archers before you can blink.
-Even worse is that back then, it felt pretty cool to be able to siege and starve out a faction's castle or spread diseases by launching sick cows. You can launch diseased animals in SC2, but its just an area of effect that deals some damage over a little bit. As for starving them out? Nope.
-False advertisement. I will quote something from the description that makes me laugh every time: "Crusader 2 recaptures the original game’s addictive, fast-paced gameplay and authentic castle simulation". What fast-paced gameplay? You mean being rushed by the AI before you can recruit one guy is fast-paced? Authentic Castle Simulation? What are you simulating exactly? Nothing. The only thing to look at in a castle are the citizens moving about, gathering resources, etc. Thats it. No feasts, no jousts, no guards chasing criminals, no criminals rotting in a jail, no criminals being tortured, no criminals period. No falconers, dung patrol guys, no jester wandering around, no women tending to the households and going about, Nothing but people walking around. Sigh. Just a boring, plain castle with next to having absolute zero life in it.
You know, if Firefly would have created a sequel by following in the footsteps of the original and grabbing a few things from the previous Strongholds, it would've been worthy of the 50 dollar price tag. I can't even fathom this game being sold for any more than 10 dollars. I would rather see the old 2D crusader ported into 3D, with the same units and stuff. That would've been much more worth it. But I just CANNOT understand HOW these guys messed up. They have the IP of a game that could quite possibly DESTROY the other RTS games out there. They could've gone more in-depth and perhaps added bigger maps, a territory system that you see in games like Rise of Nations, more units, actual strategic thinking, Hell, even some decent optimisation and a really high unit cap would've turned the tables. It seems like the graphic quality of this game surpasses the actual gameplay too.
If you read this enormous wall of text I typed out, I thank you for reading this rant. If you are thinking of buying this game, GO BUY THE STRONGHOLD COLLECTION. It costs less and just ONE of the Strongholds it comes with has LOADS more content than this... abomination. It pains me to write this because this was once a respected series, and now its come to this.

Look, this is a positive review ok? I can't recommed this game enough. It looks and sounds beautiful. The atmosphere is phenomenal. Gameplay is fluid, fun and there's enough challenge if you go looking for it. Hollow Knight is possibly... no, screw that! It is MOST ASSUREDLY the best metroidvania since the two games after which the genre "metroidvania" was named. It has given me moments of unbridled joy and existential contemplation. In the act of playing, the spectrum of my emotions has grown both wider and more nuanced. It makes me want to become a better man. Because of it, I will go back to studying entomology, exercising regularly and I will donate to the poor. And if I ever have children, I will name them after characters in this game! OKAY?!
Having said that, *ahem* I am now going to make some minor criticism concerning the very few bumps on the road to the utter and unfathomable bliss that is playing this masterpiece to 100% completion. Spoilers ahead, I suppose.
(a) Game Hiccups!
I tried playing at minimum resolution, disabling v-sync, lowering particle effects, all at once, but no dice: At certain points, the game would always freeze for only a fraction of a second, but that would be enough. Whenever I stepped on a breaking floor section, the game would hiccup immediately before its collapse, and most of the time it would be too late to avoid the spikes beneath. Traversing the Deepnest was particularly annoying because of this.
Another (infinitely worse) instance of this was battling the Radiance, who caused the game to hiccup almost every time it generated a wall of spikes. Speaking of Radiance, why do I... no, let me deliver this with the proper emphasis: WHY. THE. UNMITIGATED. ♥♥♥♥. MUST. I. KILL. THE. HOLLOW. KNIGHT. EVERY. ♥♥♥♥ING. TIME?! There, rhetorical question delivered. Next point!
(b) The map system is annoying (style over user-friendliness?) and the fast travel spots are a hundred miles away from each other and from most points of interest. Not to say that I didn't love and cherish every minute spent traipsing about the labirinthian delights of this game's visually compelling environments, but... no, actually that is exactly what I'm saying. At certain points, it got old, and then it never got young again. Some of the save/travel points are well placed, but some are irredeemably out of the way.
(c) Throughout most of the game, I kept accidentally performing Cyclone Slash instead of Great Slash, because Hollow Knight considers "up" anything in the vicinity of 45 degrees and beyond on the analog stick. This was a major source of annoyance during the Trial of Fools, specifically at the part where the ground disappears for what feels like a century of anal impalement by the trident of Satan. Eventually I conditioned myself to let go of the analog stick before releasing the sword technique, but not before spending a long time struggling with the impulse to thrust the controller into the spinning blades of a power blender and push it against them until I've prepared at least one liter of bloody joystick juice. (yes, LITER! get with the metric system already, US freaks)
(d) Salubra's Blessing
...is the reason why I no longer spend time sitting on benches to enjoy the game's scenery and music. Her giggling must have been extracted from a military program designed to research sounds which turn peaceful citizens into homicidal sleeper agents. And what do you mean "you don't have to sit"? Some of us like to roleplay, ok buddy? Stop judging me.
Just to end on a high note, I thought I might express how much I enjoyed that bit of the game where it stops being a metroidvania and turns into Super Meat Boy. I haven't cursed this loudly and often at a video game in MANY years, and I think everyone can agree that only a masterpiece of the highest caliber in terms of level design can elicit such passionate outbursts of what might have been perceived by my neighbors as the death throes of a wounded beast, but was in fact nothing but audible spasms of the sheerest mirth and appreciation.

- when attacking you just end up building roads everywhere to help your military get to where they want to go (maybe consider removing terrain walk speed slowness for hunters and military units as it just get's messy and it's a little annoying)
- Mouse scroll zoom zooms to where the mouse is instead of the center of the screen (I find this annoying, but im just nit picking this one)

So what i find is that i destroy the dwarfs and all their open portals early, then "enjoy the game," but while im "enjoying the game" i just think....  "why dont i just go to the next level, what's the point?"
- The maps are always pretty much finished before you even begin mining Iron Ore, so the iron axes are pretty much useless, unless you're just RP'ing
- Kitchens are useless.  Maybe you should impliement a lock down on food within the kitchens to prevent hungry workers from taking ingriedients and eating them.  I understand you are meant to build kitchens far away from your main base with couriers going to it to manufaction "10" food for your army, but feeding large armies is never a problem that requires this.  Also the food requires "4+5+6" foods and all you get is a "10" food...  I get this makes ur guys work for longer, but it's just not worth it at all.
- on huge maps, armies occasionally cannot find their way to new camp locations placed far away from the previous location so they just stand there bugging out until you move the camp back to a closer location

- Underwhelming feeling of victory at the end of stages.  you open the final portal, kill the 20 guards and you're riddled with feelings of "Well i could have just done this 45 minutes ago if i wanted to..." This remake of Space Hulk is a return to a video game implementation of the classic tabletop board game. Gone are the controllable first-person elements from Space Hulk: Vengeance Of The Blood Angels, which in themselves were an attempt at providing further immersion than the original Space Hulk video game (a blast from the past from 1993!) .
Of course, the graphics quality has been gently ushered into the modern age. Copenhagen developmers Full Control Apps have done a quite decent job modelling environments and characters, and an excellent job of remaining completely faithful to the tabletop edition in terms of gameplay. The music and sound-effects are very atmospheric, and immersing yourself into the feel of Space Hulk (especially the first time in the dead of night with the lights off) is really fun. Franchise fans, will find the horrific aspects of this sort of video game is very appealing in experiential terms, and the immersion in a no-way-out survival horror is probably high on the list of reasons to play.
Players can roam the hulk "Sin Of Damnation" (an expansion set for the board game) as either fearsome Genestealer Tyranids, or heroic Blood Angel Space Marines. The single-player campaign clads your squad of four in classic Warhammer: 40,000 Terminator Armor with all associated weaponry. They carry out your orders with appropriate battle cries of "For the Emperor!" and such-like. When squad members inevitably fall in close-combat with Genestealer, their death throes are accompanied with sentiments to the effect of "Avenge me, my brothers!". You will need to do a lot of avenging in the course of the campaign if you set the difficulty up high.
Unfortunately, the game is also punishing in terms of performance. Though many actions of the AI are based on six-sided dice rolls of only a few dice, the psuedorandom number generator used might well  be using floating point variables of many significant figures, for the eternity it takes to decide upon death without recourse. However, if you roll bad dice in your turn resulting in any mistake including death, there's always the Undo button. If you're terribly frustrated with a particular mission (stupid chapter artifact, why can't these pansy marines pick up a dumb chalice?) you may find yourself in a situation where spamming Undo on your turn will be the only thing which seems to get you through a difficult spot other than reducing the difficulty setting. Considering the requirements of the game, framerates go low and slow (especially with higher numbers of pixels on larger displays). This can be remedied acceptable by reducing graphics quality to medium and changing other settings. There's no pressing need for high framerates, because this a clear turn-based strategy. But smooth-scrolling around the map is necessary to keep track of what's going on. Especially when dropship teleporters malfunction during deployment! A stranded, lone Terminator faced with corridors on several sides makes an easy target for voracious Genestealers. They run in packs, don't let them get close, or even ol'lightning claws can have regrets.
The animations of Terminators heroically firing weapons gets repetitive before the end of the second map in single-player. This is quickly and easily solved by turning it off entirely in the options. The animations still play, but the camera doesn't zoom into each Terminator while firing. However, the animations still go on too long. When placing a Terminator with a Storm Bolter into Overwatch mode over a long corridor filled with Genestealers, it's time to go make coffee as literally hundreds of rounds are fired with no way to skip over the animation. It's worth marveling at this once or twice, but quickly becomes boring. The same can be said of the movement, although this can be sped up. However, at maximum speed, Genestealers are more frightening than necessary, and Terminators clump around with like humourously inarticulated style of LEGO-figurines, so fast is as fast as fast goes with that.
Of course you can always play online, and the matchmaking server will set you up against any number of eager opponents ready to kick you around the board until you just can't take it any more. I'm sure it's a long-forgotten personal motto of Blood Angels chapter librarians that in order to know the sweet ambrosia of victory one must drink of defeat until the very last bitter dregs, or something to similar effect. Whatever the cost, the Blood Angels shall redeem themselves, as their hands are mere extensions of the Emperor's will, etc. etc. So to keep things interesting, new maps and characters and campaigns must be provided for these extensions of the Emperors will, or the warp will make devils of idle hands. Or something. In typically mercenary Games Workshop style, these sorts of expansions are sold at a premium as DLC for Space Hulk. Just like the board game, so while it's a depressing monetary vacuum for fans, that Games Workshop have licensed an all-consuming Eye Of Terror for bank accounts isn't surprising. Fellow chosen of the Imperium, we must turn back this tide of Chaos! We must invoke... the Emperor's discount! In all seriousness, AU$20 is expensive for what Space Hulk offers. AU$10 would have satisfied the Emperor's chosen far more. The current asking price of AU$5/each for DLC packs is far too much. The best advice here is to wait for the bundle sale before deployment. Like the migration of Tyranid hives, a percentage off will inevitably intersect our space.

A.I. is so broken that the game is literally unplayable in it's current state (with dwarf enemies enabled)
You can play the game in a bulding/portal opening style until the point where the enemy faction shows up but, from that point it's a total mess and you either disable it in the map generator (but then the game gets boring real fast) or face the following issues.
As you cannot directly control the behavior of your troops, fighting is a nightmare given how utterly dumb and brainless your vikings are. A few examples:
- Fighters randomly engage and chase down helpless carriers while their faces are getting bashed in by enemy soldiers
- Your vikings are willing to fight basically anyone and anything in their vicinity rather than destroying the cave which countinously spawns enemy soldiers who are killing them (again you CANNOT command them to attack a specific target)
- Arrows fly so slow, that archers are basically useless against moving targets. As they cannot land one hit on moving targets the guard towers are basically rendered useless. Enemy minions are happily waltzing through my borders to expend their territory and build towers while the 5 archers eqipped with longbows are unable to hit them
- Supply depot mechanics are broken. No gold or weapons are getting delivered to your remote army camp to train and upgrade your soldiers, so you have to continously relocate your army camp back to where the goods are stored. Dudes are crying without weapons at the depot, yet your carriers will not deliver the pile of axes from the blacksmith.

- Carriers who got attacked while delivering goods will try to get that one specific item until ETERNITY at the cost of their lives
- I don't even wan't to start on the logistics part... because that is just.. insanely bad.
While the game is really atmospheric and brings back the old Settlers feeling, the disfunctioning and mindless A.I. renders it unenjoyable.
Save yourself the trouble and skip this for now until they FIX IT, or just play with the dwarf enemies disabled.

When this game was first released it was a shambolic, buggy mess.  I have heard that many of the bugs have since been fixed, but it really isn't good enough to sell a game as a full price release offering just ten or so missions, which is not even fit for purpose.  I played for 7 hours and that was really enough for me.  The initial experience has probably soured my opinion of the game permanently.  There is some strategy and enjoyment here but the game is slow, repetitive and looks terrible.  Perhaps the greatest failing for me was the complete lack of customisation or any connection the player feels towards his marines.  You can't even choose the marine's loadouts or name them and they don't increase in ability in any way in between missions.  This means you have no attachment to any of the marines and don't care when they die.  All in all, not enough time was spent making this game and it lacks any real innovation or little touches that would have made it an enjoyable title and done the IP justice.

I love the Stronghold series, but I cant reccomend this game. They got a lot wrong here in an effort to make it a game more based on war rather then economy, and the end result is unfortunately not all that fun. let me explain why.
The devs said over and over while the game was in development that they were trying to recreate the fast paced skirmish mode feel you got when you played the origional stronghold crusader. While this is a good intention, the end result pretty much adds up to the enemy sending countless waves of small suicide squadrons to your castle CONSTANTLY, never bothering to create larger seige forces as a reaction to your castle growing larger. It is flat out tedious. At the end of a skirmish match when it says you killed literally around 3,000 enemy archers, you just want to smack yourself in the face.
They also majorly streamlined the popularity and economic systems from previous games, so now keeping your people happy is as simple as making sure they have food. Making money boils down to making ridiculously high numbers of breweries and candle shops so your peasants are happy enough that you can raise your taxes. So your castle will always be the biggest candle factory and beer company in the Holy Land. Thats very realistic.
Apart from that, they also decided to take out the funny little things your peasants said when you click on them, which is kinda sad, and they descided to release more AI opponents two by two in DLCs, after only giving you an insulting eight opponents at launch, while the origional Crusader gave you eleven at launch. and for this high price? its a rip off.
Sorry Stronghold fans, this was not the redemtion from Stronghold 3 that you were looking for. At least it functions, though.

Were you ever a fan of the Pirates of the Carribean movies? The adventures of Captain Jack Sparrow to become the greatest pirate of the Carribean in his majestic Black Pearl. Ah, the memories.
What's more, if being a pirate and plundering the Carribean on your swift frigate by day is not enough, you can be an assassin by night and carry on the legacy of the previous Assassin's Creed Games.
Assassin's Creed: Black Flag follows the main character, Edward Kenway, as he goes from a lousy pirate to a fully fledged assassin for the brotherhood. The combat is very fluid and well-developed and the naval combat is surprisingly alright (besides too much smoke in battles).
Personally, I really enjoyed the 1700s feel of the game, fighting with cutlasses, and boarding other frigates and the occasional Man O' War. I put let the Pirates of the Carribean theme song loose as I jumped from the rigging onto the deck of enemy vessels and started my rampage with my trusty cutlass and the jewel encrusted set of pistols.
The story line was excellent up until the very end, where it unfortunately took a turn to a work of fiction and killed the immersion it previously provided. However, that negative did not outweight the entire game.
The game offers various clothing customization options, which are nowhere as good as the DLC costumes you can acquire. There is a fairly good selection of pistols and swords as well. Your ship, Jackdaw, is also available to be customized.
You can fight soldiers, assassinate some pesky targets, run down some thieves, board and capture military vessels, and take on the role of Jack Sparrow...literally...as you sail the high seas and make the Carribean fear your name.

Giving credit where credit is due... DTG far exceeded my expectations with TSW.  I've played it for about 10 hours and am very impressed!  Performance is adequate on my system (4790K oc'd to 4.6 with an old GTX770) using the "high" preset at 1920x1080.  Frames average in the 30's... higher with shorter consists and out in the country... a little lower (mid 20's) in the yard and when other trains are nearby.  While it could probably use a little optimizing, it is certainly not unplayable like some reviews have implied.  People need to remember that this is a sim, not a shooter... it's not going to (and doesn't need to) hit 60 fps using today's hardware.
Visuals are gorgeous.  The models exceed anything I've ever seen in a sim.  The level of detail (especially with the trees) does decrease a bit rapidly with distance; but the close-up textures are SO detailed, I imagine they had to dial in the LOD circles to maintain performance.  The night lighting and weather effects are exquisite (my only complaint is that the STARS are huge and overly bright on clear nights).
I've never been anything more than a casual train driver, so I can't comment on the physics; but everything feels about right to me.  It seems like it's much easier to control speed than in previous versions.  Controls are all logical and menu layout is much less confusing than the old TS versions.  I do agree with others that they should allow users to change the keybindings though.  I really love how I have to get off the train and walk down to the track to manually switch the rails (but can also do it via the map if I'm feeling lazy).
While you only get 3 freight locomotives and a single 60-mile route in Maryland/Pennsylvania, the scenery is beautiful with a huge amount of detail.  It seems DTG has adopted a quality over quantity approach this time around... and that works for me.  I probably have 10 routes that I bought on sale for the old TS series that I never even loaded up.  Overall, I think DTG has a winner with TSW and look forward to seeing what third-party content becomes available in the future.

My computer exceeds the "Recommended" spec and so I thought the game would run brilliantly, unfortunately I was wrong. I struggle to get more than 20-30fps in the yard and beyond the yard it only increases into the 40fps range, though it's still peppered with lag spikes. For comparison, I get solid performance with the frame rate locked at 60fps in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter Redux, which also makes use of the UE4 engine. TSW isn't unplayable because of it, but the lag spikes and perceivable low frame rates in places spoil the illusion. The real shame is that these issues were present in the Beta version and widely reported, but still the issues remain.
I also take issue with the screenshots above; I'm running the game on the highest graphics settings and they don't look as good as the screenshots above led me to believe. The game has some strange post processing which sometimes makes stuff a little washed out overall with dark edges, at times looking almost "cell shaded" in appearance. I can only assume that the above images were produced at very high resolution and then resized down to 1920x1080. You can see what I mean in the screenshot below:
The advertising screenshots above also include two cabooses, I assumed that these would be usable in game, allowing the player to sit at the back of the train and enjoy the journey from the caboose cupola; Unfortunately they only appear as static scenery and serve no other purpose. It's strange that what is effectively a scenic item is featured so prominently in the advertising images above, especially as all the rail vehicles in ALL the other screenshots are usable, giving the impression the cabooses are too.
My advice to anyone thinking of purchasing TSW is to wait until the optimization issues are rectified. There is a lot of potential for a good simulator here, with UE4 providing a much better and up to date foundation for development, as well as improved physics and expanded scope for player immersion and interaction. I just really hope DTG are able to sort out the initial issues before they move on to additional content for the game.

This game is really good, even at its early alpha stage. For the features that are in they are fairly well implemented as well as a whole, there are more features in so far then some games have at full release. Gameplay and look is similar to how games like Minecraft and similar 3d open world sandbox games where you make your own story. It is obviously in space, even though you can go onto planets.

The game at this moment is capable to being modded, with its Block Editor(which allows you to make/modify new or existing blocks). The server config which is also the configs for single player is fairly customizable, with the ability to toggle/change settings that are normally reserved for mods in other games.

Ships are dynamic in that they are all different based on what you built them with and what types of moduals you placed in them. Also the fact that you can mix and match compatible moduals together to create a new type of weapon or utility tool. The most common example is that by default a salvage(aka mining) modual will just do a burst beam, but if you connect the salvage computer to a cannon computer with just the right ratio of moduals you can get a constant steady beam for the salvage modual and mine/eat things to your heart's content.
Building is fairly straight forward for its most used functions, as well as for those who want more tools, there are more precise tools and options. Gameplay is very much like other games of it's genres. As a side effect though, with this game's many options and complexity, there will obviously be a learning curve. Where the player will need to learn how to setup the blocks and moduals, as some have their own placement rules. Thankfully there are many tutorials and Lets Play videos out there so learning will not be too difficult.
In all I recommend this game to anyone who likes; space games + open world sandbox games + lots of options, for its $9.99 USD price at this moment. As well as the developers currently have the full game for free as long as it's in early access. I bought it though, because it's pure awesome in my opinion, and I'll gladly pay the $10 for the game as well as the fact that buying the game helps to continue it's developement.

First things first...  in my opinion) this game is amazing, but far away from being flawless:
Starmade is a voxel based sandbox game in space. A game where the player is able to build massive objects like a fully functional(!) Deathstar or a Viper from Battlestar Galactica or anything else one can think of. The only limit is ones own imagination. But thats not all. There are plenty of different things to explore, like space stations or ancient ruins on planets. Or you can just adventure out into deep space, to find asteroid fields to mine. And as an nice addition, the map is gigantic!
That said, getting into the game can be a bit rough, because the tutorial, while it is very helpful and offers plenty explanations about everything in the game, is buggy as hell and pretty boring (although, that opinion can differ from person to person) .
The controls are easy to learn, but a bit, well, I would say underwhelming. You cant decide how fast you fly. It is either maximum thrust or nothing. Also, the menu system is far from perfection and very confusing at first.
And please dont even speak about the AI-quality.
So, what is it, that makes me love the game, as much as I do?
Well, here´s a list:
- Starmade is very configurable through some easy to understand config. data
- Huge fleet battles are possible if your rig is strong enough, that said, Starmade runs pretty smooth overall. Even on low end systems.
- Dogfighting is super fun.
- Weapon systems are pretty in depth
- Starmade looks astonishing beautiful, if you`re into that kind of voxel based textures.
- Multiplayer runs very smooth, as long as your ping is manageable
-And most important, the overall mixture of building, fighting, exploring, mining and more building is just fun
That said, I DONT recommend this game, if you plan on playing Starmade purely for the singleplayer experience. because, the lack of (good) AI and nice NPC ship designs is kinda meh.
On a server with dozens of people on the other hand, this game is amazing. (Or even a small one, with just you and your two or three best friends). You can even upload ships or stations you've built in singleplay onto the server.

Quick Review of the game I've played so far.
Pros:
It was challenging at first.
It is controller compatible
Nice scenery for a free game.
Cons:
It was repetetive.
It is not optimized for keyboards.
Grinding souls is tedious.
You can clip through walls like a knife through warm butter.
Analysis:
The game starts you off in the tomb. That's it. There's dialogue, but nobody reads anymore. (amirite)
Apparently you're supposed to help this Mummy guy, Ebo, lift the Curse of Mermos (GASP the game title!)
You fight♥♥♥♥♥♥ Cool. But that's about it. Sure there's a shop and all, but there's only those 5 items. Two of the items aren't even items.
The glyphs are alright IMO. They add a little bit of risk to the game while still adding worthwhile benefits such as life regen or more health at the cost of agility.
Cool♥♥♥♥♥♥ So, lets get down to the gameplay. If you're using a mouse and keyboard... So sorry. Controllers are fine! They work great with this game and almost every review besides mine has the controller influence it.
I'm gonna get down to the other stuff. Clipping.
I'm not talking about "Oh I can go through one of the pillars in the main room" clipping. I'm talking game breaking clips.
You can go through the wall behind Ebo at anytime. It's literally not there. You can go through any gate you want (closed or not) with these clips, but the cost is you can't continue your game any further. It will literally keep you in the room you are supposed to be in forever (whether or not all the enemies are killed).
The game is solid until you screw up with one roll and end up through a gate you aren't supposed to be behind.
Next thing. Saving.
There is none. I quit (after i broke my own game testing the clipping and such) and restarted, expecting to resume from where I had left off.
No. That is not a thing. You WILL have to restart if you quit.
Conclusion:
The game, if you don't break it, is solid. Great for controllers, but not for keyboard users such as myself (luckily I had a spare ps3 controller just lying somewhere). The story is straight forward with little interruptions, but the gameplay is repetetive. I give this game a 4.5/10

I rate the remake of the game Shadow Warrior (the remake is not to be confused with the original) 4.5/5. This is a truly excellent game and is possibly the most beautiful game I have ever played (tied with Skyrim in terms of beauty) but also one of the most bloody (tied with Soldier of Fortune in terms of gore).
While this is certainly a very linear action game with but one ending, this game is still outstanding. The alternate game modes (especially the one which lets you play from the start using all of the weapon and character upgrades you got the first time around) allow for a great deal of replayability. This game has truly beautiful, fantastic graphics. It's storyline is interesting (though it can seem a bit convoluted in places as it unfolds) and almost every aspect of this game (including its plot) is either a spoof of some kung fu movie or of is merely making fun of itself and yet for a game which consistently fails to take itself seriously it is able to present some very dramatic and emotional moments.
The action is visceral (the first-person-perspective sword fighting is the best I've ever seen in such a game. The sword fighting is fun, intuitive and interesting enough to cause me to often use my sword instead of other weaponry (if only The Elderscrolls games had such intuitive sword fighting in them, although a lot of the sense of intuitive sword fighting is due to the radically gory slices the game allows you to make into your enemies (and the Elderscrolls games still shy too much away from that for the sword fighting to feel either very visceral or dangerously realistic in those games).
The controls are tight and the first person perspective camera work is good (you can see your own legs when you look down. yay!), constantly giving you a good sense of where your character's body is even when most of it is not on screen, The environments are interesting and the action, while extremely constant, intense, and challenging, seldom seems either repetitive or frustrating. The voice acting is good throughout for all characters and the game has a well done, slightly over the top but witty sense of humor. The game's character is not quite an asian version of Duke Nukem (Lo Wang has a very different personality) but the things he says throughout the game often reminded of me (in a very good way) of Duke Nukem 3D, (except without very much of the sexism which Duke so often had). There is good dialogue throughout and the funny fortune cookie jokes (fortune cookies with humorous messages in them) add greatly to the game's humor, often just when things begin to feel more serious. Your character's vocal sidekick is consistently interesting as well. The music is fitting (and pretty good in many places) and the sound is truly fantastic. In a time when linear first person perspective action games are plentiful, this game is head and shoulders above the rest. This isn't just another action game. Shadow Warrior is a mythological epic which manages to feel epic and yet be silly at the same time.

It's been a while since I've played through a game that was this refreshing; while at the same time holding to more or less the first person shooter formula any gamer can recognize. Shadow Warrior, in its entirety is a pretty consistent package. Cut through hordes and hordes of the baddies and get a new toy occasionally. Sometimes, you will need to trigger a gate or find some keys to progress; but more or less you walk down some nice looking hallways and cut through more bad guys. Standard.
What makes the game for me is the execution. Shadow Warrior could've easily been a 4 or 5 hour game with some phoned in plot. Yet, its pretty surprising how far the game goes to stand out, despite its fps roots. The gameplay, writing and graphics are all pretty solid. Now, there were moments where the game just plain could've looked better, and assets are reused pretty frequently. And then there's the times when sprinting down stairs would result in an instant death. But for a 10+ hour experience, I'm willing to give it some leeway.
Minor complaints aside, this is a pretty well done experience. I really wasn't expecting a plot this well done in a game like this; that's for sure. And on top of that, the guns are satisfying to play with, and I was never bored blowing up what was basically the same enemies for the whole experience. That should say something. Rarely was it tedious; and rarely was it boring. Hats off to the developers for improving upon the Shadow Warrior formula.

Were you ever a fan of the Pirates of the Carribean movies? The adventures of Captain Jack Sparrow to become the greatest pirate of the Carribean in his majestic Black Pearl. Ah, the memories.
What's more, if being a pirate and plundering the Carribean on your swift frigate by day is not enough, you can be an assassin by night and carry on the legacy of the previous Assassin's Creed Games.
Assassin's Creed: Black Flag follows the main character, Edward Kenway, as he goes from a lousy pirate to a fully fledged assassin for the brotherhood. The combat is very fluid and well-developed and the naval combat is surprisingly alright (besides too much smoke in battles).
Personally, I really enjoyed the 1700s feel of the game, fighting with cutlasses, and boarding other frigates and the occasional Man O' War. I put let the Pirates of the Carribean theme song loose as I jumped from the rigging onto the deck of enemy vessels and started my rampage with my trusty cutlass and the jewel encrusted set of pistols.
The story line was excellent up until the very end, where it unfortunately took a turn to a work of fiction and killed the immersion it previously provided. However, that negative did not outweight the entire game.
The game offers various clothing customization options, which are nowhere as good as the DLC costumes you can acquire. There is a fairly good selection of pistols and swords as well. Your ship, Jackdaw, is also available to be customized.
You can fight soldiers, assassinate some pesky targets, run down some thieves, board and capture military vessels, and take on the role of Jack Sparrow...literally...as you sail the high seas and make the Carribean fear your name.

This is the first time I have reviewed a game. I'll make it breif. This game has potential, but it really should be an early access $20 game at this point.
The graphics look good, but need optimization. If you have a low to mid level graphics card don't buy it. Even the high end cards are having issues.
The content is limited. There are only 3 train types. The tutorials are repetitive and very shallow. There are too few scenerios to justify the price tag. You'll be done them in a couple of days.
The train controls are ok, but can't be rebound, which is a pain for me because I use a left handed mouse. The hud for train control is nice.
The game play is poor. It might just be me, but I don't want to have to climb out of the cab and walk a quarter of a mile to switch the tracks. While that might be realistic, it takes forever. The map doesn't show you which way the switches are pointing and it looks like you should be able to switch tracks from there like TS 2017, but it doesn't seem to work. They put these big 'what is ahead' markers that block your veiw of the actual signals and that totally ruin the imersion for me. I miss the old 'what's ahead' hud that TS2017 had. So maybe I am missing something, but why not a tutorial on the settings instead of 3 identical tutorial for each train. I could go on but you get the idea.
The piece de resistance - in the few hours that I play, I had the scenerios/tutorials lock up about 4 times. I say 4, but it might have been about 8.
If you want to support Dovetails development of this game then your $40 is well spent. I do not doubt that Dovetail will continue working on the game. Otherwise this is an over-hyped poor quality game and I would not recomend buying it at this time. Wait until you can get the game with a DLC bundle on sale. Maybe in a year, I would think. I love the possibilities with this game, and I recommend it to any sci-fy fan. There is a learning curve with this game, but I consider it a game worth learning.
Some things you can do in StarMade...
You can mix and match weapon systems and support systems for cool useful effects. You can save the ship you just built as a blueprint, build a ship yard, and have it make more ships. You can design functional turrets.  The logic system in the game is stunning, and with it you can make moving platforms, combine logic systems, and do other amazing things. You can explore massive galaxies, connect star systems by warp gates, raid pirate bases, mine asteroids or entire planets.
There are many things I am still learning about this game, and some small details I want fixed, but I am loving StarMade as it is, and look forward to its continued development.

Having sunk enough time into this to at least make it through all the scenarios, I have a few thoughts.
First off, I think there's tremendous potential here.  The game engine seems far more robust to me than the TS 2017 engine, even running on ultra, and it looks tremendous.  I'm disappointed that there's still such a small amount of content for this, and that it might be a while before some of my favorite things from Train Simulator show up here, especially since a lot of those things are third-party content from places like Just Trains and Digital Traction.
I'm a big fan of the way they've made the world more interactive (although I was disappointed that you seemingly can't crash a locomotive into the turntable or jump off moving trains and hurt yourself.  Haven't checked whether you can be run over yet, though).  I'm excited to see potential VR support for this game, since they way you move around the cab and they way they've modeled everything looks like it should transition well to that format.
I wish the sounds were a little meatier.  The horns, specifically, are way too quiet in the external view, and the cars aren't nearly noisy enough.  That said, the sound design is obviously more detailed than most of what you find in TS.
I could ramble on for quite a bit more, but I think I'll just end by saying that I hope they do lots more with this, and that whenever they get to steam locomotives, they actually bother to do them properly.

Was this seriously ONLY available on a PlayStation Portable prior to the PS4 and PC outing? This right here is what the internal dev teams at Square Enix need to channel when creating new and more Final Fantasy games.
Granted, Type-0's PSP roots show. We have ourselves many many "Loading" pauses in between levels, intra-level sections, rooms/corridors during exploration, loading for the Crystarium (ingame library... sigh; BUT we also have game systems that actually work in spite of these limitations. Team micromanagement that's actually not a chore. Quick and satisfying switching between numerous varied team members during battle.
And what a bloody awesome team these characters of "Class Zero" have turned out to be. Imagine for a moment that you have to somehow juggle a ridiculous three-man team of a mace wielder, a PLAYING CARD master and a girl with a rather powerful FLUTE..... Think on that last for a moment..... Moving on, imagine further that on ANY DIFFICULTY this game can throw you some nasty curveballs to the extent that you'd better not develop favorites. Please dear reader
LEVEL... UP.... EVERYONE
Keep each and every team member equal in level/hence abilities. the realtime action nature of combat forces you to do so. And believe me, the war-torn world depicted in game does this system credit. The motley crew of 14 members of Class Zero have the uneviable task of putting an end to a gruesome war waged among four nations. Each with their own motives. Each very susceptible to shifting alliances. And all not averse to a little betrayal. This story is told in a rather fascinating documentary-esque (yes, I created some word to serve this review) format with timeslots describing events in no particular order. First impressions of these approach would have you thinking that the story is ridiculously incoherent...
Except you'd be wrong. Very wrong.
For good or ill for some, this serves to create alot of suspense and poses questions that build up especially at the end of the game with its multiple endings. The explanation of which requires a second playthrough to unlock more information in the form of cutscenes and dialog. It's even more surprising that the story is so much more engaging and with real pathos as compared to FF-XIII; which incidentally shares the same "Fabula Nova Crystallis" mythos, but executed in a totally different way.
In closing, will there be niggles, yes. For now your framerate will be locked to 30FPS. Minor characters apart for Class Zero have some very dodgy texture work inluding some environmental areas and level design here had to take the portable nature of title into account. But, it is all executed very well in terms of pacing and story beats. Add in the fact that the New Game+ explains more of the story and we may have ourselves a winner here in terms of a great sub-series with mature sensibilities.
Take the plunge.

Of course I did not complete The Stanley Parable, after all the end is never the end is never the end... However I pretty much saw all of what can be seen, both by playing the game (90%) and watching some easter eggs and the art ending on Youtube (10%). I didn't give a meaningful score to The Stanley Parable, because The Stanley Parable isn't a game: it's an interactive statement regarding (mostly but not only) gaming narrative. It's basically a very well thought thesis, only it's not written in words, but with code; a thesis built around paradoxes and illogicalities, such as the clearly and purposedly paradoxical main ending, the one you reach following the narrator's instructions step by step, resulting in the only outcome permitting Stanley to obtain freedom. However there are also paradoxes created unwillingly by the developer: the Unachievable Achievement, something you literally can't achieve in game if not in a completely random way, with the developer changing the way the random process worked with each patch, ended up becoming the only real and practical achievement of the game when gamers collaborated in real life to find a way to activate it through cheating, something that ended up being very difficult in and on itself, as the developer had tried to block cheating in many ways.

I went through and played the game until wave 29 and just couldn't take it anymore. I was having fun at first but by the time I got to wave 11 I started getting very aggrivated, it's not hard or anything just annoying. Enemies spawn right on top of you so you have to constantly roll to not get hit, this is not good game design. I appreciate that you guys released it for free so I can't really complain I guess but I found myself asking "When is this going to be over"? I don't mean that in a good way either, I was genuinely annoyed by playing this. There is no point to having melee attacks at all in this either, you take way too much damage when attempting to do so and I ended up just using the bow instead. By the time you get the charge shot you realize just how broken the combat is as well, since you can't aim with the second thumbstick you have to use the lock on system which you called strafing for some ungodly reason. How about calling it what it is instead. I didn't know I could lock on until the sixth wave because of it when you decided to put a tutorial message about it in the upper right corner of the screen. You can't call those videos in the beginning a tutorial either, they just show you gameplay with no real description of whats going on. It's a good effort for a student project but if you're going to be doing game design when you get out of school there are a lot of things you need to take into consideration from this project. I honestly do not see a point in this game being released on steam other than to show off your hard work which is probably just copied and pasted from source that is already available on the web. Anyway, back to the lock on system, you'll miss more shots than you'll hit due to having to use it and since you can't aim without moving it makes things much more difficult than it should be. I don't mean difficult as in hard either I mean controlwise this game is garbage. In the later levels you'll find yourself rolling around the entire map until all of the enemies spawn and then leading them single file into your charge shots... this is not fun. With all that said, I still say good work to the devs because this is great for a school project but I just feel like there should be more to the game than there is for it to really gain traction here on steam. Eets Munchies is an adorably animated puzzle game starring a furry white rabbit/flea amalgamation, one which I honestly can't determine if cute or creepy. It's a relatively simple-to-pick up game with basic controls and (for the most part) a friendly interface; this, combined with a gradual learning curve, helps Eets live up to its all-ages claims. It's a surprisingly fun game to play, and I couldn't help but find myself enjoying each level.
-Gameplay & Controls-
The game revolves around placing a series of wooden platforms and powerups while triggering different mechanisms to help our friend Eets get to a brightly colored cake at the end of each level. Along the way, the player can also grab different candies as a sort of optional collectible; gathering the different collectibles became rather challenging as time went on. While the concept is simple, navigating through each puzzle becomes an overall enjoyable experience. With the addition of Steam Workship, the amount of puzzles for Eets to navigate is essentially endless, which should keep at least a few ingenuous players coming back for more.
-Graphics & Visuals-
Despite some initial awkwardness, I found Eets to be rather graphically charming. The different machinations and animals he uses to help him on his way are lively and animated, and I couldn't help but fall in love with the Inhale Whales. Each individual World is visually different, and in some cases rather distinctive, although I have to say that I didn't much like the desert motiff of World Two. However, the game gives off an aura of 2D eye-candy after one's intial impressions, so I have to say I'm rather sold on most of the designs.
-Music & Audio-
The tracks in Eets Munchies are rather upbeat and whimsical, although after making it few the first world or two they start to become repetitive. They're overall quite enjoyable, and they certainly add some appropraite ambience for some an adorable title, but one could have hoped for a bit more diversity as far as music goes.
-Final Thoughts-
Overall, Eets Munchies is a rather enjoyable yet simple experience for the casual puzzle gamer. It's fun and charming, and has a learning curve suitable for just about everyone. I have to say that I wasn't planning on liking the game at all when I first started playing, but it ended up winning me over within the first ten levels, and I found myself striving for every collectible. I think it's worth getting if just to play in some spare time, although I wouldn't say it's meant to be experienced in long sessions as it can struggle as far as holding one's interest. Ultimately, the game is surprisingly fun to play, and I have to say that I would recommend.

It's hard to review a game like The Stanley Parable because I can't think of any other game to compare it too.  Portal comes to mind but that's being very generous.  It's basically a choose your own adventure game as you guide Stanley through his work place either doing what the narator says or not doing what he says.  No enemies, no health bar, no weapons.  You keep making choices until you reach an ending or die due to the consequences of your choices.  With that said there is a finite number of choices you can make and number of endings to see but no two are alike which is impressive and I still haven't seen them all.  It's like being in an existential one act play being acted out in real time.  Sometimes it's funny, other times creepy, there's way more variety than I thought there would be.  To bring this review back to Earth though it does not get my highest recommendation.  It gets old quick and should be played in short sessions every once in a while.  It's the kind of game you let a friend play when they visit your house but most of the time collects dust on your game list.  It was worth the experience though just for the originality.

Honest Review - Mostly Positive
Ok,
The positive things about it.
ITS FREE! Can't beat that, also, NO ADS, it is 100% free.
It's cute, it's got a great atmosphere. The music, sound effects, artwork. It all comes together to make a great little game. It plays almost exactly like Burn Zombie Burn, except with more technical enemies, and ALOT of running around. It has a great difficulty curve, and culminates in a very natural "boss" encounter and puts all of your skills to use, I wish more games ended like this one, instead of using some weird cookie cutter boss that does not relate to your skills. I loved how the game makes you develop these natural strategies for dealing with the different enemies, and I felt like I was definitely getting better at the game the longer I played it.
Neutral things
It took me about 90 minutes to beat, in one sitting. I died twice. I'm pretty good at twin stick shooters, so your mileage may vary, but that is pretty short.
Could be shorter, given the amount of enemies, but I wish there was either more enemies, or a different level set, then just the 1 room. Also, after getting all of the artifacts, there's nothing to do for 10 levels other than wail on enemies until the final boss.
Bad Things
The control scheme really needs some work. I played this using a PS4 controller, and OMG my right thumb hurt. The game is described as a twin stick shooter, but you never use the right stick ever. It's more of strafe, and JAM the fire button as fast as you can, or the melee button. After 30 levels of doing that, in one sitting I now have a thumb cramp. I don't understand why the ranged weapon doesnt have some kind of basic auto fire on it, with the ability to fire more when you tap the button. Also, why isn't the melee button bound to right stick, and then have the charge up be bound to a trigger, instead of using the same control scheme as the ranged.
I didnt even attempt to play this using a keyboard and mouse, so your mileage may vary, but I highly recommend a controller, plays VERY well with one, control scheme not withstanding.

I rate the remake of the game Shadow Warrior (the remake is not to be confused with the original) 4.5/5. This is a truly excellent game and is possibly the most beautiful game I have ever played (tied with Skyrim in terms of beauty) but also one of the most bloody (tied with Soldier of Fortune in terms of gore).
While this is certainly a very linear action game with but one ending, this game is still outstanding. The alternate game modes (especially the one which lets you play from the start using all of the weapon and character upgrades you got the first time around) allow for a great deal of replayability. This game has truly beautiful, fantastic graphics. It's storyline is interesting (though it can seem a bit convoluted in places as it unfolds) and almost every aspect of this game (including its plot) is either a spoof of some kung fu movie or of is merely making fun of itself and yet for a game which consistently fails to take itself seriously it is able to present some very dramatic and emotional moments.
The action is visceral (the first-person-perspective sword fighting is the best I've ever seen in such a game. The sword fighting is fun, intuitive and interesting enough to cause me to often use my sword instead of other weaponry (if only The Elderscrolls games had such intuitive sword fighting in them, although a lot of the sense of intuitive sword fighting is due to the radically gory slices the game allows you to make into your enemies (and the Elderscrolls games still shy too much away from that for the sword fighting to feel either very visceral or dangerously realistic in those games).
The controls are tight and the first person perspective camera work is good (you can see your own legs when you look down. yay!), constantly giving you a good sense of where your character's body is even when most of it is not on screen, The environments are interesting and the action, while extremely constant, intense, and challenging, seldom seems either repetitive or frustrating. The voice acting is good throughout for all characters and the game has a well done, slightly over the top but witty sense of humor. The game's character is not quite an asian version of Duke Nukem (Lo Wang has a very different personality) but the things he says throughout the game often reminded of me (in a very good way) of Duke Nukem 3D, (except without very much of the sexism which Duke so often had). There is good dialogue throughout and the funny fortune cookie jokes (fortune cookies with humorous messages in them) add greatly to the game's humor, often just when things begin to feel more serious. Your character's vocal sidekick is consistently interesting as well. The music is fitting (and pretty good in many places) and the sound is truly fantastic. In a time when linear first person perspective action games are plentiful, this game is head and shoulders above the rest. This isn't just another action game. Shadow Warrior is a mythological epic which manages to feel epic and yet be silly at the same time.

It's been a while since I've played through a game that was this refreshing; while at the same time holding to more or less the first person shooter formula any gamer can recognize. Shadow Warrior, in its entirety is a pretty consistent package. Cut through hordes and hordes of the baddies and get a new toy occasionally. Sometimes, you will need to trigger a gate or find some keys to progress; but more or less you walk down some nice looking hallways and cut through more bad guys. Standard.
What makes the game for me is the execution. Shadow Warrior could've easily been a 4 or 5 hour game with some phoned in plot. Yet, its pretty surprising how far the game goes to stand out, despite its fps roots. The gameplay, writing and graphics are all pretty solid. Now, there were moments where the game just plain could've looked better, and assets are reused pretty frequently. And then there's the times when sprinting down stairs would result in an instant death. But for a 10+ hour experience, I'm willing to give it some leeway.
Minor complaints aside, this is a pretty well done experience. I really wasn't expecting a plot this well done in a game like this; that's for sure. And on top of that, the guns are satisfying to play with, and I was never bored blowing up what was basically the same enemies for the whole experience. That should say something. Rarely was it tedious; and rarely was it boring. Hats off to the developers for improving upon the Shadow Warrior formula.

Space hulk has a great old school feel and is fairly simple in terms of the more modern games that are available on the market these days. However having played the board game with friends when i was younger, as well as remembering the original versions on PC this revamp has breathed new life into what was always a successful turn based strategy game based in the Warhammer 40K universe. It has been slated by many as not being very good, but i think thats a very quick to judge reaction and most likely becuase if playing on the higher skill levels it's a very challenging game.
The single player campaigns are very scussessful and the game does a great job at setting the tension and challenge of pitting an elite fighting force of space marine terminators against overwhelming odds in the face of the sheer number of alien genestealers. as strategy games go this one has been a great one and is often challenging to the point of frustration, but i have enjoyed every minute. the revamp is also promoting the development of new content including other chapters and missions which i hope continue as it is making a classic game with a face lift even more playable and enjoyable.
I am yet to try the multiplayer component but believe that placing two human players head to head will do nothing but extend it's playability. i'm about 10 missions in now and feel everyone has been fun to complete, and many have been replayed a number of times to try and meet the additional bonus mission criteria.
In short if you are a fan of 40K this is a great game to have, if you like strategy or turn based strategy this is a great game to have, or if you like a challenging game this is a great game to have. Yes there are flasher more action packed games out there and some with better graphics. however that being said, the playability, style and action that people associate to the 40K universe and space hulk all lend themselves well to this modern revival. the terminators have the great bulky plodding feel that they should, the genestealers burst under hails of autocannon fire as you'd imagine them to, and facing down sometimes overwhelming numbers has the frustration i'm sure a space marine might feel fighting to the bitter end.
Pros:
Good game, easy to play and challenging to master, has a vintage feel with a modern take and is playable across platforms (i can play PC users from my ipad) and new DLC is now being produced
Cons:
not many to mention being a fan of the game, and the 40K universe but part of me still longs for a graphics or models update, and the desire to be able to fully customise my own chapters in game.

Hollow Knight is one of the best games I have ever played. I am a sucker for metroidvania-games, having finished among others; mainline Metroid- and Castlevania-games, Guacamelee!, Axiom Verge, Apotheon, Ori and the Blind Forest DE, Shadow Complex Remastered, Momodora: Reverie under the Moonlight, Rogue Legacy and The Swapper. Hollow Knight almost beat them all for me, I would rank it on the level of the genre-defining Super Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.
Most important, I played with an Xbox One controller on 1080p 144Hz setting and at least in this scenario the game plays amazing and you have only yourself to blame for mistakes.
Next, the graphics and music evoke a feeling in me of Studio Ghibli or Cuphead with a perhaps darker tone. I bought the soundtrack as well and listen to it a lot at the moment. FLAC inclusion is a big plus.
Difficulty level is pretty much perfect as well. Combat is fluid but does not work with mashing only, upgrades always feel rewarding and tickles the completionist nerve for sure.
The map design is great and grows to an impressive size. The lore is also interesting in a subtle way.
I have played this for over 30 hours at the time of writing but am not done. During July a free DLC titled "Hidden Dreams" will be released as well and I look much forward to it. Also, the price I feel could have been tripled and it would still have been some of my most well spent gaming money of 2017. At €15 Hollow Knight is a steal. If you like it and want to support more consider the Soundtrack DLC and/or the merch at yetee/fangamer.

I used to love playing the Settlers series of games, but that kind of ended with #2 before it got a bit too military focused, and somehow lost some of the charm. So far, I've really enjoyed Valhalla Hills - it has that charm, and more. It is still early-access so I'm not sure if/how my few cons will be addressed, but here they are:
- the game starts to get a bit choppy once your island gets more populated and you have a few buildings going, but then again I'm playing on a laptop, so this may not be a huge deal
- seems to be no way to control what goes into a stockpile, which isn't a huge drawback. Each stockpile can hold multiple stacks (of up to 5-10 items, so far), but they only have a number of stacks they can hold. The basic stockpile will gladly hold 6 stacks of 5 logs, which is inconvenient if you wanted to have it store food or something
So far, those are my only two issues with the game!
Pros:
- the pacing is good. The quests slowly introduce you to each building, but it never feels like a chore, more of a guided sandbox play, which I enjoy.
- the military aspect isn't difficult so far. There's a few dudes to beat when you want to unlock the gate to finish each level (if you choose to go military route - can bypass by sacrificing goods at the altar). Some missions have baddies roaming around, but they're fairly easy to deal with and so far they do not respawn.
- the animation is good, and I enjoy watching my little dudes march around, like the old settlers games.
- there is an interesting variety of buildings so far, and I am still unlocking more, which gives good incentive to keep playing
- the graphics are really nice, even on lower settings!
Overall if you like a chill-out-and-build kind of game, this is it. Lots of fun and I am looking forward to playing more.

If you like puzzle platformers, tilting the game world around, and M.C. Escher artstyle, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are very nice - everything is hand-drawn in black-and-white. The details in the scenery are good and varied enough to keep things interesting. The music is decent, but I quickly muted it in favor of my own.
Controls are simple and easy to learn - much of your playthrough will involve rotating the game world left or right. There is a brief tutorial and large tip popups are provided when necessary (like when you die). The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with platform puzzlers. I found most of the level solutions to be fairly intuitive and solvable through a bit of trial-and-error.
Gameplay involves you trying to reach a door to the next level. To get there, you will have to navigate through the level, most likely rotating the world in different ways to assist you. The door may sometimes be locked, forcing you to first obtain a key. As you progress through the game, new elements are added to keep you on your toes. Without wanting to spoil any surprises, some of the first additions include
. You have the ability to reverse time as far back as you wish to correct any mistakes. Some levels require a light touch - you may have to slowly rotate the world to get things where you need them to be.
Inspired by M.C. Escher's artstyle, physically-impossible level layouts require a lot of world manipulation in order to navigate to the exit. For example, you may have to do a complete 360 of the world to manoeuvre your character through several flights of stairs/ledges. The store page screenshots can give you good indications of what type of levels to expect.
Overall, the game is a fantastic puzzle platformer with a nice mechanic and a great artstyle. If you are interested in the genre, then definitely check it out.

Perhaps I was expecting too much after reading all the reviews, but the game is just too repetitive to be recommended. Yes, the naval combat is fun. Capturing the ships and destroying the forts is satisfying. Hunting animals and looking for treasures is ok too. But the rest is just a typical AC game. You just find yourself in the same situations over and over again. It could be ok if the game was challenging, but it's just too simple.
And then suddenly you start paying more and more attention to poor optimisation, twitchy camera and absolutely boring and dull combat. Overall, the first ten hours of Black Flag are fun. Then you just wish the game would end asap.
And then Ubisoft decided their game isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥ enough, so every second mission in the story is tailing someone (which is very boring). Sometimes you have to do that with the ship, which is even worse. There's also ridiculous enemy respawn in some missions.
To top that, the majority of cut scenes cannot be skipped. Because seeing the same scenes (the ship captured, Kenway unburies a mayan stone or a chest) over and over again is very fun, isn't it?
Finally, for a game with an open world there's very little actual freedom.
You are too far away from an ally. Desynchronized. You are too far away from the target. Desynchronized. This area isn't available during current memory. Or you can't leave the area. Desynchronized.
These issues were plaguing AC games from the start. And now, several games later, this isn't getting any better. The world is bigger, but the game is still very boring and repetititve. Bottom line, this is the last AC game I'm buying.
