My biggest gripes with the Bridge comes down to basically two things. The controls are kind of clumsy, and everything is SO SLOW. It's hard to be precise, and many of the puzzles requires a fair bit of precision. I very much enjoy even very hard platformers or puzzle games, when the controls are tight and you feel fully, 100% in control of what's going on. Luckily you can rewind time in this game to try again, but it takes away some of the joy when you want to do one thing and the game disagrees. It's hard to anticipate in advance what might happen when you do one thing in the more physics-heavy puzzles, which lead me to my next point. Rewinding time is slow and takes you out of the game. Restarting a puzzle takes a bunch of time as well as I had to get into the menus every time. Your character walks super slow. Gravity is low, so it takes time for things to fall in place and you to see the actions of your thoughts.
New mechanics are introduced at times but are generally poorly explained. I enjoy finding out about things on my own! But not when it involves new controls that you only find out about through random button mashing or looking at the game controls again (for an action I didn't know how/where to perform it!). I was stuck on one of the simpler puzzles halfway into the game and had to resort to a youtube video only to proclaim "how was I supposed to know I could do that!"
Perhaps I was hoping for more of a pure puzzle game rather than platformer. As it is I felt I spent too much time battling the intricacies of the game and tons of trial and error rather than thinking about how to approach things logically and figure out things in my head.
I have no doubt many people enjoy the game, but these are my thoughts and someone may find them interesting or to be an influence in whether the game is worth a try.

If you're looking for a game to engross you for hours on end, let me start by saying this is not for you. With 8.5 hours into the game, I have all but completed the whole thing. The whole story was completed within probably 6 hours, if you would consider it a story. It's more of just multiple puzzles put together to really twist your brain. With each puzzle being completed, the story get just a little bit more "interesting".
The game does make you think; afterall it is a puzzler. You simply have to walk left and right or rotate the world left or right. With just those four directional queues, you have to maneuver your way through around 50 puzzles. If you make a mistake, you can rewind time as far back as you want or need to. It feel like an indepth platformer / puzzler.
The visual appeal is there in a sense. The game doesn't project visually stunning graphics. It's meant to have a simple, trippy, and hand drawn / rustic feeling. It gits the mysterious category it is portraying. The layout of the puzzles is what causes the trippy atmosphere. All of the puzzles encompass physically impossible maps and puzzle boards. Sometimes while rotating the world and walking, my eyes would flutter and become dizzy just from trying to comprehend how what I am doing is working.

Space Hulk is a game that takes place in the Warhammer 40K Universe. Originally, Space Hulk was a board game that was released in the 80s and recieved very high critical acclaim. This success would later on adapt to Warhammer 40K, which has gained a massive following since its inception.
The game has several different campaigns with two of them being DLC. The missions are varied enough from destroying a certain room with a heavy flamer unit, to escort type missions, to even simply destroying the enemy.
The campaigns in Space Hulk follow the Blood Ravens, a chapter of the Space Marines, that are seeking revenge on the genestealers for acts against them nearly seven centuries ago. The genestealers are horrifying monsters with lightning fast movement and can tear through armor as though it were paper.
Although not the best story I've seen in a strategy game, it is adequate enough considering that this game is an adaption of a board game from the 1980s.
Visually, Space Hulk is appealing with its dark, mysterious setting. The Terminators look really cool and are modeled well as if they were Warhammer 40K action figurines themselves. The genestealers also look great and show inspiration from other works such as the Alien franchise. The maps are varied throughout the game and allow the player to play in several to different ways.
The gameplay itself is easy to jump into and plays exactly (from what I've observed) the same as the board game counterpart. You won't even need to look at the rules for Space Hulk as it is easy to just hop in and start playing with your friends or against the computer AI.
The problems. The game plays dreadfully slow even with the speed setting turned up all the way. Space Hulk only allows for most stages to have one or two ways of actually winning, often time with just placing units on overwatch, puppy guarding genestealer spawn points. The only unlockables in the game are used to customize your multiplayer banner, which you will sometimes recieve. It's a 25% chance really if you're playing on normal difficulty.
Space Hulk's developers are very engaged with their community however and I'm sure that within the future, we will see a few changes to Space Hulk and it's gameplay mechanics.
As a video game itself, Space Hulk might be something less than desirable from a strategy enthusiast. It's great adaption however of a classic board game and should be played like a board game. Not like the much more popular Warhammer 40K: Dawn of War series, which is an RTS, but a board game. I would wait for this one to go on sale for less than $20 and then grab it. The $30 isn't really justifiable.

In short: RaceRoom Racing experience is a great racing simulator to those looking for cut-throat competitive AI in offline racing. The multiplayer is shaping up to be great, but in its current Alpha state it's not quite there yet. If you're on the fence, try the free content first and if you're looking to spend a few bucks, consider either DTM '92, ADAC GT Masters 2013 or 14, or the WTCC '13 pack. Money well spent.
Look below the review for a comprehensive list of Pro's and Con's after the verdict.
R3E is a competitive title, on par with Assetto Corsa. Track textures and detail are what you expect them to be in a 2014 racing sim. Everything looks quite sharp and well detailed. Car interiors are nicely modelled as well, leaving only very few wishes to be desired. A few upcoming titles might look a bit better, but we'll see to those as they get released.
Ligthing, color and saturation in R3E seem very life-like and real. Lighting conditions can be selected from one of 5 presets: Sunrise, Morning, Noon, Evening and Sunset, with full real-time transitions coming later down the road.
In the
department, R3E really starts to shine. Or roar.
Compared to other simulation titles like Assetto Corsa, Game Stock Car Extreme and rFactor2, the cars and engines in R3E sound like they have the punch they claim to have. The sound has just the right amount of reverb to immerse you and make you think you are sitting in fact inside of the car you are pretending to be driving at your PC.
On the
side of thins, there is a lot of good to report as well: The physics feel similiar to other hardcore racing sims like rF2 or GSCE. It becomes immediately apparent whenever you push the car too hard, resulting in oversteer and overshooting a corner or massive oversteer and spinning out - or if you are lucky - just a major slide of the ideal racing line.
The game does communicate what is going on under your car really well through the
. With a little practice you can judge pretty well just by feel if you are about to lose the rear of the car, or whether your rear tyres have just locked up. This is really important in a racing sim, and in this regard R3E is comparable to Assetto Corsa and Game StockCar Extreme, but still a little off from rFactor2. To be fair, the FFB in rF2 is unmatched by any other sim.
If you're not up for racing against other people over the internet, R3E's AI will give you a good challenge. They can be either set to a fixed difficulty level (from 80 to 120%) or alternatively to Adaptive AI, which will ramp up or soften the difficulty depending on how well you do against the AI. In general, Adaptive AI is pretty good at giving you just the right challenge. You have to work really hard for a Victory, but at the same time the AI don't leave you in the dust and you always have some other cars to race against.
In their general behaviour the AI race hard against you, but fair. They don't bump you out of the way, but they will use gaps to overtake. They will defend their position with defensive lines and not just stick to a single racing line. (I'm looking at you there, Gran Turismo.) In comparision to Assetto Corsa, the AI in R3E is more aggressive, but still fair.
Unfortunately the game is missing an AI agression control, like rFactor2 and Game StockCar Extreme have. I'd like to tweak the AI not just in skill, but also in agression.
Now, some time for
There are no dedicated servers available yet, so you have to hope that your favorite track/car combination is currently running on a server hosted by Sector3 studios. The servers are "jump in and drive", meaning that if you don't pay attention you might end on a server that has just finished Qualifying and you start a race from the back of the grid. Netcode in Multiplayer is really solid. No cars warping around, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t contacts and bumps between cars that are 2 meters apart on screen. The community is okay, you get the occasional idiot who wrecks half the field and other people rage quit whenever they lose too many positions for their tastes, but additional features like ranking systems and wrecker bans are on the horizon for the Multiplayer, as well as Dedicated Servers for everyone.
Now for the most controversial part about this simulator:
: Out of the box you have access to two circuit tracks, a hillclimb track and a bunch of cars from different classes. In my opinion that's decent content for a free portion of a game. Some people might disagree, but everyone is entitled to their opinion I guess.
Tracks and Cars can be bought with
or
, and after the latest update with hard earned cash directly. This alleviates my previous criticism about having to essentially give Sector3 free money in exchange for virtual currency.
Prices are not that cheap, but they are reasonable. A new car or track will generally set you back 2€ to 4€. You can get bigger discounts if you buy more stuff in bulk, or if you get stuff in packs: The DTM '92 pack with it's 5 cars and a ton of liveries is  ~10€ compared to ~18€ when you buy them all individually.
Additional discounts are granted to everyone who owns cars and tracks of a new pack: For example, I get a huge discount on ADAC GT Masters 2014 pack, because I already own most of the tracks and cars in R3E already. I think that's a fair system.
There is an option to
all the cars on the RaceRoom Raceway that is included in the game. You can also take part in the free competitions that are changing regularly. Those competitions feature a rotating set of cars and tracks. You don't have to own them to drive them, and if you're fast you might even win a prize!
Recommendations for your first purchase(s):
* DTM '92 pack (5 cars with a lot of liveries)
* DTM Experience 2013 (3 cars, ton of liveries, 9 tracks)
* WTCC 2013 pack (5 cars, ton of liveries, 3 tracks)
* ADAC GT Masters 2013 (7 cars, ton of liveries, 6 tracks)
: If you have tried this sim half a year ago, please do come back and try it again! The driving physics and Force Feedback have been vastly improved, along with the new and fairer store pricing & discount system. R3E drives just as well as Assetto Corsa, rFactor2 and Game StockCar Extreme. It has the best single player AI on the market, apart from GSCE and the largest selection of content (sans Modding) of the currently availlable sims.
* Good Graphics
* Great sounds
* Very competitive AI
* Good driving physics and FFB
* Multiplayer a bit bare-bones at the moment
* Game can get expensive if you want to have everything

A mind-breaking game. Maybe not even a game. I would liken it to a literary work of fiction and philosophy about freedom and choices. Sid Meier's definition of game is "a series of meaningful choices", and The Stanley Parable seems to be built around this definition for the precise purpose of destroying it. What is a choice, and how to tell if it is meaningful? The game is extremely simple in its mechanics, and many would be annoyed about it: the complexity stands in the relationship between experience and choices. The barrier between developers and gamers, between reality and game, is often destroyed in delightful ways. The game itself, or the storyline the player creates, do not make any sense because, as I already wrote, The Stanley Parable is not even a game.
I recommend it as a piece of art, as a manifesto of serious and conscious games and thank the developers for their courage and passion spent for The Stanley Parable. Try it, if you can!

If you have ever looked at one of M.C. Escher's drawings of impossible buildings (with people walking on what should be a floor but you can't tell if it's actually the wall or the ceiling) and wondered what it would be like to wander around on that fantastical mind-bending playground, you need to play this game.
Imagine FEZ, but with a hand-sketched style and set inside an M.C. Escher drawing.  The mental challenge reminds me of trying to solve one of those puzzles where you have to remove the metal ring from a rope threaded through a couple blocks of wood, or try to separate different-shaped metal rings from each other.  This game provides the same sort of spatial puzzle-solving challenge.
The puzzles felt fair: nothing is hidden from you.  They do a great job with the difficulty curve: every level felt like it was just a little bit harder than the last one, and I didn't experience any big difficulty spikes.  That being said, once it gets going, this game does get quite difficult.  But if you stick with it and keep trying different things, you will keep making progress.  And every time you finish a tough level, the feeling of satisfaction and accomplishment is fantastic.
If you are looking for a tough but fair puzzle game, I highly recommend that you check out The Bridge.

Short, sweet, and utterly wonderful to look at, this eyecatching game has a knack for capturing the cerebral art of M.C. Escher perfectly, but with a price in puzzle design. In concept, his mind bending art is perfect for creating interesting navigational puzzles, but their decisions to make the character slow in movement and the trial and error methods needed to solve the later puzzles ultimately lets down on the concept. By no means does this make it a poor game, quite the contrary; the earlier puzzles are truly gratifying, and while they do grow on some interesting concepts, the shortness of the games keeps it welcoming, so that the final few puzzles barely detract. A fictional story is also told describing the relationship between Escher and Sir Isaac Newton, and adds another layer to the game that makes progression all the more enjoyable. The mirrored levels provided after the base game is completed, as well as numerous little challenges and hidden secrets keep the game very replayable, but only if you actively look for them. Otherwise, it is a charmingly brief experience that will most likely leave you with a feeling of both satisfaction and desire for a little bit more.
Providing that you have the patience to wade through its more irritating puzzles, you will find a great little game, and a wonderful hommage to the legendary artist.

- It is very poorly optimized and you will get low fps (15 to 30) even with a powerful PC and graphic card (I have a MSI GTX 980Ti 6GB)

EDIT (3 April) : Dovetail has issued a third patch that slightly improves FPS but has created some other minor problems (loss of focus). So we are beginning to get away from a slide show. However there are so many defects in the simulation (Engine, brakes, ...), bugged scenarios, defective  physics on tracks (you can run downhill at 120 mph with a 10000 coal train without derailing) and so on.

EDIT (15 April) : Dovetail has released a third official update (after 2 beta runs) with a better handling of international keyboards and a slight improvement in FPS.
However the FPS stay very poor with stuttering and sometime freezing when nearing AI trains or populated yards.
There are also many bugs still alive and many things unfinished (2D map, manual, ...)
So, sorry Dovetail, but I am not changing my recommendation : Do not buy and use you valuable 30 bucks for something else. Wait and see.

It's a basic translation of the Space Hulk board turn-based game.
The major tactical consideration is Action Points that are randomly rolled each round.
Each Terminator (termie) has a basic amount - just enought get him to move
The extra Action Points allow you to respond with flexibility to the attacks.
A lot of tension from attacking Gene-Stealers and from making sure your Termies are set up in the right direction
Also tension  in the Overwatch phase, as the moving gene-stealers can rip through your Termie.
The pace is very slow.  If you're hunched over Space Hulk on your PC as if it's an adrenaline-filled FPS, you will be driven mad by the slow speed.  Trundle would be the best description of the speed.
I use it on my lap-top while watching sports.  Relax and enjoy.
Missions
They are consistent with the WarHammer40K universe but have a limited amount of variations.
Ok length for the prologue mini-campign.
Main campaign has 9 missions that get longer with each one.  Sufficient(but at what price?)
GRAPHICS
Bog-standard average graphics. The Space Marines are very good with attention to getting it right.
But the gene-stealers are a failure.  Look like Quake models - very primitive.
The Map is pretty good but you usually miss the fine detail because you are moving about
Cut-scenes are OK
WORTH IT or NOT
Sadly the WarHammer40K fandom is used to over-paying for any WH40K content.
This falls under that category.  When you have finished the Campaign, you will have had enough.
But the tension during each mission is very good and it's a great feeling when you have won the mission.
Solidly designed and if you are a WH40K fan, it's a solid gaming experience that is worth the time.
For non-WH40K fans - wait for a steam sale.  Relax and enjoy.

It's a winner.
Pros:
- Runs just as well on my two-year old, mid-to-good gaming PC* as TS2017/2016.
- Looks FAR nicer.  The level of detail, reflections, etc. are fantastic.
- Much greater sense of freedom and immersion.  You can move from train to train through the yard, walk along your own train, open panels, flick all switches, see the conductor sitting there.
- You can pretty much do whatever you want in "Service Mode."  Service mode simulates the daily operation (daily train schedule) for CSX along this line, so trains are pretty much shuttling back and forth, avoiding each other at junctions, etc.  So you really can just sit back and pretend to be a railfan in this game.
- Choose your starting location, time of day, season of the year, weather etc. in Service Mode.
- Screenshot photos look quite good for once, with the high-res textures and bright clear colors.
- They still track "experience points" based on what you do and how you do it, but it does not force you to always drive "0.9 miles per hour over the line speed limit" in order to avoid lateness penalties.  So the atmosphere is a bit more relaxing.
- Train physics are outstanding.
Cons
- Sounds are pretty good, but some seem "missing."  The sounds are a bit inconsistent.
- There are some places and activities that push my frame rate down to less than 20 fps, but generally this doesn't happen, and as I said above, it was the same experience with TS2017.
- It's a US freight train route, no passengers.  This seems to upset so many people I'm listing it here, but for me, I actually prefer trains from my neighborhood (which these CSX units happen to be, now nice).
Summary:
Opens up some entirely new dimensions of train sim enjoyment, you won't want to miss it.  If not now, then get it when your favorite route arrives as DLC.
*Stock, Intel i5, NVIDIA GTX 960 with 2GB, 8GB Ram, regular spinning platter hard drives.  Nothing special.

This game is more or less exactly like the board game. Same mechanics, not anything else. No persistent campaign characters, no unit veterancy, no choosing squad loadouts. Just Space Hulk. Whether that is any good depends on whether you like Space Hulk or not.  With its simple campaign it doesn't compare well with X-Com, and it doesn't want to, so don't come expecting that. If you arent familiar with the board game, then you would feel like could probably spend your money just as well elsewhere, but if you buy this you will find some very neat mechanics and streamlined gameplay. Playing vs a human opponent with the space marine turn timer is the best way to do it, as the timer and encroaching horde of aliens makes for great tension.
As for the single player, it isn't too difficult, and the AI is forgiving. It seems more geared to keeping you interested than winning, as it will gleefully send single aliens to their death for no benefit, so if you dont mess up your overwatch, only some REALLY bad luck will lose you the game.
Thanks to recent patches this game is, as far as I have seen, as bug free as any game gets. They also now have an animation speed slider so if you find the animations a bit slow then you can speed that right up.  The dev seems to keep the game fairly well supported so far.
Overall probably not something for everyone, but if you are a 40K fan, enjoy board games, or turn-based strategy then this game is worth a look.

Stronghold Crusader 2, a fun gaming experience that contains castle building, sieges on your enemy, amassing large armies of mass destruction, and building your economy to support your empire. As a game worthy of the Crusader title, I would recommend it for it's nice looking graphics, smooth and fun gameplay, and large scale battles.
But as a player of their previous games in the franchise, and I think others would say the same, I feel like there's so much potential to make this an even greater game than its predecessors. Coming back to this game after playing some of the older titles makes it feel a little bland in the amount of detail that you can put into your economy and castle. With only a handful of castle design options the game doesn't leave you many choices to make a really awesome creation. Moving to the economy side of things I feel that the missing ability of an option like fear factor takes a whole lot of character out of the game. This option in previous games could really personalize your play style, and that of the AI as well. You are either the lord loved by his people who serve him with loyalty, or you become the most cruel master, your castle being littered with every kind of torturer device of that time period.
As much as I love to hear that the company is working on new DLC updates with AI, I really think Firefly Studios needs to look at adding more depth to this game with new gameplay features, to get the player more immersed into the desert warfare. Stronghold Crusader 2 is a good game, and I do like some new features that they brought in that were not in the original, but to make it the best of the series, the developers at Firefly need to make this desert experience like none other, giving the player more ways to conquer this dry landscape.
This is my humble opinion of a game that has lots of potential, and a game I really want to see succeed.

The Battle for Lopez
“Dammit Vbud don’t start the engine! Wait for everyone to get in.” Jesus, the waiting is killing me I thought as the engine puttered and choked back to sleep. Sitting inside the hot and cramped M113 armored personnel carrier I was patiently waiting for everyone to get ready. To my 2 o’clock a tall warehouse rests no more than 500 meters away. Nearby are small adobe huts and a few other scattered buildings. In the middle of it all is a derelict gas station. Over my shoulder I see Kilo and Tangible get out onto an open field. They walk to the left in front of my M113.
“Alright ground team you all ready?”
“Ready!”
“Yup!”
“What about you Billy?”
Billy close to the palm tree forest yells out,
“Yeah I’m here.”
“Ok let’s get moving.”
Maj. Kilo is leading the ground team while Ice and I are on standby with the M113s. The ground team consists of Kilo, Tangible, and Zer∅, with support from Billy and Jack. The ground team walked on an exposed dirt pathway to the warehouse. Kilo taking the lead, they inserted through the front garage and started clearing the building. I heard shots fired behind me and turned around to see the support squad under fire. I watched as Billy rolled on the ground to dodge bullets. With each round nearly missing I could see small plumes of dirt flying through the air. I looked toward the enemy base seeing tracers fly out window. Returning my eyes to the support squad I see Billy’s dead body lay on the ground. Bleeding, his head lay in the dirt blood seeping through his thick camouflage. Jack quickly sprints into Ice’s APC and closes the hatch. This is no time to mourn our lost brother, we have to find the shooter. Silence.
Silence. The only sounds I hear are the chirping of the birds in the nearby jungle. I’m just sitting here looking. Looking to find the killer. I shout out,
“Hey I think I see something on the top of that hill. Its at my 11 o’clock.”
Ice replies, “I can’t see that way its behind me.”
Jack says, “I can, I’m lookin’.”
One minute passes, two minutes, three.
“Hey I see someone, yeah I see someone he’s running down the hill!”. Jack shouts!
“I don’t see anyone. Where is he?”
“He’s right there! On the left side!”
“I see him I’m going after him!”
“Wait Vbud.”
“Come on he’s right there!”
I feel like a dog on a leash seeing a cat for the first time. I rev the engine and get ready to plow straight through him!
“Vbud go get him!” Kilo says, relieving me of my building excitement I charge at him full speed, while listening to the chirps and chimes of 7.7 rifle rounds deflecting off the M113s frontal armor. I fly across the grassy field, careful not to hit the sparse but clustered palm trees. The enemy runs away as he realizes his mistake. He dodges to my right side. I slow and turn my vehicle around a large tree. I catch him getting back up from his futile attempt to evade revenge. Calmly, I throttle up and watch his body slowly disappear out of view.
“Thud”
“I got him!”
“Alright nice.”
Now, I don’t remember what happened in between Ice and I rushing towards the enemy base, but I do remember Ice shouting,
“What the ♥♥♥♥! I’m hit!”
“Ice come on get out of there!” I say rushing towards him.
I drive up to about five meters from his M113. I hear a “Fwoomph” then an explosion. I watch as Ice’s M113 bursts into flames. The fire burning the paint and its victim inside. It must have hit a fuel line I think to myself as I call out again, “Ice get out!” Then I realize if they can destroy an M113 they can destroy me too. Once again my focus must change from mourning the loss of one of my best friends to not becoming one of those losses as well. I quickly turn right and make my way out of there. To save my♥♥♥♥♥and an expensive piece of equipment. They must have run out of 203 grenades because they started firing rifles at me. I was still a little worried but felt better knowing I was safe inside the thick armor of the M113. Drip, drip, drip. Red liquid runs down my face like wine. Dark red blood flowing from my head has covered the dashboard. Cleaning off the blood I realize the throttle is maxed out and that I’m slowly spinning in circles. The left track must have gone out. Facing the warehouse I quickly reverse and spin myself towards a road leading west away from the warehouse. Fighting the drag of the left track I pull the wheel to turn the M113 left and right to wiggle just a few inches of distance between me and the warehouse.
For 15 grueling minutes I slowly crawl the M113 towards a small row of houses. Bleeding out, I feel my hands and my feet getting colder. I watch as the color of the grass becomes more pale. The vibrant and vivid greens and blues slowly fade on to cold colorless grays. Like an overcast sky on what would have been a sunny day. As I feel my body slow down, I also slow down the M113 and park it next to the only semi-standing building within the area. Half of the living room has caved in on itself and I can see through to the kitchen. I attempt to park the M113 by the house, but I end up just hitting the tracks against some rubble. After a few minutes of waiting, most of my wounds have clotted up and I bandage up the rest that haven’t. I briefly mourn the loss of my good friends Ice and Billy, and then grab my radio and call to Kilo, “Vbud here, ready for extraction.”

Remember when games were fun to play and people reviewed them based on their gameplay elements? Instead of how well they catered to their 3000$ gaming computer? Pepperidge farms remembers.
Final Fantasy type-0 is not only a great addition to the Final Fantasy universe, but a great addition to the Fabula Nova Crystallis. Giving us a different take on L'cie and the universe in which Final Fantasy 13 exists.
It's an action RPG, unlike traditional final fantasies, It's bttle system is a great alternative to the active time battle, or turn based variety. I could honestly see myself playing every other final fantasy using this battle system. The closest thing in any other final fantasy would probably be final fantasy 12, but with no gambits. you're free to move around, and dodge every hit, block and heal and attack at any given moment. An interesting extra feature is a real time strategy/tower defense combination type of gameplay. It's hard to explain without spoiling it, but it's FUN!
The game itself is structured interestingly, you have a mission, and between missions you have some down time during which you can do side quests and expert trials (extra missions, with a higher difficulty setting).
The story is quite good, there are a few times during the story that I would squee with excitment because something awesome would happen. This story really puts in perspective the power difference between L'cies and humans. The war in the story is quite real, and the game does its best to make you personally feel the effects of that war. At times being very atmospheric.
All things considered, this game is great. And to think it was just a psp game that came out 4 years ago. My sole complaint about this game is the lack of multiplayer that was present in the psp version of the game. It might be added to the game, but in the meantime there's a fake npc version of the multiplayer aspect, which doesn't quire manage to fill the void, but still helps.
I give Final Fantasy type-0
8.5/10..

There are video games, and then there is "The Stanley Parable."
Forget about normal video game rules and discover that the end is never the end.
The Stanley Parable is an indie first-person explorer game by Galactic Cafe.
Stanley is an office worker with a very mind-numbingly boring job.
In the Stanley Parable, you play Stanley. Everyone in the office has suddenly vanished, including the boss. It’s your job to make your way through the office and… well, the actual goal of the game isn’t quite clear.
You can “beat the game” in about five minutes by finding your way outside, or you can explore a seemingly endless set of scenarios that turn an otherwise static office environment into a maze with constantly shifting directions.
You are joined on your adventure by a narrator that tries very hard to tell you what to do. You can choose to ignore him and take a different route, but you may regret that decision. Then again, you might not.
There is a demo available for the game, which plays out more as a clever introduction to the themes and atmosphere of "The Stanley Parable." The witty narrator is present, as he guides you through a number of rooms containing objects found (and not found) in the full-length game. The demo comes as highly recommended as the actual game. I think "The Stanley Parable" is the most incredible video game experiences ever created in the past few years and a "MUST HAVE"

You know the scene in Metal Gear Solid where you figure you have to change the controller slot to fool Psycho Mantis? Or the bit in an Austin Powers Movie when Mike Myers turns to the camera and gives it a great big wink?
The Stanley Parable is what happens if you make those moments into a game. It doesn't so much break the fourth wall as spend the whole "game" (note: not a game in the traditional sense with few win-lose states or puzzles) smazzing it to pieces with Stephen Fry's mordant wit.
The plot of the game features the eponymous Stanley, an average drone working in his unsatisfying job in game design for a large and slightly malovolent corporation "  *cough* EA *cough*". Your job is to help Stanley escape by choosing to follow the (totally awesome) narrators instructions.........or ignoring them completely. If you ignore the instructions the narrator gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you (a commentary on the control freak nature of creative types?) but Nonethless will still manage to free style a game of sorts for you as you embark on Stanley's journey which is of course really about commenting on the level of choice offered (or not offered) to the player in video games.
So, if you are a completionist freak like me you can play the game trying to figure out where all the imaginary branches are that slide the storyline in one direction or another (although arguably to play like this is kind of missing the point in the game) and try and get all the achievements (which includes some deliberately pointless and tedious ones poking fun at pedantic types like myself). Or you can just sit back and play it a few times and enjoy feeling smart, in the same way watching Scream makes you feel like an ironic commentator of horror movies and thus superior to your average punter.
The game is short, sweet and actually has something to say (quite a lot to say actually) about our beloved art form, what Lana Del Ray (and everyone else) calls video games. It just sounds more sultry when she says it.

Let me preface this review by saying that I have very little experience when it comes to genuine platformers, and I'm not exactly a fan of the metroidvania genre either. I never really had the chance to play Metroid when I was a kid, and about 16 years ago, I found it difficult to finish even the first level of Super Mario Bros. I've only had this slight distaste for platformers since, and it's always been something I've tolerated as a secondary mechanic.
So when I fell sick for over a week, I thought I might as well give this game a try since being an adult entails opening oneself up to new experiences and blah blah blah. I digress.
I found the art style very appealing, and the bug theme coupled with a seemingly heavy focus on exploration was what really drew me in. I bought it for aboot 11 Canadian dollars on a steam sale, and having finished this game, I sincerely regret that I can't give Team Cherry more of my money for the amazing game that they have created.
I went in with zero expectations, expecting merely to be blown away by the art style and little else.Rest assured, this is the best preset for getting your mind blown.
Much like any other game, it starts out slow but it doesn't take long when you stumble into the Forgotten Crossroads and the ominous music just draws you in. If you have played Dark Souls 1, you have undoubtedly been blown away by how well connected Firelink Shrine is to the rest of the open world- suffice it to say that the Forgotten Crossroads, though not a safe haven, is so well-connected, as a level, to the rest of the ruined kingdom, that it's now my favourite example of amazing level design replacing even FS in terms of its depth of connectivity.
It took me a while to get used to the responsive controls, and I was in fact, far more salty about my own lack of skill than the game's level of difficulty to be honest. I've beaten every boss there is in the game pre-update and I can assure you the level of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t I faced in terms of terrible game design WAS ABSOLUTELY ZERO. I'm not exaggerating.
So if you're one of those people like me, who are rather laid back (terrible) by default and just enjoy the sacred gamer's journey that begins with the magic phrase "git gud", then you will find this game a goddamn treat.
The checkpoint and death mechanics are rather similar to what has been popularized by the Soulsborne franchise- if you die, you lose all your currency and have to recover it by reaching the spot where you died.
Benches act much like "bonfires", everytime you rest enemies will respawn- of course, the small fry respawn every time you enter and exit a new "scene" of that particular level, but resting on a bench will bring back the real threatening creatures.
Combat is deliciously simple, you press one button to attack and you can eventually broaden your arsenal with spells and nail arts- most fights end up being an action packed encounter where you rush to dodge the enemy's attacks while trying to get your own in, and it never gets old in terms of how badass it makes you feel.
I've sung enough of this game's praises, though. Let me talk about it's biggest "flaw", which stems mainly from my lack of skill when it comes to platformers:
If you are a semi-completionist who enjoys finishing most, if not all, of the "core" elements that a game has to offer- mainly in terms of its story and bosses, be warned that attaining the same here requires an extraordinarily higher level of skill than the base game itself. Nearly 12 of my 50 hours were spent trying to labour through the optional content to get all the bosses and story aspects, so yeah, make sure you git gud, or have the patience to, anyway.
All in all, I enjoyed the hell out of this game and I would recommend it to anyone who's a fan of platforming, minimalistic but rich exposition, deep exploration and simple, yet thoroughly action-packed combat.
Be warned though, if you lack either patience or a willingness to improve, this might not be the game for you.

Space Hulk is a game about how terrible it would be if you and all your friends were the size of refridgerators, and you all lived in a house made of hallways so you had to walk everywhere single file, and the house contained an unlimited amount of aliens that wanted to kill you.
Space Hulk is a turn based strategy game that seems to be a pretty faithul digital recreation of the Games Workshop boardgame, transparency included (You can see the results of all dice rolls).  Throughout the game, you lead a squad (sometimes 2) of Blood Angel Terminators through a space hulk, which seems to be a ton of spaceships that have fused together in ridiculous ways.  You're given a different objectve in every mission and as you attempt to fulfill it, Tyranid Genestealers spawn from multiple spawn points in an attempt to overwhelm your squad. In order to complete your mission, you have to take and hold positions against the Genestealers and accomplish the objective, quietly hoping you never have to assault through them.
At the beginning of each mission, you're given somewhere between 2-12 Terminators, each with their own equipment and abilities, and an objective to fulfill.  Each Terminator gets 4 action points at the start of a turn, and the whole squad shares a pool of 1-6 extra points called "Command Points", which allows Terminators to perform actions outside of their allotted 4 points.  You'll move your Terminators through the narrow corridors, carefully stacking them in formation, always being wary of lines of sight and lanes of approach to reach whatever your objective maybe.
This is a game about positioning, planning, and risk management.  With the exception of a couple of missions, you'll never be able to kill all the genestealers, they simply keep coming and coming until you accomplish your objective and/or all of your troops are dead.  So, you have to establish a good defensive position, preferably with long lines of sight.  Overwatch is the most powerful ability in the game, and one that allows you to shoot at all approaching enemies as long as your bolter doesn't jam (On each shot, you roll two dice, and any time you roll doubles your bolter jams).  This allows you to dominate corridors, though a Genestealer can still slip past if your roll low enough consistently. Sometimes, the most tempting positions are ones that are only a few squares long, and you have to decide if the risk of only having a few squares to shoot at is worth sparing only one Terminator for that position.  If the overwatch fails, you could find yourself overrun.  Or, you can use 2 Terminators to guard 2 longer corridors, removing one from use in another portion of the map.
It's a fun game, and the dependence on luck makes it incredibly tense.  Granted, you can mitigate risk, but you'll never be able to remove it completely.  My understanding of the game is that its relsease was filled with all sort of weird glitches and problems, but I haven't encountered a single one yet. I haven't had a chance to try mutliplayer yet, so I can't comment on that.
If you're a fan of careful, deliberate, tense strategy, I highly recommend this.  I'm nearly done with the main campaign and enjoyed every minute of it, and I'm looking forward to moving on to the DLC.

It is like reading Lord of the Rings, the first few hundred pages are boring as ♥♥♥♥, but powering through them is so worth it.
Second, the map system is just annoying.... You start without a map (and trust me, you WANT a map in this game), even places you allready visited wont be shown on your map... so you have to navigate by heart and the gameworld is a huge labyrinth and hard to grasp in the beginning.
To enable a zone map you have to find the cartographer and pay him a fee... the map guy for the first zone is pretty easy to find, but most of the following ones are very well hidden and rarely at the beginning of a zone. You can say what you want about this map system... and you get used to it after a short time, but it adds to the slow beginning of the game and might scare people off
As I said, power through the first 3-4 hours and you will be rewarded with a game that is deserving of its reception.
You know how an Italian chef kisses his fingers and says something in Italian that translates to "A masterpiece" after tasting their own dish? That's how I feel about this game.

First off, let me say that I am a 40K player and a fan of Space Hulk the board game. I am invested in the background.
Here are my first impressions after about 6 hours of play. I will update this as I complete more of the game and the DLC.
The game sets you up with a series of missions with very specific and very basic objectives and perameters. I feel like the missions are varied within the confines of the game they developed. Unfortunately, that means that I am typically slowly moving from point A to point B killing and meeting objectives along the way. Overall, this is a good adaptation of the board game and enjoyable to play. As a player, I enjoy the methodical setup of killing fields and ensuring that all of my marines exit the level safely, and that I have completed the special objective as per the steam achievements. There is so much that could be better though. Please let me outfit my terminators and develop them from mission to mission. Let me be more connected to the game in this way and it would increase my playtime.
Graphically the game is fine. There are some animations that are silly, I have terminators shooting eachother with overlapping overwatch. The animations can often cut through the walls and through each other. This is a problem that should be fixed. I really like the camera view they offer to show what the terminators see. The atmosphere and levels are good.
We can see what is going on behind the scenes with the dice rolls. I feel like I really understand what is expected of me to hit an enemy, and my chances in combat. I almost feel like I could recreate the board game from this virtual one, and that transparency is great. With it coming down to calculated probabilities and chances, the difficulty of this game is moderate/moderate-low for very strategic gamers. I am by no means awesome, and I can get through each level with losing no one when I put my mind to it. Everything is up to these calculated risks. This is where another gripe comes to mind with this game: the undo button.. I can undo and retry combat and get a different roll/result. If I were to abuse this, it would be game breaking.
Speaking of game breaking - the game is very stable!
So.... enjoy this game, and remember to overwatch! Leave a few command points to spare - these terminators have the worst storm bolters in the world!

This is an absolutely fantastic simulation. From graphics to detail, it's very nice indeed. Though it is lacking in content and features it does have some nice little details in the menu system, for example the menu, after you select your character, shows the sky based on your computer's clock. Another thing is the music, it changes when you go to select a scenario or tutorial.
Let's move on to the actual game. The performance I get on my system is about 40-50 FPS when on foot off a train, and 30-40 FPS when on a train, on medium settings. I have 16GB RAM, an AMD FX 8350 8-core processor running at 4GHz and an AMD Radeon R9 380 Graphics card. The trains are very highly detailed, in that the physics make it feel like you're hauling a big train, when accellerating. The trains brake a bit too quickly for my liking. There's also lots of buttons and switches which you can spend an alarming amount of time seeing what combinations of buttons do what. I particularly like the swinging connectors on the front of the train and on each wagon (although this becomes hyper annoying when the game lags and they tend to go flying when you change the camera from the front of the train to the back, needs fixing) and I particularly love the first-person aspect. In conclusion, though it is a very nice simulator with a LOT of potential, I'd say wait until Multiplayer comes (something I'm very hyped for - don't muck it up, DTG!) and until bugs are ironed out and there's just in general more routes and trains.

I'm a big fan of the 40k universe, though I've never actually played the board game version of Space Hulk.
I've been told it's a very faithful adaptation that plays exactly like the board game. And that's the problem I think...
Like a board game this game is actually rolling dice. Do I hit or miss? How many extra actions do I get? Does my gun jam? Can I get the door to open?
I don't like having all these random factors determine how well I play. It works well for board games, but not so much for a PC game. I have no influence on the outcome of most things. I just place my models and hope for the best.
The Space Marines are (like their armors) incredible clunky to move around. Moving one around a corner and getting him to turn around seems like a chore. Again in a board game I would just pick the model up and place him.
The graphics are "nice" but nothing special. Frankly the 3D models looks a little dated. This game has only so many different models and models on screen at a time. I would have preferred a little more attention to polish. You especially notice this in the "action-scenes". The death animations are just sad. That is unacceptable for a game from 2013!
All that being said. Actual gameplay isn't bad per se. I disregard it was ever a board game and judge it on it's own merits. It's pretty exciting to manage your marines with the limited amount of actions each turn. A lot of planning and strategy is involved. It's more like a puzzle game in many ways. And that's it really. This could might as well have been shaved down to a candy themed facebook game!
All in all I give it 4/10
It's okay, but nothing that can keep me hooked.
If you loved the board game, take a look. If not? Well...

YOU SHOULDN'T VIEW THIS AS A FREE TO PLAY GAME.
Yes it's listed as free-to-play but it's really more of a base platform for future games (listed as DLC). You get a few cars and less than a handful of tracks to try out, but the rest of it requires money. You should approach this as something like DCS World, where it's used more of a launcher for other games/addons.
While the whole pay a metric ♥♥♥♥♥on of money for cars sucks, and something I wish SimBin/Sector3 never did, the actual DLC is topnotch. I wouldn't even call it DLC because the amount of content is equivalent to a whole new game. It still runs on the gmotor/ISImotor engine so graphics aren't the best but it's still stunning and clean. Physics aren't the best and it still feels very gMotor-y, but they still feel amazing to drive and believable. AI reminds me a lot of GTR2, fast, aggressive and (for the most part) clean, they do tend to divebomb from time to time. The thing that stands out the most is the sounds. Hands down the best on the market when it comes to racing sims. You can hear subtle variations in engine tone, track surface, debris and the little squeeks and creaks of your suspension and chassis. You can even tell which tyres are locking up based on sound. Total immersion.
It had a really rough (and imo, horrible) start but SimBin finally got their act together and I'm starting to enjoy it more and more. It's not at the level of AC, iR, or rF2 but it's damn good.

Battlerite takes all of the best parts of a MOBA and gets rid of the incredibly hard to balance item systems, the mind-numbing last hitting/laning, and limiting mana/resource systems. Instead of a game of gold gains per minute and item builds it's now a game of reflexes, smart ability upgrade choices, and skillful prediction. As someone who used to play a ton of League of Legends and getting sick of the rote strategies surrounding gold and exp gains but still loving the fighting, I LOVE this game. It's even better if you have a friend or two that you know has your back. The core gameplay feels incredibly solid. I have yet to see anything buggy happen in gameplay. I'd say the only thing in this game that seems especially rough are just some parts of the UI and the lack of a tutorial for some of the game's mechanics such as EX moves, other than that it feels pretty complete and reasonably approachable.
On top of all that, the characters ability sets are all really fun and have wonderful designs with a lot of personality.
I wholeheartedly recommend giving Battlerite a shot. At least keep an eye on it. It's already a wonderful game as it is.

So far, I'm quite impressed with this simulator. I say simulator, because I see this as a large step forward for the franchise and Dovetail, and a major shift from gameplay to simulating. They're moving away from the old system, and this is a departure in the right direction. This will offer a more open platform for developers to work with, with a plethora of available resources for them in the Unreal engine.
Now, to the simulator itself. A large step forward, no doubt, in actually SIMULATING what it's like to run a train. So far, I'm impressed with the physics, and the absolute authenticity of the available trains, including being able to do mundane tasks such as fiddling with the circuit breakers. Out of the box, this feels like a high quality DLC from other developers, such as Smokebox (if he did Diesel engines). I found myself lost inside my engines, playing around with the various new abilities, which the tutorial does well to explain (such as fueling, loading coal, connecting, computer slow speed system, etc.,) and especially enjoyed the new turntable and track switching features, which feels far more authentic. Onscreen prompts are simple, providing with the most important functions of your train, while also providing you with details on the upcoming track light and next speed limit sign. Being able to walk about your train in a first person perspective adds a level of immersion that I've been hoping to see in this type of simulator for a long time.
As others have previously mentioned, this simulator does take a toll on your system currently. Being in the simulator world for a long time, especially flight simulators, I've come to expect relatively poor performance from simulations when they first appear on market. That being said, even with a decent system, expect some stutters and 25-35ish FPS with your graphics cranked. However, drop certain items such as shadows to low, textures to medium, post effects to low or medium, and you can crank up the view distance and objects while still maintaining a decent FPS that I find quite fine (~35 for me). It still looks far better than previous iterations of the simulator, and the ability to have a higher level of functionality and physics in the trains is worth it to me. Just be aware of this, and don't go in expecting first person level shooter framerates of 50+. I have no doubt, due to the large amounts of support for the Unreal engine, that the developers will continue to tweak with the simulator and improve performance over time. For performance overall, despite what I consider a minor issue with performance (honestly, some people are perhaps making it out worse than it is), I encountered no major bugs, no crashes or freezes (despite leaving the game on for about 5 hours idling), and enjoyed the experience. Pop-up of objects can sometimes be noticable (they fade in), but I suspect this is controlled via some of the various settings, of which I've not tweaked or messed much with. I'm easy to please, honestly.
The scenery is quite good, and appears to make use of LOD/tesselated models. Passings creeks will reveal dense rocky bottoms seen through the water, and the edge of your track is covered with thick vegetation. Everywhere you go there's something to look at, and some of the towns are quite active and interesting. As you pass through busy towns you'll see traffic, people walking around, and lots of interesting and unique buildings. The track itself is quite large, and moving from one end to the other could take up hours. The grade in certain parts of the track makes for interesting scenarios, as you'll be pushing 1.8% or higher in areas, so get used to braking and really pulling out the stops when hauling very large loads.
I can't recommend this simulator enough. I'll be returning often to enjoy the dense scenery and beautiful engines. I've been waiting for a simulator like this since Microsoft Train Simulator.

This is a really solid Metroidvania type game with a SPRAWLING map to explore.
The item progression is notably a bit slow, which is good, because it gives you a lot of time for exploration and absorbing the atmosphere of the setting. This is one you can enjoy at a relaxed pace, and the serene piano-based music certainly helps with that.
Controls are slick, and the combat is tight. The difficulty is on the challenging side, but it feels very fair. There are very few "gotcha" moments but there are some, which, again, rewards exploring cautiously. That said, there are just some situations where the game completely blindsides you and when that happens it feels extra cheap, because it's so good at avoiding that most of the time.
So about that map. It's big. Really really big. It's deceptively big, and you will be revisiting areas multiple times as your capability grows. You will spend a lot of time lost, because you don't get access to the maps in game until you find the map for a given area. That's a good thing. It keeps the item upgrade power creep in check. Each upgrade you get is incremental but feels like a huge boost because the game is designed around that. A hair under 30 hours in, I just found a double-jump ability, and yet, there are still places I can't go and a couple areas I haven't been to.
Anyway, I'm taking a break by writing this review because my thumbs are too sore to play today. I'm going to have to wait until they heal and kill time playing a mouse and keyboard game, but I'm anxious to get back to it...

Making games is hard and it takes a long time. As a result of spending years making something and playing it every day, you tend to become extraordinarily, mindbogglingly good at it. For years, conventional wisdom held that if you make a game so it's challenging for you, the developer, your players will hate you, and rightly so.
Unfortunately, in 2011, Dark Souls was released, and the brain of every single independent game developer became irreparably broken all at once. Now every game has to have long sequences of frame perfect jumps, intricate boss patterns and the possibility of losing everything every time you mess up.
In one sense, Hollow Knight is a gorgeous game with wonderful art direction, a beautiful score, and a deep and evocative narrative conveyed through laconic dialogue and environmental storytelling. But in another, more immediately pressing sense, it's a frustrating, controller-throwing disaster of a game that desperately needs a round of playtesting and balance adjustment. Imagine Super Meat Boy if every time you died you had to walk ten minutes to get back to where you were probably just going to die again. Or Imagine Castlevania as made by people who actively hate you and want you to be unhappy.
Is it a good game? No. Will I keep playing it? Yes. Do I hate this game, and myself? Clearly. I'm angry at the creators and even angrier at the healthcare systems of the developed world, which have obviously failed to help independent game developers receive the proper mental health treatment to work through whatever it is Dark Souls did to them in a healthy and constructive manner instead of inflicting it on the rest of us through beautiful and terrible works of abject human misery.
I give it negative ten out of a possible ten. This isn't a game; it's a curse. It is unfit for humans and should be buried beneath a mountain in Nevada with ideographic markers placed to warn future generations to stay away. I am still going to 100% it.

The only objective is to make it to the door. In some cases, you'll need keys or be required to be a certain color to be able to make it through the door. The game requires lots of manipulation of physics & gravity. You can even turn the world itself to reach that goal. In my opinion, it has a steep learning curve as the levels get more difficult pretty fast. Although, I don't usually play platformers or puzzles which might affect my opinion. What I found to be quite astonishing was the fact that you can actually rewind time to correct any mistakes. A few of the puzzles are extremely simple, so don't overthink them, while others require a lot of thought. There's also a giant rolling ball that is also manipulated by the same mechanics as your character is. If it touches you, you will die. The only problem I have with this game is that it's incredibly short, when counting it has only 4 chapters, with only 6 puzzles each. But, with this game's cryptic puzzling, it will keep you stumped out of ideas, as you overcomplicate things and try to get things in the right motion. The visual style of this game caught my eye. Once I started playing I couldn't stop. I was a bit frustrated on a few levels, but it felt so good once I figured out what was going on.
Definitely a recommendation from me, Buy it!

I must say that I was waiting for this game a long time and bought it without hesitating.
...I shouldn't have done that.
Stronghold Crusader I is a game i played many dozens of hours, single- and multiplayer. Building a castle and prepare to defend it against hordes of enemies was always thrilling. The economy system was decent and the overall look had a lovely style. With such experiences of the first part, I simply couldn't wait for the next part, expecting new content, 3D graphics and more depth in strategy and tactics. Now i played Stronghold Crusader the Second for some hours, tried multiplayer and singleplayer. All I can say is that it has way too many flaws to give it a positive review. It's simply because of the economic system. The only profitable food source is bread, wood can be bought so cheaply on the market that woodcutter lose their sense, candle maker produce candles without any resources... I simply can't understand how they can design such a system.
The military part on the other hand is actually pretty good! The selection of the units allows great tactics for invading and defending. Archers on towers are darn difficult to kill, but there are ways to overwhelm them. Fire is still a big thing on this game, thankfully! You can still harass enemies in different ways without big attacks and every unit has weaknesses and strengths. I can't get mad at losing when I got dominated with great maneuvers.
But even if the wargame of Stronghold Crusader 2 is nice, it still feels like there's a big hole in the game. I am never satisfied when I am done building a castle because it pretty much looks the same every time: A weapon factory running on bread. Before you think about buying this game, you should take a closer look and ask yourself if you can be happy with what the game has to offer.

...And I thought Gran Turismo was brutal (S-Class License in that game was not easy to obtain, BTW. Fortunately, not a requirement in this one. I also beat GT3 and most of GT4. So I'm familiar with the overall brutality of these simulators.). Then again, it's been ages since I last played a simulation racing game (At least 5 years worth of rust on me); and now with more accurate simulation settings as such, ugh. Made a decent personal time on Get Real (without shattering my car or breaking the engine), but I needed Novice to get a better handle of when to brake overall for next time (I can survive, at least, but I'm nowhere near leaderboard-ready yet at time of post). You botch the braking anywhere (especially blind corners and chicanes), and you can mess up your entire lap, or go off course, or 180-1080 your car, and invalidate your lap (no shortcutting like I used to in GT and NFS; also no more using other cars as guardrails on certain turns either :( ).
Not stopping me from playing this more, and maybe getting an expansion pack or two to have more cars to drive with and more tracks to drive on. However, as precise I can get with a keyboard, I lack pressure sensitivity in order to draw a bead more precisely; so my skills are a tad biased (better with a gamepad for these kinds of games). +20.5 seconds (1:43.334 on a track) from 1st place (Leaderboards, that is) is not good enough for me. I gotta shave off more time... If I can clear +10 seconds from 1st, then I'll be a happier driver. +5, and I'll be impressed with myself. This game is not easy, because it's less game, and more simulator. The physics are quite familiar and rather unforgiving (like reality would be), especially in Get Real (and that mode also permits fine-tuning your car's aerodynamics, gear-shift ratios, and just about everything else under the hood; and tire wear is also quite unforgiving too, so keep those in check along with your fuel). If you seek a casual racing experience, I suggest a different game, lest you want to lose some keyboards or controllers in frustration. It can become casual, however, if you're a pro at this kind of stuff.

MINOR SPOILERS I GUESS
I enjoyed this well enough, and in terms of modern FPS games it has a ridiculous amount of polish and refinement. Still, it ain't the Shadow Warrior of my youth. I guess making Lo Wang into a snarky Asian-American (and younger for some reason) rather than the loving Asian stereotype of the original must have pleased the PC police, but I was disappointed. Especially since he also seems to have been robbed of any sort of visual distinction. When I see him in the game, I always think he looks like some sort of random Asian extra. I honestly don't even know why Lo Wang was the main character, seeing as even in the original Lo Wang was not the only Shadow Warrior. I mean, maybe in the game, but that's not what the manual said. And I'm not claiming that the first one was some sort of bordello, but I was expecting some more T&A.
I was also expecting an ending that wasn't massively ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and pointless. I appreciate that the self-important story about the demon invasion needed to be concluded, but why would I not then get to go back to Earth with the Nobitsura Kage and take my final revenge on Zilla and his sexy female assassins? It was like a fun game about cutting up demons suddenly thought it needed to have the ending to Shadow of the Colossus. I love that game, but Shadow Warrior ought to be either over-the-top nonsense like Blood Dragon, or position Lo Wang as a snarky nerd in an otherwise serious story. They sort of tried to do the latter, until it was screwed over by the ridiculous ending, which had Lo Wang acting completely unlike he should act. I guess he was supposed to have some sort of contrived character arc, but yeah, no thanks. There's actually one point in the game where Wang says 'I used to be an ###hole', and I was thinking 'what? When did I stop being an ###hole? Did I miss a meeting?' Unnecessary and galling.
Ultimately, I would have been happier if the game had just been about Lo Wang revenging himself on Zilla after Zilla sent some demons to take him out, like in the original. While I enjoyed the relationship between Lo Wang and Hoji, it again has that feel of trying to shove two puzzle pieces together that don't fit. When you try to make something like Shadow Warrior have anything more than the most barebones of stories, it just comes off as stupid. Still, the game excels in terms of gameplay and level design, and you can't beat the fun of slicing through hordes of demons with your supernatural Samurai moves. I enjoyed using the sword in the original, but it admittedly doesn't compare to the sword in this. In fact, I found the presence of other weapons kind of pointless for the most part, although I'm sure they're needed on higher difficulties, since I played on the middle difficulty. I did miss the option to fight unarmed, which would have been an amazing addition to the martial arts arsenal. Oh, and the game is also shockingly beautiful for an older title, and ran at a solid, silky-smooth 60fps with all settings maxed, even with body parts strewn all over a level after a fight. While I suspect this is at least partly due to tight, dedicated programming, I do have a relatively high-end rig; GTX980, I7 4790 CPU, and 16 gig of RAM, so your results may vary.
And did anyone else deeply miss Master Leep and his volcano-top dojo? Oh well, at least there were a host of secrets with vague references to the original. Well worth your time and money, but you might find it vaguely frustrating, especially if you enjoyed the original in your younger days. They're very different games.
Check out the original if you've never played it. I know I'm going back to it.

The Stanley Parable is clever, unfortunately it sees itself as much more clever than it actually is, which makes it very obnoxious, very fast.
The underlying message is a critic to video games that offer an illusion of choice, but only give you a few predetermined outcomes. Okay, then what would be the good way to do it ? The Stanley Parable doesn't do it, in fact it doesn't even say it. Criticism is easy but art is difficult. And this criticism feels even more pretentious when it comes from someone who doesn't even try to entertain you and instead wastes your time gloating about how much better they understand narrative gaming theory than other game companies, failing at this minimal requirement - entertaining the player - that all those other companies succeed.
What makes me dislike The Stanley Parable even more is that I recently finished another game that made me question about the notion of choices and consequences in a game universe, the relation between the player, the character and the world... while still putting some effort in other elements than endless lectures and offering an entertaining experience, showing humbly how to do right rather than criticising pretentiously those who do wrong.
Undertale.
Go play this instead, and don't waste money on Stanley Parable.

To start off, I will announce that I am a space enthusiast who has played and relatively enjoyed other space games that are in the gaming market as of right now. I can honestly say that this game seems to be more exciting than almost all of them. If you are looking for a complete game, re-direct youself to the Early-Access Notice on the Starmade store page and realize what that means. If it seems like I am being abrasive it is only because I do not want people  to judge this game as being a full game and I also want you to spend your money on a complete game if that is what you want.
That being said, I will attempt to break up this review into 2 seciton's of the Pro's and Con's of this game with a summary at the end for all of the TL:DR's.
Pro's:
- Complete Freewill with building and a massive sandbox to test your creation's.
- you can Build and Create your own Station's in space and on the surface of planets.
- Faction wars if you choose to get involved in them.
- Your Mind is the only limit to your creation's. (ie. If you want an explorer ship to fly around the galaxy, a Massive Dreadnought to take on the Pirate plague the infects the universe, a Mining ship to tear apart planets and asteroids for materials to fuel your coffers of either your own or your factions you may.)
- The game doesn't really seem to get boring unlike other sandboxes (especially with friends.)
- The mechanics of the game are smooth and have a great basis for improvement.
- The Dev's seem devoted, creative, and extremely passionate about this game.
- It is still within its Alpha stage and already feels very complete.
Con's
- Could be better building mechanics such as switching out blocks for another (on larger ships) in an easier fashion rather than just setting your x,y,z to 100 and clicking away.
- The UI could be a enhanced a tad to not only look better but also provide wider control over various aspects of your ship/character/info panels (faction, ship, navigation, etc.).
- Needs more content that allow us as the player to impact to the universe around us. (again, Alpha state.)
- A bit of a learning curve which either takes asking questions, watching tutorials, or simply tampering around and experimenting on your own (I would suggest the others if you are looking to get up to speed quick.)
- I found this game just as college was swinging back around to hit me in the face.
Overall, Great game with a solid base for improvement and a galaxy and a Dev team that allow for it expand. In my opinion, the fact that this game in in its alpha state suprises my and also gets me just as excited and crazed as a girl going to starbucks.
TL:DR- Minecraft in space, but it doesn't feel like all you are doing is slapping chickens and punching wood. Instead, you can phaser a planet and watch its molten core be exposed and your storage start teeming with loot. That can help you on your way to becoming a mogul and or fueling your passion to build Fleet of your own creations. Or you can inhabit that planet and build your very own colony that people can visit and shop at. Or you can be sucked into that planet never to enter space again because you didn't put enough thrust to your♥♥♥♥♥and thus you cant escape the planets gravity. Your Choice.

Final Fantasy Type-0 is a game I wish I could have enjoyed on my PS4.
Let me begin by addressing some of my original issues with the game.
The camera, this thing was dreaded, spun incredibly fast and made combat a huge drag that gave you motion sickness so long as you were prone to it(which I certainly am). The combat, this stemmed from the camera as I just said, having a poorly designed camera made dealing with more than one enemy at a time a misery. That was really it though, between motion sickness and dealing with enemies for way longer than necessary it ruined my experience.
Moving on though, has this game improved? Many of you seem to think it's horrific, that the game is near unplayable, that you need your mother and you need her now because only an adult can save you from this monstrosity that is Final Fantasy Type-0. It's so bad that I've gotten a girl pregnant even though I have a vasectomy. Just kidding, the improvements from those two issues are drastic.
I've only messed around a solid 15 min or so just to quickly see if the issues I had from my PS4 copy were still present, they weren't. The camera wasn't moving insanely fast when trying to look around or target enemies and following that handling with a few different enemies at once wasn't a chore and in fact simple to manage which is how a good targetting system should be.
Note: The camera isn't terrible in the PC release like people have claimed, while it's not the best I've ever played with, if you've even spent 5 minutes on PS4 or XB1 with it, this one begins to feel like the smoothest camera you've ever spun in your life.(The console was THAT bad. I'll say it's better than Devil May Cry camera angles to say the least rofl, which isn't saying much I'm sure most of you can agree xD.)
Moving on to everybody yapping about the FPS lock, it's 30 FPS, is 30 FPS doing any game justice in modern times? No. Is it making the game unplayable? Also no. It has a stable 30 FPS, something real JRPG players are very familiar with coming from xbox 360 and ps3 JRPGs. If you look past 60 FPS you'll notice something, you'll notice that the game is running flawlessly with no frame drops below 30 and that it looks smooth because of that. My friends, it's no different on the PS4 or XB1 versions.
Graphics... oh for the love of whatever god any of us believe in if you even do. Calm down, the game is a rescaled PSP game from 4 years ago. There will be some wonky textures and scaling issues present. It looks like a dated PS3 game and there's nothing wrong with that, don't set your standards of Type-0 to the height of the Empire State Building because Final Fantasy XIII looks like a modern next-gen game on PC. They're on two different engines this one on an engine designed to be compatible with mobile phone hardware, the other a poorly optimized engine that looks pretty but can't deliver. (Hence why 14 and 15 both aren't using Crystal Tools and using Luminous instead) The game is presentable and serves its purpose visually, that's fact not opinion.
Characters, every character is unique, 14 in total. Makes for the most diverse playable cast in any Final Fantasy thus far.
Lore, being part of the FNC series, Type-0 shares the same mythology as both 13 and 15. While neither of the games and their characters are related, there are a few references in Type-0 and rumored references in 15 to things we've heard of in 13. Majority of it not being anywhere even close to the same, but you get the idea.
Final Verdict?
Square did right by making me not need to take Dramamine in order to play their game, could they have made anything better? Probably, but let's be realistic here, it's not some kind of new game, this isn't the new FFVII where they're taking it and remaking it on Luminous Studio.
Final Fantasy Type-0 is an HD remaster of it's PSP predecessor that's also a fact, not an opinion.
So I recommend it to anybody like myself who wasn't able to experience it on PSP 4 or so years back.
I give it an 8/10 for the PC version. (Would have been a 6/10 had camera issues not have been fixed.)

My goodness, this game has it all. I am in awe of what this small game dev has accomplished.
First off, it is an excellent Metroidvania game true to the genre's concepts. It has the common "ability gating" where you need to pick up abilities that help you traverse the environment. With a little creativity or side-tracking however these can sometimes be ignored.
The art of this game is amazing and unique. It's 2D but the diversity between all the different environments, characters and enemies is astounding. The design of these fit together so well that they basically tell a story in and of themselves. That, in combination with all the dialogue and item descriptions, make for a very Dark Souls-esque way of world-building, which I also think is very well done.
And of course the gameplay: you start as this tiny little creature but in the end you are like a god. Not only through the powers and abilities you gain, but because of the skill you acqure by playing the game. Much like Dark Souls, again, it's your skill that determines your power. Without that power, you will simply die and die again.
This is not an easy game for people who do not have the patience to hone their skills and explore the environment. You will die. But that's why I can only recommend this game. It's you, not the player character, you, who wins. It's your skill and power that saves the world of Hollow Knight.

This is a really solid Metroidvania type game with a SPRAWLING map to explore.
The item progression is notably a bit slow, which is good, because it gives you a lot of time for exploration and absorbing the atmosphere of the setting. This is one you can enjoy at a relaxed pace, and the serene piano-based music certainly helps with that.
Controls are slick, and the combat is tight. The difficulty is on the challenging side, but it feels very fair. There are very few "gotcha" moments but there are some, which, again, rewards exploring cautiously. That said, there are just some situations where the game completely blindsides you and when that happens it feels extra cheap, because it's so good at avoiding that most of the time.
So about that map. It's big. Really really big. It's deceptively big, and you will be revisiting areas multiple times as your capability grows. You will spend a lot of time lost, because you don't get access to the maps in game until you find the map for a given area. That's a good thing. It keeps the item upgrade power creep in check. Each upgrade you get is incremental but feels like a huge boost because the game is designed around that. A hair under 30 hours in, I just found a double-jump ability, and yet, there are still places I can't go and a couple areas I haven't been to.
Anyway, I'm taking a break by writing this review because my thumbs are too sore to play today. I'm going to have to wait until they heal and kill time playing a mouse and keyboard game, but I'm anxious to get back to it...
