While I'm marking this as recommended, this game fails to avoid many of the pitfalls of modern first-person shooters.
• Confusing level design when trying to stray away from the linearity. This happens in roughly half of the "break the 3 magical seals" sections, as well as the labs level. The use of invisible walls, which are usually not too bad, really aggravates this.
• Some of the weapons are extremely situational while some others are too good in any given situation. It gives you little reason to use/upgrade parts of your arsenal.
• Tendency to pad out levels with more of the same fights, with seemingly little thought being given to how to shake things up a little. The latter half of the game degenerates quickly into "let's throw every monster at the player at once", with only the quantities varying. It's dull, it's not very fun.
• A story that doesn't know whether it wants to be funny or dramatic. Witty cheap one-liners are followed by cutscenes about complex political plots and personal sorrow. I think it's possible to mix the two but as it stands, they clash too much. I feel like it would be possible to exploit this contrast for a good effect, and without that, the writing comes off as uncertain and incohesive.
• A lot of looting. Way, way too much looting. Sure, you auto-pickup everything that's in containers, but spamming E everywhere gets old real quick.
• The game has a rating system for fights where you can get bonus experience points (karma). While it flat out tells you that you should combo and vary the abilities you use, in practice, your different abilities do NOT guarantee that they'll actually serve their intended purpose. It feels like it's a lot up to random probability.
• On several occasions I ended up becoming stuck for 10 minutes, unable to progress. On one instance, it was because a ragdolled enemy, which wasn't dead yet, refused to stand back up. On another, it's because I somehow went into a part of the level I wasn't supposed to be in, trapping myself behind locked doors. It's frustrating as hell.
• Binding the use of special abilities as tapping one direction twice + a mouse button. While it sometimes fails to register, the fact that this feels very natural really makes up for it.
• The pre-rendered story cutscenes that are like animated dioramas are absolutely gorgeous.
• Some of the writing is genuinely funny, but those moments are rare.
Finally, a word on the game's production value. It feels a little cheap, with human models and faces suffering from the uncanny valley. The animation quality varies between average and good, but nothing bad especially stands out, besides the awful animation compression (creating the jitter issue). But I don't think that's the biggest issue. To me, the biggest issue is the extremely lackluster soundtrack. For well over half the game, there is no ambient music other than the same few loops, over and over and over and over. It wouldn't normally be that big of an issue, but when the level design has trouble directing you seamlessly towards your next objective and has you aimlessly run around for 5 minutes, it gets on your nerves.
In summary, I'd give Shadow Warrior something like a 6,5/10? It's weird for an "old school" FPS to fall into modern flaws, but here we are, I guess.

Pros:
+ Puzzle mechanics (both in variety and number)
+ Art style
+ Sound effects and music
+ Cohesive design (bug/glitch-free, as far as my experience went)
Cons (all relatively minor):
- Some puzzles can be a bit... finicky.
- The 'story' is vague and doesn't really have a conclusion (as far as I can tell).
- More puzzles should be possible, given the available mechanics.
The Bridge is a great game overall, and almost all of the details are well thought out.  The mechanics and physics (which are obviously at the core of the game) are very well designed and I encountered no bugs or glitches to speak of.  The art is terrific, very appropriate for the game/story, and wonderfully reminiscent of M.C. Escher.  Putting everything together creates a marvelous puzzle experience.
Most of the complaints I have are relatively minor.  In terms of game play, a few levels relied heavily on fenagling components into position or timing certain movements through trial-and-error.  Generally, a certain amount of this is OK in a game, but a couple levels became frustrating.  (Most were a lot of fun, though.)  Also, given the variety of the mechanics, many more puzzles could have been included in this game.  The developers likely capped the puzzle sets to what were released due to time and effort constraints.  The sets they chose to include felt cohesive and had a pleasent progression in difficulty.
My only real gripe is with the 'story', such as it is.  It seemed to have a ton of potential in the beginning, but nothing was ever truly explained/resolved or even hinted at in an obvious manner by the end.  This is the one point that I feel the developers should have expounded since it seemed they had a really great story they wanted to tell.  On a related note, some collectible wisps, which seem to explain part of the story, were incredibly difficult to find without help.
Once again, though, this is a very well-designed, solidly-developed, and entertaining game.  I would definitely recommend it, especially to fans of the puzzle genre.

Let me start by saying that The Bridge is not a bad game. For an indie game the developers should be proud of what they've accomplished. If there were a somewhere-between-thumbs-up-and-thumbs-down button this is the game I would most want to use it for.
I leaned on the side of not recommending it though, for several reasons. This game is inevitably compared to Braid because it has an artsy style, time manipulation, and puzzles. But it's nowhere near the level of those other puzzle games I love, including Braid or Limbo or even Master Reboot. The reason is mostly depth and story. There simply isn't that much here. And what does exist is far too obscure and limited to be moving.
Beyond that, the puzzles range from straightforward to extremely frustrasting. The difficulty never really flattened out: I either had a level figured out in the first minute, or could stare at it forever with limited success. A few puzzles required some split second timing, which given the controls and precision in this game (they're laggy and your character can't move fast at all) made them very annoying. It was essentially just repeat forever until you happen to squeeze by.
The black and white art might have actually hurt the game more than helped, as it could be hard to tell the difference between some things that were only separated by shades of gray. As for the music, I hardly noticed it, so it didn't leave much of an impact.
My final complaint is performance. This is a 2D game with limited effects, but even on an absurdly powerful machine it got extremely choppy at points. It was somewhere down near 1 frame per 2 seconds while I was in freefall. That's just not acceptable, even for an indie game.
So overall if you're itching for a puzzle game and don't mind the lack of story, and can look past the game's other flaws, then you can pick up The Bridge and it will give you what you want for a few hours. But personally, I won't be coming back to it any time soon.

*As personally described upon being asked what the video game "Hollow Knight" was...*
Quite possibly the best side scroller I've had the fortune of playing since SNES days; soo good. Story got me like "whoa," mechanics are smooth as F and on pointtt. The hand drawn artwork is detailed and seamlessly animated to perfection. Controls are clean feeling, highly responsive, and you never quite feel like the game got you killed because it didn't act how you wanted or do what you pressed, etc.
A collective and instantly nostalgic/classic blend of bugs life meets Hayao Miyazaki (Princess Mononoke, My Neighbor Totoro, etc.) meets Hidetaka Miyazaki (Demon Souls, Dark Souls, etc.) meets metroidvania heaven. At times, the games tear jerking, unforgiving, and often challenging platforming will have you sucked in and forgetting you're even playing "just a side scroller" as you lay down a path of destruction upon any creature hindering your most epic of journeys. Alternatively, take your time soaking in the memorable beauty and atmosphere of the artists as you gracefully jump, dash, slide, and slice through the forgotten and mysterious buried kingdom.
Find yourself (borderline addictively) exploring the ancient and untouched layers or dangerously overgrown outskirts of a curiously abandoned underground city. Return to areas of the game that you otherwise thought were completed solely to re-listen to sound tracks and appreciate the game art, only to realize entire new areas have become reachable after gaining new abilities and unlocking skills. Discover secret relics and powerful abilities as you begin to peel back the shroud around this peculiar story. Gather the means and knowledge throughout your exploration to help you lay to rest the corrupted souls and infected creatures inhabiting the Hallownest. Wander through twisting and uncharted passages to uncover clues and old machines left behind by beings mysteriously long since lost to time.
Every uniquely designed area, each with it's own unforgettable atmosphere, notable life, and absolutely engrossing sound track, is lavishly hand detailed down to the pixel. Find yourself returning to areas of the game you had thought previously completed just for the music and art, only to find an entire new area open to exploring after gaining an ability elsewhere.
Hollow Knight is a modern side scroll not to be taken lightly or put on the back burner. Do yourself a favor and dive into this epic of a tale that's simple enough on the surface for casual players (and mom) to pick up, but gut wrenching and heart tugging enough for even the most seasoned veteran gamers to shed a tear once or twice. If you're looking for an original story to pull you in deep, or a game that will put your mental agility, strength, and stamina to the test, you won't regret stepping into the world of Hollow Knight.

Train Sim World: CSX Heavy Haul is the beginning of a new journey for both users of Train Simulators and the developer itself, opting to use the Unreal 4 engine. While there are many reviews talking about performance issues, frame rates, content etc, I will share my experiences thus far.
First off. Performance. I'm running i7 6850K @ 4GHz with 64GB DDR4 3200, coupled with a GTX 1080 and a Samsung 960 Pro M.2 SSD. My Steam library runs off my mechanical Western Digital Enterprise  4TB drive. Monitor is a 34" curved LG monitor running over DisplayPort. Load times are acceptable, however when launching, it wants to start SteamVR. This game does not have VR support. I had no issues with the game failing to start or crashing. I experienced a relatively smooth gameplay experience with the video settings at defauly (High/Medium). I didn't experience any major framerate issues, however there is plenty of room to improve here. Overall, the game is more than playable and I look forward to getting into it further.
Secondly, Content. Yes this game is lacking somewhat in terms of its amount of overall content. You get three (3) engines and six (6) freight wagons. I see a lot of people in the community comparing this title to previous iterations from the same developer. I'd like to point out that this is not an apples to apples comparision. The level of detail and interaction one has with the included assets is unprecedented in the train simulation world. This title is the beginning of a new type of experience both for the users and the developers. As such, rather than badge this title as just "Train Sim World", they've gone with "Train Sim World: CSX Heavy Haul". This should be an indication that the title has a specific focus. The media releases and screenshots support this. Expecting this to be a replacement for their previous simulator is simply unjustified. You get what it says on the box, and it looks just as good, if not better than expected. If you were hoping for more than what was advertised, then you shouldn't have purchased.
Overall, I found this release to be in the upper end bracket of what I am prepared to pay for a title with the amount of content it has. With DLC and new features expected to be added in future, I feel it was a fair price for the experience I am getting. Those that want a more in-depth look at where things are going, should review the developer diaries on their website. I can't want to see where this goes in the near future, and am going to have many happy hours enjoying it.
TL:DR Great game, felt price was fair, what you see is what you get, performance needs improving but is playable, looking forward to future additions and improvements.

This game is truely AMAZING, I haven't been addicted to any game in long time and then Hollow Knight came. Definitely worth its price, I would even say there is so much content it could be a bit more expensive and it would still worth a buy, not to mention any discounts/sales. I am writing this review so it gets more recognition and to share some of my thoughts.
The world is HUGE and full of surprises and secrets. Exploring it is pure fun. There is quite an amount of backtracking as the areas are twisted together, but it does not get boring - you always find something new and there are quite suprising changes as you play along.
Variety of enemies is astounding. While you progress some of them that were difficult at first get much easier while new stronger one appear. Bosses are very diverse also.
Graphics are beautiful, drawing style is very likeable. Atmosphere of the game is a bit gloomy, artstyle is very consistent yet separate areas of the game have their own unique qualities.
The game is quite challenging. Some compare it to Dark Souls series and I would agree. You can call it hard or very hard, but at the same time it is very fair and rewarding. While playing DS I was annoyed with having to repeat boss fights over and over again. Here you usually can go somewhere else, find a new upgrade and get back. Defeating boss usually demands from you a bit strategy and observation what are his/her moves. Second important thing is making proper build (choosing appropriate charms that give you special powers). Overall, I haven't found many areas in game that are frustating and too hard to beat. You have many savepoints so no need to repeat huge areas when you get killed.
As for the builds mentioned you have two main ways of upgrading your character: one is unlocking special abilities like dash, wall climbing etc. which help you in combat and to reach new areas. Second are charms scattered all over the world that give you extra boosts like you can swing your sword faster, you can regenerate your life quicker etc. Combining them in proper way can sometimes give you substantial boost when beating some parts of the game.
The controls are great (I was playing only on XBOX pad) - you have tight control over character. I got few glitches with my character running while I didn't want to, but maybe that was my cat running over the second pad :P.
Now, for the disadvantages.
Maybe it's just me, but the game feels a bit linear to some point (around 5hrs) - you have to get certain upgrades first, but then the huge world opens for you and there is so much to explore it is impossible to get bored.
It's addictive - Hollow Knight, please, I need to live my life, I cannot play 247 ;__;
There could be more vendors and things to buy (oh consumptionist me!). Some loot you find are useless, they can only be sold for money (but you don't have so many opportunities to spend the money, so what's the point).
Overall, 12/10 :)

It still has it's flaws:
- estates. I want to build castles anywhere I conquer. What is the point of estates? It just really turns it into capture the flag and a limited base building area.
- wall attack is still hard. Bring back the seige towers!
- engineers. They used to be a resource, now they come with the units which are too cheap.
and it's positives:
- its solid. you feel like defending a castle, and walls are a welcome defence in any strategy game.
- it's fun. Even the character animations have humour applied and you feel a sense of enjoyment in creation and defense of your creation.
- it's hard. The campaign gets gradually harder making you come back for one last go, go on just another attempt.
- a thing of beauty. The graphics are 3d but have that old-school charm of the original.
Final view?
Good solid move in the right direction, could do with a bit more tweaking. Worth the money, providing you spend time with it. 8/10

This is my first time I played an AC game and it sure is different from the ones I've played (Neverwinter Nights, KOTOR, FF series, RTS games, etc). I don't know about those that have been following the series for many years, and I can only compare it to my experience with Splinter Cell (2002), Fable, and Skyrim, but I find that AC4:BF is an addictive and fun game, overall.
What I liked:
+ I'm one of the lucky ones to have the game work, and so far have not lost any saved games to uPlay like a lot of the users who gave negative reviews. (Please, don't let my mentioning it jinx
this!)
+ Graphics looks nice and I'm okay with running it in 50FPS while sailing, 30FPS in towns and ship battles, 20FPS when boarding ships; using an R7 250 card, 24" BenQ Gaming monitor.
+ Assassinations. (unlike in GTA, you can only kill your targets and the guards; please refrain from killing civilians and your crew)
+ Sailing your own ship and naval battles. When you've upgraded your ship, ram that enemy ship and hear the satisfying crunch of wood, reminds me of an NFS police chase experience at sea, though I'm the one doing the chasing. :D
+ The pirate songs. Got them from iTunes.
+ Underwater exploration.
+ Being able to climb mostly anything with a handhold and go up, up, up, then jump off in a Leap of Faith.
+ Kenway's Fleet and the Companion App.
What I didn't like:
- Storyline. I mean, come on, that's it? *Spoiler: Everyone you care about dies, or leaves you. Thanks a lot.*
- Spend five hours in Kenway's POV = still feel great. Spend five minutes in player's "real world" POV = wanna throw up. Motion sickness?
- Somehow I ended up INSIDE and STUCK in an enemy ship's cargo hold after diving to escape the battle several times than I care to count. Needed to reload.
- Clunky gameplay. Got caught by guards numerous times just because Kenway keeps running into walls that can't be climbed; got surrounded by guards and Kenway can't decide who to hit first; got surrounded by guards and Kenway unleashes a flurry of sword combos on a guard then finishes combo on a completely DIFFERENT guard; thanks, you stupid camera.
- No toggle button for crouching, you have to be in Stalking Zones to be able to crouch.
- Everything becomes repetitive when played too long and too often. Find, chase, kill; fire cannons, board, loot - rinse & repeat. I recommend playing every other day for two to three hours, tops.
Every game has its flaws, and AC4:BF has its own, but I would still recommend it to others!

Battlerite is the spiritual successor to Bloodline Champions, a game developed several years ago that flew under the radar until Funcom the publisher destroyed it with some questionable microtransaction that started affecting gameplay. I played fell and in love with BLC's early gameplay and have been searching for a game like it for at least 3 years. Imagine my surprise when I discovered the same developer studio has developed a new version of the core fighting/arena based  game with all the mechanics I fell in love with years ago - Battlerite.
This game has a steep learning curve for those that have not played a game of this type before, those who played BLC have a distinct advantage because many of the old heroes have been ported in a sense to Battlerite. Once you've picked up on the learning curve the fast paced and adrenaline pumping PvP gameplay will keep you interested and engaged for fans that love competition.
The game is still in early access so there are places where it's lacking depth. The UI, cosmetics, and group management could all certainly be expanded and improved but the core gameplay mechanics are fantastic and the developers are continuing to focus on hero gameplay and new hero release prior to tackling some of the fluff that we can expect from a game that's been fully released.
Some reviews indicate that the community is 'too toxic' which can't be further from the truth. After playing hundreds of games only three of them have had a toxic player. The game can be frustrating to newer players but if you let go of your obsession with rank, play what you enjoy - over time you will improve and get a better sense for the game leading to some intense matches.
I look forward to the future developments for this game and I love the community supporting it however they can. There are weekly tournaments hosted in several regions showcasing the competitive aspect of the game. If you want a game with no fluff, no grinding, no leveling, no unfair gameplay advantages whatsoever - a game where you are rewarded exlusively for your skill and mastery of the hero you play and those you are playing against, then Battlerite is for you.
Cheers!

This is my first time I played an AC game and it sure is different from the ones I've played (Neverwinter Nights, KOTOR, FF series, RTS games, etc). I don't know about those that have been following the series for many years, and I can only compare it to my experience with Splinter Cell (2002), Fable, and Skyrim, but I find that AC4:BF is an addictive and fun game, overall.
What I liked:
+ I'm one of the lucky ones to have the game work, and so far have not lost any saved games to uPlay like a lot of the users who gave negative reviews. (Please, don't let my mentioning it jinx
this!)
+ Graphics looks nice and I'm okay with running it in 50FPS while sailing, 30FPS in towns and ship battles, 20FPS when boarding ships; using an R7 250 card, 24" BenQ Gaming monitor.
+ Assassinations. (unlike in GTA, you can only kill your targets and the guards; please refrain from killing civilians and your crew)
+ Sailing your own ship and naval battles. When you've upgraded your ship, ram that enemy ship and hear the satisfying crunch of wood, reminds me of an NFS police chase experience at sea, though I'm the one doing the chasing. :D
+ The pirate songs. Got them from iTunes.
+ Underwater exploration.
+ Being able to climb mostly anything with a handhold and go up, up, up, then jump off in a Leap of Faith.
+ Kenway's Fleet and the Companion App.
What I didn't like:
- Storyline. I mean, come on, that's it? *Spoiler: Everyone you care about dies, or leaves you. Thanks a lot.*
- Spend five hours in Kenway's POV = still feel great. Spend five minutes in player's "real world" POV = wanna throw up. Motion sickness?
- Somehow I ended up INSIDE and STUCK in an enemy ship's cargo hold after diving to escape the battle several times than I care to count. Needed to reload.
- Clunky gameplay. Got caught by guards numerous times just because Kenway keeps running into walls that can't be climbed; got surrounded by guards and Kenway can't decide who to hit first; got surrounded by guards and Kenway unleashes a flurry of sword combos on a guard then finishes combo on a completely DIFFERENT guard; thanks, you stupid camera.
- No toggle button for crouching, you have to be in Stalking Zones to be able to crouch.
- Everything becomes repetitive when played too long and too often. Find, chase, kill; fire cannons, board, loot - rinse & repeat. I recommend playing every other day for two to three hours, tops.
Every game has its flaws, and AC4:BF has its own, but I would still recommend it to others!

This is a faithful recreation of the board game, more specifically the newer re-release (which I may or may not have on my shelf), to a fault.  The underlying mechanics use simulated D6 rolls and the mission maps for the main campaign are even ripped straight from the manual.  Hard to say if it was GW or the devs, but there was some missed room for improvement and refinement of the formula.
There are no hybrids or patriarchs as in the original, instead we have the broodlords form the newer version.  It reduces the variety for anyone wanting to play genesteelers, but I suppose it makes it easier to balance.  Ultimately, there isn't too much room for strategy on the geensteeler side, which is why it's fitting the campaign plays from the Terminator's perspective.
If you enjoy the boardgame or have nostalgia for the original, there's something here to enjoy.  But if you don't know what Space Hulk or Warhammer 40K are, I'm not sure I can really recomend this.

*As personally described upon being asked what the video game "Hollow Knight" was...*
Quite possibly the best side scroller I've had the fortune of playing since SNES days; soo good. Story got me like "whoa," mechanics are smooth as F and on pointtt. The hand drawn artwork is detailed and seamlessly animated to perfection. Controls are clean feeling, highly responsive, and you never quite feel like the game got you killed because it didn't act how you wanted or do what you pressed, etc.
A collective and instantly nostalgic/classic blend of bugs life meets Hayao Miyazaki (Princess Mononoke, My Neighbor Totoro, etc.) meets Hidetaka Miyazaki (Demon Souls, Dark Souls, etc.) meets metroidvania heaven. At times, the games tear jerking, unforgiving, and often challenging platforming will have you sucked in and forgetting you're even playing "just a side scroller" as you lay down a path of destruction upon any creature hindering your most epic of journeys. Alternatively, take your time soaking in the memorable beauty and atmosphere of the artists as you gracefully jump, dash, slide, and slice through the forgotten and mysterious buried kingdom.
Find yourself (borderline addictively) exploring the ancient and untouched layers or dangerously overgrown outskirts of a curiously abandoned underground city. Return to areas of the game that you otherwise thought were completed solely to re-listen to sound tracks and appreciate the game art, only to realize entire new areas have become reachable after gaining new abilities and unlocking skills. Discover secret relics and powerful abilities as you begin to peel back the shroud around this peculiar story. Gather the means and knowledge throughout your exploration to help you lay to rest the corrupted souls and infected creatures inhabiting the Hallownest. Wander through twisting and uncharted passages to uncover clues and old machines left behind by beings mysteriously long since lost to time.
Every uniquely designed area, each with it's own unforgettable atmosphere, notable life, and absolutely engrossing sound track, is lavishly hand detailed down to the pixel. Find yourself returning to areas of the game you had thought previously completed just for the music and art, only to find an entire new area open to exploring after gaining an ability elsewhere.
Hollow Knight is a modern side scroll not to be taken lightly or put on the back burner. Do yourself a favor and dive into this epic of a tale that's simple enough on the surface for casual players (and mom) to pick up, but gut wrenching and heart tugging enough for even the most seasoned veteran gamers to shed a tear once or twice. If you're looking for an original story to pull you in deep, or a game that will put your mental agility, strength, and stamina to the test, you won't regret stepping into the world of Hollow Knight.

This is not your typical Final Fantasy. And yet, it succeeds where past entries in the main series failed: it captures the Final Fantasy magic while adding its own identity and mixing the formula. The game has its flaws, but most of them have more to do with its portable nature than game design.
The story is about a group of elite cadets called Class Zero. The game starts as your nation, Rubrum, is invaded by the adjacent empire and almost succeeds in seizing the crystal from which all of your magic comes. Class Zero manages to repel the enemy forces, but Rubrum loses a considerable chunk of territory. The plot revolves around the resulting war (and more, but let's not spoil anything, okay?)
Gameplay is fantastic. Not because it is innovative. It is an action RPG with pretty standard controllers. You dodge, attack and use special skills and magic. However, three things make it great:
1. It is incredibly smooth. This version fixed the blurry camera and you don't need to lock on enemies all the time (though you'll end up doing it anyway, because of killstrikes.) Everything is responsive and intuitive.
2. There's an enourmous cast of characters, and every one of them feels different. Some dodge better, some are ranged,  others attack faster or may even finish combos with AoE attacks. Every one of them has a distinct advantage (and disavantage) that changes the way you experience the game.
3. Combat is strategic. The game will punish you for dishing out attacks without thought (some enemies will just dodge forever.) Also, attacking at a specific window of opportunity signaled by a visual cue will kill the enemy instantly, or at least deal considerable damage, if the enemy is too strong. It rewards you for playing the game well.
As for sounds and graphics, it is a mixed bag. Soundtrack is great and sound effects are perfect, as with any Final Fantasy, but the voice acting is surprisingly bad. Most voices are decent to good, actually, but when they're bad, they're distractingly awful. Graphics got an overhaul. Kinda. Main cast looks amazing and new lighting effects make for beautiful screenshots, but most NPCs and towns look blocky and with low-res textures.
Actually, the main problem with this game on PC is that it was designed for a portable system. So the portable design is all there: it's grindy, towns and dungeons are mostly corridors and dialogues are poorly animated. But don't get me wrong: there are absolutely more good parts than bad ones. In fact, even as a portable game, it surpasses its Fabula Nova console counterpart Final Fantasy XIII in content. There are tons of sidequests, open world map with explorable dungeons, you can breed chocobos, liberate towns... You'll definitely get your money's worth in gameplay hours.
Now, the reason this game really gets to me: it is a fantastic deviation of the Final Fantasy usual tone. This game is all about death, but it chose not to take the easy route. Yes, there's a lot of killing and blood. But it doesn't stop there. It permeates the story, with its constant war. Characters in this world have their memory of the dead erased, so they can continue their neverending battles. In gameplay, fellow members of Class Zero can't be revived until the end of the mission. If they die, they stay dead until you go back. Eidolons need sacrifices to be summoned and magic is upgraded with Phantoma, which you harvest from the dead. It is a fantastic change of tone, well executed and more than welcome.
Now, this is not a good port. It is resolution and frame locked. It has terrible performance issues (I can only get steady 30fps at all times without AA.) Keyboard layout is awkward and can't be changed, so you need to play with a controller for a decent gameplay experience.  Basically, it has none of the advantages PC gaming usually has over console gaming.
But what I really want to say is:
Is this a good port? No.
Is this an incredible addition to Steam's jRPG library? Hell yeah.

TL;DR: Final Fantasy Type-0 HD, a new kind of fantasy for those looking to lose themselves in unique characters and addicting game play. Dodge!
Final Fantasy Type-0 HD, where to start, where to start...
I've wanted this game since I first heard about it in 2008. Loved the concept, loved the characters, loved the mature feel to it. And so I waited. 2011. "Only in Japan." 2011-2013. Hope. Then 2014 hit. HD remake. Full ignition of the flame, waves of hope crashed and I knew the day would come when I would play the game. The fan translation hit and I played it. Enjoyed it, but it wasn't exactly what I wanted. 2015. Steam. Boom. Here we are.
The Good:
Type-0 isn't your average, hit, wait, hit, wait, FF game. You're in full control of your character and are able to move around in battle, pulling off skills, healing, and dodging. Dodging a lot. The battles are fluid, putting you right into the action. You move left, right, attack, dodge, run, strike, magic! That freedom is what appeals to me in games. Turned based is great but sometimes you just want to pull off some sweet moves of your own accord. In terms of action of this sort, think FF 12 and a bit of 13, without the linearity of the latter and the sluggishness of the former.
Battles can be pretty easy, if you know your opponents well enough. You COULD rush in and hit everything in sight but good luck with that. Enemies like Coeurls and even soldiers will try to dodge your attacks. You could wait for your Killsight to active, a special innate power that every character has that lets you deal massive damage or instantly kill an opponent, to make things easier. Or you could use magic. Fire's always fun.
Battles can also persist, sometimes you can "feel a presence" of other enemies nearby and initiate another battle with enemies that get stronger and stronger as you remain in that battle chain. You heal after every battle chain, in other words when you exit into the world map, so that's always great, but charcaters who die can only be revived when you return to a town or Akademeia, you school and the central hub of the game. But if you're doing a mission then the character stays dead until you finish that mission so be careful with the weaker members of your party.
(Only characters who participate in battles gain EXP so be aware of that fact. You could just use any 3 character but that's no fun. Diversify~)
The 14 playable characters are all unique in terms of personality and weapons. You got your long ranger attackers, Trey (bow), Ace (cards), and Cater (gun) for example, your short range fighters, Eight (fists), Queen (rapier), and Cinque (mace), and your magic heavy characters like Duece (flute). Your party can only consist of 3 characters at any given time so pick your favorites but also be aware of the fact that their are enemies best suited for certain characters. Characters like Eight have trouble fighting airborne enemies so be mindful of that. When you level up you get AP (Ability Points I'm guessing) which you can use to learn new skills in battle. You have your passives, your attacks, and power boosts for said attacks. Experiment with different skill types cause their are a lot, and my highest level character is barely 17.
The story is pretty gritty. Like holy sh*t man, the first 10 minutes of the game and I'm already trying really hard not to cry. These are kids you're playing as. Facing a war. Facing death. Facing things some of us can't even begin to fathom on a very real level. Blood, blood everywhere! But at the end of the day, your characters can still find things to smile about and that just makes you forget what's really going on sometimes.
The music is pretty good, which is no surprise for a FF game.
The art and character models are neat but nothing astounding.
I don't care about the FPS honestly. 30 or not, it's a great game and I've loved every second of it. I don't understand why some people make such a big deal about this. I'm an avid gamer. I play a lot of games and have spent hours doing so with zero care about the FPS. Call me what you like, at the end of the day, I'm having fun and that's all that matters to me~
The Bad:
-My biggest gripe thus far is the fact that the in-game buttons only show the keys on a keyboard, nothing for a controller. I had a bit of trouble understanding what E and R did but I think I have that down now... either way, if I could have read those buttons better in the beginning I think I would have had an easier time.
Final Fantasy Type-0 HD, a new kind of fantasy for those looking to lose themselves in unique characters and addicting game play. Dodge!

When I found out about this game, I was definitely intrigued. A Final Fantasy game with action RPG combat, a large and diverse cast of characters and a much grittier story than the typical plot from the rest of the series.
Ultimately, I do not recommend the game. Here are my pros and cons:
Pros:
1. The combat system has some good depth to it.
2. The characters all feel very different, I took time to play as each one before quitting the game. All have different personalities in addition to different weapon types and playstyles.
3. Grinding, for those interested, is made easy with the repeated encounters mechanic. You no longer have to run around in circles to grind levels. You simply hit a button to fight again.
Cons:
1. Performance on PC is terrible. Sub 30fps regularly even when you're out of combat.
2. Input lag exists far beyond your typical 30fps experience. When the framerate is at its worst, a full second can pass between a button press and the execution of a basic attack. This results in occassionally frustrating combat.
3. Combat systems are nicely done, but very poorly explained for non-regulars.
4. Voice acting, even for a Final Fantasy game, is absolutely horrific. Every character sounds completely uninterested in the plot.
5. Sound in the cutscenes is completely out of sync. Sometimes sounds would happen almost a full second or two before the action happens on screen. Characters can have closed mouths and still be yelling due to the audio sync delay.
6. Texture work is actually WORSE on PC than it is on PS4. Every game I have ever played on my current system looks far better on my system than it did on PS4. When I saw my friends play this game on PS4 I was even more upset with this port.
7. The story is lackluster. I may have a blunted opinion of this because of how much the audio sync issue broke my since of immersion in the first cutscenes, but I am completely uninterested in the story other than the back story about the 4 kingdoms.
Summary: This game has a fun combat system and a great cast of characters muddled beneath a lackluster story, terrible visuals and horrible input lag. It also has TERRIBLE audio sync issues that completely ruined my experience with the opening cutscenes. Even with a controller (which is apparently preferred), I can't recommend this game to anyone. Even RPG fans or fellow Final Fantasy players like me.

Let's start with addressing the elephant in the room here, since many of the other reviewers with not even an hour of play time angrily like to point it out anyway: the game is somewhat poorly optimized at this release unfortunately. Also there's some sort of 'ghosting effect' here and there (like a motion blur) and when using the bell for a longer period of time it gets a peculiar ring to it, from time to time. Stuff like that. It will russle the jimmies of the perfectionists.
The somewhat poor optimalization is probably caused due to the developers being new with the game engine Unreal and still wanting to hit the release date with this product despite the poor optimalization. This has lead to cause that also the multiplayer functions Dovetail was planning to implement have to wait for a later update.
[EDIT]
The tutorials seem a little barebone and I would have loved to get some more technical details explained in them, like the guy in the scenarios that tells something about the areas you are driving through, but then about the locos. And overall the game is a little lacking when it comes to content: only 1 route and 3 locos.
However, that being said the game is
and when running on highest settings a pretty good looker too! Quite the step up from the previous installment of Rail Simulator (later dubbed to Train Simulator). The immersive effect from stepping in and out of the loco, being able to press and flip almost any button and switch is a great feeling. With that come some very detailed and good looking rolling stock and weather effects and it can keep you occupied for HOURS on end. This is thus far more of a simulator than any train sim previously. It starts to get close to the level of detail of that of Flight Sims.
So if you just want a shiny new train operating game that has to run smooth in every aspect, then I'd recommend you wait with your purchase and keep an eye on the updates. Don't buy it. However, if you always wanted the freedom to walk in and out of your train, press almost everything, operate a turntable from first person view and don't mind having to deal with a lower frame rate or graphics settings, then I can recommend buying it for sure! Whether the price is worth it for you, only
can decide.

Very tentative YES on this one.
Its like all the fun parts of Age of Empires II in terms of castle v castle warefare and economy management. The logistics side of things is much more important here as you must carefully manage your resources lest you totally screw yourself over (run out of food, money, weapons).
It is much more siege-like than other RTS games I feel. Don't let the trailers fool you, no one fields armies that big. Most maps don't support forts large enough to generate such armies and it takes an hour+ to even get to the start of that scale of things. Most battles are small, between packs of units and such. Finishing long before reaching epic war levels.
Additionally - It is a slower paced RTS, which I think is nice. You really must siege your enemy to win. Its almost impossible to storm a castle in one go. Instead you need to take control of resources, starve the enemy, wear them down, and then launch multiple assaults that push progressively farther and father into their defenses to get to the lord.
So, if you like those things, then yay, you'll probably have fun.
Lastly, my chief complaint is that the AI is absolutely aweful. There's no difficulty controls at all. All AI are just what they are. They are also braindead and cheaters. I've burned all my opponents' food, iron, and stone only to watch them continue to send units at me without bothering to rebuild those resources. Lemme tell you... no food = no troops. Its like fighting someone from a scripted campaign where troops are just auto-generated for the story. Its atrocious.
This is a complicated game to learn. The economy is not like other strategy games and is hard to master. I've never had a problem beating the AI, even on my first aweful try where I ran out of food and had no iron for half the game.
For the only good figthts, you'll have to PvP. That's a big disappointment for me cause I hate RTS PvP. As such, I can't tell you anything about what options there are here for that.

There is a lot for FIreFly to get over with this new game.  I see it like this:
1. those who know the old game, know it well.  That means the most frustrating thing will be learning how to play this new game where it does not match the old one, and there are lots of differences, especially in the convenience corner.  It irks me for example that I have not found yet any way to change the speed of the game to give me think time, and that a lot of my old tricks won't work any more.
2. but in the end, many suffer from the same addiction problem as I, which is we really liked the old game (even with its pittiful AI), but have also played it till the cows come home and there is nothing left in it for us.  When I bring up a scenario in the Crusader I already know how it will go and how it will end, no surprises.  So we have little choice but to get the new game if we want to get a new fix.
3. another dissappointment for me is the apparent lack of campaign missions.  You will recall from Crusader  there are 100 missions, 80 across only two of the campaigns.  This new game has maybe 15.  So there is little replayability here.  This leaves us to look towards multiplayer (maybe a good thing) and playing the computer in freeplay (like starcraft though not as good).
So I have to say, I think FireFly would have done way better if they had just taken the old Crusader game, enhanced the AI in it, and created another 50 mission campaign that they sold as DLC for that game.  @10$, everyone who played the game would have bought it.  Well... there is still time.  If they want to do this they will find a willing audience for it.
I am going to recommend the game, in part hoping that it might be like Stronghold3.  This game was immediately hated too, but for those who thought about the game and what it was really doing it turned out to be much better than originally thought with a more sophistcated resource and industry change in it that I think added depth.  It was a successful attempt to keep the old game feel, but add new options.  But  you have to be patient to see it.
So Stronghold Crusader 2, not an instant hit, not a lot of single player replayability, but if you are looking for a stronghold fix what choice do you have.  Maybe it will grow on us.

While initially it suffered from a stagnant development period, the new Sector3 and their current contributions have vastly improved this title to become my now go-to racing sim, with vast improvements in the areas of physics, force feedback, single player and multi-player and the constant rate new content is pushed out.
While graphics are impressive, other simulators such as Assetto Corsa or Project Cars lead in this area, not to say that Sector3 have done an outstanding job on their engine with impressive HDR, bloom and dynamic lighting effect. SimBin/Sector3 has always been a leader in bringing the driver the most realistic sound experience in all their titles, and this continues with R3E.
With the last major update, Sector3 have done a major overhaul of the force feedback system. Their track developers have developed a new technology to improve the presentation and feedback of their track’s road surface utilising data from telemetry to create a highly dense road surface that features small bumps and imperfections in the surface the increases the quality of the force feedback immensely.
AI does leave plenty of room for improvement, while R3E supposably utilises an “Adaptive AI”, I find many times, AI will run up the back of you like a solid lead block, causing a frustrating racing experience at the best of times with little to no effect on themselves.
Content is plentiful, with a range of cars and tracks with new content currently added recently including the ADAC 2013 GT Masters Pack and the WTCC 2013 Pack including tracks as part of each package. Still, the biggest question mark is the pricing system, while I have noticed and taken advantage of the pack discounts, standard pricing is on the expensive side. I personally would advise to hold off for specials or car packs prior to purchasing content if you consider yourself the collector, or buy one car in each class as needed. With the new inclusion of the new “Test Drive” feature, you will be able to make a sound decision prior to purchase regardless of the price.
As a free to play game, this title is worth the time to experience the improvements that Sector3 have made to bring this sim up to the standard that many sim racers will look for. If you're willing to part with your cash to race new cars on new tracks, then you will enjoy a race or two, whether its a against the AI, online multiplayer with friends, or a quick hotlapping session.

If you play this game correctly, you'll finish it in about ten minutes, without any difficulty - just do what the narrator says.
So why is this game fun?
Simple.  Try ignoring the narrator.  Or deliberately disobeying him.  How about going through the wrong doors?  Pressing the wrong buttons?  Jumping off moving platforms?  Or developing an obsession with shutting yourself away in a storage cupboard?
You see, the fun comes from doing what you shouldn't, and the reaction of the narrator (and the game) to your actions (or inaction).
Sure, it's not a game that will occupy you for months or weeks.  But there is plenty of gameplay as you explore ways in which to avoid completing the game.  And in the process, it'll give you a bloody good laugh, and a malicious sense of glee when, once again, you've peed off the narrator!

The greatest and also unique Tower Defense game with the style of a RPG.
Your goal is to defend different crystals in different maps and positions from hordes of enemies, using the building and fighting skills of your character, whose powers increases with the experience they gain while defending, and with the equipments you find scattered around the battlefield. In bigger and harder maps, you may consider getting the support of some friends in order to defend every crystal from the evil, and combining your buildings with different stats or different sets will bring your team to the victory.
If you're playing alone, you may consider to try out all of the four characters, and to use all of their buildings togheter, in order to succeed in the game;
If you're playing with some friends, coordinate each other and combine the different characters's structures in a proper way to have a chance against the wave.
: there are lots of DLCs that adds more playable characters, maps, a new difficulty, and the final part of the story of this game. This means that,
, you will have only half of the fun from this game, making yourself consider buying the whole Dungeon Defenders Collection.
Also, if you're going to play huge maps with some buddies, your friends may experience big lags, even if they have a good computer which can normally handle very huge games, making their match boring and stressful.
Though this is a magnificent game, you'll need to shell out a lot of money to really enjoy it; also you are to make sure to have a great internet connection if you plan to play on multiplayer, or else the lags are going to be an issue, depending on the host.
Usually playing with friend you know shouldn't be a problem.
Buy it at your own risk.

Rekindling back the days I played this on a friend's PSP when it was released (surprisingly couldn't finish it properly that time) and skipped getting the PS4 version (also no PS4) it was released because SE announced it's coming to Steam.
INCOMING WORDS FROM THE CLOSET
Some notes:
- It is an embodiment of the Final Fantasy franchise even if it's not a numbered
- The setting of the story is set within the Fabula Nova Crystallis series (Same mythos as FF13 and the upcoming FF15). Thus, familiar terms from the series are used in this game. But if you're worried if it seems foreign, talking to NPCs can give you a hint of the terminologies ingame, it helps!
- Some would be wondering by the gameplay, that it's not TBS as your norm Final Fantasy system but instead it's actually a quite fast paced ARPG battle system.
- THIS GAME IS GEARED FOR NEW GAME+. Some of the story contents are locked only after you finish you first playthrough.
Brief review:
+ Quite dark story surrounding the world they live in, add that to an academy of students whose purpose are to be soldiers (for the main class you're playing as, they get it worse)
+ Fast paced battle system and vast amount of versatility in roster
+ Quite alot of achievements to be obtained (not from Steam but ingame)
+ Better camera and motion blur options than the PS4 version.
+ You get to play with Square Enix staff.
- Getting some of the achievement rewards can be boring or tiring (whether doing it naturally or grinding them)
- While it has better camera, you do feel like your main boss is the camera sometimes.
- That one character.
Performance Report:
- Port wise, it's an upper touchup than the PS4 HD port from the PSP. Not a large port upgrade as normal people would expect (such as uncapped fps/superior textures/proper graphic settings), but more towards bringing the game to another market to be available without using emulators.
- I truly have no issue with the game, since I did not increase the quality of my AA (using 1080p monitor), so it didn't tax my system to make it dip in performance.
- AA settings is actually an upscale, up to 4k. That alone would affect your overall performance.

Although the game is non-optimised from the beta, the game plays nicely, and has many cool features such as being able to walk.
The graphics are great (Better than Railworks/TS2017), but don't expect to run above Medium for now. Medium for most people with higher-end systems end up with ~15-40fps, and any higher than Medium results in ~10-20fps.
The systems are great, the UI is very much improved, and the controls are also better, where you no longer have to right-click to move the view around. Using a switch or reverser etc requires a left-click and a drag in either direction, or use the same keys as TS2017.
There is a number of features still missing from the game (which I already knew wouldn't be here as of this moment, like more routes/scenario builder/route creator/Multiplayer to name a few, if not all) however the Train Sim World is really empty without them. Given this game is still technically in a "pre-release" standpoint, given a number of features are still being worked on, I would have suggested to Dovetail that this be under Early Access rather than released as a full game.
As for the number of features they added, such as the "rattling train" and "waving brake pipes" these don't move much at all and therefore are not really recognisable unless you really look for them.
As for the tutorials, they're great, although the turntable tutorial did bug out on me twice. First time, the turntable went one track too far, but the game thought that it had stopped, and the problem is that the game stops you from moving the turntable. You either have to restart or you have to have a laugh and drive the train into the railings on the side of the turntable. The second time it bugged on me is that I turned the turntable the other way, but it doesn't accept entry from the opposite end, meaning you have to turn it 180° to continue.
Bugs aside, Watching the AI travel past is a lot nicer in this game compared to TS2017. The audio quality is much better for all of the trains and wagons, meaning that you can take in the surroundings as well as the sounds of the other trains going past.
Sand Patch so far for me has been ok, I spent about 5 minutes travelling at 10mph because the limit is 15mph and you had to travel 2 miles to be able to even speed up, and even then it's only to 25mph. A lot of other time has been me trying to find the best graphical settings, which I have found a decent compromise between framerate and quality. I maintain ~20-35fps at the most demanding areas, however getting into the valley/creek allows it to creep towards 40fps at max.
Although the game is heavily unoptimised (Much like FSX in terms of performance), especially for an Unreal Engine game, it IS a good train simulator, however DO BE WARNED about the optimisation of this game prior to buying, and ensure you have at LEAST the recommended, given that the game is heavily taxing.
UPDATE (26/11/2017)
After much thought, I decided to buy the GWE expansion pack, and I do say it is quite a nice ride, with the cab/carriages wobbling along the track (not vigorous, however noticable since the camera stays still - something that DTG says they're working on trying to do - and while it is a very nice addon, it is a shame that it still runs like as if it's just another updated version of Train Simulator 20XX. It seems the main difference is the slight difference in UI, which is WAY better than the old one.
The scenarios for GWE allow you to choose a time, pick a place and either wait for a train or hop on one before it leaves the station, either hitching a ride to the next platform or just travelling as a passenger. There are plenty of trains to choose to take over, and you can take them over at any time in the journey.
Although the AI drives very well, the simulation runs at a snail's pace compared to Sand Patch. On the same settings as Sand Patch, I get between 20-30fps whereas Sand Patch is ~30-50fps. Turning the settings down below medium sets it up to over 60fps, however setting it to medium pushes it back to 20-30fps, and then going to ultra actually makes it more steady on fps at ~20-25fps. This was at Old Oak Common, during the beginning tutorial when learning to drive the Class 43.
Although it is fun, I bought this because it was to run better than TS20XX, and to my surprise, that hasn't been done. Optimisation has been getting better, however updates haven't come out in a little while, as DTG have been at work swooping up licensing deals with Virgin (WCML route coming soon to TSW?) and updating/creating new routes for TS20XX.
I'd rather they spend more time optimising code, or at least asset placement/generation or something because I don't want to have to change settings below medium just to have something that is actually not a laggy slideshow. It's dizzying watching the motion blur effect distort the whole screen making me feel as though I'm drunk, however it helps give the sense of speed, as you can't hear anything from the Class 43 since it's too quiet. They make a big thing about the 43's engine "roar to life" and "You're gonna want to hear this", however I had to turn volume up to 100 to even remotely hear it. Usually my games are set to 20-25% volume and headphones set to 50% overall.
Train Sim World is set to 100% (75% louder than my other games) and the horn is barely noticable, yet alone the actual engine run noises, even when right next to the grills on the sides! This is only on the GWE trains too. Sand Patch is plenty loud for me, and actually gets rather too loud for my headphones, so swapping between each route is stupid since I need to adjust audio settings and also graphics settings each time since I can run Sand Patch way better than GWE.

Had a few doubts about this one from reading the initial reviews, but I saw it in the Steam sale and thought ‘What the hell?’. And I'm glad that I did.
The game is pretty much exactly like the Space Hulk board game that I remember playing when I was younger, except the dice roles are handled automatically (although you can see the dice rolls if you like). In the single player campaign, you play as the Blood Angel Space Marines whilst the genestealers are controlled by the computer AI. The game doesn't particularly add anything that wasn't in the board game, which could be considered a bit of a missed opportunity but fans of the board game will probably be pleased about this. Personally, I felt that the option to change your squad setup for each mission could have added some variety to the game, and could have increased the replayability.
Overall, I enjoyed playing through the single player campaigns currently available, and would certainly recommend this to anybody who likes the board game or turn-based strategy in general. There is a mission editor planned, as well as additional DLC campaigns, which will help to provide additional content once you've polished off the main campaign. It also features multiplayer options, allowing you to play online against your friends.

This game has a near perfect set up for a fulfilling 2d slash-em-up. Much like a 2D darksouls, you'll need upgrades less than you will need skill and perfect timing. Combat is very rewarding. Although punishing, the game gives back all it takes away and gives you many tools to tune your character into a unique playstyle.
The only downside to this title is the endings. Even if you've been taking your time carefully exploring and reading any bit of lore you can find, these endings make very little sense. There are 3 endings where nearly all of them...you can't tell if you won or not. You can't tell if everything you did was even good or not. It begs for explanation and the game, sadly, does not provide it. I sunk 40 hours into the game and found this to be very...unfulfilling. After googling and watching all the endings on youtube, reading comments and theories... it seems like I had the best of the 3 endings, but I still am confused. It's a big deal when you sink so much time and fall so over the top in love with something.
Aside from the ending, just about everything else is just fantastic. The world is at the same time, sad, interesting and heart warming. As the difficulty ramps up, you unlock charms to make things easier. This goes beyond learning new moves like double jump or an air dash, but things like regeneration, a larger attack, shields and so on. Every problem you face the game will give you a solution that you can build around. It's highly satisfying.

The Bridge is a puzzle game which allows you to both move and manipulate gravity.
The two main draws to The Bridge are the art style with each level appearing like a hand drawn pencil to paper sketch and the use of an Escheresque aesthetic to the level design. The puzzles excel in requiring the manipulation of the player's perspective. And The Bridge excels when its showcasing these aspects.
The puzzles are short and tight, but by the end I felt they dragged a bit. It feels a bit tedious to push through the last 8 of the 48 total chapters. The story doesnt capture you enough to draw you into the game's conclusion. It's whimsical and vague. It doesnt tease you to draw you in, it teases you with the possibility of its existence. And ultimately, the lack of a story makes the last few levels feel like a grind instead of a reveal.
Appreciate The Bridge's beauty and level design but quit once you feel like you've seen enough.

I realize this is a "remake" of an older game, but the control scheme needed to be remade to be a bit less dated and clunky feeling. There's no attack move vs normal move, there's no queing up actions, and your soliders just do weird♥♥♥♥♥♥all the time and don't always listen to you. The "formation" thing is totally broken as it will slow your units down by a good 25% because they simply don't move if they're out of position. Your units sort of engage whoever they want to engage and they will engage enemies even if you tell them to flee. There are no hotkeys btw; you must use the UI to do every action.
The economy component is convoluted and hard to manage. Most of the time you're just totally guessing as to how much food your producing and how much gold you're making. Boosting "happiess" is a shot in the dark a lot of the times as well. I like that there's so much going on with the economy, don't get me wrong, I just don't like that you have little feedback as to the output of each building and the current demand.
Throw on top of that a set of campagin missions that get so difficult you'll be spending hours just to beat a single mission. I haven't even finished the "learning campaign" yet, I can only imagine how hard the "skirmish trails" (actual campaign?) gets.

Let me just start out by saying that this game definitely isn't for everyone. It's for people who like the board game, or want to try it out and don't want to drop $250 on a physical copy off eBay.  If you have no idea how Space hulk works, you probably shouldn't even bother. You'll just be frustrated by the randomness of the whole thing.
That said, I really enjoy it. I didn't at first, however. If you have no idea of what you do in Space Hulk, the game will feel impossible as a single Genestealer completely rips apart half your squad in one turn. Space Hulk is a dice game, where luck is a major factor. Where in the actual game, missing 5 shots in a row as your friend slowly advances a Genestealer would be just hilarious, in the video game it just becoems frustrating. Or if your weapon jams 4 times in a row.
Animations are slow for the Terminators. So you're probably best disabling the timer, as slow animaation aren't something you have to deal with in the actual game. you can speed them up, but they just look silly. The first-person shoulder cam is cinematic, but isn't used often enough, and needs an option to be bigger. Graphics-wise, it's nothing too impressive. The astetics are perfect, you really feel like you're trundling through the tight corridors of a space hulk. Sounds are good, but possibly repetative over time. I'm mostly listening to something else when I play, so I don't notice.
There are a few differenced from the board game. They don't really hurt the game, in my opinion though. They just help ease some of the frustrations.
TL;DR, If you like the board game, or like the Warhammer 40k universe, and don't mind the random element, you will probably enjoy this.  Otherwise, you may want to stay away.

To do this you must explode the red blocks which will launch the yellow blocks away from the blast allowing the blue ball to reach the platform. Most levels have multiple red explosive blocks, so your job is to figure out which ones to explode and when.
+ Creatively designed levels which keeps the game feeling fresh and enjoyable from start to finish
+ The game has the right balance of not being too difficult while still being a fair bit challenging. Some stages make the player think a fair bit in order to find the solution.

The only valid argument against this game that I can find is it's price and people having optimization problems, which I myself have suffered from but not severely. I'll agree with anyone who says that $50 dollars for this game is pretty steep, however If you get it while it's on sale I feel that it's completely worth buying. I have played Stronghold, Stronghold 2, and Stronghold Crusader. They are all really great games and I feel that this game is just as good as those.
Mechanics wise the only gripe I would have with this one is the way houses are made. The closer your house is to your Stronghold the more populated the house becomes, however it also increases in size, so therefore it costs more wood. This isn't a problem on big maps where you can build a house on the border of your territory and it only adds 2 to 3 peasants to your overall population and costs less wood, but in small maps it's difficult because you don't have enough room to make those smaller houses, and all of your houses end up being big with 6-7 more peasants added to the popultaion which naturally means you have that many more mouths to feed, so then you need more farms while the map already has little room to spare.
Overall I give this game a 7/10 I really enjoyed it.

Onto more annoying matters, after every "story-driven" mission it's pretty dry until the next one, there are very minimal rewards for going out into the world and a bad system for managing it, the whole you can only do one quest at a time thing died 10 years ago, get together with it Square. It's hard for me to review Shadow Warrior... really!
The reception is good, which means I'll probably get a load of dislikes on this review because opinions deserve to be drowned out when they disagree with the majority, but... oh well!
I played through Shadow Warrior thinking 'wow, this game is decent'... but, looking back on it now,
was it REALLY that great? It's hard to really hate on the game because of my first run through it,
but it's one of those things that feels great to experience, but upon thinking about it, you realize
just how dull and... well, EH the product is.
For what it's worth, Shadow Warrior has decent visuals, great humor, and an interesting storyline...
but one big problem and a bite-sized issue prevent me from giving this the thumbs up everybody
has been giving it.
For what it's worth Shadow Warrior takes the name and feel of an old-school shooter... while this seems good on paper, I'm left feeling like there are a few elements of old-school shooters that are better left to old-school shooters. The biggest of these things is just how repetitious everything is. Do you like being locked in a room to kill loads of enemies? I started by saying 'yes', but by the 30th time the game made me do it, slicing 'n dicing my way through the baddies felt like a chore more than it felt like fun. On top of this, the level design can be bonkers and outright ludicrous sometimes. When a puzzle game gives me a headache, that's because I'm lost, which, in the context of a puzzle game, works because it's making me think. When a First-Person Shooter gives me a headache, it's because I don't know what the ♥♥♥♥ I have to do because it's poorly communicated to me, the player. To add onto my anger: the ♥♥♥♥ing seals (the♥♥♥♥♥♥that blocks you from entrances and ends up being more of an annoyance than a challenge), some of the enemies being stupidly difficult to kill, to the point where I got so infuriated that I cheated so I could kill them easily (not kidding, either).
This game is also loaded with secrets... but, in a way that's questionable. I like a good Easter Egg or two, but only when the level is designed around that Easter Egg. What I don't like is when there is about a 100 gorillion invisible walls blocking off places where secrets
be, which wouldn't be an issue if the environments weren't at all misleading.
All in all, it's a decent game if it's your thing. Personally, while I enjoy some mindless fun every now and then, but not when the 'fun' part of that turns to pure frustration from questionable design decisions.
See you in 2 months when this has an approval rating of some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like 40-30, maybe even 50% (if I get lucky).

I was gifted this game; hence why I've tagged it as "I recieved this for free".
Hollow Knight is not like Dark Souls. Hollow Knight is also not gruelingly difficult (for the most part) like that game is often stereotyped as. Hollow Knight is closer to something like Dust: An Elysian Tail, although one may see some inspiration from Dark Souls in terms of the gloomy art direction and narrative.
Where Hollow Knight shines is the aforementioned art direction and narrative, but it also does an extremely good job at being a Metroidvania. The controls are extremely tight with maximum friction and no acceleration, so you have complete control over your movement. This is important, as Hollow Knight has a surprising amount of precision platforming involved, and the bosses are mostly well designed and really encourage skilled usage of it.
Combat is simple enough on the surface; you can swing your nail (yes, it's not a sword) in four directions, use three separate offensive spells and a healing ability that stops you in your tracks until you finish. The various Charms you can find in the game do add a bit of depth, but it doesn't go far enough to require too much thinking about it.
The map is quite large, easily surpassing Super Metroid, Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, and even Axiom Verge. Thankfully, the game does a good job with it's "fast travel" systems and doesn't feel like it overstays it's welcome as a result. It's suitably littered with secrets and items, though not quite as many as one of the aforementioned games due to it's simplicity. You get movement upgrades, spells and their upgrades, Charms, health and SOUL (basically your mana) upgrades...and that's about it. There's no dedicated ranged weapon, so you won't be finding any missile tank equivalent.
On the other hand, where Hollow Knight falters is that it's difficulty can be a bit all over the place. The curve seems pretty good at first, with most bosses at the very most taking two tries to beat, but then you can come up to a miniboss that ends up being harder than that area's ACTUAL boss, and then the game remains at a lukewarm difficulty until the next sudden spike. It's never bad enough to be gamebreaking or unforgivably frustrating, but it's definitely jarring every now and then. This alone is why I'll never even attempt the permadeath mode. Yes, there's a permadeath mode. No, it's not popular.
The worst two spikes in the game are;
the secret "final" area in the game, which out of nowhere is Super Meat Boy-levels of platforming challenges, with saws and spikes everywhere that almost don't thematically fit the rest of the game, but is required to get two of the three endings,
and one of the hidden quests required to get a health upgrade, which requires you to take a long trip from one end of the map to another without taking damage or using fast-travel, and you can't even use the new Dreamgate feature to make it easier. Most games that have a challenge like this don't have "no damage" as a part of it, and it's usually just a tedious test of patience. Here, it's far worse as you have no reliable ranged attack, and it's the one thing I'm missing for 100% completion.
However, this is honestly the only negative I can give it. Anything else I can really say are just middling nitpicks like "there isn't a reliable ranged weapon" or "you don't have any control over the duration of your dash, so you can easily overshoot". Hollow Knight all around is a fantastic experience that I can highly recommend at nearly any price. It's more than worth the money.

There have been a large number of negative reviews for this game. In terms of the arguably too-early release of the game, I can't speak to that. I understand there were major bugs when it was released. I came a bit late to the party and by the time I bought Space Hulk it was in 1.3 and I have witnessed no bugs.
In terms of the negative reviews that imply the game is boring, to that I can say this: Space Hulk is a computer implementation of a BOARD GAME. Yes, a board game that has turns and die rolls and a big rulebook and moves about as quickly as you would expect a board game to move. So in the same way that no reasonable consumer should expect a computer implementation of Monopoly to be fast-paced and action-packed, the same expectation should hold for Space Hulk. IF YOU DON'T LIKE BOARD GAMES IN GENERAL OR THE SPACE HULK BOARD GAME IN PARTICULAR THEN YOU WILL NOT LIKE THIS GAME. It is not a "translation" or a "computer game inspired by the board game." It is a direct, rule-for-rule, turn-for-turn implementation of the Space Hulk board game. If you do like board games in general or the Space Hulk board game in particular then you likely will find a lot of fun here. As a lifelong board game enthusiast and Space Hulk lover, I find this game to be near perfect.
The $29.99 price tag on the game is, in my opinion, reasonably worth it. But if you grab it during the Holiday sale for $14.99 then it is a no-brainer, great value.

Alright Hollow Knight is an absolutely awesome game but like just about every game, it has some flaws so I'm going to pro-con this shizzle:
+Fun, satisfying combat with tight controls
+some legit awesome music tracks, especially the boss themes
+epic and challenging bosses who will roast you in the tastiest way
+tons of non-linear exploration; look around and you're sure to find some interesting stuff, whether it's an upgrade, a charm with a beast effect, or even a whole new area, there's always more stuff to find
+Super beautiful graphics, so beautiful much aesthetic
+cute, lovable bugs and intense, spooky bugs are both present
+tons of different areas and a huge amount of content make it a fantastic value
Now for the cons:
-While the music is awesome, there's not really enough of it, and a lot of areas will just have ambient noises, which are sick, but they need some music with them you know?
-too much backtracking: while backtracking to find new secrets and other cool stuff is totally awesome, facing a boss, losing, then having to go through the same dudes you already fought for like 3 minutes just to get back to the boss sucks, especially if it takes you a bunch of tries to beat the boss.  Luckily this hasn't been too big of an issue for me so far, as I've never had to try that many times to beat a boss, but I can imagine it being stupidly frustrating if you get stuck on one boss and have to backtrack over and over again.
-Too punishing: many people say that hollow knight is a super difficult game but really, it's not that tough for the most part.  I think it's more of a punishing game.  Having to always backtrack to face the boss again is punishing the player, not making the game any harder than if they just put a bench in front of the boss room.  And the whole losing-your money-and-having-to-go-back-to-where-you-died-to-retrieve-it thing doesn't make the game harder either, it just makes it annoying if you fail and have to grind to get more money.
Overall, these are just small flaws in what is an absolutely fantastic game, and as long as you can put up with just a little bit of tedium sometimes, I'd highly, highly recommend it.  The feeling of exploring an uncharted world and discovering new things all the time is something that I think few games can match.

Battlerite is the spiritual successor to Bloodline Champions, a game developed several years ago that flew under the radar until Funcom the publisher destroyed it with some questionable microtransaction that started affecting gameplay. I played fell and in love with BLC's early gameplay and have been searching for a game like it for at least 3 years. Imagine my surprise when I discovered the same developer studio has developed a new version of the core fighting/arena based  game with all the mechanics I fell in love with years ago - Battlerite.
This game has a steep learning curve for those that have not played a game of this type before, those who played BLC have a distinct advantage because many of the old heroes have been ported in a sense to Battlerite. Once you've picked up on the learning curve the fast paced and adrenaline pumping PvP gameplay will keep you interested and engaged for fans that love competition.
The game is still in early access so there are places where it's lacking depth. The UI, cosmetics, and group management could all certainly be expanded and improved but the core gameplay mechanics are fantastic and the developers are continuing to focus on hero gameplay and new hero release prior to tackling some of the fluff that we can expect from a game that's been fully released.
Some reviews indicate that the community is 'too toxic' which can't be further from the truth. After playing hundreds of games only three of them have had a toxic player. The game can be frustrating to newer players but if you let go of your obsession with rank, play what you enjoy - over time you will improve and get a better sense for the game leading to some intense matches.
I look forward to the future developments for this game and I love the community supporting it however they can. There are weekly tournaments hosted in several regions showcasing the competitive aspect of the game. If you want a game with no fluff, no grinding, no leveling, no unfair gameplay advantages whatsoever - a game where you are rewarded exlusively for your skill and mastery of the hero you play and those you are playing against, then Battlerite is for you.
Cheers!
