Although would be better if there was a penilty for leaving a game, kinda annoying when an ally quits cause he died once, 1 round in. Has a lot of replay value, no pay to win, all ingame cosmetics can be obtained freely (at the time of writing this). The game is VERY polished and optimised well. Hoping to see tons more champs as I could see this becoming a world class compeditive game with many different play styles and stratagies. The gameplay it'self requires you to think on the spot, a wrong move could mean the end of your champion - and ultimlty ruin your team chances of winning, especially when it becomes 2v1 in a 2v2 match. Enjoing the cosmetics, although i think they could do with a tad more veriation. Some of the rare weapons look cooler than the legendary, while some outfits are simply just a colour change. It's a good game on it's own however one marred by several inexcusable problems that make recommending it a VERY VERY difficult sell.
If you do not own a pad, This is a painful game for kb users and I say kb not kb/m because though you can use the mouse, you will really wish you never touched it.I own a pad so this issue is not such a big deal to me but there are plenty others who are frustrated.
Issues that everyone already covered are ofc naturally the numerous threads of fps and lack of graphic options. Type 0 has 2 resolutions but AA actually scales the resolution up to I believe 1.5 and 4x the normal resolution so unless you have an extremely beefy gpu, you likely won't be able to touch these settings without massive frame drops though it will look very very nice-more clearly separating resolution and AA would have been better. The whole 30 fps thing is blown a bit of of proportion however as if you simply have a normal mid-range gpu, you can run the game at "normal" aa at 1920 which will give you a steady 30 fps, no higher, no lower which is good enough. Controls are just "acceptable" with a pad with some prebuilt keybinds but no options to actually remap keys. One INFURIATING thing everyone fails to mention too is that the mouse cursor hangs around on the screen, regardless of control type used(which is why I said you will deeply regret trying to use the mouse and have it wiggle all over your game)-think Dark Souls port. Camera controls are instead deferred to numpad which is...just...not fun.
The actual game itself is really fun and compelling despite everything. An interesting story with good action oriented gameplay where you lock onto foes and attack/cast spells in real time. 14 characters with various abilities and styles of combat. Though one gripe about this is how you instantly lock onto a corpse mid fight to "harvest" when you wish it would switch to another target. Behind the very awesome action combat(somewhat similar to crisis core) you will get a deep and very sad FF story with the beautiful OST that typically accompanies the series.
In short, it's a good game, marred by disgusting porting that cannot be recommended to the average consumer. If you are a diehard fan of the series like me, you can kind of  just justify the game with all it's issues, if not, you are better off giving this one a pass
Edit: as of Sept 18, more options were given for graphical customization especially proper resolution supports for varying displays. Similarly the horrible mouse cursor was finally patched out so no more having to drag it offscreen everytime. Controls for kb/m were GREATLY improved to actually be somewhat useable now though still severely lacking in terms of sensitivty adjustment. However, it's been improved enough to say if your 50/50 on this game, it's now enough to buy it. If you are a "30 fps" fanatic, this game will never be for you

This tower defense/direct combat hybrid game will take you in with its charming visuals and upbeat and powerful soundtrack, but give it enough hours and it will start to show its ugly side.
At low-level play the game is a blast, playing the campaign alone or with others is a fun and relaxing experience that encourages experimentation where multiple approaches are viable. You’ll learn the different classes’ ins and outs and figure out your preferred style of play, while enjoying both the tactical aspects of tower-placement and the cathartic side of directly engaging the enemies (granted, the latter in a clunky and somewhat unsatisfying manner).
At high-level play, on the other hand, you’ll find a game of tedious minmaxing armor and weapon stats in which there’s no strategy whatsoever. Just find or look up the optimal solution of stacking tower buffs into a single chokepoint or two and sit back and look at your character’s experience bar slowly fill again and again (after level 70 the requirements to level up basically double on your total accumulated experience points, making grinding a real necessity, especially with gear level requirements), since engaging in combat directly will usually mean death and a loss of bonus points. Everything you’ve learned thus far is useless, only a few select classes are useful and the rest only exist to soak up shared experience points or to get yelled at and kicked from the server.
It’s also difficult to talk about Dungeon Defenders without mentioning the DLC. While I wouldn’t go so far as saying that it’s pay-to-win, since any PvP match is a rarely-played niche game mode, there’s a couple of paid DLC classes that are absolutely required for high-level play (and you can always find another player with said classes). One effectively doubles the defenses allowed on any map and the other buffs any defense to be able to face nightmare difficulty levels. There’s also like a dozen single map/single skin DLC that award unique gear drops upon level completion, which fall under the “shady and iffy” category on my book. Sure you can trade for them in player-run shops, but if you thought grinding was a time sink you haven’t been gear hunting on Dungeon Defenders' AFK shops.
And god forbid the RNG deities haven’t favored you on a specific run and make the end of the level reward useless, forcing you to try again! (This happens more often than it should).
My advice to new players is this: if you get the game ignore the higher difficulty settings as you progress through the campaign and the DLC levels, because as it is, the game simply forces you to play it for more time than it’s worth.

I'm really new to the Shadow Warrior genre and I just bought it during a steam sale.
My first experience with the game and my take on it.
+ Astoundingly beautiful graphics.
+ Delicious gore.
+ Very original and cool weapon designs.
+ Lots of easter eggs, secrets and funny tidbits you can find when exploring the world around you.
+ Very fast-paced combat, always keeps you on your toes.
+ Wang.
+ Very nice artwork and environmental effects. Everything around you is a freaking deathtrap if you're not careful.
+ Very nice blend of horror, thriller, suspense and action.
Now for the cons.
- The head and weapon bobbing makes me a little nauseous. I wish there was an option to turn that off.
- The lighting in some are blinding and frustrating to navigate to.
- Some of the control schemes just don't make sense to me. Like the regeneration skill. Constantly pushing "D" makes you move while healing, which can be convenient at times but there are some cases where you don't want to go in the direction you're trying to heal yourself in.
- Motion blur is going to make me sick. I'm normally used and accustomed to FPS games  but this one just makes me wanna puke after playing for hours for some reason, something that most FPS games do not induce on me.
- The death count: Seriously, don't be like GTA or other games that reminds players how many times they messed up in the game. I'm a perfectionist so I had to delete my old save data just to start fresh and go for a no death run.
- There are times where Wang is just trying too hard to be funny. The accent is a little bit thick for an asian too.
- Lo Wang is not even a japanese name. I don't know Wang's backstory but when I started the game, I assumed he was Japanese. If so, disregard this.
- Experienced my first death when I misread the health number and thought it read 12 when it actuallity, it was written as "92". I panicked and ran all over the place, got mobbed and died.
Overall, my score for this game is an honest 8/10.

This game is confusing.  You will not know what to do when you first turn the game on & it will take you some time (hours or longer) to figure out exactly how to do things.
Also, ignore the 0.1 hours played since I've not been playing the game through Steam.
The game starts you out near a shop in the middle of space.  The tutorial broke for me so I couldn't use it.  I had to figure out everything by experimentation & through guides online.
The first thing you need to do is build a ship & you have no idea how to do it.  I spent 4 hours figuring out how to build a ship with some long video showing me only to have it vaporize once I went into a warp.  Not only did I just waste 4 hours of my time I ended up pennyless with no ship stranded at the starting area.  After a lot of frustration I ended up making a smaller ship after selling what little materials I had left & went to my first planet which was kind of cool in a way.  The planets aren't really planets in a sense.  More like, several pieces with their own gravity stuck together.  If you walk around you'll see dead drops & if you jump over the drop you'll be pulled down by the other sides gravity.  Sort of like a janky Super Mario Galaxy.  Only half the planet had any atmosphere & it was always the half facing the sun which I didn't understand why they did this until I realized the side with atmosphere is supposed to be daytime while the space sky is night.  I guess it works but it's wierd looking up & seeing half day/night skies.
Later, I relogged in to find my ship was gone.  Then as I searched around for it I realized it had spawned in the middle of the planet I logged out of which is kind of funny.  Here's a video of the experience.
Been playing the game a bit more & harvesting asteroids with a new ship I made which seems to be the easiest way to make money.  Harvest & then sell what you gather.  Managed to build myself a half decent ship as well even though it's unfinished.  The whole thing still rather confusing.  I don't really know what I need to get hyperdrive working properly so my ship doesn't vaporize. I'm probably not gonna be trying that again for a while. Exploring that far away might not be worth it yet anyways.
This game also has performance issues.  Being an Alpha build I guess that is to be expected because the game runs badly & locks up on me at random moments.  Usually it locks up during the first loading sequence or when I shoot something for the first time.  If you're running a lower end machine I really don't recommend running anything on high settings.  I tried having shadows on High & it dropped my FPS down to single digits.
If you do decide to buy it, do it to either support the devs or to see it through it's development cycle.  If you do plan on playing this game expect to spend several hours trying to figure out how to do anything because it's currently very confusing.  Hopefully the tutorial won't break for you like it did for me.  There's a lot of potential here & I'll probably end up playing this game more in the future & when it gets better overall.

Given the life expectancy of Terminators in this game, regular Space Marines must spontaneously combust the moment they breath space hulk air.

A warning to someone that just starts this game: You'll NEED to look up tutorials, and you'll NEED to use the wiki. (I recommend Starmadepedia). I'll summarize my expierience thus far.
Started Playing Game
Did Tutorial
Built a Crappy Ship
Combines a post I saw on steam + Some new found knowledge and made a Mining Ship
Spent upwards of 2 hours mining a small area of asteroids
Sold the minerals to the local shop
Bought a faction module to find a place to settle and claim
Bought a Space Station
Claimed a System after building a small station
Made a goal to be able to mine Asteroids in seconds
Did more Mining
More Mining
Upgraded Ship to the point it could easily eat an asteroid in a minute or less
Read a Post that said you could blow up planets
Made the ambitous goal to mine away entire planets and then blow them up (Or vice versa)
More Mining
Setup factories that were super efficient (You can increase factory outputs with Factory Enchancers)
Built a whole bunch of parts to add on to my system
Learned about Cannon Computers to Salvage Computers
Upgraded my system
Could now mine entire planets, but not destroy them
Learned about Nuke Missiles
Made a system with a Pulse Module Slaved to a Missile Module for Nukes compiling a 2.3k block array
Learned that my nuke used way to much power
Did a bunch of swearing
Tripled my power storage and reactor setup to accomadate my nuke setup
More swearing because it couldn't accomadate the setup
Doubled the reactor and power setup again, along with adding Lasers and Cannons
Finally was able to launch nukes
Blew up a world
Lagged out the Server
Got back on Server
Started raiding a nearby Pirate Station
Slowly built up ship till it could take out Pirate Station
Started helping newbies with newbie issues
Blew up another world and mined all its contents to impress said newbies
This was about 2 days worth a play time total,  and I did not regret a single second of it :)

Starmade
-Procedurally generated world, it's never the same.
-Takes imagination, or you can go download other player built ships.
-When they say "open world" they mean, "open universe". Only limitations are your own imagination and creativity
-Quite literally the universe is your sand box, build it, and they will come.
-Save Yourself some time and learn how to use advaned build mode. (but first make sure you understnad how power works)
-Oh yeah, there are ships and stuff... Did I meantion you can build whatever you want? (press "m" to spawn a station, press "x" to spawn a ship.)
-Devs are super acive in the community, makes for easy vertical communication. Which is very refreshing
Things to note:
-Little bit of a learning curve.
-Because code  for the game hasn't been streamlined perfectly yet there are some issues on multi-player servers due to lag when more than 15 players are on at one time. (this will effect game play severly)
-The community, while for the most party very informed, is actually somewhat elitest (just something to note)
-Pick the right server for your play style!! I can not stress this enough, it's very important that when playing for hundreds of hours on a server you at least like it a little bit.
-Updates are rolling out all the time, as the game is in "alpha" (updates usually fix previous bugs but always bring with them their own new bugs, remember it's in "alpha")
-I won't lie, it takes a very long time to get things done in starmade, however it is very rewarding creating your own empire.
-If you want a perfectly polished game Starmade isn't quite there yet. But it still looks and feels awesome!

No other words are necessary, my Brothers. Purge thy mind of all doubt, place this amusement construct into thine cart and purchase it without hesitation or remorse. Though the Adeptus Mechanicus has labored long and well, no construct is without fault and even the most sacred relic might fail in the searing crucible of battle. Fear not; the Machine Spirits will answer your prayers. The blasphemy of the Tyranids is such that only one solution is acceptable. Extermination.
Know what you're buying before you click the button. This game is exactly what it says it is, nothing more. It is exactly what I wanted, and I'm really enjoying it. If you like the WH40k universe, you are more likely to be forgiving of any perceived shortcomings. It is a digital reproduction of a boardgame; if you don't like boardgames or their mechanics, you might not like this. There are dice rolls, meaning luck is involved. If that bothers you, perhaps this game is not for you. It is turn based, meaning planning and tactical thought are essential to victory. This game is about close quarters battle in very confined spaces. This results in a very particular style of play which may not appeal to everyone. Tension is only elevated and enhanced by the element of randomness and luck. Your opinion may differ, if so....I think you already know the answer.
Put yourself in the mindset of a Space Marine. You are not failing if you lose Marines. If the objective is accomplished by the last man, victory is yours. Space Marines are supposed to die, they expect to die. Get out of the mindset of preserving your squad...the deaths do not carry over to the next mission. If a Marine holds a corridor alone and ends up overwhelmed, but in so doing bought enough time for the mission to be accomplished? Victory. Preserve your strength if you can, but do not be afraid to spend the lives of your Marines if it leads to victory. Fear only failure.

Stronghold Crusader 2 isn't a worthy sequel to the orginial Stronghold Crusader. If you buy it because you expect it to be as good as crusader 1 you might be disappointed. However, if you treat it as an independent castle sim, it's a decent game. The game has some performance issues and the AI tends to ignore your commands and just randomly walk around to attack peasants instead of buildings.. those are the 2 main issues which really bother me. Other than that, the game itself is quite enjoyable. The skirmish trail has less missions than the crusade but the battles feel harder in my personal opinion. Due to the difficulty, missions usually take more time and it makes up for the minor content. Multiplayer matches with friends vs. bots are also a lot more enjoyable. Crusaders main issue was, that the bots couldn't really deal with multiplayer maps and didn't do anything.. Stronghold Crusader 2 fixed (at least) that.
Short version: If you buy the game because you loved Stronghold Crusader and have high expectations... wait for a sale. If you want a decent castle sim it's worth the money though.

The graphics, soundtrack and gameplay are great and it runs well even on my measly intel 4000 integrated graphics.
The story falls a bit short, unfortunately; not only because of the writing but also because it's easy to get distracted by side activities until you can't remember what was going on anyway and probably can't be bothered to care either.
That said, it's not bad, if you don't mind a more fantasy-oriented AC game with a lot of focus on mythology and stuff, but it's not exactly the most captivating piece of AC storyline I've ever seen.
The game runs smoothly even on my laptop (Yes, I'm playing this on a laptop. Sue me.) and I haven't encountered any bugs, either (apart from the occasional sword phasing through some of the outfits, but I have yet to see a game where that doesn't happen).
The parcour pathfinding is no less aggravating than it could be in previous games, and there are some climb-able things it really hates, such as a few parts of mast and rigging, as well as the occasional tree. Fluidly running over rooftops and the like works good, though - if you can find enough rooftops to run over, that is.
You don't need to constantly hold down three keys (forward, sprint and freerunning) anymore, only two; you only need the third one for jumps deemed 'unsafe' by the pathfinding, which is definitely an improvement.
Hand-to-hand (or, well, sword-to-sword) combat is okay, but neither particularly hard nor terribly exciting. Very satisfying, though, and it looks awesome.
Naval combat, however, is fluid, streamlined and just plain fun once you get the hang of it.
The only thing that is probably even more fun than naval combat is sailing: The different weather conditions are beautiful to watch (look out for high waves during sunshine - the color of the sea when the sunlight shines through the waves is a very nice and very pretty touch), if occasionally slightly aggravating (hello there, super-dense fog and intense storms with unfortunate timing) but ah, the things you gladly suffer for a bit of realism.
The ship handles very nicely too, and the level of texture you can see even while sailing is incredible.
(Also, bonus point for
! Best thing ever. Although the soundtrack if you deactivate them is glorious, too. Win/win.)
I don't know if I've mentioned it yet, but the game is stunningly beautiful. Very detailed, very nicely textured and well made, with a very clean, intricate and atmospheric look.
If you're anything like me you'll probably end up climbing sync points more for the looks than for anything else, especially because the map is a good deal less integral to you finding your way around than it used to be.
The only thing that I don't like about AC4 is the amount of wasted potential: AssCreed needs a more captivating story than AC4 has and as much as I love it as it is, it probably would've been the game of my dreams if they'd just made a pure pirate game out of it and expanded on the pirate-y parts of it. The Assasin parts of the game do feel a bit tacked on every now and then.
Still, I don't regret spending money on this - it was totally worth every cent of it and I can full-heartedly recommend it - it may not be a perfect game, but it is a very,
good one.

Battlerite is the spiritual successor to Bloodline Champions, a game developed several years ago that flew under the radar until Funcom the publisher destroyed it with some questionable microtransaction that started affecting gameplay. I played fell and in love with BLC's early gameplay and have been searching for a game like it for at least 3 years. Imagine my surprise when I discovered the same developer studio has developed a new version of the core fighting/arena based  game with all the mechanics I fell in love with years ago - Battlerite.
This game has a steep learning curve for those that have not played a game of this type before, those who played BLC have a distinct advantage because many of the old heroes have been ported in a sense to Battlerite. Once you've picked up on the learning curve the fast paced and adrenaline pumping PvP gameplay will keep you interested and engaged for fans that love competition.
The game is still in early access so there are places where it's lacking depth. The UI, cosmetics, and group management could all certainly be expanded and improved but the core gameplay mechanics are fantastic and the developers are continuing to focus on hero gameplay and new hero release prior to tackling some of the fluff that we can expect from a game that's been fully released.
Some reviews indicate that the community is 'too toxic' which can't be further from the truth. After playing hundreds of games only three of them have had a toxic player. The game can be frustrating to newer players but if you let go of your obsession with rank, play what you enjoy - over time you will improve and get a better sense for the game leading to some intense matches.
I look forward to the future developments for this game and I love the community supporting it however they can. There are weekly tournaments hosted in several regions showcasing the competitive aspect of the game. If you want a game with no fluff, no grinding, no leveling, no unfair gameplay advantages whatsoever - a game where you are rewarded exlusively for your skill and mastery of the hero you play and those you are playing against, then Battlerite is for you.
Cheers!

Challenging, but rewarding AF. Uneven sense of humor, but overall I was laughing more than cringing (the Stan Bush sing-along in the opening sequence was brilliant). Best first-person sword fighting I've ever encountered, and a surprisingly deep system behind it. You'll be learning new moves right up until the end, meaning it doesn't get stale (neither does slicing a demon in half diagonally, a bit of service for fans of the original). enemies are a bit repetitive, but the way they're rolled out, balanced to provide new challenges just when you've grown comfortable fighting, is straight-up retro shooter. Guns felt a bit weak, for my tastes, never giving me the meaty sense of POW that games like the most recent Call of Juarez really nail. I also would have enjoyed some returning weapons from the original. The rail gun, in particular, could have been used to great effect, but it seems our fascination with that particular weapons tech died with the 90s. Surprisingly long, as well, at least for me. And the story, as many other reviewers have pointed out, is unexpectedly emotionally-charged. No Gone Home levels of emotional maturity, but certainly more than I was expecting. Also, it is, for the most part, beautiful. Bamboo groves lit up at night are a particularly pretty and mood-setting affect. However, as gorgeous as many of the settings are, they get repetitive. There's a major switch in scenery about 2/3 in, but by that point I had grown very tired of the Japanese temple/quaint village/cave surroundings. Again, my rather slow progress (lotta dying) probably contributed to this. Speedier players may not spend as much time on each level as myself. Overall, highly recommended, even to those who don't favor shooters, like myself.

Alright, after playing this for 116 hours I thought I'd share my view of this game. So first, yes I know this is an early access title, but the tutorial kinda' sucks to me. I was still clueless on what to do afterwards, but perhaps maybe I'm just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, idk. The game feels a bit empty with nothing to do, but I wasn't expecting much considering it's an early access title. The reason I've been playing so long was simply out of sheer excitement to keep building onto my ship, and even try to make a little mech or something haha (it's extremely time consuming). It's strangely addicting.
It's a sandbox space sim where you start off with nothing but a few things in your inventory. You have a ship core, you hit the X key to create a new ship, name it, and then you build onto it with parts, etc. To make stuff you need to mine of course, so you go out in space and find asteroids or planets and mine them. After you mine and get resources, you need to make factories in order to make stuff with what you mined. Pretty simple, like most crafting games. You can build ships, bases, create factions, you can claim solar systems and make them your faction territory, you can go and fight pirates and destroy their bases. But thats really all there is to it (or at least from what I've seen). With that being said, I think this game was aimed more at multiplayer.
It's not a bad game, just wish it didn't take me 100 years to figure out what to do when I first started playing. And also, the pirate stations seem to be there to troll you, as you cannot mine them after you take them out, instead you have to pay an exorbitant amount of money to repair them (15mil), which is really silly to me and kinda defeats the purpose. Idk why the devs did that. Without the help of guides and YouTube videos, i'd be lost and wouldn't have played as long as I did. I do recommend this though, I can't sit here and act like it wasn't fun. Just understand that it's early access, it has bugs, and still needs a lot of work.

TL;DR - A beautiful puzzle game revolving around a simple mechanic, with lots of content. A must-have for puzzle game connoisseurs.
A great puzzle game with a simple but interesting mechanic. The art style looks absolutely amazing, and the puzzles themselves are well-designed. The impossible architectures that are in the levels are intriguing. It reminded me a bit of Braid, mostly because of the art style, but The Bridge's main mechanic, the rotation is original, as far as I know. There is also a time-rewinding mechanic in the game, so you can undo your mistakes if yu happen to mess up, which is a nice addition, since you don't have to restart the entire level in case you fail.
There are many levels to play and collectibles to find, and after your first playthrough an alternative world is unlocked, in which you can play through more difficult versions of the original levels. I only had problems with 1-2 levels, the others can be figured out easily, or with a bit of thinking and planning.
To sum this review up, The Bridge is a very ambitious puzzle game with puzzles revolving around a simple mechanic, and with an amazing art style. I'd highly recommend it.

This is a major step up from the previous Train Simulator games, and makes other simulators look outdated next to it (on Ultra settings at least) with very high detail, great shadows, amazing reflections, high quality textures. It runs on the UNREAL ENGINE so what else were you expecting?
-
Compared to previous version of Train Simulator, the three locomotives that come with this game are very highly detailed. Pretty much every button is pressable (they also do stuff), from the main switches to the fuses everything is useable, like we have been used to in flight sims for many years. This adds a great sense of depth to the game and shows that a lot of work and thinking has gone into its design.
-
This might not sound like a very interesting feature, but it adds a whole other level of realism to the game. From the way, the train turns in a corner, to the way you first pull out with 100 wagons, to having manage your speed downhill with the 100 wagons behind you. A must for a good simulator.
-
I like the new layout of the main menu, it’s functional, simple and works well. I also like how you can just hop back in the train you were driving when you last quit the game and start from the last checkpoint.
-
This is something that not many simulators get right. From the physics to the graphics to the level of customization, it is well integrated and is functional. Driving in a blizzard really changes the gameplay compared to just driving in sunshine. This is a huge improvement from the previous games’ glitchy rain and white fog.
-
The first-person view allows you to behave like a conductor/engineer which is great. From using the turn table to fueling the locomotives to walking around and just admiring your train, first-person view and movability adds another layer of immersion.
-
Having a bit of role-play and voice-over, with fun bits of information or signaling exchanges just makes the scenarios more interesting and interactive.
-
This may not sound like a feature at all, but coming from the previous Train Simulators you will be delighted to know that the lights actually “light up things”.
-
I can play GTA V and Battlefield 1 on ultra/high settings at 1080p with ~60 FPS, so there should be no reason for getting 20-30 fps at high/ultra settings in this game. This is most likely due to the lack of optimization in the game, because lowering settings doesn’t even help reach 60 FPS. As it is a new game I will give it time and see if it gets better in the future. However low-end PCs beware, you will most likely struggle running the game.
-
Objects in the distance seem to “blur out” rather than “fade out” which makes it seem like I have bad eyesight in the game. This is most likely due to rendering of distant objects, but hopefully this will get changed or made optional through settings.
-
Although the current scenario pack and map will keep you occupied for a good while, there doesn’t seem to be much in the pipeline for future scenarios yet. Hopefully more content can be expected once third party developers jump on this.
-
While the HUD has been made simpler and more transparent, it lacks certain features that were in previous Train Simulator games that were useful like; the scenario checkpoint list, height/angulation level map and break position indicator (I find the gages and notifications a bit unclear). Also the signal/speed limit/objective indicators seem glitchy and too “in your face” rather than subtle.
-
The XP based level systems seems like a glorified play-time indicator, as it has no real function as far as I am aware. Also, why do I have to type in all my information every time I start up the game?
-
I know that this is in the works and is coming soon, but really should have been implemented from the start.
-
While the tutorials are good, they only cover the very basics. I would like to see more detailed tutorials of the individual locomotives (as they are not the same and are quite complex).
-
The current list of options is very short with little customization, therefore it is harder to configure the game for optimal gameplay on lower end PCs.
-
In the current game there is still very little communication in-between other AI and the signalers, would like to see more interactive features related to signaling in the future.

Surprisingly dark puzzler.
The levels in the game are split into 2 sets. First, you play through all the levels, then you play the "mirrored" levels which have extra things added to them which makes the puzzles much harder. It's a cool concept and gives the game some length by bringing the total number of levels ~40-50.
In the puzzles, you can control which way the world is tilting and which direction your character walks in. By doing this, you have to get your character through a door which is the exit. All the levels follow an MC Escher type theme with impossible structures everywhere. Trying to wrap your head around the fact that the levels arent flat is one of the hardest things in the entire game. The levels starts out simple enough but then you move on to adding death balls, inversions to different colors, and veils which allow you to control the balls. The additional feature is the space bar which reverses time (Braid style) so you can fine tune your movements.
The levels have a natural challenge to them as more levels get introduced. However, the last level in the main campaign has a ridiculous difficulty spike and the last two levels of the mirrored levels are insanely complex. The difficulty jumps but for someone who is really into puzzlers, you will love it. It's only 2-3 hours with me being terrible but it’s a good length for a puzzler
There isn’t much of a story. You meet a dude and he goes through the doors. But if you read the plaques at the end of each set of rooms, you will get a sense of a scientist exploring a hypercube sort of deal (which is the mirrored). It's quite dark as each time you die, you get a message which depresses you. The music is creepy and adds to the atmosphere quite well. At the end of both the normal and mirrored edge, you try and cross a bridge... and stuff happens. I'm not sure what. But something happens. Overall, there is a story but I can’t make sense of it. However, it creates a wonderfully creepy atmosphere
Overall, if you like difficult puzzlers, have fun. Otherwise, it’s not really worth your time for 10 dollars.

I was gifted this game; hence why I've tagged it as "I recieved this for free".
Hollow Knight is not like Dark Souls. Hollow Knight is also not gruelingly difficult (for the most part) like that game is often stereotyped as. Hollow Knight is closer to something like Dust: An Elysian Tail, although one may see some inspiration from Dark Souls in terms of the gloomy art direction and narrative.
Where Hollow Knight shines is the aforementioned art direction and narrative, but it also does an extremely good job at being a Metroidvania. The controls are extremely tight with maximum friction and no acceleration, so you have complete control over your movement. This is important, as Hollow Knight has a surprising amount of precision platforming involved, and the bosses are mostly well designed and really encourage skilled usage of it.
Combat is simple enough on the surface; you can swing your nail (yes, it's not a sword) in four directions, use three separate offensive spells and a healing ability that stops you in your tracks until you finish. The various Charms you can find in the game do add a bit of depth, but it doesn't go far enough to require too much thinking about it.
The map is quite large, easily surpassing Super Metroid, Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, and even Axiom Verge. Thankfully, the game does a good job with it's "fast travel" systems and doesn't feel like it overstays it's welcome as a result. It's suitably littered with secrets and items, though not quite as many as one of the aforementioned games due to it's simplicity. You get movement upgrades, spells and their upgrades, Charms, health and SOUL (basically your mana) upgrades...and that's about it. There's no dedicated ranged weapon, so you won't be finding any missile tank equivalent.
On the other hand, where Hollow Knight falters is that it's difficulty can be a bit all over the place. The curve seems pretty good at first, with most bosses at the very most taking two tries to beat, but then you can come up to a miniboss that ends up being harder than that area's ACTUAL boss, and then the game remains at a lukewarm difficulty until the next sudden spike. It's never bad enough to be gamebreaking or unforgivably frustrating, but it's definitely jarring every now and then. This alone is why I'll never even attempt the permadeath mode. Yes, there's a permadeath mode. No, it's not popular.
The worst two spikes in the game are;
the secret "final" area in the game, which out of nowhere is Super Meat Boy-levels of platforming challenges, with saws and spikes everywhere that almost don't thematically fit the rest of the game, but is required to get two of the three endings,
and one of the hidden quests required to get a health upgrade, which requires you to take a long trip from one end of the map to another without taking damage or using fast-travel, and you can't even use the new Dreamgate feature to make it easier. Most games that have a challenge like this don't have "no damage" as a part of it, and it's usually just a tedious test of patience. Here, it's far worse as you have no reliable ranged attack, and it's the one thing I'm missing for 100% completion.
However, this is honestly the only negative I can give it. Anything else I can really say are just middling nitpicks like "there isn't a reliable ranged weapon" or "you don't have any control over the duration of your dash, so you can easily overshoot". Hollow Knight all around is a fantastic experience that I can highly recommend at nearly any price. It's more than worth the money.

Alright Hollow Knight is an absolutely awesome game but like just about every game, it has some flaws so I'm going to pro-con this shizzle:
+Fun, satisfying combat with tight controls
+some legit awesome music tracks, especially the boss themes
+epic and challenging bosses who will roast you in the tastiest way
+tons of non-linear exploration; look around and you're sure to find some interesting stuff, whether it's an upgrade, a charm with a beast effect, or even a whole new area, there's always more stuff to find
+Super beautiful graphics, so beautiful much aesthetic
+cute, lovable bugs and intense, spooky bugs are both present
+tons of different areas and a huge amount of content make it a fantastic value
Now for the cons:
-While the music is awesome, there's not really enough of it, and a lot of areas will just have ambient noises, which are sick, but they need some music with them you know?
-too much backtracking: while backtracking to find new secrets and other cool stuff is totally awesome, facing a boss, losing, then having to go through the same dudes you already fought for like 3 minutes just to get back to the boss sucks, especially if it takes you a bunch of tries to beat the boss.  Luckily this hasn't been too big of an issue for me so far, as I've never had to try that many times to beat a boss, but I can imagine it being stupidly frustrating if you get stuck on one boss and have to backtrack over and over again.
-Too punishing: many people say that hollow knight is a super difficult game but really, it's not that tough for the most part.  I think it's more of a punishing game.  Having to always backtrack to face the boss again is punishing the player, not making the game any harder than if they just put a bench in front of the boss room.  And the whole losing-your money-and-having-to-go-back-to-where-you-died-to-retrieve-it thing doesn't make the game harder either, it just makes it annoying if you fail and have to grind to get more money.
Overall, these are just small flaws in what is an absolutely fantastic game, and as long as you can put up with just a little bit of tedium sometimes, I'd highly, highly recommend it. Space Hulk is one of those games that's always in my mental running for "favorite board game of all time."  It's a clean, simple design that still manages to be strategic, thematic, and atmospheric.  You don't often see all those qualities together in the same game, which makes it hard for me to not hold it with the reverence that I do.  Oh, and by the way, it's essentially the movie Aliens.  I'm not sure if we can be friends if you're not down with Aliens.  Yet I'm also a strong believer in there being something magical about playing board games face to face with friends.  I don't really do mulitplayer gaming digitally at all, since it fall short in comparison to having friends over for board games.
So here's the deal with this Space Hulk game.  It's not worth $30.  If you're looking at the game right now and it's $30, don't buy it.  It's not up to that level and Full Control are out of their minds for thinking so.  That being said, this is a _GREAT_ game at $10.  It's Space Hulk, folks, no doubt about it.  There's a couple rules tweaks here and there (clearing a jam and how the flamer works for example), but this a very well done implimention of 3rd edition Space Hulk.  So what makes this not worth $30, particularly when it's a game that I at one point spent $100 on?  Polish.  The animations are servicable, but at times requires some imagination.  Yeah, imagination, let's go with that.  It's the kind of stuff I'd be completely okay with in a $5 game I got on my iPhone, but not in a $30 one I got on my PC.  There's a couple of other nagging things like scoping out the map being a little bit slow.  The default Terminator animations are PAINFULLY slow, but you can now adjust that.  Nothing deal breaking for sure, but things I would have felt more disappointed by had I paid full price.
Bottom line is that if it's on sale, there's alot of fun that can be had here.  If you've never been fortunate to play the board game, this is a fine way to do so without selling a kidney.  It's one of the most influential board games ever published, especially in regards to video games, as you can see its DNA in games like Fallout and XCOM.
Oh, and while it's not necessary to use the timer, I certainly wouldn't dismiss it either.

UPDATE(23/09/2015): Now the game has more resolutions when in fullscreen mode and the most important thing is, MOUSE SUPPORT! You can finally move the camera with your mouse. Sadly, there isn't a mouse sensitivity settings in the game so I suppose the camera moves depending on your mouse DPI, so if you find the camera to be really slow, increase the DPI of your mouse.
Now lets start with a few simple things.
GRAPHICS
Since everyone is SO concerned about the graphics, I decide to talk about this first. The game is locked at 30FPS because it is a PSP PORT. People just tends to forget that part and starts complaining. If you are facing problems such as low FPS when playing, Lower your anti-aliasing settings. I had my AA on normal and the the rest on (except for motion blur, I turned that off) and the game runs smoothly. Cutscenes do seem a bit of a lower res than the rest of the game, so don't jusdge the game just from the cutscenes. Hop in game and start moving around to get the actual picture.
CONTROLS (OUTDATED)
I will have to say I am disappointed in the controls of this game. The keyboard controls are unplayable, that is for sure. You can't change the keyboard settings to whatever you want as well. I would advise people to play this game with a controller. If you don't have a controller (like me), you can try something else. I have a Steelseries Rival, I made a profile just for this game, changing my Mouse 1 button to F and Mouse 2 to backspace so that I can use my mouse to attack in game while I move using the keyboard. I have the camera fixed so I don't really have to worry much. In the end, it is down to personal preference.
GAMEPLAY
I only played the game for 45minutes (according to my save file). Overall, combat is fun, story seems decent. I haven't met any game breaking bugs or crashes so far.
TLDR (UPDATED ON 23/09/2015)
It is a great game, just not a really good port. The controls are better now thanks to the mouse support. But it can be rather slow if your DPI is low, and there isn't a mouse sensitivity settings. So for now, you will just have to increase the DPI of your mouse if you want to increase the camera speed. But hey, at least the game is getting better~

The Bridge is a puzzle game that takes place in a series of level that seems to be inspired by the drawings of impossible constructions by M. C. Escher. The game uses two main mechanisms that the player can use to progress in each level - walking and the ability to turn the worlds around. There's a series of submechanisms depending on the level as well, including gravity manipulation, inversions and more.
It's divided into 8 chapters (2 times 4) and as in most games the difficulty increases from each chapter. The first 4 chapter is in the "standard world" and the last 4 is in a mirrored world. The first 4 are challenging, but can be overcome with some thought, but the last 4 chapters are very, very difficult. Generally, though, each puzzle is well thought through and even levels using the same mechanisms are very different in design and the way they should be solved.
While the gameplay is nice what's the most impressive about this game is its aesthetic side - the music is great and the art style of the game is absolutely spectacular.
Overall, if you're into puzzles you're in for a treat. It's visually stunning and there's different challenges for everyone, although later levels are very difficult.
EDIT 2 months later:
I've reread the review, and while I still recommend it there should be a few notes added. It's a short game and I would not recommend picking it up for the standard €10 it goes for, but it is often for sale at around €2, which is a pretty reasonable price for a handful of hours worth of entertainment.
Also it should be mentioned that this is not an easy puzzle game. The earliest chapters are fairly straightforward, but some of the later ones are ridiculously challenging and I admit that I had to check out YouTube for a few of them in order to even make sure what I was supposed to do.
That said, if you can get it for a good price, there's still a few hours of good and entertaining exercise for the brain, but don't be supposed to find yourself a little frustrated with the later levels.

Meh. A bit of a retro take on the 40K IP. Apparently, Space Hulk was one of the original Warhammer 40k board games, and was released in 1989. I can't be sure (having never played the board game), but I bet this PC version is exactly like it.
In a departure from recent entries into the W40K series of games, Space Hulk goes back to the game's turn-based roots. I don't know if anybody remembers Chaos Gate, but this feels a lot like that. You deploy a handful of Space Marine Terminators (for those not familiar with 40K, a Terminator is a decorated veteran Space Marine that gets to wear huger armor and is therefore able to carry even blammier weapons) to undertake missions against swarms of Tyranid Genestealers.
As far as gameplay, there's not a lot of variety, and absolutely nothing innovative or unique. This is essentially the same as the old Fallout series. The different missions keep things interesting enough, but the fact that there is just the one type of enemy is a bit of a let-down. Don't get me wrong; it's fun to mow down hordes of Genestealers. But it gets old. It would be nice to throw in the ocassional... I dunno. something else.
The tactics of the game are fairly straightforward, with little (that's not to say "no") room for variation. Cover your flanks, spend your action points carefully and make sure you leave your outward-facing dudes in overwatch mode.
So, not a "bad" game, but I was expecting a lot more out of a modern re-vamp of a twenty-four-year-old board game. An XP system to improve my marines would be nice, and needn't be very complicated to be very satisfying (something along the lines of small accuracy bumps or die-roll bonuses). Some variation in units (both friendly and enemy) would also have been nice.
While I do recommend this game, I don't recommend paying full price for it. To be honest, I think you'd be better off to find a copy of the actual board game. Good luck with that, but I think it would be far more rewarding than this PC port. At least you'd get the excitement of rolling dice and the ability to change the rules to make the game more interesting after the third or fourth go-around.
So if you're a huge fan of 40K, you'll probably enjoy this trip down memory lane. If you're a fan of squad-based tactics, you'll find something to occupy yourself for a few hours. If you're neither of those things, don't bother. I can't imagine ever buying any of the DLC for this game, and I'll be shocked if the developer ever gets to make anything else for Games Workshop.

As an avid fan of the original stronghold crusader, I cannot say that this game does the original any justice whatsoever.  Many useful buildings (such as the much needed popularity buildings, and the replacement of the different religious buildings with a one-size-fits-all church or mosque) and beloved characters, including the dastardly pig, snake, etc. have been removed in exchange for a handful of what in my opinion are much worse characters.  The economy has lost much depth from one game to the next, many systems (such as leather or hunting) have been trashed in favor of unifying the materials needed to recruit troops (ex: crossbowmen now use plate armor rather than leather).  Not to mention that units such as the horseback archer, engineer, laddermen, miners, and monks have all been discarded, removing an entire aspect of seige warfare from the game.
This being said, however, there have been a few good additions to the game, namely more in-depth castle defense (meaning a handful of new defense buildings), even though the developers got rid of moats.  Those of you who have played Stronghold 3 will be glad to know that hoardings and barricades have survived into Crusader II, along with seige engine towers.  The (formerly much-needed) healer unit can now be recruited at the mercenary post.  I'm sure I missed many other changes, but those were the biggest changes that I could recall.
I'll stop here since I'm just plain tired, but in conclusion, Stronghold 1 fans should avoid purchasing this (overall disappointing) game.

This has to be one of the best modern single player campaigns I've had the pleasure to finish in a long while. Here are some reasons as to why that would be.
The combat is amazing. The traditional combat of First-Person Shooters is greatly supplemented by the usage of chi powers and the swordplay. It's visceral and to the point - many times I found myself using the sword just because it was so much fun, even if another weapons could've been the optimal choice,
The story and writing in general is entertaining. Wang's one-liners (or Wangliners, as I call them) are often hilarious and surprising. As lighthearted as the game seems at the beginning, it will turn much darker towards the end.
The ending of the game is a surprise, and frankly, left me speechless for a long while. It could be one of the most depressing and dark things I've experienced in a long while - and it still did not leave a sour taste in my mouth.
Naturally, there were some cons as well. The level design was sometimes slightly too linear, leading into needless backtracking, and the sealed door-mechanic was not very intuitive.
A fantastic game with a 12-hour singleplayer campaign. You need to play this.
Honestly, since I loved this game so much, I fear for the sequel. I hope they don't ♥♥♥♥ it up.

Intially I thought. Oh hey intel drivers break this game therefore unplayable. So the community or the devs(dont know which one) were quick to respond and help me out. A plus on that. t
Then i tried the game and OH my god is it just as bad as i hoped it not to be.
This game in its current state is filled to the brink with a large amount of bugs and is quite shame because from the trailers i expected large ships and stations filled with people to be a common core element of the game. Sadly the footage in the trailer was either impossible to get normally, takes WAY too much time to aquire as there is no way to increase building speed, and or multiplayer.
One of the features of the game, factions is present in only in multiplayer. There is no AI factions within the game. Well.. The two that are there are basically enemy faction and nuetrals. Otherwise known as standard generic name 1 : pirates( really pirates? couldnt be more like Space dudes or anything else?) and the generic nuetral faction trading guild. These are the only two NPC factions currently in the game. So then factions come down to multiplayer.
Thats where the problem lies, because this a java coded sandbox game or a sandbox game in general, to get the most out of the game you must join a high pop server. Bingo. There is already a massive problem. Finding a good high pop server in any sandbox is not only tedious but requires a large amount of time from the player to get anything done. you must make sure the server has no greifers, protection against greifers, is constantly up, does not have troll admins, is not filleld with jackasses. The devs have not implemented anything in their game to let the player know which servers could be recommend or which servers the player should avoid. It works exactly like minecraft ip multiplayer connecting. Where every server you join has that equal chance of being a gem in a sea of turds or exaclty what you would expect.
The game itself also plays quite horribly. To fly a ship you must enter the ships core, this warps you into a small space giving no visual indiction of what just happened. There is also the nice feature of switching into build mode using space. I cannot tell you exaclty how much hate i have for this design choice. Why would you make it so the building a ship requires to enter you ship itself  and make one of the most common keys for going up the one to send you into a mode REQUIRED for buildiing the ship. You dont need to do this for stations, only for ships. ITS ANNOYING AS HELL!!! Your character LITERRALY becomes the ship block. To make matters worse once inside the ship, flying becomes terrible. The ships wobble and spin all over the place as you fly and trying to rotate the ship with the slightest tap from the  c or v keys (i think thats the one) cause you to spin uncontrobble for about 45 degrees a second. So the controls suck. The ship flying sucks. Well that already ruins one of the MAJOR ASPECTS about this game. You would think in game about SPACESHIPS the devs would go ahead and make it a priority to make controls in your spaceships as good as possible.
Well alright then maybe building should be fun you say. NOPE. Getting materials is literally brain dead boring and therefore construction becomes brain dead boring. To gather materials , right click. material will be gathered by a random laser that sticks out your face and with the magic of blue box shrinking "salavages". You then collect said ore with overly complicated name that every time you wanna build something your forced to alt tab the game and go look it up on the wiki. Oh and since the deves dont wanna give someway to view a long crafting tree and or how to make certain componenets and what not, your forced to ALT TAB the friggin game every time you wanna make something. So then crafting items which is a core element of the game becomes very tedious and thus makes building boring. Also if you have played minecraft for an extended period of time you will get bored very quickly as there is no depth to the blocks. When your blocks break they splinter. While at least in minecraft out of all things, breaking block is more interactive , there is a sound to the blocks breaking, the block itself will drop as an item. As you break the block the block begins to crack. There is a feeling of life to the blocks. While in starmade the way the block building and destroying system works makes them incredibly boring. They feel and look like godamn cardboard with not effort to them whatsoever. On planets the prodcedual generation can get pretty cool from a distance. However in a game about space, and granted this is early access there is NOTHING about the planets that indicate any excitement or uniquess whatsover.
The planets range from ice planet, grass planet, rock planet. Really more like, purple planet, green planet, blue planet. It gets boring very fast. In fact the whole game becomes a repeative drag very quickly. Now this expierence might change on multiplayer. Good luck with that.
This game does have some potential however, and granted its early access i might give it some leway considring its also free. I would have really liked to get into the game as it has really cool complicated and innovated game play mechanics some how advertised. But the gameplay itself, the UI, everything about the game feels like a giant waste of tme at first which makes it REALLY difficult to play. You have to, get used to the game. Which could take SEVERAL hours of gameplay before the game would start to shine.
Is it worth it? Is it worth going through that hassle just to get ready for the game. NO. Its not and im not sure it well ever be. I wouldnt recommend this to most people. Regardless of early access and or its potenetial , the devs current decisions on how the game operates is just terrible. Maybe there is no workaround due ot how the game code works. In that case alot more thought should have been put forth before developing this game on its core mechanics, UI, basic elements... In its current state its impossbile to really get into. Unless the dev decides to overhaul the basics and resdign come core compents of the game to simply put play better, do not get this game. It fits a very small niche auidence .

I'm going to open up this review saying that it's honestly a shame that this game is getting such mixed reviews. To first put it all into perspective this was a port from a PSP game so I was going in not expecting everything to come out perfectly as it would have if it was a port from something like the PS3. I also want to point out that almost 80% of the negative reviews are from players who have played an hour or less of the game and should be taken with a grain of salt. But I will have to say learning from some of their frustrations this game is very difficult to play with a keyboard and a game pad is almost required, and the settings of the game should be played around with most notably the camera speed.
First thing that I would like to comment on is the battle system. It is actually quite fun and intense at times which brings much contrast to the other games from Final Fantasy as it is more of a Hack and Slash to a lesser extent. I would liken it to the battle system of Kingdom Hearts with a couple key differences. Overall though I did enjoy the battle system, however i did find most of the boss fights to leave something to be desired as most of them were just straightforward and not as satisfying as boss fights normally are in Final Fantasy games. i feel that the game only becomes actually challenging once the player finishes the game once and enters NG+ (Agito Mode). That being said I did find the battle system quite refreshing and did enjoy it quite a lot.
Second is the story. The story follows Fabula Nova Crystallis series which is that of Final Fantasy 13  and a couple others, which is honestly a bit confusing to start but once you start to get further into the game it makes a bit more sense. I thought the story was very entertaining with a lot of twists to it which kept the game very interesting all throughtout. The only thing that frustrated me to no end when I was only a few hours into the game is how confusing the naming of the countries were. They follow the 4 Beasts of Asian mythology which is Suzaku, Genbu, Byakko, and Seiryu which are all tied to a country Rubrum, Lorica, Militesi, and Concordia respectively. The problem is that they use words like the Dominion, Suzaku, Vermillion Bird, and Rubrum interchangably which is really confusing until you actually associate what goes with what. But overall that is just a minor thing that annoyed me.
Overall, I did think the game is quite good and the graphics are not as bad as people put them out to be in the negative reviews. The game does come with a fair bit of confusing points and takes a bit to get used to but I assure you that after playing it for a bit it is actually a very enjoyable game.

Played the PSP version.  You can find screenshots of it in my profile.
Framerate is capped to 30FPS due to engine limitations.
Uses controller mode.
***Early Impressions***
- Personally one of my favourite FF titles to date
- A much darker tone than any previous Final Fantasy titles.
- Each character has an exaggerated unique personality to differentiate
- You'll be lost/overwhelmed by what's going on in the beginning.  You may need to play the game twice to fully understand
- New Game+ has extra things you can do.  It's not the exact same game over again.
- The port allows you to change between three controller schemes
- Camera can be snappy and difficult at time
- Very brief tutorial and controls are shown in menu.  The game isn't too complicated to  learn
- SquareEnix added a snapshot mode and a Fast Forward button for the grindy parts
- When using a controller, the UI interface doesn't switch from keyboard layout -> controller layout automatically.  Must change layout settings in launcher
- Game is capped to 30FPS.  You will not be able to change this
- A very lazy graphic port.  If you look in my profile's screenshot folder for the PSP version, they barely redone any textures but the main playable characters, boss character, and academy.
- Anti-aliasing is pretty misleading.  It's basically downsampling a higher resolution.  Therefore a very high impact to performance (high - highest setting)
- The use of bloom is extremely distracting and unnecessary.  A horrible technique to mask bad textures
- Overall a pretty nasty graphic port.  The combination of oversaturation, gloss, bloom effects, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ texture is almost eye cancer.  The port strayed too far from the original artstyle intended.
- The music plays an important role in the game.  It sets the atmosphere and has a special meaning behind it.  I'm glad they stuck with the Japanese version during the dubbing.
- There is dual audio [English/Japanese].
- The gameplay style is a real-time hack-and-slash.  The closest game control-scheme wise that I can relate to is Kingdom Hearts: Birth by Sleep
- It can be grindy at times and you'll always encounter formidable foes or enemies which you must fight against during NG+
- Your AI teammates are pretty derpy.  There's a setting to sub in higher level AI to fight for you to compensate
My three true elements to a great JRPG is a great story, memorable music, and enjoyable gameplay.  I should be able to grind battles and not be sick of the music.  I should be grinding for a purpose, either for better skils or to progress the plot.
I won't comment much on the port but the game itself is worth the playthrough.  I highly suggest you to complete the game before you pass off a judgement.  You may find yourself a bit confused at first but it all comes together in the end.
Okay, if I really had to comment on the port then I'd say it's pretty sh*t.  It's not the lack of settings or 30FPS that bothers me.  It's the design change they went with the characters and lighting.  It's so freaking inconsistent with the pre-rendered videos.  I wish they stuck with the artstyle the PSP game had.
For JRPG fans, I would highly recommend this game to you.  For anyone else it depends.  As long as you enjoy JRPG style games then I would give it a whirl.  I can confidently say that it's one of the better FF titles that has come out in a while.  For once a story doesn't revolve around character romance.
Side Notes:
- Early review.  Expect changes.
Not worth £30, buy Crusader HD and save yourself a lot of money.

UPDATE - April 8, 2017:
After reading up on the forums, I decided to take the plunge and buy this game again. Performance has been improved now, to the point where I can at least maintain 30 FPS with minimal freezing. There's still a long way to go though, and I'm hoping they'll get it running at 60 fps some day.
Some of the glitchier aspects of character movement and physics have been addressed. I haven't been teleported off of my locomotive again like I did on release day, but even if I did, they've added a debug button to get around the issue and teleport you back into the engineer seat (CTRL + 0).
As for the gameplay itself, it's all gone smoothly for me. I've completed the tutorials and the first two scenarios with no issues to speak of. The biggest issue I've come across is the fact that headlights at night are extremely dim, and hardly light up the track in front of you. I hope they address this in a future update.
The graphics are still sub par though. Image quality is terrible even at 1440p if TAA is disabled, and enabling it still causes ghosting artifacts and blurring. Lighting still looks overblown and basic, but Reshade can help with this. They also still force the ugly sharpening filter on, which is probably one cause of the poor image quality. Textures also have a tendency to appear in very low resolutions, particularly the gravel under the rails, annoyingly enough...
In the end though, I'm changing my verdict to reccomended. As of right now, it's a 7/10 in my eyes, as opposed to the 4/10 or 5/10 I'd have given it at launch. The gameplay mechanics all seem to work, and 30 fps is playable enough (even though it's still poor for a PC like mine). There's also no denying that this sim has an eye for detail that hasn't quite been seen yet, allowing you to walk around and manipulate almost every aspect of your locomotive. As long as you're willing to accept that this game isn't perfect, it can be an enjoyable experience.
ORIGINAL REVIEW - March 16, 2017:
Framerate regularly dips below 30, and sometimes even 20 on anything above medium settings. The game also has a bad habit of freezing for up to a second while driving, to load in distant scenery. Graphics are also worse than you'd expect. They applied some sort of sharpening filter to the game, which actually has the effect of making everything look like a blurry painting. On top of that, there's a very noticable ghosting issue with TAA enabled (sadly the only viable anti-aliasing option, since FXAA looks terrible and supersampling makes performance even worse). They even seem to have disabled ambient occlusion, which makes lighting look very basic overall. Nothing like the screenshots.
Overall, it just feels very bad to play, and is NOT a visually pleasing experience by any means.
The cherry on the cake that made me refund this game was when I gave service mode a shot despite the poor performance. I took an AC4400CW out for a spin, and decided to walk around the train while it was in motion. When I reached the back, I was teleported into the nose of the helper locomotive, and was unable to walk back onto the lead. Basically, that run was over because I couldn't control my train anymore.
Don't buy this game. At least not yet. Wait for patches to come out.

Battlerite fills a niche that has been arguably glossed over or poorly executed since a Westwood Classic: Nox.
Nox, similar to Battlerite, was a top down, fast paced, practically entirely aimed/skill based action game. The only burdens on a player were a mixture of knowledge, planning, and reflex. No errands to be done to obtain power (Gold, leveling), no lengthy time commitments (Games rarely extend longer than ten minutes), and a variety of ways to play (Multiple characters offering varied playstyles).
I'm a filthy 30 something, dusty ancient without the time I once had. Battlerite lets me have the intense combat I crave, where WoW PvP, League, HOTS, and various others have strayed from due to design choice or burden of time investment. The no nonsense "Jump in and crack skulls" attitude is perfect for me.
Plus, even though I cannot play as much as I would like, I can still tell the difference between skill levels in players fairly clearly. The gulf between a new player and an experienced one with just a single character is fantastic. Whenever I am obliterated in a game I can think "Hey, I can do that. I wonder how he did that. Was it aiming? Skill use? Positioning? Battlerites?"
The cosmetics leave a bit to be desired and don't particularly feel properly... weighted? A recolor costs a ton of the in game currency. Regardless, the Overwatch style of loot accumulation still feels great. The avatars given are a varied, quality bunch.
For something that is in early access, I have hope for the game. There are plenty of characters not yet transitioned over from Bloodline Champions and I'm sure some will be completely redesigned alongside brand new characters, which gives me hope for overall diversity and freshness in the game. Plus, the built in tournament system hinted at being intergrated (similar to its presence in BLC) will be a fantastic hand up over other competitive multiplayer games currently in the market.
If you want something that is new and doesn't ask you to sit down for 20+ minutes minimum while also giving you a sense of skill growth, give Battlerite a spin.

On the surface Shadow Warrior is very much just a mindless hack and slash with guns tossed in. But after playing it all the way through...I realized it's deeper then that. I won't say this is the best game or it had the best ending or even that while I feel it has deeper meaning to it, I don't think it's mindblowingly deep. There are much better games out there for that. But it was surprising and a little refreshing to see it all come together in the end, and it even moved me a little.
But it's not a perfect game, and I'll explain why.
Cons:
- Several times I was able to get "outside the map" into areas where the players should not be able to get to. And I wasn't even trying very hard.
- In some of the earlier levels (I didn't see it much in the later levels) the bamboo was floating off the ground. That just looks messy and unfinished. Not something that should be in a finished game.
- I had some audio glitches in one of the last levels. No idea why.
- Some of the "boss battles" in the later stages were pure BS. A constant gang bang of demons? Seriously? I get that it's trying to give you a "challange" but it was just lazy. It was unfair and made me almost want to quit the game and stop playing.
- The story had some flaws, like why did Zilla do it.
Now for the pros.
Pros:
- Lots of fun humor
- TONS of easter eggs and nods to the classic game
- Hoji is very funny
- The cutscenes were beautiful
- Some of the levels in this game are breath takingly stunning
- The story was really good (but it had it's flaws...)
I'd say it's a good game for people who want to hack and slash through demon scum with lots of blood and body parts flying while in some stereotypical Asian settings (temples, dojos and so on...). But I'd also say get it on sale because it has some bugs and glitches that should not be in a finished game.

Imagine this game was your grumpy old dad who never ceases to tell you that playing video games is at least as ridiculous as trying to build a snowman out of water.
It basically tells you:
Listen, son. I know you spent some hard-earned-cash on this thing you call a piece of art, but you know what? Games are bloody ridiculous! You're sitting here in front of your PC screen while pressing random buttons just because the game tells you to. You're wasting your precious time! OK, I know that you will never be a rocket scientist or find the cure for cancer, but instead of video games, you should go out and enjoy the beauty of the world we live in.
How do I know that?
Well, for me it's obvious. When you follow all of the narrator's commands , you'll reach an ending where Stanley (and you at the same) shut off the so-called 'mind-control-facility' and then leave it through a garage door leading straight into a bright, greenish landscape. Shortly thereafter you lose control over Stanley who continues walking by himself and then the screen fades to black while you get an achievement that you beat the game.
But the confusing thing about The Stanley Parable is that it also offers you other endings which deal with totally different stuff.After all, it is a game about choice and consequence. Wherever you go changes the ending of the game. While it may be a game which had less budget than an AAA-title, it is by far more complex concerning the story.
The Stanley Parable is worth both your time and your cash. Buy it and let yourself be entertained by this innovative piece of art.
And then don't play it for five years and be rewarded for doing so the day you decide that you want to be Stanley again.

The Stanley Parable is a very interesting. It tells some fantastic jokes, makes some self-indulgent commentary, but then it proceeds to get stranger and more intimate and less pointed and more interesting the more you poke at it. It isn't making fun of games for the sake of some self-appointed enlightened savior of gaming and it doesn't seem to be strange for the sake of strangeness.
What makes Stanley Parable feel so fresh isn't the humor or the satire or the criticsm that's baked into it--those are enjyoable, but they weren't what impressed me. What makes it feel fresh is how intimately it converses with the player. I'm reminded very much of a game called Save the Date--though that was a smaller and simpler affair. Both games start with meta commentary and then submerge from there, talking carefully with you about how the narrator, creator or other characters think, feel and the ramifications of that for your behavior and your experience of the product. The secret of both of these games which drape themselves in the trappings of meta-narrative is that they do actually contain characters who you will learn about, be asked to empathize with, be asked to listen to, and be asked, after it all, to act on your conclusions should you have reached any.
They are games that start with the nature of games, then the nature of reality, and then quietly, timidly, reveal that at their heart they are about the same intimacies and relationships as most intersting or moving stories. For all of the delightful jokes, strangeness, non-linearity and surreality of The Stanley Parable my most clear feeling when I stopped playing was one of loss; I had run out of ways to communicate with this person with whom I formed a relationship. I had run out of things to say and ways to prove I was listening.
I was alone.

The dark fantasy world of Hollow Knight is a sprawling cavernous labyrinth, filled with exotic insectoid creatures and creepy denizens. Both hand-drawn visuals and haunting soundtrack contribute to an oppressive, foreboding atmosphere. Despite there being very little in the way of initial story, it managed to intrigue me from the very start. The story develops as the game progresses and tidbit-by-bit the lore for this universe becomes extensive. Hallownest is a Kingdom of bugs, consumed by the Infection, leading to death or worse - insanity, deformity, and mind control for nearly all the inhabitants. Even with this dark theme of death and decay there are moments of light - one of my favourite visuals is the giant sentient stag beetle, a kind and ancient being - the last of his kind - who will allow you to ride his back as he scuttles around the Stagways (fast travel).
This is a Metroidvania platformer x Dark Souls, so perhaps the most important thing is the controls and how it
to play. Movement and combat are fluid, simple and precise. Controls are responsive and intuitive - in short, everything you could hope for in this genre. If there was one word I would use to describe the combat and movement, it's tight. It's worth noting that I used a standard Microsoft controller. Although I prefer keyboard and mouse in general, if you want the most responsive movement this genre just begs to be played with a controller.
The map is huge and whilst there is a loose order in which you need to do things to progress, it is a twisting and turning dungeon that allows you an incredible range of exploration options.  One of the few downsides is that this does mean there's a fair amount of backtracking as you have to repeat sections once you've discovered something new, and I found myself traversing certain paths hundreds of times. For some, this might not be a nuisance, but I did find that part a little tiresome and tedious. More checkpoints and waypoints might have helped to alleviate the tedium as well, especially for those who are pretty bad at this sort of game - like me! There are tasks to be completed, secrets to find, items to buy, upgrades to unlock, characters to chat to and a really intriguing subterranean world to be uncovered. I was hooked from the start.
The level of difficulty for me was incredibly brutal. I often struggle with this sort of game. I enjoy them, but I'll be honest with you all - I'm not very good at them. I would rate the combat in game as some of the more difficult I've played whilst the platforming I didn't find particularly challenging at all. In that regards, this game plays out the opposite of Ori and the Blind Forest, where combat is simple but platforming challenging. Instead of falling to your death a lá Ori, you'll be getting hacked to pieces, exploded by poison clouds, shot through the heart with needle daggers and crushed in a wide variety of ways by enemy after enemy. It requires you to be on the ball with your reflexes, precision and ability to remember moves and counter them. This is definitely a game for those looking for Dark Souls style combat.
I did ragequit a couple (dozen) times and I did get frustrated with myself, but I'm not the most patient of people and sometimes my geriatric old lady hands fail me. I take a quick break and load it back up later though... that's the hallmark of an excellent game in this genre, one that keeps dragging you back in, even after you've sworn that's it, one more death and I'm done.
I haven't come close to completing the game yet and I'm not sure I will be able to - there are 30 bosses! - but I'm enjoying every moment of failure.
