There are a lot of reasons to recommend this game, but I'm going to focus on a few.
1) Tightness
The controls are the tightest I have ever experienced. I would say they are slightly tighter than Guacamelee's or even the best of the Castlevanias. I could lose to the same boss all day and not even be mad.
2) Atmosphere
This world is *enormous.* Every time I said to myself "this world is enormous" I would fall through a hole into another enormous new section. All of the regions have distinct characteristics and manage to feel completely different from one another (the fantastic soundtrack helps a lot). And this is with a really muted color palette!
And it's all so engaging! The characters are relatively simple, but the way they move in and out of the world is understated but either charming or gripping.
3) Variety
The enormous world avoids being *too* much because areas and enemies are amazingly, delightfully varied. There are a lot of ways you can gain access to most areas, so it's not even that they scale nicely with your growing power and your familiarity with the game (though they do, with the obvious exception being one of my favorite turns in a game in recent memory). It's just that they're different from one another in interesting and insightful ways. The bosses are incredible.
This is a great game.

Before I picked up this game I was aware of apparent critical dissonance. Critics liked to give Shadow Warrior a 5-6 or max 7 out of 10, but gamers found it much more enjoyable. Who is right? Sadly, I think that I'm in the first camp.
Shadow Warrior is an oldschool FPS where shooting isn't fun. I blame the design of the weapons, enemies and the skilltree system. Guns are extremely slow and they lack the significant kick and power to be joy to fire. Rate of fire for Shotgun and Revolver is atrocious without upgrades, SMG deals pee-shooter damage without upgrades, Crossbow seems redundant without explosive-bolts upgrade, Clips of many weapons are too small without upgrades. See the pattern?  It looks like the functionality and power of many guns was cut out and hidden in many, many skilltrees, for you to unlock and discover. And I can guarantee you that those skilltrees are boring, hard to navigate, and more often than not you have no idea if something you get is useful or a wasted experience point. This means that you are locked out of the "fun", until you use your EXP later in the game and even when you unlock some of the alternative fire modes and gun tweaks, weapons are STILL underwhelming.
This points us to the enemies, which are on higher difficulties (I played the game on Hard) an annoying bullet sponges. There is for example a Shaman-type demon that spawns several skeletons while alive. He takes FOREVER to bring down and as you try to shower him with bullet you slowly lose hope and start thinking that maybe you are not allowed to kill him. He eventually surrenders, but not after 30 shotgun shells that seem to bounce of him (I mentioned the rate of fire for shotgun? Those 30 shots don't go fast (those reload times, man.. reload times).
Story is also a letdown. Not only it isn't funny when it tries to, but also the out-of-our-world-Japanese-demon-drama introduced later on is annoyingly uninteresting. You just don't care for the characters.
This brings us the comparison, that I made up in the mind… You know that there is a game what does everything right, where Shadow Warrior fails? It's called Bulletstorm and if not for the horrible GFWL DRM I would wholehearthly recommend it instead of this game. Bulletstorm understands that people want guns that make enemies explode when they simply look at them. Bulletstorm knows to not clutter the purity of the gameplay with three (!) different skilltrees. It knows how to build a proper hilarious story, with a tiny bit of drama sprinkled.
Shadow Warrior isn't as good as it could be. There are good things in code written to make this game (like swordfighting and graphics engine), but unfortunately it doesn't outweigth the boredom of the rest of the game. If in the future GFWL will be stripped from Bulletstorm, buy it instead.

The Bridge reminds me a lot of Braid. It's not just the rewinding time -- it's also the slow and cerebral puzzle elements and the story based on theoretical thinking. However, due to the puzzles being more about you manipulating the environment over navigating the environment, it doesn't have the same hook as Braid and won't have the same wide appeal. (There's no platforming element or need for quick reflexes.)
The Bridge's early puzzles are too easy, but by the third room in your house they are challenging. I think it wasn't until the fourth room that I really enjoyed them because they pushed me beyond tinkering with the world to actually plan ahead to solve the puzzle.
After completing the main game, you can run through a "mirror world" that tweaks all of the old puzzles to be much harder than before.

Not a bad game by any stretch of the imagination, but it seems like it very much wants to be Braid, and it's simply not good of a game, in either gameplay or experience.  The game's biggest weakeness is that the normal game is too simple, but what seems like the "real" game, the mirror levels, is far too difficult.  The normal games puzzles are fairly easy to figure out without too much difficult, but rarely feel as rewarding as a great puzzle game often does when solving a particularly good one.  The mirror levels introduce such a level of execution difficulty that even when the solution is known, the execution level required makes the game very difficult.  Not a good endorsement of a puzzle game, in my mind.
In the end, despite completing all the normal levels and multiple mirror levels, I simply can't say this game gave me the puzzles or the satisfaction I was looking for, even when it was challenging.  Some great art and ideas, but the execution is lacking, and the cohesive whole is good, but never great.  If you love puzzle games, pick this up on sale, and you'll find some good there...but if you're on the fence, make sure you don't expect this to be another Braid, and go in with your expectation set accordingly.

Flying Wild Hog's Shadow Warrior reboot is a suburb singleplayer FPS, marrying the original game's ribald humor and chop-suey, Hong Kong bloodshed flavor with the fast-paced, challenging-but-fair new-old-school gameplay that has been on a slow rise, seen in game's like Serious Sam: BFE and Wild Hog's own Hard Reset. Much like those games, this game does an excellent job of making you feel like an unstoppable badass, a critical element of FPS that I have found sorely lacking in, say, the military shooter genre. This title sees a younger, but no less self-important Lo Wang pitted not only against his original nemesis, corporate magnate Orochi Zilla, but a new assortment of vicious demons, and he's got a new wisecracking sidekick who sees Wang for what he is: a hopeless nerd playing at being a street samurai. But while he is quick to dispense one-liners, this Lo Wang is a fay cry from the lecherous old master of the first game, and finds himself in the midst of a powerful and emotional struggle between ancient demon lords, and matures greatly as both a warrior and a person over the course of his adventure. Shadow Warrior seamlessly (More or less. The upgrade menus strike some as jarring interruptions) blends modern character progression, enemy dismemberment and bit of iron-sight aiming with movement-based, coverless shooter combat against large numbers of enemies, typical of its predecessor's day, weaving magic spells and special sword techniques into Lo Wang's already considerable arsenal of brutal firearms. The sword itself takes a much greater role then the first game and is great fun to use, rending the demons hordes into so many meat chunks. Scattered throughout the levels are a multitude of secret areas, including one lifted directly from the original game, much like the hidden Wolfenstein 3D levels in New Order and Old Blood, and you're met with a score screen at the end of the level, assessing your skills as a Shadow Warrior- I never scored particularly high, but it didn't stop me from loving the game from beginning to its surprisingly poignant ending. I eagerly look forward to playing the upcoming sequel.

Eve meets Minecraft, the game excels at letting me fly lego-like starships that I used to make as a child. Lacks some UI refinement and some polished objectives if you're in singleplayer. Also, much of the building is very, very technical in nature, sometimes needing to run equations to understand power requirements of systems.
Biggest innovation for the voxel-sandbox games - Integration of "Creative Mode" into gameplay through the "core" and "build" blocks. When you're building a ship, you start with a core block. You enter this block to build and fly the ship. In Build mode, it allows you to freely move the camera about, and even set planes to mirror building on the blocks.
Resource collection and manufacturing of blocks is meant to be done at large scale, empowering (and enticing!) you to make capital-sized ships.
Game is good now; I'd be really curious to see what it woudl be like if they applied some of the lessons from voxel games like Trove, with adding more user-tangible color and objectives to the mix.

Hollow Knight has a great graphical style, a lot content, and is a joy to move the character around the world.  The combat is tough and rewarding, and it's generally a very memorable game in a crowded genre.  The problem is that the giant world to explore is super dull.  In the best Metroidvanias, upgrades and new abilities are gained at a pretty quick clip, help reward exploration, and make backtracking worthwhile.
In Hollow Knight, new abilities are doled out at a snail's pace, and most secret or hidden areas just give you more money.  Sometimes, you'll find a charm to wear, but since you can only wear 2-3 of those (at least through the time I played) and only rarely swap them out, you're typically finding something that you won't use very often, if at all.  The money you do find is typically used to buy more of these marginally useful charms, and eventually other upgrades that take a long time to accumulate enough cash for.
The result is that much of the game feels like filler.  The parts of the game that are good are really good, and you may be able to tolerate the dullness between those parts, but I couldn't stay interested when there are so many other games that do this formula better.

Hollow Knight is hands down one of the best Metroidvanias out there, and for me personally the pinnacle of the genre, even surpassing the Kings Super Metroid and Symphony of the Night.
First of the Art Style consists of 100% hand-drawn backgrounds, characters and effects and its looks absolutely stunning, its one of the best Artistic games i have seen lately.
The World is full of different places, a Forest full of Wildlife, a City drowning in Water, a Bee hive and much more places that will make you put the controller away for a few seconds just to take in the melancholic atmosphere and the charming characters.
The Soundtrack by Christopher Larkin often fits the level tho i have to say that there were a bit too much "Sad Piano" Pieces for me, i would have liked to see a bit more variety.
But that doesnt mean the soundtrack is bad in the slightest, especially the Boss Themes will get your Heart pumping during the fights and will stay in your mind a while after that.
Normally Metroidvanias tend to be short games, rarely surpassing the 10 hour mark, with Metroid games being finishable in under 4 Hours, Hollow Knight is a big exception there, the Game is filled with Content, there are many Areas to discover that have nothing to do with the main quests leading you to alot of Items to discover and various optional boss fights, if you go for the 100 % you can easily get over 30 Hours out of Hollow Knight.
The Controlls are smooth with the exception of some problems with the downward strike, i recommend playing it with a controller tho since in some situations  it can get a bit hectical with the keyboard controlls.
The most important thing in a Metroidvania is the Level design, how much it lets you explore, and how well the Areas are connected to each other.
Hollow Knights does that very well, with you being able to take a lot of different ways to get trough the game, hell its possible to finish the game with alot of skills missing since alot of stuff is optional and left for you to discover.
Hollow Knight is a absolute must have for everyone who has even the slightest interest in the Metroidvania genre and games with a strong atmosphere.

As a FF title, you get what you pay for. It feels like it could be a handheld game -- which makes sense, it's ported from the PSP (afaik). But, it's a good title. The game could be thought of as broken into two or three categories: missions, and their derivatives, and the time you spend on campus at Akademia. How you choose to spend your time on campus is pretty much up to you. Spent carefully, you will gain insight and learn interesting information about Class Zero and individuals that come to Akademia.
Missions are exactly what this game was sold on. FFT0 probably comes off as an action game, and that's because it is. Combat is hectic, chaotic even. If you have played kingdom hearts, the combat is a bit like that, but even more fast paced and much elss forgiving. You'll be scratching your head wondering why you're dead at times. Take it with stride, and learn from your mistakes. The game rewards you for doing that. If you time your attacks right, you could do massive damage or even kill an opponent outright.
Overall, the gameplay can feel a bit repetitive. It's not a game I can pick up and -not- put down. It's something that I like playing for a while, then taking a break from. The mixture of character development and satisfying, fast paced combat will keep you coming back.

Some of the most fantastic platforming, world-exploration, boss fights and customization (via badges) in any 2D (and probably any 3D) game I've played, along with great art and sound design. The game can get fairly difficult, particularly with (optional) bosses. So many times I thought to myself, "This is ******* impossible!" But you try a few more times, you learn their attack patterns and by the time you satisfyingly beat the boss you're dodging everything they throw at you by reading the excellent attack telegraphing and audio cues.
There are some frustrations, sure; mostly due to the unforgiving world that demands all of your focus. However, the only true con to this game is that there isn't more. It did take me around 25 hours and I didn't even 100% (definitely got my money's worth), but it left me craving so much more. I NEED more of this quality title.

I'm doing this review as a counterpoint to all the negative reviews bashing this game simply for technical reasons. I haven't played a lot of the game yet (just like the negative reviewers who gave up on the game after see it was "only" 30 FPS) but I've played enough to see how the game runs and looks.
By way of a guide, I played this game on my "Steam Box" PC which is connected to my Sony Bravia 55 inch LED TV. I think the tv runs at a maximum of 120 hz. My Steam Box PC runs Windows 7. It has 16 gigs of ram, Intel i5, Gforce 980, 4T 7200 hard drive.
First off, I had zero problems getting the game to run. I downloaded on Steam, started it up, and it immediately went into a pre-game launcher. After fiddling around with various options, I hit play and within a few moments, the game started up. I had no crashes or problems.
The game has two "default" resolution options. Apparently, the game supports a number of different resolutions options but they are not intuitively set up. The game has other graphical options to fiddle around with that have varying effects on the visuals and performance. Please read Durante's PCgamer analysis in which he goes into detail about the visual options and effects. The takeaway from all of this is that the game is not simply a "lazy" port as some have described it. Square-Enix put in a lot of effort to tailor this game for PC. I like that the game has a options launcher before launching. I also liked that it was set up at default to run at 1080p in full screen.
The game started in full screen and was running at 30 FPS. The cut scenes looked amazing, the animation looked fluid, and it indeed looked like a HD upgrade. I had no lag or hiccups. There was no stuttering or skipped frames. The characters all have magical abilities with various graphical flare and these all looked great and powerful. By the way, the beginning levels are pretty detailed so I think it was a good indication of how the game runs.
As to the 30 FPS: this game indeed runs at "only" 30 FPS but what I was pleased to see is that it was a silky smooth 30 FPS. Even some 60 FPS games tend to dip and have noticable lag. This wasn't the case here. Because it was so consistent, it runs real smooth and one easily forgets that it's not 60 FPS. I'm not a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥ so I was not bothered by 30 FPS.
I have to emphasize that the game ran at full screen. I thought for a PC game to run full screen on a 55 inch TV and look great was a pretty significan accomplishment. What all the negative reviewers seem to have forgotten was that this game is a port of a game that came out in 2011.
A lot of negative reviewers have complained about the controls. I played this on a controller (who doesn't have a controller in this day and age). Game ran fine for me with a controller. One weird thing that i didn't like was the tutorial key prompts used PC keys rather than showing the corresponding controller buttons. I couldn't find a option to change this and thought it was annoying. I didn't bother to try to play this with mouse and keyboard since there wasn't much of point. If you don't have a controller, perhaps you shouldn't buy this PSP port.

TLDR: 7/10
Games got a lot going for it. Its got good music, visuals are nice, and fighting mechanics are good. There are a lot of fun things you could be looking for in a metroidvania. The reason I wont give this a perfect score is to be frank, crap difficulty problems.
To be fair, I have no problem with difficult enemies and what not. There is a difference in mechanical difficulty where you can learn in a fight how to deal with an enemy, or hard jumps that require timing and angle to get. So on so forth. These kind of things are not an issue, and the game is full of that. It's rewarding.
Bad things that are mechanically a problem is the death mechanic. This one mechanic alone is probably what frustrates me beyond no end in a double punishment system that does not work with teh rest of the games mechanics. To sum it up, when you die in this game, youre put into a 'half life' state. Youll have full hp, but your Soul meter is damaged, limiting  the use of certain abilities and skills (particularly yourself heal). This normally would not be a problem in most games, but considering the expansive nature of the dungeons, it is not extremely difficult to get lost if you dont have certain thigns with you already, like the compass.
The problem with the half life state is that on your first death, you lose all your money. But youre not totally screwed, as a 'ghost' will pop up where you died. Defeat your ghost and get your money back. The issue is the half life state makes you more vulnerable long term to enemies (though lack of skill). Pair this with the difficulty of navigating, and at times you can spend a lot of time wandering around trying to get back to your ghost only to stumble into a mini boss fight and die again, or fall into spikes, kill the wrong type of enemy you havent yet encountered that deals massive damage to you, etc etc. It makes it a little to easy to get punished hard on death. The only recourse is to take it extremely slow, and edge along.
This is bad for gameplay. Its frustrating to deal with, not fun to handle, and at times makes me simply want to quit playing all together. If you have a mechanic in your game that makes the player want to quit, thats not a good mechanic. To be frank, I woudl rather have a classic death mechanic. Die and go back to the last save point with all items intact, but progress lost. This one, with the auto save feature, ♥♥♥♥s you over at times and theres not a damn thing you can do.
There are also minor 'bugs' that are annoying. If you dont hold down heal for the full duration, you lose energy but not get the heal. Theres no reason for that to be a feature in the game. And we're not talking about enemy interrupts. If an enemy hits you while in charge and you lose the energy, thats fine. It's understandable. But not holding it down all the way and releasing a split second to early. Nope. Not a fan of that.
Overall, I enjoy this game, but yeah, there are issues that make me grit my teeth. So it could be a 10/10, but Im not going to overlook bad design mechanics.

Imagine this game was your grumpy old dad who never ceases to tell you that playing video games is at least as ridiculous as trying to build a snowman out of water.
It basically tells you:
Listen, son. I know you spent some hard-earned-cash on this thing you call a piece of art, but you know what? Games are bloody ridiculous! You're sitting here in front of your PC screen while pressing random buttons just because the game tells you to. You're wasting your precious time! OK, I know that you will never be a rocket scientist or find the cure for cancer, but instead of video games, you should go out and enjoy the beauty of the world we live in.
How do I know that?
Well, for me it's obvious. When you follow all of the narrator's commands , you'll reach an ending where Stanley (and you at the same) shut off the so-called 'mind-control-facility' and then leave it through a garage door leading straight into a bright, greenish landscape. Shortly thereafter you lose control over Stanley who continues walking by himself and then the screen fades to black while you get an achievement that you beat the game.
But the confusing thing about The Stanley Parable is that it also offers you other endings which deal with totally different stuff.After all, it is a game about choice and consequence. Wherever you go changes the ending of the game. While it may be a game which had less budget than an AAA-title, it is by far more complex concerning the story.
The Stanley Parable is worth both your time and your cash. Buy it and let yourself be entertained by this innovative piece of art.
And then don't play it for five years and be rewarded for doing so the day you decide that you want to be Stanley again.

The Stanley Parable is a very interesting. It tells some fantastic jokes, makes some self-indulgent commentary, but then it proceeds to get stranger and more intimate and less pointed and more interesting the more you poke at it. It isn't making fun of games for the sake of some self-appointed enlightened savior of gaming and it doesn't seem to be strange for the sake of strangeness.
What makes Stanley Parable feel so fresh isn't the humor or the satire or the criticsm that's baked into it--those are enjyoable, but they weren't what impressed me. What makes it feel fresh is how intimately it converses with the player. I'm reminded very much of a game called Save the Date--though that was a smaller and simpler affair. Both games start with meta commentary and then submerge from there, talking carefully with you about how the narrator, creator or other characters think, feel and the ramifications of that for your behavior and your experience of the product. The secret of both of these games which drape themselves in the trappings of meta-narrative is that they do actually contain characters who you will learn about, be asked to empathize with, be asked to listen to, and be asked, after it all, to act on your conclusions should you have reached any.
They are games that start with the nature of games, then the nature of reality, and then quietly, timidly, reveal that at their heart they are about the same intimacies and relationships as most intersting or moving stories. For all of the delightful jokes, strangeness, non-linearity and surreality of The Stanley Parable my most clear feeling when I stopped playing was one of loss; I had run out of ways to communicate with this person with whom I formed a relationship. I had run out of things to say and ways to prove I was listening.
I was alone.

There is this moment in AC Black Flag that you will find yourself in, where you are not really doing anything; you are not chasing anyone, you are not progressing the story, you are not looking for a ship to board. You are just sailing on your brig, the weather is nice, the crew is singing shanties and your trusty quartermaster is giving commands. As much as is possible in a game, in the very simple scenery mentioned above, Ubisoft have managed to create and transmit to the player a feeling of freedom and of commanding your own fate that is very rarely encountered in games.
Let me start the review by mentioning the extremely short list of the two things that are NOT good about it.
The first, after a point, are the side activities. All of them are fun, some are even challenging and many can be performed in a very stealthy – like manner, adding to the game’s immersion effect. The problem is that, after you capture your first couple of forts, kill your first two or three assassination targets and board and capture your first dozen of ships, it all becomes a rather pointless rinse and repeat, performed only to fill counters and gain achievements or in-game rewards. I would have preferred a higher sense of dread whenever a couple of men-o-war appeared and a much more sparsely populated sea.
The second of the “not good things” is the present – day setting. It is not so much that it is bad, it is actually done in a way that highlights the fact that while a player assumes the role of a character that jumps from rooftop to rooftop, he or she is actually having as much physical activity as a starfish. However, it is exactly this great disparity between the action-packed adventures of Mr. Kenway and the lackadaisical walking around of a faceless and speechless employee in the Google-like Abstergo building, incapable of calling even an elevator without a tablet, that ruin it for me; which is too bad, because the general concept and setup were pretty refreshing.
On to the tons of things that are good and make this game a must-have for every serious gamer.
Black flag is visually captivating. The environs, lush vegetation, open sea, tropical waters and jungles have been exceptionally well represented. Sailing the Caribbean is a treat to the eyes and if you add the lively cities, the smaller islands hubs and the underwater wrecks that often amaze, you have a game that seeks, and succeeds, in making you say “whoa… nice” even years after its release.
Adding to the sights are the sounds. The music of Black Flag fits wherever it has been implemented. The sounds of the sea, battles or shanties, in combat, of cities, of smaller locales – it all fits well to the occasion. Crowned with excellent voice acting, it really helps give the feeling of the era without “arrr” clichés.
Combat, on land, is some of the smoothest and best playable stuff I have seen in the series. You can do what you want, without struggling, while having just the right amount of tools for it. Moving and targeting are also upgraded and you will rarely find yourself doing what you didn’t intend to do.
Naval warfare is engaging and addictive, albeit, sadly, still having sailing vessels able to change course like motor boats. Nevertheless, it is an active and aggressive process, which makes it a lot of fun, and perhaps that is the reason why a more realistic version of naval warfare, which would feel more static and sluggish, was not opted for.
The main story line is the game’s actual forward pushing force, with all its colourful characters and interesting conversations, from legendary pirates to the Templars and Assassins and, finally, to a protagonist who is cocky and arrogant, confident and a bit megalomaniac, a pirate with his own personal drama and conflictions, mouthing off where he needs to and saying little where little needs saying. As it goes on, it becomes centered on one thing and one thing only, leaving behind the complexities of previous storylines and delivering you a straightforward, easy going motivation, unburdened by the big historical synergies that this series is so much used to. It is a good thing that it does, because this is, after all, pirateland, and it should be about loot, profit and the occasional backstabbing.
In closing, Black Flag is one of those rare games that you will play to exhaustion, because it is so very rewarding. Either in the gameplay sense or the simple feeling it gives you – the feeling of freedom the title is all about, this is a masterful title in the series and the entire industry as a whole.
Whatever else happens for you in this game, you will never forget that first time when your lookout on the Jackdaw will shout “Larboard sir! Floating booty for the taking sir!” – and isn’t this what games are all about?

I am a massive fan of the Warhammer 40k universe. I bought this game over the mediocre pro reviews and general antipathy toward the game mainly because of a sale, my fanboy status, and because, as a strategy fan, I thought I might be able to get more out of the experience than the average gamer. Ummm... no.
The developers obviously care about the source material and let that interest outstrip their collective ability to code. This game has been in the wild for months now and the general level of polish evident in the game is poor, even for an indie game. The many updates, apparently needed due to the rather shoddy state it was in at launch, dont seem to have done much to fix glaring issues such as marines shooting through walls and floors instead of at their targets, or obvious clipping issues as they move through the narrow corridors.
Beyond the technical issues, this game shows a lack of flair or dynamism in the design work. The marines are plodding and slow to move. Their movement is apparently designed to mimic a board game piece, moving in halting steps and awkward about faces on a per point basis, all leading to an excruciatingly laconic ballet as a marine saunters to your chosen position, clipping through the edges of crossroads as they go.
I can understand the attempt to faithfully recreate the board game, but the developers seem to have overlooked that board games make up for their static nature through tension generated by the close proximity, and occasional caustic banter, of friends. The video game scene works in a far more solitary fashion. Imagine watching your favorite board game play out by yourself, and you'll get a good idea of the feel of this game.
The marines themselves feel weak, with inneffective weaponry that, although supposedly surviving for millenia and defeating the most horribly effective and despicable foes of the 41st millenium, jam and miss repeatedly for no good reason. This weakness is probably due to the need for balancing in the board game, but these are supposed to be the Emperor's finest; They feel, instead, like obsteperous 6 year olds with nerf guns and foam noodle swords. Finally, the maps are samey and run together after a while. All consist of narrow corridors lacking in any real character or distinguishing features, through which your marines lumber through and, all to often, die needlessly.
Overall, then, a real shame. This game could have been a fun diversion but for the lack of technical polish, slavish adherence to an entertainment mediium that dosen't translate to video games well, and an inability to innovate.

I just finished this game for the first time and obtained the true ending with 86% completion and about 23 hours of gameplay. I didn't get the other endings but I did look them up.
That being said, Hollow Knight is probably the most fun I've had playing a game in a long time. The soundtrack and art are both gorgeous, the area are all unique, memorable, and well designed; and the characters are relatable, interesting, and fun. One thing I really liked is that every character has a small snippet of voiced text in the language of Hallownest. The way these lines were delivered and the quality of the voices said so much about what the character was like and really helped endear me to each and every NPC.
Probably the most stand-out aspect though is the gameplay and combat. As many people have said, this is a Metroidvania style platformer, with your main method of combat being your nail (a sword). As you progress through the game, you gain additional movement abilities such as a dash and a double jump that allow you excellent mobility not just in platforming but in combat as well. Every boss fight is very immersive (especially the ones with Hornet) and it is always satisfying to defeat a boss. The combat is challenging for sure, but whenever I died it was always because of something I did wrong, not because the game ate an input or something.
I also want to touch on the story, which is delivered in a bit of an unconventional style. You won't find a clear and linear narrative here: the story is delivered to you through dialogue with NPCs and through the discovery of special items. I also think that if you rush straight to the end (and get the "normal" ending) you will feel very unsatisfied because so much of the story is delivered to you as you try to get the true ending.
unless you just want to play again which in reality is not a bad choice. Probably one of my only criticisms of this game is that you can lock yourself out of the normal ending though, which could easily be fixed by
.
Overall, if you like somewhat challenging metroidvania style platformers with a focus on combat, I would make this a must-buy. Tight controls, beautiful art, and memorable characters all work together to create an experience that is both a game and a story, and succeeds admirably in both aspects.
That being said, I do have a suggestion for future content which I haven't seen tell of: a boss rush/refight. All of the bosses were great and I would love even a simple interface from the main menu that allows me to select the boss, drops me in the room just before the fight, and then lets me fight them. It'd be even better if this was worked into the game and maybe had some sort of badge reward attached to it for clearing all of the bosses in a row without dying.
Another thing of a similar nature would be the ability to refight or fight Hornet after the third time and have her get progressively stronger. The Hornet fights were always the most intense fights of the moment and I loved fighting her. A gauntlet of fighting her over and over again and her gaining more abilities as it goes on (maybe punctuated by a period of her resting and then yelling out to know you've gotten to another phase) would be great. If you want to go above and beyond even that, perhaps have her
. Another thing that might be interesting is if she used her needle to immobilize you and then
.
Anyway, that's really all I have for suggestions. The game itself is solid, I just want more! Thank you so much for making such an excellent game, and please keep releasing content for it!

Call me old fashioned, but I like turn-based strategies. It is the feeling of "stopped time" that is so appealing to me. That I have the whole of eternity (or until my laptop battery dies) to decide the fate of my soldiers for the next turn. I prefer this to RTS because, frankly I do not like the save/load system that tries to compensate for some of the tactical/strategic mistakes one might make due to rash actions and/or lack of a proper plan. And also, it is the nervous tingling you get when watching the enemy turn unfold, this lack of control for a moment that creates excitement should your plan be successful or despair as you see your best strategy go to waste by a simple stroke of bad luck. In any good game, there must be a few factors that are uncontrollable, this is what makes it interesting after all. Turn-based strategies are great in this aspect, they give you full authority for a moment, just to take it away in the next, delivering it in to the hands of chance and enemy tactical sense. This is, after all, why chess has made it this far.
Perhaps this is why I like "Space Hulk". No matter what table top fanboys might say - this game is deeply entertaining, true to the roots of best turn-based strategies like "Incubation: Time is Running Out", but it is criminally short. For a genre that is in agony (thanks to the latest XCOM, there is a faint hope of ressurection), this is like a bandage applied to an open wound.
The price is just right and do not listen to anyone who complains about it, this is way better than spending some US $200 on a Space Hulk starter kit from Games Workshop. Actually, I do not get people who play TT in digital age, or people who buy miniature plastic models for hundreds of dollars when 3D Printing and clay is practically widespread, I'm sorry. And this is despite the fact that I myself am guilty of buying things from GW in the past, but as it turns out, digital versions are much more entertaining and they are much (MUCH) cheaper too.
A little more missions and wargear would have been nice. Actually, a lot more. Also, different chapter model and colour sets and perhaps more diversity in objectives. As for TT fanboys hating on it, if I was the developer, I would make two game modes, "TT faithful" and "Video Game oriented" (you might say /tg/ and /vg/ respectively) to keep everyone happy. It's easy anyway, just cut most of the content in the first one.

I can only confirm here what I've said in my Rogue review, and that is, in comparison, Black Flag would be "GTA IV" while Rogue would be "Watch_Dogs". The comparison is due to the gameplay. Both are fairly open world (with areas becoming available the further you progress), both offer a ton of side activities that let you spend hours without playing the main mission, but there is one big difference: Black Flag is more the "just for fun", easy going pirate adventure, while Rogue is more sinister, more streamlined, and more focussed on what you need to achieve. It's more about managing yourself and your resources without imposing that all too much on you. I like both styles, so it doesn't really matter to me. Be sure to get the companion app if you have an iPhone, so you can manage your fleet when not playing the game, or while playing the game without a need to go into the Captain's Quarters.
Black Flag is a huge game, you really do get the feel of freedom, of being a privateer, of being the pirate that can do as he pleases. You can loot, hunt, explore, pillage, and upgrade your vessel, the Jackdaw, as well as yourself to your heart's content. I have literally played for hours without touching the next story mission.
You meet some historically known characters, and even if the timeline and lore don't entirely match, that's what tales are for. If you ever wanted to play Pirates of the Carribbean with a touch of GTA, then look no further matey, yarr!
I'm playing it on an i7-4770 with a GTX 750 1 GB, and 8 GB RAM at work (lunch breaks etc.), and on a Core2Quad Q9400 2.66 GHz, GTX 650 1 GB, and 8 GB RAM at home. Same resolution 1080p, and normal to high settings, except for ambient occlusion and particles. Both on Windows 7 x64. [[b]Note:[/b] Get GameSave Manager. Haven't found a better way to transfer game progress accross platforms and the internet!]
Rogue is definitely better optimized (plays smooth on higher settings), but either way, both play without significant, if any, frame drops; and then only in particularly fierce naval combat.
I would definitely recommend turning off PhysX, volumetric fog, and setup vsync via your graphics card's control panel while disabling it in-game. That will give you the highest FPS.

The Bridge is definitely one of those games that want to make you rip out your hair, in both frustration and outcome satisfaction, all for one good reason; cryptic, mind-boggling puzzles inspired by history's graphics artists makes you feel like you're on top of the world after you've unraveled through each puzzle. By the end of the game, you really do deserve a medal, is the kind of accomplishment I'm talking about.
The game consists of getting the unnamed, old chap through to the exit door in each level, to advance. The game's puzzles, inspired by the Dutch artist, M. C. Escher, who plays a massive aspect in this game, as the world and its environment is shown in grayscale with beautifully hand-drawn illustrations. Obstacles such as voids, which can suck you and other objects into a swirly mess, ''Menace Balls'' that can roll around the puzzle world and flatten you to death. Even steep cliffs that could slip you off the world and fall to your death. With all these dangers aside, you can use this to your advantage by rotating the maze world around you as well as reversing the flow of time, to cheat your demise. Along with controlling the core of elemental physics and gravitational pulls, Isaac Newton, eat your heart out.
I personally love the dark and rather gothic visual world this game sinks its teeth into. The world is truly a marvel to behold, not only for its diverse, colourless design, but for its ingenuity and artistic flare. You could literally stand there in a level, and just analyse every single little detail that had been hand-drawn and just get lost in the rich, beautiful and elegant designs. It doesn't just go for the levels, even the real world locations makes me feel as if I was reading a gothic child's book, what with its vague nostalgic environments and architecture.
The only problem I have with this game is that it's incredibly short, when counting it has only 4 chapters, with only 6 puzzles each. But, with this game's cryptic puzzling, it will keep you stumped out of ideas, as you overcomplicate things and try to get things in the right motion. I'm guilty to say that I've got stuck on one tiny puzzle that left me clueless for over half an hour. Other than that, the controls can be a little iffy here and there, as the game only allows firm movements set in the right motion and time.
Definitely a recommendation from me, if you're the brainy independent-type. And yes, I'm not that independent, as I did use a walkthrough guide for this game. Ruined the experience, I know, but definitely pick up this game and don't look for outside help as it does ruin it!

Hollow Knight is without a doubt the buggiest game of all time.
Luckily they're all dead and you're just spending your time seeing what's what in their dead bug kingdom.
From your first step in Dirtmouth, the emphasis is on exploration. It has such an emphasis on exploration that you need to explore to unlock a map to explore further. Your  first playthrough is just going to be a mess of deadends and haphazard unlocked shortcuts, but when every dead end leads to something useful and every shortcut is used multiple times it's exploration that pays off.
Levels are fairly varied, and mentally piecing them together shows them off - each level has several ways in and out and fast travel points require some getting to, which ends with you truly understanding the world of Hallownest.
This is the main driving point. This point you already knew, in the 0.2 seconds it takes to watch gameplay to see if this game's for your taste, and the rest is just how much the progression and exploration resonate with you.
Gameplay itself is serviceable. No combos or parries or anything fancy, but a solid bedrock of momentum based, gradually aerial combat with a handful of spells and quirks. You can further alter it with the "charm" system, that mostly amounts to a handful of passives.
Bosses actually use the gameplay quirks, unlike some games (with a pointed glance at Guacamelee) even if they're mostly threadbare.
A quirky collection of NPCs, bugfaced and masked, that you meet along the way are all memorable have multiple levels of environmental and mental storytelling to them. They also peter out real early, with budget cuts resulting in more than one serious anticlimax.
The budget cuts shine through in more than that one place. With boss fakeouts and some threadbare areas that obviously had more planned to them, you can feel the exact stings of "this is where we ran out of money".
As minor as they are, this is pretty much all that's negative to say about the game. They didn't push it as far as they could've. Maybe the ability unlocks are fairly rote.
That's a pretty weak detraction by anyone's standards.
Exploration in games usually means meandering around fairly boring locales waiting for something decent to happen. Exploration in Hollow Knight means something always happening while commuting from A to the B you haven't quite figured out yet. That's the vision the Hollow Knight believes in.
If that appeals to you, combined with other aspects that are inoffensive at worst, then it's a game I can easily recommend.

ACIV feels like a significant step-up in the AC franchise but also a few steps backward. Here the game shifts its premise to the open seas for the first time ever. The world is argubly the largest in an AC game so far but the various places aren't that captivating and eventually, gets quite repetitve to explore.
Above all, it's the new game features that's what truly stands out, such as harpooning, underwater exploration and naval combat on the high seas.
Perhaps of biggest significance, story-wise, is that you're no longer playing as Desmond but just a random Abstergo employee. There's much more to do in the present-day world this time round. Roam the linear Abstergo corridors and participate in boring hacking mini-games to find out more on the present day happenings.
On the other hand, the game's main missions is where I'm truly disappointed at. Many follow the same typical mission formula and this is worsened by an excessive amount of annoying tailing missions. Like all the complaints from past games weren't enough, for some reason Ubisoft thought it'd be a great idea to add
tailing missions. Or did they just run out of mission ideas?
Overall, I can't say that much of anything impressive of ACIV but the content it offered was satisfying enough, albeit the game still feels very incomplete, or to say, lacking in fullest potential and wasn't as enjoyable as I hoped.
PROs:
- Fascinating new setting
- Main mission constraints are no longer that much a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥(unlike AC3's)...but still sucks
- Interesting new features like whale/shark hunting and underwater exploration keeps things fresh...for a while
CONs:
- Too many unnecessary "tailing" missions
- Locations can get pretty repetitive

I will try to be as fair as I can be, I will also state I am writing this review based on the main games campaign since it would not be fair to tell people this game is bad or good based on DLC instead of the main game which they will want to try prior to buying the DLC's. Keep in mind DLC's were supposed to be better than the main game but having played them myself they only marginally make things better. Worthy of note I have not tried the MP aspect and I only played the game on normal mode in this review.
Initially I was struggling to decide between a recommend or avoid on this title, firstly the graphics are okay in the sense of character and enemy models. The environments are for the most part what you would expect given nature of what the game is based on being the board game. This means they are fairly generic, single lane corridor after corridor and tiny rooms that I assume are small to create an element of confined space and increase tension. For the most part the corridors serve that purpose but can seem like a rather stupid lore concept. I found myself asking such rhetorical questions like why the hell would they build spaceships with corridors that can only accomodate one person at a time through and why are the rooms always barren with nothing but floors and walls for the most part (very rarely find anything in the rooms except small open spaces). The camera angles do the game no justice but they do the job of can atleast zoom in and rotate which quite often may need to do in order to see the doors or whats around you.
The missions are generic, all text based descriptions which quite often found to be lacking in detail and can lead to confusion on some missions such as how to complete that mission. A prime example being ones like where tells you to collect a sample in one missions but does not tell you how and forced me to come online to find out how via google search or steam forums asking other players. This is not good design. The game has no cinematics through missions and even the ending was merely a text box description which left me feeling very underwelmed like being left at a bus stop in the pouring rain as your bus drives away without you...I expect to come in from the wet and feel warm and a nice feeling once completed the main campaign but felt nothing at all, still damp and still cold metaphorically speaking.
Some of the game mechanics are just plain annoying while some not so bad. For example of the bad the weapon jams constantly in an effort to create suspense and tension failed to do that for me for couple reasons, firstly whoever makes the weapons in that futuristic setting should be shot because any universe where your marines weapons jam, fail or explode that often shouldn't be making weapons. The exploding gatling guns, the flamers with hardly any ammo and even to go so far as to make a missions goal based on not using up all the flamer ammo late in the game despite you will not be using it later seems silly. I can understand why they used weapon malfunctions to make the game enemy more dangerous and attempt to increase tension but it does not work or at least not for me given the top down aerial view of the levels and knowing where all the enemy comes from.
Unlike the FPS version of Space Hulk which could create that tension because you could not see what was going on everywhere else in the level, in this one it did and not even when taking into account not knowing how many there are, you still knew where they were and could counter it before they arrived. This is a flaw that comes across from the board game where back then you had everyone in same room playing on a table. I feel should of taken advantage of such gameplay features like fog of war in the video game version, a case of less is more as far as how much show the player.
A trick I learned early on is you can place marines in the spaces in front of where the enemy come out of and it stops them from coming forth leaving less places you need to defend from later as well as some missions you never even had to kill many if any at all because when take into count a high command point roll combined with some of the mission objectives you could literally just make one marine run across the map to where need to be prior to the enemy even coming close, this again another drawback to knowing exactly where the enemy are coming from and where they are.
On the bright side I really liked the shoulder camera initially but soon realised just how pointless it is, seeing the enemy or walls though a fuzzy camera gave you no more quality scenery than just zooming in fully. In the end it is a short lived interesting function that serves no purpose. The difficuly is mostly tied to random luck of dice rolls more so than strategy and planning alone, the undo last action taken function plus save anywhere can make the game extremely easy so to make it harder you have to avoid falling back on reloads, command rerolls and undo function.
Now given this is based on the board game I should say it does stay fairly true to that so if big fan of the board game you may be more forgiving and actually enjoy this more so than a lot of general TBS genre fans as some of what I consider flaws are also flaws within the board game.
The only customisation in the game comes in the form of which order place marines on map and how your banner looks in MP for the most part. It is a combat only game, meaning no other gameplay elements like base construction, character development or customization, no research, nothing other than each mission is text based description of objective, a small map image with pointers and then drop and spank your way through the mission with preset soldiers. Once the mission is complete there is a text based well done pat on back message followed by loading of the next mission, rinse and repeat through the entire campaigns.
There is maybe half dozen weapon types, couple marine types and couple varieties of enemy type will be constantly using and fighting against through the entire thing which is I guess to be expected given what the game is based on though something you should be aware of that there is a large lack of variety in almost every aspect of this game.
If I was going to buy a Space Hulk game after playing this I probably would go back to buying the FPS versions of the past even though I am a TBS genre fan. I am not a big FPS fan unless they are RPG hybrids so when I say I prefer the older FPS versions it is saying more than would you might assume at face value. Those earlier ones were able to create more tension, more atmosphere in gameplay for me than this one. The enemy in those were more intimidating and could make you more nervous about travelling around exploring the ships while this one failed to do that for me.
This game is not bad overall however, just incredably limited in scope and variety, gameplay elements and in game content. It's the sort of TBS you might pick up and play once in a while just to grind your way through a single missions or two in short boredom breaking bite size chunks but I imagine not so many would be keen to slog through entire campaigns over and over. If your a Space hulk board game fan this may be worth purchase possibly prior to being on sale but for general TBS fans I suggest wait till it's on sale and keep in mind very little has evolved from the board game version it is based on so do not expect some grandiose large scale, large variety or even high production and high quality game. It to me comes across as a low budget fairly faithful to board game port to PC. Fun can be had but if your not a Space Hulk board game fan...probably much less than would of hoped for many.
I have read they are going to be adding more variety and such through the coming year and they did add a bit more if bought the DLC but I do not plan to wait a year till improvements have been made before writing my review.

I am a fan of the board game - I own the last published version (anniversary edition) and I had been waiting for a video game adaptation for decades.  When it came to Steam, I didn't hesitate.  But for non-hardcore fans, there are a few things you should be aware of about this version.  First, it's short.  The last patch added new campaigns, but it can all be finished in about  10 hours.  There's not a lot of replay value.  Second, there's no level editor (at least not at the time of this review).  That would make a difference - the board game is all about creating new scenarios/campaigns to play with friends.  For twitch gamers, take note this is turned base.  There are persistent bugs, like the ability to undue a failed attack and try again, that still need to be patched.  And if you know the boardgame, well don't expect the same flexibility with the rules engine in the software.  Goals and actions are limited.  AI seems basic (hunt and seek) - even just the addition of AI flanking would have made for a more rewarding challenge.
Don't get me wrong - I recommend this, at least when Steam does a price drop on it.   The sound is phenomenal, the bass is massive reverb (rapid firing a machine gun against a swarm of Genestealers will definitely move something on your desk),  the atmosphere is really well established.  It's just that it could have been so much more, and leave you wanting rather than satisfied.
However, it is fairly true to the gameplay

Before I start, I just want to address one thing:
This is the best AC game I have played so far. And I'm a diehard fan of this series.
Now let's start by a simple pros/cons:
Pros:
+The game doesn't take itself too seriously.
+You really feel like you are a pirate, so careless and free to do what ever you want.
+Almost no map limitations; after the few first missions, you are basically granted the opportunity to explore the world as much as you wish, which hasn't been possible in previous titles. And exploring is as interesting as it can get! Massive amount of islands, fisherman villages, caves, mayan ruins, plantations etc. And the game also rewards you alot for exploring.
+Character design. Edward is an interesting main character and to be honest; there has never been a side character so cool as Edward Thatch, or well, as most of us know him as, Blackbeard.
+Map. It's just... big. And full of places. After 50+ hours on the game, I'm still finding new islands to explore.
+The amount of side activities. Ranging from the usual assassination contracts to defeating legendary ships, you will not run out of things to do.
+Free roaming. Well, this isn't anything new to Assassin's Creed series, but the addition of freely sailing the seas and countering plenty of other ships to board and rob out of their cargo, this game takes freedom of play to a whole new level.
Cons:
-Optimizing is quite bad (which really isn't a surprise though), as the game will be somewhat laggy even on better gaming rigs. Don't expect too many FPS with high graphichs if your PC isn't top notch. It's not unplayable on computers that aren't as good, absolutely not, but you should be prepared for certain FPS drops and lowering your graphic quality etc.
-The story is quite short (NO SPOILERS) and sometimes feels like it's a bit too much "go there and kill him so we can be rich arrr!". Story isn't bad, I really enjoyed it, but I still hope it would've been a bit more deep in some aspects.

I've never really written a review for a game so for me to do this means something. I am in love with this game! It's such a good way to waste time and i mean that in a good way. I'll do my best to list the pro's and con's:
Pros:
-The art style seems really fresh and vibrant.
-Short rounds allow you to squeeze in a game real quick, especially if you're good and roll another team ;)
-Although some characters may remind you of other games, they are not the same. They are all unique and very fun!
-Multiple maps gives you different ways to play each game.
-No "pay to win," just crates for skins (literally just like overwatch.)
-Can be played casually or competitively.
-Each round is a level playing field. No levels, items, getting fed, etc.
-The community, for the most part, is very great and i suggest you visit the subreddit!
Cons:
-Small character pool (of course it's early and that will be fixed.)
-Personally not a fan of shift abilities.
-The skins are just recolors. Not exactly unique but again, it's early access.
Basically any con can be attributed to early access and most complaints are things that will be fixed. With this game, you get the shortness of a quick game like Hearthstone, the look of a MOBA, but the WASD movement gives it a completely different feel as well as the closed in arena. It's a perfect blend in my personal opinion and i cannot wait to see where this game goes. It is most definitely worth the money and i bought the ultimate fan pack just to support the Devs for doing such a great job for such an unfinished game.

An amazing game for the Metroidvania genre. Some of the most fantastic platforming, world-exploration, boss fights and customization (via badges) in any 2D (and probably any 3D) game I've played, along with great art and sound design. But you try a few more times, you learn their attack patterns and by the time you satisfyingly beat the boss you're dodging everything they throw at you by reading the excellent attack telegraphing and audio cues.
There are some frustrations, sure; mostly due to the unforgiving world that demands all of your focus. However, the only true con to this game is that there isn't more. It did take me around 25 hours and I didn't even 100% (definitely got my money's worth), but it left me craving so much more. I NEED more of this quality title.

What's the easiest way to get yourself killed in The Bridge? Thinking of it as a platformer. Don't even try to jump, and physics is most definitely not on your side.
The Bridge is an exercise in being both omnipotent and powerless. Omnipotent: you are the master of gravity. Powerless: Everything follows a rule. Clear-cut, and terrifying rules that force you to progressively learn on the fly about a world so infuriatingly similar to ours. Luck plays no part in The Bridge. Just as you are accountable for every mistake, you are accountable for every victory. Omnipotent and powerless. Challenging and satisfying.
Though it is by no means unsuitable for hour-long binges, The Bridge is just as enjoyable, or even more so, when played one level a session. Do not be fooled; a level is not two minutes of jumping and turtle-stomping. It is, however, refreshingly perfect for a break from work.
The backdrop of simple grayscale colours on the marvellous works inspired by M. C. Escher (I tell you, art is better than drugs) are the icing on the cake. Not only are they beautiful, but they are cornerstones of the game's mechanics: black and white are not the same, and no shape or movement. is impossible.

Having tried the tabletop game Space Hulk once, and loving it, I decided to buy the electronic version when it went on sale. I can say that it was money well spent. Space Hulk is all the fun of the tabletop game, plus more, as the visuals are gruesomely satisfying and the gameplay is very tactical and well laid-out. The controls are easy to learn, and the game provides hours and hours and hours of fun.
One feature I'm very happy it includes is that it can not only be played multiplayer online with other friends who have the game, but it includes a "hotseat" mode, where everyone can use the same computer to play out their turns. And in multiplayer, you have a chance to see things from the "other side of the hulk", or putting it simply, you can play as the Genestealers!! I am also pleased to see that DLC has been released to allow people to play through even more missions and add a little customization to their game with new "skins" for the marines and Genestealers. A feature I haven't seen in the game that would be nice, is the creation of custom map layouts and missions to play with friends.
Other than that, I couldn't ask for more out of this game!

Before I start, I just want to address one thing:
This is the best AC game I have played so far. And I'm a diehard fan of this series.
Now let's start by a simple pros/cons:
Pros:
+The game doesn't take itself too seriously.
+You really feel like you are a pirate, so careless and free to do what ever you want.
+Almost no map limitations; after the few first missions, you are basically granted the opportunity to explore the world as much as you wish, which hasn't been possible in previous titles. And exploring is as interesting as it can get! Massive amount of islands, fisherman villages, caves, mayan ruins, plantations etc. And the game also rewards you alot for exploring.
+Character design. Edward is an interesting main character and to be honest; there has never been a side character so cool as Edward Thatch, or well, as most of us know him as, Blackbeard.
+Map. It's just... big. And full of places. After 50+ hours on the game, I'm still finding new islands to explore.
+The amount of side activities. Ranging from the usual assassination contracts to defeating legendary ships, you will not run out of things to do.
+Free roaming. Well, this isn't anything new to Assassin's Creed series, but the addition of freely sailing the seas and countering plenty of other ships to board and rob out of their cargo, this game takes freedom of play to a whole new level.
Cons:
-Optimizing is quite bad (which really isn't a surprise though), as the game will be somewhat laggy even on better gaming rigs. Don't expect too many FPS with high graphichs if your PC isn't top notch. TLDR: 7/10
Games got a lot going for it. Its got good music, visuals are nice, and fighting mechanics are good. There are a lot of fun things you could be looking for in a metroidvania. The reason I wont give this a perfect score is to be frank, crap difficulty problems.
To be fair, I have no problem with difficult enemies and what not. There is a difference in mechanical difficulty where you can learn in a fight how to deal with an enemy, or hard jumps that require timing and angle to get. So on so forth. These kind of things are not an issue, and the game is full of that. It's rewarding.
Bad things that are mechanically a problem is the death mechanic. This one mechanic alone is probably what frustrates me beyond no end in a double punishment system that does not work with teh rest of the games mechanics. To sum it up, when you die in this game, youre put into a 'half life' state. Youll have full hp, but your Soul meter is damaged, limiting  the use of certain abilities and skills (particularly yourself heal). This normally would not be a problem in most games, but considering the expansive nature of the dungeons, it is not extremely difficult to get lost if you dont have certain thigns with you already, like the compass.
The problem with the half life state is that on your first death, you lose all your money. But youre not totally screwed, as a 'ghost' will pop up where you died. Defeat your ghost and get your money back. The issue is the half life state makes you more vulnerable long term to enemies (though lack of skill). Pair this with the difficulty of navigating, and at times you can spend a lot of time wandering around trying to get back to your ghost only to stumble into a mini boss fight and die again, or fall into spikes, kill the wrong type of enemy you havent yet encountered that deals massive damage to you, etc etc. It makes it a little to easy to get punished hard on death. The only recourse is to take it extremely slow, and edge along.
This is bad for gameplay. Its frustrating to deal with, not fun to handle, and at times makes me simply want to quit playing all together. If you have a mechanic in your game that makes the player want to quit, thats not a good mechanic. To be frank, I woudl rather have a classic death mechanic. Die and go back to the last save point with all items intact, but progress lost. This one, with the auto save feature, ♥♥♥♥s you over at times and theres not a damn thing you can do.
There are also minor 'bugs' that are annoying. If you dont hold down heal for the full duration, you lose energy but not get the heal. Theres no reason for that to be a feature in the game. And we're not talking about enemy interrupts. If an enemy hits you while in charge and you lose the energy, thats fine. It's understandable. But not holding it down all the way and releasing a split second to early. Nope. Not a fan of that.
Overall, I enjoy this game, but yeah, there are issues that make me grit my teeth. So it could be a 10/10, but Im not going to overlook bad design mechanics.

So, Space Hulk. The board game has been around forever, with a recent incarnation a couple of years ago. Haveing never played it before, I did pick up the board game, and excitedly assembled all the fantastic miniatures - and then it say on the shelf gathering dust after 1 game. Why? Because it took longer to setup the board than it did for my brother to beat me.
The computer game is pretty much exactly like board game - with one big difference: the miniatures move, they shoot and they talk. And of course, you don't need to set the board up. If you liked the board game, I recommend grabbing yourself a copy, even if it is for the sheer amusement of watching terminators shoot bolters and assault cannons. I quite enjoy the game for that reason alone.
If you've never played the board game before, prepare yourself for a board-game like experience because if you are after a fast action shoot-em up, this isn't the game for you.
However, things aren't all awesome in the Hulk of Space. There are things that could be improved that would make the game far more interesting:
- Custom map building. You can create your own missions with the board game, why not the computer game? Have a community map share.
- Play as 'stealers. It'd be great if after you complete the campaign, you can go back and play as the Genestealers!
- Moar skins! Bring on the Space Wolves and Dark Angels. Can I be so bold to suggest Night Lords (I want to see a Reaper autocannon!)?
This aside, I find it quite fun to pass the time.

As a casual fan of final fantasy I wasn't really sure what to expect with type 0 but to be honest so far I'm fairly impressed. For a game that was on the PSP it looks about how I would expect. Some textures are clearly left over from the PSP but all in all I can't complain to much about the graphics on a game released 4 years ago on a hand held. I haven't finished the game yet but the story so far seems interesting enough and fairly typical of final fantasy with a bit of a darker feel. The gameplay however is what makes this game a definite recommendation for me. It has completely moved away from any sort of turn based actions during combat and feels a lot like kingdom hearts in terms of combat. However, just because it has taken out the turn based actions doesn't mean the strategy is gone. Class 0 has a diverse group of skills and learning how to manage them to make the best parties to overcome certain areas takes a bit of thought. Also learning how to use each character has been fun as they all have a different play style that takes getting used too. The time management between missions I found cool as it makes you think on what is most important for your team and what you can get done in the alotted time. So if you are looking for a game with ground breaking graphics this probably isn't for you but, if you want a game that offers an fun and thoughtful action you might want to check this out.

I'm sure after enough time I'll come back and give this another go, just like I have most of the previous AC games, but like any story driven game, once you've seen the end, it's hard to play through it again as seriously as the first time. Multiplayer:
I can't comment, I haven't tried any AC multiplayer and don't really intend to.

I've never really written a review for a game so for me to do this means something. I am in love with this game! It's such a good way to waste time and i mean that in a good way. I'll do my best to list the pro's and con's:
Pros:
-The art style seems really fresh and vibrant.
-Short rounds allow you to squeeze in a game real quick, especially if you're good and roll another team ;)
-Although some characters may remind you of other games, they are not the same. They are all unique and very fun!
-Multiple maps gives you different ways to play each game.
-No "pay to win," just crates for skins (literally just like overwatch.)
-Can be played casually or competitively.
-Each round is a level playing field. No levels, items, getting fed, etc.
-The community, for the most part, is very great and i suggest you visit the subreddit!
Cons:
-Small character pool (of course it's early and that will be fixed.)
-Personally not a fan of shift abilities.
-The skins are just recolors. Not exactly unique but again, it's early access.
Basically any con can be attributed to early access and most complaints are things that will be fixed. With this game, you get the shortness of a quick game like Hearthstone, the look of a MOBA, but the WASD movement gives it a completely different feel as well as the closed in arena. It's a perfect blend in my personal opinion and i cannot wait to see where this game goes. It is most definitely worth the money and i bought the ultimate fan pack just to support the Devs for doing such a great job for such an unfinished game.

So you want a spaceship building/flying simulator, you take a look at this and it looks pretty cool. You buy it with high expectations, but as soon as you start playing you are thrown into the game with a choice to participate in a tutorial. You decide to try the tutorial so you can get a solid footing in the game. You go through the tutorial finding out you're more confused than ever and not sure what you're doing. Eventually you leave the tutorial and decide to start trying the game yourself. you get to a point where you can't make anything without some kind of factory block. You build said factory block only to find you need a direct power source, so you build a power source but can't figure out how to connect it despite what the control tips say. You end up stranded on a planet not sure what to do next until you eventually get bored and quit.
This has been pretty much the extent of my experience with this game. It seemed to have potential, but if the game interface is so user-unfriendly that you're pretty much just playing a "drift through space with only a space helmet and some blocks which can make a shoddy ship" sim, you're bound to get REALLY BORED!
To make matters worse everything is done with blocks, and the only difference between those blocks besides the function, is the color. I mean, you want to fly a ship? sure! just stuff your body into this block! (who do you think we are? solid snake?) oh but it gets more amusing when you notice there is a money system in the game. Sure, not the worst idea in voxel games, but how are you supposed to make money when you only ship you can ever make is a 3D version of the space invaders starfighter?
Ultimately I find this game to be an utter disappointment. Don't waste your money on this game!

I qualify this review in that I don't recommend it for the general masses. If you're a fan of the original Space Hulk board game or you're a fan of Warhammer 40k in general, then I would recommend buying it when it's on sale- $30 is far too much for what's offered here.
Space Hulk is pretty much a 1:1 reproduction of the Space Hulk board game, but with a few extra bells and whistles attached. The animations are well done, the voice acting is adequate and the atmosphere of the game translates well. The campaign is interesting and offers a great number of varying objectives aside from 'kill all the Genestealers', but it would have been more interesting to offer a Genestealer campaign alongside the Space Marine campaign.
My issues with it are that even with the varying objectives in the campaign, playing against the AI feels a little hollow as compared to the multiplayer experience. The AI can't substitute for a real opponent, as to be expected with board game translations, so it doesn't feel like the AI is really adapting to your strategies as much as an actual opponent would.
Overall though my biggest issue is that this game has a $30 price tag. It is definitely not worth that; though they have a few campaigns to offer, it still doesn't feel like enough to justify the price tag. Plus, all of the maps look the same aside from layout; there's a lot of blank space, and it feels wasted as opposed to claustrophobic as the developers intended.

I just finished this game for the first time and obtained the true ending with 86% completion and about 23 hours of gameplay. I didn't get the other endings but I did look them up.
That being said, Hollow Knight is probably the most fun I've had playing a game in a long time. The soundtrack and art are both gorgeous, the area are all unique, memorable, and well designed; and the characters are relatable, interesting, and fun. One thing I really liked is that every character has a small snippet of voiced text in the language of Hallownest. The way these lines were delivered and the quality of the voices said so much about what the character was like and really helped endear me to each and every NPC.
Probably the most stand-out aspect though is the gameplay and combat. As many people have said, this is a Metroidvania style platformer, with your main method of combat being your nail (a sword). As you progress through the game, you gain additional movement abilities such as a dash and a double jump that allow you excellent mobility not just in platforming but in combat as well. Every boss fight is very immersive (especially the ones with Hornet) and it is always satisfying to defeat a boss. The combat is challenging for sure, but whenever I died it was always because of something I did wrong, not because the game ate an input or something.
I also want to touch on the story, which is delivered in a bit of an unconventional style. You won't find a clear and linear narrative here: the story is delivered to you through dialogue with NPCs and through the discovery of special items. I also think that if you rush straight to the end (and get the "normal" ending) you will feel very unsatisfied because so much of the story is delivered to you as you try to get the true ending.
unless you just want to play again which in reality is not a bad choice. Probably one of my only criticisms of this game is that you can lock yourself out of the normal ending though, which could easily be fixed by
.
Overall, if you like somewhat challenging metroidvania style platformers with a focus on combat, I would make this a must-buy. Tight controls, beautiful art, and memorable characters all work together to create an experience that is both a game and a story, and succeeds admirably in both aspects.
That being said, I do have a suggestion for future content which I haven't seen tell of: a boss rush/refight. All of the bosses were great and I would love even a simple interface from the main menu that allows me to select the boss, drops me in the room just before the fight, and then lets me fight them. It'd be even better if this was worked into the game and maybe had some sort of badge reward attached to it for clearing all of the bosses in a row without dying.
Another thing of a similar nature would be the ability to refight or fight Hornet after the third time and have her get progressively stronger. The Hornet fights were always the most intense fights of the moment and I loved fighting her. A gauntlet of fighting her over and over again and her gaining more abilities as it goes on (maybe punctuated by a period of her resting and then yelling out to know you've gotten to another phase) would be great. If you want to go above and beyond even that, perhaps have her
. Another thing that might be interesting is if she used her needle to immobilize you and then
.
Anyway, that's really all I have for suggestions. The game itself is solid, I just want more! Thank you so much for making such an excellent game, and please keep releasing content for it!
