Brought this after the 1.2 patch.  Came in thinking it would be a it rubbish but as i liked the old board game so much, thought it wouldn't hurt to give Steam even more money.
As a single player digital version of the board game I actually really love it, the patch they introduced where you could speed up the movement is a definite winner otherwise it would have forced me do a squad broken all over the shop.
Multiplayer is messed up.  It's OK if you have a friend to play with, but just getting a random game is annoying and frustrating.  What they need is a quick play button, where you can just select your preferred side and play any mission.  Right now you seem to have to pick the exact mission you wish to play and just hope some other dude is wanting to play that mission as well.
You also have to create a separate account for the multiplayer, would have been alot easier just to use steamworks for that.  And setting this up and then trying to get a game with a friend can be bloody frustrating, but once finally jumped the hurdles to set it up, works pretty ok.
The actual gameplay of the multiplayer, from what I've experience is rather laggy.  The reveal mechanic of the genestealer side takes a little getting used to and can be a bit annoying with the ever pervasive lag.
That being said, the multiplayer games I did experience with a friend were Epic.  Hopefully they will brush up the MP and introduce improvements and if so then this game will be awesome.
Right now, it's a great single player rendition of the board game, I can thoroughly recommend it for that.  The multiplayer needs some work but if you have a friend to play with then it's great.

One of the most underated Sim out there. Whats hidden behind the "free to play" aspect is more worthy of a full price because all the content is worth it.
CARS:The cars are all well done and balanced so that there isnt always a dominate car but at the same time true to the real life behaviors. A great variety of racing cars, from power heavy turbo cars of the 70's and 80's to modern GT3 cars to Leman prototypes. Official series are represented, DTM, GT Masters, WTCC and more coming... feel free to test drive them all, buy what you like.
TRACKS:The tracks are well created from scratch to the point you dont care about laser scanned tracks, even though they are just beginning to utilize laser scan technology into there future tracks. The Sim doesnt allow modding, which from my opinion is a bit redundent since the other sims out there allow it but quality wise dont represent well, leaving you wanting more official quality tracks from the developer. With each track released the detail and quality is maintained, not some hack job addon.
MULTIPLAYER: One the best online racing experiences and just getting warmed up. Netcode is very good, even when racing some from the US all the way in Germany, they use a p2p connection, so close racing is possible, being able to squeeze between two cars or riding the back bumper of your opponent is amazing. Currently right now its open servers with rotating tracks, hosting a practice, qualifying and then a short sprint race. In a matter of weeks they will release dedicated servers, allowing any choice of car and track along with many of the standard features.
SINGLEPLAYER: Each official series supports the real life formats. If thats not your thing you can create your own championship, picking your own format and track calendar.
AI: Rated among the best, making a good training tool of racing hard and bumper to bumper, but be aware, be on your A game, otherwise they will punish you. There will be times they run into the back of you but thats usually because you braked too early or took the wrong racing line, so awareness isnt always there top attribute. You can choose a set pace for the AI or choose the adaptive AI and watch there speed grow with you. It isnt perfect but as they move through development, it improves.
SOUNDS: The best, you can ask anyone, even those who race in other sims, all agree RaceRoom has the most immersive detailed sounds currently. They are constantly improving them as well, adding more detail to the car and track ambient. If you dont believe me, check on Youtube and turn up the volume.
GRAPHICS: A very clean and colorful look, with motion blur that actually makes it seem like your going fast. Its improved over the past year and as usual constantly being optimized. The cars definitely fit the tracks in detail, unlike some games where the car or track look better than the other. Partnered with the sounds, its quite the visual experience. Runs well on medium range PC's but does not support SLI or crossfire yet. The game supports different times of day, sunrise to sunset, which looks beatiful across the track.
HARDWARE: They support just about every wheel out there or wheel pedal combinations.
FORCE FEEDBACK: At a glance the ffb features are overwhelming to tune, but there are many guides and user profiles to build off of. Once you have it tuned its quite a unique feeling, driving the heavy turbo cars is a handful and the modern GT3's handle with weight but finesse. They are always working towards improving the ffb and experience. My advice is patience and try out the various tweaks out there.
Final thoughts: This is a great hidden Sim that doesnt get the recognition it deserves. Most people dont believe in the free to play aspect and thats understandable, push that asside and you got something great in your hands. I advise to download and test drive the cars your interested in. Price range isnt too expensive, cheaper than iRacing but like I said its worth the price if you were to buy assetto corsa or Project cars. One thing many people miss is the fact once you buy a official series pack, you own the tracks, you no longer have to purchase them in the other packs, your only paying for the cars. My motto is build the game you want, buy the cars and tracks you like and go from there, once you try them you will want them all. Give it a fair try and enjoy the experience.
With whats ahead content and feature wise, the future is bright, so dont miss out.

The Bridge is another entry in the physics puzzle-platformer genre, and a quite ambitious entry at that!
It focuses on its one main mechanic, which is simply flipping the world, and its gravity with it. However, the levels are designed from the ground up to support it with a M. C. Escher-esque perspective, leading to some twisted and creative levels.
The game has 2 main sets, the second of which is a rework of the previous levels, with added elements that you learned to overcome in the first set. It seems a bit like an extended tutorial, as half of each chapter is about exposing a mechanic to the player, not being too challenging. The puzzles featured here are, in my opinion, better designed, and not difficult to actually finish once you know the solution.
The second, however, has a more physics-driven design, very unlike the first. This might leave you hanging a bit in the first few levels, but it's not as hard as it seemed after you realize that you actually do have to be more meticulous with the physics.
It also features a few secret Wisps (which help you interpret the story) and Achievements that can be frustrating to do if you're not using a guide, or maybe discussing clues with your friends. But none of it is mandatory, so it's a fair addition to the game.
The
of the game is most likely its main draw. It's certainly very unique and it manages to merge its visual level design with the gameplay mechanics seamlessly.
If you're familiar with Escher's work, you'll certainly see where the inspiration came from! If you're not (like I was) this is certainly an opportunity to look into it, if you find this game's aesthetic interesting at all. It's certainly a great selling point, and it's always great when games manage to teach you something as subtly as The Bridge did.
The
, on the other hand, was disappointing to me. While the game is full of twisted perspectives and characters who are near madness, the music felt a bit underwhelming as a direct result. It's not bad, by any means. It's fairly minimalistic, with a few dissonant aspects to it (which I like), but I feel like the game would benefit more from something darker and more disturbing.
With that said, it still did its job, and added to the atmosphere.
The
all come down to rotating the world around you. Your goal is to reach a door, that is often locked. It can be unlocked by picking up a key, or activating a switch with one (or more) boulder(s). The objects in the levels are also subjected to gravity, however, not necessarily the same as yours. And it's basically about figuring out which path will lead a certain object where it needs to go, in often mind-bending and maze-like levels.
There are vortices (deactivated by a pressure plate), a curtain that negates gravity (so that you can rotate freely and change only the other objects' gravity), etc.
...I almost forgot! There's also a rewind mechanic. And, of course, it made some people say the game tried to rip Braid off. Well... no. Not at all. Braid used time as its mechanic, and something needed to finish the puzzles. In The Bridge, it merely exists as a handy tool to let you undo mistakes without replaying the levels from the start.
The game has
, each with
(and then there are an equal number of mirrored levels, which are harder and provide more plot elements -- don't consider the game finished without these!). Usually, the first 2-3 levels are about introducing a new mechanic to you, and the other 3 will use them in different ways, providing more challenging puzzles.
I'll admit that a few levels (especially later ones) proved to be a bit difficult. A problem I've had with it, is that it's very hard to actually visualize the solution to the puzzles. It came down to identifying different possible paths, and trying them out until I was close enough to the solution to be able to do the rest easily. I believe this is inherent to the level design, as everything is almost made to trick your eyes, making it a real pain to predict where each path will take you. Adding the fact that you're constantly rotating, which confuses you even more (and may provoke motion sickness, so beware!).
As I said, the later ones are more physics driven, and can be substantially harder if you're not used to it.
All in all, I actually felt somewhat rewarded for finishing it all without the use of a guide (except for the wisps). Some levels took me longer than I expected, but never being too frustrating.
And it was unique, so you should definitely give it a go, if you're into the genre. If you're not, it's probably not your best choice to start out, as there are other games which teach the player its tought-patterns better than The Bridge did (at least for me).
To end it, I just want to make a comment on the
. At the end of each chapter, you'll get a sentence or two to give you a better idea of what's going on. Basically, it's a story about Escher and Newton working together. Escher, an almost mad artist, constantly trying to overcome reality, and Newton, a genius physicist, both using mathematics in unconventional ways.
It touches on finally finding someone as absurd as him, sharing interests, and then pursuing the impossible.
It's all very open to interpretation, of course, but I really liked the way it has been done. The achievements also add a bit to this, specifically the names of the ones you get from simply finishing a chapter (

)... It's definitely not the focus of a game, but I always think it's good when developers spread various elements across the game (not just in the levels, or direct exposition, but on little things like this).
If you haven't figured it out yet, I definitely recommend this game to fans of the genre. How it bridges (heh) the visual and mechanical elements of level design is awesome, and it then coats it with interesting characters and themes that should make the player interested in knowing a bit more about what it's all about.
I've certainly enjoyed it more than I expected, and makes me look forward to the developers' next games!

A pure adaption of the boardgame classic, Space Hulk comes with all you may be used to playing with on the tabletop, with none of the setup troubles, boxing the tiles and pieces after a long and tense session. It comes with an online multiplayer mode, which allows you to take the missions to the internet and test your wit against friends too far away to come over to sit around the table with you!
Full Control Studios are, without a doubt, fans of the Warhammer 40,000 universe, and Space Hulk in particular. Despite the bumpy launch the game had, their dedication to the project shows.
Space Hulk is a turn-based strategy game involving two factions - the Space Marine Terminators and the alien Genestealers.
Both sides play vastly differently - from the amount of actions a unit can take per turn, to how it achieves its goals.
The Terminators are slow, hulking figures who rely on ranged weaponry, area denial and re-rolls to fight the Xenos, while the Genestealers are numerous, fast and require to close the distance to attack a Marine with their diamond-claws. They can easily outmaneuver the opponent, and receive reinforcements every turn.
To make things worse, the number of dice a normal Marine rolls against the 'stealers, is limited to one, against the aliens' three, and the highest result wins the combat - and kills the enemy. There are no life points in this game - if a character gets wounded, he is considered dead for the rest of the game.
To balance this out, the Space Marine player receives 1 to 6 Command Points per turn, determined by (virtual) dice. Those can be used to enact additional actions beyond the 4 allowed action points of a Terminator. Even though limited and unreliable, these points, if used well, will offer a lot of tactical flexibility to the player.
The inherent strength of the Terminators lies in their weaponry - their Storm Bolters are deadly and their close combat specialists allow them to deny the Genestealers the highest of their rolls or to re-roll one of their own. The flamer can bathe a whole room or section in fire, easily burning the aliens to ashes if stepped in, denying whole parts of the map. However, its use is limited to 6 shots per mission! The assault cannon is equally limited to 20 shots, and acts like a much stronger Storm Bolter.
Overwatch, costing 2 action points, will ensure that your Marines will also shoot on any enemy that crosses into line of sight, or moves within it, giving you an advantage over the enemy's fast tactics.
The objectives are determined by the mission. They may range from simple kill count goals to evacuating a certain amount of squad members. All the main missions are adapted from the boardgame.
Yes, Space Hulk had its share of problems at launch, and probably still has some of them, but more than a few can be attributed to just how close this video game adaption is to the boardgame it was meant to represent.
Bugs and performance issues have been significantly reduced by now, the game runs smooth, and a new, albeit short, campaign has been added to the game for free.
A criticism that was brought up a lot at launch was the "sluggish" movement of the player's Terminators.
While personally I very much enjoyed the hulking Space Marines move through the corridors like that, I can understand that not everybody has the same attention span and some may like to move on more quickly (although, once an order is issued, you can move ahead and issue another to the next Terminator of your choosing - they will enact them simultaneously).
Since then the developers have introduced a new setting to the options menu, allowing the player to toggle the animation speed, resulting in a good boost in unit movements.
Another criticism leveled was the lack of satisfying squad customization - one I can understand, but not feel quite as strongly about.
The characters in the game are directly inspired by the 3rd edition boardgame set, released in 2009, which I own. Having invested a lot of time in painting the miniatures of Sergeants Gideon and Lorenzo, Brothers Claudio, Zael, Omnio and all the rest, I can attest that the ingame models are very much like those little plastic figures. They are so faithfully modeled, I felt a bit sad that the boardgame miniatures are stuck with static (though dynamic) poses.
Customizing a squad's loadout also would not work with the way the missions are written. The game presents you with a short mission context and your objectives, all presented via Terminator-like voice acting (though not of the high standard of Relic's Dawn of War II games, it is still suitably grim), a neatly animated map and iconography.
What new players may not realize, however, is that the missions, have been written with certain restrictions and loadouts in mind. There are no differences between individual Terminators apart from their equipment - changing any one of the Power Fist + Storm Bolter Terminators to another Flamer, an Assault Cannon or close combat gear would undoubtedly unbalance the missions and remove a big part of the challenge.
Space Hulk is a challenging game. Some people, myself included, would even go as far as to call it a strategic puzzle game. Knowing your pieces is vital to success, being aware of all entry points of the enemy's Genestealers is crucial. A wrong move can easily unravel your whole deployment, and turn your structured progress into a desperate run for the exit.
The randomness of the dice adds a layer of unpredictability, but similar to Blood Bowl, minimizing the risks of the dice and thinking your moves through is the key to success. A dice roll may turn sour, but there are certain contingencies to make up for the randomness, if the player is smart enough to use them. In addition, the game itself takes care of all the manual tasks and notetaking of the tabletop version, keeping you informed of your resources at all times.
The learning curve may be a bit steep for some players, I admit, but unlike the boardgame, the video game adaption offers three short tutorial missions, which should do a lot of good in making you aware of the key strokes of the game.
Thankfully for new players, the 2 minute timer the Terminator player is subject to in the boardgame (unless the players decide not to use it to add even more pressure to the Space Marine's shoulders) is turned off by default and not enforced in singleplayer games. Purists can still play the game on hard difficulty and use the timer, but I am glad they made this optional.
The level editor is still in the making, I'm afraid.
If the current 18 missions (three tutorial missions, 12 for the classic Sin of Damnation Campaign and the 3 new missions on board of the Messenger of Purgatory) aren't enough to sate your appetite (which is unlikely, as missions are very replayable and usually not beaten on your first try), there are two new DLC Campaigns available right now (Sword of Halcyon and Defilement of Honour), both of which feature a set 5 missions each and are directly inspired from old first and second edition rules of the boardgame.
Squad customization may or may not be added in the future, but first I assume there will be the teased and promised Chapter Packs, introducing more than just the Blood Angels to the game - all neatly modeled according to lore and current miniature kits. Full Control have also said that they would include those Chapter Packs with new, Chapter-unique (historical) campaigns and flavor. This is DLC I can get behind and will support.
Considering that the first priority for Full Control was using the license to recreate the 3rd edition box set of Space Hulk, which was only produced in very limited quantities back then to begin with, I can acknowledge that they did an incredible job at capturing the game's aesthetic, tone, sound and, obviously, the rules.
This is, without a doubt, Space Hulk.

Hollow Knight is a masterful metroidvania and an absolute must-play for any fan of the genre. For this review, I'm going to get the negative out of the way first, so please bear with me here.
Pacing: ★★★
To me, this is the only real flaw here. Simply put, there is too much backtracking due to the sheer size of the map and the way things are set up. Some large areas of the map don't even have a fast-travel checkpoint at all, which means that every time you want to go back to those areas, you're gonna have to walk.
This becomes a problem later on, because there are some secret passages that are very important for true completion, and on your map, it often looks as if you've already cleared those areas completely. So you end up having no idea where you missed anything, and with so few fast-travel checkpoints, it truly becomes like trying to find a needle in a haystack.
The reason I would still give the pacing an okay score is because this only starts becoming a problem later into the game, and personally, it didn't ruin the game for me at all. It just made it a little tedious near the end to find all the stuff I missed. But consider this a warning: if you absolutely despise backtracking, there is a chance that you may not enjoy this game as much after a while.
(EDIT: Apparently they've improved the pacing in an update, after I wrote this review. Now, I can't really test that accurately without erasing my memories and replaying through the whole game, but if you're playing this game for the first time, assume the pacing will be better than what I wrote above. Also, props to the devs.)
Now, onto the positives.
Gameplay: ★★★★★
I think Hollow Knight raises the bar for core gameplay mechanics in a metroidvania.
So, I've mentioned the map and the benches already, so let me elaborate on those first. Basically, your map will only update if you sit on a bench. You can look at your map by holding down LB, but it doesn't pause the game. These two facts mean that you can't constantly look at your map while exploring an area for the first time, which makes the game more immersive and adds context to the map. This ain't a GPS; it's a piece of paper that your little character updates manually by drawing on it, which I think is adorable.
Sitting on a bench also restores all your Health, acts as a checkpoint if you die, and makes all the enemies in the area respawn. It's also comfy and relaxing.
When you die, you don't lose any progress you've made (items collected, map discovery, etc), but you do drop all your money (called Geo), and it limits your Soul to about 66% of its normal capacity. To get these things back, you just need to safely go back to the area where you died. So while death itself isn't too punishing, you still have to be careful because if you die twice in a row, the money on your first corpse will be gone, yo.
Soul is basically mana. You can use chunks of it to restore your health or to cast spells. It regenerates when you strike enemies with your nail, which is your melee weapon. There are other ways to restore Soul but I won't spoil them, you get the idea.
Soul alone makes the combat loop very enjoyable, because there's always a risk-reward involved with the way you choose to use your Soul and when you choose to attack with your nail. Not to mention how snappy the controls feel. It's not floaty or anything - it feels great.
This game has no level-ups; you get new moves and upgrades purely by exploring the world. There are also Charms you can find that give you various buffs and conveniences. You can only use a few of them at a time though, and there's a lot of them, so it's nice to mix and match and try out different "builds" depending on the situation.
It's time to talk about the bosses. There are boss battles in this game, and boy, they are FUN. I can't stress this enough. Some bosses may wreck you. Some may even wreck you repeatedly. But you'll keep trying, because they're so much fun to figure out. Plus, I won't spoil the context, but some bosses are optional and can be fought later, so if they're giving you too much of a hard time, you can come back after you've become a bit stronger, so that's cool. Beating these bosses as early as possible feels like a massive achievement, though. ;)
Audiovisual presentation: ★★★★★
The hand-drawn visuals look super good, and the game is very well animated. Overall, the visuals are meant to look bleak and mysterious,
, unlike some other games. It has a really unique look and feel to it, which makes the experience extremely memorable.
The sound design is fascinating. This game just sounds so... different. There are sounds in this game that I legit had never heard before. Some of them were genuinely unsettling, which I loved.
The soundtrack is just fantastic as well, very beautiful and elegant, yet intense at the right moments. The melodies are memorable and I really like the way they add or remove instruments depending on the situation.
Also, excellent use of silence. I'll just keep it at that.
Story: ★★★★★
Some of the story is told through lore, some of it is up for your own interpretation. But I don't mean that in a pretentious way; I think they nailed what they were going for (pun intended). They give you so much to fuel your imagination, it's crazy. You encounter some really charming NPCs, too, and because of all of that, the world is very interesting to explore, which is great because that's what you spend a lot of time doing.
Overall: ★★★★½
This is an indie masterpiece, so I feel bad that I can't give it five stars just because of the poor pacing. Regardless, I would recommend this game to anyone. The amount of quality content you're getting at that price is incredible, and pacing shouldn't be what keeps you from experiencing it.

I'll preface this by saying this is the only game I never had a moment I didn't enjoy in it. No, it isn't perfect, but I took the game at face value without any expectations, and I enjoyed it. If you go in wanting something from it, you've already failed yourself.
<Gameplay>
Pros:
Very tight controls
Platforming skill is actually substantially important
The Map system is exploratory, so you only get rewarded with a map of an area via finding an NPC in that area, buying it, then exploring and resting.
Unlocked abilities, as with most Metroidvanias, allow you to backtrack through previously known areas to find new sections in them hiding items and challenges.
The only permanent upgrades are new abilities with improved functionality and your weapon damage; everything else is acquired via temporary charms that you may equip and unequip at rest points which take up a number of notches.
No charm is useless, but if you expect the game to just become progressively easier because you found an item, you have another thing coming: I used every charm at some point on my first playthrough (50 hours) in which I 100% the game.
There is no way to be coddled in the game. If you refuse to learn from your mistakes and just get mad at the game continuously, the most you can expect is a bad experience. Blaming the game for "That shouldn't have hit me," or "That heal should have been done already," rather than realizing you made a mistake will merely sour your gameplay. Consider it like... IDK, bloodborne in that regard, if you played that. Or Dark Souls if you're smart enough to realize that those games aren't even really that hard, just reward determination.
Multiple ways to solve a platforming puzzle. Believe it or not, a lot of the difficult, impossible things you are faced with without the progression upgrades to your movement can be completed prior to getting their appropriate upgrade. Once you've played the game, you'll understand this reference, but the crystal area with spikes both above and below leading upward I got through utilizing the dash and down-attacking the spikes. Got my damage upgrade quite early. You can also lure flying enemies, which I think are specifically in the game for this part, to spots that you can't jump high enough to clear, so that you can down-attack them to get up to the out-of-reach ledge.
The Story is interpretive. If you are unable to think out of the traditional appearances of good and evil, i.e. Light = good, holy forces and Dark = bad, demonic forces, then you'll simply think the game is about god being evil. Take another look at it without those biases, and you might find there are other possibilities for what's going on that are heavily implied. I won't spoil, but I did enjoy the story when I found tidbits of info from NPC appearances and details about the appearance of our friendly neighborhood plague.
Neutral:
Currency from enemies must be collected. This is an intentional detail, as it's far more easy to just increase a number when something dies, so the way I see it is that this is a way to control character progression. There is a charm which auto-collects money from enemies, but it costs a space that could otherwise be used by other charms. It is up to you to decide if you'd rather give up that space to avoid tedium, or merely realize that you will gain enough money in the long run over all your exploration anyhow, so it's not that important.
The player attack range is appropriate for their size, which is a double edged sword. On one hand, this rewards experienced gameplay and learning spacing for enemies, because the attack range is quite short, a skill which I value highly in games. On the other hand, this brutally punishes anyone who expects longer reach than they have, and has trouble learning the limits of their abilities in platformers. You can correct this "issue" with charms, though.
Cons:
Sometimes there were eaten inputs. It was mostly when you expect the game to queue up your actions and it merely takes whatever buttons you're pressing at the moment, but sometimes it did ignore maybe one button press out of a thousand. This problem actually seems to have disappeared for me, but many people do complain about it.
Some fairly vital NPCs, notably one that repairs broken charms, are extremely far away and take a fair bit of travel to get back to. You can always quit and reload the game, and after a few trips, if you learn anything and are good at the game, you can speedrun to them very quickly, but they are still a fair ways out of the way.
Your currency is left wherever you die, so sometimes it can be left in some very inconvenient places. I died somewhere around 80-90 times and a few of those deaths cost me my currency based on extremely difficult platforming and enemy placement. If you spend your currency on things you need as it becomes available, you'll only lose what you don't need, though. The more expensive items are for areas you shouldn't be going into until you can reliably get that much money again.
Travel on foot, while one of my favorite experiences in this game, is extremely long. For the majority of people playing games nowdays, they just don't have the attention span for this to be okay. I personally like the experience of walking from place to place and overcoming challenges put in front of me, even if I've seen them already, but many people do not. So I'll put this in the cons, since I'm sure this will be a huge complaint.
Do I recommend this game? Yes. Do I recommend this game if the cons OR pros are not what you enjoy about games? No. Do I think you should at least try the game, and refund it if you do not enjoy it? Yes.
I'm a terrible platformer. At least, I'm not naturally gifted with that type of gameplay as I am so many others, so a lot of this game was mind-numbingly difficult, but still I enjoyed it thoroughly, and I went across the country to get my other computer just so that I could replace my broken laptop and play it. Hyperlight Drifter is still my favorite game, but this is probably a close second, despite the fact that I normally detest platformers. So approach it fairly, and give it a shot. Everything in this game is crisp, well balanced (considering it is early access) and build straight to the point of teamfighting. The Developers are focussing all their energy on brawling heroes and it pays off. Fights feel incredibly dynamic and tactical. Hitting abilities and landing kills feels very satisfying.
If you like teamfights of MOBAS or can't stand the farming, building up phase of MOBAS this is the game for you. If you don't have time for hour long matches, this is the game for you. If you want to win by skill, tactics and determination and not by random stuff, this is the game for you. If you want access to every champion in such a game, early access is the way to go. Tired of lacklustre Early Access titles? Battlerite is the game to get your Early Access hopes up again.
But is there anything that's bad:
Not for me, really. Tutorials, ranking mechanics, champion statistics and cosmetics still need work. I'm positive the Developers will deliver on that as well.

What a GAME this is. Thoroughly satisfying from beginning to end, littered with secrets, difficult fights and fun platforming.
The controls are tight and responsive. Never had a death I could blame on anything but myself. A quick blade takes center stage in combat, in addition to a basic set of spells. You also have the choice to make both the sword and spells more powerful through charms.
The visuals are marvelous. Cartoony characters in a corrupted and dying world meshes marvelously with the simple, but often tragic subject matter.
Huge map and every reason to explore every nook and cranny. Some of the secrets are a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and you will miss them on your first pass. You can miss whole sections of the map if you're not careful. None of them are exceptionally helpful though, so it's not ruinous for anyone but the completionists.
I would like more fast travel options though. Traversing the same passages 4/5 times gets a bit annoying, and the game really doesn't need it to pad out the playtime. I played for 30 hours and only felt like stopping when I had a lot of backtracking to do. The abyss in particular is a bit of a ♥♥♥♥♥. It is an incredible area to explore at first, but annoying to get to later.
The story is a gripping one, if you can find enough pieces to stitch it together. There are bits and pieces of lore scattered around the world, but even after finishing the game I only have a vague idea of what's going on in the main story. This may be by design, but I found the feeling of being lost a familiar one by the end. What is more interesting is the small stories of the inhabitants of this strange little world. Their fates range from tragic to triumphant and they are all very engaging.
I found the music to be a little lackluster, not really inspiring, but never gets in the way. I will never look up the soundtrack, but will always remember the game's somber mood.
TLDR: I like this game a lot, and if you want 30 hours of platformy, fighty, explory goodness I think you will too.

Where do I start?
Final Fantasy Type - 0 is probably my favorite FF to date, even back when I played it on the PSP. It was a wierd turn of direction for Square, but damn was it an awesome direction to go towards. Just how Sega went a different direction with Sonic by making Shadow the Hedgehog have guns and violence, Square went a different direction with Type-0 with possibly one of the most brutal and jarring intro's to a Final Fantasy game we've seen to date. The radical departure might unease some die-hard fans, but for others it brought to light a different perspective in the Final Fantasy universe that we haven't seen.
Anyways, let's talk about the Graphics.
FF: Type - 0's HD remake has done a splendid job of remaking a PSP game into a solid PC game. As a person who generally had little faith in Square's ports (Having experienced FFXIII Being Awful, as well as FFXIII - 2) I was pretty sketchy coming into it, expecting some horribly botched port that wouldn't be worth the time of day. I was pleasantly surprised and can say that without a doubt, this is probably the best port Square's done to date for a Final Fantasy game.
The graphics have been overhauled, yet there are still remnants of it's PSP origin. Namely, some of the sprite and texture work can still be blotchy/sketchy in some areas. However, they've made an already impressively and beautiful Akademia on the PSP look even more awesome by HD'ing it. If you look at the scenery of some of the area's too, and all the pretty effects they added you can take a small moment to enjoy what they've done with the game. But let's face it, you don't care about that. You probably have one jarring question that is going to determine whether or not you buy this game.
Is it 60 FPS?
No. It's not.
Why? It's because the game itself is dependant on things operating at that speed. Try going into skyrim and disabling your frame limiter and Vsync and watch the physics engine go willy nilly. You're asking for the same thing here by complaining that you want the game to be in 60 FPS.
For once in my life, I'm defending 30FPS. ......-Facepalm- But it's true. Despite me also believing it should be an industry standard, as a person who played this on the PSP and thought the game ran -extremely- well for a PSP game despite all the crap that was happening, the same feeling extends to the PC. There are times when I hardly notice the 30 FPS either to be honest. And let me give you a pro tip. If you feel the games too slow, they introduced a speed up button to the game that makes everything move at 1.5x speed, essentially making the game feel faster both frame wise and pace-wise.
The graphics options are actually pretty plentiful, if we're being biased towards Square. The jarring fail here though is their locked resolutions of either 1920x1080p or 1280 x 720. Personally, my PC can't handle the game at 1920x1080p with all of the settings, so I usually play in a windowed mode because it also lets me keep track of other tasks on my PC. You have the options of customizing shadows, motion blur effects (which are an awesome addition to make the game feel more cinematic and action-y <--- Legit word, I promise)
Now let's talk about the Gameplay.
Type-0 is a radical departure from it's predacessors in that it's a hack and slash based game. With an impressive roster of FOURTEEN PLAYABLE CHARACTERS, EACH INCREDIBLY UNIQUE IN THEIR GAMEPLAY, you're guaranteed to find at least one member of class zero that suits your fancy. My personal favorite is Seven.
Battles happen as thus: You have your typical overfield random battles, that throw you in a sandbox-like area where you duke it out with the enemy forces in real-time hack and slash based combat. When you defeat the enemy forces, there's a chance that you have the ability to "go another round" with the same enemies, only they'll be stronger. You can do this up to four times, and the enemies levels will increase, as well as the chance of them becoming enraged. (they don't flinch and deal stupid amounts of damage)
Combat itself in the game is fast-paced and has a degree of skill to it. Essentially if you're locked onto a target a 'Kill Marker" will appear on an enemy if it's in a position that leaves it vulnerable. Striking an enemy while this "Kill Marker' is up let's you score a critical hit that usually will kill the creature in one hit.
Missions are a bit different, as they usually have some relevance to the story and pit you in a location against enemy forces. These are replayable from the main menu and can be done as many times as you want, which is a cool function if you really liked a particular mission.
When you're not in missions, you're at Akademia which is your home area. You're given a certain number of "Hours" that you can spend before your next missions starts. This is my only complain about the game, because you have to basically play through the game multiple times to experience all of Academia's scenes, as you simply won't have enough time to get through all of them. Missing events between missions can also prevent you from seeing that event in the future too, so be careful.
Eidolon's make a comback in this game in possibly their most epic form, as you can actually play as the Eidolons, or let them fight on their own. You do this by sacrificing one of 12 members of  Class zero during a mission. (12, because two aren't a part of it originally and are not under the same special circumstances as the rest of class zero) It's an epic feeling to rampage across the field as an Eidolon, and it's something I guarantee you'll fall in love with as well.
When one of your classmates falls, you can replace them on the fly with other members of class zero if they go down. You can also additionally recieve backup from Akademia itself which lets you earn some points towards unlocking some nice gear.
When I finally get around to beating it this time around and actually being able to understand the story, i'll give a story evaluation here as well, so for now this will have to do. I highly recommend picking it up, as it's a gem and deserved to be given a two-hour shot at least.
I hope you enjoy it as much as I have so far~

It's really hard to pin down what exactly this game is; the user-tags include Walking Simulator and Story-Rich, which are pretty much the game.
You play as Stanley, who may or may not follow the narrator's narration depending on what Stanley feels at the time. While the game has many different endings, I've only personally explored a handful, so my playtime does not reflect playtime from exploring all endings. The Story-Rich tag is more true than anything: this is not an action game, although it can be seen as a type of adventure game. There are no pickup items, nothing to equip.
An analogy would be like playing Portal, without the portal gun or threats; only Cave Johnson talking as you explore Aperture Science.
It's a different playstyle compared to many games on the Steam store, and it's a mindset you have to be open to, to enjoy this game. I do think if you keep an open mind, follow the game, and let the game follow you, you can have a good time and invest a few hours into this game.
Is it worth the price? Probably not unless it's on sale.

As I have clocked over 900 hours on this game, I'm going to say it's good because of the sheer amount of time I've had on this!
The main reason to why the game is and still is amazing is because of the fantastic community, This goes to people playing the game, making groups / communities for people to join and have moments which you could never have in any other game. Mods, mods are an absolute saviour for this game. The main ones as most people know, DayZ. DayZ Mod really did bring a lot of traffic to this game which people may moan about was good for the game as it has allowed communties to be formed and A LOT more content for ArmA2 available. For those that never played / did for a short while and got bored went for the "MilSim" environment of the game in which people could do PvA (Player vs AI) but not with only 4 people, you could have 150+ people at once all co-operating at once, with the help of ACE and ACRE this could not have been possible. So I highly reccomend this game to anyone who is looking for that kind of stuff.
Now... Now for the negative points of the game and why people should consider it before buying this game.
The game is poorly optimised, like really bad. Put it this way, you could have a really good gaming PC which cost you the best part of £700 ($900-$1000) and only get 20-30 FPS in this game but then for some strange reason, you could have a £400 ($550 ish) PC and get 40-60 fps... the game had it's moments where it would pick computers to be nice on and be horrible on others.
If you are from the younger generation (15 and younger) and you're looking to get into groups such as "MilSim" groups and possibly DayZ ones too you could find yourself getting turned away for "being too young" as this game is quite complex to start off with (controls etc.) is a game made for the 'mature' audience.
Finally one final point to finish this review of, ArmA2:CO. Since Gamespy went down finding a specific server (such as a certain "life" server or "wasteland" possibly "DayZ Mod" Server) seems to take a while and you could be waiting up to ~5 minutes. The only way to get around this is to have the IP and choose the "Remote" Option.
Thank you for reading my review.

Hollow Knight is without a doubt the buggiest game of all time.
Luckily they're all dead and you're just spending your time seeing what's what in their dead bug kingdom.
From your first step in Dirtmouth, the emphasis is on exploration. It has such an emphasis on exploration that you need to explore to unlock a map to explore further. Your  first playthrough is just going to be a mess of deadends and haphazard unlocked shortcuts, but when every dead end leads to something useful and every shortcut is used multiple times it's exploration that pays off.
Levels are fairly varied, and mentally piecing them together shows them off - each level has several ways in and out and fast travel points require some getting to, which ends with you truly understanding the world of Hallownest.
This is the main driving point. This point you already knew, in the 0.2 seconds it takes to watch gameplay to see if this game's for your taste, and the rest is just how much the progression and exploration resonate with you.
Gameplay itself is serviceable. No combos or parries or anything fancy, but a solid bedrock of momentum based, gradually aerial combat with a handful of spells and quirks. You can further alter it with the "charm" system, that mostly amounts to a handful of passives.
Bosses actually use the gameplay quirks, unlike some games (with a pointed glance at Guacamelee) even if they're mostly threadbare.
A quirky collection of NPCs, bugfaced and masked, that you meet along the way are all memorable have multiple levels of environmental and mental storytelling to them. They also peter out real early, with budget cuts resulting in more than one serious anticlimax.
The budget cuts shine through in more than that one place. With boss fakeouts and some threadbare areas that obviously had more planned to them, you can feel the exact stings of "this is where we ran out of money".
As minor as they are, this is pretty much all that's negative to say about the game. They didn't push it as far as they could've. Maybe the ability unlocks are fairly rote.
That's a pretty weak detraction by anyone's standards.
Exploration in games usually means meandering around fairly boring locales waiting for something decent to happen. Exploration in Hollow Knight means something always happening while commuting from A to the B you haven't quite figured out yet. That's the vision the Hollow Knight believes in.
If that appeals to you, combined with other aspects that are inoffensive at worst, then it's a game I can easily recommend.

First the specs of my PC
16GB RAM, Intel 3770, nVidia 670.  Not top of the line, but not low end either.
First let me address the 30 fps.  I could understand the limit since it's a port.  Likely there's some timings tied with the frame rate (this has been done with some racing games and raising the FPS causes oddities).
But lets talk about the HD in the name.  I had the games AA set to high (because if I set it to Highest the frame rate drops to about 18).  Which AA it's using I'm unsure as it's not actually labeled but even with the second to highest AA available there's a lot of jagged edges.  So I forced AA through the nVidia control panel.  32x CSAA with 8X super sample and I got a solid 30fps.  Which means thier implementation of AA is terrible.   Second, the only thing that is actually HD is your characters, everything else looks like it's from a PS2.  There was very little effort put into making this port or making it HD.  Constantly things they "improved" just stand out and feel out of place with the untouched environment.
The load screens/transitions.  This ties into this being a lazy port.  While the load screens are super short since I'm playing on a PC and not the original device this was released on (PSP), the fact there's so many, so frequent shows no one bothered to try to stitch these things together better.
I've only made it to chapter 2 so far, and game play/story wise I have to say it hasn't landed a hook yet.  There's been no compelling story or interesting characters so hopefully it gets better.  FF 7-10 by this point at least had your attention.  Even if the story/characters/etc. do get better, all that work was already done when it was first released.  Putting a fresh coat of paint on something doesn't entitle you to saying you built the thing.  And so far, it's a pretty shotty paint job.
At a $30 price point, I can't recommend this game.  This is a bargin bin game (since they didn't really put any work on it).  If you could find FINAL FANTASY TYPE-0 in a discount bin for the PSP and ran an emulator you'd get the same experience I feel.  It's another FF game riding the coattales of the FF name.  This may have been a spot on game back when it first released, however, to be re-release it now with putting no effort into it and call it "HD" is doing it no favors.  At best, this is a $10 game.

I wont lie, I was a little dissapionted with this game when I first stared playing, I was a big fan of its predecessor 'Stonghold crusader', this was by far one of my favorite games when I was younger.
Pros and cons:
PROS- The graphics in-game have been updated, although not as much as you might hope for, especially for the fact that the old one came out 12 years ago.
- It is much harder to appease the peasants who flock to your castle, this does make the game a bit more challenging when it comes down to 'laying siege' to an enemies castle, at least in multiplayer. You can starve your enemy in a manner of speaking.
- There are new units, athough most of these are nearly identical to the predecessors, using some of the same quotes and one-liners.
- The walls fall down in 3D, instead of dissapearing,
- Destruction of castle walls and towers, looks better,
CONS- the Opening menu was a major dissapointment, i dont really know what i expected but the predecessors kicked♥♥♥♥♥compared to this new one.
- The new AI sucks, really sucks, (eg. the enemy computer always gets free siege equipment)
- The graphics aren't that imppressive for the amount of processing power it takes to run the game.
- The price tag for what you get is practically extortion.
- If you arent familiar with the game it is quite hard to understand the mechanics of the game, depsite the introduction campaign/scenario
- The new voice acting for the AI is just generally annoying, in my personal opinion they should have used the old voices from the last game.
- The mulitiplayer menu, is the same as the opening menu, a dissapointment
- There is a building and troop limit, whilst understandably for lower end computers is unchangeable, but there should be a way to adjust it.
All in all the game leaves you feeling a little underwhelmed, to be honest if your thinking of buying this game do yourself a favour and wait until a sale, save yourself the dissapointment of spending a lot of money on something that isn't quite up to standard.
I do know that Firefly are releasing updates and extensions so hopefully in the future they may be able to fix some of the problems, and annoyances.

I never expected any deep lore from this kind of slashers, just "hey, this is big evil guy, we must destroy him by slaying one milion of smaller evil guys!". Shadow Warrior storyline could be in first approach something like that, but I think, that everyone who reccomend this game also was supprised how deep is the story and how big is immersion. Still its not broken, its ballanced and even more fun when encounters force on you to use every weapon, every skill and many time the enviroment! It's not a shame to play on easier diffulty, I played on normal and still it Was a challange to me.
Enemies are varied, but game don't throw on us every type on the beginning. Some of them we can meet in the beginning, but others in the middle/slow endgame. They are realy different from eachself and force on player to use also other tactic to single one. Everyone played their role on battlefield and every demon we encounter doing something realy different, for example support his allies or summon other minion (but also still hurting us badly). Later game mix often almost all types, and from autopsy I can said this - In this game, more is better. You need to think many times to survive in bloodshed.
Skills and equipment are satisfying. Many weapon, which every have their own advantages and cons, which makes every usefull. Upgrades maybe makes one more universal, but still not an ultimate massacre machine. You can see it especially in endgame, where its bloodbath overload. More interesing are skills, merits of swordfighting. I use katana almost everytime I can, so I can say that its created perfectly. I never felt that I need some other skill instead that i can use, same as perks.
I fully recomend this game. Its awesome, one of the best production of 2014, maybe in whole gaming history. Entartaining and challanging.
Only one con is that you can finish this game in max. 15 hours, but content loaded in this makes me fully satisfied.

I just finished this game for the first time and obtained the true ending with 86% completion and about 23 hours of gameplay. I didn't get the other endings but I did look them up.
That being said, Hollow Knight is probably the most fun I've had playing a game in a long time. The soundtrack and art are both gorgeous, the area are all unique, memorable, and well designed; and the characters are relatable, interesting, and fun. One thing I really liked is that every character has a small snippet of voiced text in the language of Hallownest. The way these lines were delivered and the quality of the voices said so much about what the character was like and really helped endear me to each and every NPC.
Probably the most stand-out aspect though is the gameplay and combat. As many people have said, this is a Metroidvania style platformer, with your main method of combat being your nail (a sword). As you progress through the game, you gain additional movement abilities such as a dash and a double jump that allow you excellent mobility not just in platforming but in combat as well. Every boss fight is very immersive (especially the ones with Hornet) and it is always satisfying to defeat a boss. The combat is challenging for sure, but whenever I died it was always because of something I did wrong, not because the game ate an input or something.
I also want to touch on the story, which is delivered in a bit of an unconventional style. You won't find a clear and linear narrative here: the story is delivered to you through dialogue with NPCs and through the discovery of special items. I also think that if you rush straight to the end (and get the "normal" ending) you will feel very unsatisfied because so much of the story is delivered to you as you try to get the true ending.
unless you just want to play again which in reality is not a bad choice. Probably one of my only criticisms of this game is that you can lock yourself out of the normal ending though, which could easily be fixed by
.
Overall, if you like somewhat challenging metroidvania style platformers with a focus on combat, I would make this a must-buy. Tight controls, beautiful art, and memorable characters all work together to create an experience that is both a game and a story, and succeeds admirably in both aspects.
That being said, I do have a suggestion for future content which I haven't seen tell of: a boss rush/refight. All of the bosses were great and I would love even a simple interface from the main menu that allows me to select the boss, drops me in the room just before the fight, and then lets me fight them. It'd be even better if this was worked into the game and maybe had some sort of badge reward attached to it for clearing all of the bosses in a row without dying.
Another thing of a similar nature would be the ability to refight or fight Hornet after the third time and have her get progressively stronger. The Hornet fights were always the most intense fights of the moment and I loved fighting her. A gauntlet of fighting her over and over again and her gaining more abilities as it goes on (maybe punctuated by a period of her resting and then yelling out to know you've gotten to another phase) would be great. If you want to go above and beyond even that, perhaps have her
. Another thing that might be interesting is if she used her needle to immobilize you and then
.
Anyway, that's really all I have for suggestions. The game itself is solid, I just want more! Thank you so much for making such an excellent game, and please keep releasing content for it!

Sorry, I usually complete a game or at least spend a decent amount of hours in it, but I cannot, just for this game, progress anymore. I just don't have the motivation to play the game anymore. It's painful.
So heres my review for this game:
Initially The Bridge might look interesting. The game definitely has that 'indie' vibe you get from games like FTL. However everything will eventually, and quickly become boring, painful sometimes. You're going to reach the point where getting the achievements is your only motivation. But for me, I couldn't care less about that anymore.
Since its an indie-game there are little mechanics. The basic being 'moving time backwards' and 'rotating the area so the orientation of gravity changes'. However you don't really have full control of the rotation due to the limit of puzzles. So none of that creating looking stuff in Portal. The game tries to be fancy by adding annoying obstacles like the 'void', but after a level or two a new toy replaces it. It's like having your gum taken away before you could finish chewing all the taste out of it. In addition, the visuals are misleading. Am I talking about the inaccessible stairs or the obvious routes you are limited to? No. See the rain (gravity) they add in stage 3.
There's so little development, all those kewl new obstacles becomes repetitive quickly. This dude is just normal. Boringly normal. Song is boring. Literally the same stuff from stage 1 to the end.
The game feels more like a chore than an interactive piece of art. I literally cannot lower my standard anymore without trying to wake myself up from bordom.

I've played every Assassin's Creed game, and I must say that this is one of the best..
At first, I didn't think that the caribbean pirate would have been a cool background character for an assassin, I thought that Ubisoft made this game just for the naval combat, and then added the usual Assassins vs Templars thing. But after finishing this game 100%, I completely changed my mind. The background story is really well done, the introduction is nice (also very pirate-style), and the end is even better. Through the game (I'll try not to spoil anything) you gradually assist at the transformation of a pirate, interested only in gold, in a real assassin. I mean, it's not instantaneous like Assassin's Creed II or III, that in two missions you become an assassin. In this game, until almost the end Edward remains in a neutral state between Assassins and Templars, because, as I said before, his only interest is gold. And I really really liked this thing, it makes the story more realistic, in a way.
But enough with the story now, I don't want to spoil anything :)
The new game engine, introduced by Assassin's Creed III, is good on some things and simply awful in others.
It's great that now you have to simply press the RT button to free-run, that's very nice, because in this way you can adjust the camera while you run. But the combat controls, in my opinion, have become worse. I don't like parrying with the B button, and honestly, I miss the dodge. Apart from the combat. though, I like this new engine and it works great.
Last, but not absolutely least, the naval combat.. Man that's marvelous! Nice controls, beatiful scenes, it really makes you live what it meant to be a pirate.. Perfect
Well done, Ubisoft.. 9,8/10

Battlerites is a team-based Arena brawler that is the spiritual successor of Bloodline champions which is effectively the same game by Stunlock studios.
It's a best of 5 rounds fighting game that's played 2v2 or 3v3. That's it. That's all there is.
You start the client, pick a champ, hop into an arena, beat 2 or 3 peasants a few times and let the cycle begin anew.
They have announced that it will become Free 2 Play with micro-transactions for cosmetic upgrades because, and I'm probably quoting the sales executive on the board meeting in which this decision took place, "it worked for League of Legends". The cosmetics are also unlockable through an ingame currency which you earn by playing.
The game also tries really hard to be an E-sport, so we should judge it as one.
First of all, there is a suprising mechanical depth behind the brawling, which makes watching a match as a player really engaging as well. The battles are tightly action-packed with enough overview to have an idea of what's going on. On top of that, the titular perks, that upgrade one of your abilities, chosen as a new round starts make for an interesting strategic draft.
The immediate downside is that this very depth also makes the game hard to explain to anyone who hasn't played it before without crashing their brainserver with ridiculous amounts of onunderstandable gibberish. It's the computergame equivalent of talking soccer with your wife.
That being said, I really like playing the game. The mechanics and maps are balanced enough to always have a way to outplay your opponents and I've always liked skirmishing over macro-wavecontrol anyway. If you're a player vs player - player then Bloodline Champions 2 is definitely a must-have for your gamelibrary.

The Bridge will bend your brain. Not as much as say Antichamber, but it will force you to think ahead with how your manipulations affect the world around you.
You play as an unnamed intellectual (who bears a striking resemblance to surrealist M. C. Escher) who starts out napping under an apple tree. After discovering your ability to rotate the world, you get him awake and discover a number of puzzle doors have appeared in his house; why and how they are here is hinted at in text descriptions given by the protagonist but nothing is really explained. A sense of dread accompanies the game's progress. The first time you meet 'the menace' (balls with huge grinning faces that kill you with one touch), there is an uneasy feeling that something is wrong with these places beyond their defiance of reality.
The art is pretty in black and white; the story that is there serves as a vehicle to put you through the puzzles. There is a sense of achievement to be had with the later ones when momentum and quick thinking rotations come into play. One mechanic that could have been explained better is "the Veil", which is a curtain that lets you manipulate the gravitational pull on certain objects. At first I thought it let me rotate objects independent of myself, but eventually deciphered its effects. I blundered through the veil puzzles a good bit before its potential hit me.
I got this for a dollar and found it easily worth that amount. Depending on your love of puzzle games, it is a good game to lose yourself in while trying to manipulate how to get the protagonist to his exit door. The downside is there is little to no replay. Some achievements help pad out the length as well as hidden collectibles, but basically the 48 puzzles behind the doors are it. The first half of the game is easy as it introduces concepts for you to play with, but then in the second half things get pretty tricky.
The Bridge would make Escher proud. Not a game you buy for the story but for the experience of solving its strange puzzles and experiencing its strange, ruined landscapes.

I don't know what it is about this game, but there's something very deeply and profoundly disturbing about it. It's like a terrifyingly beautiful nightmare. It is captivating. I love the art, the originality, and the atmosphere. But you still have this feeling of something being off. The game sucks you in and leaves you wondering what will happen to you once you've been taken. It really is just like those dreams where everything is perfectly fine, except for an uneasy feeling, you don't know what is giving you that feeling, maybe it's those boots that are laying on their side, or the absence of lint on your clothes, you don't know, but you can tell something is wrong. If you are expecting a monster or someone with a chainsaw popping up like it's a B horror flick, you won't find that here. But you will remain uneasy throughout.
I recommend this game 100%, and I'm giving it a 10/10. The experience you get from playing this game is unlike any other I've played in the past. It's very unique, it has elements I've seen in other games, rotating the map, manipulating gravity, but the ingenuity with which it was applied is unparalleled. But be warned, this game will haunt you like few other games have.

The artwork is just sad. Egyptian hieroglyph looks better than what we see here.

Take SH1, just awe at the amount of detail that it had, moss in the walls, cracks in the wood and stone. Even wind ffs.
Unfortunatly, you cannot stop and think: is this just a SH3 reskin with less bugs?
Is it a waste of time? God no. The gameplay is bland but at times, you may find some joy in it. Fans will do a fair bit of it out of pure nostalgia. Smashing walls can be fun.
In the end, the game just doesn’t do much for you to like it for very long.

This is a no-spoiler review.
Pros:
-AMAZING gameplay. Think Quake or Doom type combat, but with some additions (i.e. katana moves and special powers). If you haven't played those games, then think about what Call of Duty or Battlefield would feel like with more than two weapons.
-Nice weapons. Each one (except the pistol) feels powerful and has good sound effects.
-Fair difficulty. The game gets really tough, but it never felt unfair. Near the end of the game, it gets REALLY difficult. But there isn't a single enemy in the game that takes advantage of you. Every enemy has a predictable moving/shooting pattern. It's literally your skill vs the game designers.
-Nice graphics. Good shaders and textures used.
-Good optimization. I don't have the best PC in the world but this game runs like a beast.
Cons:
-The unoptimized karma system (which involves being innovative with killing enemies) doesn't always reward creativity. For example, I might decide to kill a certain enemy using a certain weapon, but it isn't the best and the game doesn't recognize that I did something unusual.
-Monotonous environments. The graphics are really good, but after a while, you end up seeing the same house or lab over and over again.
-Terrible boss fights. Almost every review mentions this; the boss fights suck. But don't let this keep you from enjoying this amazing game!
Summary:
8/10. There are better AAA games on Steam, but after you play those, you HAVE to play this.

One of the best indie games of all time, period.
Hollow Knight is a metroidvania that offers great 2D graphics for an extremely vast world in which you'll discover various powers, characters, worlds and secrets.  The map is huge, and it takes a long time to explore everything (between 20-30 hours). The gameplay is extremely well balanced with great and precise combat mechanics . Sometimes the game is difficult but it is never unfair; most of the difficulty comes when aiming for the true ending which requires to confront new bosses and obstacles that were designed for the best players.
The game is quite long (around 20-25 hours for a first playthrough, 30 hours if looking for the 100% completion mark) but never repetitve. Needless to say that this game is worth every penny the devs are asking for (I'd go as far as saying this game should have a higher price tag )
Special mention to the OST, composed by Christopher Larkins, which is an absolute masterpiece. No electrical or chiptune music here (I have nothing against them, but they seem quite common in indie games nowadays) but gorgeous orchestral themes that could have been made for an AAA game. Hope that we get to listen to more of his creations in other games !

So the reason with the unplayable frame-rates for Type-0 HD actually lies with the settings for anti-aliasing. Many are unaware that they were actually rendering it at a full 4k resolution. (Especially taxing if you're running mid-range systems.)
"High" and "Highest" both maintain the temporal AA, but also render the entire game at a higher resolution! PC gamers commonly call this downsampling, and we all know the enormous impact it has on both quality and performance. "High" renders at 1.5 times the resolution in each dimension, so 2.25x as many pixels, while "Highest" doubles the resolution in both dimensions, quadrupling the graphics workload.
This means that the actual rendering resolution of the game is a result of both the resolution and AA settings:
720p Resolution: 1280x720 (Off/Normal), 1920x1080 (High), 2560x1440 (Highest)
1080p Resolution: 1920x1080 (Off/Normal), 2880x1620 (High), 3840x2160 (Highest)

-Fair difficulty. The game gets really tough, but it never felt unfair. Near the end of the game, it gets REALLY difficult. But there isn't a single enemy in the game that takes advantage of you. Every enemy has a predictable moving/shooting pattern. It's literally your skill vs the game designers.
-Nice graphics. Good shaders and textures used.
-Good optimization. I don't have the best PC in the world but this game runs like a beast.
Cons:
-The unoptimized karma system (which involves being innovative with killing enemies) doesn't always reward creativity. For example, I might decide to kill a certain enemy using a certain weapon, but it isn't the best and the game doesn't recognize that I did something unusual.
-Monotonous environments. The graphics are really good, but after a while, you end up seeing the same house or lab over and over again.
-Terrible boss fights. Almost every review mentions this; the boss fights suck. But don't let this keep you from enjoying this amazing game!
Summary:
8/10. There are better AAA games on Steam, but after you play those, you HAVE to play this.

What's interesting here is that we have a game that really *shouldn't* be this bad. I mean if you look at all the different aspects of the game, they are all good. BUT when it comes to games, you NEED to have one factor above the others or it brings the whole thing down to the lowest common denominator. And that's what's happened in Space Hulk. They've got 95% of a great game here, they just ♥♥♥♥ed up the most important 5%.
The control.
I mean, why the f**k did they even bother? Imagine I cooked you a beautiful cake. It's got icing. It's a large portion. It looks beautiful, and to top it all off, it's low in calories. Great right? Well, what If I poured a big load of salt in it? It turns out that it's worthless right? The most important thing about food is that 1) You can eat it, and it 2) tastes good. Well, guess the duck what? Games aren't that different. If you want a good game the two most important things you need are 1) you can PLAY IT and 2) It's FUN.
And that's the problem! Space Hulk just isn't playable. They poured a big, big, big, big, big, big bag of salt into the games controls.
I know for a fact that the game should be fun. The game is based on a very popular board game that is *VERY* fun. So I know that the underlying mechanics of the game would be fun, they've just been implemented poorly.
To go back to our food analogy, let's pretend I have baked a new cake. Not only does this one not have an♥♥♥♥♥load of salt, but the cake tastes absolutely amazing. Now, I'm going to offer you a slice of this fantastic tasting cake. Only, the thing is, I'm not going to give you a fork and I'm not going to give you a plate. Nope, you'll have to eat it off the floor, and for every bite you take, I'm going to burn you with a lit cigarette.
And that's what it's like playing Space Hulk.

I think I've played enough to throw my perverbial hat into the ring.
This game is in effect Minecraft crossed with a successful space sim game. This is a gross simplification, for it is simply it's own entitiy.
You are able to creat in effect any spacecraft, space station, or even ship should you desire under the sun (thnks to various wedges and such) as well as pages of materials to build from, including many aesthetic blocks. Weapons too are able to be customized to your combat style, be it a close up shotgun or long range explosive sniper cannon, you have the ability to make it. It even has a stealth system. (I myself am working on a modified Normandy from Mass effect) The galaxy (or depending on the server, galaxies) are massive in scope, and even on a fully populated server you can find a place to set up your base.
Crafting is also fairly straightforward. Collect ores, pop them in a refinery, combine them by connecting factories to create a manufacture line. Very efficient. The building aspect even comes with a build mode, as well as an advanced version that allows you to place/remove alot of blocks on your creation quickly.
It does however have it's share of teething issues. Lighting glitches occur quite a bit, and the mini-radar is very ineffective in detecting threats until you're already space dust. The new rail system also has a few operation glitches, especially when creating hatches and large doorways within ships and space stations. (nothing crippling, just annoying on occasion) In the build mode there can be issues when palcing alot of blocks if you are not careful, and the "build helper" which assists with making circles is flat out useless. (cirlce is not a circle, and is not symmetrical at all. Making a sphere with it is impossible I tried)
I know nothing of the communities, but the servers can be very dangerous. Pick a remote area and high tail it there if you wish to build in any sort of peace. (I play on Red-Shift, a large active server which gives you alot of credits so you can quickly make a defendable ship and starbase in a remote area)
Overall, for the price this game is a bargain. The ship/station building system is the best I've seen, and space combat is challenging but fun. (especially with missles. BOOM) It has glitches and bugs, but given the scale of the game they can be ignored with relative content. (not that they shouldn't be fixed, obviously they should) The forums could use some better policing for trolls and "neo-nazis" harassing people who only wish to see the game grow. And this is just the Early Access! Imagine how good it will be at 1.0!
My rating for this game is a solid 7/10. Amazing in scope and execution, however has a few issues that could be annoying to novice players of survival and space games.
I adore how the game feels like it never ends, like you can always go back for more.

This isn't so much a negative review as it is a "know what you're getting into" review. Technically a No, but with a giant asterisk.
I bought this game on sale for a dollar. I definitely got my dollar's worth. I think that if I had paid full price, I would have been disappointed, but only because of the glowing 9/10 reviews. Had I expected less, I would've been more satisfied with what I got.
First, the puzzles themselves weren't great. There was no sense of build as I went on. I never felt like I was learning more about what it meant to interact in a world of impossible shapes. I had no "Aha!" moments where a shift in my thinking made the solution obvious. More than a few times my reaction was "Really? It was that easy?" The later puzzles pile on complexity but feel more like a slog than an intricate problem.
This is compounded by the second problem: The controls feel very clunky. It makes the exploratory / trial-and-error phase of learning about the puzzles more work than fun.
It's not all bad. The art and sound design are excellent. There is some fun puzzling to be had. It's just overall the game fails to deliver. I give it 6 misspent youths out of a possible 10. If you go in expecting 9/10, you will be disappointed.

A fantastic, and quite frankly enormous Metroidvania for the PC. Some great art direction, bosses and music with a huge map to explore. I managed to find most of the gear on my 100% run without a guide, which is nice.
I have a few small issues, namely a couple more obtuse strategies for obtaining items in 100%, and the game's odd input latency between abilities. Unlike something like Mega Man X, the player cannot combo abilities very well. For example, when activating the game's standard dash, you cannot jump until the animation is complete, whereas in MMX, you can combo jumping+dashing+shooting/charging in a very fluid fashion, which helps a lot in the fast-paced bosses. When you are focusing (healing), there is a small window of time after the heal where inputs seem to not register properly, so both of these issues are *extremely* annoying during some of the later game frustrating bosses. I found that this led to me getting killed via touch damage far mare often then actual enemy attacks, which just sort of gets on my nerves at times.
Overall though, this really is a great game, with some (mostly) very fair and rewarding challenges. Definitely pick this up, as some free content is on the way soon to add even more to the world as well!

Battlerites is a team-based Arena brawler that is the spiritual successor of Bloodline champions which is effectively the same game by Stunlock studios.
It's a best of 5 rounds fighting game that's played 2v2 or 3v3. That's it. That's all there is.
You start the client, pick a champ, hop into an arena, beat 2 or 3 peasants a few times and let the cycle begin anew.
They have announced that it will become Free 2 Play with micro-transactions for cosmetic upgrades because, and I'm probably quoting the sales executive on the board meeting in which this decision took place, "it worked for League of Legends". The cosmetics are also unlockable through an ingame currency which you earn by playing.
The game also tries really hard to be an E-sport, so we should judge it as one.
First of all, there is a suprising mechanical depth behind the brawling, which makes watching a match as a player really engaging as well. The battles are tightly action-packed with enough overview to have an idea of what's going on. On top of that, the titular perks, that upgrade one of your abilities, chosen as a new round starts make for an interesting strategic draft.
The immediate downside is that this very depth also makes the game hard to explain to anyone who hasn't played it before without crashing their brainserver with ridiculous amounts of onunderstandable gibberish. It's the computergame equivalent of talking soccer with your wife.
That being said, I really like playing the game. The mechanics and maps are balanced enough to always have a way to outplay your opponents and I've always liked skirmishing over macro-wavecontrol anyway. If you're a player vs player - player then Bloodline Champions 2 is definitely a must-have for your gamelibrary.
