Fan of the series? Buy it. Fan of RTS games? Buy it.
Welcome M’lord to a review of Stronghold Crusader 2.
After waiting 12 long years since the first Crusader game, Firefly Studios have released the much anticipated sequel; Stronghold Crusader 2. Whilst the later instalments of the franchise have not lived up to the critical acclaim of the earlier games, fans of the series remained somewhat optimistic in the build up to release. Personally I found myself feeling a mixture of excitement and anxiety, hoping that Firefly would rekindle the ashes of Stronghold and Stronghold Crusader and avoid giving us another flop (…cough cough looking at you, Stronghold 3)
Stronghold Crusader 2
The action starts straight away with a cinematic showcasing the iconic Templar Swordsman pitted against a Whirling Dervish, one of the newly introduced mercenary troops. A great little addition to build some atmosphere before getting to the main menu.
Jumping into single player, gamers are given a variety of options including the Skirmish Trails campaign, Custom Skirmish and Sandbox. These options include plenty of tutorials for newcomers and players who need to dust off their swords and bows before jumping in to the main campaign. Tutorial missions teach the basics of building your castle and surviving out in the desert whilst the Learning Campaigns gives players the opportunity to implement all the tools they have learned. After you’ve had your fill of practice, the main Skirmish Trails await. Acting as the main campaign, this set of Trials pits you against multiple enemies in a variety of scenarios, requiring different approaches for each enemy and terrain that you encounter. The Trials are split into a six missions trees, helping break up the relatively time consuming campaign into more manageable chunks.
My initial impressions of the tutorials missions were that they are infuriatingly restricted in terms of available buildings, troops and ways to complete the obnoxious goals such as destroying every single piece of rubble or painfully waiting for a set number of resources to be collected. My feelings about the Learning Campaigns are slightly more positive, at least they have an element of challenge and a variety of strategies to achieve the mission objectives. In hindsight I do appreciate that these missions are heavily tailored for newer players and provide an environment to learn all the basics and ante up the degree of difficulty until they reach the same playing field as more veteran fans of the series. Yet the sheer amount of training missions is what seems unnecessary, especially given that players will need to endure hours of patronising gameplay to unlock all available achievements.
The Skirmish Trials do a valiant effort at injecting some fun and excitement into the game, offering a wide variety of challenges by mixing up your enemies, allies, map size and access to resources. The learning curve is steep right off the bat, with quick decisions and a fast clicking finger being vital. There’s a fine balance to be struck between getting your economy up and running whilst also prepping your defences for the incoming attacks that happen extremely soon due to the rush-happy nature of AI opponents.
Stronghold Crusader 2
After sinking 20 hours of gameplay into the campaign I can safely say that there is an element of repetition between the missions. Is it because of the rinse and repeat approach of spamming overpowered archers until you have enough gold and troops to blitz the enemy? Is it because resources are so scarce, forcing you to twiddle your thumbs and wait? Is it because peasants spawn painfully slow and hovels are woefully overpriced? Probably a mix of all 3, plus countless other aggravating features. Talking of annoying features, let’s quickly address the voice acting and narrations. Irritating opponents such as “The Rat” have been a staple of the franchise since the initial Stronghold. Well, if the Developer’s aim was to annoy players then they sure succeeded. The voice acting seems poor quality throughout and the repetition of phrases seems more apparent than it should be for a reputable game produced in 2014. Fortunately the soundtrack provides some saving grace, providing an enjoyable ambience whilst you go about your medieval business.
There are some redeeming features to the game. The inclusion of unlimited stockpiles, granaries and armouries are welcomed additions. As are the improvements to team AI who are surprisingly competent and respond to your trade requests unlike in the first Crusader game. The easy-to-manage popularity metre is also a nice touch, allowing players to balance positive and negative popularity contributors to find the sweet spot between taxation and resources. The graphics, whilst not extraordinary, remain nostalgically reminiscent of the first Crusader game and the improvements of seeing towers shudder and walls crumble under your siege assault is certainly rewarding.
If you fancy a change from the pre-set missions there are a variety of choices to wet your castle crushing appetite. Creating your own scenarios allows players to edit maps, starting resources and computer controlled Lords. Moreover, if you crave even more customisation feel free to create your own maps in the Sandbox or download some user-created maps from the community. This contributes to the replayablility that the game offers, giving an almost infinite combination of enemies, maps and ways to conquer your opposition. There is also the option of jumping in to Multiplayer for a real challenge. There does seem to be a relative lack of lobbies though, so my recommendation would be to grab some buddies to bulk out the numbers. If, when it comes to your friends, you’re more of a lover than a fighter, there’s the chance to play co-operatively and take control of the same castle. This was one of the new features promoted during the build-up to the game, but in reality it’s quite gimmicky and leaves me with the disgruntled opinion that it’s simply more fun to control separate keeps and team up as normal.
Stronghold Crusader 2
Overall Stronghold Crusader 2 just doesn’t do enough to win me over. It’s a noticeably better game than recent instalments in the Stronghold series, but if Firefly hopes to rekindle the success of the earlier games in the franchise they still have a way to go. The lack of innovations and major improvements over the original game is underwhelming to say the least, there is also a feeling amongst the community that the focus is much more combat focused rather than actually building up your castle and infrastructure, a sign of the times in modern gaming. I frequently found myself not even bothering with a castle and opting instead for a few strategically placed towers filled with archers. Ultimately the game is a satisfactory addition to the RTS genre, but the slow paced growth and underwhelming improvements over the original game leaves me reluctant to recommend it to anyone other than hardcore fans of the series and genre.

Metroidvania + Dark Souls + Zelda.
This is a thoroughly enjoyable experience. I haven't finished the game yet (going for 100% completion on my first playthrough), but this is very well done by an indie dev. It has so much depth, yet when you read the credits, you wonder how they achieved so much with so few people working on it. Games like this help establish gaming as an art - belonging with movies and other forms of entertainment as a bona fide way for adults to responsibly enjoy downtime.
The graphics/artwork is engaging, and the music is the perfect backdrop for the constant action.
I have no problem giving this a 10/10 - if you're into Metroidvania games with a high degree of difficulty, pick up this game. The only issue players may face is that there is a fair amount of backtracking the game requires - but it doesn't feel repetitive. Rather, it is refreshing to return to an area that you just couldn't reach before in a part of the map you've cleared to see what items/enemies lie in wait - it drives the desire to complete the game and completely upgrade your character.
I was playing XCOM when I decided to try Hollow Knight - and I love me some XCOM - and this game made me put that one all the way on the backburner.
This review was written during the Steam Summer Sale. Don't delay in picking it up for that - but honestly, this game is worth buying MSRP. If the devs make a sequel, then I'll preorder it Lord willing. It's that good.

Thus far, I've only forced myself to play this game, while the original I couldn't do anything but help give hundreds upon hundreds of hours into the game. At first it's simple structure seemed likeable to me, only to realize the maps are horribly designed for Stronghold Crusader 2. You have to build your mines completely exposed, with no way to build fortifications anywhere near them to defend it, leaving you constantly buying iron, stone, and even sometimes FOOD. Yes, that's right even the oasis seems to be terribly misplaced. On some maps these disadvantages are fine, because it could prove a challenge that veteran players are looking for. However for the masses, I cannot see how this was a good move.
While it may not bother some, however it should be noted that the characters from the previous series who make a come back in this one are no where NEAR alike that of the original Stronghold, or Stronghold Crusader. You can't tell me that they can't afford better voices and animations for SHK2, everyone I've seen who liked the series purchased it immediately. Stronghold Crusader is better in many, many aspects in not only animations, but also the looks of said characters even noting the pixelation. Their voices also fit the part well, and the actors did an exceedingly wonderful job at sounding convincing. However for SHK2, their lines are corny, their voices sound unconvincing, (as if he wasn't talking about the same subject that he was) and overall their cut-seen is horribly tacky. It gives you a big, "So and so time.." and transparents to a scene with two warriors, they clash blades and.. that's all. Yep, that build up for nothing.
But let's get out of the pit of despair for a bit. They have some new units, to which are likeable. Such as the Ranger, who is capable of both range, and meleee combat, though not an expert at either.  They updated the graphics... for the most part. (again not on character models, ie when the rat portrait comes up when he's mad/attacking you) They have a simplier, clever system. Although I think overall for me this is good, this can be debated on highly. I just now thank the game that I don't have to focus on rebuilding economy/walls constantly when I'm being barraged with enemies.
If you're certain about purchasing this game, just keep in mind I was too. Overall I regret it as it stands, but if they fix the animations, voices, script for lines, and maps, then we'll start talking. In comparison to Stronghold Crusader, this game has very few gameplay hours, unless maybe you're a PvP-focused person? Not too sure how well PvP works in this game, but considering the maps.. I imagine not too fun since your economy being smashed is nothing you can really control. Unless you love fighting field battles.

Tl;Dr - Game runs fine, most people just whining about 30fps lock or having to use a controller when its no big issue. Worth getting.
So even though I don't often make reviews, the negative reviews are irritating me far too much to not do one for this.
Lets talk 30fps first, is it a problem? No. Would it have been nice uncapped? Sure, but a lot of games these days are still 30 cappedand were still making the transition to 60/uncapped in general, right now 60+fps is still a luxury, not a requirement.
There are some people even giving negative reviews because fullscreen doesn't work. Is that fair? No, because only a very minor player-base is having said issue, myself, as with most others haven't had this issue, so for giving it a negative review for your rigs issue, not exactly fair.
Controls, people are complaining about the keyboard controls being♥♥♥♥♥♥ I wouldn't know, I use a controller. But thats my point, very few JRPGS are meant for keyboards, and my god I hope they never do, at the end of the day most people who primarily use PC's for gaming should have a gamepad of somesorts now and if you dont, dont blame the devs, its a game ported from PSP - PS4 - PC, go figure its more confortable on a controller. A lot of games are, its still mainly first person games that are best for keyboards.
Now, away from my response to complaints, the game itself? Awesome, while yes the 'HD Remaster side' a lot of the time seems lazy and rushed (as seen in a lot of the ingame cutscenes) for the most part, its a nice improvement where it works.
As with any Final Fantasy, good or bad, the music is absolutely gorgeous and in my opinion one of the best soundtracks to date.
My only main gripe with the game is its camera. Oh god the camera, its aweful. While in combat locking onto targets you often find the camera surging around from target to target or the camera being stuck behind scenery where its trying to focus on a target, forcing you to briefly turn off the lock on and reset it.
The combat itself can be a little off at times, but it mainly comes down to which character you use, Ace for example (the games main protagonist) is probably one of the more boring characters, using cards as his weapon empowered with magic, you find youself just standing in one spot throwing them making you feel rooted and bland. Where as other characters such as the dragoon, nine, feels a lot more mobile and heavy.
The story right off the bat, the very first cut-scene, is intense, though depressing it certainly brings you into this new world hard and fast, which is exactly what this game is. While having a main and intruging main story the game also offers a lot of side story/lore/quests, a lot of which require a certain character from class-0 to see, making you really bond and enjoy each character seperately.
All in all, most of the 'issues' seem to be personal gripes or issues with a few rigs, which 90% of big name games have upon first release, is this an exception? Of course not, but these issues seem to be minimal and personal.
Do I recommend? Hell yes, one of the best Final Fantasys to own on PC right now.

Where to begin...
Shadow Warrior has pretty much everything I want and love. The scenery and settings are gorgeous. The gameplay is smooth and fluent throughout and never gets old or boring too quickly. Infact at all. The game doesn't give you any "here's a ridiculous and pointless puzzle as a filler to make the game longer". It's level after level of onslaught, story and exploration. The story is by far the most impressive and best thing about the game. With some games, the story can totally suck and you feel you just want to get through it and finally complete it. But Shadow Warriors story really is unique and different. It keeps on point all the time and doesn't slow down or make the game crap. Having completed the game, the story is absaloutely beautiful. The characters are unforgettable, the weapons are glorious, the melee combat is by far the best swordplay of any game I've played with the feature, and mostly what I love the most - it's a long game!
The weapons. The weapons are awesome to use. At first you may notice they feel a bit... weak. But with future upgrades they feel better and look cooler. Your arsenal will build up from a revolver, smg, crossbow to a shotgun, flamethrower, and rocket launcher. But it doesn't stop there - there's an ability to use Demon hearts and heads against foes for a gruesome but fun attack method. If that doesn't settle, there's always the swordplay which you yield gracefully in the face of combat with some amazing and deadly combos!
The enemies have some great variety and change the gameplay drastically. Yes this is a very interesting game, but would I call it entertaining?  Tell me, when you go to an art expo, do you find that entertaining?  Assuming you were just there to look at the art and nothing else?  The Stanley Parable is a very short, very artsy game that I hesitate to even call a game.
There are two flaws with the game.  One, it's short.  There are 15 endings as I remember and they can all be completed in about 10 minutes. Not that you are likely to even find all of the endings.  Some of them require looking up a guide to do and even then there are some ridiculous ones that no one is going to do. ie spend a day doing the same monotinous task until you trigger the alternate ending. Each ending reuses a massive amount of material so you aren't really playing anything different. In short, you don't get a lot of bang for your buck.  I'd say this game was worth 5 dollars, not 17...
The second flaw is the narrator.  He's a great actor, don't get me wrong.  The dialog is great as well, but I just can't stand listening to the same voice giving constant voice overs for hours on end.  No matter how great an actor is, if there's only one, it gets boring.
I think this game was rated highly because most game reviewers really didn't know how to review this product.  It is nothing like most any game you'll ever play, but you can't really call it a bad product either.  But I was bored stiff for almost the whole game.

I would describe this game as Dark Souls meets Metroidvania.
It is rich with the tight fun 2d combat, constantly improving character and emphasis on revisiting old areas like most Metroidvanias. However, the way the story is told and world is built is truly remarkable and very Souls-like. You'll meet fellow adventurers like yourself on your travels, appreciating the brief moment of companionship as you meet them in different places in the world, on quests of their own. When you die you drop your money at your death spot and have to retrieve it, the story itself mimics Dark Souls in a lot of ways (without spoiling too much,
etc.). Even some of the landscapes reminded me of Anor Londo and the like.
In terms of difficulty, It can definitely be challenging in places, but I personally thought it was overall a perfect balance of difficulty. The length is also EXTREMELY reasonable, taking me 26 hours to 100% it. Not to mention the hand-drawn artstyle is insanely good and every single environment looks absolutely stunning.
Overall if you're a fan of either genres, you will enjoy this game greatly. If you're lucky enough to be a fan of both, this game is perfect for you.

This was my go-to puzzle game when I needed to kill time. It layers each of its mechanics slowly, and, before you know it, you’re stumped in a puzzle where gravity is sideways, alternate gravity is upside-down, the map screen is tilted at a 45-degree angle, and the Newton-wannabe that you control is falling off of the platform.  Luckily, when you die, you can rewind time in a very Braid-like manner to re-attempt the puzzle. The game is built on the ability to rotate the screen, changing the gravity for the protagonist and allowing him to access otherwise unreachable destinations. In each puzzle, you must get a key and go through a door. This simple goal becomes complicated when the Escher-inspired puzzles begin rotating.  As you explore more puzzles, other features are introduced: a white plane and a black plane, the ability to change or align these planes’ gravity, and a portal that flips the 2D puzzle entirely.
I find the black-and-white art beautiful, but it’s distracting or obscuring in some puzzles. The story also takes a note from Braid: minor bits after a few puzzles, fed to you with a vague, heavy hand. I’m not sure where the Faux Newton plot is going, but I don’t care. As long as you don’t take the game as seriously as it wants you take it, it’s enjoyable.

Bought it on GoG, then bought it again because this is just too good.
Pros:
- Combat and controls in general are extremely tight, up there with Ori, Super Meat Boy and AM2R.
- Artstyle is fantastic and never got old even after almost 30 hours of gameplay. Seriously one of the best looking 2D games I've played.
- Every location feels unique and the atmosphere is great. The transitions between areas are smooth and give the world a sense of consistency very few games are able to achieve.
- Never feels unfair (well except for that one time). It gets quite challenging in some parts but I always felt like I had the tools to overcome anything the game threw at me.
- The music is memorable and adds a lot to the atmosphere, it also changes dynamically in some situations like starting combat. Some tracks are absolutely amazing.
- Careful exploration is always rewarded.
- The game is packed with consistently amazing content. +130 enemy variations, +30 cool bosses, a huge, non-linear world (is there even a bigger Metroidvania out there?) and an outstanding amount of secrets to discover.
- The lore is damn good... if you are willing to discover it. You won't have to read a thousand item descriptions here, though.
- All NPCs are memorable.
- The healing system is seriously the best.
Cons (more like nitpicks):
-
-
- There is a lot of bactracking, and until the very end game when I already knew the layout of the map by heart and could easily trace the most effective routes without constantly looking at the map it was somewhat annoying. Mostly a mid-late game issue, there is a lot to do on the first 15 or so hours before you need to start going backwards.
- The fast travel system feels somewhat off. This is something that annoyed me after completing the game when I started to go for 100% completion. During most of the normal game you can just walk everywhere and find stuff to do, but when you are already at 90% and just want to go to specific places it feels like some of the travel points are too far apart.
I read that this is going to be adressed on the next update, so I'll just remove this if it does get better (might solve the bactracking issues too).
Mixed:
- Dying and going back to the closest bench can be really harsh sometimes. Tbh I didn't die enough to care personally, and even if I did I would still fault myself for dying a lot, but I know some people would take issue on this.
TLDR: I could barely find anything negative to say about the game and all the positives completely outshine anything it does wrong. Hollow Knight is the best Metroidvania I have ever played, one of my favorite games of all time and one of the best games in a year packed with amazing releases. 100% recommended.

A comparison to space engineers, as it is similar in many ways:
Pros of this game:
- This game has less physics and graphics to be rendered, therefore it is better for people who have a low-end computer. I get around 500 fps on this game, right in a new world, space engineers only around 50-60
- As the point above, it also goes well for being able to handle many players and big ships on a server without issue.
Pros of Space engineers compared to this game
- SE has more modding support, with many mods that add new decoration and weapons.
- Better physics, with voxel damage. even though this is a big factor in lag.
Both games
- Both have practically infinite worlds, at least ones we'll never need any bigger of.
- Both can be really good for custom ship space battles.

Basically, this is one of the best "retro-modern" games out there (a retro style shooter with modern graphics).  It's an attempt to bring the fun of games like Doom or Duke Nukem 3D into the modern age.  Frankly, I'll always like that style of FPS versus the more modern types with limited weapons and complicated cover systems.
A special not about the best weapon in the game, the katana.  If you're one of these people who goes through a game crowbarring or wrenching everyone to save ammo, you'll love this game's treatment of the katana, probably the best melee weapon I've seen in this type of  FPS, they really put a lot of thought into it.  I'll note, however, there is also a good selection of upgradable firearms and special weapons, and plenty of ammo for them.
Also, the environments are very pretty and colorful, mostly.  This may seem like not a big deal, but I find it helps differentiate this game from a lot of modern FPSs.
I find the main characters (the hero gets a ghostly sidekick) to be very appealing.  He's funny and tough.  The ghostly sidekick is appropriately sarcastic.
Well, for me this was pretty much a must buy, so I highly recommend it.

TL:DR- THIS GAME IS FUN FOR BOTH CASUAL AND COMPETITIVE PLAYERS, 10/10
I purchased this game because I thought it would be fun, but I thought I'd get bored of it quickly.
It is WAY more fun than I ever expected! I have about 20 hours played so far, and it's so amazingly fun and competitive as well.
The one thing to note is, THERE IS ONLY RANKED PLAY.
Yes, thats right. There is NO "normal queue" and then "ranked queue" like you see in many games.
There is a training room where you can train and practice(and private matches if you want to play vs friends)
VS AI (which is non-ranked)
and then ANYTIME you play vs real players, you recieve points for winning, or lose points for losing, which is your "rank."
Although this system may upset people, the ranking system IS NOT designed for "gaining elo." Many people will play a game and want to gain rating, without ever improving. He or she just likes to see their special "number" rise.
Battlerite's rating system is designed for playing vs people of your OWN skill.
If you are a casual player and want to have fun, THIS GAME IS FOR YOU.
If you are an elitist who wants the utmost intense competitive play, THIS GAME IS FOR YOU.
But, if you are a player who has no interest of actually improving, and complains and cries about your rating when it's not a rating of an elitist pro, then this game is NOT for you.
This game does a great job matching you with people around your own skill, and if you are shocked or offended that you are not at the top of the world, then I am sorry.

Metroidvania + Dark Souls + Zelda.
This is a thoroughly enjoyable experience. I haven't finished the game yet (going for 100% completion on my first playthrough), but this is very well done by an indie dev. It has so much depth, yet when you read the credits, you wonder how they achieved so much with so few people working on it. Games like this help establish gaming as an art - belonging with movies and other forms of entertainment as a bona fide way for adults to responsibly enjoy downtime.
The graphics/artwork is engaging, and the music is the perfect backdrop for the constant action.
I have no problem giving this a 10/10 - if you're into Metroidvania games with a high degree of difficulty, pick up this game. The only issue players may face is that there is a fair amount of backtracking the game requires - but it doesn't feel repetitive. Rather, it is refreshing to return to an area that you just couldn't reach before in a part of the map you've cleared to see what items/enemies lie in wait - it drives the desire to complete the game and completely upgrade your character.
I was playing XCOM when I decided to try Hollow Knight - and I love me some XCOM - and this game made me put that one all the way on the backburner.
This review was written during the Steam Summer Sale. Don't delay in picking it up for that - but honestly, this game is worth buying MSRP. If the devs make a sequel, then I'll preorder it Lord willing. It's that good.

It's perhaps the only game I've played that can not only trace a clear lineage from both Super Metroid and Dark Souls, but feels more than worthy of both. But even that doesn't do it justice, because Hollow Knight is a masterpiece all its own; it manages to build upon two of the most tried-and-true formulae in the modern gaming canon and still come out fresh and original.

I normally don`t write reviews as my opinion is generally minority and unfortunately money always wins, but in this case I just have to. I love the final fantasy series and have always found their stories beautiful and captivating (apart from FF8 maybe, which was also partially war based). The game was what it`s supposed to be for me: a game (as in a thing to pass time and have fun as opposed to a second job/challenge you need to fulfill).
I don`t have a million arguments to specify all that this game does well or not, because I just could not play very far into it. The reason being that unfortunately this new type of FF has ruined my most treasured reasons why FF was unique and fun to me:
1) It was turned into yet another war game where I can`t even tell where the enemy is most of the time. Action and reflexes over thinking. We are definitely running out of good games that aren`t just killing crap the exact same way through the whole thing...
2) Excessive camera turning which makes me sick (yes, I get motion sickness from playing games so FF was actually a game I COULD play for more than an hour at a time).
3) It used to have a lighter, more spirited and funny air to it even when holding sad events and now right at the intro it`s just blood and death everywhere like all other shooters out there.
4) Controls are now more individualistic rather than an actual team play (and btw they just don`t respond properly, so fun turns into frustration very quickly). I miss the games where you didn`t have to be a one man unbeatable machine and you could see where each character`s strengths and weaknesses were and apply them properly to succeed.
5) Despite the presence of the eidolons, magic and the futuristic look it no longer feels like "fantasy", as the name would suggest, because it has gotten too close to reality (a thing a lot of games these days seem to be striving for). Sometimes you just need something NOT real to help relax from the daily crap. I miss the days where you could just do crazy, funny, impossible things as in the Lucas Arts age.
Anyway, I know most people would disagree, but this is only my opinion. And through my perspective I would not recommend it.

Square Enix. Oh, Square Enix. Why do I keep giving you my money? I love a lot of your games and I get excited whenever you port your console games to PC because I think I am going to get a great experience, but everytime I pre-order a game you port over I get let down. Whether it's inconsistent framerates, limited or low graphics options, or certain features not functional, us PC users get a lesser experience. I am a big believer of vote with your dollars and I have consistently voted in support of you porting Japanese RPGs to PC, especially Final Fantasy games, but I cannot and will not pre-order your PC games anymore, Square (if I order them anymore). I have bought Final Fantasy XIII, Final Fantasy XIII-2 and now this game, even though I already owned the console versions of these games. Out of all the aforementioned games, this is the worst port I have seen not only from Square Enix, but from a developer period (to include Dark Souls Prepare to Die Edition). Where do I start? Poor performance for Nvidia hardware, internal resolution stuck at 720p even when I select 1080p in the launcher, no proper SLI support and worse performance or graphics bugs when forcing SLI, locked FPS, only 720p or 1080p resolution options, and poor overall in-game appearance (game looks worse than PS4 version). This is just the beginning of the laundry-list of issues I have had with this game just in the first hour of playing. It wouldn't be so bad if I had faith that Square Enix would resolve these issues, but with the way they treated the Final Fantasy XIII port I doubt it. The upside? They kept true to their promise and fixed the in-game camera so now I don't feel like I am getting motion sickness in battle from the camera action, but the rest of the game just looks and plays so poorly it doesn't really matter because it's nigh unplayable. As far as the game itself, it's an enjoyable action RPG that has a pretty legit and mature story. Story and game time is progressed through completion of game quests. I would say gameplay wise, the biggest detractor is that there are 14 (yes, 14) playable characters that you have to figure out how to manage resources and upgrades. You basically have to figure out strategies and which players to use, which will lead to which characters you level up. Honestly, though, with how poorly this version plays, if you have a choice between playing this on console and PC, I would have to say the PS4 version is honestly the superior version. Square you have fooled me at least twice, but I doubt you will fool me again and I will definitely not pre-order your PC ports anymore. I guess I will just have to purchase the games I want to play on PS4, but I won't be throwing my money at you anymore. The worst part? I pre-ordered the game through Green Man Gaming at a great price. So while I saved money on the purchase, it wasn't purchased through Steam directly and now I can't get a Steam refund.

I would describe this game as Dark Souls meets Metroidvania.
It is rich with the tight fun 2d combat, constantly improving character and emphasis on revisiting old areas like most Metroidvanias. However, the way the story is told and world is built is truly remarkable and very Souls-like. You'll meet fellow adventurers like yourself on your travels, appreciating the brief moment of companionship as you meet them in different places in the world, on quests of their own. When you die you drop your money at your death spot and have to retrieve it, the story itself mimics Dark Souls in a lot of ways (without spoiling too much,
etc.). Even some of the landscapes reminded me of Anor Londo and the like.
In terms of difficulty, It can definitely be challenging in places, but I personally thought it was overall a perfect balance of difficulty. The length is also EXTREMELY reasonable, taking me 26 hours to 100% it. Not to mention the hand-drawn artstyle is insanely good and every single environment looks absolutely stunning.
Overall if you're a fan of either genres, you will enjoy this game greatly. If you're lucky enough to be a fan of both, this game is perfect for you.

For those coming from the multiple years of playing Stronghold: Crusader and all its variations, (HD, Extreme) This game fails on what could've been something so much more. Overall, FireFly really just took the game into a different, unsuccessful direction that cripples the game from the start. The failures of this game pile up the longer you play, and you won’t be playing for long.
Most of the positive reviews are from players who have never touched Stronghold:Crusader before, and are probably bots being spammed to promote sales. Almost all of the negative reviews you see for this game are from veteran players like myself whose hopes of seeing an even DECENT modern Stronghold game fade away.
-What turns me off as a 10+ year Stronghold:Crusader player-
-Stronghold:Crusader 2 just doesn’t seem like a finished game. Animations aren’t complete, this is most noticeable when watching the Duc Volpe (The Wolf’s) message animations, which are well done and smooth, to the paper mache, 5 frame animation for Saladin.
-The game is dumbed down. There are no more moats, engineers, fear factor, decorative items, or laddermen.
-The UI is ugly, and appears rushed. This looks like anyone without decent drawing skills could have done the art for the menu screens/ The main menu screen in Stronghold: Crusader looks better than the main menu in 2. The lobby UI for multiplayer doesn’t even show other players in the lobby. While some details are cool, the overall vibe is Aladdin than a brutal strategy game set in crusader times.
-The map sizes are so small, they counter this by slowing everyones economies down, to the point where its simply not fun because you have to wait forever to get resources.
-Stronghold:Crusader had epic campaigns, and Stronghold: Crusader 2 can only offer 3-5 mission mini stories that don’t feel as grand or as impactful as the original.
-The gameplay is slow. This is due to the horrendous changes they made to building costs. 20 Wood for an apple farm is reasonable, but 60 wood for a dairy farm? 100 wood for a mill? How are people supposed to develop economies without falling asleep? You are guaranteed to spend all of your starting gold on wood, or die due to you being crippled by having to wait 10 minutes to collect 100 wood.
-Castle building was thrown out the window. This is primarily due to the small map size and new clunky and slow resource mechanics. There are two wall options, thin and regular, and considering how weak walls are, if you want an enclosed keep, you have to spend at least 500-1000 stone, which by the way, will take you half an hour to accrue.
-While the graphics are nice, you would be better off playing Age of Empires 3.
Those are the primary concerns with the game. Bad gameplay, slow economy development, bad and ugly UI, and an unfinished feel, this game robs hopes of FireFly every making something as epic, or downright fun to play as Stronghold, and Stronghold:Crusader. This game is a horrendous attempt as a successor, and many veteran players would gladly go back to playing the original than wasting their time with this unfinished mess.
The anger and frustration in this review comes from the countless failed attempts FireFly has made. Stronghold 2. Stronghold 3, and now Stronghold:Crusader 2 are miserable failures, and it’s hard to comprehend why nothing has changed regarding the production of these sequels to the God-Games, Stronghold and Stronghold:Crusader. $50 is theft for an unfinished game that would never sell if it didn’t have the Stronghold name. I wouldn’t even play this game if it was free.
0/10. For $50, they are stealing money from hopeful fans. There is nothing fun or exciting about this game. You are better of buying Stronghold:Crusader HD.

Bought it on GoG, then bought it again because this is just too good.
Pros:
- Combat and controls in general are extremely tight, up there with Ori, Super Meat Boy and AM2R.
- Artstyle is fantastic and never got old even after almost 30 hours of gameplay. Seriously one of the best looking 2D games I've played.
- Every location feels unique and the atmosphere is great. The transitions between areas are smooth and give the world a sense of consistency very few games are able to achieve.
- Never feels unfair (well except for that one time). It gets quite challenging in some parts but I always felt like I had the tools to overcome anything the game threw at me.
- The music is memorable and adds a lot to the atmosphere, it also changes dynamically in some situations like starting combat. Some tracks are absolutely amazing.
- Careful exploration is always rewarded.
- The game is packed with consistently amazing content. +130 enemy variations, +30 cool bosses, a huge, non-linear world (is there even a bigger Metroidvania out there?) and an outstanding amount of secrets to discover.
- The lore is damn good... if you are willing to discover it. You won't have to read a thousand item descriptions here, though.
- All NPCs are memorable.
- The healing system is seriously the best.
Cons (more like nitpicks):
-
-
- There is a lot of bactracking, and until the very end game when I already knew the layout of the map by heart and could easily trace the most effective routes without constantly looking at the map it was somewhat annoying. Mostly a mid-late game issue, there is a lot to do on the first 15 or so hours before you need to start going backwards.
- The fast travel system feels somewhat off. This is something that annoyed me after completing the game when I started to go for 100% completion. During most of the normal game you can just walk everywhere and find stuff to do, but when you are already at 90% and just want to go to specific places it feels like some of the travel points are too far apart.
I read that this is going to be adressed on the next update, so I'll just remove this if it does get better (might solve the bactracking issues too).
Mixed:
- Dying and going back to the closest bench can be really harsh sometimes. Tbh I didn't die enough to care personally, and even if I did I would still fault myself for dying a lot, but I know some people would take issue on this.
TLDR: I could barely find anything negative to say about the game and all the positives completely outshine anything it does wrong. Hollow Knight is the best Metroidvania I have ever played, one of my favorite games of all time and one of the best games in a year packed with amazing releases. 100% recommended.

Stronghold Crusaders 2 continues the popular castle building franchise with improved graphics, several new units, and a wall physics engine.  Unfortunately, that's the end of the list of improvements.  The game doesn't bring many new game mechanics to the table and, in fact, removes many building types and gameplay elements included in previous Stronghold titles.
The new units and thier special abilities add a bit more variety to combat and the crumbling walls look very satisfying.  Other than that, this is a dumbed-down Stronghold title that needs the upcoming updates promised by the developers before I would say it is worth the $50 price tag.  That being said, I am enjoying the game and it lives up to the quality (if not the size and complexity) of previous titles in the series.
As a fan of the Stronghold series I highly reccomend this game, but would suggest you hold off and enjoy Stronghold 2 or the original Crusaders while you wait for some improvements and/or a price drop.

I really enjoyed this game. It was just a fresh breath on the FPS market in my opinion and overall a blast to play in general. However, there are a few things that got on my bad side.
- Berserkers. I hate them. I don't like them. They weren't hard, just really annoying.
- The Boss fights seemed a little too easy, I felt like the waves of enemies you have to fight are a bit harder than the actual bosses themselves, but I might chalk that up on the difficulty.
- There's a weird glitch with the dash that sometimes if you did it on stairs or down a small slope, you'll die instantly.
- Parts of the game will feel extremely repetitive and a bit boring to go through, which made it hard for me to finish this in a few sittings becuase I would get bored.
- Turret sections. Not a lot of them, but they are prevalent.
- The shield enemies. Annoying, but not hard either.
That's really it that got me negatively. I will tell anyone that if you are an average gamer or better, I definitely recommend you play higher than Normal because I only died 10 times through the entire game and only 3 of them were actual deaths and the other ones are chalked up to accidental deaths with the dashing glitch. Other than that, it was a blast.
- Looked great
- Sounded great
- Great story and gameplay mechanics
- Loved the characters (especially Hoji)
- Really loved the mini easter eggs like the arcade machines in the game, I thought those were neat.
- All the weapons and powerups were really innovative and great and I enjoyed all of them.
All in all, Shadow Warrior has some minor things about it that irked me, but nothing that took me away from a great experience and a fantastic game. It sells for $40 as of today (6/5/15) and I would honestly say wait for maybe a small discount or so because I personally just think its a bit much since you can buy the PS4 version for about 20 bucks at the stores. But, anyway you can get this game, highly recommend you do so.

Shadow Warrior caught me completely off guard.
I hadn't heard much about it when it was released in 2013, and I hadn't really played the original from the 90s either, so when I acquired it as part of Humble Indie Bundle 14, it went onto my
list.
I eventually did get around to playing it - within the first five minutes, I was completely hooked, and this quickly became one of my favorite shooters.
Shadow Warrior is a story-oriented, first-person shooter in which you play Lo Wang, a corporate enforcer. The game begins as Wang is tasked with completing a straightforward purchase of an antique katana. Wang immediately sets the tone for the game by making cracks about the seller's henchmen and the cliché nature of the cherry-blossoms-plus-koi-ponds setting.
The combat system for the game is crisp and refreshing. Not only does Wang acquire a standard complement of FPS weapons as he progresses, he's also armed with shurikens and a katana. Via a pair of skill trees, one based on "karma" (
) and the other based on "Ki crystals" that the player can occasionally locate, Wang can learn special combinations (
) that allow him to supercharge his katana attacks, immobilize nearby enemies, or even partially heal himself. These combos add a dimension of depth and challenge to combat that helps to keep it interesting and intense throughout the game.
The level design is elegant and well-thought-out, directing the player without making her feel boxed-in and giving her the freedom to explore while still making it clear how to progress. The player is often forced to double back or cross her earlier path, but there's never that feeling of having to trudge back and forth across an area, and there are often new surprises waiting in areas that have been previously visited.
The story is engaging but not heavy-handed. It's there to provide context for events and motivation to the player and the character, but the focus is definitely on the action - control isn't ripped away from the player every thirty seconds to show a cutscene or an on-rails sequence. The game is filled with comedic moments, and there's a steady stream of genuinely witty (
) commentary from Wang that kept a grin on my face as I blasted and slashed.
The Linux port was very well done. I played from beginning to end on Ubuntu 15.04, and the game runs flawlessly on my aging Macbook Pro. It took me about 19 hours to complete the game on normal difficulty, with a moderate amount of exploration and a few retried battles.
If you like old-school action shooters, Shadow Warrior should be at the top of your to-play list!

Shadow Warrior:
+ The game features lots of guns, including uzi's, revolvers, crossbows, shotguns, flamethrowers and more. There's plenty of weapon upgrades which add everything from dual wielding to explosive rounds for your firearms. In addition, two skill trees are available which focus on improving your healing abilities, movement, luck, katana mastery and defensive and offensive Chi powers, such as knockdown stuns and damage reduction blocking. There's a great amount of variation here for character building.
+ Very engaging combat for the most part, keeping you on your toes. There's several different types of enemies - standard demons, warlords, shamans, berserkers, flying demons plus others.
+ Hidden secrets to find for those who enjoy a bit of exploration, along with the often amusing fortune cookies.
+ Graphics are absolutely fine considering the obvious low budget for the game. It's clear Shadow Warrior is not a triple A game so stunning visuals shouldn't be expected. It's decent and that's all it needs to be.
+ The game takes a good 15-20 hours to finish, which is not too bad for an FPS, hack 'n' slash style title.
- Weak story, limited dialogue, somewhat hard to follow. Very linear for the most part.
- Some non-sensical environmental mechanics, cars explodes by throwing shurikens at them, or a few bullets. Fighting is very arcade-like and lacks realism.
- Really tedious and boring boss encounters, which can take 20-30 minutes per battle (hard difficulty). Often they're not that hard, just time consuming and annoying.
Overall Score: 7/10
Shadow Warrior is a nice, action packed game to pass the time. It has an acceptable amount of content for a cheap price (especially on sale) so it's well worth it.

MINOR SPOILERS – you’ve been warned.
TL;DR, There was a lot I liked about the Stanley Parable, but I keep looking at that $4 I spent on it and I can’t help but think it would’ve been better spent on other games.
Full Review:
I purchased The Stanley Parable after watching Let’s Plays of The Beginner’s Guide and Dr. Langeskov, The Tiger and The Terribly Cursed Emerald: A Whirlwind Heist; they both look enjoyable and I felt I should give their first effort a try. The game was $3.80 during a Steam Sale and I felt that thanks to the overwhelmingly positive reviews that I should give it a try.
“Quirky” is the best way I can describe the game, and it does a good of job of straddling the line between being clever and smarmy. I particularly enjoyed the “museum” sequence where you could explore the genesis of the game and abandoned pieces that never made it to the finished version.
Truth be told, I regret it, even for $4. While I appreciate alternate forms of gameplay and narrative, there simply isn’t enough here to be worth the money, certainly not at full price.
Initially you’re led to be believe that your job as Stanley is to find out what’s happened to your coworkers. But soon it becomes clear that you’re not really playing a game at all, and instead you’re exploring the philosophical ramifications of what it means to have “choice” and freewill. Distilling the plot down to a few sentences is reductive and doesn’t get to the heart of the enjoyment of the game; where the game really shines is the responses of the narrator to the choices you make, and the unexpected consequences that occur.
The purpose of The Stanley Parable is to experience all of the endings, of which there are roughly a dozen. The decisions you make will lead to different endings, some surprising, some lackluster. The endings branch off from certain decisions you make (i.e., go in one door, or the other), and this in and of itself isn’t a bad thing. However, if you play through one ending and want to see what happens if you go the other way, it necessitates starting from the beginning and retracting your steps until you find yourself at the same decision making point again. If there was a time travel mechanic that allowed you to “hop” back to these points it would make the game less tedious, but then it would also shorten the game quite a bit.
And that’s the crux of the problem. There is so much retracing of steps that it just feels like the game length has been padded. Had I not had to retrace so many times I’m sure I could’ve experienced all the endings in less than 20minutes. Is that enough game time for you to feel like you’ve gotten $4 worth of value out of it? Perhaps for you, but it’s not for me.
If you’re looking for a game with good writing, some humour, and an interesting mechanic, I would recommend “To the Moon”. The story takes you on an emotional journey that is well worth your time, even if the game can be finished in a few hours. It’s one of the few games that’s actually made me cry, and I still think about it even months after I’ve last played it – it was worth every penny.

Do I recommend this game with friends? Absolutely!
Do I recommend this game to play solo? Yes but only to certain people.
Is the community great? Oh yeah! Plenty of maps to download and online play is great!
Easy to run? Oh yeah! My computer isn't top of the line but I can still run this game at max graphics.
Gameplay: So Dungeon Defenders is a tower defense game that has a lot going on for it! It has a straightforward story that you have to defend these crystals or the bad guys win. What's awesome is that you don't have to rely on your towers to get the job done! You can jump into the chaos (which it does get very chaotic) and beat your foes head on. There's also bosses to take on too which adds more chaos because the enemies will keep coming till the boss is dead and some aren't so easy to catch up to but to help out you can switch out heroes and set up defenses the way you want and then switch to a combative hero to get the job done.
Characters: there's 4 characters to start off with all of which have additional costumes to unlock and have their own play styles. You can level them to be tower, combative, or hybrid characters. All have 2 abilities which adds on to what they can do. Through dlc you can have many more costumes and better yet MORE CHARACTERS! All of which play different which is awesome! No copy paste characters.
Maps: There's a fair amount of maps in the standard campaign which you can raise/lower the difficulty to your liking. Some are way harder than others but all easy to figure out where you want to set up defenses. Not all maps have bosses but those that do are a ton of fun adding a special enemy to the mix. There's pvp, pve, challenge, dlc, and of course community maps which some of those are crazy!(talking about the helms deep one 5/5) The dlc maps are fun but some are insane tough.
Graphics: Not crazy graphics but the cartoony and humor look is more than welcome! Cracks me up running around as the squire with heart shape boxers on hacking everything up.
Enemies: This is a bit unfortunate not a lot of variety in enemies but enough to greet you with strong challenges which is fair.  Mostly going to be facing enemies that are the same just different colors and harder to beat. From goblins to ogres to wyverns and dark elves you will have to figure out how to deal with them. What's nice here though is that not all enemies with drone their way to the crystals trying to break it. Some will hunt you down!!! Especially bosses which are fun and challenging in their own ways.
DLC: There's a lot of downloadable content for this game. However buying the dlc is where I'd say yes or no to if you want to play solo or with friends. The dlc after the game is difficult ESPECIALLY the eternial crystal quests. It seriously jumps drastically to the point just playing solo on mid difficulty you get overwhelmed so easily regardless how strong you are. Character dlc solo is fine but moving forward storyline I'd say next to impossible.
Summary review: Fantastic tower defense game that's even better with friends and those on my friends list who reads this... buy it!!! I'll gladly play with you. 8/10

Despite the fact that a character can be controlled, it's not a platformer. There is no jump button and the character moves like a snail.
So it's all about the puzzles, primarily based on turning the screen to change the center of gravity. And... it is quite boring and the mechanics become so intricate it becomes a chore to solve the level. It feels so tedious that I quit half-way, when I noticed that the next chapters were the same as before, but mirrored.
The mechanics to spice things up are a big stone ball that kills the player but is needed to press buttons, a vortex to suck up anything that gets close, portals that make the player change color to interact with different parts of the level in a specific order of events, and veils to modify the... well it has never been very clear to me what they do.
There isn't even a key to reset the current level, the player has to do it from the menu.
Lastly, the story isn't compelling.
There are clear inspirations from Braid, but it is not an experience near as enjoyable or interesting.
So I don't end on a completely negative review, I liked the art and some of the musics.

Map Editor & Co-op Play
We've received a number of queries about how and where to find the Map Editor and the new Co-op Mode, so here are instructions for everyone who is still searching:
Map Editor
1. Open your Steam client
2. Click on LIBRARY at the top
3. Select TOOLS
4. Double-click 'Stronghold Crusader 2 Map Editor' to install the editor
5. After installation, double click again to launch the editor
Co-op Mode
1. Launch Crusader 2
2. Select 'Multiplayer'
3. Select the 'Host Game' tab and create a game
4. When other players join, drag and drop players together to form a team
5. Drag and drop human teammates together to share an estate in co-op mode
Please Note: Co-op teams are limited to pairs of two players, so while you can play with a mix of up to eight human and AI opponents in one game only two players can be 'linked'. This limit does not apply to traditional teams, where each player has his or her own castle.

After almost two years of floaty physics, stuttering, bad communication, outrageous prices and lack of racing, R3E is finally turning around.
Regular sales bring the content to more sensible prices, the force feedback has been tightened up to give better information about the car, the physics are more precise and very detailed and the setup makes a big difference. Most of the racing right now is in the DTM series, but the challenges are fun and allow you to try several cars and tracks without paying a dime.
Visually, it's a bit bright and bold, but the environments look good and clear. Visibility and details are high, and the shadows passing on the dashboard look really nice. The performance on High settings with 8x AA with a 750ti is 60 fps when there's only one car, so I think the optimization is pretty good as well.
The sounds are probably the best you'll hear in a racing game, whether it's the samples themselves or just the richness of the chassis squeaking, the transmission, the tires, etc. Everything is there and sounds great. No other game comes close.
The interface is still complex and confusing, and some options are only available from the main menu. The FFB is very adjustable, but the settings are not explained much, so it takes a lot of fiddling to get everything right. For me, that means G25 and TH8RS. The modern cars don't default to auto-clutch, which is lame.
Because the game looks and sound so good, and now that the FFB is finally letting the new and tighter physics shine through,  Raceroom is becoming a killer racing game. I never thought it could be possible, but out of this could arise a GTR3 people have hoped for. In the meantime, doing time trials, challenges and racing in DTM is a lot of fun.
To newcomers: skip the free content and go straight for the competitions, this is where the higher quality content is. It cycles through cars and tracks regularly, so you can sample stuff until you find what you like. The freebies are still the old wobbly garbage from 2012, it seems. I think everything will be updated over time.

Very rough around the edges, some of the worst illustrations I've ever seen in a game, and poor UI graphic design can't stop the main event being massive fun. Stronghold is back!
Once you get past the horrible front-end, you'll find an addictive and highly engaging RTS in the style of AOE3, with a highly developed castle building element. The economy echos the Anno games too, but in a much more streamlined form.
In-game graphics are good, with nice character designs, and some good animations. Castles look well planted, and the environment is fairly interesting.
Voice acting is as excellent as ever, but it sounds like clips from the older games have been re-used, including much of the fantastic music (possible the best I've heard in any game).
The game has currently dropped a lot of the whimsical characterisation of the peasants, and certain popular features, such as the castle enhancements and punishments, have been left out, but crucially, Crusader 2 plays better than the original Stronghold. City management is easy and rewarding, castle designing is incredibly simple and flexible, and the siege element is the best in any RTS yet.
There's much more to come, according to the developers, and i believe them. Stronghold Crusader 2 is the game that should have been made years ago. It captures the Stronghold atmosphere perfectly and actually improves on the original's core game play.

The Bridge is made from M. C. Escher's nightmares.  Normally that would be a bad thing, but in this case, it's very good.  The Bridge is a puzzle game with a simple premise: Reach the exit door.  Your only tool is control over the direction of gravity though you can only change its direction slowly.  You will need to avoid deadly obstacles and obtain keys to unlock doors in order to escape.
While a few of the levels require frustrating levels of repetition and precision in order to reach your goal, most of them are very enjoyable.  In total there are 24 puzzles and 24 mirror versions which add some elements of difficulty in addition to being reversed.  Strangely I found the mirror versions of some of the hardest levels easier than their normal counterparts.  Even if you aren't into puzzle games, the Escher-like artwork is worth marveling at.
One thing I found missing in the game is music.  It seems like a greatly missed opportunity for a unique and strange soundtrack to match the level design.  There is some music in the game but it plays rarely and is very quiet.
The other major weakness I found is probably not something many players will encounter:  The collectibles.  Some are absurdly difficult to find, and one even requires you doing something that the game constantly tells you doesn't work for the entire game.  When you do locate them all, the reward is extremely anticlimactic.  It's annoying but like I said, the majority of players probably won't bother with the collectibles and those that do will most likely use guides so they don't go insane trying to find them all.
As a fan of puzzle games, I greatly enjoyed The Bridge.  You will too!

Shadow Warrior caught me completely off guard.
I hadn't heard much about it when it was released in 2013, and I hadn't really played the original from the 90s either, so when I acquired it as part of Humble Indie Bundle 14, it went onto my
list.
I eventually did get around to playing it - within the first five minutes, I was completely hooked, and this quickly became one of my favorite shooters.
Shadow Warrior is a story-oriented, first-person shooter in which you play Lo Wang, a corporate enforcer. The game begins as Wang is tasked with completing a straightforward purchase of an antique katana. Wang immediately sets the tone for the game by making cracks about the seller's henchmen and the cliché nature of the cherry-blossoms-plus-koi-ponds setting.
The combat system for the game is crisp and refreshing. Not only does Wang acquire a standard complement of FPS weapons as he progresses, he's also armed with shurikens and a katana. Via a pair of skill trees, one based on "karma" (
) and the other based on "Ki crystals" that the player can occasionally locate, Wang can learn special combinations (
) that allow him to supercharge his katana attacks, immobilize nearby enemies, or even partially heal himself. These combos add a dimension of depth and challenge to combat that helps to keep it interesting and intense throughout the game.
The level design is elegant and well-thought-out, directing the player without making her feel boxed-in and giving her the freedom to explore while still making it clear how to progress. The player is often forced to double back or cross her earlier path, but there's never that feeling of having to trudge back and forth across an area, and there are often new surprises waiting in areas that have been previously visited.
The story is engaging but not heavy-handed. It's there to provide context for events and motivation to the player and the character, but the focus is definitely on the action - control isn't ripped away from the player every thirty seconds to show a cutscene or an on-rails sequence. The game is filled with comedic moments, and there's a steady stream of genuinely witty (
) commentary from Wang that kept a grin on my face as I blasted and slashed.
The Linux port was very well done. I played from beginning to end on Ubuntu 15.04, and the game runs flawlessly on my aging Macbook Pro. It took me about 19 hours to complete the game on normal difficulty, with a moderate amount of exploration and a few retried battles.
If you like old-school action shooters, Shadow Warrior should be at the top of your to-play list!
I nominated this for the "Whoooaaaaaaa, Dude!" Steam Award 2016.

Shadow Warrior:
+ The game features lots of guns, including uzi's, revolvers, crossbows, shotguns, flamethrowers and more. There's plenty of weapon upgrades which add everything from dual wielding to explosive rounds for your firearms. In addition, two skill trees are available which focus on improving your healing abilities, movement, luck, katana mastery and defensive and offensive Chi powers, such as knockdown stuns and damage reduction blocking. There's a great amount of variation here for character building.
+ Very engaging combat for the most part, keeping you on your toes. There's several different types of enemies - standard demons, warlords, shamans, berserkers, flying demons plus others.
+ Hidden secrets to find for those who enjoy a bit of exploration, along with the often amusing fortune cookies.
+ Graphics are absolutely fine considering the obvious low budget for the game. It's clear Shadow Warrior is not a triple A game so stunning visuals shouldn't be expected. It's decent and that's all it needs to be.
+ The game takes a good 15-20 hours to finish, which is not too bad for an FPS, hack 'n' slash style title.
- Weak story, limited dialogue, somewhat hard to follow. Very linear for the most part.
- Some non-sensical environmental mechanics, cars explodes by throwing shurikens at them, or a few bullets. Fighting is very arcade-like and lacks realism.
- Really tedious and boring boss encounters, which can take 20-30 minutes per battle (hard difficulty). Often they're not that hard, just time consuming and annoying.
Overall Score: 7/10

When I first started Hollow Knight I wasn't real big on it. I loved the look and the atmosphere but the aimless nature and lack of direction in the opening hours really turned me off. It harkens back to games like Metroid, Super Metroid, and Symphony of the Night with just how little direction you are given. You're left to explore on your leisure to discover its world and the secrets therin. So much so that being able to see where you are on the map and where save points are located take up space on your limited ability to use power ups.
It wasn't until I was 5 to 6 hours in that the game truly clicked with me. When the difficulty and platforming took a sharp rise in difficulty and it felt more like I was playing Ori and the Blind Forest than your typical Metroidvania game. As of this writing I'm pushing 16 hours played and I don't see the end in sight. Granted some of that time is inflated because my aimless wondering and dying so much but even knowing where to go doesn't take away from the length. This game is a steal for $15 because I can easily see it going on for a minimum of 20 hours for a first playthrough.
If you like Metroidvania games or hardcore platformers you should seriously check this out. Just know that it's not going to hold your hand and the upgrades do not come quick. It's a slow burn that pays off in the end.

I have been playing stronghold titles since 2003, starting with Crusader and playing everything since. This series is the best Castle Sim RTS out there. With Crusader 1 being dear to my heart, and with the last title in the series, Stronghold 3 being a colossal failure, I, like many longtime Stronghold fans, was trepidatious as to how this title would pan out. Upon seeing mostly positive reviews I scooped it up and haven't regretted it since.
I have seen negative reviews complaining about some of the elements of the original being taken out. So what, you want the exact same game again? Sure things were omitted, but things were also added too. The siege equipment is much more varied and detailed, and the castle defenses offers fun alternatives, as just a small example of new material.
WHAT I LIKE:
Economy and Food Balance & ease of interface with this aspect - this element is enough to make it challenging but does not require constant micromanagement while out pillaging and rampaging.
New Troop options - offers additional new units through both the barracks and mercenary post that are worth trying. Slave Driver, anyone? A couple Whirling Dervishes?
New and Entertaining Siege Equipment - ever wanted to watch a rotting camel carcass splatter on your enemies' castle and minions? Now is your chance!
New AI Characters, plus the classics
Skirmish mode!!! Hours of fun. Hours.
Devs plan to add more content as they go
MY CRITICISMS:
AI is better than facing a mouth breathing 10 year old, but could be better still. Its really not bad, and I haven't faced everyone yet, but like the other titles most of the AI have a routine and once you figure it out that opponent is less challenging. But the skirmish maps balance that by creating difficult combinations of circumstances and oppenents. I just finished a skirmish map facing one competent opponent and one incompetent, and they had twice the starting resources as me. It was very challenging at first to get an economy, food production, and defense as they ransacked me and I had to start several times before I found an early approach that worked. But once I did get established, it was just a matter of time until I felt comfortable with the size of the army and siege equipment to finish them off. I realize how difficult it would be to design an AI like this, but some adaptations expressed by the AI late game would make that part more challenging.
Graphics aren't blow-you-away fantastic. I've seen this complaint in other reviews and I won't deny I have more graphically astute games in my collection. But I have always chosen gameplay and an engaging challenge over graphical perfection and for me this title does just fine with the graphics it has. Could they be better? Yes. Do they need to be? No way.
More content, although from posts I have seen it sounds like the devs will be actively adding to the game in the future.
CONCLUSION
For me, the pros have far outweighed the cons and I have no regrets with the money & time I have put into this title. I can't wait for a couple friends to get it so we can get medieval on each other's castles.
Happy Sieging!

There is no way I could recommend this game to anyone. When this game popped up in the store I got excited. Years and years ago I was an avid Stronghold fan. I had the warchest which came with 1, 2, and Crusader. Didnt pick up Legends till years later and liked it, but not nearly as much as the juggernaut that was Stronghold Crusader. After the abysmal dissapointment that was 3, I was ready to give up on the series. Then I saw this...
I was first struck by the asking price. 50 dollars is a lot to ask for a game like this, but if it means what is (supposed to be anyways) a more modern and updated version of Crusader, then the asking price is worth it. Only that is not what I bought. What I bought was another farce.
The reasons it sucks:
1 - Lacking in depth - where did the happy/sad castle adornements go? why cant i build monks at the church? why take out units for that matter? why are there so many weapons shops when we used to be able to dictate what weapons the shops made? no leather armor for that matter?
2 - combat is ridiculous - no engineers guild? what is the deal with the seige towers? anyone else notice how freaking fast all of the troops run? enemies are way too persistent in their attacks as well.. why the hell cant i build a moat anymore? and just how exactly do i even use the horses in my stable?! 3 seige weapons are just slightly bigger versions of the catapult..
3 - maps - maps lack any creativity whatsoever. none of them seemed very fun to me.
4 - characters are no longer fun - I remember the good ol days when the skirmish leaders were entertaining and had distinct personalities. now theres not as many to choose from and they seem like perverted versions of their former selves. troops as well...no more "WE ARE THE MACEMEN" or "HEEEERE COMES BESSIE"
5 - bad AI - I cant tell you how annoying it is when I'm building up my castle and all of the sudden my teammate builds a seige camp in the middle of my town. (For that matter, why do we even need seige camps!? they should never have changed the engineers guild mechanic)
All in all it seems like all the devs tried to do was improve graphics and make the game more fast paced, which is something it DID NOT need. The original Stronghold Crusader rules and moves at a perfect pace. Perfect. Like i said before, you are purchasing a farce, not a game here.

I have hundreds of hours in this game and yet I had to sit here for a few minutes to just decide what I was going to say about StarMade. In short, it is completely overwhelming. I spawned into my server and did the tutorial..... twice. I then realized how poorly made the tutorial is and proceeded to go find youtube videos on how to get started. This helped tremendously and I returned to the game ready to become a space exploring master.
I quickly built my first little ship and flew to a shop to buy some more parts with my starting credits. I had my first mining ship ready to go in a little over an hour and from that point the game has only gotten more awesome. I soon lost my first ship to a wave of rogue pirates and had to start over. I was upset but it taught me the simple truth that space is not a friendly utopia. My next ship was still a mining ship but I equipped weapons, light armor, and some shields to ensure my long worked for investment would not be lost again.
I now have some friends on the server with me and we have all started building capitol ships, cruisers, and stations. The game's building system is the most wonderful thing I have experienced in a "voxel" style game. The ability to mirror on all 3 axes, bulk block place, free rotation camera, copy/paste options, undo/redo buttons, and template saving/loading are just a few of the functions this game offers IN ALPHA. You can even save/upload ship templates from the registry or your computer into the game server for purchase and building! I could not ask for a more appropriately envisioned building system.
If you see the reviews stating the game has a steep learning curve, they would be right. But don't let that dissuade you from grabbing a copy for free while in alpha! Its free, what do you have to lose other than some time? It is definitely worth a look at least.
The controls are a bit clunky but that is because the range of motion and movement directions and ship menus are so plentiful they had to map nearly every key on the keyboard to a button. It takes some getting used to especially the getting around in 0G part.
The game is buggy and occasionally runs out of memory or has a java fatal exception. Its an EARLY ACCESS title and to expect perfection is just not realistic. It isn't even that common of an event honestly.
Even with the few negatives I've mentioned above this game is still unreal. The scope and size is just absurd. I looked at my first galaxy where I spawned in and realize it would take months to explore all of those stars. Then I found several neighboring galaxies and the realization dawned..... YOU ARE SO TINY AND INSIGNIFICANT. You are a speck of dirt in one solar system, in a galactic neighborhood with thousands of other solar systems, in a galactic cluster containing thousands of galaxies, in a universe containing thousands of galactic clusters..... It blew my mind to see the scale on the map. Sure it sounds "big" when its written out in text or as you see the stars from in the game. But opening that galactic map.... it is so overwhelming.
TL;DR
If you want an overwhelming space experience, like building spaceships, want something different from many other games on the market, and are willing to accept and understand what EARLY ACCESS means, then please download the demo and get started. I chose to purchase a 4 pack of this for myself and some friends not long after getting the demo version. It is that good.
I don't do this often, but if you would like, add me and I would be happy to help walk you through some of the basics. I have several private servers up and running on US East Coast including one to provide a slightly safer "new player" friendly environment.

I've been looking forward to this game since before it ever even came out on psp. I really loved the concept and I loved how it looked. At the time.
Unfortunately, the pc port has some significant issues:
It's extremely unoptimized and can barely hold 30fps on medium settings with AO and camera blur disabled entirely. It usually dips into the 15-20fps range. I have 2x GTX 660ti's in sli. A game that is essentially a psp port with slightly reworked textures and models should not run this badly. I could emulate the original with better results.
I'd complain about the 30fps cap but honestly anyone without a ridiculous build couldn't even run it higher than that in the first place, even on minimal settings. It's disgraceful. An action game like this should definitely support 60fps and be better optimized, especially one that looks as bad as this.
Even worse, it leaves all the graphical settings, which because of the aformentioned optimization issues you'll need to constantly tweak to get a solid framerate, in a pre-game launcher, meaning you can't tweak ANY of these settings in-game. This is outright damning.
Also I'm just disappointed in general at how bad it looks and how long it took to come out in the US, much less on current gen consoles and pc. The original was released on PSP originally in 2011. 4 years and the hd remake still looks like it should've been on PSP.
I'm going to give SE a week to at least announce a patch before refunding this game, but I recommend you wait until it's been fixed to pick it up...
