Overall, I like this game. I, to be honest, expected something along the lines of Forza or Grand Torismo standards, but in my eyes, it met a fraction of those standards. I have to admit though, this is a very nice and sharp looking game when it's on it's highest settings (it set mine to the highest setting because my computer is very powerful). I am very fond of how many cars there are in the game and I love how each and every one of them has their own different sound. Although i'm not a car expert, if fact I don't really know much about cars in the first place....but I still wanted to try this game as I have heard it looked amazing and was a very good free to play game. They were right. Although this game has a lot of good stuff about it, I feel it has quite a lot of negative stuff about it. To start off, I noticed how there was a MAJOR lack of music unlike Forza or Grand Torismo or most racing games combined. This really annoys me because I feel that the music can bring a certain video game to life (ex: Saints Row 3, I actually got hooked on it because I started listening to it's soundtrack and just fell in love). I also didn't like how a good 75% of controls are unbinded at default, which I don't know if that's because the developers just wanted to let the player bind them his/herself or because they were just too lazy. Another problem is with every single car. What I noticed is how they all fail to break especially on very hard turns. I always find myself in 5-6th gear and then a very hard turn comes and I slow down, but I slow down enough that i'm still in 3rd-4th gear which doesn't help with the turn (I stop nearly 2 seconds before the actual turn). This is also a problem because I don't know if I properly binded a key; handbrake. I binded it to space (it shows I binded it correctly in the settings, but i'm just not sure) and when I press space while the car is just rolling, nothing happens. If I use it when i'm turning, slight to nothing really happens. In most case senarios I feel it does virtually nothing, when compared to other racing games where the handbrake is vital to the game. Handbrake wasn't even pre-binded when I started the game. Set aside all the negative stuff about the game, I would like to focus on the positive stuff in the game. What I think I enjoy the most about this is how it's actually more of a formula one racing game as you don't see day-to-day cars in the game like Forza. I personally love the formula one cars because they always give me a sence of how it would really feel if I was in one. With a computer so heavily powered and with a game that looks so amazing as this one does, they make up well to fulfill what I like most about formula one cars. I also like how there are LOTS of cars and tracks to choose from (there aren't many default and free tracks and cars, but there are a TON of paid tracks and cars). Although I don't have a lot of time under my belt playing the game, I can see it will turn out to be a very well made game. 7.9/10

After getting all three endings, I can say wholeheartedly that Hollow Knight is one of the best games I've ever played. Not flawless, mind you, but it has an immense level of polish and fun that I haven't seen since Dark Souls 1. On another note, while I think this game is awesome, if you didn't like Dark Souls, chances are you won't like this, sadly.
PROS:
- Fun, solid Metroidvania gameplay all around.
- HUGE world that offers 25+ hours of gameplay that almost never gets stale or repetitive.
- The art is some of the best, if not THE best 2D art I've ever seen in a video game.
- Music is great and fits the game perfectly.
- Tons of unique enemies and bosses that are fun to fight (for the most part).
- Progression is very satisfying, and every item feels useful in their own unique way, including most charms.
- Story is great, even though it's basically the Dark Souls story of "people are sad and everything's about to die and/or is dead"
CONS:
- The game has the Dark Souls III syndrome of "anime fights," that is, putting in way too many boss fights that sacrifice fun for trial and error for the sake of looking cool. Granted, the majority of the bosses aren't anime fights and even some of the anime fights are fun, but still though.
- The art, while great, tends to stick to one palette per area.
- Some attacks have no right to do the same amount of damage as other attacks, this is especially frustrating regarding contact damage and some of the dream bosses (because obviously bumping in to a small bug deals the exact same amount of damage as a giant knight swinging a sword three times the size of your body at you)
- DEEPNEST. Screw this area.
- A select few enemies are a complete pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥(cough cough Soul Warriors)
- The final boss is pretty easy,
All in all, Hollow Knight is absolutely worth your time and money if you're a fan of Dark Souls. Hell, even if you're not, you might end up liking it anyway. It has the quality and polish of a triple A game for only 15 dollars! In conclusion, I give this game a 9/10.

It turns out, it's merely a freemium game, with full-on microtransactions, and you can't do anything in the game besides doing practice on one track with one car without paying money. It's essentially the Real Racing 3 of computers, except Real Racing 3 allows you to progress through the game without microtransactions and offers much more without paying a cent.
Let's talk about the game itself. The physics kinda work, but the car feels slippery, much like a bar of soap, and the graphics are representative of a phone game-no, not even, Real Racing 3 looks much better. Especially the interior view of the car is very messy and poorly textured at best.
Is it a bad game? Not necessarily, I'm guessing the game is merely developing, but I feel that it is not worth playing let alone spending money on at this state. Definitely get Assetto Corsa instead, it looks great even in alpha state and it looks like the developers really care rather than this pay-to-have-fun affair. Or, if you're broke and need a free racing game, I'd recommend Trackmania Nations Forever, which has course creators and frantic online multiplayer, or even the demo of GRID 2, which has online multiplayer.

I have a 2500k @ 4.5 and a 7970, while not new I can handle most games at high quality and high fps. This struggles to stay at 30 with everything at "normal". They tagged a "HD" onto the title when that's crap. 720p or 1080p. Textures are a mess, like they just upscaled an already blurry, bland texture.  I game at a different resolution, 2560x1080, so everything looks even worse stretched across that extra portion of the screen. There are no config files to speak of, so anyone hoping to try their hand at altering files, not going to happen. Its all DLL files. It was just an overall disappointing experience.
I understand the reviews trying to support the game itself, and from what I saw it does look like a good game. But I can't support poor quality ports, and I certainly won't spend my time playing them when there's better things out there. Shame on me for pre-ordering.

I cannot even begin to stress how much I regret purchasing this game. I probably would not have minded it so much if it hadn't made me install something called "Uplay" before I could even begin to play it. I use the word "play" in the loosest possible sense here, because this utterly useless program did nothing but slow my system down. "Uplay" turned out to be an entirely superfluous shell program (think of it in terms of a SECOND Steam launcher, running on top of the first!) whose only purpose seemed to be to launch the program, only to then run it
s-l-o-w-l-y!  For reference, I run two overclocked SLI:d GTX 980:s on an i7 4790K with 16 GB RAM, and the game
hardly managed to scrape by averaging ~50 FPS with all settings maxed! Yep, that sure is slow, all right!
What's more, "Uplay" also slowed down
Steam games while I had it installed, even though these games did not even
Uplay, and the program appeared not to even start while running them! "Shadow of Mordor" ran in a molasses-like ~55 FPS when I had it installed. The second I uninstalled Uplay and rebooted my system, however, the game immediately returned to its original FPS, which is something in the vicinity of 75-80 FPS! This makes me believe Uplay is probably running in the background somehow, intruding on the framerate, even though it appears to terminate when closed normally. Sneaky, and entirely untrustworthy!
"Uplay" also refused to save many of the changes I made. I repeatedly set AC4:s in-game menu language setting to "English", as the Swedish menus (Swedish being my native tongue) were so incredibly poorly written (think machine-translated) so as to make them almost wholly unreadable. Still, the game refused to acknowledge my change to the menu language and merrily returned the menu language to Swedish EACH AND EVERY TIME I started it!
The only way to temporarily disable this linguistic malfunction turned out to be to set the menu language to "English" and then immediately let the game reboot itself. This way, when it does reboot, it will be in English. However, once you start the game again, your native language will again return, complete with horrendous machine-translation! I tried precisely
to avert this, including changing my system language, Steam launcher language and Uplay language settings, but nothing worked! Now imagine doing this, over and over again, for
, rebooting your system numerous times as you go along! I even tried using RegEdit, but nothing helped! AAARRRGGHHH!!
As for the game itself, it did show potential, but utterly blew it by the horrible launcher. I only got as far as Havanna before I noped out of this mess, and even then the game was lagging horribly (see above). The in-game sailing system did show promise, but the fighting system was overwhelmingly stupid since the enemies just repeated the same few moves over and over again, without any variation. I was disappointed in the treasure hunting system, as treasure chests lurked around pretty much every street corner, and in every nook and cranny. Also, there are way more than 4 pages in the Voynich manuscript! I might still have overlooked all these things, however, and just kept playing, if Uplay hadn't turned out to be the horror that it did.
Imagine a parasite that intrudes on your system and which requires you to allow it to suck you dry before undertaking any kind of activity. However, by this point, the parasite has weakened you so much that you can no longer enjoy anything because you are too weak and are no longer able to move as quick as you once did. This is Uplay, an entirely superflous launcher whose only purpose is to intrude in your system and slow you down. You are better off installing the nearest malware instead, as it will probably hurt your system less than this piece of garbage. Never again.
I have removed Uplay from my system. This also required me to remove ACIV, however, I consider this trade-off to be entirely reasonable, since I am now able to play the rest of my games normally again, without any lag. I greatly regret wasting 20 Euros on this game, and strongly urge you - the reader - not to do the same.
Do yourself a favour and buy another game instead. Trust me, you'll thank me for it. As for me, I only hope my system is back to full functionality, and that there aren't still any uninstalled traces of Uplay lurking around!

I have virtually no complaints about this game. The default keyboard controls felt very unintuitive to me, but of course they can easily be changed to suit your personal preferences. The fast travel system is limited, and while I can see how some people would have an issue with this, it's designed that way because there's so much exploration to do in areas you've already been once you acquire new skills. This takes away most of the tedium of backtracking that is all too common with Metroidvanias, and Hollow Knight executes this flawlessly. There is a plethora of enemies and bosses to fight, each providing their own unique challenges without feeling impossible or unfair. The game is also visually impressive and has a great soundtrack that really captures the atmosphere and mood of each area you traverse. If you're a fan of these types of games, you should definitely check this one out. And for the price, it's got an insane amount of content with free upcoming content packs.

I'm going to start by saying that the more I play this game, the more I like it. It's very different from many other games, especially FF games I have played in the past, but it is keeping me engaged and I'm used to the mechanics already.
So on to the technical stuff: This is a game from 2006... from a MOBILE console... from 2006. This was when the game had a preview build put together for E3. It never had the budget or time given to it compared to the other games, so it took them longer to get it to market, and even longer to port it to the PS4, and now to the PC. IF your PC can handle it, the "Higher" and "Highest" AA settings in the game affect a lot more than AA, which can make the game look very crisp, which is a lot better than the PS4 version already... if not, then the "Normal" mode still delivers a great gaming experience.
O.K., now that we have that out of the way, this is a PSP port that was ported to the PS4, while really being more of an [early] PS3 game even in it's 'HD' version.
Yes, the game is forever locked to 30fps, if that is all you want in a game, then just stop here, and don't buy.
Now, if you are still reading, that means you might want to experience a PSP game at about half the price (granted I got mine on sale from another source for about $10 cheaper), that had only a handful of effects and textures upgraded... no, this is not a full "HD" game, and no, it won't support anything above 1080p and 30fps as of the time of this review. Does it matter? That's entirely up to you.
My system is an i7 4820k with 32GB of high-frequency RAM, and 2x 3GB 280x Black Edition cards from XFX. The game on my 1440p monitor is pretty much a PS3 game (yes, PS3, not PS4) with no stutters or graphic problems... except that it only supports 1 graphics card, and the requirements are low enough that you DON'T need my system to play at the same level as I do.
I have not gotten very far in the game, but so far the story is relatively standard FF-fair, in that the voice acting is great, and the music with the cut scenes are fairly 'epic'-feeling.
Gameplay is solid, although simplistic. Keyboard controls work just fine, and while you CAN pan the camera and move around with the mouse, I did not like that as much as just using the standard keyboard control (with no mouse). I did not experiment with a controller, but I never much liked using a controller with PC games anyway.
In short, if you can get past the graphics being a slightly-imporved PSP port from 2006 (most of the graphics are straight from the PSP), and being stuck at 1080p (for now) and 30fps, then you may enjoy this if you are a past Final Fantasy fan and want another fix. If you want the best graphics ever, then you have other game options, and you will probably just abandon this.
For somebody looking for a gem in the rough, which is an action RPG with a Final Fantasy vibe... from 2006... you will probably enjoy this game just as much as I have so far.
The opening cinematic was heart-felt and just about drove me to tears, while the combat and story so far has kept me entertained.
For me, this game was $20, and so far worth every penny. I'm looking forward to putting more time into this game, and if they can increase the resolutions to my native 1440p, it would make the experience that much sweeter... 1080p is still perfectly playable, though.

Enjoyable and short puzzle-platformer where the "gimmick" is the ability to rotate the entire level in order to manipulate the gravity of you and other objects around you. The rotation is similar to And Yet It Moves in that regard, and there's a simple time-rewind mechanic in order to undo your mistakes (although this does not actually factor into any of the actual puzzles for the most part). There's also an "overworld" that consists of your house, the yard around it, and multiple doors to the different, numbered worlds (and individual doors to each of the sub-levels in those worlds). So in those two regards (overworld layout and the simple "undo your mistakes" button), it somewhat reminds me of Braid. The art style is interesting, complete with odd geometry and floating objects, but the lack of color for the main game gets a bit tiring. The puzzles have a good difficulty curve, and getting all the achievements requires some work (and/or guides). It's not very long and feels like And Yet It Moves with touches of Braid, but the mechanics and difficulty are both solid. I'd buy it on sale for a few dollars.

This juvenile pre-remake for Shadow Warrior set in the 80s starts strong and the implementation of sword play works nicely with the special abilities that you gain and use through button combinations (like in a fighting game). Unfortunately the fun level doesn't rise but rather stagnates as you go through waves of the same enemies over and over again. I kept wishing there was some way to do combos like in 'Darkness 2' or 'Bioshock', and also some finishing moves would have been nice. The other thing missing is the stealth element, in the original game you could become invisible and choose when to attack a pack of baddies...hence the title of the game. Here you have to kill everyone in an orderly fashion to open the doors that lead you to the next part of the level (effectively annihilating any replay value). Still the game looks great if not entirely original - sometimes I felt I was playing 'RAGE' or 'CALL of DUTY' with a sword- it's fast and furious speed is noteworthy. In a way it falls shy of greatness, although there are 17 chapters, there are only 14 levels (and 3 bosses) and only 3 different enviromments (Japanese villa/town and forest/cemetery, Shipyard, and mountain lab/castle) clocking around 20h on HARD for a first playthrough. Maybe one day we'll get more Wang with a cool DLC but the fortune cookie says it's doubtful at this point in time.
PS: There's a survival mode with 3 levels but no multiplayer all. Sniff.
PPS: Whatever happened to the black and white twin sisters?

This game is a pleasure to watch and a delight to play.  The puzzles are all fairly solvable for the first half, but for the second half...  well I've been consulting the walkthrough info regularly.  I'd say this is one of my favorite games now.  It combines a unique/compelling visual style with an enjoyable set of puzzles that all involve manipulating gravity by rotating the world.  I really loved the hand-drawn artwork and simple but effective animation.  The visual and audio cues are all very helpful in solving the puzzles.  I don't think the game ever relies entirely on audio, so it's a game that hearing impaired folks will be able to enjoy.  The gameplay is mostly about reasoning out a problem, rather than twitch based controls (although there are a few occasions on which timing and twitch mechanics were employed).  I hope more people realise what a bargain this game is.  I think it has the hand-drawn aesthetic of Braid with the puzzle satisfaction that Portal brings.  Also, you don't die, you just rewind so you can really take your time in solving puzzles, and you never lose your progress.  Great Game!

Like many of this genre, The Bridge has a beautiful art style, going for a hand drawn look. It plays into the designs of impossible structures held by nothing while containing abstract obstacles and items. With the main focus of turning the world I was immediately reminded of fez. I quickly found however that most of the puzzles are pretty one note, at least in early segments. The game shapes the world in a sort of makeshift labyrinth like the wooden ball in a maze puzzles. It's all well and good until you realize that the world isn't hiding secret details you're overlooking or hiding ways to use the mechanics that you didn't notice. That aspect which turned games like Braid and The Swapper much harder by revealing what was right in front of you part by part made them maddening puzzles, which clear inspiration from the former for level selects, and story building tends to feel egregious when it ignores these same aspects in order to layer new mechanics or objects without expanding the base ones. That said, the game is still both beatiful and interesting, making it hard to ignore even with it's setbacks.

I have a love-hate relationship with most platformer titles simply due to timed trials and ridiculous boss battles.
thankfully avoids these pitfalls and offers a genuine puzzle-platformer experience.  The gameplay involves rotating the screen while simultaneously moving the character towards their goal--an unlocked door.  Sound easy?  Well it is...at first.  This is one of the most challenging puzzle games I've ever touched.  Any frustration generated fades away instantly as the solution aligns and warm satisfaction carries the player to the next level.  While
was interesting and fresh, it became unnecessarily complicated in an effort to scale with the player's progression.  On the other hand,
is an exercise in perspective rather than a gauntlet of reflex-based challenges and quite simply a joy to play.
The Good:
- eerie sound design that never becomes excessive
- surreal art style that feels like the offspring of M.C. Escher with Edward Gorey's eyes
- difficult puzzles (when I say puzzles, I mean actual puzzles not reflex challenges) that merely frustrate rather than enrage
- time reversal element similar to
that allows for quick adjustments instead of forcing a complete restart
- rudimentary story that allows the player to draw their own conclusions and never gets in the way
The Bad:
- engine can be sluggish at times (recent patches have improved this somewhat)
- clunky installation (I have yet to uninstall, so this may have improved since launch)
The Ugly:
- honestly, nothing; one of the rare games that shines just enough not to create an unpleasant glare

Battlerite is a fast, fun and easy to play multiplayer game.  It is not a  typical MOBA with creeps camps and lanes.  Its all team fighting all the time.  It also has a surprising amount of depth of gameplay with counters, cancel casting and everything is skill shot.  Every hero essentially has 9 abilities to use.  On top of that each round you pick a battlerite (think HOTS talents) that adds even more depth.
It is well balanced hero wise for a game this early in development which it should be as there are only 15 heroes to play so far. From my persepctive there's only one hero that is sub par and one a bit too strong.  The devs have already done some tweaking to the game balance to I expect this to only get better. Each hero has its own feel and playstyle.  The voice acting is decent.
The best part for me is games are fast.  I'm averaging less than 15 minutes a game and that includes queue times and such.  You can do most daily quests in an hour which is great for people who dont have a ton of time to invest.  The other thing I will say is this game is great fun even if you're not great at mobas (like me).  I'm a low grade player and its still a blast to play.
Cons:
I will say as of this writing (10/10/16) the cosmetics are a bit of a disappointment.  I undestand there is going to be a patch later this month with added outfits etc so this should improve.  How much has to been seen.  Right now there are very few items that excite me and make me want to purchase.
There are a couple minor  bugs like orbs not being visible on occastion but nothing game breaking from my experience.
Overall this is a great game and certainly worth the price tag for entry if you like multiplayer team fighting.

Now that I have actually BEATEN the game, I think I can give a truly complete review:
Slightly different from its predacessors, Type 0 plays more like an Action RPG closer to Kingdom Hearts and the like. You can customize your actions, abilties, spells and equipment. Furthermore, you get all of your team members at the beginning of the game and to play at your leisure/play style (all of which have unique combat styles and tactics they use to fight/support in battle) It takes on a darker setting of a world at war with itself, without leaving out the horrors that come with it. That's your basic premise.
Now lets talk more about the aspects of the game itself. It has both keyboard and controller (360) interface (which I feel handles better than the PSP version). Very minimal resolution settings for windowed mode selecting from 1920x1080 and 1280x720, most of the commands you can't edit either. Normally I wouldn't have a problem with this as they're very natural for the most part... however there's a speed up button bound to the L3 button, which I keep bumping into during intense combat, making it even more awkward to control at times (this experience might be just myself, but if I could edit it, it wouldn't be an issue is all I'm getting at)
While I found the combat to be very enjoyable and varied, I found the enemy variety to be somewhat lacking once you get about 3 chapters into the game. Dodging is a very important mechanic to the point you are generally better off trying to spam rolls over any defensive countermeasure like Protect  or the like. And you WILL die a LOT in this game, not necessarily fail a mission, but HP is for the most part arbitrary as you'll find on Officer difficulty and above, most enemies possess the ability to take you down in just a few attacks (having you tag team in another party member to keep fighting). Fortunately, there are SOME countermeasures to the consistent dying, but are very VERY situational to the point without another human player to execute them, they won't work very often (which was how the PSP version was designed), which brings me to another issue: The AI. You're going to be tearing your hair out a lot on the AI's lack of discretion and general skill/situational awareness, as expected its an AI. But when you lose a potential tagout as a result of their poor decision making, it can be very frustrating on harder missions (of which, I would often just solo one character through and tag out as I went along) The AI understands basic tactics like using cure when you're below a certain HP threshold, but will actually attempt to engage certain "high level" enemies indiscriminently (you will know what I'm talking about once you're up to about chapter 3)
I didn't care for the overworld layout much either, most of the land in the game never actually can be explored until very late game, and even then spawns lvl 99 monsters in the process. There's a FEW caves you can explore but the rest is intended for VERY high level characters which I'll touch base on in a minute, but for the most part its City A, B, C, with very little difference between them, other than equipment. And that brings me to another point, equipment is handled very differently than other Final Fantasies: most of it is very very focussed. For example, instead of a proper armor that provides a variety of defenses, you'll end up with a piece of gear that only protects against a certain damage type, which makes it VERY hard to prepare ahead of time. The so-called "armory" in akademia isn't very helpful either only having the lowest of gears through most of the game (at least until you play on agito) As far as random battles are concerned, they do attempt to aid this with chocobos and teleport stones to escape, but it can be a little annoying, nothing I didn't expect from a JRPG though. Grinding though is actually helped out a bit with a real time background grinding feature in the colliseum, which makes it easier to level up characters you dont use much. However thats not quite enough.
Remember those high level dungeons I mentioned earlier, while with fanatic level of dedication often only ending in recieving a minor trinket can be overcome whenever, are intended for 2nd and 3rd playthroughs of the game. That's right, you are expected to play the game again, just to beat those expert missions and side dungeons. For some this might be a relief that will let them just beat those missions later, but for me, I feel like it doesn't do much for me. Moreover, without giving away spoilers, much of the game's ending/plot is influenced by things only available in the 2nd/3rd playthroughs, and also in a mobile game that hasn't been/probably won't be released in America, called Final Fantasy Agito.
So you'll find the story having quite a few holes as a result of that, the rubicum will only give you so much information on the lore, that it's almost irrelevant to the more key plot points.
I know it sounds like I'm complaining a lot, but what kept me to finish the game was the gameplay. Like I said, while frustrating at times, a creative person actually has more freedom than they think: Example, you can give a character Reraise, summon an Eidolon, then once thats done, come back as if they never sacrificed themselves. And man, controlling the Eidolons is very VERY satisifying, you actually feel like a proper demigod.
I would reccomend trying the game on PSP first if you can, then decide if you like that kind of gameplay, if you can enjoy the game for that, you won't be dissapointed.
Again, a flawed gem, not bad though. Probably won't be bothering with a second playthrough for awhile.

My first Assassins Creed game, so I can't really compare it to any other games in the franchise. As a standalone game, it is excellent.
The game can be quite demanding on hardware, but if your rig is good enough it can be truly stunning.
The gameplay is pretty fluid. The free running can be a little annoying as I often run up walls instead of going through the door I want to get through. The combat is a little bland, i.e. attack attack attack block kill, but satisfying if you pull off a perfect chain of kills.
The open world is where this game really begins to shine. The map is set in the Carribean in the Golden Age of piracy (early 18th century), with multiple large islands with open ocean in between. It isn't a true open world like Skyrim, where if you can see it you can get there, but it doesn't matter as the areas you can get to are so large and diverse you'll have more than enough adventuring to do. The main map is split up into sections. No loading screens, but you must defeat naval forts to make each section safe for you and reveal all the items in the section. Same goes for the smaller sub areas, such as the cities, where you have to reach vantage points to reveal all items within the immediate area.
The islands and cities themselves vary greatly, some being heavily populated, others barren. Some areas are affluent while others are slums. Most are unique and feature stunning landmarks and natural wonders. The cities can have really immersive atmospheres, with just enough NPCs and a great outlay.
The open ocean is where you'll spend most of your time. Here you'll sail to new areas, attack enemy ships , weather fierce storms, defeat hostile forts and dive for sunken treasure. Attacking ships can be addictive and naval combat is what really keeps me playing this game (it's that good), but I imagine it can get a little repetitive after an extended amount of time.
Collectables and unlockable are well done for the most part. Some areas have relatively few collectable items and can be completed in a short amount of time, while larger areas can be a big of a slog to find every last chest and shanty. Shanties have to be chased, so some parkour skill is needed there. Items for you ship are bought with gold until the last upgrade which must be found (random loot from chests mostly). Outfits and weapons can be bought, unlocked through the Edwards Fleet mini-game or community challenges, or simply found as random loot. Some outfits are very similar, but there are enough that stand out to give your Edward a personal feel.
I havn't completed the story as of writing this review, but my experience so far has been mixed. There are quite a few "Tail X" and "Eavestrop on Xs conversation" missions, and the story can feel quite slow if you're doing alot of exploring between missions. Edward is a great, relatable character however and I enjoy spending time playing as him and meeting other pirates along the way. It's just a good thing the campaign isn't the main draw to this game.
In conclusion, Assassins Creed IV Black Flag is an excellent adventure game, possibly one of the best I've played on PC or console. Impressive visuals, a large and diverse map, good gameplay and a robust main character do more than enough to make up for an average storyline. AC4 is definitely worth your time if you enjoy open world adventure games.
~Brysk

There are literally all kinds of ways to make money in this game, for anyone to be "broke" in this game is ridiculous when it's so easy to make money. You can whale and sell the procedes from that, you can (of course) raid other ships for new crew members and items to sell, you can make money from treasure hunting and various other 'business ventures' as well.

For fans of the original, I can't necessarily say this is a faithful reboot, considering how clunky it was even compared to contemporary shooters like Duke Nukem or Doom. However, this is hands down the closest you will get these days to an old school chaotic shooter like the original FPSes.
You will routinely face dozens of enemies on screen at once, and mow them all down in bloody glory with guns, rockets, flamethrower, a variety of katanas and a wonderful crossbow. Each of them is somewhat versatile as well and demons will enrage, making them harder and faster, if you do not kill them quickly. Many of the enemies have various attacks and the game continues to introduce new demons until the very end of the game, at which point it begins to throw all of them at you the same time, like old Doom would on high difficulties.
The voice acting is ridiculous, the asian (mostly Chinese) stereotypes are cliche and borderline offensive, and the control system is downright wonky to master. You may not even realize how to do half your abilities until the end of your first playthrough.
I wouldn't recommend the game for $40 as it doesn't have much content beyond the campaign, but the next time it's on sale, if you are a fan of true FPS, definitely grab this game.

On my daily game browsing, I was looking for anything interesting. I came across this game. This is one of the coolest games I have ever played. Some people say this is a Space Engineers clone...it is not. And I am sure (Idk who or why) someone has called this a Minecraft clone...GOD no. (It's in space, come on now.) I will break this up into different sections, with a TL;DR at the end, as well as a section for those who read the whole thing! Thank you.
ONE MORE THING: The demo unlocks the whole game for free. The developer said it will stay that way until it goes out of early access, and that buying it is mainly just to support development.
Why it is awesome:
1. Customization. You can build any kind of ship you want. A ship for transporting things, a ship for mining, a fighter, a massive battle ship, a mining ship with salvage beams (Those are beams that mine for you. SO you shoot at something, it being an ore, rock, or even parts of another ship or station) or any combination of all. (This is not all, of course)
2. Fighting. The fighting is incredible and fun, and fast paced action. It is like a Star Wars battle. You can have your fleet of 20 ships versus another player's fleet of 20 ships or against Space Pirates, or in single player, you versus a bunch of pirates (Idk yet if you can have computer controlled fighting allies in singleplayer) The complex weapons systems are for a whole other part of the review.
3. The complex weapons systems. There is the basic cannons, lasers, and missiles, and they are fun and damaging. You can make the cannons and any other weapon touch each other to make 1 very damaging weapon, or you can space them out to have many of that weapon firing at once. Here is where it gets complex. You can combine weapons. *SPOILER HERE* So you can combine the cannon and the missile to make a shotgun like weapon on your ship. *SPOILER END* Cool right? And there are over 80 combinations (so I have read). So lots of fun to be had with weapons. (And don't be afraid to stack them up a ton. If you have the weapons available, and the power available, make some crazy weapons systems.)
4. NPCs. This is where Space Engineers is lacking so far, but will have them in the future. There are, like I said, Space Pirates. They have killed me many times. But if you have the power and the numbers, fight them back and steal from them and you shall be granted rich reward...so I assume. There are also NPCs at some shops.
5. Shops. You can go to a shop and buy anything in the game. You need a lot of money for many things, but you can get a lot of money fairly easy with the right knowledge of what is really valuable, like ores and glass. (More fun with shops later in the review)
6 Space Stations. You can do a lot of the same stuff with stations that you can do with ships. I am not sure what it has weapons wise, but I am sure there are good things with that. I know there are turrets. Automated turrets and controllable I think. Very customizable. To make a space station though, you need 1,000,000 credits. Which tbh, isn't that bad. I saw one guy get like 2 million credits from selling a bunch of salvaged (collected) glass. And with a faction you can claim a station as yours and make it invulnerable to damage and stealing. It also makes any docked ships invulnerable too. So griefers aren't a problem with this HAHA!
7. Factions. You can make a faction and build on faction points with players to join it (Idk if npcs can join or not), taking over sectors and systems, defeating enemies, and so on. With a faction you can claim a space station and make it invulnerable to damage and stealing. And you can claim a whole system as your territory. Again, there are 128 x 128 x 128 (I think) sectors in a system, so that is a TON of space as yours. With a faction, you can also make your own shops! You can price items how you want, decide what is on your market, and sell things to other players, and maybe even npcs. (You may not need a faction, you may only need a space station to make a shop. I can't remember) And with a faction you can keep growing your territory until you take over everything MUAHAHAHAHAHHAHA! (Not even kidding though)
8. Build mode/Advanced build mode. Who doesn't love a good build mode for easy ship/station construction? With regular build mode you can do all the basic stuff like placing/deleting blocks, flying, sped up flying, connecting blocks and groups, and all that stuff. With advanced build mode, you can use symmetry (For precise building), copy/pasting/saving pieces of ships or stations as templates, mass building with placing up to 10 blocks in every axis at a time (So you can build a 10 x 10 x 10 cube with one click), rotating blocks, and a few other things. So very fun and easy to use. Makes for easy building of a massive ship.
9. Jump drives/Warp gates. *SPOILER HERE* The jump drives and warp gates are a great way to get around fast, but you need alot of power. With a jump drive, you can "jump" up to 8 sectors away. With warp gates, (I think) you can warp up to 128 sectors away. So very convenient.
10. Asteroids, planets, stars, stations. These are all procedurally generated. Very cool.
Now, for the cons. However, some of these are personal opinions and may not matter to you.
1. *PERSONAL OPINION* This game has blocks, not voxels. Sometimes I prefer voxels instead of blocks because realistic smooth surface terrain is cool, but it is not a big deal, this game is still great.
2. Memory issues. I have noticed a lot of people having memory issues where it gets very laggy and a message pops up in game and says you are running low on memory, and to increase the max and min memory in the launcher, you can edit the memory settings like it says, but some people still get the issue. I have fixed it for the most part, but some people can't. Maybe the devs will fix this or optimize it.
Other than these, that's all I got for the cons. Great right? lol
Now, this section is WHY it is NOT a clone of Space Engineers.
1. It is blocks, not voxels.
2. It has planets, stars (Stars that you can actually go to and burn up and die, not just the background sun), sectors, systems, and galaxies.
3. It ALREADY has NPCs, I know SE will have them, but this game already does.
4. It has customizable weapons and complex combination systems.
5. It has more than just 1 type of metal block. Just saying lol.
6. Build mode/advanced build mode.
7. More content with factions (SO FAR).
*Don't get me wrong, I still love and play Space Engineers, but I wanted to clear this up for people who think this is a clone because it most certainly is not*
*ONE MORE THING BEFORE WE WRAP THIS UP* It is still early access (For those who don't know what that means), it is still being developed, it will change, get worse, get fixed, get better, and maybe even become something different.
*TL;DR*
Now, for the people who didn't feel like reading all of that, here is a basic summary:
It is an incredibly fun game with many unique features, and very few bugs that I have noticed. Not many cons at all, and I suggest this to any person. STILL early access so things will change, get worse, get fixed, get better and maybe even become something different. NOT a clone of Space Engineers. (I covered that in the above section)
*FOR THOSE WHO READ THE WHOLE THING*
Thanks for taking the time to read and I hope you found this helpful. :)

I'm writing my review based upon my experience playing the PSP version of the game and because I hate to see this game have a negative review score due to people complain about "muh graphixs" and "muh bad mouse and keyboard controls"
Final Fantasy Type-0 is a mission based Final Fantasy game originally released only for the PSP in Japan.  Thanks to some fans, there has been a fan-translated ISO of it floating around for a while now. Earlier this year, the game was released in NA for PS4 with updated textures, resolution and improved framerate. Now, none of these are perfect due to it originally being a PSP game (Look at Metal Gear Solid: Peacewalker HD), but it does look better than the PSP. Especially when you stretched a 480p game to 1080p in the ISO. Sadly, some less important areas and non-main characters or main NPCs have low textures still, giving it early PS2 graphic quality, but it's fine for it being a PSP port.
Gameplay wise, it feels a bit clunky at first, but once you get the hang of it it becomes very fast paced and enjoyable.  Plus they finally added the second control stick to be camera moving away from the awkward camera controls on the PSP. The world may feel a bit small or cramped due to the mission based gameplay, but if you ever played MGS Peacewalker, it feels the same way as the missions for that. You bring 3 of the 13 classes to battle with each one representing a Job from Final Fantasy games (though with many liberties taken) each using a unique weapon. You upgrade their stats and what abilities they have in the hub world, the Military Academy.
Story wise the game is top notch. The opening cinematic to the game is pretty dark for a Final Fantasy game, but war isn't pretty. You get a combination of teen angst, Final Fantasy VI-ish story and a bit of XIV's Garleans vibe with this game. And turn on Japanese audio unless you want to hear Christina Vee throughout the whole game.
If you are a Final Fantasy Fan, I'd say this is a must have, especially if you don't want to buy a Bloodborne Machine (PS4) just for this game. If you enjoy PSP games like Peacewalker or Monster Hunter, this is a must have for you as well.  If you are not too big on games in this style, this game isn't going to make you change your mind about them.
Overall Score: 8.5/10
It's a wonderful game, has some very minor kinks, and the graphics are PS2 graphics, but it's wonderful for a PSP port.  I recommend using a controller for this game.

Overview: A good expansion of the Assassin's Creed universe, taking on the role of a semi-neutral character that doesn't care much for the Templar-Assassin conflict (though leans closer toward the Assassins since he's a pirate, and doesn't like to be told what to do).
STORY - above average
Characters are very well developed, and you definitely identify with some of their personalities. Blackbeard, the tough-on-the-outside pirate, who also shows his gentler and wiser side to his close friends, is sorely missed when he dies. Many of the Templar villains are also very likeable, and in fact, portrayed to be very human instead of outright evil.
The story itself was above average, because depending on your personality, you might not relate to Captain Kenway. I had a hard time feeling sympathy for pirates, because they're just consumers rather than creators of value. As the Sage put it, all Kenway was capable of was "Murder and Mayhem."
The meta story in the real world was horrendous. I did not care at all, and wish it could be skipped completely.
GAMEPLAY - good while new
Naval warfare is great fun, for the first dozen battles. Then you upgrade your ship, and it gets pretty old quickly. The naval minigames on the companion mobile app is very fun though.
Combat on land is very repetitive, and it doesn't progress through the game at all. Same enemies, same tactics, same weapon effects, even with upgrades.
Missions are also hit or miss. I enjoy the story missions, but the stealth tailing missions are very frustrating. On the other hand, the assassination missions are much more enjoyable.
VISUALS - good, but not optimized
There's a lot of scenery complexity, especially when it comes to plant life, and rain effects. This can bog down your framerate, without actually adding to the visual experience in a positive way. To be honest, I preferred AC2's visuals to Black Flags. Just too chaotic for a 3rd person wide-FOV game.
SOUND - average
Soundtrack is okay. Nothing memorable. Sea shanties when sailors sing are painful on the ears.
Overall Rating: 7/10.

Stronghold Crusader II is a game developed by Firefly Studios in a long line of the Stronghold series.  First, some background on me.  I was playing games when DOS was still around and when Age of Empires 1 was the new thing on the MSN gaming zone.  My video game history encompases every genre but primarily focuses on Strategy games, FPS games, and the occasional RPG.  Stronghold 1 and Stronghold Crusader were essentially the same game with a different atmosphere and some unit changes.  Both were excellent games and the sucessors to follow did not so well.  Stronghold 2 was mediocre at best, the fantasy mythic Stronghold and Stronghold 3 were bad.
Firefly split from their old publisher and became their own, just as many developers are doing these days because publishers like to add their two cents to game they know nothing about.  Stronghold Crusader II takes what the original did and improves upon it further.  The music and sound and very similar from the first and well done.  Some of the original quotes from the units are still there as you move your catapults and archers.  The villagers no longer speak to you when you click on them, instead it simply tells you what they are doing.
One of the things that made Stronghold so great for me back in the day was destroying the castles and watching the walls crumble.  The massive armies going at it with each other and heads rolling.  The physics in this game are much improved as to be expected.  When catapults slam their boulders into a wall bodies standing near the point of impact are screwed.  See those thirty archers in a tight group?  Well now they are at the bottom in a pile where they belong.  Trebuchets have great range and destructive power and still need to be setup while the catapults have less range and can be shot by archers. Overall the military feels well done, especially that mace men frenzy charge that leaves nothing standing as they spit and scream their way into battle.
While on the topic of military, some things have been reworked.  The laddermen are gone, which wasn't really a surprise, who ever used them anyways?  Moats and tunnelers have also been removed. At the time of this review sieging a castle isn't an easy task.  Strongwalls are not an option but the time it takes for any military unit to chip away at a wall or gatehouse isn't worth that route.  Almost your entire military force would be dead while they were picking away at the walls.  While I would still like the strongwall option, it works well as it stands.  As said before, catapults, trebuchets that fire boulders, cows, camelheads, and pigs, a bigger version of a catapult, rams, firecarts, and troop carriers are all the siege units.
Archers have remained the same but the crossbows no longer use animal hide as armor.  The swordsmen are still slow but the knights can get horses to get them from point A to point B quickly.  There is a new unit called the Sergeant at Arms which gives a bonus to troops within an area of effect, this can boost your other swordsmen, pikes, or whatever else you got nearby.  Of course, the higher military units cost a fortune to field but can essentially soak up arrows while your catapults lay waste to the walls and mace men haul tail into the base to wreck everything.
While building a military you will notice that you run out of gold quick unless you run an efficient economy.  Churches, breweries, and extra rations are all ways to keep your citizens happy to so you can generate more taxes.  The market will let you auto-sell and/or auto-purchase items.  This can be set as high or as low as you want.  Iron, stone, wood, pitch, all the basic resources sell for the least while the armors and weapons sell for the most.  Unlike the previous Crusader game, Inns providing ale do not need to be spammed but rather you adjust how much ale is consumed much in the same way as you would food.  This will increase happiness to get you the desired level but just make sure you have the hops farms and breweries to accomodate the usage level.  Churches act in much the same way in that you only need one but have to provide them with candles.  Once again, here you can adjust how many candles are used for the desired happiness.
So far I have played through the tutorial and the lionheart campaign.  The story isn't that great but the game does a good job at preparing you for harder battles.  Some are so difficult that if you don't complete the level quick enough the army forces become so numerous it is a massive chore to keep them at bay while you invade.  Additionally, I have played many skirmish matches, which is where the game is at for me.  I like setting up from scratch and playing massive 4v4 battles.  The game hosts 8 players, human or computer.  As in the old ones, the rat is the worst player while the wolf and some of the new comers bring a better challenge.  I have only had one crash to the desktop at the time of this review and that was right after intial installation and launching of a skirmish.  I loaded that same map again a second time and it worked fine.
That brings me to the bugs.  Most people were holding off on this game because of the reputation Firefly has.  Since Firefly is now technically a "indie" developer as they separated from their publisher, I would like to take away the fears of  purchasing this game.  Other than a few issues with selecting units or them getting stuck in a gatehouse I haven't had any issues.  Below are my specs just in case you are wondering and want to compare.
i5-2500k OC'd to 4.4 Ghz
16 GB of G Skill Ripjaws RAM
Dual 7970 Radeons
EVGA FTW Motherboard
2 OCZ Vector SSDs in RAID 0
1200 Watt PSU gold from Corsair
H100i CPU Cooler
With that setup I have no issues.  Some people have reported problems while others have not.  I am not sure how well they maintain their computer or what they have going on, as a system is going to be different from the next.  I run a tight ship on mine and have zero problems with running the game.
Final Thoughts:
Stronghold Crusader II is a well designed game that is being constantly updated with both fixes and soon to be new content.  On their forums they have laid out a plan on how they wish to progress with supporting this game.  It appears as though their heart is where it should be and a fleshed out game was designed.  Is it worth 50 dollars is the next question?  I would say no, 30 or 40 dollars maybe but not 50.  There isn't enough new content to justify the price but if you are a big fan of the original then price might not matter much to you.  I waited for 24 hours and looked at what people were saying before I purchased the game.  I hope this review helps you decide for yourself but please watch YouTube videos of the gameplay and try to find the glitches some are talking about and the ones I spoke of.  If any of that puts you off, give it a week or two then come back.

Stronghold Crusader is the successor of Firefly Studio's Stronghold. It is a real time (midevil) strategy game set in the Middle-East Crusades. Stronghold Crusader 2 is the sequel to the critically acclaimed original crusader which sets you back in the middle east versing some familiar foes (Rat, Lion, Shah, etc) and some new comers to the series.
As this game came out recently (September 23rd, 2014) it can obviously be expected that there are some minor bugs that occur (such as small series of lag, misplace of troops, etc)
In comparison to Stronghold 3 this game is far better as it has a better hosting connectivity, less troop lag, and improved physics.
Massive armies, easy to lay castle wall design, and town square layout design makes this game far easier to play. I have heard mixed reviews of this game- but after 6 hours in my first sitting I can say that it brings me back to the days of the Original Crusader. With massive armies, tactical maps, and strategic footholds- I am impressed with my first hands on experience.
I would recommend this game to those who loved the original crusader as it is very much like the original.
Pros:
-Ability to amass huge armies of up to 500 units.
-Ability to heal units using Arabic healers
-Quick place buildings in a easy to use square metrics system
-Smooth wall building and stair integration
-Army formations (Columns, Lines, etc)
-Variety of siege equipment bonuses
-Map variety
-Skirmishes mode
-Build your own multiplayer maps
Cons:
-Small community available
-Easy to defend (turtle) castles
-Some connectivity issues
-Soldiers sometimes bug out when you are replacing features of your castle (i.e. Barracks/Gate into wall)
-No Moats
-No Tunnelers
The guys, who makes these games must be sick in their heads. But nonetheless its still a very entertaining bloodbath of a game.

I know this review is long, but I promise if you read it you will have a very clear understanding of what this game is.
I do not write many reviews, but the folks who developed this masterpiece, Team Cherry, have earned my time and public praise.  I had not played a platformer in many many years, but I was looking to shake things up and this beauty caught my eye.  I could not possibly be happier about taking the leap and giving it a try.  In this review, I will do my best to paint you a portrait of why this game is so excellent, without spoilers or discussing content.  Instead I will focus on the concepts and mechanics that make this a truly incredible game.
Pros:
– Every area of this game was designed with a specific concept, purpose or intention in mind to challenge a player to use their mind and abilities differently than they had before.  It is extremely apparent that there was not a single moment of laziness while the twisting labyrinth of Hollow Knight was being designed, and by extension, offers a world that a player can never fall to laziness and hope to succeed.  Every gap between jumps, every enemy placed, every inch of this land was cared for and taken into serious consideration while being designed and built.  The variability of each level is still staggering to me, ~26 hours in.  I am still uncovering new and unique areas, at a nearly alarming rate.  And with each new area, with each new enemy I am challenged in a way that the previous 25 hours had not done.  If you purchase, I would strongly suggest you pace yourself, this is a marathon of beauty, not a sprint.
(You can skip this paragraph if you’d like to get back to the actual review) – Here is my anecdote on level design:  I conquered the first few areas masterfully.  There were bumps in the road, but equipped with my map, I was able to traverse the danger and make it through.  But then I entered the caves.  Slowly, my confidence turned to fear, and eventually my fear into panic.  I had not found the map of these area early on like usual, no, instead I wandered aimlessly into the darkness.  Surrounded by enemies as unfamiliar as the terrain.  An hour in, the thought finally bubbled up in my mind;  I was going to die.  With the thought festering in my mind, and as so often happens to those who are lost, I panicked, and ran.  Jumping and fighting through the twisting caverns, too quickly.  Suddenly, I had lost all sense of direction. I knew not where I had entered, or how to escape this hell.  Forward I pressed, I think it was forward.  My health dwindling, my spirit fading into the endless darkness of this place, giving up.  And just then, as the last of my hope left me, a familiar blue glow shone above me, the light of salvation itself.  I climbed, out of the dark, and into familiarity.  I clawed my way into that beautiful blue light and found my way home.  After a time, I had regained my health and my wits, and as I entered that all-consuming darkness again, I found myself reinvigorated.  With new found confidence I managed to keep my wits about me, and conquered those hellish caverns.
– To me, this is the crown jewel of Hollow Knight.  First off, it’s important to know this game’s combat is centralized around the idea of the protagonist gathering “Soul” each time he strikes an enemy.  This soul can be expended to cast spells, but is much more frequently used to heal himself.  The protagonist only has 5 health, and each hit, whether delivered by the strongest badass or the littlest grub, does 1 damage.  So every combat is significant.  This mechanic is brilliant, as it forces you to continue fighting in order to collect soul, but you can never combat enemies lazily, because if you do, they will likely damage you more than the soul you collected can heal.
Alright, now to the creatures that populate Hollow Knight.  First, I’ll discuss the non-boss battles, the enemies you face throughout an area.  This game has a huge cast of enemy types, I believe the description of the game says 140, I have seen about 110 thus far.  Each type enemy possesses a unique algorithm for how they will approach combat and try to kill you.  This is not a new concept, in fact it is nearly as old as video games themselves, spanning all the way back to the 4 ghosts of Pac-Man.  Each one behaves in a different way, and alone they are easy to master and avoid, but put them all together and you’ve got yourself a challenge.  Hollow Knight does this beautifully.  It will often introduce a new enemy to you, 1 v 1, so you can scope it’s movements and attacks, but as you progress it will introduce fights with varying enemies and areas, all behaving in a unique fashion offering up seemingly infinite combinations for combat, constantly engaging and challenging you in new ways.
Boss Fights – One word comes to mind, elegant.  Bosses have a series of attacks/moves that generally have no particular pattern to them, but with practice you learn to identify them and avoid damage.  The first time you fight each boss, they will likely smote you with ease.  But remain patient, with each battle you will learn their moves a bit more, until finally you can vanquish them with relative ease.  To me, this type of learning is deeply satisfying.  To go from attempt 1, dying and hitting the boss 0 times, to attempt 6 and barely being hit and slaying your enemy is a sign of balanced difficulty, which to me this game does masterfully.  You’ll die, but not in the frustrating way.  You will die or survive by the quality of your own skill, nothing else.  The game is never “unfair” or frustrating for the sake of frustrating, it is the perfect balance of difficult and satisfying, which is most frequently felt in the conclusion of each boss battle.
Final notes on combat – This game offers Dark Soul’s-esque combat, but IMO far more enjoyable.  It’s not as difficult as DS, but offers that similar feel of action-puzzle solving in which a player must learn the patterns and attacks of each creature before hoping to be successful.  The change from 3D to 2D makes all the difference for me.  The loss of a dimension and a camera center-focused on the protagonist offers a combat experience in which all the information you need is readily available, which then leads to a truly satisfying combat.  Nothing will sneak up behind you because your camera isn’t facing the right way, you won’t back into those spikes accidentally, no, none of that “difficulty.”  As I said, you will die and survive on your own merit, not chance or frustrating accidents.  The 2 dimensional world only helps to feed into this utterly satisfying combat.
-  I will not write much about this, because that would require spoilers and this review is already approaching 1,500 words, but all you need to know is this game is absolutely packed to the freakin’ gills with content.  Every nook and cranny likely offers some secret or badass content you had not seen before.  The progression of your platforming skills, both in game and as a player will have you revisiting familiar areas, but with a new lease on traversing it.  This often leads to discovering sweet new gear and offers even more reason for a player to respect each level design.  As a completionist,  this will likely be the death of me, but dammit I had fun in the meantime!
Cons:  I have yet to find one.  Will edit if I do.
TL;DR – Difficult, beautiful, elegant, masterfully crafted, labor of love. 10/10.

I completed the game (99%, because of the Colosseum mentioned further...) and would like to share my opinion about it.
NOTE: This review probably isn't very helpful for people looking to buy the game. The review is more focused on people who have played at least a part of the game.
First of all, I would like to say that I agree with many other: This game is indeed a piece of art. But, just like many other pieces of art, does this one contain imperfections. These imperfections can be anoying, frustrating and can destroy the joy of playing the game for moments. I will sum some good and bad thing up about this game:
The good:
-Great diversity of zones.
-The background music is amazing (although the boss music could have been a little bit cooler/heavier).
-You will experience the sad admosfere in its full glory. The game is sad, but can be a bit lovely aswell.
-The art design is absolutely stunning!
-Controls are fine when using a controller.
-Charms allow a little bit of fighting style customization.
-Finally killing bosses can be very rewarding.
The bad:
-Maps. This was my greatest annoyance. You don't start of with the map of a newly entered zone. Navigation is almost impossible without a map, so you just end up using walkthroughs or maps from Google. After acquiring the map of a zone (which is extremely hard, because you need to find the cartographer in the zone you don't have a map for), only part of the zone becomes visible on the map. The undiscovered parts remain black until you visit them, which is fine, except for the part that these parts are only updated on the map when resting at a bench. Because of that, you will travel through parts of the zones without being able to use the map, which isn't making navigating easier either.
-You come across a lot of places you can't reach yet (because you miss abilities). This is fine, except that you mostly don't know you don't need to go that way because of the horrible map navigation.
-You need to get to zones in a specific order to get abilities which help bypassing some area hazards. Unfortunately, you have absolotely no idea which zone to visit without using a guide...
-At the beginning of the game (after Dirtmouth) you have absolutely no idea what to do or where to go.
-The amount of fast travel points is too low, especially in the lower parts of the map. There should be more stag stations, for example. Now you end up using the King's Station hundreds of times in one playthrough.
-Some zones really need some extra benches (safe spots). Also, finding benches can be extremely hard because of bad navigation.
-Showing yourself as an icon on the map requires a charm slot (really!!!?).
-Some combinations of enemies and room hazards are reaaaally cheeky.
Bad things about some quests:
-The White Palace feels completely out of place. The White Palace is a very difficult optional parkour that is needed to be completed to get acces to two additional endings. This place is hard, frustrating and doesn't really belong in this game.
-Colosseum of fools: The trials are way too long (especially the last one). Some rounds are disproportionate and way too difficult (mostly the ones with grounds spikes and/or no possibility to heal). Luckely, this colosseum is also optional.
-The delicate flower quest: WTF!? You are asked to travel from one side of the map to the other without being hit. Getting to the right place costs around ten minutes, and you end up failing lots of times (after which you need to walk back). I finally did it on my 6th try (yeeeeeh). The most tricky/cheeky part is actually near the end of the path you need to walk. Before reaching the right place, you need to traverse an area filled with thorns (which deal damage, ahem). So... They made a quest where you have to walk ten minutes without getting hit and put the hardest part at the end (which results in A LOT of wasted ten minutes).
Conclusion: The dreadful navigation, shortage of fast travel and safe points and the presence of some horrendous quests are the reason I give this game a negative review. I still enjoyed this game a lot, but the imperfections I summed up also destroyed my fun an awful lot of times. This game had a lot of potential and at times it did live up to that. Other times, it really felt like a burden to play. Shame...

Now granted this may look like a quick review having only 30 minutes into the game at the moment, however I have also played this on consoles so I have a lot more experience than it may seem with this game. I have not come across any sort of technical problems, such as glitches(graphical or otherwise). There are some odd things however. You can't exit the game easily when you want to. The main menu has no exit game choice, that I do admit is odd, so I had to use my window key to get out of it. Alt-Tab will probably work as well. However the rest of the game is fantastic. They brought back an overworld to the FF series which imo was sorely missed. Graphically when you look closely the graphics aren't that impressive, you can tell the game came from the PSP, however rather than focusing on the details and instead looked at as a whole when it comes to its graphics, it's actually a beautiful game with beautiful design. I loved the combat in Crisis Core FF7 on the PSP as well as Kingdom Hearts, if anyone has played those, you'll be somewhat prepared for the combat. Unplayable until they support more than Xbox360 controllers. The KB/M setup is horrendous. I will not waste my time.

EDIT: I finally got a controller to get recognized in the game using x360ce. There was an option for "Force Feedback Passthrough" in the Advanced tab.
Full PS4 controller setup that I used.
I have InputMapper already running and working
set x360ce like Bar0th says to:
download x360ce (64 bit version) from
. Place it in the WIN\ subdirectory of the game folder. Run it, let it create the DLL, and configure for your controller.
Switch to the Game Settings tab, add the exe for the game (the one in the WIN\ folder - fftype0hd.exe), and make sure COM, DI, PIDVID, and 64-bit v9.1 are checked for that game profile. Checking PIDVID should set the Fake VID to 1118, and the Fake PID to 654 (if not, use those values).
Make sure Force Feedback Passthrough is checked in the Advanced tab. You may have to uncheck the one above it to get it.
Once configured, exit x360ce_x64, and rename xinput1_3.dll to xinput9_1_0.dll (if you don't see the .dll extension, rename xinput1_3 to xinput9_1_0).
screenshot of my settings:
Now that the controller works, the game is enjoyable. I would recommend it now, ONLY if you can use your controller. The KB/M setup is terrible still.

This game caught my eyes while I was browsing games to buy in the steam shop.  I saw the trailer and I bought it right after that.
I have probably spent 95% of my playing experience in singleplayer.  I didn't have any help from real players so this review will be in that perspective
First, I'll go with the cons.  You can get pretty lost in the launcher for the game.  Also, if you don't set your memory to a good level and don't set the graphics to a level your computer can handle, you might not even be able to run the game at a good speed (or at all).  There is also a bit of a learning curve to the game.  For the first few days you play, you will probably spend just as much time playing the game as you will watching youtube videos trying to figure out how to make things work properly.  As for the youtube videos, a lot of them are a bit outdated, and finding a recent video can be difficult.  There's also not a lot of content when it comes to singleplayer, but that's because this game was built more for the multiplayer experience.  Although there are many planets and systems, they are very similar to each other so the only thing that makes you explore is having to move to the next system to find more resources.  For where the game is at, I think the build mode is pretty great, but it could use some tweaks to make it faster and easier.  For example, I find it a bit tedious to have to go into 'advanced edit' and having to press an arrow 5-10 times and look at a tiny picture of the selected piece, trying to find the right orientation of the block you're trying to place everytime I switch to a different part of a ship.  And I find that most of the time, I get the wrong orientation because in some lightings it's very difficult to tell which direction the block is facing in the tiny picture if it's all one color.  I think a system where you could click and hold the mouse button then move your mouse in different directions to change the orientation would make building 1000% easier (maybe they already have an easier way and I don't know about it).  That's all I really have for cons.
For the pros, this game is just amazing.  If the thought of building your own ship and scavanging the galaxy for resources excites you, this is the game for you.  If you want to build a ship with a ridiculous amount of salvage modules so you can mine to the core of a planet in the click of a button, you can do that.  If you want to build extravagant space stations where you can store all your ships, you can do that.  If you want to kill pirates and plunder their stations, you can do that.  All this I'm explaining is still only scratching the surface.  Once you get into multiplayer, there are factions you can join and wars you can fight.  This game is so fun and is only going to get better with every update.

After getting all three endings, I can say wholeheartedly that Hollow Knight is one of the best games I've ever played. Not flawless, mind you, but it has an immense level of polish and fun that I haven't seen since Dark Souls 1. On another note, while I think this game is awesome, if you didn't like Dark Souls, chances are you won't like this, sadly.
PROS:
- Fun, solid Metroidvania gameplay all around.
- HUGE world that offers 25+ hours of gameplay that almost never gets stale or repetitive.
- The art is some of the best, if not THE best 2D art I've ever seen in a video game.
- Music is great and fits the game perfectly.
- Tons of unique enemies and bosses that are fun to fight (for the most part).
- Progression is very satisfying, and every item feels useful in their own unique way, including most charms.
- Story is great, even though it's basically the Dark Souls story of "people are sad and everything's about to die and/or is dead"
CONS:
- The game has the Dark Souls III syndrome of "anime fights," that is, putting in way too many boss fights that sacrifice fun for trial and error for the sake of looking cool. Granted, the majority of the bosses aren't anime fights and even some of the anime fights are fun, but still though.
- The art, while great, tends to stick to one palette per area.
- Some attacks have no right to do the same amount of damage as other attacks, this is especially frustrating regarding contact damage and some of the dream bosses (because obviously bumping in to a small bug deals the exact same amount of damage as a giant knight swinging a sword three times the size of your body at you)
- DEEPNEST. Screw this area.
- A select few enemies are a complete pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥(cough cough Soul Warriors)
- The final boss is pretty easy,
All in all, Hollow Knight is absolutely worth your time and money if you're a fan of Dark Souls. Hell, even if you're not, you might end up liking it anyway. It has the quality and polish of a triple A game for only 15 dollars! In conclusion, I give this game a 9/10.

Hello eveyone.
Now I've played quite a few early access games in my time on steam (Years of gaming that aren't all on this account.) and I've seen some terrible alpha's that probably will never go into beta or release for real.
StarMade is a beautiful exeption. (be ready for semi-long rant)
I jumped into the game thinking it would just be some half-baked copy of Minecraft. I was so wrong. Many people who are familiar with Minecraft will wonder why that game isn't as advanced as StarMade has become. Building you're own ship that flies, uses complex energy algorithms that contribute to everything from shields, to weapons, and many other sci-fi mechanics for spaceships is so satisfying! You can make the most amazing ships! It is a little more difficult to build then minecrafts style, but the game is no where near finished and it will probably be updated to be easier later on.
And that's another great point. The game is no where near finished.
That might not sound great, but with all the content you already have hours of enjoyment. I spent most my time building a mid-sized ship and that took me 20 hours! I see people with ships 3x, 5x, even 10x larger then mine. The system is so much more advanced then redstone and the massive amount of technology that you can create is astounding and will keep you tinkering for hours. If you want to build more then a basic ship you'll have to look at the sites wiki because energy production and storage have some pretty complex rules but most of it will be explained in the tutorial. The game generated structers are amazing as well. Screw Hexxit and other Minecraft dungeon mods. The pirate stations are deadly and great challanges, and the space stations you can discover floating around are awe-inspiring. You can even generate your own. Planets and Stars are still a little buggy, but the physics system is solid so far. Gravity works pretty well. (Though the Mass-to-Gravity ratio seems strange.)
Since I've been praising the game I'll give you a little more about the cons.
The HUD is a little strange. Kinda bare bones in my opinion. There's a lot of helpful information but it could be better. Although the Navigation system is pretty good, there is no way to save coordinates as far as I know. (Unless you write them down yourself.) The radar/map thing you have isn't very helpful.. you have some dots that might be something close by.. but up or down or wherever you can't really tell. It is suppose to be updated soon. The AI isn't that developed yet. You can make an AI for your ship but its honestly pretty stupid and doesn't always work. I hear it is suppose to be able to fly your ship and stuff later on in development though. You can still use it for autoturrets but it can go rouge every once in a while. Pirate stations are OP on the other hand. They can take a massive amount of damage to their shields and some of their turrets do crazy amounts of damage. I had shields that very few other people on the server could take down easily, I nearly got my core destroyed in two shots from a pirate station.
Planet shapes are also a real bi*!#. They are 3D pentagons as far as I remember at the moment. Maybe hexagons. Jumping around corners and having your gravity reorient is really disorientating. Also big ships can get stuck on them if you don't have a high thrust. So taking off is really difficult if you've got a 1500 mass battleship. It's usually better to make a small mining ship and dock it to you're bigger ship. Leaving the big one in orbit.
The size of the game is really overwhelming too. Like.. you thought minecraft is big... It took me 20 minutes to get to the edge of the core systems.. I was still had half my galaxy to go before reaching the outer rim. Jump drives shorten the time if you have enough power to charge them a lot.
Anyways I'm done ranting on about the game. Right now the Demo is the same as the full Alpha that you can purchase now. It will only be free for a limited time though. So try it out and see for yourself. Most people will help newbies if you ask nicely.
I'm off to build a spacestation and conquer a star system. ;)
