The game is still in alpha, let alone Early access, but I will put my experience to your service.
Overview:
This game is a voxel-based space sandbox with a bunch of original content.
In this game, you can build ships, and fully customize it with the hundreds of blocks at your disposition.
If you feel like taking a true challenge, you can go on and build a space station.
The game includes factions, and faction battles. Factions have absolutely no player capacity limit. You can easily end up with five hundred factionmates with you.
Now, let's talk about the pros and cons.
PROS:
CONS:
Now this game might be for €9.99, but it sure is worth twice as much, if I had one gift to do to a bored gamer, it would be this game.
It has been on developpement for about 4 years (More, already ?), but is still progressing at a sustained pace. The community can't wait to see further progress, and neither can I.
Ships will become overpowered exponentially with their mass, if one dreadnought is 50 megatons in mass, it will still be much stronger than 200 corvettes of 500 kilotons. This is due to the exponential increase in stats the more blocks you have connected in one array. This is sad because that can inhibate epic space fleet battles. Fighters will never be able to breach through larger ships due to the former having weak weapons compared to larger ships, and the latter having too much shield recharge rate for the former.
Schema and the developpement team plan on upgrading this though, to make smaller ships stronger and more of a threat, and larger ships more exposed to swarms of smaller ships.
I guess I'll take my leave, before this review scares other people.

Mediocre port, but good game. A few things you should know on the technical level:
30FPS lock (As mentioned by the Framerate Police)
Resolution option is Output Res ala Dark Souls - Actual resolution is linked to Anti-Aliasing, as goes:
None - 720P
Standard - 1080P
Maximum - 4K
Mouse and Keyboard controls are awful, gamepad is practically mandatory (Glorious WiiU Pro pad here)
Mouse renders on top of the screen at all times, cannot be used in menus, and the mouse controls are blatantly Analog Stick emulation. Worst of all, there is no rebinding keys, just two control-schemes with minimal difference between them.
Now, onto the game itself -
Decent Action-RPG built off of FF7 Crisis Core, with a touch of Monster Hunter. 14 playable characters with different abilities that need to be used in their own ways. There's a world-map with places to explore, for the first time in an FF game since the PS1 FF games.
Prepare to die a lot, it's somewhat difficulty, especially since your party members have barely any health. Running is advised if enemies 5+ levels higher are encountered.
Also, RTS elements as well, quite interesting departure from where the series has gone before IMO - Though I recall something similar in the SNES FF games.
All in all a good experience if you can look past the issues of the port.

I don't hardly know where to begin with this game, it was a fantastic experience. You play as Lo-Wang, a smartass samurai , who constantly drops rediculous one-liners, very similar to the original Shadow Warrior. Make no mistake though, this is a  reboot, and very good one at that. The story is surprisingly serious though it's hard to take it that way with all the silliness going on, but there is some seriously dark stuff going on behind all the shenanigans. Although it won't exactly suck you in, it's just adequate.
As you progress through the game you find several guns to use, and while cool, they are nothing compared to endless joy your Katana will bring you as you slice through hordes of demons. You also gain special powers that will help you in battle such as healing, a knockback, and a shield. All the powers and weapons can be upgraded. Weapons use money to upgrade, generally gaining both passive bonuses as well as new funtions. While powers use Ki Crystals to gain new effects. There are also kharma points, gained from killing enemies, finding secrets, and completing a battle with high ratings. You use these points to buy passive upgrades for Lo Wang, increased max hp, abilities heal you, find more money, etc. Honestly all this is above and beyond anything I'd expect in a reboot of such a simple shooter, and seriously the Katana combat is amazing. Enemies have only average variety, giving many of the different weapons/powers their place in the game at least, but be prepared to see the same enemies a lot.
Graphically the game is pretty nice looking, it's nothing new, but your eyes won't be disappointed. Especially when you slice demons into a dozen bloody chunks. While you look around and admire the scenery, you may come across one the game's many secret areas, some of which use the same textures and level design as the classic shadow warrior as a throwback. If you haven't figured it out by now, this game is literally jam packed with references and easter eggs, many of which are done in corny ways that make the retro gamer in me giggle.  Level-designwise, it's done well. It's linear at times but doesn't feel that way. The levels feel similar to serious sam in a lot of ways, though they are more detailed and generally at a smaller scale.
I didn't really come across any glitches aside from a enemy becoming stuck and forcing me to reload once. And the only real gameplay mechanic that behaved oddly at times was the dashing (Sprint+Direction). To elaborate when you would quickly dodge down a set of stairs or ramp, rather then hug the ground you'd fly out and sometimes die of fall damage if it was a particularly steep incline. Dashing in particular seemed to cause me to randomly splat when done against certain walls, though I only ran into this twice.
All things considered, I can't imagine anyone hating this game if they even remotely enjoy the FPS genre. Even if the jokes aren't to your tastes (As corny as they are at times), you'll enjoy slicing demons up with the Katana garanteed. The game clocked in at about 9 hours on normal, by a experienced player. The game is well paced though, it doesn't feel too short, or too long. These guys made a seriously excellent game, show them some love and pick this game up if you are even remotely interested (At least get it at the next sale if you have any doubts).
TLDR: It's old school, but it's new, and it has swords, guns, mystic powers, and demons. It's awesome and it's cheesy. You'll laugh, you'll cry. Buy it! Buy it! Buy it!

A great game. This AC is brighter and nicer to look at than ACIII, and not just because of the enahnced graphics. The bright sunlight makes you feel like a hearty pirate, not that depressing cloudy GTAIV-esque lighting they had in the previous title (because to me personally ACIII just looked really dreary). But now to address the real issue at hand, which happened to me and tempted me to walk away from this game and never return. Me: Buys game. Plays game for like 5 hours. Leaves open overnight. Repeats for about a week. So here's me, who's put over 35 hours into this game, to one day finally close it and reopen it, just to find out that all my save data was gone. I cried inside (and maybe a little outside). But I didn't give up. I didn't give in. I didn't give down. I didn't give out. I investigated, and here is my solution (it worked great for me, even if it is a little inconvenient). The file with your save data in it is called 437. Open it, and if I remember correctly, there should be some suspicious files in there like something_DELETED. Yeah those are bad, delete 'em. The only things left should be 1.save, 1.save.upload, 2.save, 2.save.upload, 3.save, and 3.save.upload. What I found out is, whenever you leave the game while your save is in that folder, it wipes it back to zero. So make a new folder called "AC4 Saves" or something, and whenever you open the game, put whatever save file you used in that folder. Ex. I used save slot 1. I would put 1.save in 437 when I open the game, and before I close it I would put 1.save in AC4 Saves. That way, the files don't get corrupted whenever you quit. I got my 40 or so percent save slot back like this, but I always move the file back to 437 when I open the game, and move it to AC4 Saves BEFORE I close the game. Hope this works for you, and good luck. ;)

This game feels to me like it's trying to be Braid 2, with esoteric rhetoric, simple-yet-convoluted symbolism, and pensive vibes (not to mention a rewind mechanic). Unfortunately, for me it just falls flat. What made Braid really work for me was how well-executed the rewind mechanic was, how versatile it was, and how everything built off of time to create a unique and thoughtful atmosphere, rather than a bunch of random puzzles thrown together. The controls were tight, the artwork beautiful, and the puzzles complex enough to keep me thinking about them and coming back to them for days.
I can't really say the same applies here. While the mathematician-style of abstract thought and thinking in several dimensions is present here, the game comes across as something simple trying to be something pensive. The controls are slow. Your character moves the speed of a snail in molasses frozen in an iceburg buried under a mountain. While this does aid in the pensive vibes I get from this game, nothing about this game is all that pensive (and I was feeling this even BEFORE I played Antichamber, which succeeds dramatically where this game does not). The puzzles are extremely simple, at least for the first three chapters, and everything can be done with minimal experimentation. I would really like it if i could think about the puzzles at my own pace, rather than solving a puzzle mentally in seconds and having to slow my mind down to a crawl as the character ever so slowly meanders across the screen. Antichamber and Braid do this brilliantly; you can move around and come back at any time if a particular puzzle looks too hard, and solve it in seconds if you finally figure out how. Here, there's no such joy of discovery, since you'll likely discover the solution on accident as you wander ever so slowly back and forth.
Unfortunately, this game also suffers from what a lot of indie games seem to nowadays: a terrible difficulty spike for no reason. The first three chapters (and half the fourth) were unbelivably simple and required no thoughtwork whatsoever. Then, one level abruptly is insaely complex, time-consuming, and far more difficult than anything before it, with nothing leading up to it at all. That's not how you design a puzzle game. That's not how you design any game.
Lastly, new mechanics aren't introduced well. It's totally fine to have new mechanics as a game progresses, but it took me quite a few minutes to realize that those arrows flip gravity. Why? Because the flipping-gravity effect looks nothing like it has anything to do with flipping gravity. I would expect something straightforward; rotate the camera 180 degrees, grey out the screen a bit, maybe flash a two-way arrow, something simple. Instead, there's a circle wipe from the center outwards reminiscent of a Powerpoint slideshow, and the level kinda looks like it's changed in the process, but I can't really tell because the level is vertically symmetrical anyway. Oops. Oh, and gently touching one of those boulders kills you dead on the spot, because why not.
It's stuff like this that just irks me about a game. Especially because, just with a few more months of beta-testing and polish, this game could be absolutely amazing. They've got some fantastic ideas here, and they've executed them horribly. That's just the saddest thing for me, because I like games that are great, and this one just barely isn't there.

I'm going with a 'yes' to 'do you recommend this game ?', but that 'yes' needs to be qualified.  If you want an easy arcade style game, as a lot of the other reviews suggest to me, then move on, this isn't a game, it's a serious simulation.  Like most serious simulations, you can't expect to get everything in one download.  You buy the base and then you add the elements that interest you, just like people did with scalextric or electric train sets back in the good old days :)  The advantage of this offering is that the first part is free.  It doesn't include a lot, but if you have some patience, there is enough to get a feel for what is on offer and decide if you want more.
I have tried both Assetto Corsa and RaceRoom Experience this past week.  My first impression was that Assetto Corsa was better.  It cetainly has the better interface and the option to set up the cars to some degree is attractive.  RR3 has some problems with it's server and the current Nvidia drivers, but, while frustrating, these are not major issues, assuming these will be fixed in the near futures.  Both simulations promise multiplayer options, although it looks like the RR3 option will be limited to the DM Experience DLC for now.  For me the availability of the DM Experience tips the odds in favour of RR3 for the moment, but I'm happy to follow both for now and see what the future brings.

Not worth the time or money, really. I only finished the game out to completion because I'm that way. Sometimes it's simply because I spent the money and other times it is because of my OCD. There are games that I have just dropped completely, however, but this wasn't one of them.
The Bridge had a very interesting idea, but it was poorly executed. Braid was a MUCH better game that you should go purchase right now and not waste your money on this cheap "sequel."
For me, the puzzles just got too annoying too quickly and required too much painstaking effort to make sure the littlest piece didn't mess up. As OCD as I am, I usually enjoy immense effort in things like that, but this game just rubbed me the wrong way.
The gameplay was also very slow. Even if you know what to do in a level, it takes forever to get it done. The walking and turning is just terribly slow in something like 95% of the levels. Some people argue that it's because it is level-dependent, but there were only like 2 levels where I noticed the pacing was increased vastly. Other than that, all of them seemed the same slow drag to me.
Besides that, the color palette and lack of a story made it boring. Braid told a story and looked beautiful doing it. I usually don't hold games up side-by-side in a review, but this game tried to repeat Braid's success and failed. The game would have looked much better styled up like Braid (and it even shows that in two different 5 second scenes) and it really needed a story.
Overall, it seemed like a boring slog through annoying puzzles that led to no real payout of any kind.

Charge attack is just so damn slow (without the charm) rendering it nearly useless, but that might be a personal thing.

And even if you have the charm you need to wait before a screen transition so your money can catch up or you will leave without it. This is balanced by giving you money each kill and there's some good places to farm money too.
Cons:
That son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ stole my girlfriend. >:(
Final thoughts:
The game took me about 16 hours to beat and I ended with 76% completion because I was tired of searching so much for secrets. I was totally hooked on the game and really enjoyed it. If you liked Super Metroid, then you'd like this game too.

A great game. This AC is brighter and nicer to look at than ACIII, and not just because of the enahnced graphics. The bright sunlight makes you feel like a hearty pirate, not that depressing cloudy GTAIV-esque lighting they had in the previous title (because to me personally ACIII just looked really dreary). But now to address the real issue at hand, which happened to me and tempted me to walk away from this game and never return. Me: Buys game. Plays game for like 5 hours. Leaves open overnight. Repeats for about a week. So here's me, who's put over 35 hours into this game, to one day finally close it and reopen it, just to find out that all my save data was gone. I cried inside (and maybe a little outside). But I didn't give up. I didn't give in. I didn't give down. I didn't give out. I investigated, and here is my solution (it worked great for me, even if it is a little inconvenient). The file with your save data in it is called 437. Open it, and if I remember correctly, there should be some suspicious files in there like something_DELETED. Yeah those are bad, delete 'em. The only things left should be 1.save, 1.save.upload, 2.save, 2.save.upload, 3.save, and 3.save.upload. What I found out is, whenever you leave the game while your save is in that folder, it wipes it back to zero. So make a new folder called "AC4 Saves" or something, and whenever you open the game, put whatever save file you used in that folder. Ex. I used save slot 1. I would put 1.save in 437 when I open the game, and before I close it I would put 1.save in AC4 Saves. That way, the files don't get corrupted whenever you quit. I got my 40 or so percent save slot back like this, but I always move the file back to 437 when I open the game, and move it to AC4 Saves BEFORE I close the game. Hope this works for you, and good luck. ;)

(*Beginning initial review*)
So, I'm a little over 14 hours in and thought I might give my initial thoughts on the game (scroll to bottom for final quick thoughts):
This game is not like anything I've ever enjoyed. I tried playing minecraft for a grand total of 5 minutes and was like - this is dumb, why do people play this - and never touched the game again. I saw Starmade on steam and my initial thought upon seeing that it was another one of those dumb block games was that it would be horrible. Well I watched the trailer and saw all these neat ships and all this space combat and was like... maybe I should give this a try.
I played Eve Online for a few months and really enjoyed the game, however the problem with that game is that to be anywhere near good at it you have to spend an incredible amount of time farming, learning to fly ships, learning what ship counters what, losing tons of ships, farming to replace those tons of ships. It was just boring honestly and I saw these guys with these huge ships that they had to train for months just to be able to get into them and I got discouraged and left.
I thought my time in space was over, then I bought Starmade on a gamble. For 10 dollars, I figured I would give it a shot. I can honestly say that this 10 dollars is the best 10 I've spent in a long time.
Final thoughts:
DO buy this game - if you enjoy making your own content. If you want to join a server with a small group of people who you can interact with and grow to know (or hate).
DO buy this game - if the thoughts of building your own specially designed space ship for combat, mining, transportation, or anything you can possibly think of makes you want to pee for excitement.
DO buy this game - if you enjoy games which have a high degree of rules which govern stats and laws. Ship building is not just connect the blocks and win. DON'T buy this game - if small glitches are a huge turn off for you (the game is still in early release when I'm writing this)

Shadow Warrior is not a bad game. I don’t recommend it because it has a lot of really great ideas that could have made it much much better, but fails in that, creating something mediocre. It has cool weapons, great level designs and creates an awesome horror – parody atmosphere. I also really liked the hidden jokes and references to older games, TV shows and movies. The story to me feels a bit incoherent and in parts unfinished, but in these types of games I don’t think it matters much.
Where SW wore out its welcome and starts to kill all the joy and fun out of the game is the combat. It has 17 quite different levels, each with its own atmosphere, but basically 10 different types of enemy monsters / demons, (and 3 of them introduced as boss monsters in the beginning). The gameplay gets harder by throwing more and more of the same things at your face, to the point where it begins to feel an endless challenge mode. Which is fun in the first few times, but after that, even with the weapon and ability upgrades, it becomes EXTREMLY REPETATIVE. In my opinion the second half of the game, (roughly the last 6 out of 17 levels, which felt like the same amount like the first 11 levels), is basically an almost endless challenge mode, with the same few monster types and slowly changing background. Throwing the same things at you only more at once became really difficult to the point it became so frustrating and enraging that made me write this anti-recommendation.
There is a saying among entertainers: “always keep your audience wanting more” which the developers should have heeded, because that would helped this game a lot. If Shadow Warrior would have been shorter, keeping its fast(ish) pace from the beginning till the end, I would say that this is a really great game, but it forced the same combat on me so many times, that to me at least, lost all its charm and became a grind that took away the fun I’ve had in the beginning.
If you buy this game, play thru chapter 11 and forget the rest. After that point you will only see some new backgrounds and cut scenes with the same everything before which becomes a grind.

There are parallels between this and Space Engineers. Starmade was here first, though space engineers has made leaps in areas SE hasn't, Starmade has made leaps in area SE hasn't. Starmade is more likely to run on your system. :P At the time of this writing, I fit the system requirements for SE but can BARELY play it while Starmade runs well.
*Starmade is easier to fly unbalanced craft (forward is forward, no matter WHAT the weight distribution whereas I've seen in SE unbalanced craft might want to pitch down or whereever because the center of mass is off-center. This could be seen as easier or more casual. Your pick.
*Starmade has AI pirate enemies. A unified enemy for everyone whereas in SE, I believe it's bainly PvP.
*Starmade does NOT have ramming physics like SE, at least I don't believe it does. Ramming might send you offcourse but likely won't cause damage.
*Starmade's OPTIONS... are INCREDIBLY hard to grasp, but useful for the power user wanting to squeeze every last frame pers second. SE's options are.. three settings off a dropdown menu. There's no turning off shadows in SE.
The good:
It's Minecraft in space. People's creativity can be set free and lucky factions might be able to field a gigantic capitol ship or super-titan warship they created themselves.
You can save your ships as blueprints which you can take to and from MP and singpleplayer.
And at the moment of this writing, it's $9 which is a steal.
The bad:
Starmade is an EARLY alpha. It has more bugs than Timon and Pumba from the Lion King can eat. It crashes often, at least for me. Maybe this is attributed to my fairly weak PC, but visiting a planet is impossible for me because my framerate TANKS despite framerate smooth as silk elsewhere. And that options menu great for the power user? I would be very hesitant messing with memory settings as that seems to be capable of making it so the game won't even start.
There is also a lack of goal in this game. Sometimess it just feels deserted, lifeless. Then again, maybe space is supposed to be this way. But you're very likely going to want to play with others in factions.
Do I recommend this game?
Yes, but like Space Engineers, it's a niche. Starmade is a less expensive niche.
And I apologize for all the SE references, but the two share a similar spirit, despite being different in many ways.

Best FPS I've played in a long time. There is no multiplayer, but the campaign is stellar. Plays like an FPS from late 90's-early 2000's, but with modern functions (sprinting, leveling/character building, etc).
Combat is phenomenal - between your katana, ki powers, pistol, SMG(s), crossbow, shotgun, flamethrower, rocket launcher, and demon bits (yes, you use pieces of demon as weapons. yes, it's as awesome as it sounds), combat is varied and exciting. There are probably an infinite number of ways you can approach any fight. The swordplay is pretty great - the lack of a parry  is a slight downer, but the ki powers make up for it.
The dialogue is drop-dead hilarious. Lo Wang's one-liners never get old, and the constant banter is what really gives this game its personality (IMO).
The story might be linear with not too many surprises, but if you can get by that and take this game for what it is (a throwback to late 90's shooters) you will enjoy yourself.

This is an early access review and may change as the game progresses.  Also I ONLY tried the single player game.
I really really wanted to love this game, and even now I'm struggling to give it a thumbs down because it has such promise and potential.  I want to support the developers so they make this the game that I hoped it would be.  I just don't feel it's right for me yet.
based on the comments I will add some amendments to my review.  I only played single player and thus had no explanations outside of the tutorial.  I'm not big on pvp and didn't want to spend as much time on a wikki as I did playing, but love space exploration type games.  It sounds like multiplayer is more fun.  I didn't know about cameras, shields, ect... because I dove into single player and was never able to survive long enough to upgrade my tech far enough to get any of those things.
--Space is big and I LOVE that aspect.  Some people were complaining that it takes too long to get anywhere but I felt that helped with the emersion.
--Ship building is an awesome idea but the controls let it down.  Movement is not intuitive and I'm not sure how to fix that.
--In "battle" I often accidentally switched to build mode making the slaughter even worse.
--I've never won a fight against the AI.  They always seem to hit my critical systems with amazing accuracy.
--The game universe is huge, but feels empty.  The only thing to do is build a target for the AIs and mine on large asteroids that I think are supposed to be planets.  If they are planets they are very small.  I guess you can build a base on one if you wanted.  There's not much else going on.
--I had trouble figuring out how to set a waypoint marker so I could come back to a world I liked.  Never did figure it out.
--The map is practically useless.  I couldn't tell where I was, which direction I was going, and whether it even mattered if I went that way.
--You have to put your most important piece of the ship in the front or try to fly with the ship right in your face in 3rd person mode (taking up most of the screen) because you can't see anything if the core is buried.  (apparently there are cameras that help with the view.  I never survived long enough to advance my tech that far).  Perhaps if I understood the map better I could mine and advance in safe territories before fighting.
--it doesn't matter where you put your most important piece of the ship because the random enemies that attack for no reason will crush right through any armor you put over it.  (apparently there are shields that help keep them from disabling you before you realize you're being attacked but once again I never got that far.)
I wanted to love it, and I still want to love it.  Please developers make the single player better!  As for the multiplayer, I can't speak for it at all.  Sounds like a good game for people who like pvp, or don't mind spending some time studying the wikki.  For me, I'll wait till a few updates roll in and give it another shot.

There seems to be a lot of negative reviews on Steam about this game, especially revolving around the pricing structure, and while I agree that the price looks quite high I have to say that I think the items are so good that to me they're worth the outlay.  You get what you pay for and the quality here outshines any misgivings regarding prices.
Graphically it's stunning especially with everything turned high and running at 60fps with 22 cars on the track, for which I'm referring to DTM experience, but the hot lapping in the base game with Ai turned on gives you an insight into what the finished game will feel like and in my opinion they have got it spot on.
I can only assume that the base game is yet to be optimised because I get lower FPS on the same tracks, with only a couple of cars out than I do with the 22 cars in a full race of DTM. Same graphics settings for both but with a 10 fps drop in the base game?
Sounds are incredible, I've never been so engrossed in the sounds of any game as this one and playing with headphones on just highlights the beauty of these cars.
Gameplay is great especially on the Get Real setting, althought the Ai needs a little bit more speed as its currently too easy to catch and overtake.
I'm currently using a Razer Sabertooth gamepad and once setup it works perfectly but I can only imagine how much more fun a steering wheel would make this and it's the game which will likely push me to make that commitment.
It's that good that I've bought pretty much most of the buyable stuff, except for a couple of livery options, within just a few days of trying it.
EDIT : May 26th 2016
After having set myself up with some decent hardware to get the most out of driving games I can say that this is my favourite driving experience on the PC. I own most if not all of the PC racing sims but there's something about Raceroom that makes it very special to me, and that's the feeling you get from the overall atmosphere that this sim creates. From the sounds to graphics to driving feel, once set up correctly this is such a cool experience with AI that can keep up and give you a thrilling racing experience.

How to bake a Hollow Knight cake:
1 - Add a cup some Dark Souls Flour.
2 - Add 2 tablespoons of Ori and the Blind Forest.
3 - Toss in an ounce of...A C T U A L   B U G S!
4 - A dash of cuteness for visual appeal.
5 - Add water and mix them goods up real nice boi.
6 - Cook for a good 20-30 minutes.
Your final result should be one hell of a platformer that is visually beautiful in most, if not every sence of the way, a ear pleasuring sound track with fitting sound effects, and very fluid controls and sense of fun from this gem of a game.
It's an overall amazing game that I find myself wanting to play more and more each day to progress further, which is something I usually have a hard time doing with most games, including that big named ones that are already renowned by the public. Not only is Hollow Knight a fun platformer to play, it also has very cute character designs and voice acting, which makes it even more adorable and likable. I will admit, there are some parts that can begin to frustrate some, but it's not enough to make me stop loving this game. It's a challenge well thought out and very well presented.
This is one of the few games that I can find myself replaying over and over again.
10/10 would bake again!

Shadow Warrior is an FPS reboot of the classic game of the same name. You play as Lo Wang, a sword and gun wielding one-liner machine on a mission to save the world from demons.
What sets apart Shadow Warrior from the multitude of other FPS games is the swordplay. While the gunplay is not the most exciting you will see in the genre, with the guns not feeling powerful enough, the swords are really second to none. There are many special moves, each with their own uses, and there is a great sense of satisfaction to be felt as you see limbs and heads fly off your enemies. The best approach is probably to mix up the two weapons, but the more fun approach may be swords only.
The graphics are ok if not spectacular for their time. There was recently a new graphics overhaul released for free, but I did not notice much of a difference. Maybe this is due to the graphics being a little forgettable in the first place.
The story and writing is ridiculous and par for the course for 90's FPS games. Save the world while killing hordes and hordes of bullet sponge enemies. How Lo Wang finds time to think of his witty remarks during his genocidal spree, I may never know.
The issue I found with Shadow Warrior is that it all starts feeling a little samey after a few levels. I kind of lost my will to continue shooting and chopping up demons after about 4 hours. I wouldn't say that makes the game a failure, just that I got my fill before it was over. The story is definitely secondary to the gameplay, which I enjoyed, but I really had no wish to see the game the whole way through. Overall I felt like I got my money's worth out of the game, but I got it on sale. Would I be happy if I paid $40, probably not. I couldn't recommend it at that price. But is it worth a play if you find it on sale? Absolutely.
Grade: B

Slice a demon in half with a katana. Behead a demon with a crossbow bolt. Shoot a demon with a sticky bomb, then detonate him near an explosive barrel and start a room-clearing chain reaction. Even better is the continued support of this game by the dev team, who released a massive update 2 years after the game was published, fixing tons of bugs, adding x64 DX11 support, porting the game to Mac and Linux, and making the campaign even more exciting! Admitted; one of the achievements is to find all the wisps, and I wouldn't have been able to find all of them without the use of a guide. "The Bridge" is right on the borderline of a good/bad game.  It's advertised as a strategy (puzzle) game and that's what it is (no problems there).  All the puzzles are interesting and involve walking through an environment, rotating that environment, and inverting yourself.  In general, each "level" consists of multiple "stages."  The early stages in each level tend to be easy and the final ones tend to be hard.  Again, no problem.  What I have issue with is that several of the puzzles hide the mechanism for solving it instead of just making the solution more complex.  Specifically, there are broken edges to the world that in almost every case, you can't walk/rotate around.  But, in a couple of puzzles, you can (and must).  There's also a problem with the velocity of the transit.  And then, there's the final Steam Achievement:  Collector.  It's pure gamification.  There's not a chance in the world that anyone could ever find more than one of these naturally.  The only way to find them is to do a search online.  Because of this unnecessary frustration, I was "this close" to rating the game down.  But, I did get several hours of thought out of the game.  So, I'm sticking with a Thumbs Up.

Difficult yet rewarding, harrowing yet charming. Beautiful graphics and tight gameplay set Hollow Knight far beyond any other 2d retro-inspired 'Metroidvania." Hollow Knight feels like the lovechild of both Dark Souls, and, Ori and the Blind Forest. Quick, tight gameplay in a hand drawn world that as you explore, sinks its teeth into you. I must admit, the learning curve is a little high but once you get a feel for the controls of this platformer, it comes alive.

The story picks up as you explore different areas. In typical Metroidvania fashion, you explore an area until completion, or until you hit an obstacle, unbeatable enemy, unscalable wall, etc. Then you go onto the next area (maybe find a powerup or two) and return to conquer what held you back before. Save points are few and far between which encourages a huge risk/reward style of gameplay. Until you get a feel for it, it may feel like the save points are holding you back. A few moments of frustration after losing to a boss can be remedied by exploring a little bit more to find a save point near their lair.

The art and animation style seem as though they'd feel more at home in a cartoon or animated series but are so supremely well done that it pulls you in. Team Cherry could have gone for the standard “2D PIXEL ART RETRO METROIDVANIA PLATFORMER” that seems to pop it's head up every 10 minutes, but the art style gives it a level of credibility that is unparalleled in most independant games. The music is somber, strings and keys. The atmosphere can go from a quiet hallway to a tense battle and the music changes dynamically. Sound design is excellent as well, from skittering of beetles, squishing and popping of bubbles, swords clanking on metal, everything sounds unique and as if it belongs. Nothing sounds canned, or picked out of a sound effect library.

Honestly, I’m in love with this game. I feel like I may have rushed through it, but I’m clocked at 13 hours right and at 56% completion. I’m going to go back and and try and find everything in every nook, cranny, and corner I can find.

This game is not what anyone would call a 'solid purchase'. It is by no means unplayable - the game itself is very playable. It just under-delivers on everything that it does manage to bring to the table, and I mean everything.
Just starting with the basics, menu set-up and game customization:
UI:
The user interface is somewhat standard faire - bottom menu bar, mini map, pop-up tooltips. But even these are lacking. The minimap provides little detailed useful information and is a general blotchy mess - there are no 'pings' to deliver location information for any contextual information provided, the representation of units and buildings on it is pixellated like you wouldn't believe, and for the size of the screen that it covers is basically an eyesore in the corner of the screen. Not that this is any different from the rest of the UI - the main displays for buildings and unit types are incredibly bland, the artwork is horribly un-inspired, and the tooltips provide very little actual information as to what capabilities anything brings to you. You cannot re-bind bind keys. You do not get a running list of resources that are available to you; you must hover over either a building in the action bar to view buildable resources available, or hover over your food/ale/perishable resources in the top right bar (because this couldn't all be done on one bar?) to see what you have left. Even with your perishable items, the game does not calculate total usage/production over time - only immediate production with immediate usage, so you have a harder time trying to figure out the optimal number of any production buildings you'll need to use.
Graphics:
Anyone that doesn't believe that graphics don't provide for gameplay is fooling themselves. The graphics need to match the setting, and this is something that Stronghold Crusader 2i is also lacking in. Playing the game on its highest settings, you will legitimately feel like your machine was transported ten years in the past. There is no reason for any game being released to look as poorly as this one does, it even performs poorly - there is no unit collision in a $50 game released in 2014? Regardless of how hard either of these things are to implement, you're charging full price for a game that does not deliver full-price accomodations in anything, and the extremely, extremely dated graphical and physics engine showcase that like nothing else in this game.
Sound:
Aside from the lackluster voice acting, the actual scripts that the units and characters use in the game is chuckle-inducing at best and absolutely, ear-gratingly, cringeworthy at worst. This begins with the very first playthrough of the game - while the initial tutorial Scribe voiceover is not bad, every other aspect of what the game uses for units and sounds is. Wall crumbling? Sounds like build-a-blocks falling with a microphone placed next to them. Battle? *clang clang*. The music is absolutely stereotypical for both the time period and the game, which would not be bad, if the music weren't so low-quality, and if the music didn't randomly stop playing at times leaving your ears to drown in the abyss that are the original soundbytes of the few other things happening around you.
Gameplay:
The gameplay itself is one of the only saving graces of this game, and that being said, its a literal re-cycle of the last Stronghold Crusader. Even so, that gameplay has its merits, and when the sieges get going, there are some enjoyable moments. Besieging Castles, when the lackluster gameplay and units come together like they were originally intended, becomes fun, well-paced, and engaging. The problem is, that this does not happen often. The game itself is buggy, unit animations are terrible, and the control scheme is just as bad.
All in all, this is an extremely disappointing outing for what was a very promising line of games, Stronghold 3 not included. 5.5/10. I would not recommend this game to anyone, not even with a sale, as there is just better out there to be had right now. While the gameplay remains a constant throughout the playable games in the series, the latest iteration is not a step in any direction but sideways for the franchise, and for the cost, you're better off going with a less buggy, more complete version of the original in HD.

Shadow Warrior is an FPS reboot of the classic game of the same name. You play as Lo Wang, a sword and gun wielding one-liner machine on a mission to save the world from demons.
What sets apart Shadow Warrior from the multitude of other FPS games is the swordplay. While the gunplay is not the most exciting you will see in the genre, with the guns not feeling powerful enough, the swords are really second to none. There are many special moves, each with their own uses, and there is a great sense of satisfaction to be felt as you see limbs and heads fly off your enemies. The best approach is probably to mix up the two weapons, but the more fun approach may be swords only.
The graphics are ok if not spectacular for their time. There was recently a new graphics overhaul released for free, but I did not notice much of a difference. Maybe this is due to the graphics being a little forgettable in the first place.
The story and writing is ridiculous and par for the course for 90's FPS games. Save the world while killing hordes and hordes of bullet sponge enemies. How Lo Wang finds time to think of his witty remarks during his genocidal spree, I may never know.
The issue I found with Shadow Warrior is that it all starts feeling a little samey after a few levels. I kind of lost my will to continue shooting and chopping up demons after about 4 hours. I wouldn't say that makes the game a failure, just that I got my fill before it was over. The story is definitely secondary to the gameplay, which I enjoyed, but I really had no wish to see the game the whole way through. Overall I felt like I got my money's worth out of the game, but I got it on sale. Would I be happy if I paid $40, probably not. I couldn't recommend it at that price. But is it worth a play if you find it on sale? Absolutely.
Grade: B

- Controls are very weird and ahrd to get used to. Controls are not too bad, but can be challenging to get used to.
Overall, I really do recommend this game, even at full price, but just be informed that it has issues. This game certainly will not be for everyone, and this certainly is different from other finaly fantasy titles, but I still urge people to purchase this great game.

The Bridge is an homage to the art of M.C. Escher. If you don't know who that it is, it doesn't really matter as the game stands alone well enough. The puzzles are complex enough to be challenging at times but not in a cerebral manner. More often than not I knew what I was supposed to do to finish the puzzle, I simply had difficulty doing it because it required a precise maneuver. This became very frustrating to me at times as on some of the levels I ended up getting smashed by the little lion marble things over and over again simply because I couldn't fall or move precisely right. Having also played games like Antichamber, Portal and Portal 2, I found this games puzzles to be much more annoying than the puzzles which those games present (which wasn't a good thing) as the puzzles of those games didn't rely so much on that precision.
In many ways, the game is essentially a digital version of this little marble game I played as a kid. The game consisted of a marble which you had to guide (by titling the board) through a maze rife with holes. If your marble fell into one of the holes as you were tilting the board, you had to start over. The game was never a riddle as you knew you had to tilt the board to get by the holes, but it was difficult because of the skill required to move the marble precisely how you wanted. The Bridge is basically an updated version of this.
The game does boast a fairly unique build and look and the artwork at times is intriguing. There is little to no storyline however and what little they do incorporate is very esoteric. The game does feature an interesting soundtrack, but it is underutilized.
The gameplay was interesting enough to me to finish it (which took less than ten hours) and so I think I can recommend it if you can purchase it while the game is on sale. If it's not, you may not feel like you're getting your money's worth and you probably shouldn't buy it. If, in the end, you are an enthusiast of Escher's artwork and impossible figures and structures (such as endless staircases etc) then it may be worth the full price of the game, but otherwise just wait for the price to drop.

The Bridge is a puzzle platformer heavily inspired by M.C. Escher's works. It's main feature is its crazy impossible space and really cool space manipulation mechanics. It also features some time-manipulation mechanic that reminds me of Braid - You can rewind time if you make mistakes, so there isn't really a "game-over" state.
For the most part, solving a level is just a matter of figuring out how to navigate the weird space you find yourself in. That is not an easy feat since you can easily get disoriented by the impossible geometry. In a few levels timing your moves plays significant role too.
There are 4 worlds with about 6 levels each. In each world a new gameplay mechanic is added making the game more complex the further you progress. After you complete the game, you can revisit each level in a 'mirrored' mode which features new and more difficult puzzles.
Depending on your ability and on how much time you spend looking for hidden items and completing achievements, the game can probably take anywhere between 4 to 10 hours. It took me about 7; although I did use a guide to find in what levels each of the hidden items are located, I did take me a while to finish some of the harder levels.
So, if you like puzzle platformers and enjoy M.C. Escher's works, you'll definitely like this game!

Shadow Warrior is a reboot/prequel of the obscure 1997 shooter developed by 3D realms (creators of the legendary Duke Nukem.) The reboot was developed by Flying Wild Hog and published by Devolver Digital. After playing the original game along side the two expansion packs I was eager to get my hands on the reboot once it was announced on May 10, 2013 the trailer showed promise and looked like what a reboot should be.
Once I finally purchased and started playing I was introduced to our main hero and one-liner zinger Lo Wang an assassin who works for the powerful Japanese industrial magnate, Orochi Zilla. He is sent to a mission to purchase an ancient katana from a collector named Mizayaki for 2 million dollars. Mizayaki refuses the offer and Lo Wang tries to take the sword by force which takes a horrible turn for the worse. "Let's see... briefcase full of cash... blade... million dollar smile... ready for school, ma!" This game has a soild presentation and reinstated the hopes I had for the game. The story does do its job right with interesting, funny and downright awesome characters, and the plot keeps you engaged thoughout.
Gameplay wise it is almost flawless, old school with exploration for secrets in well designed levels and run and gun combat with modern elements and amazing sword fighting. Gunplay is soild and fun with great toys to play with against anything that bleeds although I would have liked to see abit more weapons and some more returning guns like the riot gun (a gatling shotgun) from the original game. Sword play really stands out and is really satisfying with full control of different swings to hack and slash any foe that dare crosses you alongside with special chi moves to bend reality to your will, you can also upgrade guns, skills and power to create more havok. There are some problem with the game unfortunately the maps can be a wee repatative, the guns are way to underpowered with the katana killing enemies with ease and the later demons can be way too annoying on the hardest difficulties.
Visually the game is stunning and alot of work has been done to make the game look jaw dropping there are some low quality textures even on highest settings and some cutscenes animations look terrible but they get a pass due to being rare. On launch this game was brutal to run but thanks to a recent patch it did help abit however it is still very terribly unoptimized which is unacceptable for a PC launch games, a huge bummer that ruins the experience. The game is out on Windows and with the recent patch Mac OSX and Linux is now supported. Music, sound and voice acting are pretty good aswell with a kickass soundtrack, witty and hilarious voicework and writing and satisfying sounds this game has a good amount of polish but could have been a little better.
Overall Shadow Warrior has to been one of my favourite shooters of all time and if your even slightly curious do play it I 100% recommend it. Packed with tons of content I have not completed still and you can even play the original free on Steam.

First of all It is part of the "New Crystal" setting, like XIII and XV, meaning that it shares mythology/world concepts with them (while they are not the same world, the death/rebirth of life as a cycle is a major part of said mythology), which means that you will see concepts like l'Cie and fal'Cie, superpowered servants of Crystals (though you will not be playing one, unlike XIII), Magitek technology also plays a prominent role taken directly as it was in VI.
Gameplay-wise it is closer to an action RPG style brawler, combat is real time in a party of 3, but from the get go you maintain a group  of 12+ characters, if one of your current party member dies and you do not res them, you can replace them with another one from your Ship on the fly. You can switch which party member you control on the fly and there is at least basic AI programming and they generally are fairly competent.
Boss fights can be a little bit underwhelming, but overal the game plays nice enough for a PSP (?) port and at least imo gameplay was solid.
The games story is told via "missions" which typically have save points during them, but have to be completed using the stuff you currently have on you. You can cancel your mission, though  and grind up if you need to when you find yourself stuck, though that has happened to me literally only once. In between missions you have a set amount of actions you can take, like attending classes, talking to other people (which typically gets you stuff), doing side quests or exploring. Unlike some other jRPGs that use similar mechanics, what you do during those segments has no real influence on the storyline though, it's all on rails (which isn't unusual for an FF of course)
Each character uses a different weapon and has different traits/abilities that you unlock as you level up (though some abilities, especially passives, tend to overlap) and while it's fairly possible to just maintain a group of your favorite 3, there are multiple segments where you have to split up your group. You do not have to grind to catch up too much though, as you can attend lectures that at least somewhat level up the party members you do not use and you get enough money/loot to keep them all updated. Maintaining the entire party is sort of a ♥♥♥♥♥ at times, though.

NEW REVIEW:
Coming back to this game a few years later, especially after actually playing Stronghold 2, I've come to appreciate this game a lot more. Using Stronghold 2 as the adjustment into 3D Stronghold games from the original Crusader really helps a lot. Q and E don't work in Crusader 2 for moving camera however, so the mousewheel problem still persists. It's a lot more balanced and you can definitely set up defenses fairly well now. It does feel satisfying to play, and it's pretty difficult so it's very rewarding to get through some of the missions. I can honestly say I recommend it now even if you prefer the old Strongholds, just make sure you use Stronghold 2 to ease into the 3D games as it'll teach you what you need to know to gitgud here.
OLD REVIEW:
It's not a bad game, but it's certainly not as good as the original Crusader. The graphics are horribly optimized, the controls aren't fluent at all (turning the camera around with mouse wheel feels terrible, the x-asis isn't inversed and isn't inverted, also you use left click to select troops then right click to move them/attack stuff, feels so wrong in Stronghold), and it feels extremely slow paced without any way of increasing game speed. It takes ages to get food/wood/stone/iron/weapons ect. in, and everything costs way too many resources to build. Taxes come in slowly and there's no good things/bad things that I found. It isn't very balanced, either. It's extremely easy to attack and very hard to defend. Catapults (not even trebuchets) out range the highest archer tower and ballistae do very little damage. Walls crumble (and kill all your units on them) in 1-2 catapult shots that are built and start shooting within a few seconds. There's no way to repair towers or gatehouses. Archers on towers/walls are nearly useless. So you're better off building little defense and focusing on keeping your opponents on offense all game. Lords are extremely tanky and can be healed with a new healer unit, which makes the game more about bursting him down than getting passed his defenses which is no where near as fun as the original. Knights (Called Templar in this game) come in un-mounted and you have to mount them manually which is really buggy. Combat between troops isn't visceral and satisfying like it was in the original. Voice acting is atrocious, probably the worst I've heard in 10+ years. I am happy about no moats though as units weren't programmed very well to dig it out so it was a pain to fight against in the original Crusader.
A lot of these things can be fixed in patches but I wonder if Firefly will see them as issues at all.﻿ If you're a fan of the original Stronghold and Crusader, definitely give it a shot, you'll probably like the changes more than I do. If you're just looking for a solid RTS, wait for some patches or a sale first.

I was generously gifted The Stanley Parable, as I thoroughly enjoyed the demo and was waiting for it to go on sale; it's been on the top of my wishlist for several weeks.
I played it for 2 hours, try many things and getting many of the endings. I had a laugh here and there, and the first few playthroughs were intriguing and enjoyable. Then I continued to play. After piercing the tip of the iceburg of what the game has to offer, I've found that the bulk of the game can be summed up in two words:
Underwhelming and boring.
It's unfortunate when a game's demo is more entertaining and appealing than the game itself.
I was expecting it to be as much of a hilarious, satire-filled walking simulator as the demo was, but instead I get an anticlimactic nonsensical ending no matter what I do. I try every branching possibility that I can think of, retrace my steps on every playthrough, do things differently, and it always ends relatively the same. The entire game feels like one of those gifs that loops some sort of buildup that implies an inevitable conclusion, only to deny that conclusion and continue looping until you've realized you've been bamboozled into just watching the same bait over and over.
... Unless that's the entire point of The Stanley Parable, which has been made very clear.
Some of the achievements are just ridiculous, and I'm not talking about "difficult"; One of them requires you leaving the game on for an entire 24-hour Tuesday. Another requires you to not open the game for 5 years. One of the final achievements requires you to do something completely unrelated to the game; the "Impossible" achievement, but this review isn't the place to discuss that. Achievements and unlockables usually provide motivation to play a game, but the achievements in this game don't feel very compelling at all.
I really wanted to enjoy this game, but the game just left me feeling empty, baited and sometimes frustrated.

Dungeon Defenders allows you to play multiple classic fantasy RPG character types in a co-op, action, tower defense game dealing with waves of dungeon monsters (e.g., gobbies, orcs, ogres, etc.). The graphics are beautiful, the systems -- except for character balancing -- well thought out, and the experience pretty glitch free. It's a well-thought, well-executed, fully integrated Steam title.
As for play, each round you will do a build phase and then a combat phase. Good smarts in the build phase, especially with the best builder types, will make or break your victory. The basic game has levels that progress smartly with the balance of your defenders, and there are numerous scenarios and some duplicate characters in the DLC. All four of the basic characters are duped in a gender-opposite DLC model.
The most serious complaints I have about the game are these: First, the different character types do not balance at all. As much fun as the barbarian is to play, he can't hold a candle to the characters who can build destructive defenses, like the squire, the apprentice, and the robot. The rangers' defenses are so expensive compared to the middling damage they do, that he / she can be frustrating to play: The apprentice gets a LOT more bang for the buck. The sorcerer, who summons "living" towers, like elves, spiders, orcs, and so on, is a tremendous amount of fun to play even though his bang for the buck is not as good as the apprentice or squire either. One advantage for the sorcerer is his / her summoning points are counted apart from the defensive points of the strutures.
My second complaint is, perhaps because the number of strong characters is small, the replay value on this game is probably less than I expected. Of course, if one were completionist on the DLC, that would give you some hours of play.
Loot in the game is fun, and you will find yourself making important tactical choices in how to equip your own defender.
All in all, I won't go back to Dungeon Defenders as often as I do my best faves, but I will go back. This is a nice gaming experience and co-op is fun. Enjoy!

After the update that the game got yesterday, I've played the game again in hopes that Square-Enix actually fixed stuff. And you know what? I'm actually surprised, they DID FIX STUFF! I think it's the first time Square-Enix has tried to ♥♥♥♥ something in their Steam Final Fantasy games. Anyway, since the game has gotten rid of most of the problems, and I'm actually having fun playing it (and not getting annoyed by not even being able to play it Fullscreen), I think it's time to make a SERIOUS review of the game, talking about both the good and bad stuff the game has to offer. And as usual, I'll go with the bad stuff first:
While the Fullscreen bugs are fixed, and the Pre-game menu ACTUALLY WORKS NOW FOR EVERYBODY, the game still seems to have some performance issues. At times, the FPS drop bellow 20, and it seems to happen when there are a lot of NPC's arround. I haven't yet suffered any game breaking bugs, but that being said, I haven't yet gone too deep into the game. If I find any of that, I'll quickly rewrite this part of the review.
Something that also bothers me way more than it should is how Square-Enix keeps working on these "HD" ports. They take a lot of effort into making main characters look GREAT, and some of the areas are quite good... But then, they seem to be TOO LAZY to make EVERYTHING look decent. Because of that, some areas of the game look extremely pixelated, which looks ridiculious when you go arround with extreme HD-looking guys. This gets even worse in cut-scenes, when a lot of secondary characters are pixelated as hell, and some models look extremely aged. I know this is a PSP-port, don't get me wrong: What I'm saying is that, if you start making the textures and models look good, for f#ck sake, finish the job and make everything look decent as well. Take this as an hilarious example, this guy appears like, 40 minutes into the game, and I've seen multiple cases just like it so far:
Now go ahead and tell me if it looks okay to you or not.
Another issue some people had with the game are the controls. Playing the game with a keyboard is like using over-sized condoms: Not only it won't work, but you'll look like a jack#ss. I actually TRIED to play it with a keyboard after hearing they would try to adapt the controls for PC a bit, but they failed MISERABLY. You can't even control the camera properly. I switched to my Xbox360 controller in less than 2 minutes of gameplay, and I advise you to get a decent controller before attempting to play this.
The last thing that I really don't like about the game is more of a personal thing: How the characters go. You have 12 characters to play with after the tutorial stage. What's the problem with that? In 90% of the RPG games you'll play on your life-time, characters appear gradually, and you'll actually get to know them a bit. Well, not in here, after the tutorial you have twelve guys to choose and bring to missions, but all you know about them is that they're all fixed to go with a different set of weapons and skills. That's it. It makes all characters look dull and life-less. I think the game would have benefited WAY MORE if it went with an approach similar to the Disgaea games, were you can create your own characters, and choose which of them to bring into the battlefield or leave on the base.
That being said, is the game good or bad? Well, I'm even surprised myself, but the game is quite good. Why do I say that? Well, Final Fantasy games have been garbage for the latest years, and I wasn't thinking too much about this one. Quite stunned, really! That being said, the story is really different for what you'll see in most FF games: Let's just say that the story is as mature as Final Fantasy Tactics; War of the Lions, while the gameplay is similar to Final Fantasy: Crisis Core, but having more than just 1 character by your side. And you know, it works really well.
The gameplay is fun and simple: The characters that you bring into battle will gain experience, uppon leveling up you get points which can unlock more moves or upgrade others. Each character is also stuck with a type of weapon, and you can also call a reserve character incase you lose one during a fight (though that character will not get anything, after being defeated).
The effects on battle look quite good (while most models look like from Half-Life 1), and the battle system seems to be balanced. During most fights on the over-world, you can choose to keep fighting monster of a higher level or leave, something that will help players level up weaker characters.
The story seems to go arround the same universe of FFXIII and all of those other games: I won't call that a bad thing, mainly because Lighting and all of those hideous characters don't seem to appear anywhere.
Do I recommend the game? Yeah. But I think only a Final Fantasy fan would pay the full-price. If you're not too much into it, then maybe you should wait for a sale.
Oh and, I'll edit this Review as I go through the game, as I said up there. If I find anything that needs to be told, then I won't shut up about it.

Overall i really enjoyed Shadow Warrior, having played the original back in the day.
Pros
- Modern graphics with retro feel
- Retains the humor of the series, many one liners and fortune cookies brought a smile to my face
- A wide variety of weapons and unlocks to keep this interesting. Want to solo the game with just the sword? Very doable.

- Good enemy variety and are generally quite intelligent as well
- Good length for a Modern FPS, it took me about 10 hours or so to finish my 1st playthrough
Cons
- Fall damage. I lost count of the amount of times i used shift to move quickly in a direction, fell and instantly died... it was not much fun haha
- The game difficulty spikes hard in the last 3/4 of the game, there are SO many enemies that it almost felt like luck if i didn't simply get sandwiched and almost insta killed because there was so much stuff flying in my direciton (and this was on the 2nd difficulty)
- I got stuck not knowing where to go several times as, while there is good variety to the levels, having to sometimes backtrack made me get lost for a good while
I picked this game up for a couple of bucks from a Humble bundle, but i would definitely get this one even on sale, it's worth it =)

Like a lot of other players, I was immediately sold on The Bridge's concept and art style. Both are certainly very solid: Mind-bending puzzles in a graphite or charcoal sketch style inspired by the works of M.C. Escher. Puzzles work by rotating the level and moving your character, and solutions often require managing gravities that work in several different directions within the same level. There's little not to love with that description, and that is ultimately what sold me on the game.
What ultimately comes out of that concept, however, is little beyond an exercise in tedium. There are several details in the game's execution that leave more to be desired. (Full disclosure: I reached about halfway through Chapter 4 before realizing that I was not enjoying myself in the slightest.) First, and most noticeably, is the ambling pace of both the character's movement and that of the level rotation. Many times, I found myself just idly holding a direction for several seconds, waiting for the level to reach the desired orientation while my character impotently shuffled about trying to gain footing on the shifting ground. Or I'd end up dragging my feet along a "twisting" path -- which usually turns out to be ultimately linear -- to my destination, long after having worked out the solution. I appreciate a good, thoughtfully paced puzzle experience, but perhaps the motion of the level and character should actually match that speed of thought.
Perhaps more egregious, though, is that the puzzles, while sometimes fairly challenging, never actually feel satisfying to solve. Unlike other more clever puzzle platformers, there were never any "Oh, yeah! THAT'S how I'll do it!" moments while playing The Bridge. Everything seemed to just kind of putt along, and reaching a solution seemed like a given more than an actual achievement. Perhaps it gets more interesting after Chapter 4, but that's the point that I gave up.
Other objections could be made of how highly derivative -- downright imitative -- the game is of a certain other time-bending puzzle platformer. One could suggest that shoehorned time reversal mechanic adds absolutely nothing to the game experience other than harking to another better game. Arguments could be made that the narrative and level structures are almost identical to that one game with the timey wimey stuff. One could do all that, if one wasn't enjoying playing Braid so much more.
Overall, I wouldn't personally recommend The Bridge, unless you picked it up on sale and don't mind tediously trudging through admittedly very competently illustrated puzzles for a few hours. I commend the developers and wish them the best for their future games, but hopefully next time they won't try to make Braid 2: The Rebraidening.

This review is from someone who wanted Crusader 2 to be really similar to Crusader 1.
Let's start at the beginning. The intro...
The intro looks like it's from 2006 or 2005 or even older. The animations are choppy and you don't even get the purpose of it. At least I did not.
You can give your email to get another 10 icons... yeah, I mean shield icons. Such an amateur way to get subscribers to their newsletters and stuff. (You can uncheck those though) But you still get into their system.
In the mainmenu, the announcer starts with "Welcome to Stronhold Crusader 2 my liege.". O K.
The menu is just nothing like Stronghold Crusader 1's. It looks amateur, simple and hell, there are not much of skirmishes. The menu itself is just, I don't know, confusing? I don't know why they chose the drag and drop team arranging, but it sucks. When you select a map in the menu, there is a slight delay which is irritating. I guess it is because of loading the minimap of the map, but whatever.
The voice acting is... well... you better check it out yourself. The peasants has no voice, nor image like we used to in Crusader 1. (Nor does the workers by the way)
The fact that they changed Lionheart's character, makes me sad. He used to be my favorite character in the game, but now... they ruined him. They changed his voice too.
Also, the announcer keeps telling you what is happening, if an enemy is attacking, you are going to be noticed. I also found hard to see what's going on on the battlefield as there are 3-4 players fighting, and you just can't distinguish the units' colors.
The UI is horrible, nothing like Crusader 1's, you just search for things mid-game, but that is not a problem, because the game itself is so slow in pace, that you can go out and cook some meal while you are waiting for resources. Building your castle became horrible, you can no longer twist the stairs, nor you can get your men at the wall through the gatehouse. Which seems more realistic of course... but eh.
Estates... yeah well. I captured an estate on one of the maps in custom skirmish, but no one gave a ♥♥♥♥ about it. From the estates, oxes(I guess) deliver resources to your main state, and yeah, guess what. They are slow.
(I have rechecked and found that you can click on the minimap and it goes there, but only if you don't move your cursor, not even accidentally.)
If you thought at least you can click on the minimap to move the camera there, you are going to have a bad time. You can only drag the camera with the minimap which is what the f. I was very surprised, so you got to scroll around.
There are dashes indicating the end of the map, which you can't hide, or at least I did not find a way to do it so. Bugged the hell out of me.
No collision detection! HURRAY! Although this can ease the gameplay, and makes the battles easier, it would be still nice in 2014.
So the main reason I played only 30 mins after paying 35€ is that I can't stand the pace of the game, the stronghold 2 like graphics and the whole UI design it is just horrible. Don't judge by the videos they put on the store page. Check a real gameplay on youtube or something.
Don't buy it until you are sure that you want this. Waste of money in my opinion. Thanks Firefly for ruining the Stronghold Crusader series.

Pros:
Main character is a cute lil' bug.
Combat is tight.
Movement controls are responsive.
World has interesting lore and the story is pretty neat (if a bit obvious).
Characters are unique and interesting.
Map system is pretty neat.
Fast travel system is cool and very useful.
You feel like a badass while murdering stuff.
Atmosphere is phenomenal.
Great music which adds to overall theme of despair.
Different areas of the map FEEL different with sound and enemies.
Transitioning to different areas of the map feels natural. If you're heading toward the mushroom-themed area, before you get there, you will start to see some mushrooms and mushroom enemies.
Customizable "kit" using charm slots so you can be better at the way you want to play the game.
None of the required content is too difficult, but it's still challenging and fun. Bosses (and enemies) have clear animations and attack patterns.
Puzzles are well-thought out and gated exploration areas are well designed.
Neutrals:
Charge attack is just so damn slow (without the charm) rendering it nearly useless, but that might be a personal thing.
Lots of backtracking even with the fast-travel systems.
The boss isn't at the end of the game, it's sitting around right in the middle. Makes it feel less of a climax.
The death mechanic where you have to fetch your "shade" is okay, but it didn't feel all that necessary in this kind of game. It's fine though since usually I do want to go back to the place I died anyway.
Gathering money is a chore without the charm that does it for you since it flies all over the damn place. And even if you have the charm you need to wait before a screen transition so your money can catch up or you will leave without it. This is balanced by giving you money each kill and there's some good places to farm money too.
Cons:
That son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ stole my girlfriend. >:(
Final thoughts:
The game took me about 16 hours to beat and I ended with 76% completion because I was tired of searching so much for secrets. I was totally hooked on the game and really enjoyed it. If you liked Super Metroid, then you'd like this game too.

This is without a doubt the best Stronhold release to date. I have played Stronhold since number one came out on demo disc in my quarterly PC gamer when I was 12. Everything that made me smash my mouse and spit at the screen in Stronghold 3 has been addressed in Crusader 2. Good pace and balance, buildings a good size, easy placement, graphics options, scaled tutorial missions. Most importatnly, the ability to quench my insatiable thirst to buld castles, man the walls, and slaughter dirty desert peasants.
My only hope is that the $50 I spent on Stronghold 3 have gone towards making this game as good as it is, and that the $50 I just spent on Crusader 2 go towards a celebration party for a job well done.
Edit: Notable improvements: smaller lumberjacks (1 pop requirement), better housing system (max 8 pop with generous placement radius), better happiness scale (less insane micromanaging food-tax-population), square building placement (no more awkward slightly turned buldings ruining my OCD), faster and smoother ox tethers.
I think I'm having an existential crisis because of this.

I got The Bridge as a gift, and I'm sure glad I did.  By far, it's the best "mind opening" game that I've ever played.  The graphics are done in an interesting "DaVinci's Notebook" style (at least that's what I would call it.), and the sparse storyline is absolutely perfect for what it is.
The puzzles are great!  The frustration that comes with them is of the good kind.  You're never felt wondering "why did they make it like that???!!!"  Instead, you'll have that "Omg, how didn't I see that sooner" sort of frustration that really puts you in awe of the game's design.  I LOVE IT.

Thus far, I've played through chapter 4 (each chapter has several subset levels).  It's starting to get pretty damned challlenging!  I'd definitely recommend avoiding any sort of guides for the game, as that could easily ruin the experience the developers intended, which they pulled off perfectly.
10/10, will play again, will achievement hunt, will speedrace.  Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥what a gem.

A good game? Yes. A good Crusader sequel? Not entirely.
Let me be clear by saying I don't hate the game and its actually quite fun but my main issue is it feels half done. There aren't too many bugs and the game runs smoothly on either of the systems I've run it on. (A desktop with two year old parts and an average laptop that's around four years old. When I said the game feels half done I mean to say that the game feels flavourless and at times even dull. The art, animation and design are fairly basic and simplistic; one of my biggest disappointments is the lack of interesting voice acting from the computer opponents to the humble peasants that populate my castle all the voice acting is bland or in the case of the latter. totally absent. The music is half recycled from the original and half stereotypical pseudo middle-eastern. With only 8 AI opponents there isn't a large number of challenges and it was disappointing to not see the likes of the Pig or the Snake. The appearance of familiar opponents like the Wolf and the Rat was welcome but I'm confused why they recorded new voices for those two characters when many of the units (European Archers for example) use the exact same voice recordings from the first Crusader title.
All in all Stronghold Crusader 2 is a solid game and quite fun to play but in my own opinion it doesn't live up to either the hype or the legacy of the original Stronghold Crusader.
P.S. I personally would buy Stronghold Crusader HD for cheap and wait for this game to come down in price. It's not worth the $50 price tag but will be more than worth while to snag on a Steam sale.
