I'm sorry to say that I was greatly disappointed with this game. It looks like it would be a lot of fun, but there are some glaring problems with it.
First and foremost, there is about a second delay when trying to jump, which in a platforming game should be a criminal offense. It's odd really, because there doesn't seem to be any delay when attacking. But the jumping delay turns simple platforming sections into death traps. The difficulty of facing a flying enemy is also greatly exaggerated. By the time  you've launching yourself into the air to meet them, they've long since changed position.
Jumping in general seems like a foreign concept in this game. You character jumps somewhere between 3 to 4 times his own height. There are no quick little hops to reach the next platform. Instead you have this ungainly, frantic rise into the air that brings back memories of Luigi from Super Mario Bros 2. I can only imagine your character's little feet are pedaling madly beneath his robe. Once in the air, you have to adjust for reentry and hope you reach the appropriate landing spot. But I suppose any landing you can walk away from...
There also really needs to be a roll or dodge in this game as well. Everything about the game play just seems to scream out for the need of one, but given that your character can't even jump without seriously thinking about it first (you know, weighing the pros and cons of it all), a dodge/roll probably wouldn't be all the helpful.
The art of the game is quite nice, but there isn't a clear enough distinction between background and foreground. Often times I would simply walk off ledges because I coudln't tell where the edge was. In one section early on, there was a lake of acid (or a dangerious looking green liquid at least). There was a platform and then what looked like a little island of rock. But I honeslty couldn't tell if this island was part of the foreground or the background just by looking. I finally reasoned it had to be foreground and made a leap of faith onto it. But until I actually landed, I couldn't honestly have told you what was about to happen. That's how poor the distinction is, although some areas are better/worse than others.
Finally, while not nearly as problematic, I feel I should also mention that the lack of an interactive map in a game that has a "metroidvania" tag seems like an unnecessary addition to the game's difficulty. You get maps (you have to buy them), but they're just static images on the screen. You'd be better off going old school and keeping a pen and paper nearby to draw your own. Then maybe place a coin or other small object on the paper to indicate which room you're currently in. Really, that would be a lot more helpful than anything the game offers.
Overall, the game is just a struggle to play. Not because the game or gameplay itself is difficult, but because the mechanics and design of the game are poor enough that they hinder the player. Really, with a few tweaks, I think this could be a great game or at least a much better one. But as it is, it's just not worth the time.

The Bridge is a neat journey that offers a vigorous challenge and some (slightly) new concepts to those well versed in puzzle games.
Gameplay revolves around manipulating  gravity around your character, who can't run or jump, and various objects in order to reach a door. As the games goes on more mechanics are added: locks, fast moving boulders, and so on. After the first play though you could always challenge yourself in the mirrored world (which is more than just inversions) or try to find all the wisps.
The art and animation are praiseworthy. Impossible architecture fills out the hand-drawn world. The M.C. Esher style is well done and makes this game stand out. Though I enjoyed the art, at times I felt like Air Force academies could use this game to train pilots.
In many ways this game is companion to Braid. Where Braid revolved around the concept of freedom in gameplay (running around and messing with time), while The Bridge seems to deal with restraint (physically limited and trapped in gravity). Braid's vivid water-colors also act as a counterpoint to The Bridge's hand drawn black and white style. Though I am simplifying, these differences (and many more) are interesting to note and for that I think the Bride deserves more attentino.
There is a lot of depth to this game (upon close inspection) and it is brimming with challenge. Puzzle fiends should have a great time with The Bridge, casual puzzle fans will find a nice challenge.

Shadow Warrior (2013) is a fun reimagining of the original Shadow Warrior. Gameplay is best described as "Serious Sam Lite" due to the hordes of enemies that can get thrown at players as you progress through levels. The aresenal wielded by players includes the typical firearms you'd wield in an FPS along with a sword (that's a personal weapon you'd wield more, especially since the viseral melee combat can be much more fun) that is complete with its own moves. The story itself is also fleshed out in comparison to its original, involving a sword and some family drama between ancient beings. The only con I can think of from playing the game is that guns feel more suited for boss though that may be due to the fact that fighting with a sword can be fun, especially with the dismemberment that comes with slashing your foes.
The game itself also makes throw backs to the original in form of not just the main character and his (soon to be former) boss but also in fortune cookies complete with their own quips and sayings, arcade machines of the original Shadow Warrior (along with some other games like Serious Sam), and even the bathing anime girl from the original Shadow Warrior (unfortunately, Wang doesn't make any response to her though luckily she doesn't try to shoot you).
If fighting hordes of demons from the Shadow Realm interest you, I recommend it. If you are a fan of the original Shadow Warrior, I recommend it.

I have been a fan of Minecraft for many years, and have played many spin off games. None have come close to Minecraft, and Minecraft with Mods just seemed like all you could ever need when it came to games in it's genre.
However, there were things that Minecraft, even with Mods, never did perfectly. For example, I built Ships in Minecraft and enjoyed it, but they weren't the best. First, they were fixed in place. May as well be a building, even if it was a pretty good looking building at that. Second, they didn't really DO anything. They looked cool and you could walk around them, but that's about it. I mean, you could add redstone functions and stuff but they really didn't have a purpose. Also, once Minecraft or the mod packs were updated, you would have to restart your world from scratch or try migrating your saved world to the new server. Good luck with that!
Enter StarMade- a game which does so many things right. If you ever found yourself wanting to build ships from scratch like in Minecraft, this is your game. Period. It's not just the fact you can make ships block by block- you can actually FLY them. I mean, through space. You can add functions to them, such as shields, thrusters, doors, turrets, lights, and armor. You can add Weapons like Missiles, Beam Lasers, Cannon lasers, pulse weapons... You have to build power for your ship, and you can make use salvage beams to gather materials. You can dock to other ships or space stations, meaning you can effectively have carrier ships. Ships have artificial gravity, and best of all- it's all multiplayer as well.
How cool is it that you can build a carrier ship with your friends onboard, have them fly off in fighter jets as you pilot the large carrier ship? As cool as it gets if you ask me. You can also build space stations and explore small planets with their own gravity. You can use black holes to travel across the galaxy, and there is infinite space to explore. Of course, don't forget space pirates you can fight.
While the game is early access, you get a very amazing experience for the money. Crafting isn't the same as Minecraft, but it is still fun. The core of the game is about making your own fun, but there is a growing community of people and plenty of online servers you can explore.
While there are of course cons to the game. Some may find the lack of clear goals a turn off, or how their is an initial learning curve with how the ships work, however, If you can make your own fun building with friends, salvaging, and attacking pirates, and aren't afraid of looking online if you have a quick question, than you are in the right place. While the game can use more content, there is plenty here to warrant getting into the game now as there is plenty to keep you busy. Money well spent.
If you are still on the fence, I would like to tell you about the Blueprint system. You can save Blueprints of ships you build, allowing you to create the same ship again, even on other servers. You can even take ships you create in solo play to multiplayer servers, or take ships you create from old versions of StarMade and play them as StarMade is updated. I have not lost a ship through all the updates we have had in the last year thanks to the blueprint system- compared to Minecraft where I have had to restart servers and lose everything every time.

With the many platformers and puzzle games constantly being released, The Bridge changes up the puzzle genre with an extremely unique take on puzzles. This game forces the player to view the game in different ways. The mind-bending puzzles has the player's reevaluate the preconceptions they've had on physics and perspective of the world.
"It is Isaac Newton meets M.C. Escher."
The puzzles consist of one or many intricate architectures where the player has to manipulate gravity to complete the levels. The levels of the puzzles gradually increase, leaving a sense of accomplishment after completing them. The beginning puzzles start out extremely easy, letting the player finish in a minute or two, but the puzzles towards the end can leave a player stump for days unless they look up a guide or have someone else look at the puzzle (a different set of eyes can look at the puzzle at a different angle).
Not only is The Bridge a highly intellectual game, the artwork is something to behold. Many art enthusiasts would enjoy the game, simply for the art. The art style is hand drawn black-and-white lithograph. At first glance, the art did not appeal to me, but after completing the game 100%, I saw how beautiful something so simple can be.
With all that said, I dare you, reader, to complete this game 100%. The puzzles can leave you weary and your brain hurting, but the sense of accomplishment is well worth it.

The Bridge is a 2D puzzle game with beautiful Escher-like architecture and level design, hand-drawn black-and-white art and its own laws of physics. It is divided into 48 levels with the first half requiring minimal use of logic and feeling like somewhat of a pushover; fortunately, this is mostly remedied in the second half—a mirrored version of the first with additional obstacles thrown in and where a greater number of puzzles actually make you think.
The puzzles start off easily enough, with simple gravity manipulation and key collection, then introduce additional elements consistently: deadly balls which roll as you rotate the environment and can adhere to their own laws of gravity; points which invert gravity and shift you between black and white dimensions where you may only interact with objects matching your current color; vortexes which suck anything near them into place and hold them there until deactivated; mirror images of yourself which require entering multiple doors or picking up multiple keys simultaneously to progress; and gravity curtains, where you may remain stationary while rotating the world to work objects into their desired positions relative to your own.
The Bridge features Steam achievements and some well-hidden collectibles to find.  Gamepad is natively supported and the controls are very simple, consisting of walking, rotating the environment clockwise or counter-clockwise, and rewinding time when you make a mistake.  It feels very reminiscent of Braid at times, but the puzzles aren’t as satisfying or clever as those in Braid and the overall difficulty curve should have been based on the second half of the game. Anyone who stops before the mirrored world is doing themselves a disservice and, if I had to judge the game based on the first 24 levels alone, I would have to judge it much more harshly. As a whole, The Bridge manages to be a worthwhile puzzle game and to feel very solid despite being made by two people.

Battlerite is a mix of the World of Warcraft arena, the adrenaline of a 1v1 fighter like Mortal Kombat or Street fighter and the character style of a MOBA like league of legends or DOTA 2.
It's well wort your attention and you should really try it out if you have ever played any of the above. Already in early acces it's a balanced and competitive experience.
The gameplay is fast and rewarding, there is no RNG wich means that if you are better than your opponent you can and  will kick their♥♥♥♥♥ The 2v2 format is perfect for a "solo que" system as it makes teamplay possible whilst minimizing the chanses for afks or trolls. It also gives your actions much more meaning and bigger consequences. If you play bad in Battlerite you are going to lose because you're half your team whilst in a game like LoL or DOTA 2 where there are 5 players in each team you can still get carried if you play bad and you can still lose even if you play good.
The characters are designed in a way that allowes for outplays to happen. There are no fixed abillities (other than shields) and everything can be dodged. Majority of caracters also have ways of becoming "imaterial" or ignoring all effects for a small period of time.There are many "trances" or counters that make your caracter enter a state where if you get hit by a projectile or melee strike you get a benefite. This allows for great moments and mindgames as you try to trick your opponent into using their trance and get them to trigger yours. All this and more makes winning feel rewarding as you can clearly tell how you played better than your opponent.
I have personally felt in love with this game after spending the last 6 years playing League of Legends. This game has been really refreshing for me because of how little time you spend waiting for things. Playing a game of league takes so long and is filled with so much nothing. In battlerite farming is replaced with fighting, walking form lane to lane is replaced with trying to get the last hit of the middle orb befor the enemy, watching your allies carry you for 20 minutes after a lost laningphase never happens because there is no laningphase or snowballing as that would ruin the competitivness, instead of getting smashed to pieces by a vayne your bot lane fed you are picking the right battlerite for the next round after you lost the last because of a stupid misstake your never going to do again. All there is is fighting. Positioning, outsmarting, maximising damage and settign up cc combos with your friend is all you do. And it never gets old.
The negatives for me have been the lack of progression. You have a level on each caracter that you can level up to ten but the rewards haven't been to intriguing. There is no way of showing of these levels either and the time it takes to get a caracter to level ten isn't to long. A simple fix would be to take away the cap of the levels and let you brag about it in some way. Otherwise there is really nothign but the ranking system to progress through. As far as I know there have been no talk about a progression system either unfortunatly.
What keeps me playing is the rewarding feeling of playing better than the other guy.
Over all I hope you give this game a try when it is released and becomes free to play in early 2017.

It warms my heart to say that the final review of Review Series I was a very positive experience. Let’s get this rolling.
I – Story [10/10]
Shadow Warrior is a first-person shooter from Flying Wild Hog. It is a reboot of the classic Shadow Warrior released in 1997 by 3D Realms.
The player assumes the role of Lo Wang; an assassin who works for the Japanese industrial magnate, Orochi Zilla. Wang is sent to purchase an ancient katana (the Nobitsura Kage) from a collector named Miyazaki. Miyazaki refuses the offer, so Wang tries to take the sword by force. Wang is ultimately captured, but escapes when demons attack Miyazaki’s compound. Miyazaki himself is killed in the attack and Wang allies himself with a demon named Hoji. Hoji explains that the Nobitsura Kage  is capable of slaying immortals and cannot be touched by demons. He also explains that the Nobitsura Kage is actually three swords and so, Wang seeks them out.
Through the course of the game, Wang hunts several “Whisperers” (magical golems which contain a memory that a god chose to hide away). By slaying these Whisperers, Wang absorbs the stored memories and learns of the history of the immortals. In the Shadow Realm (the realm of demons) the rain is created by the weeping of Hoji’s sister, Ameonna. Hoji and Ameonna had an incestuous affair, which made her happy and stopped the rain. This caused a drought throughout the realm and, when the affair was discovered, Hoji’s brothers separated the pair and disfigured Hoji as punishment. Ameonna accepted her responsibility to bring rain to the Shadow Realm and Hoji was became bitter. Hoji then conspired to poison his sister, putting her into an eternal slumber and, thus, causing a second great drought. Hoji was consequently banished to the mortal realm. Enra, the ruling immortal of the Shadow Realm, saw that only the sacrifice of a god could revive Ameonna and began to seek the Nobitsura Kage. Enra hired the mortal Orochi Zilla to find and assemble the sword, promising a cure for his paraplegia and an army of demons with which Zilla could conquer the Earth.
Wang tracks down the swords that comprise the Nobitsura Kage and assembles it. He then proceeds to the Shadow Realm to confront Enra. Wang is captured by Enra and has the Nobitsura Kage taken from him. Enra tries to sacrifice Hoji to revive Ameonna, but Hoji disarms Enra’s Whisperer and hands the sword back to Wang, forcing Enra to retreat from them. By touching the Nobitsura Kage, Hoji dooms himself. Lo Wang corners Enra, who allows Wang to kill him, since he is the only sacrificial candidate left. Ameonna awakens and, upon seeing the lifeless body of Hoji, she weeps and brings rain back to the Shadow Realm.
I thought that the story was very original and had a lot of great characters. I had a great time playing through it.
II – UI [9/10]
The user interface in SW was almost perfect for how the game was set up. It was easy to see where your health and stamina were located, how much ammo remained in your guns and in your ammo reserve, and everything else you needed to know in combat. Even items that could be interacted with glowed when you got close to them.
My one actual complaint was the complete lack of a map of any kind. I got lost once or twice doing some quest-related backtracking and a map would have been invaluable.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
I don’t know that I will be able to throw enough praise at the gameplay of SW. In a world of gaming that is utterly infested with substandard FPS games, Shadow Warrior was a gory, profane breath of fresh air.
For starters, the katana that you’ll have (and most likely use) the entire game was easily the most fun you’ll have when it comes to combat. If that katana was Oprah Winfrey in another life, everyone was getting free dismemberment and decapitation. You can just have at it and hack and slash your way through raging hoards of demons, or you can actually apply yourself and use some sweet, sweet special Ki attacks.
Not once did any gun lose it’s relevance during the course of the game (assuming you were diligent in applying upgrades). They all had alternate modes of fire as well, arguably the best of which is the hammer fanning feature on the revolver. And you don’t just have to Clint Eastwood fools to death, no, you have a variety of choices in your deadly arsenal. We’ll cover that more in the Content section though.
The aspect of gameplay that I enjoyed the most though, is the back and forth between Lo Wang and Hoji (and not to mention Wang’s one-liners). I would be amazed if you could play this game for ten minutes without chuckling at least a little bit.
IV – Content [10/10]
There was a pleasant and comfortable amount of content in Shadow Warrior. There are ten different weapons you’ll find during the course of the game. There are the standbys of all FPS games (shotgun, rocket launcher, flame thrower, etc.), but you also have access to exotic and unique weapons like demon hearts or demon heads. To clarify that just a little bit, the demon heads shoot huge beams of energy from their mouths and, yes, you decapitated it yourself. Each weapon has it’s own set of upgrades as well.
You have a good set of upgrades to work your way through as you play the game. Some you’ll consider more worth it than others, but when isn’t that the case? Also, the campaign was a good length and a good difficulty (at any setting you’ll feel challenged).
V – Visual [8/10]
The graphics in Shadow Warrior are, admittedly, not the best the generation has to offer. That being said, they’re still good graphics. The demon models are fantastic and the sheer amount of gore displayed is enough to sate even the most avid Mortal Kombat veteran. The weapons are all very unique and each one has it’s own endearing quality in an aesthetic way.
VI – Audio [10/10]
When a game gets the music it right, that’s a good thing. When a game get’s the music perfect, that’s an amazing thing. There are some quality, metal backing tracks that set the perfect mood for relieving demons of their appendages. Whether your scrounging for cash or impaling those obnoxious winged ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to walls, you’ll have some good tunes to accompany you.
VII – Overall [9.5/10]
Overall, Shadow Warrior is a great game and a shining example of what a FPS can be. If you’re sensitive to gore or profanity (why are you here?) you may want to steer away from this one. If that sort of thing is right up your alley and severed limbs don’t bother you, this is the game for you. It is absolutely worth the price tag, but if you can get it on sale, even better.

Arms Race in Space
It’s been about two hours of furious clicking, and I still haven’t finished this battlecruiser. I am so focused on getting this done so that I can as soon as possible take it into outer space and blow the crap out of my rivalling faction’s outpost that lies 9 solar systems away. I must prove like many other factions in StarMade, that the “ACE Pirates” is a faction that are to be taken seriously and I am sure that when this battlecruiser is done, they will never even consider launching a missile at even the weakest of our mining ships.
StarMade is all about building spaceships and continuously upgrading them as time flies by while having such a blast. Whenever one thought that one’s interstellar battlecruiser was too big, an hour or two later they will not think so anymore. StarMade creates this need, this addiction to keep on destroying, keep on mining and to keep on building that spaceship of yours that you will brag about to all the people on the server – until someone with some space dreadnought that is twice your size shoves a missile down your throat. When such things happen, StarMade emotionally attached you to that ship, and it emotionally attached you to making that ship beat someone else’s. StarMade makes you think of your spaceship as your children, you want the best out of them and you keep on encouraging them – or even force them to be better that others. That’s what happens when you get this thought; “how shall I build this weapon system to one-shot that guy?”.
At first StarMade would seem very similar to Minecraft – which it is in both its aesthetics and fundamental gameplay. They are both games based on blocks and building. But apart from that it has what Minecraft lacked and made me stuck to the game ever since, namely to be able to build space ships. Not only are the textures so much sharper, and the building materials come in different shapes apart from cubes, but the scale of StarMade is just outstanding. Robin Promesberger spent a decade to code the engine for it and runs so well on even low end pcs. With this you soar the universe, explore millions of different planets, solar systems and galaxies. There is not one world, but hundreds to explore – all in one game!
If you thought space was lonely and think that it’ll be like that in StarMade, I’m sorry but you thought wrong. StarMade’s multiplayer is a fantastic experience of interacting, trading, obliterating and befriending your fellow astronauts in this vast universe of space. Not only is it fun to mine and survive in space alongside them, but joining a faction by teaming up and creating a coalition can be just as exciting. A fully established faction will sometimes be forced to operate in such a way that is almost as complex as modern day politics! For example, a leader that divides certain members to either build, produce blocks, fight or mine. Mine where? When? How? With what? These are all fundamental questions that must be solved within the faction, forcing the players themselves to figure out what’s best for them and for the faction so that they can stand out as a better faction. This is StarMade’s multiplayer experience, which is both unique and enjoyable for the casual to hardcore gamer.
I mentioned continuously upgrading your spaceship and how this hooks you onto the game. To be able to continuously upgrade your ship by adding more modules, more shields, more guns, you have more or less no limits opposed to other scifi shooting games. Your ship depends all on how well you can plan, how well you choose to get resources, and of course how well you design your ship with all these resources you get. Much like the modpacks for Minecraft such as tekkit and feedthebeast, you can build huge factory complexes. In StarMade these are the essential and fundamental parts for wrecking space scrubs in the universe. It takes a long time to get a hang of it, and there is quite a steep learning curve, but you’ll eventually understand the game, and when you do you can do anything you ever wished to do in in space. The part of StarMade that I find most satisfying is when you explode someone’s ship with a missile whilst piloting the spacecraft made of all those resources which you collected and strived hard to turn into modules in your factory complex. It is very amusing to watch the guy’s dead ship drift away for you to take.
Like more or less everything in this universe, there has to always be the downsides. StarMade unfortunately lacks many sounds for certain parts of the game and gives a less immersive feel. Currently the game has a very limited AI simulation, which means that playing the single player mode will feel very lonely. However this can be quickly solved by hopping on to the first multiplayer server in the conveniently placed server list that exists in the launcher. StarMade also lacks a proper third person view perspective, something I and probably many other people think is a natural view point in games.
But for being in alpha, that is quite alright, and the gameplay itself is outstanding and addictive to say the least. StarMade is about building stuff, and sometime later blow stuff up with that stuff. The intense multiplayer creates the competitiveness to progress with designing your ships, and forces this competitiveness to go on. And in the process, forces you to blow up one another in this blocky arms race in space.
The Good
+ Infinite universe,
+ Smooth immersive multiplayer,
+ Well established ship building system
+ Rewarding progression
The Bad
- Lack of AI simulation
- No third person view
- Few sounds.

I personally loved this game, but I will use this review to highlight a few things that may turn off players.
The lack of convenient fast travel was probably the most frustrating thing for me, especially since I usually go for the 100% and thus need to backtrack a lot. I guess I could handle it because I enjoyed the area design so much, but it was definitely a major issue. Sometimes you had to backtrack though lengthy areas just to get from point A to B, with the trip simply being a chore. Exploring an area for the first time is amazing, but you really don't need to do it ten times.
Then there is the charm issue that some people often complain about. Some charms seem mandatory for fixing what seems to be missing features, most notably seeing yourself on the map or automatically picking up currency. I personally argue that these charms are needed only for exploration, and that you can just choose a different loadout for bosses, which is where you mostly need strong charms, but it is still aggravating at times.
People also seem to have an issue with getting back to a boss after dying. I personally didn't mind that much, the trips weren't that long (1-2 minutes at most), but a safe point right in front of at least major bosses would have been nice, if only not to be thrown out of the flow, so to speak.
High enemy health also seems to be a common complaint, but I personally had no issue here. It was simply up to the player to figure out the fastest way to dispatch enemies, and once you did, most enemies could be dispatched quickly, even with unupgraded weapons. The absence of health also didn't bother me, as it created intense situations where you found yourself low on health but hoped that just a few more hits would finish the fight.
Some people also seem to complain about controls, but I believe that is entirely unjustified. The controls are incredibly responsive and tight, allowing you to evade even narrowly and take any opening that presents itself. If you get hit, it's your fault.
Lastly, I should mention that this game is hard and unforgiving. If you get frustrated easily, you may want to turn back now. There is no easy mode, and the only way to overcome challenges is to "git gud". If you're not into dying against the same boss 10+ times, only to get a little better each time until you finally make it, this game is not for you.

***EDIT-2015***
If you had told me at the time I first wrote this review that things were just about to turn around and that this would become one of my favorite games of 2015 (and hopefully later) I would have had you committed.
But that's exctly what happened. Big shake ups went on at Simbin and the company is now called "Sector 3". But more than that, whoever it was that made the majority of the wrong decisions about this game must either be gone or he/she has seen the light.
I have changed my review to reflect the great advances this game made. I will also write a more comprehensive review at some point in the future, but for now suffice to say that this game should be in every race enthusiast library.
-------------------OLD REVIEW BELOW-------------------------------
It pains me not to reccomend this game. I own every single Simbin game ever published and I still race in a GTR2 league with weekly races where we manage to have 30 to 40 rivers per 1h or 1:30 hour race. Every week, year around.
Naturally, GTR2 is showing its age, but it is still the only racing simulator with day/night transitions, full pit experience, large fields and all the other features that make a simulator awesome.
We waited for GTR3 for a long time and we were very excited by Simbin early previews of their new sound engine. It was truly something to behold.
Then GTR3 fizzled and Raceroom Racing Experience came out as a "free to play" game. Initially I was quite impressed. The sound was awesome and far superior to anything else out there. The graphics, while not the best, were better than their latest offering (the Race07 series). The car handling was OK. Nothing too advanced, but passable.
Even as a free to play game it had promise and initially we belived it would become something at least playable if not a substiotute for GTR2.
After the launch, which only included hotlapping as an activity and an "Apex hunt" game that, while a good training tool, seemed forced and certainly no substitute for the missing features. However, since it was a new game  I even purchased about $70 of content, betting on the upcoming and promised availability of AI cars and multiplayer.
While we knew that as a league we would be looking elsewhere for our future platform, R3 held the promise of being a good offering for casiual online racing.
Then time passed and the only new offerings were cars, tracks and ugly, useless "liveries".  The promised AI is still (as of this writing) missing in action and there is no multiplayer to speak of, just boards with hot lapping results.
The choice of available cars goes from the uninspired (cars that every sim seems to have) to some unique cars that are indeed exciting, except that they all seem to drive like one another.
Frankly, if I could go back in time I would buy only the Zacspeed Ford and the additional hillclimb track. The free cars are OK, with the BMW hillclimb car being the best of the lot and the hillclimb challenge is really the only bright spot in this game. Considering that the BMW and the hillclimb are free, I would suggest thst if you like the genre you download this game, but don;t buy anything else. Maybe the other hillclimb track and a car or two that you fancy. All the rest is just repetitive and uninteresting.
There is no weatehr, no day/night transitions, no pit stops, no telemetry to speak of, even the liveries, which are not free and there is no way to design your own, are ugly.
To me it is truly unbelievable that a company like simbin released this stillborn game. It could have been so much more, but in truth, they fooled me into spending more than double what I ever paid for GTR2 so maybe they made their money from me for the next two years. But no more. They released a DTM game that suffers from the same limitations (it has AI, but it is very weak) and for the first time since I ahve been simracing I did not buy it.
Maybe one day they will come to their senses and they will offer the same features as GTR2 offered almost 10 years ago. Maybe they'll relent anmd let players create their own liveries and the promised "Adaptive" AI will really be what they promised. Maybe one day you'll be able to compete against other humans online too, and maybe even at night and in the rain. Maybe.
When that happens, buy this game. Until then, perfect your hillclimb skills (that is really a lot of fun) and save your money.

My first StarMade Experience:
1st-2nd hours:
I get on the server (redshift). I am so damn overwhelmed by the cool spawn and spaceships docked there. I have no idea of what to do, so I request help from a fellow player. One thing leads to another, and I am now in this guy's faction. its just the guy, his friend, and me. He surprisingly has about six ships, 2 for mining, one with a jump drive, a few fighters, and some other huge ship with unknown purpose,also a space station orbiting a terraformed planet. Guy teaches me the basics, and then logs off. You can not blame me for wanting to try out the stuff. First I try building my own ship, a core, a power supply and a thruster, and I realize the ship is simple and fast. I land on the planet. I forget to press shift. ship flies off even with me getting out of it. I'm stranded in the planet. SHEEEEIIIIT. I start mining blocks, and build a pilar trying to reach the space station. I am successful, and get back on.
3rd Hour:
I now am familiar with the basic controls of the game (I took a while to get used to the controls of this one). I am curious, so I decide to take the warpship for a spin. The jumpdrive jumps about 8 sectors per jump. I start charging and jumping all over the universe,the setting is relaxed, I'm listening to some slow trance,and I am actually having a lot of fun exploring. Suddenly I see another station. "I should dock there" I thought. As I arrive near the foreign station my systems begin to fail, and I start getting blasted. I mean BLASTED by lazers and projectiles of all sorts. The ship is dead. THE SHIP IS ♥♥♥♥ING DEAD!!! THE GUY IS GONNA KILL ME!!!!!! How would I look him in the eyes, the one person who helped me out, who took me under his wing, I was ashamed. I managed to find my way back to my faction's station, and about half hour later the faction leader who took me in logged on. oshitoshitoshitoshitosheeit. First thing he asks me: "hey man, have you seen the jumpship, you know the one that looks kind of like a satellite?" "Y-yes I s-s-aw s-someone stealing it". He looked at me, then he kicked me out of the faction, and blew me back to spawn.
10/10 would steal a jumpship and lie about it again

How could Duke Nukem Forever go so wrong, yet the new Shadow Warrior go so right?  All the things that made old school FPSs work back then are brought back here with just the right tweaks to fit in with the younger Halo/COD crowd.  For starters, health doesn't regenerate like in newer FPSs, but you get a dandy healing spell early on that you can cast while on the move.  The spell has its limits to keep players from wading into every hail of fire, but stays effective enough to keep you in play.
Then there's the melee combat.  All I can do is agree with every other review out there on Shadow Warrior.  The makers got this one right.  As for the rest of the weapons, even the first pistol feels like it can drop a demon at ten paces.  Each new weapon is encountered in such a way that feels integral to the story and game.  And no, you don't have to drop a weapon to acquire a new one as we see so often in modern FPSs.
For fans of the original Shadow Warrior, know that the humor has changed.  There's less reliance on Asian stereotypes and gratuitous T&A.  There is genuine wit as you listen to Lo Wang mutter to himself to stay sane, and the back and forth dialog with your partner Hoji makes you actually care what happens to these characters.
The game is also longer than I would have expected.  So you definitely get your money's worth.

Let me just add my positive review to the pile...
Frankly I'm surprised the metacritic rating is so low for Shadow Warrior. It's a well-polished game with very nice graphics, good game-play, interesting combat that rewards not spamming the same technique all the time, has a really nice and emotionally involving story (that ending!), includes Easter eggs referring to the original game for nostalgia (and refers to other popular games too), and it somehow balances a line between being ludicrously cheesy (try to keep count of how many Wang puns there are, or better yet: take a drink every time there is a Wang joke!) and being somewhat self-deprecating because they know how stupid it is, but for Shadow Warrior to not have Wang jokes and over the top cliche'd settings would just not be Shadow Warrior.
This is how you breathe new life into a game franchise. Other devs should take notes on this game, because there's a lot of childhood favourites that I would like to see get this kind of treatment.

BUY THIS GAME.
I'm writing this review at the end of 2014, and I must say that StarMade turned out to be a bit of a dark horse contender for my personal GOTY (and that's going up against amazing games like Shadow of Mordor, DA: I, and Endless Legend). I've had more fun with it than I ever had with Minecraft, despite the obvious similarities between the two games. I find myself thinking about StarMade when I'm at work, plotting out new ship designs and planning raids on other factions. I cannot recommend this game highly enough.
So what's the appeal? Why is StarMade so great?
For me, the answer is that it fulfills the promises of games like Space Engineers, Eve, STO, and even legendary franchises like the X series. It is one of the first sci-fi games I've ever played that strikes a perfect balance between space combat, ground combat, ship design, strategy, and a vibrant in-game economy. The game is still early-access, and this is somewhat obvious at times (particularly on planets, which currently do not spawn pregenerated structures or mobs), but there's just so damned much to DO - particularly if you're playing online - that you'll rarely care.
One of the most appealing aspects of the game is ship and station design. You'll start off floating in the void of space, somewhere near the center of a proc-gen galaxy. You have 25, 000 credits and some basic building components, which can be used to make a large fighter, or, more likely, a small, all-purpose vessel. Whatever you decide, every single aspect of the design is up to you. Want a donut-shaped ship? Do it! Want to fly Moya, the Galactica, or the USS Enterprise? It'll be expensive, but it's totally doable. Want turbolifts between decks, drone racks, or a tractor beam? Build the right components and you can install them anywhere you want on your ship. Be careful though, because every block you place serves an important purpose - and every block can be destroyed. This means you can lose gravity partway through a fight, potentially jettisoning your friends into the void of space. Or perhaps the logic that controls your turbolifts will go down, trapping you on the command deck until repairs can be made. StarMade is, IMO, the most complex and well-executed science-fiction simulator available, with its infinite possibilities offering countless moments of drama, terror, and triumph.
I could keep raving about how great this game is, but, well, I kinda want to play it instead. I HIGHLY recommend that anyone who's a fan of sci-fi or sandbox games give the game a whirl. Trust me, the $10 or so that they're asking for is an absolute steal.

Hollow Knight.
Well, when asked howI would describe this game, the first thing that occurs to mind, is if Dark Souls was a 2D platformer, this would be the likely result, however that's not completely fair to how great of a game this gem is.
Even when you're starting the game, and going through the options, you can already get a feel in the ambience created by the music, and the opening is done in amazingly brilliant and wonderful artwork, and that's where a lot of this game really shines, in my opinion.
The Artwork is, in a word, fantastic. There's so many other words, but that would make the review too long and I can't say enough how much of an amazing job it does to not only set up the world the game is set in, but keep you feeling like you're exploring this vast and wonderous kingdom. Each area has it's own atmospheric parallax and level designs, as well the enemies you face with give a unique, and beautiful feel, polished to a tee, experience.
The Soundtrack is possibly one of the best I've even come across in a game of this style and size. As you explore the giant bug kingdom, melodies brought to life by melancholy piano, or haunting strings, help to immerse you in this dark and tormented world. Are you move through the areas, the tone changes to match the world around you and keep you feeling like a real part of the story.
The Gameplay itself is polished, clean and smooth all over. Animations are sleek during combat and moving around the world and the controls are simple, gaining a little more complication as you gain new abilities, but always without any real hitches or clipping, or even delays and for a game that has fast, responsive combat, this is something that I feel is very important and glad to see that is part of the game.
The Combat, like with many sidescrollers, ranges from easy enemies you can defeat by standing your ground and striking them, to difficult enemies that you have to continuously dodge and only strike at the perfect time, usually from an unexpected angle and this is one of the major parts that adds to the overall difficulty of the game. Sure, you don't die in one hit, but many monsters don't give you time to heal and can knock you backwards, leading to nasty situations in which you'll likely find yourself dead. But don't fear, you can always recover yourself and try again after taking a short rest on the bench.
All in all, I'd say that this is a fantastic game that's definately worth picking up, especially if you're a fan of challenging 2D sidescrollers and if you're a fan of games set in dark, twisted worlds, as opposed to fluffy unicorns and rainbows.

Reviewing Early Access.
The game will go Free to Play but I honestly think the 20€ it asks for the Early Access are a legit price for all the fun it gives.
First of all, don't call it a MOBA. There are no towers, no minions and no base to destroy. It's just fights, teamfights over and over. 2v2 and 3v3. You move your character with WASD and aim with the mouse.
First team to win 3 rounds wins the game, every round is won by killing the enemy team. Think of it as a Team Deathmatch.
Every round you unlock a new talent (called Battlerite in the game, but they are talents just like in HOTS) that enhance your character's skills like adding damage, decreasing cooldown or other interesting new properties. With this talent system the game doesn't feel flat and predetermined as there are many viable ways to build a hero. You may want to go more offensive or more defensive depending on the enemy team composition and playstyle.
I'm finding the hero balance good so far, but this may change in any patch. Please don't.
The only negative bit I found about the game is the tutorial. It is lacking. So much important stuff isn't even mentioned in it, like what the central orb does, what the EX moves are and how to use them, how to fake-cast...
But this can be fixed with a rework of the tutorial.
I definitely think (and hope) that once this game hits release as free-to-play, we will be talking about a huge success. Keep up the good work developers.

Lastly, at the risk of making too direct of a comparison to League of Legends, the developers at Stunlock are pretty on point in terms of communication and messaging; so far i haven't seen any of the content-lacking buzzword-heavy "riotspeak" from Stunlock, and they've even gone as far as to specifically lay out how their match making works. Good luck getting anything like that from Riot.
Definitely a solid buy if you like these kinds of games, and if Stunlock plays their cards right they'll have a really solid eSports product on their hand by the end of 2017.

Let me just add my positive review to the pile...
Frankly I'm surprised the metacritic rating is so low for Shadow Warrior. It's a well-polished game with very nice graphics, good game-play, interesting combat that rewards not spamming the same technique all the time, has a really nice and emotionally involving story (that ending!), includes Easter eggs referring to the original game for nostalgia (and refers to other popular games too), and it somehow balances a line between being ludicrously cheesy (try to keep count of how many Wang puns there are, or better yet: take a drink every time there is a Wang joke!) and being somewhat self-deprecating because they know how stupid it is, but for Shadow Warrior to not have Wang jokes and over the top cliche'd settings would just not be Shadow Warrior.
This is how you breathe new life into a game franchise. Other devs should take notes on this game, because there's a lot of childhood favourites that I would like to see get this kind of treatment.
Edit: I bought the special edition because I love Hotline Miami, and really it wasn't worth the extra money, even on sale. I'm not sure what I expected with that promo sword, but it's just not worth it. Definitely buy the standard edition.

Currently the ONLY reason to buy this is to support the developer, which I have no problem doing, but based on the history of early access games on Steam - most buy an EA game, and then are upset at the lack of features, even though the EA concept is clear.  So, if you are one of those people - pass on this for now.
For others, I'll state that while you can build some ships and travel through space, flying through space is very slow and as others have noted, there isn't really much to do - you can mine stuff and you can salvage stuff - oh, and you can sell stuff to the shop in order to buy stuff.  There's stuff, stuff and pirate stations...
Despite the lack of other stuff, the game shows potential.  I really like the build aspect for the spaceships as it allows for lots of customization, but flying the ship isn't that great because of the overall control scheme - switching between flying and building shouldn't be so easy that you do it by accident and end up exiting and losing the ship in deep space.
I didn't play this game before it came to Steam, so don't know how the planets were before, but the current design is...interesting.  They have a good size to them and I actually like the multi-faceted appearance, but travelling from one face of the planet to another is kind of weird (in both a good and bad way).  One thing I don't like so far is that there doesn't appear to be liquids - lava is simply a glowing non-flowing block - dig one out from under another and the hole remains with the other lava block just "floating" over it.
Another thing I feel needs to be improved - space stations.  I know they pushed an update that changed the mix of abandoned versus pirate stations, but considering how long it takes to fly anywhere, it is still a pain to travel a long distance only to see you're being shot at by a pirate station or that the station is degraded, thus only good for scrap - and you'll need more than scrap if you want to upgrade your engines in order to fly faster.
To summarize - unless you simply wish to support the dev and/or really like space games/sims, I'd wait until more of the features are added to the game.  At that time I'll revisit this review and hopefully change that "no" to a "yes!"

This is the story of a man named Stanley.
Stanley worked for a company in a big building where he was Employee #427. Employee #427's job was simple: he sat at his desk in room 427 and he pushed buttons on a keyboard. Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk, telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order. This is what Employee #427 did every day of every month of every year, and although others might have considered it soul rending, Stanley relished every moment the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job. And Stanley was happy.
And then one day, something very peculiar happened. Something that would forever change Stanley; something he would never quite forget. He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he realized that not one single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow. No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say 'hi.' Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation. Something was very clearly wrong.
Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time. But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.

A MOBA in the truest sense of the word. You play in game modes of 2v2 or 3v3 as champions with different skillsets.
The game has no lanes or NPC minions/creeps, it is a non-stop teamfight until one side wins and the other loses.
If you become skilled in Battlerite you can quickly climb the ranks above other players as the game is based on nothing but skill. In a 2v2 you are 50% of your team and can change the flow of the battle quite a deal. This alone changes the frustration that I've had in previous games like DotA 2 or League of Legends where you are also depending on 4 others to not suck.
Battlerite is pure action, pure skill, all of the time. If you are the type of person who loves teamfights in games similar to DotA then this game is for you.
Currently the only customization for skins are recolours but I'm sure they will add more later on. You can swap out what your weapon looks like for each champion you play, swap out what mount you start the game on etc.
I'd highly recommend this game if you are a competitive person who loves the idea of different skill kits on very well designed characters.

I was a fan of the old Shadow Warrior back in the day, and was admittedly a bit skeptical about this reboot.  I agonized for days over whether or not to buy it, as the $39.99 price tag is about twice as much as the most I would pay for any game, but I finally pulled the trigger.
And boy am I glad I did!  Every part of this game glistens with care and attention, from the beautiful visuals at every level of detail to the smooth, fun, and never impossible combat.
Oh man, the combat!  It absolutely makes the game.  You are given a sword and some guns, a pat on the back, and a "go get 'em, tiger" by the game, and anything beyonf that is up to you.  Upgradable weaponry, special powers you can use on the fly without having to think too hard--or even use a special button!--to use, and best of all, some of the best sword mechanics I've EVER seen.   Your sword is lethal without being overpowered, and deeply satisfying to use, as enemies fall apart in various exciting ways when hit with it.  You can do special moves with it, if you so choose.
What stood out to me immediately was the way the enemies acted in combat.  In many modern games about fighting supernatural creatures, developers seem to forget that enemies need to feel pain.  It's an important part of how powerful weapons feel.  You'll never be disappointed in this aspect, as every enemy reacts to you: demons big and small react when shot, lesser demons sometimes cower in fear for a few moments, some enemies can have body parts blown off and still fight, but not nearly as well, and sometimes the smaller enemies will actually commit suicide in fear when you're doing some major damage!
The story was wonderful: simple and straightforward, yet growing in complexity as the game progressed, while never being unsatisfying.  Each level of this game is very long and satisfying, and it even includes a survial mode!
All in all, a fantastic game, and WELL worth the money!

Good Things:
This is a good addition to the AC series, although not my favorite, the sailing/pirating aspect is great as I really enjoyed those minor sailing missions in ACIII, the crafting and upgradable ship is good and has been improved upon and streamlined since the menu mayhem which was the ACIII crafting system.
The story is enjoyable and a breeze to play through, not a single boring or chore-like mission in the main plot that I can remember and the underwater stuff was fantastic, avoiding sharks was actually quite a challenge! I didn't think I would like how the modern day elements of the story would be implemented since the end of ACIII but it was alright, especially as you begin to hack into various parts of Abstergo to gain more information on what they've been doing and gain some extra knowledge about Desmond. The Abstergo/Modern Templar/First Civilisation stuff is something that has always interested me throughout the series so I'm pretty happy so far with how it's going and look forward to what Unity has to offer.
Bad Things:
Due to the pirating/sailing nature of the game you don't really spend a lot of time in the major towns in the game, and for me that's a problem, although you get immersed in the ocean aspects of the game the town activites are severely lacking and you just don't care so much about those places (In my 80 hours of gameplay I re-visted Havanna just once after spending about 20-30mins there in the beginning!). This is something that has genuinely been missing since ACII, in ACII you played so much in those locations that you could get around without using your map because you got to know the towns and cities so well and I really miss having that level of connection and immersion with the locations and the stories being told in them.
Sadly the stealth mechanics haven't changed at all, which is fine as for the most part in ACIV I found that stealth was better implemented than before, but as always moving from one piece of cover to another involves standing up and near-by guards all being alerted to your presence; the ability to crouch whenever you want is /still/ baflingly absent from the series at this point (something thankfully rectified for AC:Unity).
Ubisoft still insist on cluttering the UI with ridiculous amounts of information and options to turn those things off aren't specific enough to be useful. Overall I would give the game a solid 3.5 out of 5. It has it's unique qualities in the pirating/sailing/underwater things, but the story isn't as interesting as ACIII and the game itself is nowhere near as immersive as ACII

Assassin’s Creed has drifted away from the era of Desmond Miles to a totally new story arc. Gone is the convoluted plot of hunting down magical glowing orbs to protect the Earth from a decimating Sun flare. This time around, Assassin’s Creed goes all meta, making you play a game while you are playing a game with the end point of developing a game. Confused? It’s all good.
This time around you will play an up and coming Abstergo Industries employee, tasked with dwelling into old genetic memories from the Kenway line, set in the early 18th century, the time of roving pirates. Abstergo now operates as a multimedia entertainment company, much akin to Ubisoft, perhaps, and in the e-mails and conversations you will hear, it seems the developers are fully aware and enjoying this murky ambivalence between both the real and the virtual company. AC4 does a very good job in portraying Abstergo and, ultimately, the Templars in a different light. Before, they were the all ending evil bound to enslave humanity. This time around? Maybe not so much. Some of it is actually likeable.
But enough introduction. Enter: Edward Kenway, charming rogue pirate born in Wales and decided to make a fortune in the Caribbean Seas. Leaving his young wife behind, he sailed forth to make a name for himself, thinking little beyond his own profit. When it comes to character likability, Edward is light-years ahead of predecessor and pinnacle of blandness Connor. The game makes a solid effort to dwell deep into Edward’s character building and spins a convincing tale of tragedy, loss and motivational changes – while keeping it substantially different from Ezio’s initial revenge forays.
The gameplay is fluid and intense – both at sea and on land. Edwards moves with haste, and is a daredevil with the double swords – and the double hidden blades. The game introduces several changes to combat gameplay while improving on AC3 revamped counter system. You can approach combat head-on, swords flaring, and feel like a total badass; or you can run up to unsuspecting enemies and end them with the new running execution moves. The game also introduces blow darts – a new, silent way, of dispatching enemies, either by putting them to sleep for a few moments, or making them go on a berserker rage, attacking everyone in sight. That addition of the rope darts, that can be used to pull or hang enemies is also a welcome one, but comes a little bit too late in the game to be of proper use. It would be so much better to have had this in a feudal Japan setting, wouldn’t it? Hint hint.
While at sea, you will command the Jackdaw, a very competent Brig that you can, and very much should, care for and upgrade as much and quickly as possible. By late game your ship should be very capable to stand up to massive Man-o-Wars and you’ll feel like an invincible terror of the seas, indeed. Among the great mechanics introduced to naval battle, you can now fire long range, heavy hitting mortar shots, sail-wrecking chain shots, highly destructive heavy side shots and drop fire barrels from the back of the ship to hinder pursuing enemies. You can now board and take over ships when they are damaged enough, plundering them for materials you will need for repairing and upgrading the Jackdaw and creating your own war fleet. Naval battle has been refined into an intense affair, especially when set up between several enemies, rough seas and rogue waves. It is, by far, the best pirate naval warfare simulation out there (sorry, Sid Meier!).
The new out-of-the-Animus section has become a first-person small exploration game as you wander around Abstergo’s Google-like offices, hacking computers as commanded by your IT overlord, collecting post-its and peeking through security cameras. The hacking games are extremely easy and nowhere near as frustrating as the old painting puzzle games from the past. The unlocked information that you get by completing these challenges is nice enough to guide a new player through the most recent events of AC, and to provide the seasoned player with a lot of nice lore. Still, the whole history seems too convoluted to make much sense, at least in these early stages.
All in all, I’d say the lacklustre point in Assassin’s Creed 4 is the Assassin’s storyline itself. It never feels quite up to par with previous instalments, and never manages to grip the player’s attention as strongly as Kenway’s own personal storyline. As an entertainment, AC4 is truly the best instalment in the series since AC2, with a streamlined gameplay that makes combat, exploration and completion more intuitive and, above all, more fun.
Extremely recommended whether you like Assassin’s Creed as series (especially if you felt let down by AC3), or if you need a great action-adventure game that will scratch your pirate itch. For crying out loud, Blackbeard’s in it! So go forth, and live the good life!

Reviewing Early Access.
The game will go Free to Play but I honestly think the 20€ it asks for the Early Access are a legit price for all the fun it gives.
First of all, don't call it a MOBA. There are no towers, no minions and no base to destroy. It's just fights, teamfights over and over. 2v2 and 3v3. You move your character with WASD and aim with the mouse.
First team to win 3 rounds wins the game, every round is won by killing the enemy team. Think of it as a Team Deathmatch.
Every round you unlock a new talent (called Battlerite in the game, but they are talents just like in HOTS) that enhance your character's skills like adding damage, decreasing cooldown or other interesting new properties. With this talent system the game doesn't feel flat and predetermined as there are many viable ways to build a hero. You may want to go more offensive or more defensive depending on the enemy team composition and playstyle.
I'm finding the hero balance good so far, but this may change in any patch. Please don't.
The only negative bit I found about the game is the tutorial. It is lacking. So much important stuff isn't even mentioned in it, like what the central orb does, what the EX moves are and how to use them, how to fake-cast...
But this can be fixed with a rework of the tutorial.
I definitely think (and hope) that once this game hits release as free-to-play, we will be talking about a huge success. Keep up the good work developers.

Assassin's creed is a series i hold near and dear to my heart so this review will be a little biased, fair warning.
The true mark of being streamlined is having several features taken out that at one point seemed as simple as buttering toast, this game suffered a great bit of that but still came out as an amazing game. Several parts from previous games were polished to a shine and the story is the best i've seen in a game in a long time.
Combat mostly focuses on the sea and fighting other ships, the times you fight sword to swod is often simplified to shooting as many people as possible then countering the rest until all your enemies are dead, with a very limited selection of weapons it's pointless to use anything other than your hidden blades and a few smoke bombs. The naval combat is fun but very easy once you have any sort of upgrades, it's not impossible to defeat a man 'o' war with no upgrades but is very very difficult.
The game has a very strained crafting system that cannot really be avoided so expect several stops at different islands to skin animals for that new gun holster or expect to attack every ship in sight to get wood for that new hull upgrade. The game would be so much better without this system but if you don't want to waste time you can pay for a "dlc" that gives you just about everything.
On the subject of pointless systems the game has a sort of "trade route" system where you sent stolen ships to get money or items from different locations, it's very time consuming and pointless, avoid it at all costs if you can. The game's shining grace is the well crafted story that tosses you in the shoes of a low life with no future and ends with a tear jerking song and credit screen that leaves you rethinking everything that was done and everything that was said.
Overall this game was a bit of a dissapointment and was a far shot from what the franchise was known for, the secondary "real world" story was a bit of a let down but was still done well, i'd give black flag a 7/10, worth it for the story but the rest is just meh.

Get. This. Game.
It's easy to get into, and deceptively complex.  For example, they have logic blocks, aoe triggers, effects (on pretty much everything from lights to weapons) that you can do all kinds of  things with.  Those are  just a few examples.
The game is freaking huge...not sure if it ever ends tbh...so many sectors in a system, systems  in a galaxy, galaxies in π and you have 42 (Gorilla math was used).
The exploration is like a box of chocolates.  You could find a random shop to buy and sell  things, you could find a pirate station with turrets and ships attacking you, or asteroids, and I even hear you can find  a city but I've yet to find one.  There's planets and asteroids to mine, stations to build,  ships of every kind to make.  There's cloaking, radar jamming, scanning, jump drive (warping / long distance travel), push / pull weapons (tractor beam anyone?), drainers of all types, cannons, missiles, you name it, they probably have it.
You can save your ship designs locally and on servers (multiplayer) and load them onto  another server using blueprints.  Think template that you fill with all the components and when the blueprint has all the parts it  needs you can spawn it.  You can build bases and outposts, or repair undiscovered /  unclaimed stations and  claim them as your own  / build on it.  There's factions (corps  / guilds) and every faction gets to claim 1 home base which is invincible to damage unless  they run  out of faction points (hard to do unless you claim alot of systems or die alot),
Very customizable server settings so each multiplayer server you play on is probably different from every other.  You can customize your singleplayer server.cfg as well if you so choose.
The cons:
This is more on the servers you play on but when there's alot of people it tends to lag / warp.  (It's Alpha).  The initial RAM settings for the game is 1024  which  is really low.  If you are on a  64 bit OS you will want to download the 64 bit Java and change the RAM settings.  You can do this by going to the menu in the launcher > Options > Memory settings
I have 16GB RAM so I changed mine to 8192 1000 1000  and I stopped getting running out of memory errors  in game.  You will also most likely want to disable procedural background if you get alot of lag...caused me several seconds delay getting out of my ships in high pop servers.  All these options can be changed in the launcher, there's also advanced settings in  the launcher.
All in all, this is a very fun game I would highly recommend it and I would buy it again.  I figured sooner or later there wont be a free demo and the price will most likely go up so why not support the devs now and not have to worry about it later on.

Really amazing sandbox game.  One of the best early access games I've tried and well worth the money.  The scope is very ambitious but even in this early state it's a TON of fun to play.  If you like the building elements of Mincraft and don't mind a similar rough art style this has similarities in the building aspects but it stands apart in scope.  Explore hundreds of planets.  Build buildings, spacesports, starships, space stations, mine asteroids and planets,  and combat pirates and loot their stations and ships to make yourself a fortune, make friends trading (or enemies).  There is a simple but broad crafting tree (lots of possibilities for more and a ton in already)  Full instrumentable logic elements and basic animation capabilities (eg open/close doors, elevators etc) Automated build via chained factory systems with upgrades are in.  Weapon and mining systems for ships are customizable (down to color and damage effects eg. explosions, EMP etc)  Cloaking devices, jump drives and shielding are all customizable and craftable for your fleet.  There is a faction/claim system for most entities (ships/stations/planets/sectors)  The universe feels massive with lots to explore including derlict ships ripe for the plundering if you can keep the pirates from one shotting you.   Multiplayer servers allow combat and/or cooperation.  Private server support and hosting services are already established and work well.  There are a few graphical and sound bugs that are an annoyance but no showstoppers.
The Dev's are clearly passionate about their work and have posted several videos/tutorials.   You'll definately get your money's worth.  The learning curve for the interface is a bit steep but there are a number of in game tutorials to get you in the right direction and after a bit of a rocky start I'm feeling very comfortable and can quickly spin up new ships, turrets, stations etc with relative ease.
I expect I'll be spending a lot of time in the starmade universe!
Oh and full Oculus support (head tracking and 3d)  WOOT!

I have now, when I'm writing this review, finished the game the second time. And this, by far, won't be the last time!
Before you read on, you should consider that I haven't played the original Shadow Warrior from 3D Realms. So everything I say may or may not be applicable to the old title and could be credited to 3D Realms instead of Flying Wild Hog.
Shadow Warrior is based on the Havok Engine (yes, the very same engine Skyrim uses, in which you can't even walk over random stuff laying on the floor without hurting yourself...).
Another thing I don't like about the game is the poor transition between ingame and cut scenes (e.g. the sheathing animation of the sword right before a cut scene, in which you suddenly have your sword drawn again).
But the biggest disappointment was the sword fighting. I hoped for it to be just like in Mount & Blade (for the ignorant reader: being able to direct the slashes with moving the mouse while attacking), but it isn't. The direction is changed randomly from attack to attack.
Well, you may ask, why did I upvote this game? Easy question, easy answer: The story owns!
In this case it's gold!
The previously used word 'disappointment' was an overstatement, to be honest. I got this game cheap at the Steam Summer Sale or a Humble Bundle (I just don't remember) and I didn't expect anything of it. The bigger was my surprise as something that started so humbly with retrieving a sword from a rich guy for another rich guy turned out to be something so big that it goes beyond everything we know. Sadly, I can't really go into detail without spoiling it. But I experienced the story as touching, unique and new, one that truly differs from the mud of rehashed stories put into games and Hollywood movies (Yes, it contains love, but doesn't everything contain love? Everything except jobs in office-cubicles, of course).
When it comes to first-person swordfighting, you don't get the control you are used to at the Mount & Blade Series, but on the other hand you are able to unleash pure havoc on the battlefield (decapitation will be the least of all things ;) ). So both games equal out somewhere. And if you are sick of cutting hordes of demons into piles of flesh and intestines, use one of the other weapons and blast them to pieces! :D (the one and only Torque would be proud of this game)
So this is what you get when you buy this game: Fun and humorous gameplay with a flagship of a story, all seasoned with a load of eastereggs and secrets, which even a good Serious Sam title couldn't deliver better... and there is the Shadow Warrior edition of Viscera Cleanup Detail, a little tongue-in-the-cheek extra.
And I didn't even mention the skills, talents and weapon improvements.
Thank you so much for this experience Flying Wild Hog!

Battlerite is a mix of the World of Warcraft arena, the adrenaline of a 1v1 fighter like Mortal Kombat or Street fighter and the character style of a MOBA like league of legends or DOTA 2.
It's well wort your attention and you should really try it out if you have ever played any of the above. Already in early acces it's a balanced and competitive experience.
The gameplay is fast and rewarding, there is no RNG wich means that if you are better than your opponent you can and  will kick their♥♥♥♥♥ The 2v2 format is perfect for a "solo que" system as it makes teamplay possible whilst minimizing the chanses for afks or trolls. It also gives your actions much more meaning and bigger consequences. If you play bad in Battlerite you are going to lose because you're half your team whilst in a game like LoL or DOTA 2 where there are 5 players in each team you can still get carried if you play bad and you can still lose even if you play good.
The characters are designed in a way that allowes for outplays to happen. There are no fixed abillities (other than shields) and everything can be dodged. Majority of caracters also have ways of becoming "imaterial" or ignoring all effects for a small period of time.There are many "trances" or counters that make your caracter enter a state where if you get hit by a projectile or melee strike you get a benefite. This allows for great moments and mindgames as you try to trick your opponent into using their trance and get them to trigger yours. All this and more makes winning feel rewarding as you can clearly tell how you played better than your opponent.
I have personally felt in love with this game after spending the last 6 years playing League of Legends. This game has been really refreshing for me because of how little time you spend waiting for things. Playing a game of league takes so long and is filled with so much nothing. In battlerite farming is replaced with fighting, walking form lane to lane is replaced with trying to get the last hit of the middle orb befor the enemy, watching your allies carry you for 20 minutes after a lost laningphase never happens because there is no laningphase or snowballing as that would ruin the competitivness, instead of getting smashed to pieces by a vayne your bot lane fed you are picking the right battlerite for the next round after you lost the last because of a stupid misstake your never going to do again. All there is is fighting. Positioning, outsmarting, maximising damage and settign up cc combos with your friend is all you do. And it never gets old.
The negatives for me have been the lack of progression. You have a level on each caracter that you can level up to ten but the rewards haven't been to intriguing. There is no way of showing of these levels either and the time it takes to get a caracter to level ten isn't to long. A simple fix would be to take away the cap of the levels and let you brag about it in some way. Otherwise there is really nothign but the ranking system to progress through. As far as I know there have been no talk about a progression system either unfortunatly.
What keeps me playing is the rewarding feeling of playing better than the other guy.
Over all I hope you give this game a try when it is released and becomes free to play in early 2017.

The game launches, it seems great, I click new game... Then I bear witness to easily one of the best introductions since Mass Effect. I won't spoil it, but it's got the touch.
You're quickly thrown into a rather beautifully crafted world rich with detail, and a fair amount of graphic settings to go with it. Even on an entry-level build I was able to average 40-60 frames on medium, and still got 30-40ish when I cranked up the post-processing. So it runs well, for sure.
The gameplay is ridiculously solid. I can hack and slash and cast all sorts of spells, using these to regenerate health with certain upgrades, or keep my distance and use skills with a large arsenal of weapons. Even the Revolver from the start of the game is... Well I slew the final boss with it. The upgrade system isn't unique, but it's certainly useful. Buy an upgrade, save up money, buy a new upgrade, repeat. But every single upgrade feels beefy and serves a purpose. Unfortunately not as much can be said about Ki and Karma upgrades. But they have a lot of use regardless. New abilities, health regeneration, ammo and money become easier to aquire, that sort of stuff. But you'll probably fall into a playstyle that renders a lot of upgrades useless to you. And that's absolutely okay.
The sprint system is coupled with a dash system. Hold shift to perform a dash in the chosen direction, and then keep sprinting. Once I learned to dash, fights became a lot more fun and intense. It won't save you from some attacks, but it will make the game more fun, and when used correctly, can make you a true Shadow Warrior.
Exploring is fun. The story is linear at best, but it sticks true to the old ways and allows for a lot of exploration, and usually rewards you for it! Not many games get to say that these days.
All in all, the game plays solid, it has replay value with NG+ and a truly hardcore mode that's even more difficult than the standard difficulties.
8/10. A lot of effort clearly went into this, and it most definitely pays off. From start to finish the game plays well, even if the occasional corpse looks like a turd.
