TL;DR Nothing new with the game play, but the story telling was amazing
To be honest, I came into this game with a negative bias because of the bigest mechanic to the game, being the ship sailing, was ripped from a mini-game portion of assassins creed 3. However, this was not a deal breaker for me.
First about the aforementioned ships. Ship combat was easily the most difficult part of the game, and that not a bad thing. The combat sequences where smooth and hit detection was never a problem, and boarding and taking over ships was actually quite fun.    The things I did not like about the ships was the upgrading portion of the ship. I often found myself grinding for materials to upgrade my ship because it wasn't powerful enough to take on a man o' war and I would get ripped to shreds. Which would normally be a good thing, but grinding for something in a game is never fun.
The land based game play was alright. There was nothing new there except for maybe dual weilding swords. It was easy and predictable, and stealth was almost laughable by how easy it was. but nothing too game breaking.
Performance regarding graphics: As a video game design major working on 3D assets such as Character design and the like, there were some things that really broke immersion for me that I'm sure a lot of people didn't even notice. For one, the clothes that you wear often had collision issues and would clip threw its self, even if you were standing still, which for me, that is unacceptable from a professional production such as this, but of course this is minor. Otherwise, the game ran smoothly for the most parts. In times there was some frame rate issues, but they were all minor. I ran the game on max settings all the time with an Nvidia gtx 770 graphics card and 8 gig of ram.
Free running in this game felt quick and fluid mostly. There were some times where my character would not go the direction I was pointing him. He would continually do the same useless move that got me no where no matter which way I pointed, thus ending in a game over from detection. This happened rarely however and otherwise the freeruning was bug free
Now time to take to the story. The story for this game is fantastic (I mean come on, its pirates, even ubisoft cant mess that up.) all the characters within the game are vibrant and colorful and they actually make me care for each one individually. Character development of your character and all the others around you is also very prominent, and only lends to enrich the environment. \
Outside the animus story on the other hand was not as good. There were a few short segments in-between long stretches of pirate looting, and each one was basically the same and then out of nowhere a plot device that had no reason for being there appeared suddenly.

The Stanley Parable. A clever, charming little game. Nothing too major but to me that is what is great about it. It's subtle messages and basic concept give the game it's style. The thing I love most is the narration. Within the entire game, meeting, becoming best friends, and even not knowing wether to trust the narrator is a wierd but somehow enticing experience. Not to mention the voice acting really brings him out. He is simply a charm throughout the game. With that, there are still some flaws. For one thing, the replay value is just shot down, once all the endings are discovered. It is fun to re-experience endings a few times but after that, it's over. And for a game this interesting, it's dissapointing when it ends that quicky. Another thing that bugs me is, the lack of secrets this game holds. This game has about 3-4 unique secrets that I can say are pretty interesting. But thats it. This game could have been incredible if there were more hard to find treasures within the game that broaden the story and gameplay. The last significant flaw is the lack of continuity. When you get all the endings, you are left with a lot of questions. How much do we know about stanley? or the narrator? Where did your co-workers really end up? What else is there to be learned about the company's dark secret and how it came to be? I hate to say it but this is one of the few games I wouldnt mind spending a few bucks on DLC. Just to be thrown back into the mystery. In the end, the game is a good little experience that leaves you wanting more. for that I give it a 79/100

I'll write a long review detailing everything more thouroughly later, but for now, this is a must buy at this price if you like metroidvania games. For those that don't know the term, this means exploration and platforming focused games, typically 2D.
tl;dr version: Great music and art, has something to offer for both casual and hardcore players. This game feels like a steal for the price even for the full $15. Personally I think this game is definitely worth at least $30, if not full $60, and personally I could not put the game down except when I went to work. Couldn't put the game down except when I had to go to work.
Pros:
+Amazing Soundtrack
+Incredibly detailed handdrawn art
+Great, surprising story, told piecemeal in a Dark Souls-esque fashion. Leaves just enough unkown to speculate, but if you pay attention it won't leave you guessing or unsure about the main story. For those who want to know everything, most of the big answers can be found, with little intricate details left for you to form your own ideas and opinions on.
+Extremely fluid and well thought out combat system. Charm system allows multiple builds to be built, primarily focused around melee combat, defense, spellcasting, and maneuverability, as well as a few basic quality of life charms such as a compass that shows your location on the map. Personally I stuck with melee and speed focused build the whole game, but I have heard of various builds that can truly break the game in tremendously satisfying ways when executed properly in the right areas. Every boss is very unique and interesting, all standing out in my memory in some way. And due to this charm system, bosses could be designed in very different ways. If one build isn't working for you or you are struggling to beat a boss with your preffered playstyle, you can switch things up and try again in an instant.
+As far as difficulty goes, this is a game that can be enjoyed casually for those just looking for a fun, quick romp without too much effort, but also has plenty of optional challenges for the more hardcore and adrenaline seekers.
++While simply beating the game does not require too much difficult combat, heavy exploration, or nerve-wracking platforming, those that wish to complete the game or uncover all the mysteries to achieve the "True End" will have quite a challenge ahead of them. Without spoiling specifics, there are three great challenges for the three main pillars of this style of game. An end/post game area known as the White Palace is an incredible challenge for platforming. The true final boss, as well as the highest difficulty of a hidden colosseum area are soul crushingly difficult but highly rewarding combat challenges that truly make you feel like you earned your victory in ways only games like Dark Souls have been able to replicate consistently. And an optional hidden escort quest that truly tests your navigation and survival skills.
+++All of this on top of not even mentioning Steel Soul Mode. For the truly masochistic, Steel Soul mode is a one life mode, where if you die, the game ends. You have to beat the game on a single life, and there's even an achievement for 100%-ing the game on this mode. Needless to say, I haven't even come close to this, nor am I sure I wish to do so, but for those seeking a true challenge, this is it. For the gods amongst us, there is even a speedrun 100% achievement. COMPLETE the game in it's entirety in under 20 hours. Personally, on my first run, I spent nearly 30 hours and haven't even gotten 100%.
Cons
-Honestly, none so far. I played the whole game and the only glitch I encountered was the final boss soft-locking where they stood still and I couldn't progress the fight. But I didn't even have to close the game to fix it, simply go to main menu and come back.

Shadow Warrior, though being a relatively recent title, clearly is a tribute to the older 1993 game of the same name, and as a matter of fact, to oldschool shooters in general. There are no annoying quicktime events, the cutscenes generally are more on the short side, and the enemies would probably laugh at you if you tried to make use of the oh-so-tedious cover mechanic found in modern titles. Instead, the game gives you a bunch of guns, a large number of enemies, even more enemies, several cleverly hidden and often humorous secrets/easter eggs, and a protagonist that can move faster than a squirrel on crack - just like in the shooters of old.
Of course the term "shooter" is not quite the right word here - while the game does, as mentioned above give you a few different guns, you will spend the vast majority of your time outside of bossfights hacking and slashing your way through the aforementioned hordes of enemies, rapidly dashing to and fro to avoid enemy blows or close the distance with those that would avoid you. Besides of a basic damage system that allows you to sever limbs and heads based on where your blows land, the game also gives you some nifty special abilities that can be unlocked via a RPG-like experience system, ranging from the classical whirlwind attack to more mystical powers such as summon a shockwave to send enemies flying, or keeping them paralyzed in a levitation field. Together with the weapon itself, this makes the combat in shadow warrior extremely fast - and insaleny fun atop of that.
On clear difference between Shadowrun and it's oldschool ideals is the presence of an elaborate background story. While it's nothing comparable to the writing of a Planescape:Torment, this game decidedly has a better story than both the "old" oldschool shooters (Aliens have landed on Earth, kill them!) and even many modern titles (Terrorists have landed in Eagleland, kill them!).
The only really weak points of the game are the rather repetitive boss fights, some minor inconsistencies in the story, and a handful of (non-gamebreaking) bugs, but other than that, Shadow Warrior definitely is one of those hidden gems for people that can't stand the three-hundreth "Call of Battlefield"-sequel and long back to the days of Duke Nukem, the Doomguy, or (the slightly later) Serious Sam.

This game is most definitely intersting.
It's got quick matches so there's more to be desired, meaning you finish a match and you just want more and more of it! Sometimes matches can last and become an anxious filled, edge of your seat, last man standing kind of deal and that's fantastic!
The music is pretty good to listen too. It's not utterly repetitive, or too extreme. It has a sort of calming feel that allows you to think and just become one with the background. Some MOBA's hype it up severely and have music that's just too over the top, even in the character selection screen and stuff, so its nice.
The characters are various and some of them are unique. Albeit they are also unbalanced in some cases, of course this is only early acess so I assume they are going to spiffy it up and balance it out in due time. I look forward to this. The customizational part is also to be desired. It's bland and many of the weapons or mounts don't really scream out "I WANT IT!" Though, I expect some more interesting looking skins, instead of recolored clothing for second teir loot.
The loot system is like Overwatch. You don't know what you'll get. It's all random. I don't personally like gachapon loot. I like to know that I'll at least get something for characters I like to play. Maybe this will change in the future, but as of right now.. eh.
The maps are bountiful for the time being. Though they're pretty much almost the same map repeatedly. MOBA's have this weird issue where they make one map design and kind of stick with it. Why not a diamond shaped map? Or a hexagon? Don't be that MOBA. I expect great things to come in the future, and this is one of them. The reskined colors and themes are neat though.
The gameplay varies with each character. There are no minions. No Turrets. No jungle. It's literally a MOBA, a Massive Online Battle Arena. 2v2, 3v3, maybe a 5v5 in the future? 10v10!? Each character has unique moves that seperate them from each other and it all goes with their backgrounds and themes. You got your Healers, Marksmen, Fighters, Tanks, Ninjafrog. wat? It's very engaging and cooperative heavy. If you and your partner don't see eye to eye you're gonna have a bad time. Prepare yourself though, with every MOBA comes the horrible stereotype of toxic players. It's inevitable, expect it, but luckily you don't have to see any of it. Turn chat off, leave it off. No big deal. It can be fast paced, especially if you're panicking.
That's pretty much it. I'll edit this as time goes along and revise. All in all, I would give this game a 7/10. Still work to be done, but it's still really good. Most certainly reccomend.

Shadow Warrior, though being a relatively recent title, clearly is a tribute to the older 1993 game of the same name, and as a matter of fact, to oldschool shooters in general. There are no annoying quicktime events, the cutscenes generally are more on the short side, and the enemies would probably laugh at you if you tried to make use of the oh-so-tedious cover mechanic found in modern titles. Instead, the game gives you a bunch of guns, a large number of enemies, even more enemies, several cleverly hidden and often humorous secrets/easter eggs, and a protagonist that can move faster than a squirrel on crack - just like in the shooters of old.
Of course the term "shooter" is not quite the right word here - while the game does, as mentioned above give you a few different guns, you will spend the vast majority of your time outside of bossfights hacking and slashing your way through the aforementioned hordes of enemies, rapidly dashing to and fro to avoid enemy blows or close the distance with those that would avoid you. Besides of a basic damage system that allows you to sever limbs and heads based on where your blows land, the game also gives you some nifty special abilities that can be unlocked via a RPG-like experience system, ranging from the classical whirlwind attack to more mystical powers such as summon a shockwave to send enemies flying, or keeping them paralyzed in a levitation field. Together with the weapon itself, this makes the combat in shadow warrior extremely fast - and insaleny fun atop of that.
On clear difference between Shadowrun and it's oldschool ideals is the presence of an elaborate background story. While it's nothing comparable to the writing of a Planescape:Torment, this game decidedly has a better story than both the "old" oldschool shooters (Aliens have landed on Earth, kill them!) and even many modern titles (Terrorists have landed in Eagleland, kill them!).
The only really weak points of the game are the rather repetitive boss fights, some minor inconsistencies in the story, and a handful of (non-gamebreaking) bugs, but other than that, Shadow Warrior definitely is one of those hidden gems for people that can't stand the three-hundreth "Call of Battlefield"-sequel and long back to the days of Duke Nukem, the Doomguy, or (the slightly later) Serious Sam.

So I know I have 2000 hours in an early access game with a negative review. The casual shopper may look at that and may wonder why that is. If I've played the game for so long, surely I must enjoy it!
I've been playing this game for about four years now. In that time I've had amazing experiences and made great friends. I've become intimately familiar with the development of the game and interacting with the community. Two years ago I would support buying this game. Maybe even last year. But not now.
The game has been in a state of alpha development for its entire existence. The developers insist that beta is around the corner, but multiple flaws in gameplay persist. Gamebreaking bugs are common place. Improper math leads to broken balancing and combat.
After four years the development team wants to completely revamp how ships are designed. Were this much earlier in development, this wouldn't be a problem. However, the developers now have to update nearly a thousand existing ingame assets in order to make them compatible with the update. Pirate, trader, and derelict stations have yet to be updated to use the current docking system, leaving them with out of date ship systems, although the update dropped over two years ago. Stock pirate vessel assets do not function properly. With the developers teasing and discussing this upcoming update, history would suggest that they will again abandon their existing assets to become utterly useless.
Another major issue comes with the lack of self-awareness that the developers have regarding the marketability of their product. After four years in alpha and three years on steam, Schine has yet to realize that not only is Starmade a niche game, but that gameplay bugs have alienated much of starmade's likely playerbase.
The final issue I'll touch upon (there are others I can discuss) is that starmade cannot handle the scale at which it is marketted. In the trailer on steam, you can see ships zooming past a massive station facility, populated by "players" interacting in a cantina scene. While this is possible, it is hardly feasible. Players desynchronize when switching between entities and at random. Ship positions desynchronize between players, causing much confusion in combat. Multiple station entities are present in a single sector, while in reality this can produce console spam and slow down the sector. Many players build massive ships, dwarfing planets in size. Yet when these ships enter combat, server and client performance comes to a halt. A common performance issue in starmade is having too many turrets on a ship. With the only limiting factor for ship design and production being patience and base storage, this results in multiplayer servers being clogged with ships with hundreds of entities that damn near crash the server every time they enter combat or load into memory.
I have other grievances with this game, but I concede that I got 2000 hours worth of fun out of it. It was a great ride, but I doubt that someone purchasing the game today could get the same enjoyment that someone who purchased the game two years ago would have.

StarMade is less appealing today than it was in 2013. The best memories I have of this game are building evil harvesting ships, going to abandoned planets and eating up damaged bases and old satellites where there was once war. I remember starting my own planet and building a factory to produce a resource, made from some plant we grew in fields.
None of that is really possible anymore. Planets have been redesigned into dodecahedrons, with visible gaps on the edges and glitchy gravity. I find this disgusting and a massive step backwards, but some have defended it as "more realistic" which is odd, given very little about the game is or needs to be.
Harvesting old materials is now severely limited. You can't go and eat up an abandoned space station anymore, according to a friend who tried.
StarMade feels like the work of a programmer, and not an all-round developer. The textures are still odd. The player model looks disturbing. Overall it lacks the creative substance to feel satisfying. I suspect this kind of design focus isn't of priority to the developer.
I fear that the community around the game is too accepting of progress for the sake of progress, instead of working forwards to make the game feel right. I waited ages for it to come to Steam, and now I've lost my love for it.
I can't recommend this game on the basis that I'm not convinced it will evolve into the game it should be. I feel it will continue to change, for better or worse, and end up a niche game, that neither wins as a sandbox or an exploration adventure. I think it is too abstract and awkwardly executed to have mass appeal, and you really need to have enthusiasm for space games to enjoy it currently.

The Stanley Parable. A clever, charming little game. Nothing too major but to me that is what is great about it. It's subtle messages and basic concept give the game it's style. The thing I love most is the narration. Within the entire game, meeting, becoming best friends, and even not knowing wether to trust the narrator is a wierd but somehow enticing experience. Not to mention the voice acting really brings him out. He is simply a charm throughout the game. With that, there are still some flaws. For one thing, the replay value is just shot down, once all the endings are discovered. It is fun to re-experience endings a few times but after that, it's over. And for a game this interesting, it's dissapointing when it ends that quicky. Another thing that bugs me is, the lack of secrets this game holds. This game has about 3-4 unique secrets that I can say are pretty interesting. But thats it. This game could have been incredible if there were more hard to find treasures within the game that broaden the story and gameplay. The last significant flaw is the lack of continuity. When you get all the endings, you are left with a lot of questions. How much do we know about stanley? or the narrator? Where did your co-workers really end up? What else is there to be learned about the company's dark secret and how it came to be? I hate to say it but this is one of the few games I wouldnt mind spending a few bucks on DLC. Just to be thrown back into the mystery. In the end, the game is a good little experience that leaves you wanting more. for that I give it a 79/100

As of now the game is in it's early stages, there are much to fix and add, and fix again. So don't be expecting the most perfect game, that has a lot of content. It is not as buggy as when I first started playing, so I am glad for that.

I think this game is best described as a puzzle game where finding all the different endings and secrets are the solutions of the puzzles.
Solving the puzzles is as simple as walking through the right doors which you can freely choose.
What makes you want to see all the endings? It is the 'fun' interaction with the narrator who interacts with what you do (or what you didint do).
This game is made to be started over multiple times so dont be scared that you have seen everything after the first ending that can come very quickly.
The biggest problem of the game is that you are never certain if and when you have found all the endings as some actions can change a part of the game but eventually will still lead to the same ending (or not?).
Spending hours trying to figure something out what may have no effect at all is more a time waste than a way to prolong the game.
My advice is to try to find all the possible endings by choosing the obvious different paths.
After 3 hours (for me) when you have the feeling you explored every outcome look up the other possibilities to find the remaining endings and secrets which prolongs the game by an hour or so.
And yes, you need to look up stuff anyway if you want to experience everything as 1 room is locked under a cheat command, which is more of an easter egg/ fun room, but then again so is 90% of the game, or is it?
I also expected some more life lessons or something greater out of the game (main reason for with i went looking for other solutions) but in the end we all just are pressing buttons anyway.
Value wise due to the short playtime and low replay-ability (after you have seen it all, although still usable to let others play it when they come over) I recommend to pick it up at a discount for which any value under €10 seems right.

Regardless of my personal experience with Dungeon Defenders, this game does the genre justice, and even though I might not play the game again, it's a highly recommended title!

Shadow Warrior, Shadow Warrior... where to begin?
The short and sweet of it: As someone who grew up with the original game and others like it I spent almost the entire game thinking in the back of my head "remember when video games were made for fun? Just... fun?" Because this game sure does. It's so riddled with little things here and there that show how much care and joy the devs put into it. Between old 2D or early 3D easter eggs (or even the fact that there are secrets all over the levels) and the blissfully chaotic combat you spend the majority of Shadow Warrior not taking yourself too seriously and enjoying it the whole ride. To finish up the quick summary, nobody who knows the roots of this company should go into Shadow Warrior expecting a good story. That said, I found myself actually enjoying what they had done with it and thought the ending was a not-breathtaking but totally satisfying conclusion to the story.
Extra notes for Purchase Consideration:
-Sword combat should be put on the expert mode for you combat enthusiasts. The type of slashing is based on the movement of the player and/or camera so you can do some serious precision work if you ever find yourself having time. Sometimes it just melts into a giant mess of "SLASH SLASH SLASH SLASH" and who knows what you're hitting at any given time. You can get some extras like slicing open demon chests to find their hearts (a bonus weapon that's a little tricky to use properly) or just extra points for beheading and limb seperation.
-For you min/maxers, you should know that you will not complete everything on your character in one playthrough. There IS a newgame+ mode if you really want to, but choose your points wisely as you progress. I played through on Hard and found that my power level rose steadily and evenly to the challenges presented.
-IT IS WORTH YOUR TIME TO DO STUPID THINGS. You are taught this by the game, even, as in earlier levels some of the easter eggs are blatant and shoved in your face so you know to keep looking. This will later manifest in ways such as "That's a suspicious wall" or "I hear a weird noise over here" and next thing you know you are crawling through an obvious secret getting money to upgrade your guns or other goodies. A lot of the easter eggs are 100% tongue in cheek which was a major plus in my book.
-Graphically it's not top-of-the-line gorgeous on the surface (some of the models look weak on close inspection), however the environments created from them and how it's all used make it a beautiful game in and out of combat and best of all can run really well on medium rigs.
-A note to parents, etc.: There is a LOT of vulgarity in this game. Your character's name is Lo Wang and you WILL be bombarded with "wang" jokes and other foul mouthery. It's not in-your-face shock factor humor like you might find in, say, South Park, but it is there and it is well done if you're an adult who isn't trying to shelter innocence.

I haven't even finished the main questline, but I'm going to review anyway, which is unusual for me.
And here's why: It's Just That Good.
I am not exaggerating when I say this is the game I've been searching for my entire life.
I have always longed for a proper adventure game - not the genre of "Adventure Games", but games about going on an adventure. I wanted something that would make me feel like Frodo Baggins, or Indiana Jones, or Jack Sparrow.
A game about high adventure and exploration, treasure hunting and ancient ruins, fending off wild beasts, and having dramatic battles.
This is that game. Now, it won't make you feel like Frodo, but Jack Sparrow and Indiana Jones? Absolutely!
If you want to sail around enjoying the truly gorgeous scenery, you can do that.
You can go whaling or shark hunting. Or if you prefer land-based prey you can hunt deer, jaguars, iguanas, and any number of other animals.
If you want to feel like a bold explorer, you can delve into the jungle, climb ancient Mayan ruins, or explore beaches, searching for hidden treasure chests and other secrets. The islands are incredibly varied, meaning that exploring them does not feel repetetive, and there are a hell of a lot of them! There are even a few puzzles hidden about.
If you like assaulting fortresses, there are plenty of those for you to attack, and it feels like something out of a movie.
And of course there are naval battles. This game, and the minigame in ACIII that inspired it, are probably the first examples of naval combat done right in a character-based (as opposed to RTS) video game. The ship combat is well done, and the boarding is seamless. The combat on board the ship is dramatic and immersive.  Fight with a pistol (that you can aim freely instead of autoshooting, if you so desire), swords, hidden blades, or your fists, according to your tastes. Counterattacks and the like are both beautifully animated and delightfully un-frustrating to use. This game also does not seem to suffer the "stand by and wait to counter" problem previous AC games had. The attacks are also extremely varied, without too awful much complexity on the player's part, so the battles are cinematic without feeling clunky - speaking of feeling cinematic, you can swing on ropes, which comes in handy when boarding ships! But if you don't feel like jumping to the other ship? You can just man one of the swivel guns and use that instead. If it's there, you can probably interact with it in some way.
I mean it when I say you can do just about anything you could possibly want to do in this world. You can even play board games with guys at taverns and pet the dogs that wander the towns! That is how varied the activities in this game are!
And unlike so many games these days, the colors are not greyed out, but exactly as vibrant as you would expect the Carribean to be - except during a storm, of course!
The downsides?
- The accessible portions of the islands are a little smaller than I'd like, but the number of them somewhat makes up for this.
- The game is buggy sometimes. It's an Assassin's Creed game, what do you expect? It's nowhere near as bad as Unity, though, and most of the bugs can be easily fixed by rebooting the game - which is not very painful, because this game saves much more frequently than previous AC games. (The one bug I encountered that couldn't be fixed by rebooting was one where the game would freeze on going near an enemy fortress - turning on volumetric fog in the graphics options fixed it.)
- You can't climb cliff walls (presumably so that the devs could get away with only giving you a small portion of the larger islands to explore). But you can still climb literally everything else - buildings, ships, trees, ruins...
- It is EXTREMELY system intensive. Be SURE you check the system specs! Just because your machine runs ACIII does not mean it will run this!
These are minor drawbacks at best, except for the one about system requirements. But that's hardly something for a review to hinge its conclusion on. With that taken into account, and how amazing I've found this game to be, I am going to call this the ultimate adventuring game: it is like playing a Pirates of the Carribean movie.
If I were to give it a ranking out of five stars, I'd give it 30.
If you can run this game, BUY IT. You will not regret it.

I am 3 hours into this game at the time of writing, and I just had to say that I think Ubisoft have really turned the series around with this instalment. I feel like they really listened to the criticism of the previous two games, particularly AC3, which I spent 30 hours in and had much less fun with than I have with this one so far! This is the best AC experience I've had since AC2, and I feel like it might even turn out to be the best of the series full stop.
The pirate setting is wonderful. The gameplay so far really takes me back to the endless hours of fun I used to have with Sid Meier's Pirates! I can definitely see myself losing a ton of hours to simply sailing around the sea, boarding other ships, building up booty and exploring islands.
One thing that I really love so far is that the game is infused with a wonderfully self-effacing humour. Suddenly we're playing from the perspective of an Abstergo employee, and Ubisoft makes itself the butt of jokes constantly. If you read the historical notes on buildings, there are really funny notes and comments added in from Abstergo employees, joking about how the consumer won't notice historical inaccuracies etc. The humour goes further than that; I laughed when one of my optional challenges was to 'air assassinate an ocelot'. There are a lot of nice little details so far that have really made the world of Black Flag a pleasure to explore.
The optional challenges relating to storyline missions are now actually doable without replaying them 10 times. I simply gave up on trying to get 100% synch on AC3 because it felt like a chore and the requirements were often counter-intuitive. Here, the optional challenges always make sense.
For the first time in the AC series, the menu system finally feels like it was actually designed for a PC instead of lazily ported from a console, so if like me you prefer a mouse and keyboard, you no longer feel like you are disabled.
I will almost certainly update this review once I've put in a bunch more hours, but from what I've seen so far I have to say Ubisoft has really done something great here!

This game is actually really good. If you're into the Metroidvania style of games then this game is for you. It's also basically a 2D version of Dark Souls which is cool in its own way. Basically, instead of bonfires you have benches and when you die you have to go kill your own ghost where you died to restore your soul orb and get all your currency back. The powerup system in this game is brilliant too. Every boss or so you get a new powerup (kinda like Mega Man) and these powerups let you reach new places. Some are optional to get but most you HAVE to get to progress. My favorite is the Crystal Heart ability so far which lets you blaze through a room in mid-air until you hit a wall or decide to stop, useful for going through long passages. The bosses all have attack patterns you need to learn and dodge. Some are fairly simple while some are just challenging and there's a few that are plain unfair but can beat with the right strategy. This game can take you at least 10 hours long depending in how good you are but is generally supposed to be about 25 hours, 50 if you collect everything. I still have yet to beat it but I am nearing the end and cannot recommend this game enough.
Pros:
Great Gameplay
Hand Drawn Visuals
Fun Bosses
Cool Abilities and Powerups
Decent Music
Cons:
Repetitive Settings (All of them have the same dark gloomy feel, I get that's the point but mix it up a bit. The Crystal Peak is the only thing I've seen so far that is different in terms of design and look but has an unfair boss that is luckily not required to be defeated to progress the game)
Otherwise, I give this game a 9.8/10

I'll begin by saying the amount of hours I have playing this game, according to steam, is in no way relevant, as the game was just moved to steam very recently.
I've been playing starmade ALOT. I've seen this game constantly change every month with new updates, each one improving the overall experience dramatically. This is still an early release, and like any other early release, your experience is not a guarenteed satisfactory one. There will be bugs. You will get frustrated. But overall it is worth it. And like many others that have reviewed this game, I agree that Starmade is one of very few early access games that I'd be ok with calling a "full" game, even though it is still not officially released.  Despite the occasional crashing and glitches, it is a very enjoyable game. But it is also a sandbox game, which means it is whatever YOU want it to be.
I would not call this a minecraft clone. Do not listen to anyone who says it is. I do believe one of the developers of the game mentioned they based it off of minecraft, but it is a totally different experience. Some people have tried comparing it to the minecraft mod galacticraft, but even that is totally inaccurate. Still, if I had to compare, I'd say starmade was a mix of Eve Online, Dayz, and yes, Minecraft.
Building: The building mechanics in this game are EXTREMELY advanced, and surpass minecraft by a long shot. It has everything I wanted in minecraft and more. There is a symmetry mode when building a ship or space station, there is an "advanced building mode" (activated by holding down ctrl in build mode), and there is an option to build more than one block at a time, and choose how many blocks on each axis (x, y or z) you want to place at once. This is customizable in the config, though the default is a max of  10x10x10. On one server, you could build up to 50x50x50. Now if you use x, y and z symmetry (and you have enough blocks for it) you can build quite a large mass in one click (though I wouldn't recommend it due to the lag involved). There is also wedges, coming in I believe 4 different types, and a wide range of different colored blocks. Overall, the things you can do with build mode is just insane.
Pvp: On many servers, they have an "anything goes" rule to pvp. Essentially, this feels alot like rust or dayz, or even EVE online.  People can easily betray you, destroy your ships and stations and then warp out of your star system before you even knew what happened. Due to a recent update, factions are now extremely important in controlling and maintaining multiple star systems in your galaxy. There is always a risk in forming an alliance with people you don't know, but it is usually worth it. I'd advise to keep some secrets, however. Don't go around the server bragging about your new ship, or how many credits you made in a recent raid on a pirate station. If you are in a faction with random people, try to keep a hidden storage box somewhere in a remote system with backup supplies in case the faction falls apart.
As for the actual combat, it can get pretty chaotic. There's three really basic weapons, cannons, damage beams and missile blocks. Theres also effect modules and computers to modify your weapons. If you connect an explosive effect computer to a missile computer, it increases the missiles blast radius. Connecting an ion effect computer to a cannon computer decreases the enemy ship's power, useful for stopping the enemy from warping away from you or cloaking. Theres also blocks like the stop effect computer, which can stop a ship from moving completely.  The shield capacitor block gives your entire ship some shields that stop your actual blocks from recieving damage. The shield recharger will recharge your shields automatically (if you have enough power) after you take damage. The amount of customization means no two pvp battles are the same, everyone is constantly improving their ships and experimenting with different ratios to try and find the perfect balance between damage and manueverability, or power consumption and protection, etc.
Mining and crafting: I can't say too much about this, as I haven't really experimented enough with the new crafting system. Mining was not very profitable before, it was too hard to find resources and the amount of work involved did not seem very worth it to me. Due to the new universe and faction update, as well as the new shop update, mining has become pretty much a neccessity if you're playing on a survival server. If you are in a system that your faction owns, you get a bonus amount of minerals when you mine a block. This does help quite a bit, and with enough people in your faction it shouldn't be too much of an issue. But if you're playing solo, don't expect to make a multi-million block ship anytime soon. The largest ship I've ever made was about 20 million blocks, though I mostly used credits to buy the blocks i needed in shops, as well as having a friend using the (very old) crafting system supply me with the rest.
Also, NOTE: This game, for the time being, IS FREE TO PLAY! It has always been free to play. HOWEVER!!! Like when minecraft was in beta, this will only be temporary. When the game is finally released, the price will go up and you will no longer be able to play for free. Ignore the title "demo version", it is not a demo. You have full access to the game for free right now. But I highly suggest buying the game as soon as possible, as it is getting closer to release every day.

Shadow Warrior asks a few simple questsions: What's better than shooting hordes of demons in the face with a bunch of cool guns? Shooting demon hordes in the face and also hacking at them with a katana. Now, what could possibly be better than guns and swords together? Guns and swords and also here's some magic. Yes its all just as much fun as it sounds. Its like peanut butter and jelly and then someone threw some honey into the mix.
It would be one thing to have all of this in a video game, but Shadow Warrior actually does it incredibly well. I don't think I have ever played another hack n slash game that does swordplay so well. The non-sword based magic is mostly on the support side of things, but the further you get into the game the more you would be wise to use it. The guns are all standard FPS guns, though they manage to look cool and none of them manage to be the "usless gun". There's a time and place for all of them. They might actually be the only "downside" to the game, due to how none of the guns are original. If you have played an FPS before, you have seen every single one of these guns. Its less of a downside and more of a neutral thing though, as though all the guns have been done before they're still done well here due to the aforementioned fact that you'll end up using all of the guns, and not just sticking to a small few like in so many other FPS's. This is of course helped by the fact that you can sever a greater demon's head, then shoot other demons with it. This is, of course, just as badass as it sounds.
The dialogue is all top notch and some of the funniest I've ever seen in a video game, or any medium for that matter. Possibly most amazing is that while the protagonist throws out a healthy portion of quips and one liners, I don't think any of them are ever re-used. The developers seem to have realized that just because something is funny the first few times, doesn't mean its going to be funny the next dozen times you hear it. The story isn't ground breaking, but it is still very good. With the incredibly addictive gameplay, they could have easily slapped on an excuse plot and called it a day. No one would really complain because the rest of the game is so fun. Instead I actually found myself wanting to move forward for both addicting gameplay AND plot.
Perhaps most importantly is that there's a demo available, so you can go see first hand how perfect this game is before throwing all of your money at the developers. This game is going to go down as one of my favorites of all time. I can easily tell when a game is instant classic material for me, its when I sit down to play it and some time 8+ hours later some outside force has to stop me from playing the game. When the gameplay is best described in terms of satisfaction as "♥♥♥♥♥♥ic", you need this game.

I in turn love this game and Ill explain why.
Parkour: The parkour of Assassins Creed 4 is similar to the outdoor free running of AC3 but with some great changes. First you don't just randomly start climbing a wall when running. It feels very smooth and clean but a notorious run up a wall and jump off that is terrible.
Combat: The combat is relatively easy unless you come across an officer or heavy soldiers. These special soldiers can parry and counter attack. The two swords make the fighting very interesting with some bad♥♥♥♥♥animations. The pistols are slightly unrealistic because when you reload it does the normal reloading animation then does the same animation 2-4 times depending on how many pistols you carry. The pistols have great variety and are made for every players needs.
Combat Extended: One of the weapons you come across is the blow gun, it can shoot 2 profectiles, a sleep dart(Knocks them out for a period of time) and a Beserk Dart(It makes the victim start attacking others. You also have an array of odd weapons. Such as the throwing knife(Self Explanatory) and the Rope Dart. The Rope Dart can be used to hang or pull soldiers to you, I didnt use these much but when I did they were extremely useful. You also have two hidden blades.
Gadgets: Some of the gadgets or items you get include the: Smoke Bomb and Money. The smoke bomb stun and blind soldiers whilst the gold draws civilians with means you can blend in.
Ship Gameplay: The ship gameplay is acclaimed and overall extremely fun and diverse. The weapons you have include the: Mortar(A long range upward firing cannon that shoots a shell that explodes over the target spewing it with cannon balls.), The Chain Shots(Used to fire at sails and slow ships), Round shot(Normal Cannon shot) Heavy shot(A flaming cannonball of close ranged death) and the swivels(After you make a solid hit against the the solid part of the ship, it leaves weakpoints that the swivels fire at dealing massive damage). After you decapicate a ship you can board it and have to kill crew and/or cut a flag and/or kill a captain and scouts. After doing this you can repair your ship the Jackdaw or send it to your fleet, you can also lower your wanted level(If your wanted level is high enough pirate hunters come after you.).
There is also assassin contracts which involve killing a target, bonus for remaining stealth, Naval contracts which you hunt down ships. You can also save pirates and unlock taverns.
Story: The story is brilliant, there is character development is solid as titanium, and the story in general is SIMPLY BRILLIANT. Nope, no spoilers.
In conclusion this game is the best in the franchise.

Simply put, it's a MOBA without any laning, pushing and farming mechanics. Right from the start, you're thrust into fighting enemy champions immediately (and only enemy champions). What's so great about this game is that it's all about skillshots and rewards fast reaction (through counters and escapes) and there's no crit chance modifiers or hit procs. Combines action elements with free form (no grid) tower defense and PG-esque levels and loot collecting for a fun, addictive, and eventually very challenging multiplayer experience. My only complaint is that defenses become unbalanced at higher levels, but if you get that far you've already gotten your money's worth.
This game is very easy to get sucked into with 5 difficulties and a lot of variation between classes. The classes have differing strengths, which makes it best experienced with 2 or 3 friends with everyone playing a different role (from the monk's enemy weakening auras, the huntresses high damage AOE traps, the apprentices more direct firing towers, or the squires strong walls). Players can also attack with their characters, leading to the constant balancing between tower boosting and player boosting stats.
There are several DLC levels and classes, which are pretty cool, but don't feel like you need them to enjoy the game. The biggest weakness of Dungeon Defenders is the unbalanced scaling which makes some defenses completely useless at higher levels. For instance the apprentice's single target magic missile tower does less damage per defense unit than the area of effect fire tower, and there's really no reason to ever build them. Also, the DLC necromancer class builds units that don't compete for resources with other players, which unbalances the game quite a bit at higher levels. Those complaints really only apply to nightmare difficulty though, and you could probably get 50 hours in before bumping into any major balance issues.

If you haven´t played the original shadow warrior, you should at least try it in my opinion. It gives you a bit of an insight to what shooters were like years ago and where does this ´´reboot´´ take it´s inspiration from. Now, I don´t mean inspiration in the sense that it reuses the same mechanics and what not, but rather the main character , some of it´s lines, the katana of course and it´s easter eggs. I´ve managed to fin most of ´em. What is the game like though. Well, here´s the short version: looks good, plays exquisit, sounds amazing, repetition level high. Here´s the longer version. Shadow warrior takes place in Japan (no♥♥♥♥♥♥right?) and you take the role of♥♥♥♥♥♥joke named hit man called Lo Wang. At the beggining of the game your mission is to buy the sword from guy named Zilla with hilariously clichéd mansion, with even Wang saying that he couldn´t have picked a more clichéd place to make a deal. In a true ´´gamey´´ fashion everything goes to hell and you are greeted with some of the most fun sword combat I´ve had pleasure to play around with. You can literaly cut their head off an continue cutting ´em until they are just legs. Aside from the chopin´ up yer foes action you´ll be gettin´ on, you´ll notice that this game is quiet prety, no realy, this game goes from looking great to looking jaw dropping, especially by the end where the game takes you to some varied, colorful and huuuge environements and it´s quiet a sight to behold. An astoundingly elegant adventure game in the style of Metroid with a fairly open-world exploration system. Combat can be brutal and requires precise timing, and overcoming bosses requires anticipating and reading moves rather than pattern recognition with figuring out which specific combination of attacks and feints will give you the necessary advantage to overcome your opponents.
The two most interesting mechanics are the healing system and the regret system. The former requires you to hold down the "focus" button in order to charge your healing spell, which uses up energy from your pool of soul. However, if you take a hit or release the focus button ahead of time, you lose the focus you spent without your healing being activated. However, you infinitely regenerate soul with each hit delivered to enemies. This creates a clever, frantic tug-of-war where overcoming your opponent is primarily offense-oriented.
The second of these mechanics is the regret system, which has some resemblance to Dark Souls. Your soul reserve is decreased and all of your currency has been lost until you track down your shade and beat them in one-on-one combat. This usually requires you navigating through dangerous terrain beforehand, and you don't get any additional bonuses for succeeding, but chances are you're going to end up dying during a boss fight, which means some small chance that you'll be fighting both your own shade and a leaping, tumbling, flying boss at the same time while trying not to die.
Mastering combinations of moves and figuring out what bonuses work best from your accessories (known as charms) gives a lot of life to this game and it can get a little addictive. The game is pretty hefty size-wise, so you'll get a lot of practice.
Enthusiastic 10/10.

So, the first thing to keep in mind is that this game is absolutely beautiful. At 97% completion with 50 hours into it, I could probably just go back inside and start wandering through the strange Bug's Life-meets-Redwall-meets-Lovecraftian cosmic horror laid out.
***SPOILERS***
***SPOILERS***
What fascinated me the most was how the game takes the grotesque realities of miniature life and reinvents it through an epic fantasy lens to give brain-eating fungi sinister purpose and make the birthing practices of bloatflies into whimsically monstrous epic bosses. All of this is charming and somehow natural given the setting, and I applaud the inventiveness at work. The environments are detailed and gorgeous with some fantastic parallax, and the variety from lush green gardens to the crumbling ash of burned corpses provides a fantastic sense of place. The movements of the enemies are lively and given the nature of combat necessary for telegraphing their actions with an excellent amount of personality.
The game lore goes deep, waiting to be discovered through conversation, hidden paths, ancient relics, empty buildings, and discarded corpses on long-ago battlefields. There's even some very clever dialogue and memorable characters to interact with, although there are no real dialogue options to delve any deeper.
Combat, as I mentioned before, is satisfying, and it proves to be so after dozens of hours in the way only a finely-tuned system can be. And this is excellent as the game can be downright brutal to the inattentive. Platforming is precise, but the analog jump matches that precision. Enemies don't attack in patterns as one would expect from an action-adventure, instead relying on telegraphs and phases of attacks that seem to increasingly be focused on countering your particular playstyle and making life harder for you. Luckily, the ability to turn instantaneously, deflect sword attacks to protect yourself from a blind hit, and an ever-increasing series of more complex movesets will match that as well.
For the most part, I cannot say there is too much about this game I find that comes up short if you are to play it from beginning to end with nothing in the middle. That said...
***BIGGER SPOILERS***
***BIGGER SPOILERS***
This game has a few elements that are downright obtuse.
First, similar to Dark Souls before it, this game has a habit of giving you charms (items that upgrade your abilities/stats/health) the effect of which it refuses to tell you about. Or, worse, just plain lies to you about. I found "hiveblood" that says outright that you regenerate health over time. What it ACTUALLY does is slowly regenerate *the last health point you lost* and that's it. While this is still useful in certain situations, it's not the description as stated. There are many charms that function similarly, concealing their usefulness (or lack) behind vague descriptions that don't state precisely how they work until you are in a situation where they completely fail to do what you think and you get smashed.
And then there's the map system. You enter an area, you track down Cornifer by following pieces of paper until you hear the sound of scribbling and humming, you find Cornifer and pay him for a map. This map will not add locations until you rest on a bench. You will not know where you are on the map unless you use a charm slot for a compass. There is no minimap either. Navigating territory will often be you memorizing locations after repeated experience or stopping to check your map page (which actually doesn't stop the game at all but allows you to keep walking slowly while holding it open).
This leads me to a few♥♥♥♥♥♥moves the game took to heart that were unnecessary:
1. There are a lot of hidden pathways, and while they are usually portrayed as cracked walls or crumbling stone, there are more than a few not visible in any way until you accidentally stumble upon them. For a game with a world this big and a map so frustrating It's downright douchey.
2. Accessing some of the game world requires interacting with things that don't seem to be interactive. A full 15% of the world is unreachable until you wander down a random back path and find a single item AND THEN figure out what parts of the transport to interact with and when. But given the map design, you may not even know there is anywhere else to go!
3. Upgrading the Howling Wail requires going into the Abyss, wandering into a room that has NOTHING TO INTERACT WITH, and activating your special ability. The clue to it is extremely vague and requires the player to interact with the environment in two separate ways the game has never suggested will ever produce any results except for this one instance. It's a bizarre choice and reads like the devs just didn't want you to know about it.
4. Unlocking the TRUE ENDING requires using one of those modes of interaction with a thing designed in such a way that it in no way implies you can interact with it. Which means, again, another big part of the game walled off behind obscurity.
5. The Radiance is an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Random attacks, skill spamming, and double damage with STACKABILITY sometimes makes it impossible to dodge. It's amazing how much was just luck and hoping you don't get four sword walls + the sword star which shoves an extra sword through the gap you would otherwise be jumping through but not so tightly that a shadow dash clears both, forcing a cheap hit knocks you into ANOTHER sword wall that you can't avoid because you just used up your shadow dash. This happened more than once. I won when he instead decided to sit still and spam an easy attack instead.
I got good, HORNET, but The Radiance is still a♥♥♥♥♥♥
6. Mr. Mushroom!? I'm sorry, but WHAT? The fourth ending requires wearing a charm unrelated to the tablet in the hidden room and then solving riddles at an arbitrary time in order over the whole map? GTFO!!!!!

If you haven´t played the original shadow warrior, you should at least try it in my opinion. It gives you a bit of an insight to what shooters were like years ago and where does this ´´reboot´´ take it´s inspiration from. Now, I don´t mean inspiration in the sense that it reuses the same mechanics and what not, but rather the main character , some of it´s lines, the katana of course and it´s easter eggs. I´ve managed to fin most of ´em. What is the game like though. Well, here´s the short version: looks good, plays exquisit, sounds amazing, repetition level high. Here´s the longer version. Shadow warrior takes place in Japan (no♥♥♥♥♥♥right?) and you take the role of♥♥♥♥♥♥joke named hit man called Lo Wang. At the beggining of the game your mission is to buy the sword from guy named Zilla with hilariously clichéd mansion, with even Wang saying that he couldn´t have picked a more clichéd place to make a deal. In a true ´´gamey´´ fashion everything goes to hell and you are greeted with some of the most fun sword combat I´ve had pleasure to play around with. Seriously, this combat is so good that in probably first 10 chapters you´ll be using that more than the actual guns IN A FPS GAME. The sword combat is basic, atleast until you get some great powers, but the thing that makes it sooooo much fun is the way enemies come apart. You can literaly cut their head off an continue cutting ´em until they are just legs. Yeah, they don´t come apart into tiny itsy-bitsy pieces like they do in metal gear rising: revengeance, but I feel like combat in this game is more tight even though as I´ve said...... written, it is quiet basic, but that´s not a bad thing at all. Aside from the chopin´ up yer foes action you´ll be gettin´ on, you´ll notice that this game is quiet prety, no realy, this game goes from looking great to looking jaw dropping, especially by the end where the game takes you to some varied, colorful and huuuge environements and it´s quiet a sight to behold. The game also sounds awesome. All weapons and especially the shotgun, sound beefy and are model with a lots and I mean lots of detail. You can also upgrade your guns and yourself and your powers even further more. The game is around 14-15 hours long which is great even though you might expect more from a modern single-player only fps. Yes, there ain´t no multiplayer in this game. That´s not a bad thing because it allows the game to be more focused than it would be with a multi-player or co-op game modes. The game gets repetitive after a while, but that happens to almost all games, but the game is linear with a bit of a widened path and you get into these rooms that enemies spawn in and you do this over and ver and over. It would be a very bad thing if the combat was boring, but it isn´t as I´ve mentioned earlier so that shortens a quiet a bad thing. The game can be also cheaply hard sometimes. It throws these enemies that take 20 rockets to take down and charge at you and can kill you in 3 hits if you don´t heal yerself. And by the end it has the tendency to throw atleast two of these guys at ya tripled with another enemy that takes a beating before he goes down. I´m almost at the end currently and I´m facing the frustrating problem with these doubled tough enemies, but hey, I don´t mind, I´ll get a rest from the game and than come back again. So for single-player purists this is a no brainer to pick up, for folks somewhere in hte middle I strongly recommend and for multi-player folks I still recommend, ´cause come on, who deosn´t like choppin´ his enemies into bits. Shadow Warrior is a hell of a game. And I actualy realy enjoyed the characters too , later on they have some great dialogues even if they start of quiet weak. You should go get it, it doesn´t mattrt on sale, average price it´s very much worth you time.

Hollow Knight blends melancholy, whimsy, and tight-but-punishing gameplay into a masterpiece.
I honestly don't even want to list the minor gripes I had because the rest of the game just eclipses them overwhelmingly. I'll just note that there are a couple of platforming bits that are questionable (one in particular stands out as an absurd change of pace and design) and that the sheer amount of freedom given to the player necessarily results in some awkward difficulty spikes.

The soundtrack is gorgeous, the sprite work/animation is some of the best I've ever seen, and the nonsense-voices are so damn charming that I was never annoyed by them.

It's easy to setup for DayZ. In order, do:
Download Arma2, play one tutorial to learn some controls.
Download Arma2 OA, play the tutorial to learn the other controls.
Download the DayZ mod (about 300mb) (Steam).
Download the DayZLauncher (Non-Steam), and use it's internal services to download Dayz Overwatch, Epoch, and Overpoch (about 6gb).
Then to play, load up steam, then use the DayZLauncher to find your favourite sever.
It's a little buggy, but definately worth playing with friends. Also, find a server with some good server side scripts/events, it's more fun like that.
Epoch/Overpoch is as good as legacy Rust, and provides more adrenaline moments too :)

First of all I would like to say...
WOW!
Ok this is a space Minecraft style sandbox game but for a fresh release on early access on Steam...
it's amazing !
THE LAYOUT:
After a quick tutorial (some aspects of the game are still missing...), you start near a "cotton bud" looking space station.
You are an astronaut and with few credits and items you are left in a huge universe.
First you have few blocks to build a basic spaceship. If you are smart enough, you will be able to go anywhere and enjoy the huge number of planets, asteroids and stations you can find (nearly infinite).
THE GAMEPLAY:
Ship and stations designs are easy. By pressing Space after entering a Ship core, you can launch building mode.
The Ship core it some kind of box where the player can enter and control the ship.
It's a strange way to use vehicles but the designer is enough well made to compensate this strange design.
Like in Minecraft you use blocks, you place them with left click and delete with right click (you have tons of other contols by pressing left ctrl).
For every ships, you have to plan it's energy usage and mass.
The bigger the more expensive it will be for you: like the cloak wich needs more energy depending of the size  of the ship. The interresting aspect of this mode is the way you use weapons and tools.
Every items needs a computer to be used. You put an appropriate computer and the weapon or tool block related, and you conect them. The funny thing is that you can mix weapons and some upgrade blocks to change their effects, like EMP or Shield Drain, ect...
You can even place turret docking blocks with AI blocks to create an automated sentry capable to fire anything you want from missiles to beams.
For tools you have less possibilities but you can put more blocks and computers to create massive Salvage beams (some kind of mining laser) or even create you own Antenna relay to scan your sector and spot anything that moves.
You can even hold personnal weapons or tools (you have a basic mining laser) but you can't upgrade it much, like for the ships.
You can also place a building block on a planet or a location you own ( with a faction block), to customize it.
From the plants to the soils, being able to change a planet so quickly is excellent and gives you plenty ways to create.
But you can't harvest materials by this way, you have to clear a path with the editor and go mining yourself.
About crafting, it's not a good aspect of the game. Because you have too much materials and it becomes quickly too complicate to build nice recipes (bad crafting menus when you use crafting stations). In fact you will spare tons of time by harvesting raw materials and selling them to the Galatic Traders. These guys are the owners of the "space cotton buds" They are neutral npc that sells all blocks you can imagine and they buy everything you can bring !
When you got the way to gather quickly, you get quite a lot of credits (the actual currency in the game).
But space is a dangerous place...
Players can be hostiles, you will notice that with a nice Faction system. By yourself you can create a faction, claim locations in its name and even conquer other players properties. Before doing that you need faction points with the help of other faction members and enough fights against enemy factions. This system is really good and surprises by it's quality for an early acess game.
But your not alone because some pirates are roaming...
They hide in somes big space stations with heavy turrets that does quite a lot of damage.
But if you can manage to enter them... you will get tons of items !
Be ware pirates are fliying in fast ships and dying is quite normal when you begin.
Don't forget to buy enough stuff to build few basic ships when you first spawn.
And find a nice planet to land.
At this moment you will have time to study the blocks, the ways you have to earn money and CONQUER THE UNIVERS !
TO CONCLUDE:
Starmade is a real surprise. Quite impressive and cheap (the price will change), the gameplay it offers is amazing for an early acess.
Ok i have to admit the game is rough around the edges: need some balance about the trade and crafting system. The tutorial wich is empty especially in front of game mechanics such as Factions or Logics. The physic for ship flights needs to be better because it's like driving in a "soapbox" or the punch of weapons wich are a bit weak especially on foot. Physic on blocks would be cool, like on some planets where lava "floats" in the airs.
But the overall quality is really good for this kind of game, the developpers are even planing to add creatures (actually there is one alien spider you can see in the tutorial). And seriously, being able to build so much crazy things with turrets, landing zones, weapons, antenna and even warp gates...
it's amazing !
N.B: The game is quite stable, even if i had to play it on an old computer.
You can also play alone on a dedicated server and set the difficulty of the AI. Life in space has never been so easy !

This game is about fun.
There's no micromanagement here worrying about running low on ammo or if I should save that health pack for later.  The game feeds you enough ammo and health so that you can just focus on your main goal: ripping demons to shreds.
This game has been compared to the fps shooters of the 90s, but that doesn't matter and don't let that comparison to a 20 year old genre turn you off.
I was a bit relucatant to purchase this game, having missed playing the original (although I thoroughly enjoyed Doom and Duke Nukem at the time) and I was worried I was just getting a prettier version of one of those games.  Perhaps I'd just forgotten how enjoyable games like those were, but I was very muched impressed with this remake.  Yes, it has the old standards, the pistol, machine gun, shotgun, rocket launcher ... red, green, and blue doors.  But it also captured the charm and excitement of dispatching large hordes of enemies with whatever the heck weapon you want to use in your arsenal.
It took me by surprise though, the start of the game is campy and pokes fun at the genre. The main character is an over the top an oriental version of Duke Nukem, that I did not take this game seriously.  I started the game mildly interested in seeing where it would take me and a couple chapters later I found I was engrossed in a deeping storyline.  The charm of the game sneaks up on you.
I was honestly worried about an FPS centered around a sword wielding character. How would a shooter game deal with that game mechanic?  The melee action in FPS games always seem to me to be a last-ditch weapon, and I usually find them to be clunlky and not very usable.  But this is not the case here; it didn't take long for me to realize that the sword was going to be my favourite and go-to weapon when the going got tough. The range of the sword is good enough to be effective, but not too overpowered.  For those monsters within range, well, there's comes some good satisfaction in slicing off the arms of a demon right before he claws at your face.
The Ki skills were a little bit distracting and confusing at first. They could have been better intergrated into the game play.  I was having so much fun shooting and slicing, once I topped up my healing powers I honestly didn't bother with the ki magic.  Perhaps this might give it some replay value for me.
Finally, as an FPS, I know there is a level of gruesomeness to be expected, esp in a game like this, where you are literally
disembowelling monsters.  But what I found strange was the level of blood everywhere- but not having anything to do with your story.  There were pools of blood* and bloody and skewered bodies that seemed out of place in the scenery. Is this an homage to the original?
Conclusion:
- Shadow Warrior 2013 is a fun game; it throws armies of demons at you and it gives you to tools to slaughter them however you like.  There is much enjoyment in how they let you do this.
- It is built in the spirit of its 1990 ancestors, but instead of a rehash,  it feels like a fresh take on the genre, especially in this age of retreaded COD-like rail shooters.
- Using the sword to cut up phantastic foes much more fun than I anticipated.
*Ok I concede the Pool of Blood thing has a connection to the story, but it seemed out of place in the story.

The music is pretty good to listen too. It's not utterly repetitive, or too extreme. It has a sort of calming feel that allows you to think and just become one with the background. Some MOBA's hype it up severely and have music that's just too over the top, even in the character selection screen and stuff, so its nice.

The customizational part is also to be desired. It's bland and many of the weapons or mounts don't really scream out "I WANT IT!" Though, I expect some more interesting looking skins, instead of recolored clothing for second teir loot.
The loot system is like Overwatch. You don't know what you'll get. It's all random. I don't personally like gachapon loot. I like to know that I'll at least get something for characters I like to play. Maybe this will change in the future, but as of right now.. eh.
The maps are bountiful for the time being. Though they're pretty much almost the same map repeatedly. MOBA's have this weird issue where they make one map design and kind of stick with it. Why not a diamond shaped map? Or a hexagon? Don't be that MOBA. I expect great things to come in the future, and this is one of them. The reskined colors and themes are neat though.
The gameplay varies with each character. There are no minions. No Turrets. No jungle. It's literally a MOBA, a Massive Online Battle Arena. 2v2, 3v3, maybe a 5v5 in the future? 10v10!? Each character has unique moves that seperate them from each other and it all goes with their backgrounds and themes. You got your Healers, Marksmen, Fighters, Tanks, Ninjafrog. wat? It's very engaging and cooperative heavy. If you and your partner don't see eye to eye you're gonna have a bad time. Prepare yourself though, with every MOBA comes the horrible stereotype of toxic players. It's inevitable, expect it, but luckily you don't have to see any of it. Turn chat off, leave it off. No big deal. It can be fast paced, especially if you're panicking.
That's pretty much it. I'll edit this as time goes along and revise. All in all, I would give this game a 7/10. Still work to be done, but it's still really good. Most certainly reccomend.

The good:
- A tutorial - as in there actually is one and it's moderately useful
- Various texture packs built in to the client so it looks less Minecraft-like
- You can build *massive* ships and there is a decent selection of utlity modules
The middling:
- OK build tools - far better than Minecraft, maybe worse than Space Engineers
- The star systems are basically all the same - pick any one and you can find every resources you need, no reason to explore
- There are NPC enemies, and they will pester you, but don't expect to be challenged by cleverness.  Tenacity perhaps...
The bad:
- The crafting interface.  Yes it has a filter to search, but no categorization.  Browsing a small list is painful.
- The UI elements.  Ok, this is early access, some of it is likely developer art.  Recommend these guys go look at Space Engineers for a better example of UI.
- The flight model.  Flight games *scream* for a joystick and rudder system - this system only supports one controller at a time so unless your stick does everything, it comes out to be much less useful.  Using a keyboard and mouse to fly anywhere near a planet is basically an exercise in frustration - get a gamepad at the minimum for when you step inside a ship.
This game is like Minecraft in space, but without so much grinding trying to find resources (they are in fact very easy to get once you build a salvage ship - you will spend more time waiting for the resources to process than actually acquiring them.)  If you like *building* things, you will enjoy this game.  If you like *fighting* things, your enjoyment will probably be short-lived.  If you like *exploring*, you're enjoyment will also be short-lived.
But it's still Early Access, so give it some time.  It will no doubt improve (just see how far Space Engineers has come along.)

This game is about fun.
There's no micromanagement here worrying about running low on ammo or if I should save that health pack for later.  The game feeds you enough ammo and health so that you can just focus on your main goal: ripping demons to shreds.
This game has been compared to the fps shooters of the 90s, but that doesn't matter and don't let that comparison to a 20 year old genre turn you off.
I was a bit relucatant to purchase this game, having missed playing the original (although I thoroughly enjoyed Doom and Duke Nukem at the time) and I was worried I was just getting a prettier version of one of those games.  Perhaps I'd just forgotten how enjoyable games like those were, but I was very muched impressed with this remake.  Yes, it has the old standards, the pistol, machine gun, shotgun, rocket launcher ... red, green, and blue doors.  But it also captured the charm and excitement of dispatching large hordes of enemies with whatever the heck weapon you want to use in your arsenal.
It took me by surprise though, the start of the game is campy and pokes fun at the genre. The main character is an over the top an oriental version of Duke Nukem, that I did not take this game seriously.  I started the game mildly interested in seeing where it would take me and a couple chapters later I found I was engrossed in a deeping storyline.  The charm of the game sneaks up on you.
I was honestly worried about an FPS centered around a sword wielding character. How would a shooter game deal with that game mechanic?  The melee action in FPS games always seem to me to be a last-ditch weapon, and I usually find them to be clunlky and not very usable.  But this is not the case here; it didn't take long for me to realize that the sword was going to be my favourite and go-to weapon when the going got tough. The range of the sword is good enough to be effective, but not too overpowered.  For those monsters within range, well, there's comes some good satisfaction in slicing off the arms of a demon right before he claws at your face.
The Ki skills were a little bit distracting and confusing at first. They could have been better intergrated into the game play.  I was having so much fun shooting and slicing, once I topped up my healing powers I honestly didn't bother with the ki magic.  Perhaps this might give it some replay value for me.
Finally, as an FPS, I know there is a level of gruesomeness to be expected, esp in a game like this, where you are literally
disembowelling monsters.  But what I found strange was the level of blood everywhere- but not having anything to do with your story.  There were pools of blood* and bloody and skewered bodies that seemed out of place in the scenery. Is this an homage to the original?
Conclusion:
- Shadow Warrior 2013 is a fun game; it throws armies of demons at you and it gives you to tools to slaughter them however you like.  There is much enjoyment in how they let you do this.
- It is built in the spirit of its 1990 ancestors, but instead of a rehash,  it feels like a fresh take on the genre, especially in this age of retreaded COD-like rail shooters.
- Using the sword to cut up phantastic foes much more fun than I anticipated.
*Ok I concede the Pool of Blood thing has a connection to the story, but it seemed out of place in the story.

This game sometimes feels like it's got a little too much of everything: blood and gore, too many colors, wang jokes. Stylistically it seems to be a wild mix with influences from Japan and China and probably others that I don't recognize. But the whole experience is great if you're up for some old school monster killing. When looking in detail, it is certainly not like the original "Shadow Warrior" where the whole level was basically a huge playground, with some of the strongest weapons available right from the start. This one here is more linear but with enough complexity in the level design to keep you hunting for those secrets for a bit, especially in the later, bigger levels. Don't let the first ones fool you. Additionally, the skill system and weapons upgrades are a good motivation to look for all hidden stashes of "money" and "karma".
And I have to mention the story telling. For a monster-slaying first person shooter I found it quite original, with beautiful cutscenes, and even the in-engine parts are well done: smooth animations with distinctive body language for the characters, voice acting quite good mostly, especially Lo Wang and Hoji whom you'll hear most often. It is no BioShock, but it doesn't want to be, and for what it wants to be, it is really really good.
Despite its over-the-top violence and occasionally kitschy looks and flat jokes, it can be quite subtle at times if you're willing to look for and listen to details between the hectic fights and explosions.
If you like shooters with a lot of melee action and some non-standard weapon techniques that require a bit more than a quick trigger finger to get the most out of, go for it. You won't be disappointed.
